This study examines the thinning of supported liquid films driven by thermocapillary forces, focusing on oil layers initially tens of microns thick. Localized, moderate heating of the underlying glass substrate generates a thermocapillary flow that produces ultra-thin films. We demonstrate that, within a specific timeframe, the thinning dynamics of submicron films are controlled by thermocapillary stress. This results in a straightforward time-dependent relationship for thickness profiles, confirmed by the collapse of data onto a single master curve. This curve depends solely on liquid properties and the thermal gradient, enabling the measurement of the latter. However, as films thin further into the range of molecular interactions, deviations from the master curve emerge. Despite all tested oils being fully wetting on glass, the nature of this deviation varies between alkanes and silicone oils. We attribute these behaviors to differing signs of disjoining pressures, a conclusion supported by numerical solutions of the thin-film equation. Consequently, we propose that thermocapillary flows offer a precise method for probing molecular interactions.

Typically, quantum fields evolving in time-dependent backgrounds result in particle production; however, this work focuses on "unexciting" scenarios where the net production is zero. We begin by examining the simple harmonic oscillator to explicitly derive all time-dependent frequencies that prevent excitation. This foundation enables the construction of homogeneous field theory backgrounds with no particle production in any specific mode, although we demonstrate that no such homogeneous backgrounds exist where particle production vanishes across every mode simultaneously. We subsequently develop general inhomogeneous unexciting backgrounds for field theory. Finally, the complete set of these unexciting backgrounds is constrained by the selection of physical interactions, leading to a compelling open problem.

Large sequence-to-sequence models, commonly used for tasks like Neural Machine Translation (NMT), typically undergo training on hundreds of millions of samples. However, training represents only the initial phase of a model's lifecycle; real-world applications necessitate ongoing behavioral adjustments as new requirements arise or existing limitations are identified. Generally, removing unwanted behaviors requires full model retraining, while adding new behaviors relies on fine-tuning, both of which constitute data-driven model interventions. This study offers a preliminary investigation into rank-one editing as a direct intervention technique for eliminating specific behaviors in encoder-decoder transformer models. We introduce four editing tasks tailored for NMT and demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves high effectiveness, requiring only a single positive example to correct an erroneous (negative) behavior.

This paper first demonstrates the local well-posedness of strong solutions to the incompressible Hall-MHD system for initial data $(u_0,B_0)$ belonging to $H^{\frac{1}{2}+\sigma}(\mathbb{R}^3)\times H^{\frac{3}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ where $\sigma\in (0,2)$. Specifically, by utilizing the novel formulation of the Hall-MHD system identified in \cite{MR4193644}, we show that when the viscosity and resistivity coefficients are identical, the parameter $\sigma$ can be lowered to $0$. Furthermore, for small initial data, we establish global well-posedness within the same function spaces with $\sigma\in (0,2)$ and derive the optimal time-decay rates for the solutions, thereby advancing upon earlier research.

We establish a lower bound for bottleneck sizes in uniform quadrangulations that holds across all scales simultaneously. Leveraging this result, we derive upper bounds for the uniform mixing time of both the lazy random walk on uniform quadrangulations and its dual. The proofs rely on an explicit calculation of the Laplace transform regarding the number of faces within truncated hulls of the uniform infinite plane quadrangulation.

As our world and the web's content continuously evolve, languages—which often reflect reality—are inherently dynamic. Yet, most existing contextual language models remain static and fail to adapt to temporal shifts. This paper introduces TempoBERT, a temporal contextual language model that incorporates time as an additional textual context. Our method involves enriching texts with temporal data and implementing time masking, a specialized masking technique for this supplementary information. We apply this approach to semantic change detection and sentence time prediction, testing it across diverse datasets that vary in time span, size, genre, and language. Our comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that both tasks significantly benefit from the use of time masking.

While music evokes emotions, these feelings are intangible and challenging to quantify for algorithmic use in composition. To address this, we introduce Mugeetion, a new musical interface that captures users' emotional states through facial gestures and maps them to specific musical parameters. This system converts qualitative emotional data into quantitative inputs suitable for sound generation. We demonstrated and tested Mugeetion during the "Hearing Seascape" sound installation exhibition, where audience facial expressions directly influenced the background audio. This project advances research in gesture tracking, emotion-sound modeling, and the interplay between auditory output and facial expressions.

The contrast sensitivity of the human visual system can be accounted for by specific low-level vision processes, such as filtering retinal noise and correcting optical blur, but not by others like chromatic adaptation or reconstruction following simple bottlenecks. This finding remains robust even when stimulus statistics shift significantly, for example, when comparing natural images to cartoon-like ones (Li et al., Journal of Vision, 2022; Preprint arXiv:2103.00481). In this note, we introduce a method for generating original cartoon-like images that align with the statistical training parameters of the aforementioned study. Echoing Magritte's (1929) famous assertion, the stimuli produced by our method are explicitly not the objects they depict ("Ceci n'est pas une pipe"). By clearly distinguishing between the generated representation and actual reality, we mitigate potential issues regarding the use of these stimuli in academic, non-profit publications.

Optimal transport has emerged as a valuable technique in machine learning, particularly for comparing probability distributions. Notably, distributionally robust optimization applications inherently rely on Wasserstein distances to model uncertainty, accounting for data shifts and worst-case conditions. Building on the success of regularizing Wasserstein distances within optimal transport, this paper investigates the regularization of Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization. We first establish a general strong duality theorem for regularized Wasserstein distributionally robust problems. Subsequently, we refine this duality specifically for entropic regularization and present an approximation result applicable as the regularization parameters approach zero.

We introduce techniques for investigating the scalar sector of multi-Higgs models characterized by large discrete symmetry groups that undergo soft breaking. In the limit of exact symmetry, the model is defined by a minimal parameter set and allows for analytical study; however, the introduction of soft breaking generates a proliferation of quadratic couplings, rendering the general analysis complex. We distinguish between two categories of soft-breaking terms: those that maintain the alignment of symmetric vacuum expectation values and those that disrupt this alignment. Concentrating on the alignment-preserving terms, we examine which structural characteristics of the original symmetric model remain intact and which are altered. Our results highlight specific structural features inherited from the parent symmetric model that endure even in the complete absence of exact symmetry. This general methodology is demonstrated through the case of the three-Higgs-doublet model with the softly broken symmetry group $\Sigma(36)$.

While bandit problems featuring linear or concave rewards have received extensive research attention, studies addressing non-concave rewards remain scarce. This work investigates a broad class of bandit scenarios where the underlying reward function is non-concave, specifically encompassing low-rank generalized linear bandits and bandit problems involving two-layer neural networks with polynomial activations. For low-rank generalized linear bandits, we introduce a dimension-minimax-optimal algorithm, thereby disproving conjectures found in [LMT21, JWWN19]. These algorithms rely on a unified zeroth-order optimization framework that is highly versatile and achieves optimal rates across various structured polynomial settings relative to dimensionality. Additionally, we illustrate the utility of these algorithms in reinforcement learning within generative model contexts, achieving superior sample complexity compared to previous methods. We also demonstrate that standard optimistic algorithms, such as UCB, suffer from sub-optimality by factors of the dimension. In the noiseless neural network setting with polynomial activations, we propose a bandit algorithm whose sample complexity matches the intrinsic algebraic dimension. Furthermore, we show that optimistic approaches yield inferior sample complexity, which scales polynomially with the extrinsic dimension and can be exponentially worse than our method depending on the polynomial degree.

We have analytically determined the precise statistics for any arbitrary quantum observable. Because the sequence of intermediate measurements is inherently probabilistic and environmental interactions introduce stochastic fluctuations, the final measurement outcomes function as random variables. This study presents the exact large-deviation form of their probability distribution, characterized by an exponential decay relative to the number of measurements. Furthermore, we derive the most probable distribution of outcomes for a single realization of the system's evolution, thereby extending predictions beyond simple expectation values. These theoretical findings are validated through numerical simulations of a two-level system with a stochastic Hamiltonian, which is reproducible in experimental settings.

We introduce a leptoquark framework designed to concurrently address recent experimental anomalies concerning the muon's anomalous magnetic dipole moment and the $b\to s \mu\bar\mu$ decay process. Our model adheres to rigorous constraints, including $\mu\to e\gamma$ and meson mixing limits. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these leptoquarks facilitate the generation of minute neutrino masses at the one-loop level without requiring extra symmetries. Numerical analyses are presented to illustrate the extent to which our parameter space is constrained.

The swift advancement of quantum technologies and thermodynamics has created a critical need for the precise control and measurement of microscopic matter's temperature at the quantum scale. Although numerous quantum thermometry protocols have been suggested, accurately measuring low temperatures remains difficult because sensing errors typically diverge as temperature drops. We introduce non-Markovian quantum thermometry utilizing a continuous-variable system to assess the temperature of a quantum reservoir. We identify a mechanism that ensures the sensing error $\delta T$ scales with temperature $T$ according to the Landau bound ($\delta T \simeq T$) across the entire temperature range. Our analysis indicates that this heightened sensitivity arises from the quantum criticality of the combined thermometer-reservoir system. By effectively circumventing the issue of error divergence, our findings provide an efficient method for the precise measurement of low temperatures in quantum systems.

Recent years have witnessed swift advancements in characterizing topological band structures through symmetry eigenvalue-based methods. However, growing theoretical and experimental focus has shifted toward multi-gap dependent topological phases that fall outside this traditional framework. These novel topologies emerge from the braiding of band degeneracies located between distinct bands, which carry non-Abelian charges owing to $C_2T$ or $PT$ symmetry, resulting in invariants like the $\mathbb{Z}$-valued Euler class. This work introduces a universal formulation for Euler phases grounded in their homotopy classification, linking them to the Skyrmion profiles of a single unit-vector in three-level systems and two unit-vectors in four-level systems. Furthermore, by systematically constructing 3D models from pairs of lower-dimensional Euler phases, we demonstrate that transitions between any two inequivalent Euler phases are facilitated by adjacent (in-gap) nodal rings connected to sub-gap nodal lines, creating trajectories that correspond to the braiding or unbraiding of nodal points. We also establish that the stability of these linked nodal rings is signaled by an Euler class monopole charge matching their $\mathbb{Z}$-valued linking numbers. Finally, we systematically examine the transformation of Euler phases into descendant Chern phases when $C_2T$ or $PT$ symmetry is broken. All discussed topological phases are validated using explicit minimal lattice models, which can directly drive experimental investigations or support theoretical analyses, thus reinforcing the potential of this emerging field.

Bacteria frequently navigate complex natural settings, such as soils, oceans, and the human gut microbiome, where carrier fluids like mucus or reproductive fluids exhibit non-Newtonian rheology and intricate structures. Fundamental questions regarding navigation in these challenging environments remain largely unanswered due to their inherent complexity. Recently, significant attention has focused on how swimming bacteria interact with nematic liquid crystals. In these structured fluids, bacterial motion kinetics are restricted by the orientational molecular order (director field), leading to novel spatio-temporal patterns driven by this constraint and interactions with topological defects. However, a key unanswered question is how bacteria alter their swimming direction within such environments. This study investigates the swimming mechanism of a single *E. coli* bacterium constrained to follow the director field of a lyotropic chromonic liquid crystal (LCLC) confined within a planar cell. In this setting, the bacterium's natural run-and-tumble motion becomes frustrated because liquid crystal elasticity prevents flagella unbundling. Interestingly, to change direction, the bacterium performs a reversal motion along the director field, propelled by relocating a single flagellum to the opposite side of its body, a process termed a "frustrated tumble." We provide a detailed experimental characterization of this phenomenon using a two-color Lagrangian tracking technique that captures the exceptional spatial and temporal resolution of bacterial and flagellar dynamics during swimming. Furthermore, we propose a plausible mechanism explaining the frustrated run-and-tumble motion that accounts for these observations.

Hierarchical Bayesian inference serves as a fundamental method for analyzing the population characteristics of compact binaries detected via gravitational waves. The core objective involves deducing the unknown prior distributions governing binary black hole and/or neutron star parameters, including component masses, spin vectors, and redshift. These distributions provide critical insights into the life cycles of massive stars, the formation and assembly sites of binaries, and cosmic evolution across time. In hierarchical analyses, the binary black hole population is modeled using a prior distribution conditioned on hyper-parameters inferred from observational data. However, employing a misspecified model can result in erroneous astrophysical conclusions. This paper addresses the inquiry: for a given dataset, which prior distribution, selected from the space of all possible priors, maximizes the population likelihood? This optimal distribution, denoted as $\pistroke$ (pronounced "pi stroke") and which does not represent a physical prior, yields the associated \textit{maximum population likelihood}, $\Lstroke$ (pronounced "L stroke"). We hypothesize that the structure of $\pistroke$ comprises a linear superposition of delta functions. Furthermore, we demonstrate how $\pistroke$ and $\Lstroke$ facilitate model exploration and criticism. We apply this $\Lstroke$ framework to investigate the population of binary black hole mergers observed in the third Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog from LIGO--Virgo--KAGRA. Finally, based on our findings, we propose potential enhancements for gravitational-wave population models.

We introduce a machine-translation method for automatically creating playlist titles from a collection of music tracks. By adapting the sequence-to-sequence framework—utilizing both Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Transformers to music data—we process track IDs as input and generate word sequences for playlist titles as output. Acknowledging that tracks within a playlist lack inherent order, we propose two strategies to eliminate input sequence ordering: data augmentation through shuffling and the removal of positional encoding. Additionally, we restructured existing music playlist datasets to produce phrase-level titles. Results indicate that Transformer models consistently outperform RNNs, and performance is further enhanced when the input sequence order is removed.

Building on the concept of measurement-induced nonlocality [Phys. Rev. Lett. 106, 120401 (2011)], we propose a novel metric to quantify nonbilocal correlations. For arbitrary pure input states, we demonstrate a straightforward relationship between nonlocal and nonbilocal measures. When examining mixed states, we derive two upper bounds for the affinity-based nonbilocal measure. Lastly, we investigate the nonbilocality arising from various combinations of input states.

Machine learning is increasingly delivering cutting-edge results in environmental domains, including streamflow forecasting within hydrologic basins. Nevertheless, constructing precise large-scale streamflow models remains difficult in practice because of the variability in dominant hydrologic processes, which are most effectively represented by process-specific basin attributes. Current basin attributes often contain noise and uncertainty, factors that negatively affect model accuracy. To address these issues, this paper introduces a novel Knowledge-guided Self-Supervised Learning (KGSSL) inverse framework designed to extract system characteristics from driver and response data. This pioneering framework delivers robust performance even when characteristics are corrupted. We demonstrate that KGSSL achieves state-of-the-art outcomes for streamflow modeling on the CAMELS (Catchment Attributes and MEteorology for Large-sample Studies) dataset, a widely adopted hydrology benchmark. Specifically, KGSSL surpasses other methods by up to 16% in characteristic reconstruction. Moreover, we show that KGSSL exhibits greater resilience to distortion compared to baseline approaches and exceeds the baseline model's performance by 35% when utilizing KGSSL-inferred characteristics.

Block modularity is introduced as a generalization of standard modularity, serving as a quality function that assesses label assignments relative to specific block patterns. This approach allows for the comparison of arbitrary network structures and the determination of an optimal block matrix, distinguishing it from conventional modularity methods. Several algorithms for optimizing block modularity are presented and tested on networks containing planted structures, frequently resulting in the successful recovery of these structures. Instances of failure are examined, revealing that strong degree correlations can account for the planted patterns; consequently, the detected structure is more surprising than the original under the configuration model. Furthermore, applying this method to well-known networks such as the Southern Women and Zachary's Karate club datasets demonstrates its ability to automatically deconstruct the networks into a highly useful summary of their primary characteristics.

We derive explicit height-dependent eddy viscosity coefficients for the Ekman layer based on convex wind speed profiles. These solutions are parameterized using the relative deflection angle between wind directions at the flow's upper and lower boundaries, along with geostrophic wind speed and a velocity scale representing the vertical transfer rate of horizontal momentum. Furthermore, these solutions enable the inference of Ekman layer thickness across a range of deflection angles that differ from those of the classic Ekman spiral.
We demonstrate that for most positive integers $n$, the $Kn$-smooth component of $a^n-1$ (where $a$ is an integer greater than 1) grows at a rate of $a^{o(n)}$.

Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) has advanced significantly in handling complex control tasks through temporal abstraction; however, existing HRL methods often struggle with severe data inefficiency as environments scale. This inefficiency arises because expanded components, such as the goal space and episode duration, place constraints on both high-level and low-level policies, which share a single total episode horizon. To address this, we introduce Decoupling Horizons Using a Graph in Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (DHRL), a technique that separates the horizons of the high and low levels and connects them via a graph structure. By enabling a high-level action interval that can be freely extended, DHRL supports deeper temporal abstraction and accelerates training in intricate tasks. Our approach surpasses state-of-the-art HRL algorithms in standard environments and successfully executes lengthy, complex locomotion and manipulation operations.

Collaboration networks, defined by nodes representing authors and edges indicating co-authorship, are essential for analyzing how knowledge is consumed, produced, and disseminated. Driven by social dynamics, biases, and constraints, these networks naturally form tightly knit communities with varying degrees of segregation. This study aims to measure the extent and consequences of such segregation within collaboration networks, specifically focusing on the field of Computer Science using the Semantic Scholar Open Research Corpus. By employing the Spectral Segregation Index (SSI), we categorize communities into three groups: non-segregated, moderately segregated, and highly segregated. We concentrate on comparing the structural topology and core positioning of non-segregated and highly segregated communities within similar size ranges. Our findings reveal no significant differences in density or clustering between these groups, yet we observe distinct variations in their core locations. As community size grows, they tend to occupy positions closer to the network's nucleus; however, when controlling for size, highly segregated communities are more likely to be situated near the periphery compared to their non-segregated counterparts. Furthermore, we examined how community segregation levels influence citation counts. Notably, researchers in highly segregated communities achieve higher citations per publication when located in the periphery and receive more citations from within their own community regardless of the core location. In contrast, researchers in non-segregated communities accumulate more citations per publication when situated in intermediary or central cores. To our knowledge, this research represents the first effort to characterize segregated communities in scientific collaboration networks and to explore their connection to citation-based impact.

We present a novel method for characterizing Ehresmann semigroups using left and right étale actions of a meet semilattice on a category. Furthermore, we identify the specific Ehresmann semigroups that correspond to the set of all subsets of a finite category. In practical applications, we demonstrate that any restriction semigroup can be elegantly embedded into a restriction semigroup derived from a category, and we delineate the conditions under which a restriction semigroup can be similarly embedded into an inverse semigroup.

The Internet of Drones (IoD) represents a networking architecture emerging from the convergence of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) and wireless communication technologies. While networked drones can trigger transformative scenarios across various application areas, fully realizing their potential necessitates precise modeling techniques capable of capturing the nuanced details of UAV characteristics, wireless protocols, and networking standards. To address this need, this work introduces the Internet of Drones Simulator (IoD-Sim), a comprehensive and flexible open-source solution designed to cover multiple aspects of the IoD. Built upon Network Simulator 3 (ns-3), IoD-Sim utilizes a three-layer architecture: (i) the Underlying Platform, which supplies telecommunication primitives for standardized protocol stacks; (ii) the Core, which encapsulates fundamental IoD scenario features; and (iii) the Simulation Development Platform, which offers a suite of tools to expedite graphical design for diverse use cases. To demonstrate the proposal's significant potential, three distinct scenarios are evaluated from both software and telecommunication perspectives. The unique attributes of this open-source tool hold particular value for academic researchers, who can leverage it to model future specifications such as mobile networks and satellite communications. Furthermore, the tool is highly relevant to the industry, as it can accelerate the design phase and reduce the time-to-market for IoD-based services.

This paper investigates approximate circular pattern matching (CPM) under both Hamming and edit distances. Given a text $T$ of length $n$, a pattern $P$ of length $m$, and a threshold $k>0$, the goal is to identify all starting positions in $T$ where fragments are within distance $k$ of some cyclic rotation of $P$, or simply to determine if such a match exists in the decision variant. Prior research on approximate CPM primarily relied on heuristics or average-case bounds, with the exception of Charalampopoulos et al. [CKP$^+$, JCSS'21], who addressed only the Hamming distance. For the reporting version under Hamming distance, we enhance the algorithm from [CKP$^+$, JCSS'21], reducing the time complexity from ${\cal O}(n+(n/m)\cdot k^4)$ to ${\cal O}(n+(n/m)\cdot k^3\log\log k)$. Additionally, we present an ${\cal O}(nk^2)$-time algorithm for the reporting version under edit distance. Regarding the decision version, our Hamming distance algorithm achieves ${\cal O}(n+(n/m)\cdot k^2\log k/\log\log k)$ time, nearly matching the performance of Chan et al. [CGKKP, STOC'20] for the standard problem. For edit distance, our ${\cal O}(nk\log^3 k)$ approach nearly matches the ${\cal O}(nk)$ runtime of the Landau-Vishkin algorithm [LV, J. Algorithms'89]. As a foundational contribution, we introduce an ${\cal O}(nk\log^3 k)$-time algorithm for the Longest Prefix $k'$-Approximate Match problem [LMS, SICOMP'98] for all $1 \le k' \le k$. Furthermore, we establish a conditional lower bound indicating a polynomial separation between approximate CPM under Hamming distance over a binary alphabet and its linear counterpart. Finally, we demonstrate that a strongly subquadratic-time algorithm for the decision version of approximate CPM under edit distance would contradict the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH).

We derive classical solutions for $\l$-deformed $\s$-models utilizing $SL(2,\mathbb{R})/U(1)$ and $SU(2)/U(1)$ coset spaces. By employing two distinct coordinate systems, we identify two separate classes of solutions: the first relies on hyperbolic and trigonometric functions, while the second utilizes elliptic functions. We examine the characteristics of these solutions, their associated boundary conditions, and the string systems they represent. Notably, the solutions from the second class exhibit a resemblance to pendulum motion.

The connection between finite-volume multi-hadron energy levels and matrix elements, on one hand, and two-particle scattering phase shifts and decays, on the other, is established; however, incorporating long-range interactions like QED presents significant challenges. Addressing QED is crucial for correcting systematic errors in $K\to\pi\pi$ decays. This presentation introduces a technique to incorporate a truncated, finite-range Coulomb interaction within finite-volume lattice QCD simulations. We demonstrate that the errors resulting from truncation can be recovered through an infinite-volume analytic calculation, ensuring the final result is free from power-law finite-volume errors beyond those inherent in standard Lüscher phase shift determinations. This methodology enables the computation of QED-corrected infinite-volume phase shifts for $\pi\pi$ scattering in Coulomb gauge—a vital component for $K\to\pi\pi$ analyses—while temporarily excluding transverse radiation.

Traditionally, researchers have relied on native speakers to annotate widely used benchmark datasets. However, recruiting native speakers is challenging for certain languages, making it valuable to explore whether language learners could perform these annotations. This study examines the potential of language learners to contribute to benchmark datasets. Through a rigorously controlled experiment, we engaged 36 language learners, offering them supplementary resources such as dictionaries and machine-translated sentences, while administering proficiency assessments. The study focused on three languages—English, Korean, and Indonesian—and covered four NLP tasks: sentiment analysis, natural language inference, named entity recognition, and machine reading comprehension. Our results indicate that language learners, particularly those with intermediate or advanced proficiency, can generate reasonably accurate annotations when provided with additional support. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the process of data annotation enhances learners' language skills, specifically in vocabulary and grammar. These findings suggest that expanding annotation efforts to include language learners could facilitate the creation of benchmark datasets for languages where recruiting native speakers is difficult.

Recently, a new trend has emerged focusing on sparsity to accelerate neural network training, specifically within the paradigm of edge computing. This paper introduces the Memory-Economic Sparse Training (MEST) framework, designed for accurate and rapid execution on edge devices. The MEST framework integrates Elastic Mutation (EM) and Soft Memory Bound (&S) enhancements to maintain high accuracy even at elevated sparsity ratios. Unlike existing sparse training approaches, this work highlights the critical role of sparsity schemes in determining both accuracy and training speed on actual edge hardware. Furthermore, the study leverages data efficiency to further expedite sparse training. Our findings indicate that unforgettable examples can be identified in-situ during the dynamic adjustment of sparsity masks, allowing their removal to boost training speed on edge devices. Compared to state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, our MEST framework achieves significantly higher Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet using the same unstructured sparsity scheme. Systematic evaluations of accuracy, training speed, and memory footprint demonstrate that the MEST framework consistently outperforms representative SOTA solutions. We also address a reviewer's strong objection, which was based on incorrect assumptions and misunderstandings, by incorporating data efficiency for additional acceleration and exploring how model sparsity, sparsity schemes, and training algorithms affect the number of removable examples. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/boone891214/MEST.

We introduce new explicit bounds for the Gaussian approximation of Poisson functionals by utilizing fresh estimates of the moments of Skorohod integrals. By integrating these with the Malliavin-Stein method, we obtain bounds in terms of Wasserstein and Kolmogorov distances that rely on minimal moment conditions regarding add-one cost operators, thus generalizing findings from Last, Peccati, and Schulte (2016). Our applications encompass a Central Limit Theorem (CLT) for the Online Nearest Neighbour graph, confirming a conjecture by Wade (2009) and Penrose and Wade (2009). Furthermore, we employ our methodology to establish quantitative CLTs for edge functionals of the Gilbert graph, the $k$-Nearest Neighbour graph, and the Radial Spanning Tree, addressing scenarios where both qualitative CLTs are established and where they remain unproven.

Recent self-supervised visual learning methods employ a pretext task, which functions as an imitation classification objective by assigning labels to augmented or transformed input images, with the aim of predicting the applied transformations. However, it has been noted that transformations already inherent in a dataset may be suboptimal for learning robust self-supervised representations. Leveraging this insight, we introduce a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) based framework designed to automatically identify transformations absent from the input dataset, thereby enhancing self-supervised learning efficacy. This automated policy enables the estimation of a dataset's transformation distribution and the construction of a complementary distribution, from which training pairs for the pretext task are sampled. We validated the effectiveness of this automated transformation strategy across multiple visual recognition datasets.

Comprehending the structural and evolutionary dynamics of solar plasma and magnetic fields across multiple layers is crucial. The force-free magnetic field model, which serves as a precise approximation of the solar corona owing to its low plasma $\beta$, has been extensively utilized to represent coronal magnetic architectures. Although the force-free condition holds true in the corona, the lower solar atmosphere deviates from this state due to elevated plasma $\beta$ values. Consequently, a magnetohydrostatic (MHS) equilibrium, which incorporates plasma forces including pressure gradients and gravity, offers a more suitable framework for modeling the lower atmosphere. This paper provides a review of both analytical and numerical extrapolation techniques grounded in the MHS assumption for deriving magnetic fields and plasma characteristics in the solar atmosphere from observed magnetograms.

Extreme multi-label text classification (XMTC) involves assigning relevant labels from an extensive predefined set to each document. Although recent large pre-trained Transformer models have significantly boosted XMTC performance—typically by using the special CLS token's embedding as a global semantic representation to match against candidate labels—we contend that this global vector fails to capture semantics at varying granularities. Consequently, integrating local word-level features with these global representations could yield further improvements. Building on this insight, we introduce a method that fuses both local and global features derived from Transformers to enhance classifier prediction capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed model either surpasses or matches the performance of state-of-the-art approaches on benchmark datasets.

Recently, the concept of distributed linearly separable computation was introduced to mitigate straggler delays and communication overhead in distributed tasks. In this model, a data center partitions input datasets among various servers, which process assigned subsets by generating coded packets returned to the user. The system is designed so that the user can reconstruct the desired function from responses provided by a subset of servers, thereby tolerating stragglers. This paper extends that framework by establishing a novel secure architecture, ensuring the user recovers only the target function without gaining any information about the underlying datasets, even upon receiving all server responses. To guarantee input privacy, a common randomness variable, independent of the datasets, is integrated into the transmission. We demonstrate that any existing non-secure linear-coding scheme for this problem can be rendered secure without incurring additional communication costs. Furthermore, we address the scenario where server computation costs are minimized, aiming to reduce the randomness variable size while maintaining optimal communication efficiency. We begin by deriving an information-theoretic lower bound on the required randomness size. Subsequently, we develop secure computing schemes utilizing two established data assignment strategies: fractional repetition and cyclic assignment. Finally, we introduce a new scheme based on a novel assignment method that strictly surpasses the performance of the previous two approaches, alongside several additional optimality findings.

When a charged particle travels through a medium faster than light's phase velocity within it, it emits Cherenkov radiation. Similarly, a strong electromagnetic field can polarize quantum fluctuations, granting the vacuum an effective anisotropic refractive index that enables Cherenkov radiation from the quantum vacuum itself. This study examines the characteristics of such vacuum Cherenkov radiation within intense laser pulses and the magnetic fields surrounding pulsars, identifying conditions where it becomes the primary radiation mechanism. This phenomenon may offer an explanation for the surplus high-energy photon signals detected in astrophysical observations.

Using St\"uckelberg's divergence theorem within Minkowski space, the relativistic continuity equations for extensive thermodynamic quantities are established. This covariant method yields a relativistic expression of the first and second laws of thermodynamics. In a relativistic perfect fluid, internal energy density and pressure possess inertia, resulting in a relativistic coupling between heat and work. The continuity equation governing relativistic inertia is derived, and the relativistic corrections to the Euler equation, as well as the continuity equations for energy and momentum, are identified. This theoretical framework enables a rigorous derivation of the relativistic transformation laws for temperature, pressure, and chemical potential, utilizing the known transformation laws for energy density, entropy density, mass density, and number density.

Determining the origins of greenhouse gases like methane from limited sensor data is a critical step in addressing climate change. Although the complex atmospheric dispersion of these pollutants is well-described by the Advection-Diffusion equation, directly solving this inverse problem to locate sources and quantify their magnitude is challenging due to spatially sparse and noisy observations, where concentration data exists only at specific sensor points with limited sensitivity. This study introduces a multi-task learning framework capable of generating high-fidelity reconstructions of the concentration field and identifying key emission characteristics, such as source location and strength, from these sparse inputs. We demonstrate that this approach successfully achieves accurate reconstruction of methane concentrations from limited measurements and precisely determines both the location and emission intensity of pollution sources.

The extended coset leader weight enumerator for the generalized Reed-Solomon $[q + 1, q - 3, 5]_q$ code is calculated, treating the problem as one within finite geometry. This requires classifying points, lines, and planes in projective three-space that remain invariant under projectivities preserving the twisted cubic. There exists a correspondence where a line in three-space defines a rational function of degree at most three, and conversely. Additionally, the double point scheme of a rational function is examined. Specifically, the pencil generated by a true passant of the twisted cubic, provided it does not lie in an osculation plane, yields a genus one curve as its double point scheme. Utilizing the Hasse-Weil bound regarding $\mathbb{F}_q$-rational points, it is demonstrated that such a passant is contained within a 3-plane.

This work introduces the fractional variant of oriented coloring and begins its investigation. We establish fundamental results and analyze the parameter for directed cycles and sparse planar graphs. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any $\epsilon > 0$, there is an integer $g_{\epsilon} \geq 12$ such that every oriented planar graph with a girth of at least $g_{\epsilon}$ possesses a fractional oriented chromatic number no greater than $4+\epsilon$. In contrast, it is established that an oriented planar graph with a girth of at least $g_{\epsilon}$ can have an oriented chromatic number of exactly 5. Furthermore, we determine the precise value of the fractional oriented chromatic number for directed cycles, revealing that this value is contingent upon the prime factors of the cycle's length.

**Abstract.** We characterize classes of filters $\mathbb{D}$ such that the full subcategory $\operatorname{fix}\operatorname{A}_{\mathbb D}$ of $\mathsf{Conv}$, consisting of convergences defined by the adherence of filters in $\mathbb{D}$, is simple within $\mathsf{Conv}$. Additionally, we clarify conditions under which distinct filter classes yield identical categories of adherence-determined convergences. Applying our primary result, we demonstrate that the category of hypotopologies lacks simplicity, thereby resolving a question posed in [25].

When two messages are presented as linear sequences of characters, it is straightforward to determine if one can be transformed into the other using a simple letter substitution cipher. Conversely, when letters are attached as labels to nodes in topologically isomorphic unordered trees, the problem of identifying a valid substitution is known as the marked tree isomorphism problem in academic literature and has been proven to be as computationally difficult as the general graph isomorphism problem. While a left-to-right approach yields the letter cipher for linear messages, a tree isomorphism serves as the cipher for messages structured as unordered trees. Because the number of isomorphisms between two trees grows exponentially with their size, exhaustively searching for a cipher is highly inefficient. This paper introduces a method designed to overcome the combinatorial complexity of the isomorphism search space. We demonstrate that, in linear time relative to the tree size, we can reduce the cardinality of this search space by an exponential factor on average.

Sequential decision-making in cost-sensitive scenarios is exceptionally challenging, particularly for high-stakes real-world applications like malaria control and treatment recommendations. Policymakers primarily struggle to learn effective policies from scratch through limited interactions within complex environments. To address this, we present Variance-Bonus Monte Carlo Tree Search (VB-MCTS), a practical and data-efficient model-based reinforcement learning approach designed to facilitate rapid learning with minimal trials. By employing Gaussian Process (GP) regression to explicitly model environment transitions, the method mitigates model bias. Furthermore, a proposed variance-bonus reward mechanism leverages the GP world model to quantify uncertainty, thereby enhancing exploration efficiency within the MCTS planning process. Theoretical analysis demonstrates polynomial sample complexity, confirming VB-MCTS's sample efficiency. Extensive experiments and superior performance in a competitive world-level RL benchmark validate its advantages over state-of-the-art methods on the demanding malaria control task.

This study investigates the inclusive production of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) charmonium states across varying centrality classes in p-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 8.16$ TeV at the LHC. Using the ALICE detector and analyzing the dimuon decay channel, the measurement covers rapidity ranges of $-4.46 < y_{\rm cms} < -2.96$ (Pb-going) and $2.03 < y_{\rm cms} < 3.53$ (p-going), extending down to zero transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$). Production cross sections for both states are calculated as a function of centrality, determined by the energy deposited in the zero-degree calorimeter in the Pb-going direction. Differential $p_{\rm T}$ cross sections for J/$\psi$, along with mean $\langle p_{\rm T} \rangle$ and $\langle p^{2}_{\rm T} \rangle$ values, are reported for multiple centrality bins at both forward and backward rapidities. Nuclear effects on these charmonium states are examined via the nuclear modification factor. In the p-going direction, a suppression of both states is observed, intensifying from peripheral to central collisions. Conversely, in the Pb-going direction, the centrality trends diverge: the J/$\psi$ nuclear modification factor rises from below unity in peripheral collisions to above unity in central ones, whereas the $\psi$(2S) remains at or below unity across all centralities without significant dependence. These findings are compared with p-Pb data from $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV, revealing no notable energy dependence, and are further evaluated against theoretical models incorporating various nuclear matter effects.

The Poisson's ratio in spring network systems has been demonstrated to rely not merely on geometry, but also on the balance between angle-bending and bond-compression forces. We derive a straightforward analytic finding: when spring interaction strength equals bond-reorientation strength, the Poisson's ratio becomes exactly zero and remains independent of the network's geometric configuration.

Although Differentiable Architecture Search (DARTS) has been widely adopted in various vision tasks, its direct application to Transformers is often impractical due to excessive memory consumption. To address this, we introduce a multi-split reversible network integrated with DARTS. Our approach employs a backpropagation-with-reconstruction algorithm, ensuring that only the outputs from the final layer need to be stored. This reduction in memory requirements enables the search process to utilize larger hidden dimensions and a broader set of candidate operations. We assessed the resulting architectures on three sequence-to-sequence benchmarks: WMT'14 English-German, WMT'14 English-French, and WMT'14 English-Czech. The experimental findings demonstrate that our network consistently surpasses standard Transformers across all evaluated tasks. Furthermore, our method achieves performance comparable to large-scale Evolved Transformers while reducing computational costs by approximately an order of magnitude.

We present equations for the Variance Gamma process because we go beyond the standard definition as a time-changed Brownian motion. This approach leads to a novel non-local equation, valid even in the drifted case and involving generalized Weyl derivatives. Subsequently, we examine the relationship with special functions and investigate a space equation for the process. Finally, we conclude by noting the convergence in distribution of a compound Poisson process to the Variance Gamma process.

The development of thermal machines has progressed from traditional steam engines to recently introduced nanoscopic quantum systems serving as working fluids. These systems adhere to quantum open system dynamics and often function under non-equilibrium conditions, yet the impact of such dynamics on the performance of quantum heat engines remains unresolved. This study examines and optimizes the efficiency and power generation of two-stage quantum heat engines powered by non-equilibrium steady states. In the initial charging phase, a quantum working fluid—comprising either a qutrit or two coupled qubits—is linked to two reservoirs at distinct temperatures, creating a heat current that accumulates ergotropy within the system. The subsequent stage involves a coherent driving force that extracts work over a finite duration; afterward, the external drive is deactivated, allowing the machine to begin a new cycle.

This study introduces and evaluates a predictive eco-driving assistance system (pEDAS) designed to help drivers in battery electric vehicles adopt more efficient driving habits, thereby lowering energy use while boosting safety and comfort. The system utilizes two model predictive controllers (MPCs)—specifically a reference-tracking MPC and a car-following MPC—which integrate data from onboard sensors, traffic signal phase and timing (SPaT) messages, and route geography to calculate energy-optimal speeds. Drivers receive these optimal speed recommendations and advisory guidance through visual feedback. pEDAS continuously encourages energy-efficient behaviors, such as optimal car-following, maintaining safe speeds on curves and turns, adhering to dynamic programming-derived speeds on freeways, and utilizing green-wave speeds at signalized intersections whenever feasible. To assess the system's effectiveness, user studies involving 41 participants were conducted on a dynamic driving simulator. Analytical results demonstrated that pEDAS enabled drivers to achieve average energy savings of up to 10%, decrease speed limit violations, and eliminate unnecessary stops at traffic signals. Additionally, user acceptance was assessed using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), revealing a generally positive user attitude where perceived usefulness and perceived behavioral control emerged as the key drivers of the intention to use pEDAS.

Resource allocation scenarios involving restricted agents competing for resources often map to maximum matching problems on bipartite graphs. This work examines situations where agents possess constraints rendering them incompatible with specific resources. Under this framework, a central authority selects a maximum matching stochastically, thereby assigning each agent to a resource with a certain probability. Agents aim to enhance their matching probabilities by adjusting their constraints within defined boundaries. The authority's objective is to counsel a dissatisfied agent to relax these constraints such that the total relaxation cost remains within an agent-specified budget while maximizing the probability of resource assignment. We demonstrate computational hardness for certain variants of this budget-constrained optimization problem and provide algorithms for others. Furthermore, we empirically assess our approaches using synthetic data alongside two new real-world datasets: one concerning vacation activities and another regarding classroom assignments.

A primary benefit of multi-level cache-enabled (MLCE) networks is their ability to bring content closer to the network edge by proactively storing it across various transmitters, including small base stations (SBSs), unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), and cache-enabled device-to-device (CE-D2D) users. This strategy mitigates fronthaul congestion between the core network and numerous transmitters. To achieve this, we leverage network coding (NC) to schedule multiple users for transmission from the same node. Our focus is on a throughput maximization problem that jointly optimizes network-coded user scheduling and power allocation, adhering to constraints on fronthaul capacity, transmit power, and network coding. Due to the problem's intractability, we decompose it into two distinct subproblems: the first addresses network-coded user scheduling with a fixed power allocation, and the second optimizes power levels based on the user schedule derived from the first. To solve the first subproblem, we propose an innovative *two-layered rate-aware NC (RA-IDNC)* graph, while the second subproblem is addressed using an iterative function evaluation (IFE) method. Finally, simulation results demonstrate the throughput improvements of our proposed approach compared to existing solutions.

This work investigates final state observability estimates for bi-continuous semigroups acting on Banach spaces. Specifically, it addresses the problem of determining the state at a final time $T>0$ for any given initial value, utilizing the trajectory of that value over the interval $t\in [0,T]$ as measured by an appropriate norm. A sufficient condition is established, relying on an uncertainty principle and a dissipation estimate. Furthermore, two specific bi-continuous semigroups—the Gau{\ss}--Weierstra{\ss} and the Ornstein--Uhlenbeck semigroups, both defined on the space of bounded continuous functions—are shown to satisfy such final state observability estimates. Additionally, the duality linking cost-uniform approximate null-controllability and final state observability is extended to locally convex spaces for bounded and continuous control functions; this generalization appears to be novel even within the context of Banach spaces.

This paper introduces a new method for automatically building a parallel discourse corpus tailored for dialogue machine translation. The process begins by crawling parallel subtitle data and corresponding monolingual movie scripts from the internet. Using an information retrieval technique, metadata such as speaker roles and discourse boundaries extracted from the scripts are mapped onto the subtitle data, thereby aligning monolingual discourse with bilingual texts. Beyond evaluating these mapping results, the study also incorporates speaker information directly into the translation framework. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves 81.79% and 98.64% accuracy in annotating speakers and dialogue boundaries, respectively, while speaker-based language model adaptation yields an improvement of approximately 0.5 BLEU points in translation quality. Finally, the authors publicly release a dataset of roughly 100,000 parallel discourse entries, manually annotated with speaker and dialogue boundary information.

Recent years have seen large, pre-trained Transformer-based language models drive significant advancements in various natural language understanding tasks. To accommodate the growing scale of these models, practitioners often expand batch sizes to utilize multiple GPUs, thereby enhancing training velocity. However, enlarging the batch size frequently complicates optimization, resulting in sluggish convergence or suboptimal generalization, which can necessitate exponentially more training time to reach equivalent model performance. This paper investigates the loss landscape steepness associated with large-batch optimization when adapting pre-trained Transformers to domain-specific tasks, revealing it to be notably complex and irregular, thus hindering generalization on downstream applications. To address this issue, we introduce ScaLA, a novel and efficient technique designed to accelerate the adaptation of pre-trained transformer networks. Distinct from previous approaches, ScaLA employs a sequential game-theoretic strategy by incorporating lightweight adversarial noise into large-batch optimization, substantially boosting adaptation speed while maintaining model generalization. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that ScaLA achieves 2.7 to 9.8 times faster adaptation compared to baselines on GLUE benchmarks using BERT-base and RoBERTa-large, while matching or exceeding the accuracy of current state-of-the-art large-batch optimization methods. Furthermore, we examine the theoretical dimensions of large-batch optimization with adversarial noise, offering a theoretical convergence rate analysis for ScaLA grounded in techniques for non-convex saddle-point problems.

Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a fundamental technique in machine learning. When handling large datasets (N), SGD typically constructs an unbiased gradient estimator of the empirical risk by sampling a small subset, known as a minibatch. While standard practice involves uniform random sampling, researchers have investigated alternative methods to reduce variance, specifically exploring Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs). DPPs generate minibatches that prioritize diversity among selected items, and empirical results indicate their effectiveness. However, establishing a systematic and theoretical explanation for why DPPs improve performance has proven challenging, similar to difficulties encountered in recent coreset applications. This paper introduces an orthogonal polynomial-based DPP framework for minibatch sampling within SGD. By leveraging the specific characteristics of the data distribution, this approach offers enhanced sensitivity and power compared to data-agnostic techniques. We validate our method through a rigorous theoretical analysis of convergence properties that bridges the gap between discrete datasets and continuous domains. Specifically, we demonstrate that particular DPPs, combined with controlled approximations, yield gradient estimators whose variance decreases with batch size more rapidly than uniform sampling. When integrated with existing finite-time guarantees for convex SGD objectives, this results in a tighter bound on mean square approximation error compared to uniform minibatches. Furthermore, our estimators are compatible with recent algorithms that sample linear statistics of DPPs (the gradient estimator) directly, bypassing the need to sample the underlying DPP (the minibatch) and thus lowering computational costs. Finally, we support our theoretical findings with comprehensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world data.

We establish an abstract framework for proof-theoretic analysis extending beyond ordinal numbers, creating an analog to Ordinal Analysis focused on $\Pi^1_2$ theorems. This is achieved by substituting ordinal numbers with uniform, wellfoundedness-preserving functors within the category of linear orders. Generalizing the concept of a proof-theoretic ordinal, we introduce the functorial $\Pi^1_2$ norm for a theory, proving its existence and uniqueness for $\Pi^1_2$-sound theories. Building on this, we define $\Sigma^1_2$- and $\Pi^1_2$-soundness ordinals, which respectively measure the maximum strength of true $\Sigma^1_2$ theorems and the minimum strength of false $\Pi^1_2$ theorems in a given theory. We investigate these ordinals to develop a proof-theoretic classification for recursively enumerable extensions of $\mathsf{ACA}_0$. Employing methods from infinitary and categorical proof theory, generalized recursion theory, constructibility, and forcing, we demonstrate that an admissible ordinal serves as the $\Pi^1_2$-soundness ordinal of a recursively enumerable extension of $\mathsf{ACA}_0$ if and only if it is not parameter-free $\Sigma^1_1$-reflecting. Furthermore, we identify the $\Sigma^1_2$-soundness ordinal of $\mathsf{ACA}_0$ as $\omega_1^{ck}$ and characterize the $\Sigma^1_2$-soundness ordinals of recursively enumerable, $\Sigma^1_2$-sound extensions of $\Pi^1_1{-}\mathsf{CA}_0$.

Contemporary multivariate machine learning and statistical techniques estimate key parameters by incorporating prior knowledge of associations among outcome variables. However, existing methods that model these relationships typically rely on an error covariance matrix within multivariate regression, a limitation that prevents their application to other model types. This article introduces the MinPEN framework, which simultaneously estimates regression coefficients and inter-outcome relationships under mild assumptions. By employing a novel penalty function based on the minimum operator, MinPEN leverages detected response relationships to improve estimation. To address the resulting non-convex optimization challenge, an iterative algorithm that extends current state-of-the-art approaches is developed. Theoretical contributions include high-dimensional convergence rates, model selection consistency, and a framework for post-selection inference. Furthermore, the framework is extended to various exponential family loss functions, with specific emphasis on multiple binomial responses, and includes strategies for tuning parameter selection. Finally, simulation studies and two real-world data applications demonstrate the framework's finite-sample performance.

Computer science curricula typically aim to teach both the theoretical foundations of programming languages and best practices alongside practical development skills. However, in massive courses involving hundreds of students, instructors cannot adequately supervise the practical components; thus, process automation and student incentives are essential to guide learners effectively. The primary objective was to design an automated infrastructure for programming assignments capable of supporting such large-scale courses. This system was intended to encourage students to adopt key software engineering practices—specifically automated testing, configuration management, and Integrated Development Environments (IDE)—while helping them master the corresponding tools. We identified widely used development tools that support these practices and integrated them into our exam assignment management workflow. This experience report details the outcomes from the previous academic year. The developed infrastructure operated throughout a full year, facilitating four exam sessions for over a thousand students, with students reporting generally high satisfaction levels.

This work examines the character theory of metabelian and polycyclic groups to explore Hilbert-Schmidt stability, utilizing the character-theoretic framework established by Hadwin and Shulman. Given the strong link between stability and the dynamics of automorphisms on compact abelian groups, we establish that finitely generated virtually nilpotent groups, free metabelian groups, lamplighter groups, and upper triangular groups defined over specific rings of algebraic integers all possess Hilbert-Schmidt stability.

This study employs a damped potential to describe the running coupling constant of QCD within the confinement phase. Utilizing a phenomenological framework for the Debye screening length, the derived coupling is compared against the Brodsky-de T\'eramond-Deur and Richardson models, with results suggesting that the proposed model aligns more closely with the Richardson approach. Additionally, the Debye screening mass in the confinement phase relies on a small parameter that approaches zero in the non-confinement phase of QCD.

Hawkes processes are self-exciting stochastic models designed to capture scenarios where historical events elevate the likelihood of future occurrences. This study introduces a flexible methodology for modeling a discrete-time variant of these processes. While standard Hawkes models typically depend on a parametric form for the triggering kernel—the function quantifying the influence of past events—this approach may fail to accurately represent complex excitation patterns. By employing trans-dimensional Markov chain Monte Carlo inference, the proposed model allows the triggering kernel to assume any step function form, offering substantially greater flexibility than traditional parametric alternatives. The model's effectiveness is first validated through an extensive simulation study covering both univariate cases and multivariate scenarios involving multiple interacting Hawkes processes. Subsequently, the model is applied to various case studies, including the interplay between Italy and France during the early to mid-phases of the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as terrorist interactions between Indonesia and the Philippines, and within three distinct regions of the Philippines.

Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are fundamental to the chemical and hydrodynamic development of exoplanetary atmospheres and protoplanetary discs. Should these molecules endure the planet formation process, they could participate in prebiotic reactions that generate complex compounds like amino acids and nucleotides—the building blocks of life as we understand it. Nevertheless, the specific abundance and function of PAHs in these settings remain largely obscure due to the sensitivity and wavelength constraints of existing and past space-based observatories. Emerging infrared space spectroscopy missions, including Twinkle and Ariel, offer a distinct chance to identify PAHs within both exoplanetary atmospheres and forming discs. This study introduces synthetic observations derived from conservative numerical simulations of standard protoplanetary discs and a transiting hot Saturn orbiting a solar-type star. Our models indicate that both Twinkle and Ariel could detect the 3.3-micron PAH signature within feasible observation times for both discs and transiting planets, provided PAH abundances reach at least one-tenth of interstellar medium levels.

While current state-of-the-art object detectors offer speed and accuracy, they depend heavily on extensive, well-annotated training data. Acquiring such large volumes of task-specific fine-grained annotations is often prohibitively expensive. Conversely, extracting common-sense relationships from text—such as the fact that a table lamp is a lamp resting on a table—is significantly more accessible, and relationships like "on-top-of" can be annotated in a task-agnostic manner. This paper introduces a probabilistic model that leverages this relational knowledge to convert an existing coarse-grained object detector into one capable of fine-grained detection. Our method, RelDetect, shows performance comparable to state-of-the-art baselines that rely on fine-tuning, even when only a minimal fraction ($0.2\%$) of fine-grained annotations is available. Furthermore, RelDetect effectively exploits the transferability of relationship data to outperform these baselines by $5$ mAP points on unseen datasets, achieving zero-shot transfer. Overall, we highlight the efficacy of incorporating relationships into object detection, particularly when fine-grained categories can be connected to coarse-grained ones through appropriate relational links.

This paper introduces a framework designed for rapid trajectory planning in unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Adapted from a pre-existing bilevel optimization structure, the approach assigns the lower level to determine the optimal trajectory for a given time allocation, while the upper level refines the time allocation via analytical gradients. Originally, the lower level included safety-set constraints as inequality conditions within a convex quadratic program (QP). Our method accelerates computation by removing these safety constraints from the lower-level QP and relocating them to the upper level. There, feasible waypoints and time allocations are jointly updated using analytical gradients facilitated by OptNet. Simulation results demonstrate that our method's computation time grows linearly with the number of safety sets, offering a significant improvement over state-of-the-art techniques, which exhibit exponential scaling.

Proof by induction is vital for mathematics and formal verification, yet automating it remains a persistent challenge in computer science. To tackle this, we created sem_ind, a tool that suggests arguments for the inductive method based on a given problem. We enhanced sem_ind's precision by introducing definitional quantifiers, which enable an analysis of both the syntactic structure of inductive problems and the definitions of relevant constants in a domain-agnostic manner. Our evaluation demonstrates that this improved version boosts recommendation accuracy from 20.1% to 38.2% for the top candidates within a 5.0-second timeout, while reducing the median execution time from 2.79 seconds to 1.06 seconds.

Leveraging the strong expressive power of graphs, graph-based methods have delivered remarkable results across diverse biomedical domains. However, most current approaches rely on manually constructing adjacency matrices from meta-features and subsequently derive node embeddings via Graph Representation Learning (GRL). This reliance often hinders generalization to unseen samples and overlooks the intricate correlations between different modalities, ultimately limiting the ability to provide accurate patient information for reliable diagnosis. To address these issues, this paper introduces an end-to-end Multimodal Graph Learning (MMGL) framework for disease prediction. By employing amodal-attentional multi-modal fusion, the model effectively integrates features from various modalities, capitalizing on their complementarity and inter-correlations. Instead of manually defining adjacency matrices, MMGL captures latent graph structures through adaptive graph learning, which is jointly optimized with the prediction model to uncover intrinsic sample connections. Unlike traditional transductive methods, our approach supports inductive learning, making it applicable to unseen data. Extensive experiments on two disease prediction tasks demonstrate that MMGL achieves superior performance. Additionally, we visualize and analyze the learned graph structures to offer more robust decision support for clinicians and inspire further disease research.

We demonstrate that the hierarchy of higher antibrackets—also known as higher Koszul brackets or braces—for a linear operator $\Delta$ acting on a commutative superalgebra can be characterized by universal formulas based on iterated Nijenhuis-Richardson brackets of $\Delta$ and multiplication operators. Consequently, this result allows for an immediate extension of higher antibrackets to noncommutative algebras, maintaining the validity of generalized Jacobi identities.

In contemporary drug development, the increasing access to high-dimensional observational data enables researchers to investigate subgroup heterogeneity, particularly when randomized clinical trials are unfeasible due to ethical or financial limitations. However, the common practice of naively identifying subgroups with high treatment levels is often deceptive because of "subgroup selection bias." Furthermore, the inherent characteristics of high-dimensional observational data have intensified the difficulty of accurately estimating treatment effects within these subgroups. To address these challenges, we introduce novel inferential tools utilizing resampling techniques to evaluate the replicability of subgroups identified post-hoc in observational studies. Supported by rigorous theoretical validation and comprehensive simulations, we demonstrate that our proposed method yields asymptotically sharp confidence intervals and debiased estimates for selected subgroup treatment effects even in the presence of high-dimensional covariates. Additionally, we illustrate the advantages of these methods through an analysis of UK Biobank data.

To enhance decision-making regarding immunization strategies, this study integrates a stochastic cellular automaton into the SEIR model by accounting for two vaccine doses. We evaluate three vaccination scenarios: (i) unlimited doses, (ii) limited doses targeted at susceptible individuals, and (iii) limited doses randomly distributed across the entire population. Our findings indicate that the total volume of vaccinations and the timing of initiation are more critical factors than vaccine efficacy, the interval between the first and second doses, or the gap between vaccinated groups. In scenario (i), the system can rapidly converge to a disease-free equilibrium even when only a fraction of the population receives the first dose. Scenario (ii) demonstrates that dividing a limited number of doses into fewer applications reduces infections more effectively than spreading them across many applications; additionally, waste is minimal for the first dose but rises for the second. Scenario (iii) exhibits a steeper increase in dose waste from the first to the second application compared to scenario (ii), with total wasted doses rising linearly as the number of applications grows. Finally, in scenario (iii), the quantity of effective doses administered to consecutive groups declines exponentially over time.

Using the SU(3) flavor symmetry framework of a constituent quark model, we investigate the $\Lambda$ baryon spectrum. Our findings indicate that it is challenging to fit certain negative-parity $\Lambda$ resonances as single $q^2s$ ($q = u, d$) configurations within the traditional three-quark model. Consequently, we evaluate the ground-state mass spectrum of $q^3s\bar q$ pentaquarks and propose an interpretation: the $\Lambda(1405)1/2^{-}$, $\Lambda(1670)1/2^{-}$, and $\Lambda(1800)1/2^{-}$, along with the $\Lambda(1520)3/2^{-}$, $\Lambda(1690)3/2^{-}$, and $\Lambda(2050)3/2^{-}$ resonances, are understood as three-state mixtures comprising two $p$-wave $q^2s$ states and one ground-state $q^3s\bar q$ pentaquark state.

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) represent astronomical events observed at the highest energy levels. These gamma-ray photons, possessing energies in the mega-electronvolt range, originate from point-like sources uniformly scattered across the sky. Typically, a burst manifests as a pulse lasting approximately one minute. Since Earth's atmosphere is opaque to such high-energy radiation, these bursts are detected by satellites orbiting the planet. The total energy output of GRBs, calculated from the integrated energy flux per unit area of a detector, indicates that we are observing immensely powerful explosions that release enormous power over a brief interval. The only known mechanism capable of generating such colossal energies in the universe is the disruption of a star.

Inspired by recent computations of the SL(K+3,C) symmetry within n-point Lauricella string scattering amplitudes (SSA) for open bosonic string theory, we determine the ratios of solvable infinite linear relations for arbitrary n-point hard SSA (HSSA). Our findings reveal a universal stringy scaling behavior applicable to all n-point HSSA across every string loop order. Specifically, for the n=4 case, this scaling behavior simplifies to the infinite linear relations and constant ratios among HSSA previously conjectured by Gross [8] and subsequently verified using the decoupling of zero-norm states method [11].

This paper investigates monetary mechanisms for two-sided matching. While mechanisms following the deferred acceptance tradition, including those with monetary components, primarily prioritize stability, this work proposes a straightforward, auction-based approach that guarantees social welfare. We analyze the "Marshallian Match," a descending-price mechanism introduced by Waggoner and Weyl (2019) but previously unanalyzed. Under the assumption that all potential match values are positive, we demonstrate that the Marshallian Match, when paired with a "rebate" payment rule, achieves a constant price of anarchy. This finding generalizes to scenarios involving costs for acquiring value information and to hypergraph matching models. However, when valuations can be negative—such as in job markets—the problem becomes more complex. We define concepts of approximate stability and highlight their positive effects on welfare. Nevertheless, establishing constant factor welfare guarantees within an "ex ante stable equilibrium" remains an open challenge.

We examine multilevel fermions within an optical lattice governed by the Hubbard model featuring on-site SU($n$)-symmetric interactions. We demonstrate that, under suitable conditions, this system can be transformed into a spin model characterized by all-to-all SU($n$)-symmetric couplings. Raman pulses targeting internal spin states alter the atomic dispersion and generate spin-orbit coupling, effectively creating a synthetic inhomogeneous magnetic field that rivals the SU($n$) exchange interactions. We analyze the mean-field dynamical phase diagram of this resulting model across varying values of $n$ and initial configurations reachable via Raman pulses. Aligning with prior research for $n=2$, we observe that certain initial states yield two distinct dynamical phases following simple scaling laws with $n$. Furthermore, for $n>2$, we discover that dynamical behavior can be profoundly sensitive to initial intra-spin coherences. These predictions are easily verifiable in existing experiments involving ultracold alkaline-earth(-like) atoms.

Photoacoustic images derived from linear arrays are typically reconstructed using the conventional delay-and-sum (DAS) beamforming technique. While DAS is effective for forming PA images, the resulting reconstructions frequently suffer from noise, sidelobes, and other significant artifacts caused by inaccurate assumptions regarding PA signal correlation. This study aims to create an inversion method that mitigates these artifacts and sidelobes to enhance overall image quality. We introduce a novel beamformer utilizing higher-order signal correlation, which combines and sums a greater number of delayed PA signals than the traditional delay-multiply-and-sum (DMAS) approach. The proposed technique offers substantial improvements in resolution, contrast, and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) relative to conventional beamformers. Notably, the computational complexity of this method remains at the same order as DAS, $O(N)$, enabling real-time photoacoustic image reconstruction. GPU-based timing studies indicate that the proposed method executes in time frames comparable to both DAS and real-time DMAS. The algorithm was validated through both numerical simulations and experimental testing, with higher-order DMAS beamformers demonstrating superior reconstruction across all scenarios. Quantitative evaluation using an ex-vivo phantom revealed that the proposed method achieves 51% and 6% improvements in full width at half maximum (FWHM), as well as 81% and 39% improvements in SNR compared to DAS and DMAS, respectively. In conclusion, the proposed algorithm shows significant potential and promise for real-time photoacoustic imaging and its associated applications.

We develop a transparent metric to quantify chirality in single-electron ionization occurring within inherently achiral atoms. This study focuses on Argon atoms driven by novel optical fields composed of two non-collinear laser beams, which generate spatially varying chirality across the focal region. Our calculations incorporate realistic experimental parameters. To establish this chirality measure, we first determine the sign of the scalar triple product of the final electron momentum, $\mathrm{{\bf{p}}_{k}\cdot ({\bf{p}}_{i}\times {\bf p}}_{j})$, and multiply it by the ionization probability for specific values of $\mathrm{p_{k}}$ and $\mathrm{p_{i}p_{j}}$. We then integrate this product over all possible values of these momentum components.
