The observed suppression of infection clusters in the GPP-based model suggests that such distancing strategies are effective, particularly when infectivity levels are relatively low.

This paper examines the strong convergence of Faedo-Galerkin approximations toward a strong T-periodic solution of the torso-coupled bidomain model, where T represents the activation period of the heart's inner wall. Initially, we define the torso-coupled bidomain operator and establish its key properties essential for this study. Subsequently, we formulate the abstract evolution system associated with the model and define the concept of a strong solution. We demonstrate that Faedo-Galerkin approximations possess the regularity required of a strong solution and identify specific constraints on initial conditions that ensure the sequence converges fully to a global strong solution of the Cauchy problem. Finally, these results are applied to prove the existence of a strong T-periodic solution.

Colloidal gels behave as soft solids when stationary but flow like liquids under applied shear. When a fluidized gel, subjected to a shear rate $\dot\gamma_{p}$, suddenly stops flowing, it undergoes a liquid-to-solid transition during which stress relaxes to a \textit{residual stress} $\sigma_{\rm res}$, reflecting the material's prior shear history. This study examines the liquid-to-solid transition in boehmite (an aluminum oxide) gels, revealing a notable non-monotonic relaxation of $\sigma_{\rm res}(\dot\gamma_{p})$ defined by a dual response relative to a critical shear rate $\dot\gamma_{c}$. If the initial shear rate exceeds this critical value ($\dot\gamma_{p}>\dot\gamma_{c}$), the resulting gel forgets its shear history, and $\sigma_{\rm res}$ remains negligible. Conversely, when $\dot\gamma_{p}<\dot\gamma_{c}$, the gel retains a memory of the shear, and $\sigma_{\rm res}$ rises as the shear rate decreases, thereby enhancing the gel's viscoelastic properties. Furthermore, both $\sigma_{\rm res}$ and the viscoelastic characteristics increase logarithmically with the strain accumulated before flow cessation. This shear-induced "overaging" effect offers significant potential for tailoring the rheological behavior of colloidal gels.

Emotion and expressivity within music have long captivated researchers in music information retrieval. Recently, mid-level perceptual features have been proposed to clarify computational models of musical emotion. However, we observed that the diversity of styles and genres in existing datasets is insufficient for these models to generalize effectively to specialized acoustic domains, such as solo piano music. This study demonstrates that combining unsupervised domain adaptation with receptive-field regularized deep neural networks can substantially enhance generalization to this specific domain. Furthermore, we show that these domain-adapted models are capable of more accurately predicting and explaining the expressive qualities found in classical piano performances, as perceived by human listeners.

This study introduces a general methodology for computing a compressed representation of the exponential $\exp(h)$ of a high-dimensional function $h$. These exponential functions are crucial in various Uncertainty Quantification tasks, such as approximating log-normal random fields or evaluating Bayesian posterior measures. Typically, such high-dimensional objects are numerically intractable and can only be accessed pointwise via sampling techniques. In contrast, the proposed method constructs a functional representation of the exponential by leveraging its property as the solution to an ordinary differential equation. By applying a Petrov--Galerkin scheme to this equation, we obtain a tensor train representation of the solution and derive an efficient, reliable a posteriori error estimator. Numerical experiments involving a log-normal random field and a Bayesian likelihood demonstrate the method's performance compared to other recent low-rank representations for these applications. While the current work focuses on a specific differential equation, the approach is applicable in broader contexts. We demonstrate that composing a generic holonomic function with a high-dimensional function yields a differential equation suitable for our method. Furthermore, the differential equation can be adjusted to tailor the norm used in the a posteriori error estimates to specific problem requirements.

Model ensembling is a prevalent strategy in machine learning, yet the standard practice of averaging predictions from multiple models often becomes impractical due to memory and computational constraints that scale linearly with the number of models. To address this, we introduce a layer-wise fusion algorithm for neural networks that employs optimal transport to align neurons across different models before averaging their parameters. This method enables successful "one-shot" knowledge transfer between networks trained on heterogeneous, non-i.i.d. data without requiring retraining. Our results demonstrate that this approach significantly surpasses simple averaging in both i.i.d. and non-i.i.d. scenarios and serves as an efficient alternative to full ensembling with moderate fine-tuning. We evaluate its performance on standard architectures, including VGG11, ResNet18, and MLPs, across CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and MNIST datasets. Furthermore, the method offers a principled framework for merging parameters of neural networks with varying widths and has potential applications in model compression. The implementation is available at https://github.com/sidak/otfusion.

Over the last few decades, there has been a growing focus on deploying social robots as behavioral coaches for Autism Spectrum Disorder interventions [4]. We argue that robots integrated into therapeutic settings could also deliver quantitative diagnostic data by monitoring patient behaviors. Given the social characteristics of ASD, achieving this requires robots to identify the internal states of their human counterparts, such as confusion or engagement. Addressing this challenge involves two key inquiries: (1) which robot-accessible cues can indicate internal states, and (2) how can a system classify these states to generate sufficiently granular diagnostic insights? This paper examines these questions thoroughly, proposes a novel conceptor-based classifier, presents initial findings from a proof-of-concept study, and outlines directions for future research.

We establish a link between the Hawking radiation spectra of various Taub-NUT black hole classes and the radiation generated by the relativistic motion of an accelerated, perfectly reflecting Dirichlet boundary in (1+1)-dimensional flat spacetime. We show that both particle and energy spectra become thermal at late times, with particle production being suppressed by the NUT parameter. Furthermore, we calculate the radiation spectrum for rotating, electrically charged (Kerr-Newman) Taub-NUT black holes and their extremal limits, explicitly illustrating how these parameters influence the outgoing particle and energy fluxes.

Using the standard basis operator method, we examine the momentum distribution and excitation spectrum of the ionic Bose-Hubbard model. We derive Green's functions within the random phase approximation across the Mott insulator, superfluid, charge density wave, and supersolid phases. Our results indicate that the superfluid and supersolid phases exhibit gapless Goldstone modes alongside gapped modes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the momentum distribution displays a peak at the zone corner for both the charge density wave and supersolid phases near the phase boundary. Additionally, we establish that the momentum distribution can be understood through the excitation spectrum and spectral weights associated with hole excitation modes.

This work offers several contributions aimed at connecting supervisory control theory with service coordination to investigate the boundaries between these two domains. First, we adapt the classical synthesis algorithm from supervisory control theory to generate the most permissive controller, enabling the creation of orchestrations and choreographies for service contracts modeled as contract automata; this is made possible by introducing a new concept of controllability. Second, we introduce an abstract parametric synthesis algorithm that encompasses both the classical synthesis and the specific syntheses for orchestration and choreography. Finally, using this novel abstract synthesis, we demonstrate that the concrete syntheses adhere to a refinement order. A practical example from the service domain is provided to illustrate these contributions.

The dimension of a partition $\lambda$, denoted as $f^{\lambda}$, refers to the count of standard Young tableaux with that specific shape. McKay originally enumerated partitions possessing odd dimensions, a work later expanded upon by Macdonald. Defining $a_i(n)$ as the quantity of partitions of $n$ where the dimension is congruent to $i$ modulo 4, this study refines previous findings by determining $a_1(n)$ and $a_3(n)$ for integers $n$ lacking consecutive 1s in their binary form or having a binary digit sum of 2, while also supplying values for $a_2(n)$ across all $n$. Additionally, analogous results are provided regarding the irreducible representations of alternating groups.

Integrating a product of linear forms over the unit simplex is solvable in polynomial time when the number of variables $n$ remains fixed (V. Baldoni et al., 2011). This note demonstrates that such integration is equivalent to computing the normalizing constant of state probabilities for a widely used class of Markov processes in queueing network theory. Leveraging this equivalence, we review computational algorithms from queueing theory capable of performing exact integration. For instance, provided certain regularity conditions are met, these algorithms can exactly integrate a product of linear forms with a total degree $N$ by solving $N$ systems of linear equations.

This study investigates the static and dynamic characteristics of the antiferromagnetic material Zn$_{2}$(VO)(PO$_{4}$)$_{2}$, specifically examining the effects of substituting non-magnetic Ti$^{4+}$ ions at the V$^{4+}$ sites. $^{31}$P nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra and spin-lattice relaxation rates ($1/T_1$) both confirm the establishment of long-range antiferromagnetic ordering below $T_N= 3.8-3.9$\,K. The critical exponent $\beta=0.33 \pm 0.02$, derived from the temperature evolution of sublattice magnetization measured via $^{31}$P NMR at 9.4\,MHz, aligns with three-dimensional spin model universality classes. The isotropic and axial hyperfine couplings linking $^{31}$P nuclei to V$^{4+}$ spins are determined to be $A_{\rm hf}^{\rm iso} = (9221 \pm 100)$ Oe/$\mu_{\rm B}$ and $A_{\rm hf}^{\rm ax} = (1010 \pm 50)$ Oe/$\mu_{\rm B}$, respectively. Magnetic susceptibility measurements above 6.5\,K and heat capacity data above 4.5\,K are accurately modeled by quantum Monte-Carlo simulations of the Heisenberg model on a square lattice, yielding an exchange constant of $J\simeq 7.7$\,K. This $J$ value agrees with results from NMR shift analysis, $1/T_1$ measurements, and electron spin resonance (ESR) intensity studies. Introducing non-magnetic Ti$^{4+}$ into Zn$_2$VO(PO$_4)_2$ results in a slight increase in the $J$ value alongside the dilution of the spin lattice. Unlike recent \textit{ab initio} predictions, no evidence of monoclinic structural distortion or magnetic one-dimensionality is observed in samples doped with up to 15\% Ti$^{4+}$. Furthermore, the Néel temperature $T_{\rm N}$ exhibits a linear decline as the concentration of the non-magnetic dopant increases.

We investigate electroweak corrections linking the running $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ mass $m_b$ of the $b$ quark within the five-flavor QCD$\times$QED effective theory to its counterpart in the Standard Model (SM). Utilizing the $b$ quark's pole mass $M_b$ as an intermediary, which is calculable in both frameworks, we bridge these two parameters. Although the running mass is not a fundamental component of the SM Lagrangian but rather the product of the running Yukawa coupling $y_b$ and the Higgs vacuum expectation value, the specific definitions of the latter introduce variability into the derived relations. While all such definitions can be interconverted via perturbation theory, we advocate for a specific gauge-independent prescription. This yields a relation enabling the direct determination of the $b$ quark's Yukawa coupling at the electroweak scale from its effective QCD running mass, facilitating the systematic resummation of large logarithms $\ln(m_b/M_t)$. Numerical results confirm that corrections to this proposed relation are significantly smaller than those observed between $y_b$ and $M_b$.

Intracellular transport is critical for supplying essential components throughout the complex, branched structures of neurons, ensuring their survival and function. Since disruptions in this transport mechanism are linked to numerous neurodegenerative diseases, understanding how neurons regulate transport to deliver materials to specific sites is vital. In this study, we introduce a new optimization model to simulate the traffic regulation of material transport within the intricate geometries of neurons. This transport system is managed to prevent congestion by minimizing a specific objective function. The optimization is subject to a set of partial differential equation (PDE) constraints that represent the material transport process using a macroscopic molecular-motor-assisted model for intracellular particles. We solve this PDE-constrained optimization problem within complex tree-like structures using isogeometric analysis (IGA). By varying simulation parameters, we induce traffic jams to investigate neuronal responses to such issues. Specifically, our model successfully replicates and elucidates traffic jams resulting from a reduced density of microtubules (MTs) and MT swirls. In summary, the proposed model effectively simulates material transport in healthy neurons and accounts for the formation of traffic jams in abnormal neurons. Our findings highlight that both neuronal geometry and MT structure are crucial for achieving an optimal transport process.

Positioning systems are fundamentally expected to deliver reliable location estimates to users. Furthermore, providing an assessment of the uncertainty associated with these estimates significantly enhances user utility. Although the idea of dynamically estimating the accuracy of fingerprinting-based positioning has been occasionally explored in recent literature—primarily through handcrafted rules relying on domain expertise—the rise of IoT devices and the abundance of data from Low Power Wide Area Networks (LPWANs) have enabled data-driven methodologies for determining positional certainty. This study examines a data-driven approach to Dynamic Accuracy Estimation (DAE) within the broader framework of a positioning system. Specifically, utilizing a public LoRaWAN dataset, the research investigates the optimal allocation of the training set between location estimation and DAE tasks, evaluates the strategy of selecting the most reliable estimates, and assesses how the spatial distribution of data influences DAE accuracy. Ultimately, this work offers a comprehensive overview of data-driven DAE determination within the overall design of positioning systems.

Given a finite group $G$ and an inverse-closed generating set $C$, let $Aut(G;C)$ denote the automorphisms of $G$ that fix $C$. We define an $Aut(G;C)$-invariant normal subgroup $\Phi(G;C)$ with the following property: for any $Aut(G;C)$-invariant normal generating set of $G$, removing all elements belonging to $\Phi(G;C)$ leaves a set that remains an $Aut(G;C)$-invariant normal generating set. While $\Phi(G;C)$ always contains the Frattini subgroup $\Phi(G)$, the inclusion can be strict. A Cayley graph $Cay(G,C)$ is termed normal edge-transitive if $Aut(G;C)$ acts transitively on the pairs $\{c,c^{-1}\}$ within $C$. We demonstrate that for such a graph, the quotient modulo $\Phi(G;C)$ represents the unique largest normal quotient isomorphic to a subdirect product of normal edge-transitive graphs of characteristically simple groups. Consequently, when $\Phi(G;C)$ is trivial, normal edge-transitive Cayley graphs of characteristically simple groups can be regarded as fundamental building blocks for all such graphs. The discussion further examines questions arising from these findings, including those regarding the collection of inverse-closed generating sets for specific group families. Specifically, this framework is applied to classify all $4$-valent normal edge-transitive Cayley graphs for dihedral groups; this classification introduces a novel construction of an infinite family of examples and refutes a conjecture by Talebi.

Creating realistic artificial preference distributions is essential for simulating electoral systems. Although this topic has been explored extensively for single districts, many relevant systems involve multiple districts. Approaches that either treat district preferences as independent or disregard the district structure entirely fail to produce satisfactory outcomes. This paper introduces a model extending the classic Eggenberger-P\'olya urn scheme, where each district corresponds to an urn and correlations exist between them. We demonstrate that this method features a minimal set of tunable parameters, offers computational efficiency, and generates distributions that appear realistic. We plan to apply this model in future research on electoral systems.

The DANSS detector is situated immediately beneath the core of a commercial reactor at the Kalinin Nuclear Power Plant, providing a vertical overburden of approximately 50 meters water equivalent. This location places the detector in an intermediate position relative to cosmic rays, between surface and underground facilities. Its sensitive volume consists of one cubic meter of finely segmented plastic scintillator equipped with both PMT and SiPM readout, enclosed by multi-layer passive and active shielding. The detector is capable of reconstructing muon tracks traversing this volume. The primary objective of the DANSS experiment is to measure antineutrino spectra at different distances from the source; this is accomplished using a lifting platform to collect data from three specific positions: 10.9, 11.9, and 12.9 meters from the reactor core. Muon data were gathered over nearly four calendar years. Parameters including the overburden characteristics $\langle E_{thr}\cos\theta \rangle$ and $\langle E_{thr} \rangle$, along with temperature and barometric correlation coefficients, are evaluated independently for each of the three detector positions. Within each position, these evaluations are conducted across three zenith angle ranges: nearly vertical muons ($\cos\theta>0.9$), nearly horizontal muons ($\cos\theta<0.36$), and the entire upper hemisphere.

A minimal gene expression model, comprising a switchable promoter and the generated messenger RNA, is mathematically equivalent to a Poisson channel driven by a binary Markovian input. Calculating its capacity involves optimizing two parameters: the mean sojourn times in the promoter's active (ON) and inactive (OFF) states. By analytically solving the associated filtering problem at the distribution level, an expression for mutual information is derived. Under a fixed peak power, three bandwidth-like constraints are applied by setting lower bounds on: (i) the average sojourn times, (ii) the autocorrelation time, and (iii) the mean time until a transition. For all three constraints, optimal solutions favor the OFF state, mirroring typical results for the Poisson channel. However, constraint (i) reveals a region favoring the ON state, while constraint (iii) displays local optima that also favor the ON state.

U Sco is a recurrent nova system characterized by eleven recorded outbursts, with the most recent occurring in 2010.1 and 2022.4. This study presents data from a monitoring program initiated in 1989, focusing on measuring the quiescent eclipse timings and brightness of U Sco between 2010 and 2022. Following the 2010.1 eruption, the orbital period experienced a sudden increase of +22.4 ± 1.0 parts-per-million (ppm), a change significantly larger than the near-zero shift (+3.9 ± 6.1 ppm) observed after the 1999.2 eruption. This magnitude of change cannot be attributed to standard mechanisms; instead, it suggests the dominant influence is the poorly understood process of asymmetric nova shell ejection. Between 2010.1 and 2016.78, the observed-minus-calculated (O-C) curve indicated a substantial, steady period decrease with a P-dot value of (-21.0 ± 3.2) × 10⁻⁹, which far exceeds the steady declines recorded in the two preceding inter-eruption intervals (-3.2 ± 1.9 and -1.1 ± 1.1 × 10⁻⁹). This large, variable, and negative P-dot is attributed to magnetic braking acting on the companion star's rotation. Beginning around 2016.9 ± 0.6, the O-C curve displayed a distinct kink, signaling a sudden period jump of +35.4 ± 7.1 ppm associated with a nova event. Quiescent brightness measurements post-2010.4 indicate that the white dwarf accreted sufficient mass to trigger the next eruption by 2017.1 ± 0.6. Photometric data further constrain the timing of this missed eruption, suggesting its 60-day peak occurred undetected within a 75-day observation gap in 2016, thereby narrowing the eruption date to 2016.78 ± 0.10.

Drawing upon the contributions of Ma and Wu\cite{Ma} and Climenhaga\cite{Climenhaga}, this paper proposes a novel definition of topological pressure for a semigroup of maps, grounded in the Carath\'{e}odory-Pesin structure (C-P structure) relative to any given subset. Furthermore, utilizing Bowen's equation, we provide a characterization of the Hausdorff dimension for arbitrary subsets comprising points with positive lower Lyapunov exponents that adhere to a specific tempered contraction condition.

We investigate how pressure-induced non-geodesic effects influence epicyclic modes within pressure-supported, perfect fluid tori orbiting Kerr black holes. By applying a perturbation approach, we establish fully general relativistic expressions for the eigenfunctions and eigenfrequencies of both radial and vertical epicyclic modes. These formulas apply to slightly non-slender tori with constant specific angular momentum, accurate up to second-order terms in torus thickness. We analyze the behavior of axisymmetric modes as well as the lowest-order ($m=\pm 1$) non-axisymmetric epicyclic modes. For black holes of any spin, we determine that non-slender tori experience negative pressure corrections relative to the epicyclic frequencies of free test particles, resulting in lower frequencies. These findings align qualitatively with recent pseudo-Newtonian studies utilizing the Paczyński-Wiita potential for a similar problem. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for high-frequency Quasi-Periodic Oscillation (QPO) models involving epicyclic oscillations.

This paper introduces a deep neural network (DNN)-based detector for uplink single-carrier index modulation nonorthogonal multiple access (SC-IM-NOMA) systems. In SC-IM-NOMA, users transmit data modulated via subcarrier index techniques over a shared set of subcarriers. Specifically, SC-IM-NOMA users simultaneously send their data at varying power levels, enabling receivers to perform successive interference cancellation (SIC) for multi-user detection. However, existing detectors for this system, including joint maximum-likelihood (JML) and maximum likelihood SIC-based (ML-SIC) methods, are plagued by high computational complexity. To mitigate this, we propose a DNN-based detector that utilizes a model-based SIC structure to jointly detect both M-ary symbols and index bits for all users, trained on extensive simulated data. Simulation results indicate that the proposed DNN detector achieves near-optimal error performance while significantly reducing runtime complexity compared to traditional hand-crafted detectors.

This study examines the maximum length of words definable in First-Order (FO) and Monadic Second-Order (MSO) logic using formulas of size $n$. For both logical systems, we establish an upper bound for this length as an exponential tower whose height grows linearly with $n$. This result is derived by counting types relative to a fixed quantifier rank. Conversely, we derive lower bounds for both FO and MSO that also take the form of an exponential tower, where the height scales with a rational power of $n$. These lower bounds are demonstrated by providing explicit formulas that define word representations corresponding to levels within the cumulative hierarchy of sets. Furthermore, we analyze the Löwenheim-Skolem and Hanf numbers for these logics applied to words, achieving analogous bounds for these parameters as well.

Dynamo theory posits that stars with convective envelopes efficiently produce surface magnetic fields, appearing as activity like starspots, faculae, and flares when their rotation period is shorter than their convective turnover time. While most red giants have slowed down significantly due to expansion and typically lack spots, a prior analysis of approximately 4,500 red giants from the NASA Kepler mission revealed that roughly 8% exhibit spots, with about 15% of those belonging to close binary systems. This study addresses a specific anomaly: red giants in close binary systems with rotation periods under 80 days show photometric modulation approximately ten times larger than single red giants of similar age and rotation. We investigate whether tidal locking in binary systems enhances magnetic field strength or if differences in spot distribution account for this discrepancy. By measuring CaII H & K line chromospheric emission for 3,130 of the 4,465 stars previously analyzed via the LAMOST survey, we demonstrate that red giants in close binaries with spin-orbit resonance exhibit significantly higher chromospheric emission than single stars. This indicates that tidal locking generates stronger magnetic fields at a given rotational period. Beyond offering new observational insights into binary system evolution, this finding could enable machine learning pipelines to automatically distinguish between single and binary red giants.

Nearest neighbor search serves as a fundamental computational tool widely applied across computer science research, particularly when handling vast datasets. However, its algorithmic application is often constrained by the challenge of defining "nearness" between data points. Current research trends focus on large, intricate networks where nodes signify entities and edges denote relationships, making community detection a critical area of study. Typically, community detection algorithms define an objective function to identify significant clusters by optimizing this metric. This article investigates the nearest neighbor search problem within complex networks by establishing a tailored notion of nearness. First, we analyze exact nearest neighbor search using a metric tree on a proposed metric space derived from the network. Subsequently, we address approximate nearest neighbor search through locality sensitive hashing. To evaluate our approach, we applied it to the community detection problem. Our methods yield results that are highly competitive with established algorithms in the literature, as verified on various real-world networks. Furthermore, our algorithm demonstrates significantly lower execution times compared to popular existing methods.

We re-examine the Haake-Lewenstein-Wilkens (HLW) methodology applied to the Edwards-Anderson (EA) Ising spin glass model [Phys. Rev. Lett. 55, 2606 (1985)]. This method involves evaluating and analyzing the probability distribution of configurations across two replicas of the system, averaged over quenched disorder. This distribution yields the squares of thermal spin copies from the two systems, averaged over disorder, which constitute the terms defining the standard EA order parameter, qEA. Utilizing the saddle point/steepest descent technique, we compute the average of Gaussian disorder in higher dimensions. Our approximate findings suggest that qEA remains positive for temperatures between 0 and Tc in both 3D and 4D. The 2D case appears more nuanced, as the competition between domain wall energy increases and boundary/edge effects is more pronounced; nevertheless, our approach still predicts spin glass ordering at sufficiently low temperatures. We speculate on how these results align with or challenge prevailing views: i) that the EA model possesses only a single ground state (up to spin flips) in 2D, 3D, and 4D; and ii) whether a spin glass transition occurs in 3D and 4D (or not in 2D). This work is dedicated to the memory of Fritz Haake and Marek Cieplak.

The Panoramic SETI (PANOSETI) experiment is designed to identify and measure optical transients with timing precision ranging from nanoseconds to seconds across a vast field of view of approximately 4,450 square degrees. To satisfy these demanding constraints regarding timing and wide-field coverage, PANOSETI will deploy two groups of roughly 45 telescopes each. These assemblies utilize custom-built fast photon-counting detectors paired with $f/1.32$ focusing optics to eliminate false signals through coincidence detection. Preliminary observations using pairs of prototype telescopes covering 100 square degrees have evaluated instrument performance and false alarm rates. The results indicate that positioning telescopes more than 1 km apart, rather than side-by-side, while surveying the same area, significantly lowers the rate of false positives caused by nearby sources such as Cherenkov showers. Additionally, the report outlines design parameters for the proposed all-sky PANOSETI instrument and its anticipated field-of-views.

The paper introduces DICHASUS, a distributed massive MIMO channel sounder designed to collect extensive channel state information (CSI) datasets. This data supports applications such as machine learning for user localization, joint communication and sensing (JCAS), channel mapping, and facilitating massive MIMO in frequency-division duplex (FDD) scenarios. Unlike prior architectures, the proposed system features fully autonomous single-antenna receivers, allowing for flexible, spatially distributed deployments and near-infinite scalability. Additionally, channel coefficient vectors can be optionally annotated with precise ground-truth location data, sourced from GNSS receivers for outdoor use or various indoor positioning methods.

Target localization beyond the convex hull of anchors is a common yet under-researched challenge in vehicle-centric, UAV, and self-localization systems. This paper investigates the optimal placement of anchors for Time-of-Arrival (ToA) localization methods to minimize the worst-case Dilution of Precision (DOP). Leveraging existing findings on DOP scaling laws for beyond-convex-hull scenarios, we introduce a new metric called Range-Normalized DOP (RNDOP). We demonstrate that the problem of minimizing worst-case DOP can be reduced to minimizing worst-case RNDOP. However, this formulation remains non-convex and computationally intractable under practical constraints. To address this, we develop iterative anchor addition strategies that yield a tractable, albeit still non-convex, problem. By utilizing the structure of the resulting rank-1 updates, we create three heuristic approaches with different balances between performance and computational complexity. Furthermore, we establish upper and lower bounds for optimizing worst-case 3D and 2D positioning errors. These findings inform a unified iterative framework for robust anchor placement, alongside an analysis of the proposed methods' computational costs. Numerical experiments confirm the accuracy of our theoretical derivations, while extensive Monte-Carlo simulations evaluate the positioning error and execution time of each iterative scheme. These results highlight performance tradeoffs and offer critical design insights for localization systems operating beyond the convex hull.

Daily, 800 women and 6,700 newborns lose their lives due to pregnancy and childbirth complications, most of which could be prevented by well-trained midwives. By leveraging data science models and logs from online learning platforms for midwives, we can enhance their professional skills. This approach aims to utilize rich behavioral data to shift digital education toward personalized content and adaptive learning pathways. In this study, we assess various forecasting techniques to predict the future content preferences of app users, segmented by profession and geographic region.

AI and machine learning-driven decision-making systems are already deployed across diverse sectors such as finance, healthcare, law enforcement, and education. It is increasingly plausible to imagine a future where autonomous systems manage entire business operations and support large-scale infrastructure to address society's most complex challenges. However, issues of bias and discrimination are prevalent in human decision-making and often persist or are exacerbated in machine-driven contexts due to a lack of transparency, accountability, and fairness. To bridge this gap, we present a framework for *causal fairness analysis* designed to understand, model, and potentially resolve fairness issues in decision-making. Our core approach connects observed data disparities with the underlying, often unobserved, causal mechanisms that generate them, a challenge we term the Fundamental Problem of Causal Fairness Analysis (FPCFA). To address the FPCFA, we investigate the decomposition of fairness metrics and data variations, attributing these differences to specific structural mechanisms and population subgroups. This work culminates in the Fairness Map, the first systematic effort to organize and elucidate the relationships between various fairness criteria in existing literature. Furthermore, we identify the minimal causal assumptions required for causal fairness analysis and introduce a Fairness Cookbook, enabling data scientists to evaluate the presence of disparate impact and disparate treatment.

We present a successful navigation and docking control system for the John Deere Tango autonomous mower that relies solely on a single camera input. This vision-based approach is valuable due to its cost-effectiveness, simplicity in manufacturing, and elimination of the need for external sensors, distinguishing it from current systems that depend on integrated position sensors and GPS. Our solution integrates the state-of-the-art object detection model, You Only Look Once (YOLO), with a reinforcement learning (RL) framework, Double Deep Q-Networks (Double DQN). The object detection network identifies mower features and transmits this information to the RL network as a low-dimensional representation, facilitating rapid and robust training. Subsequently, the RL network learns the necessary navigation strategies to reach target locations within a custom simulation environment. Upon testing on physical mower hardware, the system achieves centimeter-level docking accuracy from arbitrary starting positions and orientations.

This study introduces a scalable framework for channel estimation and reflection optimization tailored to reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems. The proposed method initially constructs an offline training set comprising RIS reflection coefficient vectors. For each vector in this set, the scheme estimates solely the end-to-end composite channel and executes transmit power allocation. Consequently, RIS reflection optimization is streamlined by selecting the optimal vector from the pre-designed training set that maximizes the achievable rate. Unlike traditional methods, this approach flexibly adjusts training overhead based on channel coherence time. Furthermore, the paper evaluates the computational complexity and analyzes the theoretical scaling of the achievable rate relative to the number of training slots. Simulation results confirm that the proposed scheme outperforms existing techniques by reducing training overhead and complexity while enhancing rate performance, even under channel estimation errors.

Supervised learning models are increasingly employed to make critical decisions in domains like hiring, lending, and college admissions. However, these models often inherit biases from their training data, leading to discrimination against protected attributes such as race or gender. Beyond unfairness, the deployment of such models raises privacy risks by potentially exposing sensitive personal information. Among various privacy frameworks, differential privacy has gained significant traction. This study investigates the feasibility of employing a differentially private exponential mechanism as a post-processing technique to simultaneously enhance fairness and privacy in supervised learning. Distinct from prior research, we focus on a scenario where a model must select a fixed, limited number of candidates due to constrained positions, a setup applicable to job recruitment and university admissions. Utilizing "equal opportunity" as our fairness metric, we demonstrate that exponential mechanisms can achieve perfect fairness in the decision-making process. Furthermore, experiments on real-world datasets indicate that this approach improves both privacy and fairness, albeit with a minor reduction in accuracy compared to models without post-processing.

This study introduces a low-power, high-accuracy embedded algorithm for recognizing hand gestures, specifically designed for battery-operated wearable devices utilizing low-power short-range RADAR sensors. The approach integrates a 2D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) that processes range frequency Doppler features with a Temporal Convolutional Neural Network (TCN) to handle time sequence prediction. The resulting model is compact, comprising only 46,000 parameters and a memory footprint of 92 KB. Evaluation was conducted on two datasets featuring 11 challenging gestures performed by 26 individuals, totaling 20,210 instances. On this dataset, the system achieved 86.6% accuracy with 26 users and 92.4% with a single user, figures that rival state-of-the-art performance (87% for 10 users and 94% for a single user). Notably, this accuracy is attained using a TCN-based network that is 7,500 times smaller than existing state-of-the-art solutions. Additionally, the classifier was deployed on a Parallel Ultra-Low Power Processor, proving that real-time prediction is viable with just 21 mW for the full TCN sequence and a total system power consumption under 100 mW. All associated code and data are available open-source at tinyradar.ethz.ch.

Banking fraud results in billions of dollars in losses globally, making graph-based approaches essential for uncovering intricate transaction patterns and emerging fraud schemes. This study investigates graph patterns within a real-world transaction dataset by identifying and analyzing network motifs, with a specific emphasis on heterogeneous motifs given the nature of banking graphs. Furthermore, we introduce a new randomization method capable of generating valid synthetic banking graphs. Our exploratory analysis demonstrates that extracting these network motifs yields insightful and interpretable patterns.

The rise of large, irregular, and sparse relational datasets has spurred the development of new storage and analysis platforms designed to overcome the performance and functional limitations of traditional database technologies. These systems leverage graph structures and analytical methods to allow users to ingest, update, query, and compute on the topological relationships defined as edges connecting vertices. To handle Facebook-scale data, such platforms must support billions of edges, sustain update rates in the millions per second, and execute complex analytical kernels. Furthermore, they require intuitive interfaces that empower both graph experts and novice programmers to implement common graph algorithms. This paper investigates a range of graph analysis and storage platforms, comparing their capabilities, interfaces, and performance by executing a suite of real-world graph algorithms on synthetic datasets containing up to 256 million edges. In the interest of transparency, several authors involved in this study are affiliated with the development of STINGER.

Bayesian neural networks and deep ensembles are two contemporary methods for quantifying uncertainty in deep learning, yet they face significant scaling challenges due to memory inefficiency, as they necessitate storing parameters multiple times larger than deterministic models. To overcome this, we enhance the weight matrix of every layer by incorporating a minimal set of inducing weights, which projects uncertainty quantification into a low-dimensional space. Additionally, we adapt Matheron's conditional Gaussian sampling rule to facilitate rapid weight sampling, ensuring our inference method retains competitive runtime efficiency compared to ensembles. Crucially, our technique delivers performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods in both prediction and uncertainty estimation using fully connected networks and ResNets, while shrinking the parameter count to no more than 24.3% of that required by a single neural network.

Transactional stream processing (TSP) is rapidly gaining prominence. The primary objective of TSP is to establish a unified model that simultaneously delivers guarantees for both transactions and stream processing. Over the last ten years, significant work has led to the creation of various TSP systems, allowing for an analysis of their shared characteristics and distinctions. Nevertheless, a universally accepted standard for combining transactional capabilities with stream processing remains absent. Current TSP systems generally concentrate on a narrow range of application features, often necessitating complex design trade-offs. This survey first investigates diverse transaction models applicable to streams and TSP-specific transactional properties, followed by an analysis of how specific design choices impact system implementations. Next, we present representative scenarios where TSP is utilized and address several open challenges. The survey has two main goals: first, to offer insights into the varied requirements and techniques associated with TSP; and second, to stimulate the design and development of new TSP systems.

In recent years, Domain Adaptation (DA) has gained significant interest from deep learning researchers due to its ability to enhance test accuracy using out-of-distribution labeled data. However, most current state-of-the-art DA algorithms are computationally demanding and require extensive hyperparameter tuning because they rely on large batch sizes. To address these challenges, we introduce a rapid and straightforward DA approach comprising three phases: (1) domain alignment via covariance matching, (2) pseudo-labeling, and (3) ensembling. We term this method **PACE**, an acronym for **P**seudo-labels, **A**lignment of **C**ovariances, and **E**nsembles. PACE operates by training on fixed features extracted from an ensemble of modern pretrained backbones, eliminating the need to train a neural network. On most benchmark adaptation tasks, PACE surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods by **5–10%**. Furthermore, compared to existing DA techniques, it cuts training time and hyperparameter tuning time by **82%** and **97%**, respectively. The code is available at: https://github.com/Chris210634/PACE-Domain-Adaptation.

Soft robots are often modeled as low-dimensional systems, particularly when employing learning-based techniques, which restricts their ability to capture the vast array of deformation modes and interactions inherent to these devices. This paper introduces a deep-learning framework that constructs high-dimensional visual models of soft robots by integrating multimodal sensorimotor data. The approach utilizes end-to-end learning, eliminating the need for intermediate sensor processing or data grounding. We demonstrate the efficacy and benefits of this modeling strategy using a soft anthropomorphic finger equipped with embedded sensors. Furthermore, we illustrate how this method can be scaled to enable higher-level cognitive capabilities, such as self and environment identification, as well as object manipulation skills. Ultimately, this research advances the convergence of soft robotics and developmental robotics architectures, paving the way for next-generation intelligent soft robots.

Let $\mathcal{F}$ denote a hereditary collection of finite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$. This paper presents and characterizes $\mathcal{F}$-(almost) greedy bases. For a given family $\mathcal{F}$, a basis $(e_n)_n$ in a Banach space $X$ is defined as $\mathcal{F}$-greedy if there exists a constant $C\geqslant 1$ such that for every $x\in X$, $m \in \mathbb{N}$, and any greedy sum $G_m(x)$ of order $m$, the inequality $\|x - G_m(x)\|\ \leqslant\ C \inf\left\{\left\|x-\sum_{n\in
A}a_ne_n\right\|\,:\, |A|\leqslant m, A\in \mathcal{F}, (a_n)\subset
\mathbb{K}\right\}$ holds, where $\mathbb{K}$ represents the scalar field. By definition, every $\mathcal{F}$-greedy basis is quasi-greedy, positioning the concept of $\mathcal{F}$-greediness between that of greedy and quasi-greedy bases. We establish that a basis is $\mathcal{F}$-greedy if and only if it is $\mathcal{F}$-unconditional, $\mathcal{F}$-disjoint democratic, and quasi-greedy, thereby extending the classical characterization of greedy bases by Konyagin and Temlyakov. A corresponding characterization is also provided for $\mathcal{F}$-almost greedy bases. Additionally, we offer several examples of bases that exhibit nontrivial $\mathcal{F}$-greediness. Considering the Schreier family $\mathcal{S}_\alpha$ of order $\alpha$ for a countable ordinal $\alpha$, we demonstrate that for each $\alpha$, there exists a basis that is $\mathcal{S}_{\alpha}$-greedy yet fails to be $\mathcal{S}_{\alpha+1}$-greedy. Consequently, we prove that the following implications cannot be reversed for countable ordinals $\alpha < \beta$: $\mbox{quasi-greedy}\ \Longleftarrow\ \mathcal{S}_\alpha\mbox{-greedy}\ \Longleftarrow\ \mathcal{S}_\beta\mbox{-greedy}\ \Longleftarrow\ \mbox{greedy}$.

Legged robots equipped with manipulators can interact with and alter their surroundings. However, planners for these systems must account for how the contact forces produced by the manipulators influence overall stability. Existing approaches either treat these forces as fixed during the planning phase or fail to optimize them in real-time. This paper introduces STORMMAP (Stability and Task Oriented Receding-Horizon Motion and Manipulation Autonomous Planner), a method that generates continuous trajectories for both motion and manipulation forces to ensure dynamic stability and feasibility while prioritizing user-defined tasks. By solving a nonlinear optimization problem and assuming known contact locations (provided by a user or external algorithm), STORMMAP operates in real-time. Simulated experiments on a quadruped with a torso-mounted manipulator demonstrate its versatility. Unlike current state-of-the-art methods, STORMMAP produces continuous plans in under ten milliseconds, representing a tenfold speed improvement over previous strategies.

This study presents the initial Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) observations of the "extra-galactic" diffuse gamma-ray emission (EGB). Characterized by a generally isotropic or near-isotropic distribution across the sky, this emission component comprises various contributions noted in existing literature. The EGB was derived through comprehensive modeling of the bright foreground diffuse Galactic gamma-ray emission (DGE), identified LAT sources, and solar gamma-ray emission. Our results indicate that the EGB spectrum aligns with a power law, exhibiting a differential spectral index of g = 2.41 ± 0.05 and an intensity of I(> 100 MeV) = (1.03 ± 0.17) × 10^-5 cm^-2 s^-1 sr^-1, where uncertainties are primarily systematic in nature. Compared to spectra derived from EGRET data, our EGB spectrum is softer, less intense, and devoid of features.

Internal wave reflections generate shear that significantly influences sediment transport and resuspension in oceanic environments. Notably, the \textit{critical reflection} phenomenon can induce exceptionally high shear in the reflected waves. However, isolating the reflected wave from the incident wave is technically difficult because they share the same temporal frequency. This study presents experimental measurements of internal waves within a \textit{critical reflection} setup, analyzed using the 2D-VMD-prox decomposition method. We adapted this technique specifically for internal wave critical reflection, demonstrating enhanced performance compared to existing decomposition methods. By confidently isolating the reflected wave, we were able to compare our findings with viscous and non-linear models for critical reflection, which accurately describe how the shear rate at the boundary depends on experimental parameters.

This paper introduces generalized inverse operators, which play a significant role in operator theory, and establishes a Douglas-type factorization theorem for Hilbert pro-$C^{\ast}$-modules. We define atomic systems and $K$-frames within this context to investigate their interrelationship. Furthermore, we utilize the established factorization theorem to derive several properties of $K$-frames. Finally, we demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the sum of two $K$-frames in a Hilbert pro-$C^{\ast}$-module remains a $K$-frame.

Artificial neural networks have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in fault detection for the Tennessee Eastman process; however, their massive parameter count necessitates significant memory resources. To enable online real-time fault detection, three deep compression strategies—pruning, clustering, and quantization—were employed to alleviate computational demands. An extensive evaluation of seven distinct combinations of these techniques revealed that all approaches achieved compression rates exceeding 64% while sustaining high detection accuracy. The optimal configuration, which integrates all three methods, reduced model size by 91.5% while maintaining accuracy above 94%. Consequently, this approach minimizes storage needs in production settings and facilitates smoother real-world deployment.

We employ polarization-resolved resonant Raman spectroscopy to study optical transitions between spin-polarized bands in the quasi-two-dimensional Rashba system BiTeI. Our analysis identifies chiral excitations connecting states of opposite helicity and aligns experimental spectra with predictions from a three-band model. By examining the resonant Raman excitation profiles, we extract Rashba parameters and band gaps for higher conduction bands adjacent to the Fermi level, subsequently comparing these findings with results derived from ab initio density functional theory (DFT).

This Letter investigates the radial velocity variations of the chemically peculiar star Epsilon Ursae Majoris ($\epsilon$ UMa), specifically derived from the sharp cores of its hydrogen lines. The analysis utilizes ELODIE archival data collected at various stages of the star's rotational cycle. The observations reveal low-amplitude radial velocity fluctuations with a period of P=5.0887 d. A best-fit Keplerian model determines an eccentricity of e=0.503 and a minimum mass of approximately 13.7$M_{\rm Jup}$, assuming the star's rotational axis is perpendicular to the orbital plane. These findings indicate that the companion is a brown dwarf, characterized by a projected semi-amplitude of radial velocity $K_{\rm 2}$=135.9 km/sec and an inclination-scaled semi-major axis of $a_{2}$sin(i)=0.055 au.

Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) enable direct communication between electronic devices and the brain. While decoding tasks for medical applications often suffice with data from multiple neurons or local field potentials, neuroscience research requires the isolation of individual neuronal activity. However, as large-scale silicon technology and probe channel counts have grown, manually interpreting and labeling spikes has become increasingly impractical. This paper introduces a novel framework called the Adaptive Contrastive Learning Model, which derives spike representations through contrastive learning grounded in a maximizing mutual information loss function. Leveraging the principle that data sharing similar features share the same labels—regardless of whether the task is multi-class or binary—we decompose the multi-classification problem into several binary-classification tasks. This approach enhances both accuracy and computational efficiency. Additionally, we implement a series of spike enhancements to address classification inaccuracies caused by overlapping spikes.

Requirements frequently define anticipated system behavior through causal relationships, such as "If A, then B." Automatically identifying these relations facilitates key requirements engineering tasks, including the automatic generation of test cases and the detection of dependencies between requirements. Nevertheless, current tools struggle to extract causality from natural language with satisfactory performance. This paper introduces CiRA (Causality detection in Requirements Artifacts), marking an initial step toward automating the extraction of causal links from requirements. We evaluated CiRA using a publicly available dataset comprising 61 acceptance criteria (32 causal and 29 non-causal) that outline the functionality of the German Corona-Warn-App. Our approach achieved a macro F_1 score of 83%, demonstrating its feasibility.

This paper establishes a fundamental $p$-adic comparison theorem for smooth rigid analytic and dagger varieties defined over $C$, the algebraic closure of a $p$-adic field. It demonstrates that within a stable range, $p$-adic pro-\'etale cohomology corresponds to a filtered Frobenius eigenspace of de Rham cohomology (specifically over $\bf{B}^+_{\rm dR}$). The central calculation involves transitioning from absolute crystalline cohomology to Hyodo-Kato cohomology and constructing the associated Hyodo-Kato isomorphism. Furthermore, the authors "geometrize" the comparison theorem by formulating $p$-adic pro-\'etale and syntomic cohomologies as sheaves on ${\rm Perf}_C$, the category of perfectoid spaces over $C$; this geometric perspective is essential for proving the $C_{\rm st}$-conjecture in the subsequent work.

This note introduces a technique for minimizing discretization errors encountered when solving Quantum Field Theory on a hypercubic lattice within both position and momentum spaces. By leveraging artifacts that disrupt rotational symmetry, the method recovers rotationally invariant results for two-point Green functions. We demonstrate that combining findings from position and momentum spaces can effectively identify rotationally invariant artifacts through their approximate Fourier transforms in the continuum. The approach is first illustrated using a Klein-Gordon propagator, followed by a direct application to the gluon propagator in quenched lattice QCD.

Let $B_1$ denote the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^N$ where $N \geq 2$. Consider a function $f \in C^1([0, \infty), \mathbb{R})$ satisfying $f(0)=0$, $f(\beta) = \beta$, $f(s)<s$ for $s\in (0,\beta)$, $f(s)>s$ for $s\in (\beta, \infty)$, and $f'(\beta)>\lambda^{r}_k$. D. Bonheure, B. Noris, and T. Weth [Ann. Inst. H. Poincaré Anal. Non Linéaire 29(4) (2012)] established the existence of nondecreasing, radial, positive solutions to the semilinear Neumann problem $-\Delta u+u=f(u)$ in $B_1$ with $\partial_\nu u=0$ on $\partial B_1$ for the case $k=2$. They further conjectured that a radial solution possessing exactly $k$ intersections with $\beta$ exists whenever $f'(\beta) >\lambda^r_k$ for $k>2$. This paper confirms that this conjecture holds true.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are known to be susceptible to adversarial attacks, a concern that has recently intensified regarding 3D point clouds. Despite growing interest in this area, existing methods for generating adversarial point clouds suffer from poor transferability and are easily countered by defenses. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces AOF, a novel attack strategy that emphasizes the low-frequency components of point clouds. By integrating losses derived from both the original point cloud and its low-frequency representation, AOF crafts adversarial samples that demonstrate significantly improved transferability compared to state-of-the-art (SOTA) attacks and exhibit greater resilience against current 3D defense mechanisms. Furthermore, unlike clean point clouds, the adversarial samples generated by AOF contain more significant deformation than typical outliers.

While Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at solving real-world problems, their high computational demands often prevent deployment on edge devices. Pruning, which introduces zeros into model weights, offers a valuable balance between accuracy and efficiency, making it a standard technique for model compression. However, the choice of pruning granularity presents a significant trade-off: at identical sparsity levels, coarse-grained structured sparsity performs better on traditional hardware but sacrifices accuracy, whereas fine-grained unstructured sparsity improves accuracy but struggles with hardware efficiency.

Conversely, modern processors now feature fast on-chip scratchpad memories and dedicated gather/scatter engines capable of performing indirect memory operations. This work introduces a new set of sparse patterns, termed Gather-Scatter (GS) patterns, designed to leverage these hardware features to accelerate neural network inference. Accompanying these patterns is a compact sparse format. Together with a novel pruning methodology, the GS patterns resolve load imbalance issues, yielding models that nearly match the accuracy of unstructured sparse models while approaching the computational efficiency of structured ones. Experimental results demonstrate that GS patterns consistently outperform conventional structured sparse patterns in balancing accuracy and efficiency, reducing DNN component runtime by two to three times without compromising accuracy. This improvement was validated across three distinct deep learning tasks using popular models: GNMT for machine translation, ResNet50 for image recognition, and Jasper for acoustic speech recognition.

Recently, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) for semantic segmentation has gained significant interest due to its potential benefits in label-scarce real-world applications, such as autonomous driving, robotics, and medical imaging. Although substantial progress has been made, existing research primarily addresses single-source single-target setups, failing to accommodate more practical scenarios involving multiple or even unseen targets. This paper explores open compound domain adaptation (OCDA) for semantic segmentation, which simultaneously handles mixed and novel target situations. We introduce a new framework built upon three core principles: discover, hallucinate, and adapt. Initially, the method clusters compound target data by style to uncover multiple latent domains (discover). Subsequently, it employs image translation to hallucinate corresponding latent target domains within the source data (hallucinate), ensuring a pairing between source and target latent domains. Finally, the model learns target-to-source alignment independently across these domains (adapt). Fundamentally, our approach transforms the challenging OCDA problem into a series of simpler multiple UDA tasks. Evaluations on the standard GTA-to-Cityscapes benchmark demonstrate that our method achieves new state-of-the-art results.

This paper details the integration of binary and ternary neural networks into the hls4ml library, a tool engineered to automatically transform deep learning models into digital circuits for FPGA deployment. Beginning with benchmark models trained in floating-point precision, we explore various techniques to minimize resource usage by lowering numerical precision to binary or ternary levels. We analyze the trade-offs between model accuracy and resource efficiency, demonstrating how to optimize the balance between latency and accuracy by maintaining full precision on specific network components. As case studies, we examine two multiclass classification problems: handwritten digit recognition using the MNIST dataset and jet identification from simulated proton-proton collisions at the CERN Large Hadron Collider. The results indicate that binary and ternary implementations achieve performance comparable to higher-precision counterparts while significantly reducing FPGA resource consumption.

Standard contrastive learning typically applies $\ell_{2}$ normalization to extracted features, yet this approach often fails in domain adaptation tasks. The primary limitation is that class weights—parameters of the final fully connected layer—are excluded from the optimization process, preventing the generated features from clustering around the source data's learned class weights. To address this, we introduce Probabilistic Contrastive Learning (PCL), a concise yet effective method that yields compact features while explicitly aligning them with class weights. Specifically, PCL diverges from the traditional feature-plus-$\ell_{2}$ normalization paradigm by substituting features with probabilities and eliminating normalization. This shift compels the probabilities to approximate a one-hot distribution, effectively minimizing the distance between features and class weights. Due to its simplicity and versatility, PCL is applicable across various tasks. We evaluated our method extensively across five domains: unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), semi-supervised domain adaptation (SSDA), semi-supervised learning (SSL), UDA detection, and UDA semantic segmentation. Experimental results indicate that PCL delivers substantial performance improvements. Notably, in segmentation tasks, PCL achieves or exceeds the performance of CPSL-D with reduced computational costs (1×3090 GPU for 5 days versus 4×V100 GPUs for 11 days). The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/ljjcoder/Probabilistic-Contrastive-Learning.

In 2015, the system CaMn$_{2}$Al$_{10}$ was discovered and hypothesized to be an itinerant magnet; we have since applied the robust self-consistent renormalization (SCR) theory of spin fluctuations to this material. Our calculations of the inverse static (paramagnetic) susceptibility show excellent agreement with experimental data (Phys. Rev. B 92, 020413, 2015). Additionally, we computed spin fluctuations across various temperatures and determined the electronic correlation strength within the Hubbard Hamiltonian to be $I=0.3136$ eV. The quantitative alignment of our SCR-based analysis of the inverse susceptibility data leads to the definitive conclusion that CaMn$_{2}$Al$_{10}$ indeed exhibits itinerant magnetism. Furthermore, our DFT and DFT+U results support the critical role of strong Mn-Al hybridization in driving this magnetic behavior. The estimated correlation strength established here serves as a basis for future investigations into itinerant magnetism within this system.

Federated learning enables mobile devices to collaboratively train a global model without transmitting private data to a central server. While significant research has focused on the performance guarantees of the global model, the specific impact of individual clients on the collaborative training process remains unclear. To address this, we introduce a new concept termed {\em Fed-Influence} to quantify this impact on model parameters, alongside an efficient algorithm for its estimation. Our approach offers several key advantages: (1) it avoids the need for retraining or retracing, imposing only linear computational costs on both clients and the server; (2) it adheres strictly to federated learning principles by ensuring no client's local private data is exposed; and (3) it performs effectively on both convex and non-convex loss functions without requiring the final model to be optimal. Experiments on synthetic data and the FEMNIST dataset demonstrate that our estimation method approximates Fed-Influence with minimal bias. Additionally, we illustrate a practical application of Fed-Influence in model debugging.

Over the last ten years, research into multi-scale structure formation within the cold interstellar medium has expanded rapidly, driven by both theoretical advancements and observational breakthroughs. High-resolution spectral line observations at (sub-)millimeter wavelengths have offered critical insights into the kinematics of dense gas in star-forming regions, supported by extensive dust continuum surveys mapping the column density of molecular clouds and polarization data revealing the influence of magnetic fields. These efforts are matched by increasingly complex numerical simulations that incorporate new physical processes—such as supernova feedback, cosmic rays, non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics, and radiation pressure—alongside advanced techniques like zoom-in simulations for multi-scale analysis. Collectively, these new datasets underscore the anisotropic growth of dense structures across all scales, ranging from giant ISM bubbles driven by stellar feedback (50–100 pc) down to molecular filaments (pc scales), dense cores (< 0.1 pc), and protostellar disks (< 1000 au). By integrating observational data with theoretical models, we construct a unified framework for the formation and evolution of these structures, outlining a comprehensive physical scenario for the initial conditions and early phases of star and disk formation.

Adapting the Modulation and Coding Scheme (MCS) in Cellular Vehicle-To-Everything (C-V2X) sidelinks offers significant potential for applications such as congestion management, handling variable packet sizes, density-aware rate adjustment, and enhanced unicast support. Nevertheless, implementing MCS adaptation introduces complex implications for C-V2X radio resources, bandwidth usage, power level calculations, and scheduling operations. This paper introduces the first detailed analysis and implemented model examining how MCS adaptation affects the Sensing-Based Semi-Persistent Scheduling (SB-SPS) mechanism in C-V2X sidelinks. Specifically, the study analyzes the performance of MCS adaptation for distributed congestion control across various vehicular densities. The findings suggest that while MCS adaptation can alleviate channel congestion by lowering resource occupation, it does not necessarily enhance the overall packet delivery rate unless subchannel usage is also reduced. Ultimately, this research establishes a foundation for further exploring MCS adaptation applications within the C-V2X sidelink framework.

Quantum mechanics establishes that particles correspond to wave functions, where the likelihood of detecting a particle at a future position is proportional to the square of its wave function's amplitude. While this statistical link is well-defined, its interpretation remains contentious, dividing physicists between the traditional Copenhagen view and variations of de Broglie-Bohm pilot wave theories. Recent experiments involving Hydrodynamic Quantum Analogs (HQAs) reveal that fluid droplets can enter stable dynamical states where their interaction with self-generated ripples mimics the motion predicted by pilot wave guiding equations. Consequently, many effects once considered uniquely quantum now appear as emergent phenomena in these macroscopic systems. This has inspired an investigation into whether quantum mechanics itself arises from fluid dynamics on a genuine quantum-scale fluid. We demonstrate that if such a fluid exists with HQA-like dynamics, it must be a superfluid operating on the surface of a 4-dimensional hypersphere. Furthermore, under cosmological inflation, we show that these bouncing droplets would exhibit an apparent rest mass, while principles including inertia, momentum, mass-energy equivalence, general relativity, the uncertainty principle, and the emergence of a time-like dimension can all be derived as purely emergent results of this fluid's dynamics. Therefore, we argue that this model warrants serious consideration as a potential foundation for a unified theory of physics across all scales.

The introduction of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for handwriting recognition represented a major breakthrough, achieving high accuracy despite significant variations in writing styles. While sequential architectures are well-suited for modeling text lines due to their temporal nature and ability to learn character and word sequence distributions, they incur training costs because their linear pipelines hinder parallelization. This paper presents a non-recurrent solution using transformer models to recognize handwritten text. We propose a novel method that eliminates recurrence entirely, employing multi-head self-attention layers at both visual and textual stages to handle character recognition and capture language dependencies within decoded sequences. Our model operates without constraints on a predefined vocabulary, enabling the recognition of out-of-vocabulary words. We significantly outperform previous methods, demonstrating that satisfactory recognition accuracy is achievable even in few-shot learning scenarios.

Fluid Antenna Systems (FAS) represent an emerging technology capable of delivering substantial diversity gains within compact environments. Driven by the transformative potential of liquid antennas, researchers in wireless communications are exploring a system where a solitary antenna moves freely along a short linear trajectory to capture the strongest incoming signal. Unlike traditional setups, FAS element spacing does not strictly adhere to the half-wavelength separation rule. While prior studies simplified FAS channel parameters to derive single-integral expressions for outage probability and performance insights, these models may fail to accurately reflect port correlations described by Jake's model. This study advances the state of the art by accurately approximating the FAS channel while preserving analytical tractability through a two-stage process. The first stage significantly reduces the complexity of multi-fold integrals in the outage probability formula, and the second stage yields a single-integral representation of the FAS outage probability. Additionally, the performance of this innovative technology is examined under a more realistic correlation model. Numerical results confirm the validity of the proposed channel approximations and indicate a modest performance improvement under practical assumptions. Furthermore, this work paves the way for future research into scenarios where FAS outperforms conventional multiple-antenna solutions.

We examine the electromagnetic and gravitational waves produced when a white dwarf star is tidally stripped while orbiting a black hole. Using the quantum hydrodynamic equations, we model the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet to simulate the binary system's evolution. During periastron passage, the white dwarf sheds a small amount of mass; this material falling into the black hole generates intense electromagnetic and gravitational radiation. Each periastron passage triggers bursts of ultraluminous radiation, a phenomenon resembling the recurrent X-ray flares recently identified by Irwin et al. Gravitational energy bursts are primarily emitted at very low frequencies. Additionally, the accretion disc formed from the stripped white dwarf material eventually begins to contribute continuously to both electromagnetic and gravitational radiation.

Until recently, measuring the neutral atomic gas in individual galaxies at vast cosmological distances was challenging due to the faintness of the hyperfine HI 21-cm transition. This study estimates the HI gas mass for a sample of main-sequence star-forming galaxies at redshifts $z\sim 6.5 - 7.8$, selected via [CII]$-158\mu$m emission within the Reionization Era Bright Emission Line Survey (REBELS), utilizing a recent calibration of the [CII]-to-HI conversion factor. Our results indicate that HI gas mass excess rises with redshift, averaging $M_{\rm HI} / M_\star \approx 10$, which corresponds to HI mass fractions of $f_{\rm HI} = 90\%$ at $z\approx 7$. Using the [CII]-$158\mu$m luminosity function from this sample, we constrain the cosmic HI gas mass density in galaxies ($\rho_{\rm HI}$) at this epoch, measuring it as $\rho_{\rm HI} = 7.1^{+6.4}_{-3.0} \times 10^{6}\,M_{\odot}\,{\rm Mpc^{-3}}$. This value is approximately ten times lower than estimates derived from extrapolating damped Lyman-$\alpha$ absorber (DLA) data and relies heavily on the adopted [CII] luminosity function. Nevertheless, this reduction in $\rho_{\rm HI}$ aligns with recent simulations; we argue the discrepancy likely stems from DLA sightlines primarily sampling the significant HI reservoirs in high-$z$ galactic halos, while [CII] traces HI within the star-forming interstellar medium. We project this evolution of neutral gas, noting that at $z\gtrsim 5$, only about $10\%$ of the cosmic HI gas is contained within galaxies and linked to the star-forming ISM.

Ranking tasks that rely on pairwise comparisons, particularly in online gaming, frequently deal with extensive item pools where performance gaps between items are substantial. In such scenarios, winning probabilities for the strongest and weakest items may approach zero or one, and comparisons are often limited to subsets, meaning not all pairs are observed. This paper evaluates the Bradley-Terry-Luce model for ranking under more realistic conditions than previously studied. Specifically, we account for near-degenerate winning probabilities and arbitrary comparison designs. We derive new findings regarding the existence of the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) and the associated $\ell_2$ estimation error, removing the standard assumption of bounded winning probabilities and accommodating any graph topology. Our methodology centers on using the Fisher information matrix to analyze how graph structures and winning probability values influence estimation risk and MLE existence conditions. While our bounds encompass existing results as special cases, they offer broader applicability.

Developing cost-efficient and efficient photocatalytic materials capable of driving water splitting under visible light remains a paramount challenge in contemporary environmental materials science. Although numerous photocatalysts exist for green hydrogen production, systematic and rational strategies to engineer their optoelectronic properties for optimal performance are still lacking. Piezoelectric materials offer a promising avenue by modulating their band gaps and alignments in response to mechanical stimuli, enabling precise catalyst design. Nevertheless, piezo-photocatalysts remain scarce and have received limited attention. This study introduces a high-throughput screening of approximately 1,000 bulk piezoelectrics, utilizing a straightforward electrostatic model combined with first-principles calculations. The analysis theoretically identifies roughly 10 previously neglected binary and tertiary bulk compounds as highly promising piezo-photocatalysts, attributed to their favorable optoelectronic characteristics and exceptional tunability of band alignment through uniaxial strain.

Three-body semileptonic tau decays provide a pathway to investigate light hadronic systems and CP symmetry violations via electric dipole moment searches. In electroweak physics, the hadronic components of final states have historically been characterized using form factors. However, spectroscopic details, categorized by orbital angular momentum quantum numbers, are most effectively obtained through an explicit decomposition of the hadronic current within an orbital angular momentum basis. Driven by anticipated large datasets from B factories, we offer a complete description of hadronic currents decomposed into the quantum numbers of the hadronic final state using the isobar model. We provide formulas for orbital angular momenta up to three and utilize rules derived from hadron spectroscopy to construct decay chains for arbitrary-mass hadronic three-body systems. Furthermore, we translate this formalism into the language of form factors, addressing inadequacies identified in prior analyses of three-body hadronic final states.

Research into low-redshift galaxy clusters indicates that the intra-cluster medium (ICM) underwent non-gravitational heating during cluster formation. By employing simple phenomenological heating models, we simulated the impact of this preheating on the nascent ICM within galaxy proto-clusters and investigated its influence on Lyman-$\alpha$ (Ly$\alpha$) forest tomographic maps. Our analysis utilized a series of cosmological zoom-in simulations of proto-clusters, examining the relationship between Ly$\alpha$ transmission and the dark matter (DM) density distribution. We found that greater energy injection into the proto-ICM at $z$ = 3 results in a high-DM density distribution that shifts toward higher Ly$\alpha$ transmission. This finding was validated using both low-resolution simulations with an entropy floor preheating scheme and higher-resolution simulations utilizing an energy floor scheme. Additionally, we demonstrated that the evolution of this distribution's slope varies with redshift. The methodology presented here can be applied to existing and future Ly$\alpha$ forest tomographic survey data to better constrain feedback models in galaxy proto-clusters.

Bipolar disorder is a mental health condition characterized by mood fluctuations spanning from depression to mania. Typically, diagnosis relies on patient interviews and caregiver reports, often depending on the clinician's expertise, which can lead to misdiagnosis with other conditions. Automated diagnostic tools can offer quantitative metrics and facilitate extended patient monitoring. Additionally, the demand for remote diagnosis and treatment surged during the COVID-19 pandemic. This thesis presents a multimodal decision system utilizing acoustic, linguistic, and visual data from patient recordings, trained on the Bipolar Disorder corpus. The study conducts a thorough evaluation of unimodal and multimodal approaches, including various fusion techniques. While analyzing entire sessions with unimodal features, the research also investigates task-level performance on video clips. By integrating acoustic, linguistic, and visual features through multimodal fusion, the system achieved a 64.8% unweighted average recall score, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art results on this dataset.
