This study details the observation and analysis of newly identified coherent structures within the L1688 region of Ophiuchus and the B18 region of Taurus. Utilizing data from the Green Bank Ammonia Survey (GAS), we pinpointed areas characterized by high density and nearly constant, almost-thermal velocity dispersion. This analysis revealed eighteen distinct coherent structures—twelve in L1688 and six in B18—each exhibiting a sharp transition to coherence in velocity dispersion near their peripheries. These findings offer a valuable opportunity for the statistical study of coherent structures in molecular clouds. The identified structures, which we term "droplets," typically possess a radius of 0.04 parsecs and a mass of 0.4 solar masses, generally being smaller than the coherent cores previously documented by Goodman et al. (1998), Caselli et al. (2002), and Pineda et al. (2010). Unlike earlier coherent cores, these droplets are not virially bound by self-gravity but are primarily confined by ambient pressure. Their density profiles are shallower than those of a critical Bonnor-Ebert sphere, and their velocity (VLSR) distributions align with dense gas motions traced by NH3 emission. These characteristics suggest a formation mechanism driven by pressure compression and turbulent processes within the dense gas. Furthermore, we compare these findings with magnetohydrodynamic simulations of star-forming regions and speculate on the relationship between droplets and larger, gravitationally bound coherent cores, as well as the role these structures play in the star formation process.

Utilizing atom-in-jellium calculations to determine the Einstein frequency and equation of state, we predicted how the shear modulus varies from zero pressure up to approximately $10^7$ g/cm$^3$ for various elements pertinent to white dwarf stars and other self-gravitating systems. This study represents the broadest range of reported electronic structure calculations for shear modulus, covering conditions from ambient environments through one-component plasma to extreme relativistic regimes. Our predictions relied on a relationship between Debye temperature and shear modulus, which we estimate to be accurate within the order of 10%, marking the inaugural application of atom-in-jellium theory for this purpose. We evaluated the method's overall accuracy by contrasting our results with experimental data and more detailed electronic structure calculations conducted at lower pressures.

Transition-edge sensors (TESs) serve as highly sensitive thermometers within microcalorimeters designed to detect various wavelengths. Specifically, in soft X-ray astrophysics, achieving the high resolution required by scientific objectives relies on TESs paired with appropriate absorbers. Many applications also demand a large number of pixels, necessitating multiplexing during the readout phase. Frequency Domain Multiplexing (FDM) is a prevalent method and serves as the baseline for the ATHENA mission; however, this technique requires biasing the TES with an AC signal at MHz frequencies. Recent reports indicate that performance degrades under AC bias compared to DC bias. Consequently, to evaluate TES suitability for FDM, it is crucial to compare the performance of the same device under both AC and DC conditions. This comparison necessitates two distinct measurement setups with different characterization procedures. This work presents preliminary results from characterizing a single pixel TiAu TES first under AC bias and subsequently under DC bias across various facilities. The study compares the extraction of dynamical parameters and noise performance in both configurations as an initial step toward a broader AC/DC comparison of these devices.

We introduce novel approaches for refining polygonal grids by leveraging Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Our findings demonstrate that CNNs effectively identify the "shape" of polygonal elements, enabling the development of tailored refinement criteria for adaptive strategies. We present two such strategies that utilize CNN-based shape classification at minimal computational expense. These methods were evaluated using two families of finite element techniques capable of handling arbitrarily shaped polygons: Polygonal Discontinuous Galerkin (PolyDG) methods and Virtual Element Methods (VEMs). The results indicate that our algorithms significantly enhance discretization schemes, improving both accuracy and grid quality. Furthermore, because the training phase occurs offline and is independent of the specific differential model, the overall computational costs remain low.

Given the constraints of limited battery life and computing power inherent to individual unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), processing demanding deep learning tasks like convolutional operations is challenging. UAV-based networked airborne computing (NAC) offers a viable solution by enabling resource sharing through inter-UAV links, allowing collaborative execution of intensive computations. This study examines vector convolution within the NAC framework and introduces a new privacy-aware dynamic coded convolution strategy. This approach is designed to accommodate specific NAC characteristics, such as node heterogeneity, fluctuating network topologies, and variable communication and computational resources. Simulation outcomes demonstrate the strategy's high efficiency and robustness against uncertain stragglers.

**Context:** Regarding the solar coronal heating problem, magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) waves are a proposed source of the high temperatures observed in the corona. Energy transfer via these waves may occur through the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability (KHI) developing within coronal loops. **Aims:** This study investigates whether standing slow waves in solar atmospheric features—including coronal loops, prominence threads, sunspots, and pores—can induce KHI by creating oscillating shear flows at the structure's boundaries. **Methods:** We developed an analytical model using linearized nonstationary MHD within a Cartesian frame. This model represents a compressible plasma adjacent to a discontinuous interface between two homogeneous regions, where each region contains an oscillating velocity field with constant amplitude parallel to the background magnetic field and the interface. We then applied the analytical results to assess the interface's stability under both coronal and photospheric conditions. **Results:** Our findings indicate that interface stability is governed by a Mathieu equation, allowing for either stable or unstable outcomes depending on the equation's parameters. Under both coronal and photospheric conditions, the interface remains stable against KHI. While a parametric resonance instability is theoretically possible, it appears physically improbable. **Conclusion:** Consequently, in this simplified framework, standing slow waves alone cannot trigger the KHI without the contribution of additional physical processes.

Creating scalable quantum network nodes faces a significant hurdle in efficiently engineering and characterizing the coupling between cavities and emitters. Traditional *ex-situ* defect creation hinders real-time monitoring, while existing *in-situ* techniques either necessitate additional processing to enhance emitter quality or are restricted to bulk substrates. We present a method for directly laser-writing spin defects integrated into cavities using a nanosecond-pulsed laser operating above the bandgap. In 4H-silicon carbide, photonic crystal cavities function as nanoscopes to track the formation of silicon monovacancy ($V_{Si}^-$) defects within a $100~\text{nm}^3$ mode volume. Our observations reveal defect spin resonance, cavity-integrated photoluminescence, and excited-state lifetimes that align with standard formation protocols, all achieved without subsequent thermal annealing. Furthermore, we note an exponential decrease in excited-state lifetime as laser fluence nears the cavity amorphization limit and demonstrate single-shot local annealing of intrinsic background defects at the sites of $V_{Si}^-$ creation. This real-time, localized *in-situ* defect fabrication, combined with the verification of cavity-integrated defect spins, represents a pivotal advancement in optimizing cavity-emitter coupling for quantum networking.

This paper presents an optimization framework for designing proper scoring rules. The scenario involves a principal seeking an agent's forecast regarding an unknown state, where the agent may choose to report their prior belief or acquire a costly signal to report a posterior belief. With a defined set of potential posterior distributions, the principal aims to construct a bounded scoring rule that maximizes the agent's worst-case increase in payoff from reporting a posterior rather than a prior. The study examines two distinct scenarios: static and asymptotic. In the static case, where the agent accesses a single signal, an efficient algorithm is proposed to determine the optimal scoring rule for finite distribution sets. In the asymptotic case, the agent can indefinitely and adaptively refine their predictions. For a sequence of posterior distributions with vanishing covariance, representing general estimators with large samples, the quadratic scoring rule is proven optimal. Furthermore, when the posterior follows a Beta-Bernoulli process, the log scoring rule emerges as optimal. Additionally, the optimality of the log scoring rule is demonstrated over a restricted set of functions for categorical distributions utilizing Dirichlet priors.

Mobile applications frequently encounter failures, yet developers typically prioritize issues that negatively impact the user experience. While current methods mine extensive logs to identify technical failures, there is, to our knowledge, no existing approach specifically designed to detect whether a user has actually perceived a failure. This paper introduces a novel method for identifying user-perceived failures in mobile apps. By utilizing frontend user traces, our approach constructs an app page model and employs an unsupervised detection algorithm to determine if a failure has been noticed by the user. The core insight driving this algorithm is that when a user perceives a failure on a specific page, they tend to backtrack and revisit that page to retry the action. Preliminary evaluation results indicate that our approach achieves strong detection performance using a dataset gathered from real-world users.

This study presents a search for $W'$-boson production in the $W' \rightarrow t\bar{b} \rightarrow q\bar{q}' b\bar{b}$ decay channel, utilizing 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of 13 TeV proton-proton collision data recorded by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider during 2015 and 2016. The analysis interprets the results for both left-handed and right-handed chiral $W'$ bosons across a mass spectrum of 1 to 5 TeV. Hadronically decaying top quarks are identified using jet substructure tagging methods derived from a shower deconstruction algorithm. No significant discrepancy from Standard Model predictions was found; consequently, upper limits on the $W' \rightarrow t\bar{b}$ production cross-section times branching ratio were established as a function of the $W'$-boson mass. These findings exclude $W'$ bosons with right-handed couplings below 3.0 TeV and those with left-handed couplings below 2.9 TeV at the 95% confidence level.

In a nanocomposite composed of reduced graphene oxide (RGO) and BiFeO$_3$ (BFO), room-temperature measurements on a pristine sample reveal that remanent ferroelectric polarization exhibits a nonmonotonic dependence on magnetic fields ranging from 0 to 20 kOe. This polarization was quantified through both direct electrical testing of nanoparticle assemblies and powder neutron diffraction patterns collected under varying fields up to 20 kOe. Approximately 20 nm BFO nanoparticles are anchored to RGO sheets via Fe-C bonds, which simultaneously enhances the covalency of Fe-O bonds. The observed nonmonotonic polarization behavior is attributed to a field-dependent competition between positive and negative magnetoelectric coupling mechanisms; these arise from magnetostriction driven by interface and bulk magnetization, respectively. Furthermore, the formation of Fe-C bonds alters the magnetic and electronic structure at the interface, significantly influencing the coupling between ferroelectric and magnetic properties. This interface reconstruction offers a novel approach for tuning magnetoelectric characteristics in graphene-based multiferroic heterostructures.

This study examines the two-dimensional dynamics of a self-propelled, asymmetric bent rod. Utilizing slender body theory alongside the Lorentz reciprocal theorem, we calculate particle trajectories across various geometric arrangements and surface activity profiles. Our findings demonstrate that all resulting trajectories conform mathematically to circular paths. The particle's rotational velocity governs the frequency of this circular motion, whereas the ratio of translational to rotational speeds determines the trajectory's radius. We establish that geometric asymmetry alone is sufficient to generate self-propulsion, even in the absence of non-uniform surface activity. Specifically, under uniform surface conditions, we observe that (i) equal arm lengths result in pure translation, and (ii) maximum rotational and translational speeds occur when one arm is roughly four times the length of the other and the inter-arm angle is approximately $\pi/2$. We attribute these trends to the geometry's influence on the hydrodynamic resistance tensor and active driving forces. Ultimately, these results quantify self-propulsion in composite slender bodies and encourage further investigation into highly asymmetric self-propelled particles.

Jimenez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced a family of "symmetric Tversky ratio models" denoted as $S_{\alpha,\beta}$, where $0\le\alpha\le 1$ and $\beta>0$. The function $D_{\alpha,\beta}=1-S_{\alpha,\beta}$ constitutes a semimetric on the powerset of any finite set. We demonstrate that $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ qualifies as a metric if and only if $0\le\alpha \le \frac12$ and $\beta\ge 1/(1-\alpha)$, a finding formally verified within the Lean proof assistant. The boundaries of this parameterized metric space correspond to $J_1=D_{1/2,2}$, known as the Jaccard distance, and $J_{\infty}=D_{0,1}$, which serves as an analogue to the normalized information distance proposed by Li, Chen, Li, Ma, and Vitányi (2004).

The 3D ternary Li$_2$GeO$_3$ compound, a potential electrolyte for Li+-based batteries, displays unique characteristics in its lattice symmetry (orthorhombic), band structure, charge density, and density of states. These fundamental properties have been thoroughly examined using first-principles calculations. Detailed analysis reveals that the atom-dominated electronic energy spectrum, space-charge distribution, and atom-/orbital-projected density of states adequately identify critical multi-orbital hybridizations within the chemical bonds: specifically, 2s-(2p$_x$, 2p$_y$, 2p$_z$) and (4s, 4p$_x$, 4p$_y$, 4p$_z$)-(2s, 2p$_x$, 2p$_y$, 2p$_z$) for Li-O and Ge-O interactions, respectively. The system features a large indirect band gap of Eg = 3.77 eV and contains numerous significant covalent bonds characterized by notable non-uniformity and anisotropy. Furthermore, spin-dependent magnetic configurations are entirely absent. This theoretical approach can be extended to explore key attributes of anode and cathode materials associated with lithium oxide compounds.

This study investigates the dynamics and stability of charged solitons in trans-polyacetylene (tPA), specifically re-examining their stability when subjected to an external electric field aligned with the polymer chain. Employing the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) formalism, we solve the coupled equations for electrons and classical nuclei at the mean-field level, focusing on the low-field regime ($E$) where soliton motion is adiabatic. By analyzing observable quantities in both real and frequency spaces, we pinpoint the microscopic mechanisms that induce dynamical instabilities. Furthermore, we propose a new quantitative metric for assessing soliton stability, addressing a question previously left unresolved. Beyond its fundamental significance, this research holds potential relevance for designing novel organic electronic devices that rely on soliton-mediated transport.

Pyroptosis, an inflammatory form of cell death, plays a significant role in the cytokine storm observed in severe COVID-19 cases. This process is driven by the NLRP3 inflammasome, which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2. Certain anti-inflammatory medications have the potential to suppress inflammasome assembly and, consequently, pyroptosis. This study introduces a single-cell mathematical model, structured as a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs), to simulate NLRP3 inflammasome formation, pyroptotic death, and the impact of interventions that block inflammasome development. Our findings indicate that anti-inflammatory drugs can postpone inflammasome formation, potentially shifting cell death from the inflammatory pyroptosis pathway to non-inflammatory modes like apoptosis. In partnership with a multidisciplinary group studying within-host COVID-19 dynamics, this model is being integrated into the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator. This paper offers an overview of that simulator and emphasizes the cellular-level effects of pyroptosis.

Sticky diffusion processes spend a finite duration (and finite mean duration) on a lower-dimensional boundary. Upon reaching this boundary, the process resumes after a random interval, during which it may follow dynamics distinct from those in the interior. These behaviors can be defined by a time-derivative within the boundary condition of the governing equation. By employing time changes derived from right-inverses of appropriate processes, we characterize fractional sticky conditions and their corresponding boundary behaviors. Our findings indicate that fractional boundary value problems, specifically those involving fractional dynamic boundary conditions, result in sticky diffusions that spend finite time (but infinite mean time) on a lower-dimensional boundary. This phenomenon can be interpreted as a trap effect from a macroscopic perspective.

3D neural networks have gained widespread adoption across numerous 3D vision applications, such as object detection, segmentation, registration, and other perception tasks involving 3D inputs. However, research has predominantly focused on developing custom 3D operators or network architectures to address the sparsity and irregularity of 3D data, often neglecting network size and parameter efficiency. This study presents the first comprehensive investigation into the weight sparsity of spatially sparse 3D convolutional networks, introducing a compact model termed WS³-Convnet designed for semantic and instance segmentation on real-world indoor and outdoor datasets. By applying various network pruning techniques, we demonstrate that WS³-Convnet achieves a minimal performance degradation of only 2.15% while reducing the parameter count by 99% and computational costs by 95%. Furthermore, we systematically analyze the compression patterns within WS³-Convnet, revealing consistent sparsity structures that enable a 45% acceleration in inference speed.

\keywords{Efficient network architecture, Network pruning, 3D scene segmentation, Spatially sparse convolution}

Missing data presents a significant challenge in data science. This paper reviews imputation conventions within Automunge, an open-source Python platform for tabular data preprocessing, specifically highlighting "ML infill," where auto ML models are trained on partitioned training subsets to estimate target features. Validation experiments benchmarked these scenarios against downstream model performance, revealing that ML infill frequently surpassed other methods for both numeric and categorical targets, or at worst performed within the noise range of alternatives. Additionally, evidence indicated that augmenting ML infill with boolean support columns to flag imputed values generally improved downstream model results. Consequently, we recommend adopting ML infill as the default for tabular learning and incorporating support columns to indicate imputation presence, both of which can be executed effortlessly via Automunge's push-button interface. Our contributions encompass an auto ML-based imputation library for the Python ecosystem, fully integrated into a preprocessing suite with extensive feature transformation capabilities, featuring a novel production-ready design that anchors imputation models to a designated training set for consistent handling of new data.

We characterize the local stellar velocity field by utilizing position and velocity data for 4 million stars from Gaia's second data release. Within approximately 27,000 spatially defined bins, we calculate the components of the mean or bulk velocity. Our approach assumes these quantities form a Gaussian process, where the correlation between bulk velocities at different locations is governed by a straightforward covariance function or kernel. By employing a sparse Gaussian process algorithm based on inducing points, we develop a non-parametric, smooth, and differentiable model for the underlying velocity field. Our estimates for the Oort constants A, B, C, and K align exceptionally well with prior findings. Velocity field maps within 2 kiloparsecs of the Sun expose intricate substructures, offering compelling evidence that the local disk is currently in a state of disequilibrium. Furthermore, we provide the inaugural 3D map of the stellar velocity field's divergence, highlighting specific disk regions that appear to be experiencing compression and rarefaction.

This study models time-structured multi-turn injection for an enhanced Main Injector utilizing an 8-GeV Superconducting RF proton driver, alongside configurations based on ILC-style or Project-X linacs. Mismatches in radio-frequency parameters between these linacs and the upgraded Main Injector generate parasitic longitudinal painting within the RF phase. Various scenarios were analyzed, considering different RF settings for both single and dual RF systems under conditions of longitudinal space charge. Microbunch injection simulations conducted with ESME (2003) indicate that a dual RF system, configured with suitable RF parameters, can surmount the space-charge limits imposed by beam intensity during multi-turn injection. Specifically, a dual RF setup featuring a harmonic ratio (R_H = H_2/H_1) of 2.0 and a voltage ratio (R_V = V_2/V_1) of 0.5 is identified as the optimal choice for minimizing both longitudinal and transverse space-charge effects in the Main Injector.

Current deep learning approaches for motion deblurring rely on pairs of synthetic blurry and sharp images to train models that directly restore blurry inputs. However, this strategy is heavily dependent on the quality of synthetic data, which must be generated prior to training and is costly to scale. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an on-the-fly data augmenter capable of generating blurry data dynamically during both training and testing phases. We further integrate an unconventional deblurring framework that follows a blur-deblur-reblur-deblur sequence. This process utilizes a reblurring module (synthesizer) to generate pseudo-blurred versions of sharp or previously deblurred images. Additionally, this module incorporates hand-crafted priors derived from a state-of-the-art human body statistical model. These priors guide adversarial learning by distinguishing between human and non-human regions, enabling the model to better capture the characteristics of motion blur caused by human articulation and scene dynamics. Consequently, this adaptive approach yields superior performance compared to recent state-of-the-art deblurring algorithms.

We present the first spatial detection of three novel pure hydrocarbon cycles in TMC-1: c-C3HCCH (ethynyl cyclopropenylidene), c-C5H6 (cyclopentadiene), and c-C9H8 (indene). The derived column density for c-C3HCCH is 3.1×10^11 cm^-2, while the latter two exhibit comparable abundances ranging from 1 to 2×10^13 cm^-2. Despite their substantial molecular size, cyclopentadiene and indene are remarkably abundant, existing at levels only five times lower than the ubiquitous cyclic hydrocarbon c-C3H2. This high abundance, combined with previously identified high levels of the propargyl radical (CH2CCH) and other hydrocarbons such as vinyl and allenyl acetylene (Agundez et al. 2021; Cernicharo et al. 2021a,b), enables us to begin quantifying the hydrocarbon ring content in cold dark clouds and pinpointing the intermediate species likely responsible for the in situ bottom-up synthesis of aromatic cycles in these regions. Although c-C3HCCH is most probably formed via the reaction between the CCH radical and c-C3H2, the observed high abundances of cyclopentadiene and indene remain challenging to explain with current chemical mechanisms. Additional research is required to determine how five- and six-membered rings form under the cold conditions present in clouds like TMC-1.

This study investigates nonlinear effects arising during perturbation propagation in a dusty electron-ion plasma, utilizing a fully relativistic wave framework. By employing a multifluid model for the particles, a Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation is derived. Generally, two soliton solutions emerge: one corresponding to a slow wave mode and the other to a fast wave mode. The analysis demonstrates that soliton behavior—whether compressive, rarefactive, or nonexistent—is contingent upon specific system parameters, with relativistic effects proving significantly more impactful for ions than for electrons. Furthermore, it is observed that relativistic influences can markedly reduce soliton amplitudes in the slow mode, while in the fast mode, they may induce transitions between compressive and rarefactive solitons (and vice versa), a phenomenon dependent on the dust charge density in both modes.

This research examines adversarial attacks designed to manipulate opinion dynamics within complex networks. It introduces a straightforward attack strategy that keeps individual opinion states aligned with a specific target in voter model dynamics. The findings suggest that even if a single opinion holds a majority, the final vote result can be reversed—shifting toward the opposing view—by introducing strategically placed, minute, and difficult-to-detect perturbations across social networks. Such adversarial attacks prove more potent in complex, large-scale, and dense network structures, demonstrating that opinion dynamics can be subtly distorted without awareness.

The AstroSat mission includes multiple high-energy detectors designed for rapid timing analysis of cosmic sources. To achieve high-precision multi-wavelength timing, it is crucial to calibrate the absolute timestamps of these instruments with maximum accuracy. This study details the absolute time calibration of the AstroSat LAXPC instrument, leveraging the broadband electromagnetic radiation from the Crab Pulsar to cross-calibrate against the Fermi-LAT satellite and ground-based radio facilities, the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT) and the Ooty Radio Telescope (ORT). By applying pulsar timing techniques, we calculate the fixed timing offsets of LAXPC relative to these reference instruments and compare these offsets with those derived from another AstroSat instrument, CZTI.

We present several novel infinite families of rational $\tau$ values, including those that are squares of rationals, for which the group or semigroup generated by the matrices $\left( \begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right)$ and $\left( \begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \tau & 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right)$ fails to be free.

This study establishes metrical patterns as a superior marker of authorial style within classical Latin hexameter. By applying four distinct machine-learning models to pairwise classification tasks involving five first-century authors (resulting in ten comparisons), the research relies exclusively on metrical data. The findings indicate a two-label classification accuracy of at least 95%, achievable with as few as ten lines and no more than eighty lines (approximately 500 words). These required sample sizes are ten times smaller than those typically advised for 'bag of words' or n-gram methods, yielding exceptionally high accuracy. Furthermore, the paper investigates novelty or forgery detection through 'one-class classification'. Specifically, an analysis of the contested Aldine Additamentum (Sil. Ital. Puni. 8:144-225) yields a p-value of 0.0013, demonstrating a statistically significant divergence in metrical style from the remainder of the poem.

We introduce Baihe, a SysML framework designed for AI-driven databases. This framework allows existing relational database systems to be retrofitted with learned components for tasks such as query optimization or learned indexing structures. To ensure practicality and real-world applicability, Baihe's high-level architecture adheres to key requirements: separation from the core system, minimal third-party dependencies, robustness, stability, fault tolerance, and configurability. Building on this architecture, we describe a concrete implementation of Baihe for PostgreSQL and present example use cases involving learned query optimizers. To serve both practitioners and researchers in the database and AI4DB communities, Baihe for PostgreSQL will be released under an open-source license.

Existing studies in the automotive sector have highlighted security vulnerabilities in the CAN protocol. While application-layer attacks involving malicious packet creation are remotely feasible and detectable by modern Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS), newer link-layer attacks are more subtle and disruptive, though they traditionally require physical bus access. This paper introduces CANflict, a software-only method enabling reliable data link layer manipulation of the CAN bus from an unmodified microcontroller, surpassing current state-of-the-art solutions. We demonstrate the capability to launch stealthy link-layer attacks from a remotely compromised ECU against another ECU on the same network. By exploiting pin conflicts between microcontroller peripherals, we create polyglot frames that grant attackers bit-level control over CAN traffic, effectively bypassing protocol rules. Our experiments validate the approach across high-, mid-, and low-end microcontrollers. Furthermore, we release an extensible tool to facilitate future research, allowing implementation on various platforms and aiding in the development of data link layer countermeasures.

While the overlap of quantum states serves as the standard metric for distinguishing between two states, it fails to adequately assess the intricate configurations of many-body systems. This limitation extends to widely used measures like quantum state fidelity and associated distances. We propose a novel class of information-theoretic metrics known as weighted distances, which address these shortcomings. These measures evaluate the difficulty of discriminating between multi-particle quantum states by accounting for the architecture of the necessary measurement equipment. Consequently, they offer a means to assess both theoretical and experimental efficacy in complex quantum systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the newly defined "weighted Bures length" between the input and output states of a quantum process establishes a lower bound for the experimental cost of such transformations. This finding reveals an exact quantum limit on the capacity to convert physical resources into computational power.

Determining the total radiative output, or bolometric luminosity, across all wavelengths is essential for understanding how active galactic nuclei (AGN) influence their host galaxies and the broader cosmic environment. This work outlines a method to estimate this luminosity by utilizing quasar accretion disk spectral energy distribution (SED) templates, which are defined by black hole (BH) mass, Eddington ratio, and spin. We calculate the bolometric luminosity by integrating these disk SEDs from 1$\mu$m to 10keV. This approach naturally fills observational gaps and excludes reprocessed emission from the torus. The resulting accretion disk SED, and the derived bolometric correction, vary significantly based on BH mass, Eddington ratio, and spin. Specifically, corrections in the visible spectrum (at 5100$\,\mathring{A}$ and 3000$\,\mathring{A}$) are highly sensitive to BH mass, while those in the X-ray range depend strongly on the Eddington ratio; dependencies weaken as wavelengths approach the SED peak. Furthermore, maximally-rotating (spin = 1) quasars necessitate higher bolometric corrections than non-rotating (spin = 0) ones across all wavelengths. The SEDs and bolometric corrections presented here enable the calculation of radiative power for samples of radio-quiet to radio-loud Type 1 AGN, provided observations between 1$\mu$m and 10$\,$keV are corrected for extinction.

Fluorine holds significant interest for nuclear and stellar astrophysics. Its abundance was first measured in non-solar stars in 1992, initially in a select group of metal-poor stars thought to have originated in the early Universe. The primary sources of fluorine remain debated, with candidates including asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, the $\nu$-process in core-collapse supernovae, and Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars. Given variations in progenitor star mass and lifespan, observing fluorine at high redshifts offers a means to constrain production mechanisms in massive galaxies. In this study, we report the detection of HF (S/N = 8) in absorption within a gravitationally lensed, dusty star-forming galaxy at redshift z=4.4, characterized by a high ratio of $N_{\rm HF}$/$N_{\rm{H_2}}$ of approximately $\sim2\times10^{-9}$. This suggests a rapid acceleration of chemical enrichment in this high-redshift system. At z=4.4, AGB stars of a few solar masses are improbable as the dominant enrichment source; instead, we demonstrate that WR stars are necessary to account for the observed fluorine levels at this epoch, with other mechanisms gaining importance later. Consequently, these observations shed light on the processes driving the 'ramp-up' phase of chemical enrichment concurrent with swift stellar mass assembly in young, massive galaxies.

This study reports on a search for pair-produced particles with masses exceeding 100 GeV, each decaying into at least four quarks. Utilizing 2015-2016 data from the CMS experiment at the LHC, which corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 38.2 fb$^{-1}$, the analysis identified reconstructed particles grouped into two large, similarly massive jets, each exhibiting substructure consistent with four partons. No statistically significant excess over background predictions was found in the distribution of average jet mass. Consequently, pair-produced squarks with dominant hadronic $R$-parity-violating decays into four quarks, spanning masses from 0.10 to 0.72 TeV, are excluded at the 95% confidence level. Likewise, pair-produced gluinos decaying into five quarks are excluded for masses ranging between 0.10 and 1.41 TeV at the same confidence level. These findings represent the first constraints on pair-produced particles with masses below 400 GeV decaying into four or five quarks, thereby filling a substantial gap in the exploration of $R$-parity-violating supersymmetry parameter space.

Previous research indicates that human expressions contain more positive than negative words, a pattern usually explained by positivity bias—the inclination to view reality favorably. However, the linguistic characteristics of negative reviews warrant examination. Using multiple datasets, we demonstrate that English negative reviews also feature a higher frequency of positive words compared to negative ones, aligning with earlier findings. We resolve this apparent contradiction by integrating prior insights into the pragmatics of negation, revealing that negative reviews commonly pair negations with positive vocabulary. Moreover, sentiment analysis shows that in these reviews, most sentences containing positive words ultimately convey negative opinions, suggesting the presence of negation.

Current national laboratories are increasingly developing new high-gradient RF cavities for high-energy physics, achieving ultra-high gradients of approximately GV/m through ultra-compact sub-THz structures. However, experimentally determining the primary RF parameters for these compact designs is complex and prone to inaccuracies, while RF simulations demand substantial computational resources. Specifically, calculating the reflection coefficient—a critical parameter for accelerating structures—poses significant challenges. To address this, we have formulated an electromagnetic theory based on Bethe's small aperture polarization approach (also refined by Collin) to provide a rapid and precise analytical estimation of cavity-waveguide coupling. This paper presents an exact analytical formula for the reflection coefficient as a function of the system's physical parameters, applicable to any geometry, material, or frequency.

We present CircuitQ, a Python-based open-source toolkit designed for analyzing superconducting circuits. This tool enables the automated generation of a symbolic Hamiltonian from a given circuit layout and provides a dynamic numerical representation of the Hamiltonian with adjustable basis options. Additional capabilities include estimating T1 lifetimes of circuit states across different noise mechanisms. We revisit established methods for circuit quantization, reformulating them to support efficient software implementation. The toolbox's utility is demonstrated through its application to practically significant qubit circuits, with results compared against specialized solvers. Our quantization approach accommodates a broad range of circuit designs, and the software is made publicly available. Consequently, we provide a valuable resource for developing new quantum circuits for quantum information processing.

Golan and Sapir \cite{MR3978542} established that the Thompson's groups $F$, $T$, and $V$ exhibit linear divergence. In this work, we investigate the divergence characteristics of various generalizations of these groups. First, we examine the Brown-Thompson groups $F_n$, $T_n$, and $V_n$, demonstrating that they also possess a linear divergence function. Subsequently, by analyzing the braided Thompson's groups $BF$, $\widehat{BF}$, and $\widehat{BV}$ in conjunction with findings from \cite{Kodama:2020to}, we conclude that these groups likewise have linear divergence.

Predicting the future movements of dynamic agents is a critical yet difficult challenge in robotics, particularly for self-driving systems, due to agents' hidden intentions and the complex interplay between them, their surroundings, and the map. This paper introduces LaneRCNN, a graph-based motion forecasting framework. By utilizing a specialized graph encoder, we derive a local lane graph representation (LaneRoI) for each agent to capture its historical trajectory and the immediate map topology. Additionally, we implement an interaction module that enables efficient message passing between these local graphs within a shared global lane structure. Furthermore, we define output trajectories using lane graphs, offering a more suitable prediction parameterization. LaneRCNN effectively models both agent-to-agent and agent-to-map relationships in a distributed, map-aware fashion. Our approach was evaluated on the Argoverse Motion Forecasting Benchmark, where it secured first place on the leaderboard and substantially surpassed prior state-of-the-art results.

Randomized field experiments, exemplified by A/B testing, have traditionally served as the benchmark for assessing the value new software delivers to users. However, in automotive embedded software development, conducting such randomized trials is often unfeasible, undesirable, or ethically problematic. To address these constraints, this paper proposes employing Bayesian propensity score matching for causal inference within observational studies specific to the automotive sector. We introduce a method grounded in the Bayesian propensity score matching framework, tailored for the unique context of automotive software engineering. This approach enables the creation of balanced control and treatment groups derived from observational online evaluations, allowing for the estimation of causal treatment effects even when the treatment sample size is limited. We validate this method through a proof-of-concept study in the automotive domain. In this example, a large control fleet of 1,100 vehicles running the existing software was compared against a small treatment fleet of 38 vehicles receiving a new software variant. Because shipping the new software to all users was restricted, a fully randomized experiment was impossible. Consequently, we applied Bayesian propensity score matching using 14 observed covariates as inputs. The results demonstrate significantly more balanced groups, making them suitable for estimating causal effects from the observational data. We provide a detailed description of the method, share our specific configuration, and discuss its applicability for evaluating new software via online experiments with small sample groups.

Veldkamp polygons are specific graphs $\Gamma=(V,E)$ where, for every vertex $v\in V$, the subgraph $\Gamma_v$ carries a symmetric, anti-reflexive relation denoted $\equiv_v$. These relations are entirely trivial if and only if $\Gamma$ constitutes a thick generalized polygon. A Veldkamp polygon is defined as flat when no two vertices share an identical set of opposites in a natural sense. This study investigates the relationship between Veldkamp quadrangles and polar spaces, leveraging this link to provide a complete classification of flat Veldkamp quadrangles where some, but not all, of the relations $\equiv_v$ are trivial.

Over recent years, deep learning models for learning analytics have gained significant traction, yet their adoption in practical applications remains limited, likely stemming from concerns regarding trust and transparency. This paper addresses this challenge by integrating explainable AI techniques into black-box neural networks, specifically within the domains of online and blended learning for student success prediction. Utilizing a pairwise study design, we examined controlled variations across five course pairs that differed in a single educationally relevant factor, applying two prominent instance-based explainability methods: LIME and SHAP. We conducted a quantitative comparison of explanation distances between courses and methods, followed by a qualitative validation involving 26 semi-structured interviews with university educators. These interviews explored educators' perceptions of the most impactful features for student success, their level of trust in the generated explanations, and how they might apply these insights to improve course design. Our findings reveal significant quantitative disagreement among explainers regarding feature importance and a qualitative lack of consensus among experts concerning which explanations are most trustworthy. All code, extended results, and the interview protocol are available at https://github.com/epfl-ml4ed/trusting-explainers.

The manufacturing sector has increasingly embraced the reuse of machine components to lower expenses and promote sustainability. A critical step in this workflow involves identifying reusable features within part designs and locating their counterparts in existing databases. This project leverages fully convolutional geometric features to extract and learn high-level semantic attributes from CAD models using inductive transfer learning. These extracted features are subsequently matched against other CAD models in the database via the Frobenius norm to retrieve identical items. Furthermore, passing these features through a deep convolutional neural network equipped with a spatial pyramid pooling layer significantly enhanced retrieval performance. The results demonstrated that the model effectively captures geometric elements associated with machining features.

Jean-Marie Souriau, a French mathematician and physicist, investigated Gibbs states arising from the Hamiltonian action of a Lie group on a symplectic manifold, exploring their potential applications in physics and cosmology. This work provides detailed proofs for all stated results. Furthermore, by adapting the cross product to pseudo-Euclidean three-dimensional vector spaces, we present multiple examples of these Gibbs states and their corresponding thermodynamic functions across various two-dimensional symplectic manifolds, such as pseudo-spheres, the Poincaré disk, and the Poincaré half-plane.

We report measurements of the cross section for anti-neutrino charged-current quasielastic-like scattering on hydrocarbon, utilizing the medium energy (ME) NuMI wide-band neutrino beam, which peaks at an average energy of approximately 6 GeV. These results are presented as functions of the longitudinal momentum ($p_{||}$) and transverse momentum ($p_{T}$) of the resulting muon. This study complements our earlier high-statistics neutrino channel measurement and extends the prior anti-neutrino data from the low energy (LE) beam (averaging $\sim$ 3.5 GeV) up to a $p_{T}$ of 2.5 GeV/c. Existing theoretical models fail to fully describe the data in this previously unexplored high $p_{T}$ region. Furthermore, the single differential cross section as a function of four-momentum transfer ($Q^{2}_{QE}$) now reaches 4 GeV$^2$ with high statistics. Analysis of the cross section versus $Q^{2}_{QE}$ reveals that the MINERvA collaboration's tuned simulations, which previously aligned well with low-energy beam data, do not match the medium-energy beam results as accurately. In contrast, newer neutrino interaction models, such as the GENIE 3 tunes, demonstrate superior capability in simulating high $Q^{2}_{QE}$ scenarios.

A convex body can be approximated using polyhedra by solving an associated multiobjective convex program (MOCP) to a desired degree of accuracy. Benson-type algorithms address this MOCP approximately by generating both inner and outer polyhedral approximations of the problem's upper image, from which polyhedral approximations of the convex body are derived. We establish error bounds, expressed via the Hausdorff distance, for these polyhedral approximations of the convex body, contingent upon the stopping criteria used in the primal and dual Benson-type algorithms applied to the corresponding MOCP.

The open-domain dialogue system Alquist aims to achieve social intelligence by fostering coherent and engaging conversations. As the fourth iteration developed for the Alexa Prize Socialbot Grand Challenge 4, it introduces two primary innovations: enhancing coherence and improving engagement. To address coherence, the system employs a novel hybrid strategy that integrates hand-crafted responses with a generative model. This approach leverages pre-designed dialogues to guide users through high-quality conversational paths, utilizes out-of-domain detection to identify when a user strays from these predefined flows, and deploys a neural response generator. The neural component analyzes the dialogue context to appropriately react to unexpected inputs, steering the conversation back within the boundaries of the hand-designed framework. Regarding engagement, the innovations are largely inspired by the exploration-exploitation dilemma. Effective engagement requires balancing exploration—learning the partner's preferences and interests—with exploitation—applying acquired knowledge to maintain interaction. This paper details the principles and mechanics of Alquist's individual components, along with the experiments conducted to evaluate them within the context of the Alexa Prize Socialbot Grand Challenge 4.

Myocardial perfusion MRI quantification offers the promise of rapid, automated, and user-independent ischemia assessment. Nevertheless, high noise levels, limited temporal resolution, and complex tracer-kinetic models often lead to unreliable parameter estimates during model fitting. Bayesian inference addresses this by integrating prior knowledge to enhance estimation reliability; however, its reliance on Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling to approximate posterior distributions makes the process computationally expensive. To overcome this, the proposed work involves training convolutional networks to directly predict kinetic parameters from signal-intensity curves, using Bayesian estimates as training data. This approach enables fast parameter estimation with performance comparable to that of Bayesian inference.

Camera localization is a critical task for numerous robotic applications, and deep learning has recently emerged as a dominant approach in this field. However, these methods often struggle with robustness against significant domain shifts, such as variations in season or lighting between training and testing datasets. While data augmentation offers a promising solution without requiring new data, current techniques indiscriminately perturb all pixels, leading to suboptimal results. To address this limitation, we introduce RADA, a system designed to focus perturbations specifically on geometrically informative regions of the image. Consequently, RADA learns to produce minimal yet effective perturbations that challenge the network. Our findings demonstrate that incorporating these generated examples as augmentation significantly enhances robustness. Furthermore, our method surpasses prior augmentation techniques and achieves up to twice the accuracy of state-of-the-art localization models (such as AtLoc and MapNet) when evaluated under unseen, challenging weather conditions.

Multi-modal magnetic resonance (MR) imaging holds significant promise for the diagnosis and analysis of brain gliomas. While standard sequences like T1, T2, and FLAIR are routinely acquired simultaneously, obtaining contrast-enhanced images (T1ce) necessitates extra time, cost, and contrast agent injection. Consequently, developing methods to synthesize these missing modalities is clinically valuable, as the generated data can serve as additional inputs to downstream tasks, such as brain tumor segmentation, to improve performance. This study introduces an end-to-end framework called the Modality-Level Attention Fusion Network (MAF-Net), which innovatively employs patchwise contrastive learning to extract multi-modal latent features and dynamically assigns attention weights to fuse various modalities. Extensive experiments on the BraTS2020 dataset demonstrate that MAF-Net achieves superior T1ce synthesis performance, with an SSIM of 0.8879 and a PSNR of 22.78, alongside accurate brain tumor segmentation, yielding mean Dice scores of 67.9%, 41.8%, and 88.0% for the tumor core, enhancing tumor, and whole tumor, respectively.

Observing numerous quantum effects, including optomechanical squeezing and entanglement, relies fundamentally on strong coupling within optomechanical systems, with normal-mode splitting (NMS) serving as its primary indicator. This study demonstrates that NMS, detectable in both the movable mirror's spectrum and the output field, can be precisely tailored by integrating optical parametric amplification (OPA) with coherent feedback (CF). Furthermore, NMS intensity can be significantly amplified by fine-tuning key parameters, such as input optical power, OPA gain and phase, and coherent feedback strength defined by the beam splitter's amplitude reflectivity.

Direct imaging of exoplanetary giants requires achieving the highest contrasts (dH ~10 magnitudes) at the smallest angular separations (~0.1'') from their host stars. We introduce an adaptive optics technique known as "star-hopping," recently implemented as a standard queue observation for the SPHERE instrument at the VLT. Unlike previous approaches, this method acquires images of a reference star for PSF subtraction within minutes of observing the target using reference difference imaging (RDI). Our objective is to achieve significantly higher contrast than conventional angular differential imaging (ADI) to search for a fifth planet in the HR 8799 system at separations under 10 au, located interior to the known four giant planets. We collected 4.5 hours of simultaneous integral field spectroscopy (R~30, Y-H bands with IFS) and dual-band imaging (K1 and K2 bands with IRDIS) of the HR 8799 system alongside a reference star. The reference star was observed for approximately one-third of the total duration, exhibiting a color difference (dR) of ~1 mag and an angular separation of ~1-2 degrees. Star-hopping occurred every 6-10 minutes, with only 1-minute gaps in integration between hops. We failed to detect the hypothesized fifth planet at the most likely separations of 7.5 and 9.7 au, down to mass limits of 3.6 MJup at high signal-to-noise ratios. As noted in prior studies, the spectra of red field dwarfs closely match those of the planets. Furthermore, we demonstrated that star-hopping RDI can improve contrast by up to 2 magnitudes at 0.1'' separation. Since this method does not require ADI, meridian transits, or sky rotation, the observation window is expanded by a factor of 2-3. Generally, star-hopping is applicable to stars fainter than R=4 magnitudes, as suitable reference stars are typically available for them. The reduction software utilized in this study is now available online.

This report details the calculation of variance for joint conditional model and state residuals within multivariate autoregressive Gaussian state-space (MARSS) models, defined by the equations $x(t)=Bx(t-1)+u+w(t)$ and $y(t)=Zx(t)+a+v(t)$, where $w(t)$ and $v(t)$ represent multivariate normal error terms with covariance matrices $Q$ and $R$, respectively. While Harvey, Koopman, and Penzer (1998) provided a recursive algorithm for these residuals conditioned on potentially incomplete data $y$, this work derives the residual equations using conditional state variances and the covariance between unobserved data and states. This approach enables the computation of variance for unobserved residuals, a capability beneficial for leave-one-out cross-validation. Furthermore, the report outlines modifications to the Harvey et al. algorithm to handle missing values and to generate non-normalized conditional residuals.

This paper demonstrates the end-to-end fine-tuning of the complete Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. We outline the primary engineering hurdles required to accomplish this goal and show that the end-to-end approach surpasses the original RAG design in question-answering tasks. Additionally, our implementation has been made available through the HuggingFace Transformers library.

Our previous research utilized a spatially dependent propagation (SDP) model combined with the nearby Geminga supernova remnant to concurrently address cosmic ray (CR) spectra and anisotropy; however, the resulting anisotropy phase remained inconsistent with experimental findings. Recent data indicate that below 100 TeV, the anisotropy phase aligns with the local regular magnetic field (LRMF) detected by the Interstellar Boundary Explorer (IBEX), suggesting that diffusion along the LRMF is a critical factor. Consequently, this study incorporates the LRMF and accounts for associated anisotropic diffusion to better explain CR anisotropy. We demonstrate that when the diffusion coefficient perpendicular to the LRMF is significantly lower than the parallel coefficient, the anisotropy phase shifts to approximately R.A. = 3ʰ, matching observations below 100 TeV. Furthermore, we examine how the ratio of perpendicular to parallel diffusion coefficients influences anisotropy and its energy dependence. Our results show that as perpendicular diffusion decreases, the anisotropy phase transitions from the direction of the nearby source to the LRMF below 100 TeV, while shifting from the galactic center (GC) to the opposite LRMF direction above 100 TeV. Additionally, if the perpendicular diffusion coefficient increases more rapidly than the parallel one with energy, diffusion becomes isotropic at high energies, causing the anisotropy phase to move from the LRMF toward the GC above 100 TeV. These findings may assist in determining the energy dependence of diffusion coefficients.

This note presents a manageable example of a polyhomogeneous solution space for four-dimensional electromagnetism at null infinity. From this framework, we derive the electromagnetic memory effect and discuss its relationship with asymptotic symmetries.

Offensive material is widespread across social media platforms, posing significant concerns for both corporate and governmental entities. Recent research has explored various detection methods for such content, including hate speech, cyberbullying, and cyberaggression. However, the majority of these studies focus on English due to the prevalence of annotated English datasets. This paper leverages existing English resources by utilizing cross-lingual contextual word embeddings and transfer learning to generate predictions for low-resource languages. Specifically, we map our findings to comparable datasets in Arabic, Bengali, Danish, Greek, Hindi, Spanish, and Turkish. Our approach achieved an F1 macro score of 0.8415 for Bengali in the TRAC-2 shared task, 0.8532 for Danish and 0.8701 for Greek in OffensEval 2020, 0.8568 for Hindi in HASOC 2019, and 0.7513 for Spanish in SemEval-2019 Task 5 (HatEval), demonstrating competitive performance against top systems in recent shared tasks for these languages. Furthermore, we report strong results for Arabic and Turkish using the OffensEval 2020 training and development sets. Collectively, these outcomes validate the robustness of cross-lingual contextual embeddings and transfer learning for offensive content detection.

Energetic particles are primarily generated by strong shocks in collisionless plasmas, including those from supernovae and coronal mass ejections. Because heavy ions have a distinct mass-to-charge ratio compared to protons, their interaction with the shock layer varies, making their injection into acceleration mechanisms difficult. This study presents the first direct observational proof of alpha particles being magnetically reflected from a high-Mach number quasi-perpendicular shock, based on in-situ spacecraft data. The intense magnetic amplification at the shock front, driven by nonstationarity, alters alpha particle trajectories; some particles gyrate within the enhanced magnetic field, travel upstream, and undergo further acceleration. These findings underscore the critical role of high magnetic amplification in initiating the energization of heavy ions at nonstationary, reforming shocks.

The secondary component of GW190814, denoted as $m_2$ with a mass range of $(2.50-2.67)\,\text{M}_{\odot}$, occupies the mass gap between the known maximum neutron star mass and the minimum black hole mass, a fact that remains highly debated. While various hypotheses exist, one prominent suggestion is that $m_2$ is a superfast pulsar, though its stability against r-mode instability driven by the Chandrasekhar-Friedman-Schutz mechanism via runaway gravitational radiation remains uncertain. By evaluating a set of 33 unified equations of state (EOSs) developed by Fortin {\it et al.} (2016)—which consistently apply the same nuclear interactions from crust to core and satisfy all current astrophysical and nuclear constraints—we compare the minimum frequency needed for $m_2$ to sustain a mass exceeding $2.50\,\text{M}_{\odot}$ against the critical frequency triggering r-mode instability. Employing two extreme damping models (one assuming a perfectly rigid crust and the other an elastic crust), and relying on the stability of 19 observed low-mass X-ray binaries as evidence that rigid crust damping dominates, we conclude that $m_2$ remains r-mode stable at frequencies above 870.2 Hz (0.744 times its Kepler frequency of 1169.6 Hz), provided its temperature stays below approximately $3.9\times 10^7\,\text{K}$. These findings further bolster the hypothesis that the secondary component of GW190814 is a supermassive and superfast pulsar.

This work derives expressions for polarization and magnetization in magnetically confined plasmas, incorporating full gyroradius expansions to account for both equilibrium conditions and microscopic electromagnetic turbulence. These expressions establish relationships between particle densities and flows and their counterparts at gyrocenters. At the first order of the normalized gyroradius expansion, the mean particle flow comprises the sum of gyrocenter flow and magnetization flow, aligning with the established magnetization law in drift kinetics, whereas the turbulent component includes polarization flow. Collisions introduce an additional contribution to the second-order particle flow. The mean particle flux crossing magnetic surfaces, which is a second-order effect, encompasses classical, neoclassical, and turbulent transport mechanisms. By applying a Lagrangian variational principle, the gyrokinetic Poisson and Ampère equations are derived to properly integrate both mean and turbulent components, facilitating full-$f$ global electromagnetic gyrokinetic simulations. It is determined that the second-order Lagrangian term, representing the inner product of the turbulent vector potential and the drift velocity (which includes curvature and $\nabla B$ drifts), must be retained to ensure the derived Ampère equation correctly captures the diamagnetic current, a requirement particularly critical for full-$f$ high-beta plasma simulations. Furthermore, the turbulent components of these gyrokinetic Poisson and Ampère equations are validated against results obtained from the WKB representation in previous studies.

Many natural language processing (NLP) tasks inherently suffer from class imbalance, as certain categories appear far more often than others in real-world data. Consequently, existing NLP models often struggle to perform well on underrepresented classes. Although addressing this imbalance is a prominent area of research, identifying the optimal solution for specific tasks and scenarios remains challenging. This survey serves as the first comprehensive overview of class imbalance in deep learning-based NLP, offering guidance for researchers and practitioners facing imbalanced datasets. We begin by examining different forms of class imbalance, ranging from controlled environments to real-world settings. The survey then details approaches explicitly designed for imbalanced NLP tasks or methods adapted from computer vision that have been tested in this domain. These techniques are categorized by their underlying mechanisms: sampling strategies, data augmentation, loss function selection, staged learning, or model architecture. Finally, we address remaining challenges, such as handling multi-label scenarios, and advocate for systematic benchmarking and reporting to advance the field collectively.

This study utilizes computer simulations employing effective-medium theory (EMT) potentials to investigate Cu$_x$Zr$_{100-x}$ alloys (where $x=36, 50, 64$) in both liquid and glassy states. Our findings demonstrate significant invariance in both structural and dynamic properties when expressed in reduced units along the system's isomorphs. The investigated state points span a density range of nearly a factor of two, with temperatures ranging from 1500 K to over 4000 K for liquids and from 500 K to above 1500 K for glasses. Comparative results along isochores for similar temperature shifts reveal minimal invariance. Typically, a binary system's phase diagram is defined by three axes: composition, temperature, and pressure (or density); however, the presence of isomorphs reduces this to two axes, or just one for a fixed composition. We conclude that, at a fixed composition, the liquid and glass regions of the thermodynamic phase diagram for this metallic glass former are effectively one-dimensional. This is because numerous physical properties remain invariant along specific curves, meaning that exploring the phase diagram requires traversing only these invariant paths.

Extracting insights from health data accelerates clinical decision-making, enhances treatment quality, facilitates disease prevention, lowers costs, and fosters innovation within the healthcare industry. Nevertheless, the sensitivity of such data necessitates compliance with strict regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) to safeguard patient privacy. While removing or anonymizing identifiable information is the primary step toward regulatory adherence and privacy protection, it is not a complete solution. This paper reviews existing anonymization techniques and their applicability to both relational and graph-based health datasets. Furthermore, we examine potential attacks on anonymized data, demonstrating through a reconstruction attack that anonymization alone is insufficient to guarantee patient privacy. Finally, we explore available tools designed to facilitate the anonymization process.

Density functional theory calculations reveal that vacancy-centered hexagonal armchair nanographene (VANG) exhibits excellent reversibility in hydrogen uptake and release. The VANG structure features a triply hydrogenated vacancy (V$_{111}$) at its center, which acts as a self-catalyst to lower the activation energy for hydrogen absorption and desorption. Notably, the activation barriers for hydrogen uptake and release are nearly identical, measured at 1.19 eV and 1.25 eV respectively. The process is slightly endothermic during hydrogenation and slightly exothermic during dehydrogenation, indicating high efficiency. Under high hydrogen coverage, a quintuply hydrogenated vacancy (V$_{221}$) forms, with hydrogen atoms situated on both the in-plane and armchair edges. This configuration facilitates exothermic hydrogen release from the in-plane sites with an energy barrier of 2 eV or less. These findings offer a promising solution to the low reversibility challenges associated with organic chemical hydrides used for hydrogen storage.

Living organisms are treated as open systems, utilizing Prigogine's thermodynamic framework. This approach enables the formulation of a law governing the individual growth and development (ontogenesis) of life, accounting for the fact that system functioning operates under a distinct internal program. A thermodynamic equation for growth is employed to estimate an organism's specific entropy. When compared with experimental data, including entropy estimates for various species, the theory reveals a reduction in specific entropy across the evolutionary lineage, progressing from yeast to insects, reptiles, and finally birds.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) and Hyperparameter Optimization (HPO) democratize deep learning by automatically selecting network architectures and tuning training pipeline parameters, making the field accessible to non-experts. Although both areas have been extensively researched recently, most NAS methods assume fixed hyperparameters, while HPO typically assumes fixed architectures, leaving a significant gap in joint NAS and HPO research. Moreover, NAS is increasingly framed as a multi-objective optimization problem to account for factors like resource constraints. This paper introduces methods that extend existing approaches to jointly optimize neural architectures and hyperparameters across multiple objectives. We aim for these methods to serve as simple baselines for future investigations into multi-objective joint NAS and HPO. To support this, all our code is publicly available at https://github.com/automl/multi-obj-baselines.

The high-energy tails observed in charged- and neutral-current Drell-Yan processes offer crucial constraints on light quark and anti-quark parton distribution functions (PDFs) within the large-x regime. Simultaneously, short-distance new physics phenomena, as represented by the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT), are expected to produce smooth distortions in these same high-energy tails. This study is the first to evaluate the interaction between PDFs and EFT effects for high-mass Drell-Yan processes at the LHC, specifically quantifying how a consistent simultaneous determination of PDFs and Wilson coefficients influences the resulting bounds on the latter. We examine two theoretically motivated new physics scenarios: $1)$ electroweak oblique corrections $(\hat W, \hat Y)$ and $2)$ four-fermion interactions that may explain the LHCb anomalies in $R(K^{(*)})$. Utilizing existing Drell-Yan data, including both unfolded cross sections and search results, we also perform dedicated projections for the High-Luminosity LHC. Our primary conclusion is that although the interplay between PDFs and EFT effects is currently moderate given the available dataset, it will present a significant challenge for EFT analyses at the HL-LHC.

Heavy flavour physics offers significant avenues for indirectly probing new physics at extremely high energy scales and investigating hadron properties to deepen our understanding of the strong interaction. Since the LHC began operations roughly a decade ago, the LHCb experiment has been at the forefront of this field, achieving numerous high-precision measurements and unexpected discoveries with profound implications for particle physics. This review focuses on a curated selection of LHCb's most impactful results regarding CP violation, rare decays, and heavy flavour production and spectroscopy, derived from data collected during the collider's first two operational runs. Additionally, the review briefly outlines the LHCb upgrade plan and its associated physics prospects.

Identifying gene regulatory regions, characterized by high motif frequencies in DNA sequences that code for transcription and enhancer proteins, remains a significant challenge in bioinformatics. Predicting alignment scores between subsequence k-mers and specific motifs allows for the detection of candidate regulatory regions associated with protein transcription. We introduce a one-dimensional (1-D) Convolutional Neural Network trained on k-mer sequences interspersed with motif patterns to forecast pairwise alignment scores between the consensus motif and these subsequences. The architecture comprises fifteen layers, organized into three rounds of 1-D convolution, batch normalization, dense, and 1-D maximum pooling layers. Training utilizes mean squared error loss across four distinct datasets featuring randomly inserted motif patterns: the first three include zero, one, and two mutations per motif, while the fourth uses a position-specific probability matrix. To assess performance, we employ a novel metric, $S_{\alpha}$, derived from the Jaccard Index, alongside 10-fold cross-validation. This metric evaluates accuracy by determining the proportion of the top 15 highest-scoring 15-mer indices in the predicted scores that match the actual scores within a selected $\alpha$ region. Results from the best-performing dataset demonstrate that, on average, 99.3% of the top 15 motifs were correctly identified within a one base pair stride ($\alpha = 1$) in out-of-sample data. To our knowledge, this represents a novel approach demonstrating how intelligently formatted data can be effectively extrapolated using machine learning.

Precise future measurements of the Higgs mass and couplings at dedicated Higgs factories can probe the parameter space of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM). By employing a multi-variable $\chi^2$ fit focused on the primary contributions from the stop sector, this study examines how these Higgs precision data constrain the MSSM. The findings indicate a strong complementarity between indirect searches conducted at Higgs factories and direct searches performed within the current LHC program.

This study introduces the luminosity function (QLF) for type-1 quasars at redshift $z\!\approx\!6$, derived from the Pan-STARRS1 (PS1) survey. The PS1 dataset comprises 125 quasars within the range $z\approx5.7-6.2$ and absolute magnitudes $-28\lesssim M_{1450}\lesssim-25$. By augmenting this with 48 fainter quasars from the SHELLQs survey, we extend the QLF evaluation to cover $-28\lesssim M_{1450}\lesssim-22$. Utilizing a double power-law model with exponential density evolution ($\Phi(z)\propto10^{k(z-6)}$; $k=-0.7$), we apply maximum likelihood fitting to our data. Our results yield a break magnitude of $M^*=-26.38_{-0.60}^{+0.79}\,\text{mag}$, a faint-end slope of $\alpha=-1.70_{-0.19}^{+0.29}$, and a steep bright-end slope of $\beta=-3.84_{-1.21}^{+0.63}$. Based on this model, the comoving spatial density of quasars at $z\!\approx\!6$ with $M_{1450}<-26$ is determined to be $1.16_{-0.12}^{+0.13}\,\text{cGpc}^{-3}$. Comparisons with existing literature indicate that quasar density evolves with a constant rate of $k\approx-0.7$ spanning from $z\approx7$ to $z\approx4$. Furthermore, we calculate an ionizing emissivity of $\epsilon_{912}(z=6) =7.23_{-1.02}^{+1.65}\times 10^{22}\,\text{erg}\,\text{s}^{-1}\text{Hz}^{-1}\text{cMpc}^{-3}$ using the QLF measurements. Combining this with standard assumptions and the recent mean free path measurement by Becker et al. (2021) at $z\approx6$, we derive an HI photoionizing rate of $\Gamma_{\text{HI}}(z{=}6) \approx 6 \times10^{-16}\,\text{s}^{-1}$, which strongly suggests that quasars did not play a dominant role in hydrogen reionization.

This study investigates both resonant and non-resonant pair production of Higgs bosons within the $b\bar{b}\tau^+\tau^-$ final state, utilizing 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected by the ATLAS experiment at the LHC ($\sqrt{s}= 13$ TeV) during 2015 and 2016. The analysis encompasses both fully hadronic and semileptonic decay modes of the $\tau$-lepton pairs. No significant deviation from the predicted background is observed. Consequently, the cross-section times branching ratio for non-resonant Higgs pair production is limited to below 30.9 fb, which corresponds to 12.7 times the Standard Model prediction, at a 95% confidence level. Additionally, the data are employed to search for resonant Higgs pair production, setting constraints on a two-doublet extended Higgs sector and a Randall-Sundrum bulk graviton model. These results establish upper limits on the resonant cross-section times branching ratio, thereby excluding simplified hMSSM minimal supersymmetric model resonances $X$ with masses between 305 GeV and 402 GeV (for $\tan\beta=2$) and bulk Randall-Sundrum gravitons $G_{\mathrm{KK}}$ with masses between 325 GeV and 885 GeV (for $k/\overline{M}_{\mathrm{Pl}} = 1$).

Recently, numerous Knowledge Graph Embedding (KGE) methods have been developed to map entities and relations into dense vector spaces for downstream applications like link prediction. While some techniques prioritize interpretability by aligning relation connectivity patterns (e.g., symmetry, inversion, composition) with geometric concepts such as rotations, others enhance expressiveness by utilizing higher-dimensional spaces, notably four dimensions. However, operating within a 4D space often sacrifices interpretability. This paper introduces HopfE, a novel KGE framework designed to maintain interpretability while leveraging four-dimensional modeling. Our approach first represents structural embeddings in 3D Euclidean space, treating relation operators as SO(3) rotations. Subsequently, entity embeddings are mapped from this 3D space onto a 4D hypersphere via the inverse Hopf Fibration, incorporating semantic information derived from the knowledge graph ontology. By integrating both structural and semantic entity properties, HopfE preserves both expressiveness and interpretability. Empirical evaluations across four established benchmarks demonstrate that HopfE achieves state-of-the-art performance in knowledge graph completion tasks.

Using ultrafast optical spectroscopy, we detected significant oscillations in the differential reflectivity of 9 nm and 60 nm BaFe$_2$As$_2$ (Ba-122) thin films. These oscillations arise from propagating longitudinal acoustic (LA) phonon wave packets that exhibit strong dependencies on both thickness and temperature. Specifically, the measured oscillation frequency for the ultra-thin 9 nm film approaches 50 GHz. Our calculations indicate that the Young's modulus of the 9 nm film is approximately four times greater than that of the 60 nm film, aligning with experimental findings. This increase in Young's modulus with decreasing thickness is attributed to a reduction in the parent Ba-122 tetragonality ($c/a$) near the film-substrate interface caused by material-substrate mismatch effects. Additionally, the temperature-dependent variation in LA phonon frequency for the 9 nm film is linked to changes in the parent Ba-122 orthorhombicity, defined as $(a-b)/(a+b)$.

A $\sigma$-frame is defined as a partially ordered set equipped with countable joins and finite meets, where binary meets distribute over countable joins. This paper aims to demonstrate that $\sigma$-frames, or equivalently $\sigma$-locales, constitute a branch of Formal Topology, representing an intuitionistic and predicative approach to point-free topology. Specifically, every $\sigma$-frame $L$ corresponds to the lattice of Lindel\"of elements within a particular formal topology; this topology serves as a presentation of the free frame generated by $L$. Furthermore, we provide a constructive characterization of the smallest (strongly) dense $\sigma$-sublocale of a given $\sigma$-locale, thereby establishing a "$\sigma$-analogue" of Boolean locales. This development relies on the axiom of countable choice.

This work introduces the notion of energy-variational solutions for the Ericksen--Leslie equations in three-dimensional space. This framework offers greater precision than dissipative solutions and ensures weak-strong uniqueness. Under a specific regularity weight selection, the existence of energy-variational solutions guarantees the existence of measure-valued solutions; alternatively, by choosing a different weight, we construct an energy-variational solution using an implementable, structure-preserving space-time discretization method. Computational experiments are conducted to demonstrate the practical applicability of the proposed algorithm.

We report observations of zero-to-$\pi$ phase transitions triggered by Rabi oscillations within an unbalanced Ramsey atom interferometer. By adjusting the polarization or duration of Raman lasers, we experimentally examined the resulting phase shifts and visibility, with outcomes that align well with a theoretical framework. In such interferometers, $\pi$-phase flips arise not merely from the sign of the Rabi frequency but also from the Rabi oscillation itself.
