This study introduces a multi-modal, humour-annotated dataset comprising approximately 40 hours of stand-up comedy clips. We propose a novel scoring mechanism that assigns a humour quotient score based on audience laughter, calculated as the normalized duration of laughter relative to the total clip length. This method yields a humour coefficient on a five-point scale (0-4), which was validated against manual annotations, achieving a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.6. Utilizing this dataset, we trained a model to predict a "funniness" score (0-4) from audio and text inputs. By evaluating various neural language models for humour rating, we attained an accuracy of 0.813 in Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK). The "Open Mic" dataset and accompanying code are now publicly available to support further research.

In contemporary software engineering, Continuous Integration (CI) has become an essential practice for systematically managing the software development lifecycle. However, large organizations often face challenges in maintaining their pipelines efficiently due to the high volume of incremental changes, feature additions, and the involvement of multiple developers across various platforms. These changes necessitate rigorous testing; yet, as teams and projects expand, comprehensive testing becomes increasingly burdensome. Consequently, it is crucial to identify the most pertinent test cases early on without sacrificing software quality. To address this, we have developed Neural Network Embedding for Test Case Prioritization (NNE-TCP), a novel Machine Learning framework. NNE-TCP analyzes file modifications occurring during test status transitions and learns relationships between files and tests by mapping them into multidimensional vectors based on similarity. When new code changes are introduced, the tool prioritizes tests most likely associated with the modified files, thereby reducing the resources required to detect newly introduced faults. Additionally, NNE-TCP facilitates the visualization of entities in low-dimensional spaces, enabling alternative methods for grouping similar files and tests to eliminate redundancies. Our application of NNE-TCP demonstrates, for the first time, that the correlation between modified files and tests is both significant and competitive compared to traditional approaches.

We establish two linear relationships connecting an arbitrary (real, tempered, second-order) generalized stochastic process defined over $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with White Noise processes on the same domain. First, we demonstrate that any such generalized stochastic process can be generated as a linear transformation of White Noise. Second, subject to dimensional compatibility constraints, we show that a generalized stochastic process can be linearly transformed into White Noise. These arguments depend on the regularity theorem for tempered distributions, which facilitates the derivation of a mean-square continuous stochastic process subsequently expressed via a Karhunen-Loève expansion in a suitable Hilbert space. The initial linear relationship further implies that every generalized stochastic process admits an orthogonal series representation composed of deterministic tempered distributions weighted by uncorrelated random variables possessing summable variances. This representation serves as the basis for deriving the second linear relationship.

We investigate the collective behaviors and constraints arising from aggregating individual cooling units through the lens of statistical mechanics. These units, modeled as Thermostatically Controlled Loads (TCLs), represent zones within large residential or commercial buildings. Their energy consumption is managed centrally by an Air Handling Unit (AHU) that supplies cooled air, thereby coupling the TCLs. To identify key qualitative characteristics of the AHU-to-TCL interaction, we developed a realistic yet simplified model and analyzed it under two distinct operational regimes: Constant Supply Temperature (CST) and Constant Power Input (CPI). In both scenarios, our analysis focused on the relaxation dynamics of individual TCL temperatures toward a statistically steady state. We found that while CST dynamics are relatively rapid, causing all TCLs to cluster around the control setpoint, the CPI regime exhibits the emergence of a bi-modal probability distribution characterized by two potentially widely separated time scales. Specifically, the two modes in the CPI regime correspond to all TCLs simultaneously occupying either a low or high temperature state, with occasional collective transitions between these states reminiscent of Kramer's phenomenon in statistical physics. To our knowledge, this phenomenon has been overlooked in multi-zone building energy engineering despite its direct implications for the operation of centralized cooling systems. This finding highlights the necessity of balancing occupant comfort, which depends on individual temperature variations, with the power output predictability that is central to demand response (DR) schemes.

With social media gaining significant traction among young children, it is crucial to investigate the specific needs and requirements of this demographic. To initiate this inquiry, we organized an exploratory design workshop involving children aged ten to eleven to identify their expectations from these platforms. By analyzing the paper prototypes generated during the session, this discussion highlights the social media features most coveted by this age group.

Let \(G\) be a finite group, and let \(\Delta(G)\) represent the \emph{prime graph} constructed from the degrees of the irreducible complex characters of \(G\). It is established that if \(\Delta(G)\) is connected, its diameter does not exceed \(3\). In this paper, we characterize the finite solvable groups where the diameter of this graph reaches this maximum value. Furthermore, this analysis allows us to verify several conjectures put forward by M.L. Lewis.

The $\varLambda^0_b \to \varLambda^+_c K^+ K^- \pi^-$ decay has been observed for the first time using a dataset from proton-proton collisions at center-of-mass energies of $\sqrt{s}=7$ and 8 $\rm{TeV}$ recorded by the $\mbox{LHCb}$ detector, with an integrated luminosity of $3{\rm{fb}^{-1}}$. The ratio of branching fractions for $\varLambda^0_b \to \varLambda^+_c K^+ K^- \pi^-$ and $\varLambda^{0}_{b}\to\varLambda^{+}_{c}D^{-}_{s}$ is determined to be
\begin{equation*} \frac{\mathcal{B} ( \varLambda^0_b \to \varLambda^+_c K^+ K^-
\pi^-) } {\mathcal{B} ( \varLambda^0_b \to \varLambda^+_c D^-_s)} = (9.26 \pm
0.29 \pm 0.46 \pm 0.26)\times10^{-2}, \end{equation*}
where the first uncertainty represents statistical error, the second is systematic, and the third arises from the uncertainty in the $D^-_s \to K^+ K^- \pi^-$ branching fraction. No structure is detected in the invariant mass spectrum of the $\varLambda^+_c K^+$ system, which aligns with the absence of an open-charm pentaquark signal.

Releasing all-pairs shortest path (APSP) distances on general graphs under Differential Privacy (DP) is a notoriously difficult challenge. Previous efforts, such as Sealfon (2016), attempted to achieve DP by adding Laplace noise to edge weights or output distances, but this resulted in a maximal absolute error of roughly $O(n)$ with high probability, where $n$ is the number of nodes. While this error could be reduced for specific graph types, doing so for general graphs remained an open problem, specifically whether the error could be lowered to sublinear in $n$.

We overcome this linear error barrier by proposing an algorithm that privately releases a constructed synthetic graph. For a fixed privacy parameter, computing APSP on this synthetic graph yields an error of $\tilde O(n^{1/2})$. Our approach relies on a novel augmentation of the graph diameter through the creation of "shortcuts." By introducing a specific set of shortcut edges, we ensure that every node pair possesses a shortest path with a link length of $\tilde O(n^{1/2})$. Subsequently, by adding noise with a positive mean to the edge weights, we demonstrate that the augmented graph satisfies differential privacy. This allows the graph to be published for standard APSP computation while answering all pairwise shortest path queries with $\tilde O(n^{1/2})$ approximation error.

Furthermore, we address graphs with a small feedback vertex set (FVS) number. The FVS is the smallest set of vertices whose removal eliminates all cycles, and its size is denoted as $k$. For such graphs, we propose a DP algorithm that achieves an error rate of $\tilde O(k)$.

We develop a microscopic framework to compute cross sections for radiative neutron capture on neutron-rich nuclei, utilizing the continuum random-phase approximation (cRPA) within the time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT). Targeting the r-process, where statistical reaction models are often inadequate, we employ a unified many-body cRPA-TDDFT approach to model the transition from an incident neutron state to a final gamma-decay state. The cRPA method allows for the description of diverse excitation modes in $(n,\gamma)$ reactions, such as soft dipole excitations, giant resonances, non-collective excitations, and single-particle resonances. Additionally, it facilitates the treatment of reactions where gamma transitions terminate in low-lying surface vibrational states. We validate this theory through numerical calculations of the $^{139}{\rm Sn} (n,\gamma) ^{140}{\rm Sn}$ reaction, highlighting features absent in the single-particle model, including narrow and wide resonances arising from non-collective and collective excitations, as well as the influence of low-lying quadrupole and octupole vibrational states.

Current widely used semi-supervised learning techniques based on Graph Neural Networks, including Graph Convolutional Networks, are theoretically incapable of mastering a broad range of neighborhood mixing relationships. To overcome this limitation, we introduce MixHop, a novel model capable of learning such relationships—including difference operators—by iteratively blending feature representations from neighbors at multiple distances. MixHop achieves superior performance against challenging baselines without incurring extra memory usage or computational costs. Furthermore, we introduce sparsity regularization to enable the visualization of how the network prioritizes neighborhood information across various graph datasets. Our analysis of the learned architectures demonstrates that neighborhood mixing strategies differ depending on the specific dataset.

Majority voting is a fundamental technique for enhancing the reliability of outcomes, extensively applied across computer science and other fields. Although this method can improve the accuracy of quantum devices producing classical results, no equivalent procedure existed for quantum outputs. We propose a "quantum majority vote" task: given a product state $|\psi_1\rangle \otimes \dots \otimes |\psi_n\rangle$ where each qubit resides in either of two orthogonal states ($|\psi\rangle$ or $|\psi^\perp\rangle$), determine and output the majority state. Our findings demonstrate that an optimal algorithm for this task achieves a worst-case fidelity of $1/2 + \Theta(1/\sqrt{n})$. Furthermore, if it is promised that at least $2/3$ of the input qubits align with the majority state, the fidelity improves to $1 - \Theta(1/n)$, converging to $1$ as $n$ grows.

We also examine the broader challenge of computing any symmetric and equivariant Boolean function $f: \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ within an unknown quantum basis. We show that an extension of our quantum majority vote algorithm is optimal for this generalized task. The optimal parameters and worst-case fidelity for this generalized approach can be derived via a simple linear program of size $O(n)$. The algorithm operates with a time complexity of $O(n^4 \log n)$, where $n$ represents the number of input qubits.

Standard classification methods often fail to achieve desired performance when applied to real-world datasets containing noisy labels. To address this, we propose Gaussian Mixture Discriminant Analysis (GMDA) tailored for noisy labels within each class. Our approach incorporates flipping and class probabilities, utilizing the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm to resolve the discriminant problem in the presence of label noise, accompanied by detailed convergence proofs. Experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms four other state-of-the-art techniques.

Network alignment, which involves identifying significant node correspondences across different graphs, is a crucial graph mining task with wide-ranging scientific and industrial applications. A fundamental principle in this field is matched neighborhood consistency (MNC), which dictates that nodes situated near each other in one graph should be mapped to nodes that are also proximate in the other. We theoretically establish a strong connection between MNC and alignment accuracy. Since many current methods fail to maintain topological consistency in challenging scenarios, we propose a refinement approach that enhances their MNC to improve results. Our method, RefiNA, is easy to implement, supports scalable sparse approximation, and can be applied post hoc to any existing network alignment algorithm. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that RefiNA boosts the accuracy of various unsupervised alignment techniques by up to 90%, rendering them robust enough to handle graphs that are five times more topologically dissimilar than previously studied.

Species extinction is a critical issue supported by extensive research. This study examines a differential equation model of population dynamics to identify conditions under which multiple species—represented by the coordinates of a bounded solution—are compelled to die out exponentially. Typically, each coordinate corresponds to the population density of a specific species. Our primary method involves constructing "die-out" Lyapunov functions, where a single system may possess numerous such functions, each dependent on a distinct subset of coordinates. The existence of a specific die-out function indicates that at least one species within its associated subset will vanish exponentially for almost all system coefficient choices. By assembling a "team" of these functions, we demonstrate that $k$ specific species must go extinct, with $k$ being determined independently. Additionally, we introduce a "trophic" condition for generalized Lotka-Volterra systems that ensures the existence of a globally attracting trapping region, thereby guaranteeing that all solutions remain bounded.

The range closest pair problem involves building a data structure for a set $S$ of $n$ planar points that identifies the closest pair within any axes-parallel query rectangle $R$ intersecting $S$. While Xue et al.~(SoCG 2018) achieved the best prior result with a structure of size $O(n \log^2 n)$ and query time $O(\log^2 n)$, we demonstrate that a structure of size $O(n \log n)$ can be built in $O(n \log n)$ time. This new structure answers queries in $O(\log n + f \log f)$ time, where $f$ represents the rectangle's aspect ratio; notably, for fat rectangles, the query time reduces to $O(\log n)$. This improvement is derived by reducing the range closest pair problem to standard range searching on the points in $S$.

In baseball, every field play is quantitatively assessed and influences both individual and team tactics. While the weighted on-base average (wOBA) is a recognized metric for a batter's hitting contribution, it overlooks game context—such as base runners—which coaches and hitters account for when devising multiple hitting strategies, despite the effectiveness of these approaches remaining unclear. This uncertainty likely stems from two factors: the inability to directly observe a batter's strategy and the difficulty in estimating its impact. To address this, we introduce a novel estimation method utilizing counterfactual batting simulations. Specifically, we developed a deep learning model capable of adjusting batting ability metrics in response to changes in batting strategy. This approach enables the estimation of various strategic effects, overcoming traditional limitations imposed by actual game data. Our findings indicate that when switching costs between strategies are negligible, employing diverse strategies increases run production; however, when switching costs are factored in, the conditions for gaining an advantage become more restricted. Validation results suggest that our simulation effectively elucidates the impact of utilizing multiple batting strategies.

We establish a structural theorem regarding the semi-conjugacy of orientation-preserving actions of finitely generated solvable groups on real intervals. Applying these findings, we address a problem originally posed by J. F. Plante concerning the conditions under which such actions are semi-conjugate to affine transformations on the line. We demonstrate that for $C^1$ diffeomorphisms acting on closed intervals, this semi-conjugacy always holds. In contrast, while Plante showed this is not universally true for arbitrary homeomorphisms, we prove that a local semi-conjugacy to an affine action persists near the interval endpoints in the form of germs. Furthermore, for a broad category of solvable groups—encompassing all solvable linear groups—we establish the robustness of the family of affine line actions: any homeomorphism action on the line sufficiently proximate to an affine action is semi-conjugate to one. However, this robustness does not extend to all solvable groups, a limitation highlighted by a specific counterexample.

Integrating percolation theory into conformal field theory demands demonstrating that connection probabilities approach a conformally invariant scaling limit. We establish that for critical site percolation on a triangular lattice, the probability of $n$ vertices sharing an open cluster possesses a well-defined scaling limit for all $n \geq 2$. Furthermore, the resulting limit functions $P_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ exhibit covariance under Möbius and local conformal transformations, mirroring the behavior of correlation functions for primary operators in conformal field theory. Specifically, these functions remain invariant under translations, rotations, and inversions, satisfying the scaling relation $P_n(sx_1,\ldots,sx_n)=s^{-5n/48}P_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ for any $s>0$. This property ensures that the ratio $P_3(x_1,x_2,x_3)/\sqrt{P_2(x_1,x_2)P_2(x_1,x_3)P_2(x_2,x_3)}$ remains constant regardless of the positions of $x_1,x_2,x_3$, thereby validating a prediction from physics literature. Additionally, we introduce a site-diluted spin model whose $n$-point correlation functions $\mathrm{C}_{n}$ are expressible via percolation connection probabilities, granting them a well-defined scaling limit with identical characteristics to $P_n$. Notably, $\mathrm{C}_{2}(x_1,x_2)$ equals $P_{2}(x_1,x_2)$. We demonstrate that the magnetization field linked to this spin model converges to a well-defined limit within a suitable space of distributions, transforming covariantly under Möbius transformations with a scaling dimension of $5/48$. A heuristic examination of the magnetization field's four-point function indicates the existence of an extra conformal field with scaling dimension $5/4$, representing percolation four-arm events and corresponding to the "four-leg operator" in conformal field theory.

We report on three Core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) located in elliptical galaxies, identified by the Zwicky Transient Facility Bright Transient Survey (BTS). SN 2019ape, a SN Ic, occurred within the core of a standard elliptical galaxy and aligns with the characteristics of a typical SN Ic progenitor. A secondary peak in its g-band light curve may signal ejecta interaction with circumstellar material (CSM), while an H$\alpha$-emitting source at the site points to residual local star formation. SN 2018fsh and SN 2020uik are SNe II that erupted near the edges of elliptical hosts. SN 2020uik exhibits standard SN II spectra, whereas SN 2018fsh displays a boxy nebular H$\alpha$ profile indicative of CSM interaction. By combining these three events with seven from existing literature, we analyze the host galaxies as a collective sample. We provide multi-wavelength photometry for these hosts and compare it with archival data for all BTS hosts. Based on the spectroscopically complete BTS, we determine that $0.3\%^{+0.3}_{-0.1}$ of all CCSNe take place in elliptical galaxies. We calculate star-formation rates and stellar masses for these host galaxies, contrasting them with properties of other SN hosts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that CCSNe in ellipticals maintain larger physical distances from their host centers compared to SNe Ia in ellipticals, discussing the implications for star-forming activity within these galaxies.

Dynamic computed tomography perfusion (CTP) imaging represents a valuable technique for diagnosing and assessing acute ischemic stroke. This process involves generating hemodynamic parametric maps of the cerebral parenchyma by analyzing repeated CT scans during the initial passage of iodinated contrast through the brain. However, the high radiation exposure resulting from these repeated scans necessitates dose reduction for routine use, making image denoising essential for ensuring diagnostic reliability. This paper introduces a self-supervised deep learning approach for CTP denoising that eliminates the need for high-dose reference images during training. The network is trained by mapping each CTP frame to an estimate derived from its neighboring frames; since the noise in the source and target frames is independent, this strategy effectively removes noise. The ability to operate without high-dose training images allows for easier adaptation to various scanning protocols. Validated on both simulated data and a public real-world dataset, the proposed method outperforms conventional denoising techniques in image quality. Furthermore, when applied to real data, it demonstrated superior spatial resolution and contrast-to-noise ratio compared to supervised learning models trained on simulation data.

Sound propagation within a fluid is fundamentally nonlinear. We investigate the implications of this property for the analogue gravitational field governing sound waves. Our approach begins by outlining how the nonlinearity in the phase fluctuation equation influences the background definition, thereby modifying the effective space-time metric. Next, we employ Riemann invariants for one-dimensional motion to calculate source terms within the effective gravitational field that arise from this nonlinearity. Finally, we demonstrate that these nonlinear effects can be experimentally observed using Bose-Einstein condensates in ultracold gas laboratories.

Let $V: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}$ (with $k \geq 2$) be a nonnegative, smooth potential possessing multiple zeros. We define a curve $\mathfrak{q}: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^k$ as a connecting orbit if it satisfies the autonomous system of ordinary differential equations $\mathfrak{q}'' = \nabla_{\mathbf{u}} V(\mathfrak{q})$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$ and approaches a zero of $V$ as $t \to \pm \infty$. The primary objective of this work is to investigate the existence of such orbits for the aforementioned problem via variational techniques. Although there is extensive literature on the existence of connecting orbits for various second-order systems, to the best of our knowledge, only those orbits that minimize the associated energy functional within an appropriate function space have been established to exist for autonomous multi-well potentials. This paper contributes by establishing existence results for non-minimizing connecting orbits within a specific class of such potentials. These findings are closely aligned with similar results derived by J. Bisgard in his 2005 PhD thesis from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, which addressed non-autonomous periodic multi-well potentials while effectively excluding autonomous cases. Our methodology relies on several refined formulations of the classical Mountain Pass Lemma.

Optimal Power Flow (OPF) is a long-standing domain in power systems aimed at determining the optimal operating points for electrical plants, requiring solutions every few minutes in practical applications. However, nonconvexities inherent in power generation have prevented the development of a rapid and robust technique for solving the full Alternating Current Optimal Power Flow (ACOPF). As power grids have transformed into dynamic, nonlinear, and large-scale control systems, finding faster and more effective ACOPF solutions has become increasingly critical. The emergence of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) enables the natural application of Machine Learning (ML) to graph-based data like power networks, while Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) is renowned for tackling complex decision-making tasks. Although existing literature features solutions utilizing these methods individually, no approach has yet integrated their respective strengths. This paper proposes a novel architecture combining Graph Neural Networks with the Proximal Policy Optimization algorithm to address the Optimal Power Flow problem. The goal is to create a system that learns to solve optimization tasks while maintaining the ability to generalize to unseen scenarios. Our proposed solution is compared against DCOPF based on cost performance, following the training of our DRL agent on the IEEE 30-bus system and subsequent OPF calculations on that network with modified topologies.

We establish novel bounds for the additive energy of regular measures conforming to the Ahlfors-David type in both one and higher dimensions. These findings yield expansion theorems for sums and products of the corresponding regular sets, extending further to broader nonlinear transformations of these sets. Additionally, as a consequence of our higher-dimensional results, we derive new instances of the fractal uncertainty principle applicable to odd dimensions.

This paper determines the asymptotic behavior of recurrence coefficients for polynomials orthogonal against the logarithmic weight $w(x){\rm d}x = \log \frac{2k}{1-x}{\rm d}x$ on the interval $(-1,1)$ where $k > 1$, thereby confirming a conjecture by A. Magnus regarding these coefficients. While employing Riemann-Hilbert and steepest-descent techniques, we deviate from standard approaches due to the absence of a known parametrix for the Riemann-Hilbert problem near the logarithmic singularity at $x=1$.

Obtaining high-quality human labels from crowdsourcing services such as Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) proves more difficult than anticipated. Factors including task instructions, Human Intelligence Task (HIT) structure, and compensation levels significantly influence annotation quality. To prevent low-quality data from skewing the assessment of automatic summarization systems, we propose a three-step qualification pipeline for recruiting superior MTurk workers. Our findings demonstrate that this approach effectively screens out unreliable annotators prior to their participation, yielding high-quality results while optimizing resource allocation. This study offers a foundational framework for recruiting qualified annotators in other complex labeling scenarios.

We investigate a straightforward complex scalar singlet dark matter (DM) model incorporating $Z_3$ symmetry within the type-II seesaw framework. This model accounts for the electron-positron flux excess observed by the AMS-02, DAMPE, and Fermi-LAT collaborations, attributed to triplet decays resulting from DM annihilations in the Galactic halo. Specifically, we examine the non-degenerate scenario where the DM mass exceeds that of the triplets and we intentionally reduce the DM's leptophilic nature to amplify semi-annihilation effects. Under the constraint of $Z_3$ symmetry, fitting antiproton data from PAMELA and AMS experiments reveals that the DM cubic terms and DM-Higgs couplings are tightly restricted, resulting in a semi-annihilation cross-section fraction below $3\%$ for a DM mass of 3 TeV.

This work investigates a variant of the fractal uncertainty principle within the joint time-frequency domain. Specifically, we examine Daubechies' localization operator, which projects onto spherically symmetric Cantor sets formed by $n$ iterations using an arbitrary base $M>1$ and alphabet $\mathscr{A}$. We establish an asymptotic upper bound for the operator norm, up to a multiplicative constant, expressed as a function of the base $M$ and the alphabet size $|\mathscr{A}|$. For any fixed base and alphabet size, we demonstrate the existence of Cantor sets where this asymptote is optimal. Notably, the asymptote is exact for the mid-third Cantor set, previously analyzed in Part I. However, this optimality does not hold universally for all Cantor sets, as we present examples where the optimal asymptote remains unattained.

Since their breakthrough in machine translation, Transformers have become an essential component of text generation models. Previous research credits their success to query-key-value dot-product attention, which offers a strong inductive bias through fully connected token graphs. However, we identified a significant limitation in self-attention: when predicting the (i+1)-th token, it relies primarily on the i-th token as an information source and tends to prioritize tokens similar to itself. Consequently, much of the historical context preceding the i-th token is overlooked. Building on this insight, we introduce Bird-Eye Transformer (BET), a novel architecture that enhances Transformer performance by reweighting self-attention to prioritize crucial historical information. We evaluated BET across various text generation tasks, including machine translation (2 datasets) and language modeling (3 datasets). Our experiments demonstrate that BET outperforms baseline Transformer architectures on all tested datasets. The code is available at: \url{https://sites.google.com/view/bet-transformer/home}.

Deep subspace clustering networks have gained significant traction by employing an auto-encoder to non-linearly project input data into a latent space, combined with a fully connected self-expressiveness module that learns an affinity matrix using standard regularization techniques like sparsity or low-rank constraints. However, these conventional regularization methods often overlook intra-subspace connectivity, thereby restricting clustering efficacy. Moreover, the existing framework struggles with the interdependence between the auto-encoder and self-expressiveness modules, complicating the training process. To address these limitations, we introduce the Maximum Entropy Subspace Clustering Network (MESC-Net). This approach maximizes the entropy of the affinity matrix to enhance connectivity within subspaces, ensuring that elements belonging to the same subspace are uniformly and densely distributed. Additionally, we propose a new framework that explicitly disentangles the auto-encoder and self-expressiveness modules. We further provide a theoretical proof demonstrating that the learned affinity matrix adheres to the block-diagonal property under independent subspaces. Comprehensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations on standard benchmark datasets confirm that MESC-Net significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art methods.

This paper investigates numerous homogeneous Markov decision processes characterized by transition probabilities and costs that are coupled through the empirical distribution of states, a framework known as mean-field. In this setup, the state of any single process remains unknown to the others, resulting in a fully decentralized information structure. The goal is to minimize the average cost, defined as the empirical mean of individual costs, for which a sub-optimal solution is presented. Notably, this solution is independent of the number of processes but converges to the optimal solution of mean-field sharing as the number of processes approaches infinity. Under mild assumptions, the convergence rate of this proposed decentralized approach is demonstrated to be proportional to the square root of the inverse of the number of processes. Typically, deriving this sub-optimal solution requires solving a non-smooth, non-convex optimization problem over an uncountable set; to address this challenge, a combinatorial optimization problem is introduced that attains the same convergence rate.

This report investigates the dynamics of passive quenching in a single-photon avalanche diode. Our analysis relies on a microscopic model of the electron-hole avalanche integrated with the device's equivalent circuit, which comprises a quench resistor and junction capacitance. Analytic formulas for the resulting signal waveform are derived for straightforward electric field setups, while efficient numerical methods are provided for practical device geometries. Additionally, simulations incorporating space charge effects generated by the avalanche reveal that while these effects distort the signal shape, they do not modify the fundamental characteristics or the core quenching mechanism.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) has recently been utilized for sequential estimation and prediction, specifically to formulate hypothetical treatment strategies for septic patients, with a focus on offline learning using observational data. In practice, effective RL depends on deriving informative latent states from sequential observations to optimize treatment plans. However, determining the best method for constructing these states within a healthcare context remains an unresolved challenge. This paper presents an empirical study evaluating various information encoding architectures using data from septic patients in the MIMIC-III dataset to generate patient state representations. We assess the influence of representation dimensionality, correlations with established acuity scores, and the resulting treatment policies. Our findings indicate that sequentially constructed state representations enable effective policy learning in batch environments, supporting a more deliberate approach to representation learning that respects the sequential and partial characteristics of healthcare data.

This paper demonstrates that generic symplectic quotients of a Hamiltonian $G$-space $M$, where $G$ is a compact connected Lie group, can also be realized as symplectic quotients of the same manifold $M$ by a compact torus. This specific torus action is derived from particular integrable systems defined on $\mathfrak{g}^*$, the dual of the Lie algebra of $G$. Notable examples of these systems include the Gelfand-Cetlin systems developed by Guillemin and Sternberg for unitary and special orthogonal groups, as well as integrable systems constructed by Hoffman and Lane for all compact connected Lie groups. Our abelianization theorem applies to smooth quotients and extends more broadly to quotients that form stratified symplectic spaces, consistent with the definition by Sjamaar and Lerman.

We introduce an alternative perspective on established derivative computations for regular expressions, attributed to Brzozowski, Antimirov, and Lombardy and Sakarovitch, to generalize the abstraction of underlying data structures (such as sets or linear combinations) through the concept of a monad. Leveraging this generalization, we propose a novel derivation technique grounded in the graded module monad. Furthermore, we extend expression operators to accommodate any n-ary functions defined over value sets, encompassing standard operations (like negation or intersection for Boolean weights) as well as more complex ones (such as algebraic mean for rational weights). Additionally, we demonstrate how to construct a potentially infinite automaton from these extended expressions by utilizing the categorical definitions of automata proposed by Colcombet and Petrisan; these category theory principles enable a unified construction process regardless of the specific monad employed. Finally, to exemplify our contributions, we offer a Haskell implementation featuring advanced functional programming techniques, accompanied by a web interface for exploring concrete instances.

Anderson acceleration (AA), typically used to hasten the convergence of fixed-point iterations, can also be adapted to enhance optimization techniques. We introduce a new optimization algorithm by applying AA to the energy adaptive gradient method (AEGD). Although AEGD is not a fixed-point iteration, we validate the proposed method based on AEGD's established convergence properties. Furthermore, we quantify the acceleration factor of AA in gradient descent, which corresponds to the gain achieved at each Anderson mixing step. Experimental findings indicate that this algorithm demonstrates rapid convergence with minimal hyperparameter tuning.

This study calculates the two-loop QCD helicity amplitudes for Higgs boson production alongside a bottom-quark pair at a hadron collider. Utilizing the leading colour approximation and a five-flavour scheme—where bottom quarks are treated as massless yet retain a non-zero Yukawa coupling—we derive analytic expressions through numerical evaluations over finite fields. The results are expressed using an independent basis of special functions capable of reliable evaluation across the entire phase space.

The ultrapower $T^{\ast}$ of any ordered set $T$ is presented as an infinitesimal extension, constructed from equivalence classes of sequences in $T$ under a relation defined by an ultrafilter on the natural numbers. It is demonstrated that $T^{\ast}$ invariably satisfies Cantor's property, whereas necessary and sufficient conditions for $T$ to ensure that $T^{\ast}$ is either complete or possesses the open completeness property are identified. Specifically, the open completeness of the extension is governed by the density of the original set $T$, while the completeness of $T^{\ast}$ is determined independently by the cardinality of $T$.

This research examines the summation of finite multiple harmonic $q$-series defined on $r\text{-}(r+1)$ indices at roots of unity for $r=1,2,3$. Furthermore, we establish equivalent conditions for two recent conjectures by Kh. Pilehrood, T. Pilehrood, and R. Tauraso concerning cyclic sums of finite multiple harmonic $q$-series with $1\text{-}2\text{-}3$ indices at roots of unity.

I propose a scenario in which the dense, compact circumstellar matter (CSM) observed when supernova ejecta collide with it within days of a core collapse supernova (CCSN) explosion originates from a specific zone. This zone, surrounding red supergiant (RSG) stars, contains gas that fails to achieve escape velocity alongside the stellar wind. Within this effervescent region, dense clumps are ejected near the RSG surface, expand to distances of tens of astronomical units, and subsequently fall back. By examining two simple velocity distributions for these clumps, I determine that the density of this bound mass can reach tens of times that of the escaping wind, effectively simulating an extremely high mass loss rate. This dense, compact CSM zone offers four key explanations: (1) it accounts for the early collision of CCSNe ejecta with dense CSM; (2) it facilitates high mass loss rates during powerful pre-explosion activity; (3) it forms dust that obscures the progenitor in visible light; and (4) it enables efficient mass transfer to a nearby stellar companion if one exists at tens of astronomical units. Since this effervescent zone can persist for thousands of years or longer, the effervescent CSM model eliminates the need for many Type II CCSN progenitors to undergo a massive outburst only months or years prior to explosion.

Luttinger's pioneering 1964 study established the connection between thermal transport and gravity, a relationship that has since been extensively explored, particularly regarding the thermal Hall effect. This review examines new concepts linking thermal transport to space-time geometry and quantum field theory anomalies. Special attention is given to the interdisciplinary exchange between emergent phenomena in condensed matter physics—specifically Weyl and Dirac semimetals—and gravitational and scale anomalies derived from high-energy physics. The discussion concludes by connecting these ideas to recent experimental progress and outlining several open challenges.

Public goods frequently face inefficiencies, such as overconsumption without regulation or total underutilization, as exemplified by the social distancing measures imposed during the Covid-19 pandemic to cap occupancy in shared spaces. This study addresses this gap by implementing market-based mechanisms to efficiently allocate capacity-constrained public goods. Drawing on Fisher market theory, we assign each agent an artificial currency budget to purchase these goods. While Fisher markets offer a robust framework for resource allocation, they are restricted to scenarios involving only two constraints: individual budgets and good capacities. To overcome this, we propose a modified Fisher market that incorporates additional physical constraints for individuals, defining its solution properties and proving the existence of a market equilibrium. To handle these extra constraints, we formulate a social convex optimization problem where agent budgets are perturbed; the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions of this perturbed problem then yield equilibrium prices. Finally, we introduce a fixed-point algorithm to calculate these budget perturbations, supported by numerical experiments demonstrating convergence. Consequently, our approach resolves a fundamental limitation of classical Fisher markets, which fail to account for constraints beyond capacity and budget.

It is a well-established fact that the maximalization of a locally compact group's coaction on a C*-algebra possesses a universal property. We demonstrate how this significant property can be derived from a categorical framework by utilizing specific characteristics of the maximalization functor for coactions. Additionally, we present a dual proof regarding the universal property of coaction normalization.

This research utilizes fuzzy-based membership-mappings to enable practical, secure distributed deep learning through fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). To overcome the prohibitive computational costs associated with performing secure deep learning on FHE-encrypted data, the study introduces fuzzy attributes. These attributes are derived from locally trained deep models that employ robust, globally convergent variational membership-mappings. By integrating these local models in a flexible and resilient way, the approach allows the global model to be evaluated homomorphically and efficiently via boolean circuits built from bootstrapped binary gates. Despite maintaining privacy within a distributed learning environment, the proposed method ensures accuracy, practicality, and scalability. Its effectiveness is validated through extensive experiments, including demonstrations on the MNIST and Freiburg Groceries datasets, as well as a biomedical application focused on detecting mental stress in individuals.

We enhance the computation of elastic motions caused by dark matter impacts on the surfaces of mirrors used in interferometric gravitational wave detectors. Our study specifically examines the discovery potential of such dark matter signals using the Einstein Telescope, the third-generation European gravitational wave observatory. By incorporating mirror thickness into our model, we predict the existence of multiple resonances within the high-frequency sensitive band of the interferometer. We find that if the dark matter mass exceeds a few PeV or if it is highly boosted, the resulting signal-to-noise ratio could surpass unity, enabling the Einstein Telescope to detect this dark matter signal.

While superradiance in black holes is a well-established concept, a comprehensive framework for superradiance in stars has been absent until now. This gap is notable considering the relative ease of observing isolated neutron stars and the diverse observational signatures that stellar superradiance could produce. This work introduces the first systematic pipeline for calculating superradiance rates in rotating stars. Our approach is adaptable to any Lagrangian describing the interaction between the superradiant field and the star's constituents. The methodology consists of two stages: first, we demonstrate how finite-density field theory can model the absorption of long-wavelength modes as microscopic scattering events, yielding a damped equation of motion for the bosonic field. Second, we integrate this into an effective long-wavelength theory (the worldline formalism) to characterize the amplification of superradiant modes across arbitrary multipole moments for rapidly rotating stars. By establishing a robust theoretical foundation, our method enables the calculation of superradiance rates for any interaction between a bosonic field and stellar matter.

In composite Higgs (CH) frameworks, substantial mixing between the top quark and a new strongly interacting sector is necessary to account for the top's large Yukawa coupling. Consequently, precise measurements involving both top and left-handed bottom quarks provide a valuable avenue for investigating these new physics scenarios. This study examines the effects of third-generation quark pair production at future lepton colliders, converting anticipated effective-field-theory sensitivities into constraints within the CH parameter space. The findings indicate that the top portal can explore a considerable portion of the natural CH parameter space, particularly at center-of-mass energies in the TeV range.

The application of parity-time (PT) symmetry, characterized by balanced gain and loss, has opened diverse avenues in electronics, ranging from wireless energy transfer to telemetry sensing and topological defect engineering. Yet, current implementations typically rely on ad-hoc methods at low frequencies and struggle with large-scale integration. In this work, we present a fully integrated realization of PT symmetry using standard complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology. Our demonstration highlights key PT features, including phase transitions and the capacity to control broadband microwave generation and propagation, surpassing the constraints of previous approaches. Compared to conventional oscillatory microwave generation, the system achieves a 2.1-fold increase in bandwidth and a 30% reduction in noise. Furthermore, in non-oscillatory mode, it exhibits significant non-reciprocal microwave transport between 2.75 and 3.10 GHz, driven by enhanced nonlinearities. This methodology has the potential to expand integrated circuit (IC) design beyond current performance boundaries and facilitate the investigation of topological effects in high-dimensional non-Hermitian systems using scalable IC technology.

We propose a van der Waals (vdW) charge qubit, electrostatically trapped within two-dimensional (2D) vdW materials, as a potential component for future quantum computers. This proposal is systematically evaluated by examining the two-level anti-crossing energy difference ($\Delta$), using bilayer graphene ($\Delta \approx 0$) and a vdW heterostructure ($\Delta \gg 0$) as representative cases. The qubit's state is defined by the tunable electronic properties achieved through an external electric field. By integrating density functional theory with quantum transport calculations, we identify optimal operational conditions grounded in charge stability and energy-level diagrams. Additionally, we introduce a single-electron transistor (SET) measurement setup utilizing trilayer vdW heterostructures capacitively coupled to the charge qubit, offering reduced decoherence and enhanced measurement capabilities. Our findings indicate that a $\Delta$ exceeding 20 meV causes rapid qubit state mixing, thereby diminishing measurement metrics such as contrast and conductance. With appropriately optimized designs, qubit architectures based on 2D vdW structures could be integrated into a fully electronic quantum computing platform.

This paper explores the foundational concepts of Modern Coexistence Theory (MCT), a quantitative approach to ecological coexistence. To apply MCT in inferring species coexistence, researchers must bridge complex real-world simulation models with simplified frameworks that encode existing coexistence theories. This process involves three stages: 1) linking coexistence to invasion growth rates, 2) mathematically decomposing these rates into distinct coexistence mechanisms, and 3) connecting these mechanisms to established simple explanations. While prior work has mainly addressed stage 2, this study examines the remaining critical steps and their significance for identifying coexistence drivers in natural communities. Our analysis of stage 3 acts as a heuristic for generating hypotheses in new models and clarifies common misconceptions; for instance, it clarifies that the storage effect is distinct from bet-hedging or robust life-history storage, notes that relative nonlinearity likely fosters coexistence more than previously believed, and identifies fitness-density covariance as a composite of various explanations such as the competition-colonization trade-off, heteromyopia, and spatially varying resource ratios. Furthermore, we review additional MCT topics, including the function of "scaling factors," the approximate nature of coexistence mechanisms, the relative importance of invasion growth rate magnitude versus sign, Hutchinson's resolution of the plankton paradox, and the scale-dependence of these mechanisms, among others.

We thoroughly examine two distinct mechanisms responsible for the loss of non-Gaussian correlations in an isolated quantum system undergoing out-of-equilibrium dynamics after interactions are switched off. The first mechanism relies on spatial scrambling, leading to locally Gaussian steady states in large systems over extended periods. The second, termed "canonical transmutation," involves the mixing of a pair of canonically conjugate fields: one initially displaying non-Gaussian fluctuations and the other Gaussian and dynamically dominant. This process results in relative Gaussianity even at finite system sizes and times. We assess signatures of these two potential mechanisms in a recent experiment involving an atom-chip controlled ultracold gas where Gaussification was observed, concluding that canonical transmutation, rather than spatial scrambling, drives this phenomenon in the experiment. Both mechanisms share the characteristic that the Gaussian correlations dynamically revealed by the quench were already present at the initial time, albeit practically inaccessible. Along the way, we introduce novel observations based on the experimental data, including clustering of equilibrium correlations, analysis of full counting statistics dynamics, and tomographic reconstructions of quantum field states. Our work aims to offer an accessible overview of the potential of atom-chip experiments to investigate fundamental aspects of quantum field theories through quantum simulations.

Constructing many-body interaction Hamiltonians is a fundamental objective in quantum simulation, yet synthesizing interactions involving more than two spins remains a significant challenge. By leveraging techniques from quantum optics, we successfully engineered a five-body spin-exchange interaction within a superconducting quantum circuit. This was achieved by simultaneously exciting four independent qubits using time-energy correlated photon quadruples derived from a qudit. Throughout the dynamic evolution of this five-body interaction, a Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state was generated in a single step with an estimated fidelity of 0.685. Furthermore, we analyzed how noise impacts three-, four-, and five-body interactions to advance our understanding of the quantum origins of chiral molecules. Additionally, we demonstrated a many-body Mach-Zehnder interferometer that exhibits potential Heisenberg-limit sensitivity. This research establishes a pathway for quantum simulations encompassing complex many-body interactions and highly excited states in quantum circuits.

The significance of precisely modeling two-way coupled interactions between complex-shaped particles and rarefied gas flows is increasingly critical in fields like aerospace and semiconductor manufacturing. These transport phenomena are frequently simulated using an Euler-Lagrangian Point-Particle framework, which incorporates rarefaction effects through phenomenological Cunningham corrections applied to drag forces. However, standard Point-Particle methods typically ignore explicit dependencies on finite particle size, shape, orientation, and momentum accommodation coefficients. This study addresses this limitation by developing heuristic drag force models for ellipsoidal particles of varying aspect ratios, derived from fully resolved DSMC simulations. These models integrate predictions for gas-surface interaction effects via the tangential momentum accommodation coefficient (TMAC). The resulting corrections can enhance standard Euler-Lagrangian Point-Particle simulations in rarefied gas flows by accounting for shape, orientation, and TMAC influences. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these drag corrections, originally valid for unbounded flows, may also apply to scenarios where particles move near solid walls. This conclusion is supported by an investigation into near-wall drag effects on prolate ellipsoids; while confinement increases drag compared to unbounded conditions, these effects remain negligible at large Knudsen numbers, even when the particle contacts a solid wall.

In filter-bank multicarrier (FBMC) systems, intrinsic interference poses the primary obstacle to achieving full diversity gain in multi-input multi-output (MIMO) channels. This paper introduces a new multicarrier architecture termed the FBMC offset upper-lower polyphase network (FBMC/OULP). To eradicate intrinsic interference, this system transmits complex-valued symbols alternately through the upper and lower branches of the polyphase network with a time offset. The FBMC/OULP maintains a symbol density of one complex-valued symbol per time-frequency lattice point. Furthermore, when operating over frequency-selective channels, a minimum mean square error (MMSE) estimator is utilized at the receiver to mitigate interference resulting from channel frequency selectivity. Leveraging the circular convolutional property, the proposed scheme effectively suppresses interference between symbols in the upper and lower polyphase branches. Consequently, by employing complex-valued symbols and minimizing interference, the system achieves full diversity gain from orthogonal space-time block codes (OSTBC) in MIMO environments using a computationally efficient maximum likelihood (ML) detector. Simulation results comparing this approach to orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) demonstrate that the FBMC/OULP system delivers superior performance in fast multi-path fading scenarios and competitive performance in slow multi-path fading conditions.

Standard neural networks often fail to generalize when facing distribution shifts. In computer vision, the leading method for out-of-distribution generalization currently involves averaging weights throughout a single training run. This paper introduces Diverse Weight Averaging (DiWA), a modification that averages weights from multiple independent training runs instead of one. Surprisingly, this approach performs effectively even under soft constraints despite the network's nonlinear nature. The primary goal of DiWA is to enhance functional diversity among the averaged models; models from different runs exhibit greater diversity than those from a single run due to variations in hyperparameters and training procedures. We justify the necessity of this diversity through a novel bias-variance-covariance-locality decomposition of expected error, drawing parallels between DiWA and standard functional ensembling. Furthermore, this decomposition reveals that DiWA succeeds when the variance term is dominant, a condition we demonstrate occurs when the marginal distribution shifts at test time. Empirically, DiWA consistently outperforms the state of the art on the DomainBed benchmark without incurring additional inference costs.

We examine the empirical validity of the monocentric standard urban model (SUM) using a distinctive dataset of gridded variables—including population density, rents, housing sizes, and transportation—across 192 global cities. The findings suggest that the SUM effectively captures the internal structure of urban areas in both developed and developing nations. Consistent with theory, cities expand when they are wealthier, more populous, or when transportation and farmland costs decline. Specifically, 100% and 87% of the cities display the anticipated negative gradients in density and rent, respectively; on average, a 1% drop in income net of transport costs results in a 21% reduction in density and a 3% drop in rent per square meter. Furthermore, we analyze variations among cities regarding their degree of monocentricity, informality, and amenities based on their distinct characteristics.

We begin by examining the electrodynamics of charges and currents in a vacuum before extending these findings to describe dielectric and magnetic media, first using spatial algebra (SA) and subsequently space-time algebra (STA). By defining a polarization multivector $\tilde{P} = \boldsymbol{\tilde{p}} -\,\frac{1}{c}\,\boldsymbol{\tilde{M}}$ and an auxiliary electromagnetic field multivector $G = \varepsilon_0\,F + \tilde{P}$, we formulate the Maxwell equations for material media within SA. In STA, introducing a bound current vector $\tilde{J} = J -\,c\,\nabla\cdot\tilde{P}$ allows us to express the Maxwell equations accordingly. The wave equation for a material medium is derived by applying the gradient operator to the Maxwell equation. For a uniform medium characterized by induced electric and magnetic dipoles, the stress-energy momentum vector is expressed as $\dot{T}\left(\dot{\nabla}\right) = \frac{1}{c}\,J \cdot F = f$, where $f$ represents the electromagnetic force density vector in space-time. Ultimately, the Maxwell equation for a material medium can be reformulated in STA as a wave equation governing the potential vector $A$.

We implement a novel null geodesic approach to identify gravitational memory, locating the bulk memory within the Newman-Unti gauge near the boundary of conformally compactified spacetime. We demonstrate how conserved charges emerging in the subleading terms of the large-$r$ expansion of BMS charges allow us to define gravitational memory at each order of the non-linearized gravitational theory. Additionally, we determine the gravitational shift along the $r$ direction. It is established that the longitudinal displacement at the $1/r$ order corresponds to the relative change in detector radius originally derived by Strominger and Zhiboedov.

Composition serves as a critical aspect of specification languages, facilitating the construction of complex systems from their constituent parts. Equally vital is decomposition, which allows for the analysis of a system's structural properties. Typically, however, a system admits multiple decomposition strategies, each tailored to optimize distinct criteria. This work extends an algebraic component-based model for cyber-physical systems to address decomposition. In this framework, components combine via a suite of algebraic products and separate, under specific conditions, using a corresponding set of division operators. We employ division to define system invariants and to represent preferred updates. Finally, we apply this framework to the design of a cyber-physical system involving robots navigating a shared field, utilizing the division operator to identify desirable updates.

Strong gravitational lensing serves as a distinct observational instrument for analyzing the distribution of both luminous and dark mass within and between galaxies. Due to the presence of substructures, contemporary strong lensing observations necessitate more intricate mass models than smooth analytical profiles, such as power-law ellipsoids. In this study, we present a continuous neural field capable of predicting the lensing potential at any location within the image plane, facilitating a nearly model-independent characterization of the lensing mass. We tested our approach on simulated Hubble Space Telescope imaging data featuring various perturbations applied to a smooth mass distribution, including localized dark subhalos, populations of subhalos, and external shear effects. By assuming knowledge of the source surface brightness, we employed the continuous neural field to model either the perturbations in isolation or the complete lensing potential. In both scenarios, the generated model successfully fitted the imaging data, enabling the accurate recovery of properties for both the smooth potential and the perturbations. Unlike many other deep learning techniques, our method explicitly incorporates lensing physics (specifically the lens equation) and introduces high flexibility only where necessary, within the lens potential. Furthermore, the neural network does not rely on pre-training with large labeled datasets and derives the potential from a single observed lensing image. Our model is integrated into the fully differentiable lens modeling framework known as Herculens.

This study reports the simultaneous detection of flux variations in the massive young stellar object G036.70+00.09 (G036.70) across both maser emission and mid-infrared (MIR; $\lambda=3$--$5$~$\mu$m) wavelengths. By analyzing approximately a decade of data from the ALLWISE and NEOWISE archives, sampled every six months, we confirmed that G036.70 exhibits stochastic year-long MIR variability without corresponding color changes in the W1 (3.4~$\mu$m) $-$ W2 (4.6~$\mu$m) bands. Cross-referencing these MIR observations with high-cadence 6.7~GHz class II methanol maser flux data, previously identified as having a 53.0--53.2 day period via a Hitachi 32-m radio telescope, reveals flux correlations at both daily and yearly timescales. Such dual-timescale correlations in MYSOs have not been previously reported, except during accretion burst phases. These findings support the hypothesis that class II methanol masers are energized by infrared radiation from the accretion disks of MYSOs. We further explore potential origins for the observed MIR and maser variability. To reconcile the stochastic year-long MIR variability (characterized by minimal color change) with the maser-MIR correlation, we propose that changes in the mass accretion rate and line-of-sight extinction caused by nonaxisymmetric dust density structures within a rotating accretion disk are plausible mechanisms. Future spectroscopic monitoring of accretion-related emission lines is crucial for definitively identifying the source of the variability in G036.70.

This study theoretically examines the nonlinear propagation of heavy-ion-acoustic (HIA) waves within a four-component multi-ion plasma, which consists of inertial heavy negative ions, light positive ions, inertialess nonextensive electrons, and positrons. Utilizing the reductive perturbation method, the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation is derived. The results indicate that this equation predicts modulational instability (MI) in HIA waves and the emergence of heavy-ion-acoustic rogue waves (HIARWs), phenomena driven by the interplay of nonlinearity and dispersion during wave propagation. Key conditions for MI and fundamental characteristics of the resulting HIARWs are identified. Furthermore, it is noted that critical features of these waves—including instability thresholds, MI growth rates, and the amplitude and width of HIARWs—are substantially altered by factors such as the nonextensivity of electrons and positrons, the mass ratio between light positive and heavy negative ions, the density ratio of electrons to light positive ions, and the temperature ratio of electrons to positrons. Finally, the relevance of these findings to both laboratory settings, such as laser-plasma interaction experiments, and space environments, including cometary comae and Earth's ionosphere, is highlighted.

Text-video retrieval holds significant practical importance and has garnered growing interest, with learning spatial-temporal video representations emerging as a key research focus. However, current state-of-the-art video retrieval models typically employ fixed pre-trained vision backbones for their video encoders, limiting their ability to evolve and generate fine-grained spatial-temporal representations. To address this, we introduce the Token Shift and Selection Network (TS2-Net), a novel transformer architecture designed for dynamic token sequence adjustment and the selection of informative tokens across both temporal and spatial dimensions. The token shift module facilitates back-and-forth shifting of token features between adjacent frames to maintain complete representations and detect subtle movements, while the token selection module isolates tokens most critical for local spatial semantics. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that TS2-Net achieves state-of-the-art results on leading text-video retrieval benchmarks, setting new records on MSRVTT, VATEX, LSMDC, ActivityNet, and DiDeMo.

Langevin MCMC gradient optimization has become a widely adopted approach for estimating posterior distributions. This study investigates the application of this algorithm in a decentralized environment, where agents distributed across a network collaboratively solve the problem via peer-to-peer gossip communication. Theoretically, we establish three key results: 1) the time-complexity required to achieve $\epsilon$-consensus in the continuous-time stochastic differential equation framework; 2) the convergence rate in the $L^2$ norm toward consensus for the discrete implementation utilizing the Euler-Maruyama discretization; and 3) the convergence rate in the Wasserstein metric to the optimal stationary distribution under the discretized dynamics.

This paper introduces an efficient numerical solver for the A-Phi formulation in electromagnetics, utilizing the discrete exterior calculus (DEC) framework. The A-Phi approach is particularly suited for broadband and multi-scale analysis due to its immunity to low-frequency breakdown. By employing the generalized Lorenz gauge, the method decouples the A and Phi equations. The formulation is discretized via DEC, which represents a discretized form of exterior calculus from differential geometry. Essentially, DEC extends the finite difference method by naturally preserving Stokes' and Gauss's theorems. Unlike the finite difference method, which relies on rectangular grids, DEC supports unstructured mesh schemes, such as tetrahedral meshes. Consequently, the proposed DEC-based A-Phi solver is inherently stable, free from spurious solutions, and capable of efficiently modeling highly complex structures. The study provides background on the A-Phi formulation and DEC, along with technical details for implementing the solver under various boundary conditions. Numerical examples are included to validate the approach.

This review focuses on the features of topological superconductivity in two-dimensional systems lacking spin-orbit interaction, specifically those with long-range non-collinear spin ordering or magnetic skyrmions. It also provides a concise overview of the emerging concept of higher-order topological superconductivity in two-dimensional systems, including those with spin-orbit coupling. The discussion covers the generation of Majorana modes through magnetic textures, emphasizing the roles of effective triplet pairings and the odd fermion parity of the ground state wave function across various systems. We detail the unique characteristics of magnetic skyrmions that facilitate the creation of Majorana modes and the defects where these modes become localized. Furthermore, the review examines braiding phenomena in two-dimensional systems, with particular attention to higher-order topological superconductors.

This study investigates the application of multi-modal data, specifically combining accelerometry and Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals, to classify animal behaviors. We derive three novel features from the GNSS data: distance to water, median speed, and median estimated horizontal position error. To integrate information from both sensing modalities, we employ two strategies. The first involves concatenating features from both sensors and feeding the resulting vector into a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) classifier. The second strategy fuses the posterior probabilities generated by two separate MLP classifiers, where each classifier processes features from a single sensing mode. We assess the efficacy of these multimodal classification algorithms using two real-world datasets gathered via smart cattle collar and ear tags. Leave-one-animal-out cross-validation demonstrates that both methods significantly enhance classification performance compared to using data from a single sensor mode, with particularly notable improvements for infrequent yet critical behaviors such as walking and drinking. Both algorithms demand minimal computational and memory resources, making them well-suited for deployment on the embedded systems within our collar and ear tags. However, the algorithm based on posterior probability fusion is superior to the feature concatenation approach, offering higher classification accuracy, lower computational and memory complexity, greater robustness to sensor failures, and improved modularity.

We establish that flavour-changing neutral currents within the top sector, facilitated by leptophilic scalars at the electroweak scale, can readily emerge in new physics frameworks, specifically composite Higgs models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that while current experimental data offers limited constraints on these interactions, the LHC can probe them through rare top decays and, more broadly, via the process $pp\to tS(S)+j$, where $S\to\ell^+\ell^-$. Our dedicated analyses reveal that with an integrated luminosity of $\mathcal{L} = 150$ fb$^{-1}$, cut-off scales up to $\Lambda\sim$ 90 TeV can be investigated.

Among humanity's earliest mathematical investigations may have been the study of geometric patterns found in nature. The spiral arrangements seen in cactus spines, sunflower seeds, and leaf placement on branches display a remarkable regularity that illustrates complex mathematical principles. Remarkably, the count of these spirals often corresponds to consecutive pairs within the Fibonacci sequence (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55...), which follows a straightforward rule where each number is the sum of the two preceding ones (e.g., 1+2=3, 2+3=5). This article explores how physics elucidates the origins of this phenomenon by connecting it to the mechanics of deformable lattices that grow and restructure under stress.

This paper introduces Differentiable Network Adaption (DNA), a new approach that tailors existing networks to specific computational budgets by differentially adjusting their width and depth. By leveraging gradient-based optimization, DNA automates the tuning of these dimensions, overcoming the limitations of prior heuristic methods that depend heavily on manual human expertise. Furthermore, we propose an elastic search space capable of flexibly expanding or contracting during optimization, enabling bi-directional adjustments to network width and depth. Through DNA, we successfully optimize network architectures by dynamically condensing and expanding across both dimensions. Extensive experiments on ImageNet show that DNA can adapt pre-existing networks to meet various computational targets with superior performance compared to previous methods. Additionally, DNA further enhances the accuracy of high-performance networks generated by state-of-the-art neural architecture search techniques, such as EfficientNet and MobileNet-v3.

This work introduces a sheaf-theoretic framework for differential calculi on quantum principal bundles defined over non-affine bases, with quantum flags serving as our primary examples. For a first-order differential calculus on the bundle's total space that is covariant under the quantum structure group, we construct calculi on both the base and the structure Hopf algebra when the base is affine. In cases where the base is projective, we instead construct calculi on the sheaf of localizations; these induce canonical differential structures on the base sheaf and the structure Hopf algebra, and conversely. The specific instance of the quantum principal bundle $\mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SL}_2)$ over $\mathrm{P}^1(\mathbb{C})$ is examined in depth.

This paper constructs a tropical moduli space that parametrizes divisor roots on tropical curves. We investigate the relationship between this space and the skeleton of Jarvis's moduli space of limit root nets on stable curves. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the combinatorial structure of the tropical roots moduli space is controlled by a poset of flows, which parametrizes specific graph flows.

High-resolution observations frequently reveal jets within light bridges (LBs) on the Sun, yet the specific contributions of convection versus the magnetic field in initiating these jets remain uncertain. We present a detailed study of a small, fan-shaped jet observed along an LB using the 1.6-meter Goode Solar Telescope (GST) equipped with the TiO Broadband Filter Imager (BFI), the Visible Imaging Spectrometer (VIS) in Hα, and the Near-Infrared Imaging Spectropolarimeter (NIRIS), capturing both spectral data and Stokes parameters. The instruments' superior spatial and temporal resolution enabled a thorough analysis of the jet's features. By constructing Hα Dopplergrams, we determined that the plasma initially moved upward before flowing back during the jet's second phase. Analysis of time-slice diagrams revealed the propagation speed of the jet's bright base and fan; the fan-shaped structure emerged within minutes with diverging beams. At its base, a bright point slid along the LB before invading the sunspot's umbra. Similar to Ellerman bombs, the Hα profiles of these bright points showed enhanced intensity in the wings. Simultaneously, extreme ultraviolet brightenings formed at the front of the dark jet material and traveled at the same velocity as the fan, suggesting that the jet material compressed and heated the surrounding coronal plasma. Our multi-wavelength analysis suggests that magnetic reconnection across highly diverging fields in the lower chromosphere may have generated the fan-shaped jet, causing an apparent slipping motion along the LB. However, we did not detect the opposing magnetic polarity at the jet base typically associated with such reconnection. Consequently, we explore alternative triggering mechanisms involving waves and convection.

We present Graphene, an Open IE system designed to produce accurate, meaningful, and comprehensive propositions to support diverse downstream semantic tasks. To achieve this, we convert syntactically intricate input sentences into clean, compact core facts paired with their contexts, simultaneously identifying the rhetorical relations connecting them to maintain semantic integrity. This approach preserves the contextual information of relational tuples extracted from source sentences, creating a new lightweight semantic representation for Open IE that significantly improves the expressiveness of the generated propositions.

We establish a collection of fully Lorentz-invariant wave packets that span the associated one-particle Hilbert subspace and, consequently, the entire Fock space, complete with an explicitly Lorentz-invariant resolution of the identity. The position-momentum uncertainty relation governing these Lorentz-invariant wave packets differs from the standard Heisenberg uncertainty principle but converges to it within the non-relativistic limit.

Given an odd positive integer $n$ and an odd prime $p$, we establish an infinite collection of quadruples of imaginary quadratic fields, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d+1})$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d+4})$, and $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d+4p^2})$ where $d \in \mathbb{Z}$, such that the class number of each field is a multiple of $n$. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of an infinite family of quintuples consisting of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d+1})$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d+4})$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d+36})$, and $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d+100})$ with $d \in \mathbb{Z}$, where all class numbers are divisible by $n$. These findings offer a comprehensive proof of Iizuka's conjecture (along with a generalization thereof) for the case $m=1$. Additionally, they positively resolve a weaker variant of a generalized Iizuka's conjecture for $m \geq 4$.

Addressing the intricacies of network data, we introduce a directed hybrid random network that combines preferential attachment (PA) and uniform attachment (UA) mechanisms. Upon the creation of a new edge, it adheres to the PA rule with probability $p\in[0,1]$; otherwise, it connects two nodes chosen uniformly at random. This blending results in slower growth rates for both in- and out-degrees of a fixed node compared to a pure PA model, thereby producing lighter distributional tails. We subsequently develop and apply inference methods for this hybrid model to both synthetic and real datasets. Our findings demonstrate that the additional flexibility provided by parameter $p$ enables the hybrid network to better align with real-world scenarios, specifically those characterized by lighter tails in in- and out-degrees.

With the exponential growth in data volume and scale, federated learning has become increasingly critical for high-performance computing and machine learning applications. Although it was once assumed that sharing gradients during training would adequately protect local data privacy, Zhu et al. [2019] proved otherwise by demonstrating that raw data could be reconstructed from these gradients using generated dummy data optimized to minimize distance from the real dataset. Building on this, Zhao et al. [2020] enhanced the attack's effectiveness by substituting the standard loss function with cross-entropy loss, thereby achieving a higher fidelity threshold. To counter such threats, this paper introduces an additional dropout layer prior to the classifier input. This approach significantly mitigates raw data leakage; specifically, even after 5,800 training epochs with a dropout rate of 0.5, the model fails to converge to a low Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), indicating successful protection of the training data.

Long-Tailed Semi-Supervised Learning (LTSSL) focuses on training models with class-imbalanced datasets containing limited annotations.
