This study calculates numerical approximations of such solutions for NSE on two-dimensional domains featuring non-periodic boundary conditions and empirically examines the convergence of both these approximations and their associated observables. The numerical solver employed combines Monte Carlo sampling with a deterministic solver based on H(div)-FEM. Numerical experiments involving high Reynolds number turbulent flows indicate that the statistics and observables of the approximations indeed converge. Furthermore, we introduce a new algorithm designed to compute structure functions on unstructured meshes.

A high-dimensional artificial neural network interatomic potential for molybdenum has been developed. This potential was trained and validated using density functional theory (DFT) calculations on structural and property data relevant to fracture, including elastic constants, surface energies, generalized stacking fault energies, and surface decohesion energies. The model achieves a root mean square error of less than 5 meV per atom for total energies in both the training and validation sets. Subsequently, the potential was utilized to examine screw dislocation core characteristics and perform extensive fracture simulations. These studies indicate that the 1/2$\langle111\rangle$ screw dislocation core is non-degenerate and symmetric, while mode I fracture exhibits brittle behavior. Consequently, this potential is expected to be highly effective for large-scale atomistic simulations of plasticity and fracture.

This study introduces a robust adaptive algorithm for smooth graph signal recovery grounded in generalized correntropy, accompanied by a specifically defined cost function. The algorithm is derived, and a variant utilizing kernel width learning is proposed; simulation results demonstrate its superiority over the version employing a fixed correntropy kernel. Furthermore, the paper provides theoretical analysis, beginning with an examination of the cost function's convexity, followed by an investigation into the algorithm's uniform stability, mean convergence analysis, and complexity assessment. Additionally, both synthetic and real-world experiments highlight the proposed algorithm's advantages relative to other adaptive methods found in the literature on graph signal recovery.

A junction connecting two superconductors via a normal metal supports Andreev bound states, creating a phase-dependent energy spectrum with a minigap that drives a periodic supercurrent. At finite frequencies, phase-dependent dissipation arises from the relaxation of these bound states. Although dissipation and supercurrent responses near thermal equilibrium have been studied, their nonequilibrium behavior remains unclear. By measuring the ac susceptibility of a graphene-superconductor junction under microwave irradiation, we observe that the supercurrent response diverges from the adiabatic ac Josephson effect when the irradiation frequency exceeds the relaxation rate. Remarkably, as the frequency rises above the minigap, dissipation increases at phase 0—where the minigap is widest and equilibrium dissipation is lowest. We attribute this to a nonequilibrium distribution function enabling additional transitions within the same side of the minigap. These findings indicate that phase-dependent dissipation is more sensitive to microwave irradiation than supercurrent, offering a novel approach to exploring photon-assisted physics in proximitized superconducting systems.

Identifying jets that originate from beauty and charm quarks is crucial for analyzing Standard Model processes and searching for new physics. This study evaluates the performance of algorithms designed to select $b$- and $c$-quark jets using LHCb data from proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV (2011) and $\sqrt{s}=8$ TeV (2012). For jets with transverse momentum $p_{\rm T} > 20$ GeV and pseudorapidity $2.2 < \eta < 4.2$, the identification efficiency is approximately 65% for $b$ jets and 25% for $c$ jets, with a light-parton misidentification probability of 0.3%. Additionally, the analysis examines how performance varies with the jet's $p_{\rm T}$ and $\eta$.

All-optical ultrasound detection offers distinct advantages for photoacoustics, such as broader bandwidth, enhanced signal-to-noise ratio per unit area, and reduced vulnerability to electromagnetic interference. These benefits have made optical detection a pivotal technique for photoacoustic applications in biological and medical fields. Nevertheless, free-space detectors are prone to optical aberrations, which can diminish pressure sensitivity and compromise image quality. Although fiber-based spatial mode filtering has been suggested to mitigate these issues in Fabry-Pérot pressure sensors, its practical efficacy has not been thoroughly examined. This study provides a rigorous and quantitative comparison between free-space and fiber-coupled detectors using a custom correlative setup. The results demonstrate that fiber-coupled systems outperform free-space counterparts in both signal strength and image quality within realistic all-optical photoacoustic tomography scenarios.

Countable locally standard measure algebras are parameterized by a pair consisting of a Steinitz number and a real number that is at least 1. This result serves as an analogue to the theorems established by J. Dixmier and A. A. Baranov.

This paper addresses the pointwise approximation of solutions to stochastic differential equations (SDEs) driven by an infinite-dimensional Wiener process and additional jumps from a Poisson random measure. We provide upper error bounds for the suggested truncated randomized Euler scheme. Furthermore, we derive matching upper and lower bounds (up to constant factors) for $\varepsilon$-complexity, demonstrating that the proposed algorithm is optimal within the Information-Based Complexity (IBC) framework. Additionally, we present results from numerical experiments conducted using GPU architecture.

We report an $L$-band (2.98--3.96$\mu$m) spectroscopic analysis of eight young L dwarfs spanning spectral types L2 to L7. Utilizing the Gemini Near-InfraRed Spectrograph, we obtained spectra with resolutions ($\lambda/\Delta\lambda$) ranging from approximately 250 to 600. Our investigation focuses on the young $L$-band spectral sequence, specifically tracking the evolution of the methane $Q$-branch absorption feature at 3.3 $\mu$m. We observe that this feature emerges between spectral types L3 and L6, consistent with findings from older field dwarfs. Additionally, we assessed how well five distinct grids of atmospheric models reproduce both the $L$-band and published near-IR (0.7--2.5 $\mu$m) spectra through fitting procedures. Comparing best-fit parameters derived from combined near-IR and $L$-band data against those from near-IR data alone reveals that incorporating $L$-band observations lowers the best-fit effective temperature by roughly 100 K. Furthermore, models including clouds and a vertical mixing rate ($K_{\mathrm{zz}}$) favor configurations with thick clouds and elevated $K_{\mathrm{zz}}$ values. For five objects with previously published effective temperatures, surface gravities, age estimates, and bolometric luminosities derived from evolutionary models, we compared model spectra against our data. This comparison indicates that disequilibrium chemistry and clouds are necessary to match the established temperatures. Finally, as three of these objects belong to the AB Dor moving group, we demonstrate the temperature dependence of the methane $Q$-branch.

We provide a combinatorial proof for a formula expressing the partial sums of the $k$-bonacci sequence as alternating sums of powers of two multiplied by binomial coefficients. As a corollary, we derive a formula for the $k$-bonacci numbers.

We provide initial findings from the first convergent global analyses of multiple minimal composite Higgs frameworks. These fits utilize the differential evolution tool $\texttt{Diver}$ and incorporate diverse physical constraints, notably a broad spectrum of Run 2 LHC exclusion limits on heavy resonance production. Additionally, as an outcome of these fits, we examine the collider signatures of the lightest new up-type and down-type resonances within the viable model regions, identifying several low-mass candidates accessible to future collider experiments.

Many-body systems with long-range interactions can persist in quasi-stationary states far from thermodynamic equilibrium, typically manifested as counter-propagating density clusters or a single non-homogeneous core-halo structure within the particle phase-space. Through particle simulations utilizing the Hamiltonian mean-field model, we demonstrate that this framework accommodates stationary states featuring multiple clusters or particle holes in phase-space density. Furthermore, we outline a mechanism driven by wave-wave and wave-particle interactions responsible for forming these clusters and define these novel quasi-stationary states according to the simulation's initial parameters.

Differential privacy (DP) applied to text rewriting offers robust theoretical safeguards for individual privacy within documents. However, current systems often struggle to verify their privacy claims, resulting in issues regarding transparency and reproducibility. To address these challenges, we present DP-Rewrite, an open-source, modular, and highly customizable framework for differentially private text rewriting. This system integrates diverse downstream datasets, models, pre-training protocols, and evaluation metrics to facilitate flexible research and validation in private text rewriting. As a practical demonstration, we conducted a case study on the ADePT system, utilizing our framework to identify a privacy leak within its pre-training methodology. Publicly accessible, we aim for DP-Rewrite to enhance the accessibility and transparency of DP text rewriting research across the community.

This study investigates how Run 2 LHC data influences general Composite Higgs models, specifically examining scenarios where non-linear effects, mixing with extra scalars, and new fermionic states jointly alter Higgs characteristics. We derive updated experimental constraints on the compositeness scale, the mixing between the Higgs and singlet or doublet states, as well as the mass and mixing angle of top-partners. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in frameworks involving new fermions in electroweak symmetry breaking, there is a significant interconnection among measurements of Higgs couplings, boosted Higgs attributes, SMEFT global fits, and direct searches for singly and doubly produced vector-like quarks.

This paper addresses the fundamental challenge of determining a maximum cardinality matching in general graphs $G = (V, E)$. To date, the most efficient algorithm for this task, attributed to Micali and Vazirani \cite{MV80}, operates in $O(m \sqrt{n})$ time; notably, this same bound applies to general bipartite graphs, as does the algorithm by Karp and Hopcroft \cite{HK73}. While $O(m)$ time algorithms exist for regular bipartite graphs, recent advancements by Goel, Kapralov, and Khanna (STOC 2010) \cite{GKK10} have further optimized this to $O(n \log n)$. We introduce a randomized algorithm grounded in the Markov Chain Monte Carlo framework that achieves an $O(m \log^2 n)$ runtime, marking a substantial improvement over the Micali and Vazirani approach. Our method employs a Markov chain akin to the \emph{hard-core model} utilized in Glauber Dynamics with a \emph{fugacity} parameter $\lambda$ for sampling independent sets from the Gibbs Distribution \cite{V99}. A pivotal aspect of our result is that the mixing time of this chain remains independent of $\lambda$, contrasting sharply with recent studies \cite{GGSVY11,MWW09, RSVVY10, S10, W06} that rely on computational transitions at specific $\lambda$ thresholds. Consequently, we develop a randomized algorithm running in $O(m \log^2 n)$ time that significantly surpasses the Micali and Vazirani runtime. Furthermore, leveraging conductance bounds, we establish that the mixing time is $\Omega(\frac{m}{k})$, where $k$ denotes the size of the maximum matching.

The AWAKE project proposes a novel plasma wakefield accelerator driven by a proton bunch from the CERN SPS. This proton bunch travels through a 10-meter rubidium plasma column, which is created by an ionizing laser pulse. The laser pulse co-propagates with the proton bunch to trigger self-modulation instability, converting the single bunch into a train of hundreds of bunchlets that generate wakefields; consequently, the plasma radius must be larger than that of the proton bunch. To measure the plasma radius at both ends of the vapor source, Schlieren imaging is suggested. Using this technique, we estimated the radius of a column of excited rubidium atoms. A tunable laser with a narrow bandwidth was split to serve two purposes: exciting the rubidium vapor and facilitating visualization via Schlieren imaging. By employing a wavelength nearly identical to rubidium's D2 transition line (780 nm), we successfully excited a column within a compact vapor source, recorded the resulting Schlieren signal, and calculated its radius. This document outlines the methodology and presents the measurement outcomes.

We present hankl, a lightweight Python implementation of the FFTLog algorithm designed for cosmological applications. FFTLog extends the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to handle logarithmically spaced periodic sequences, enabling the efficient computation of Hankel transformations. These transformations are essential for numerous modern cosmological analyses that rely on power spectra or multipole moments of the 2-point correlation function. The code is open source, publicly accessible, and thoroughly tested.

Detecting Twitter bots presents a significant and difficult challenge. Current detection methods struggle to handle community-based attacks and disguises, often missing bots that mimic genuine users while coordinating collectively. To overcome these specific hurdles, we introduce BotRGCN (Bot detection with Relational Graph Convolutional Networks). This approach tackles the community aspect by building a heterogeneous graph from follow relationships and utilizing relational graph convolutional networks. Furthermore, BotRGCN leverages multi-modal user semantic and property data to eliminate the need for manual feature engineering and enhance its capacity to identify bots employing diverse disguises. Comprehensive experiments on the TwiBot-20 benchmark, which includes follow relationship data, show that BotRGCN surpasses competitive baseline methods.

This study presents a numerical investigation into the collapse of a magnetic, rotating protostellar cloud with a mass of $10\,M_{\odot}$. Initially, the ratios of thermal, magnetic, and rotational energies to the gravitational energy modulus are 0.3, 0.2, and 0.01, respectively. The research focuses on the evolution and characteristics of the quasi-magnetostatic primary disk that forms during the isothermal collapse phase. Simulation results indicate that the disk's size grows from 1500 au to 7400 au, while its mass increases from $0.3\,M_{\odot}$ to $5.2\,M_{\odot}$. Within the cloud envelope, the magnetic field is predominantly quasi-radial, whereas it is quasi-uniform inside the primary disk. Additionally, a toroidal magnetic field develops behind the leading edge of a fast MHD shock wave originating at the disk boundary and within the outflow region near the first hydrostatic core. Observations of magnetic field geometry and angular momentum distribution can help reveal the hierarchical structure of collapsing protostellar clouds.

We present the application of reinforcement learning (RL) methods to the conformal bootstrap framework. We show that appropriate soft Actor-Critic RL algorithms can conduct efficient, low-cost searches in high-dimensional spaces of scaling dimensions and OPE-squared coefficients, yielding meaningful results for tens of conformal field theory (CFT) data points derived from a single crossing equation. This paper evaluates the approach on established 2D CFTs, specifically examining the Ising and tri-critical Ising models alongside the free compactified boson CFT. We report findings from searches reaching up to 36 dimensions, relying solely on the expected count of operators per spin within a truncated conformal-block decomposition of the crossing equations. Our investigation of 2D CFTs relies exclusively on the global $so(2,2)$ sector of the conformal algebra, with our methodology remaining applicable to CFTs in higher dimensions. When integrated with existing numerical and analytical techniques, we anticipate that our method will provide a novel perspective on the non-perturbative structure of arbitrary (unitary or non-unitary) CFTs.

This study theoretically explores the design and controlled preparation of entangled atomic states arising from spin-exchange collisions in spinor Bose-Einstein condensates for atom interferometry that remains resilient to common technical constraints, such as finite detector resolution. Through both analytical and numerical modeling of the spin-exchange mechanism, we demonstrate that initiating these entangling collisions with a small classical seed instead of vacuum fluctuations yields superior sensitivity and greater robustness against technical noise, even though the resulting atomic state ideally possesses less metrologically valuable entanglement. These findings offer valuable insights into optimizing the generation and design of entangled atomic states for quantum-enhanced matter-wave interferometry.

We introduce a Bogoliubov method to calculate the laser emission linewidth within the framework of generic semi-classical laser dynamics described by the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation. This approach offers a unified view of the Henry and Petermann treatments, attributing both broadening mechanisms to the non-orthogonality of Bogoliubov modes existing in a space with doubled degrees of freedom. As an illustrative application, the method enables the analysis of the interplay between driven-dissipation, interactions, and spatial inhomogeneity characteristic of polariton condensates. We demonstrate that the conventional theory of Henry and Petermann factors fails significantly when substantial polariton-polariton interactions are present. Specifically, even under strong confinement, accurately describing phase diffusion in the Henry manner requires accounting for the intrinsically multi-mode nature of density fluctuations.

Dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) are defined by the nonanalytic behavior of physical observables over time. In systems subjected to periodic modulations, these nonanalytic signatures recur cyclically, giving rise to Floquet DQPTs. This study systematically investigates Floquet DQPTs within a class of periodically quenched one-dimensional systems exhibiting chiral symmetry. By adjusting the quench strength, we identify multiple Floquet DQPTs occurring within a single driving cycle; notably, systems initialized in Floquet states with higher topological invariants exhibit a greater number of such transitions. Each transition is accompanied by a quantized jump in a dynamical topological order parameter, which remains quantized over time provided the underlying Floquet system resides in a gapped topological phase. We validate this theory using a piecewise quenched lattice model rich in Floquet topological phases, which is amenable to realization in quantum simulators such as nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamonds. Consequently, our findings offer new avenues for the Floquet engineering of DQPTs and the dynamical detection of topological phase transitions in Floquet systems.

We examine five blue stellar systems located toward the Virgo cluster, similar to the mysterious SECCO 1 (AGC 226067). Identified through their optical and UV morphologies, these objects were further studied using HI observations from the VLA and GBT, MUSE/VLT spectroscopy, and HST imaging. Our new data reveal that one system is a distant galaxy group, whereas the other four are extremely low-mass ($M_\ast \sim 10^5 \; \mathrm{M_\odot}$) systems dominated by young, blue stars. These four exhibit highly irregular, clumpy morphologies spanning only a few kiloparsecs but contain abundant metal-rich HII regions with $12 + \log (\mathrm{O/H}) > 8.2$. Such high metallicities suggest they formed from gas stripped by more massive galaxies. Despite their young stellar populations, only one system shows HI detection, while the other three possess minimal or no gas reserves. Additionally, two systems are unexpectedly isolated, lacking any plausible parent galaxy within $\sim$30' ($\sim$140 kpc). While tidal stripping remains a possible formation mechanism, ram pressure stripping more naturally accounts for their characteristics, especially their isolation, due to the higher relative velocities achievable. Consequently, we propose that most of these systems originated from ram pressure stripped gas ejected from newly infalling cluster members, surviving long enough in the intracluster medium to separate from their parents by hundreds of kiloparsecs, thereby representing a novel class of stellar systems.

In numerous practical applications, including forming processes and impact simulations, treating one contacting body as rigid provides a highly accurate approximation of the physical reality. This study applies the established dual mortar method to enforce interface constraints during finite deformation frictionless contact between rigid and deformable bodies. The efficiency of the proposed nonlinear contact algorithm stems from two primary advancements. First, a variational formulation based on the Petrov-Galerkin scheme is explored; this approach significantly simplifies the process by eliminating the necessity to explicitly compute dual basis functions, with detailed presentation of the resulting first-order dual mortar interpolation. Additionally, the work addresses second-order interpolation by utilizing a piecewise linear scheme that crucially preserves the geometric fidelity of the finite element mesh. Second, a novel definition for a nodal orthonormal moving frame attached to each contact node is introduced. This innovation minimizes geometric coupling among nodes, thereby reducing the bandwidth of the stiffness matrix. Collectively, these contributions lower the computational complexity of dual mortar methods for rigid-deformable interactions, particularly in three-dimensional contexts, without compromising accuracy or robustness.

Drawing inspiration from developments in categorical probability, we define non-commutative almost everywhere (a.e.) equivalence and disintegrations within the framework of C*-algebras. We demonstrate that C*-algebras (respectively, W*-algebras) and a.e. equivalence classes of 2-positive (respectively, positive) unital maps constitute a category. Furthermore, we establish that whenever non-commutative disintegrations exist, they are unique up to a.e. equivalence. Finally, we offer an explicit criterion for the existence of disintegrations in finite-dimensional C*-algebras and present the corresponding formulas.

The circumstellar disk surrounding HD 169142 is hypothesized to contain several embedded planets, based on the diverse structural features observed in its dust distribution. We examined archival ALMA data covering $^{12} \mathrm{CO \ (2-1)}$, $^{13} \mathrm{CO \ (2-1)}$, and $\mathrm{C}^{18} \mathrm{O \ (2-1)}$ to detect large-scale kinematic patterns indicative of additional embedded planets in the outer disk. At a distance of 125 au, we detected a coherent flow extending from the disk surface down to the midplane, visible across all three CO isotopologues, which we interpret as a meridional flow possibly caused by an embedded planet. By analyzing variations in gas rotation speed to map the physical structure in this region, we found that at 125 au, CO emission highlights areas of elevated gas pressure even where surface density is at a minimum. Using a straightforward analytical model, we showed that the gap's physical configuration can exhibit complex responses to surface density variations, aligning with prior thermo-chemical simulations and observational inferences. Extending this method to various sources will enable a direct comparison between observations and theoretical models of gap formation in protoplanetary disks.

HD163296, a Herbig Ae star, launches a bipolar knotty jet extending approximately 6000 astronomical units. While there is strong evidence for planets within its disk, companions around jet-driving stars can influence jet morphology, potentially causing axis wiggling and periodic knot spacing. This study examines the HD163296 jet's morphology, including width and axis position, along with its proper motions to gain deeper insights into the system. Data were collected via optical integral-field spectroscopy using VLT/MUSE in 2017. By analyzing spectro-images and position-velocity diagrams from the MUSE data cube, we determined the number and locations of jet knots. We compared these findings with 2012 X-Shooter data to estimate knot proper motions and analyzed jet width and axis position relative to distance from the star from the extracted images. Our observations reveal knot merging and identify two previously unseen knots. Measurements of the jet axis position show a consistent deviation pattern across all forbidden emission lines within the first 20 arcseconds, which we interpret as resulting from asymmetric shocks rather than axis wiggling. The detection of new knots and their positions challenge the 16-year ejection periodicity suggested by earlier research, indicating a more complex jet system than previously thought. Furthermore, the absence of jet axis wiggling allows us to rule out companions with masses greater than 0.1 solar masses orbiting between 1 and 35 AU; any object inferred at these distances via other methods must therefore be a brown dwarf or planet. We consider both precession and orbital motion scenarios in our analysis.

We contend that selecting the appropriate boundary condition for the wave function in quantum cosmology relies on the ultraviolet completion of general relativity. To illustrate this, we present a specific braneworld model where de Sitter cosmology emerges on the surface of a Coleman-de Luccia bubble within a five-dimensional AdS space. By requiring consistency with established bubble nucleation physics, the relevant boundary conditions are uniquely determined, thereby selecting the Vilenkin weighting for the amplitude when viewed from four dimensions.

The halo mass function (HMF) plays a pivotal role in analyzing galaxy cluster catalogs within cosmology. This study quantifies how uncertainties in HMF parameters affect cosmological constraints derived from catalogs resembling those from Planck, as well as those anticipated from upcoming Euclid, Roman, and Rubin surveys, and a hypothetical larger future survey. By analyzing simulated catalogs for each scenario while progressively relaxing priors on HMF parameters, we assess the resulting degradation in cosmological precision. Although current HMF uncertainties do not significantly hinder Planck-like surveys, they can substantially weaken constraints for Euclid-like surveys. Consequently, the present level of HMF precision will be inadequate for Euclid, Roman, Rubin, and potentially larger future surveys. To avoid compromising cosmological parameter constraints, future experiments must rigorously account for HMF parameter uncertainties, necessitating improved precision in HMF modeling.

This note explores the concept of symmetric self-duality within shaded planar algebras, a framework that enables the elevation of shadings on subfactor planar algebras to construct Z/2Z-graded unitary fusion categories. Consequently, this establishes the proof of the existence of unitary fusion categories possessing fusion graphs 4442 and 3333.

Although Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) are increasingly favored for processing data on irregular domains, their underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood due to the opaque nature of neural networks. This work revisits GCNN operations to demonstrate that their convolution layers function as matched filters, aligning input data with specific patterns or features. By adopting this matched filter perspective, we offer a unified explanation of GCNNs, extending the framework to include nonlinear ReLU and max-pooling layers. Furthermore, the paper provides a detailed walkthrough of information propagation and learning processes within GCNNs, illustrating how standard CNNs and fully connected networks emerge as special cases. A carefully selected numerical example accompanies these explanations, offering both visual and quantitative insights into the various stages of GCNN operation and learning.

This study demonstrates a strong inverse correlation between temporal fluctuations in the toroidal magnetic field component of the solar tachocline (the base of the convective zone) and the Y-component of Earth's magnetic field. We explore the hypothesis that solar axions, which convert into photons within external electric or magnetic fields via the inverse Primakoff effect, serve as the mechanism linking the Sun's convective zone magnetic field to Earth's magnetic field modulation. We propose an axion-based model connecting the solar dynamo and geodynamo, wherein energy from a specific solar axion flux component—emitted during M1 transitions in $^{57}\text{Fe}$ nuclei—is first modulated by the solar tachocline's magnetic field through the inverse coherent Primakoff effect. This energy is subsequently resonantly absorbed in Earth's core, acting as a modulator for the planetary magnetic field. Based on this mechanism, we derive estimates for the axion-photon coupling ($g_{a \gamma} = 7.07 \times 10^{-11} \text{ GeV}^{-1}$), axion-nucleon coupling ($g_{an} = 3.20 \times 10^{-7}$), axion-electron coupling ($g_{ae} = 5.28 \times 10^{-11}$), and axion mass ($m_a = 17 \text{ eV}$). Furthermore, these derived axion parameters are shown to remain consistent with all known experimental and theoretical model-independent constraints. Additionally, we examine the impact of 17 eV axion dark matter on the extragalactic background light (EBL), finding that the theoretical spectral intensity of EBL generated by axion decay aligns well with experimental observations across the near-ultraviolet, optical, and near-infrared ranges (1500–20,000 Å).

Model-based approaches currently dominate robotic control, yet their success relies critically on model precision. While deep neural networks have been employed to learn robot dynamics from data, they face challenges regarding data inefficiency and the difficulty of integrating prior knowledge. We present Structured Mechanical Models, a flexible framework for mechanical systems that overcomes these issues by being data-efficient, readily accommodating prior knowledge, and compatible with model-based control techniques. This work aims to showcase the advantages of adopting Structured Mechanical Models over black-box neural networks for robot dynamics. Our results indicate that these models generalize more effectively from limited datasets and produce more reliable model-based controllers across diverse simulated robotic environments.

This study assesses the Fokker-Planck equation, characterized by linear force coefficients, as an approximation for the kinetic equation governing homogeneous isothermal multicomponent condensation. By starting with a discrete balance equation for the temporal evolution of multicomponent droplet distribution functions and applying Taylor series expansions to convert it into a differential form near the free energy surface's saddle point, we determine the specific parameters whose smallness is required for the kinetic equation to assume the Fokker-Planck form with linear force coefficients. If these parameters are not sufficiently small, the resulting equation may include third-order or higher partial derivatives of the distribution function, exhibit non-linear force coefficients dependent on droplet variables, or display both features, thereby compromising the accuracy of conventional multicomponent nucleation predictions. As a numerical demonstration, we performed calculations for isothermal condensation across five binary systems with varying degrees of non-ideality at 293.15 K: 1-butanol/1-hexanol, water/methanol, water/ethanol, water/1-propanol, and water/1-butanol. Our findings indicate that under typical experimental conditions, the classical nucleation theory kinetic equation for binary nucleation likely requires a two-fold modification, suggesting that the standard expression for steady-state binary nucleation rates may be insufficient for accurately comparing theoretical predictions with experimental data.

Defined appropriately, quantum complexity serves as a valuable probe for the late-time dynamics of black holes, especially within the AdS/CFT framework. This concept can be effectively quantified by measuring the temporal evolution of an operator's spread within Krylov space. Notably, complexity is anticipated to exhibit distinct behaviors in chaotic many-body systems versus integrable ones. This paper examines Krylov complexity in finite-sized interacting integrable models, revealing that complexity saturation is suppressed relative to chaotic systems. We link this phenomenon to a new form of localization on the Krylov chain by mapping complexity growth to an Anderson localization model featuring off-diagonal disorder. Our analysis indicates that localization is more pronounced in integrable cases due to enhanced disorder in hopping amplitudes, which effectively dampens Krylov complexity. We validate these findings using the interacting XXZ spin chain and a phenomenological model we developed; this model encapsulates the core aspects of our study and successfully reproduces the observed behaviors for both chaotic and integrable systems through an adjustable disorder parameter.

This paper introduces two finite-time control strategies based on bearing measurements for acyclic leader-follower formations. In these formations, leaders follow bounded continuous reference velocities, while each follower adjusts its position relative to three other agents. The first strategy relies solely on bearing vectors, achieving finite-time convergence through the appropriate selection of state-dependent control gains. The second strategy incorporates both bearing vectors and inter-agent communication, wherein each agent simultaneously localizes itself and tracks a virtual target. The finite-time convergence of the desired formation under both approaches is demonstrated via mathematical induction and validated by numerical simulations. (10.1109/LCSYS.2021.3088299)

Recent studies have demonstrated that numerous Gustafson integrals arise within investigations of ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ spin chain models. We anticipate that a broader class of Gustafson integrals can be derived by examining spin chain models possessing alternative symmetry groups. This paper examines the spin magnet under ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{C})$ symmetry, considering both periodic and open boundary conditions, to establish several novel integrals.

This work investigates rigid surface operators within $N=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theories possessing $SO(n)$ and $Sp(2n)$ gauge groups. Building on Wyllard's explicit proposals regarding the action of the $S$-duality map on specific subclasses of these operators via the maps $X_S$ and $Y_S$, we further analyze these mappings. By employing a convenient methodological trick, we streamline the construction of the symbol invariant for rigid surface operators. Through consistency checks, we both recover and extend Wyllard's proposed $S$-duality maps. Additionally, we identify new subclasses of rigid surface operators linked by $S$-duality, attempt to elucidate the exceptions within these maps, and discuss the application of techniques from $B_n/C_n$ theories to the $D_n$ context.

Using exclusive $J/\psi$ production data from HERA and LHCb, the low-$x$ behavior of the gluon density $xg(x,\mu^2)$ at a scale of $\mu^2=2.4$ GeV$^2$ is established within the collinear factorization framework at next-to-leading order (NLO). Analysis reveals that within the range $3\times 10^{-6} < x <10^{-3}$, the gluon distribution function follows a power-law growth, $xg(x,\mu^2)\propto x^{-\lambda}$, with an exponent of $\lambda=0.135\pm 0.006$. The influence of these experimental findings on global parton distribution function (PDF) analyses in this low-$x$ region is assessed, and no evidence supporting parton density saturation is found.

The global COVID-19 pandemic triggered abrupt and significant transformations in university and research operations, frequently yielding adverse effects that disproportionately impacted minorities, women, and individuals from low-income backgrounds. These challenges exacerbated existing hardships for these groups, particularly by heightening the barriers marginalized students face when pursuing careers in STEM fields. Established to assist underrepresented students in physics and astronomy through research opportunities and sustained mentorship, the National Astronomy Consortium (NAC) adapted to pandemic-related shutdowns by converting both its summer research program and annual fall conference into fully virtual formats. This discussion outlines the modifications the NAC implemented to ensure a successful transition to a remote environment and offers both immediate and enduring recommendations for initiatives aiming to support marginalized undergraduate and graduate researchers in the future.

In resource-limited environments focused on reducing bias, such as law enforcement, it is crucial to identify the origins of unfairness before implementing real-world mitigation strategies. Unlike prior research that merely warns against discrimination or addresses bias post-generation, this study offers a dual toolkit: the Unfair Edge Prioritization algorithm for mitigating unfairness during data generation, and the Discrimination Removal algorithm for de-biasing data afterward. The approach assumes a provided non-parametric Markovian causal model representing the data generation process, where edges originating from sensitive nodes (e.g., race) are treated as the primary sources of bias. First, we quantify Edge Flow as the belief of observing a specific outcome Y influenced by a specific input X along an edge X -> Y. Next, we define Edge Unfairness using a non-parametric formulation based on these edge flows. We demonstrate that cumulative unfairness against sensitive groups in decisions, such as bail determinations, vanishes when edge unfairness is absent, a result proven even in non-trivial non-parametric settings where cumulative unfairness cannot be directly expressed via edge unfairness. Furthermore, we measure the potential to reduce cumulative unfairness by decreasing edge unfairness. Leveraging these metrics, we propose the Unfair Edge Prioritization algorithm for policymakers and the Discrimination Removal Procedure, which de-biases data distributions by eliminating optimization constraints that scale exponentially with the number of sensitive attributes and their values. Extensive experiments confirm the validity of the proposed theorems and the measures used for quantification.

Differential dynamic microscopy (DDM) has gained prominence in soft matter physics and biophysics for analyzing the motion of microscopic objects across various wavevectors via optical microscopy. However, conventional DDM is constrained to detecting dynamics that are no faster than the camera's frame rate. This study introduces an enhanced DDM approach that sequentially illuminates the sample with spectrally distinct light while capturing images with a color camera. By pulsing blue and red light with a lag interval significantly shorter than the camera's exposure duration, this two-color DDM technique enables the measurement of dynamics occurring at speeds far exceeding the standard camera frame rate.

The formation of a black hole during a core-collapse supernova is anticipated to cause a unique and sudden decline in neutrino luminosity. This drop results from the consumption of the primary neutrino-generation zones and the intense gravitational redshift affecting the remaining escaping neutrinos. While earlier studies of the cut-off profile relied on specific trajectories or simplified bulk transport models, this study integrates over simple "ballistic" geodesics to examine the impact of including all emission angles from a collapsing surface within the Schwarzschild metric and from a contracting equatorial mass ring in the Kerr metric. Our findings indicate that non-radial geodesics soften the cut-off profile in both scenarios. Furthermore, extreme rotational speeds significantly alter the shape of the tail, changes that could potentially be detected by future neutrino observatories or detector arrays.

LiteBIRD is a Strategic Large-Class mission led by JAXA, aimed at detecting primordial gravitational waves generated during cosmic inflation by measuring their imprint on the polarization of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB). To achieve this, the mission will conduct full-sky observations at large angular scales across 15 frequency bands ranging from 34 GHz to 448 GHz, requiring exceptional sensitivity. The instrument suite comprises three telescopes: the Low-, Medium-, and High-Frequency Telescopes (LFT, MFT, and HFT). This paper outlines the design of the Medium-Frequency Telescope (89-224 GHz) and the High-Frequency Telescope (166-448 GHz), collectively known as the MHFT, which fall under European responsibility. These systems are cryogenic refractive telescopes cooled to 5 K. Each features a continuous rotating half-wave plate as the primary optical component, two high-density polyethylene (HDPE) lenses, and over 3,000 transition-edge sensor (TES) detectors cooled to 100 mK. We present an overview of the concept design and discuss the remaining specific challenges necessary to meet LiteBIRD's scientific objectives.

We experimentally evaluated simple physics-based models against data-driven neural-network models for the offline training of programmable photonic chips utilizing Mach-Zehnder interferometer meshes. For chips exhibiting thermal crosstalk, the neural-network model surpassed physics-based approaches, resulting in improved testing accuracy.

This paper investigates the deployment of Model Predictive Control (MPC) for object manipulation within highly uncertain settings, such as retrieving items from densely packed, semi-flexible bins. While MPC serves as a robust, real-time, perception-driven feedback controller capable of handling environmental uncertainties, our experiments reveal that its myopic nature prevents it from successfully executing motion sequences in heavily occluded environments. We conclude that integrating a high-level policy to adaptively modify the MPC's optimization problem would be beneficial.

Sequential effect algebra serves as a crucial framework for investigating quantum measurement theory. In 2005, Professor Gudder proposed 25 open problems to encourage further research, with the 20th question asking whether the square root of an element within a sequential effect algebra is unique. This inquiry can be extended as follows: For every integer $n>1$, does there exist a sequential effect algebra where an element $c$ possesses a non-unique $n$-th root, and this $n$-th root is distinct from any $k$-th root of $c$ where $k<n$? We have recently provided an affirmative answer to this strengthened problem.

An experimental investigation into $\omega$ photoproduction on protons was performed at the Mainz Microtron MAMI, utilizing the photon tagging facility alongside the Crystal Ball and TAPS multiphoton spectrometers. Differential cross sections for the $\gamma p\to\omega p$ reaction were measured with 15-MeV binning in photon energy ($E_\gamma$) and complete angular coverage, spanning from the reaction threshold up to $E_\gamma=1.40$ GeV (corresponding to a center-of-mass energy $W=1.87$ GeV). The high quality of the data acquired near the threshold enables the exploration of various physical phenomena; for instance, it allows for an estimation of the $\omega N$ scattering length, $\alpha_{\omega p}$.

The photoneutron reaction $^{181}\rm{Ta}(\gamma,3n)^{178m,g}\rm{Ta}$ was studied using the LUE-40 electron linear accelerator at NSC KIPT. Employing the residual $\gamma$-activity method, researchers measured the flux-averaged bremsstrahlung cross-sections ($\langle{\sigma(E_{\rm{\gamma max}})}\rangle$, $\langle{\sigma(E_{\rm{\gamma max}})}\rangle_{\rm{m}}$, $\langle{\sigma(E_{\rm{\gamma max}})}\rangle_{\rm{g}}$) and the isomeric ratio $d(E_{\rm{\gamma max}})$. Theoretical predictions for these averaged cross-sections and isomeric ratios were generated using partial cross-sections from the TALYS1.95 code across six distinct level density models (LD 1–6). While the experimental $d(E_{\rm{\gamma max}})$ values align with existing literature, they deviate from theoretical predictions regarding both absolute magnitude and energy dependence trends. Comparing the measured averaged cross-sections with calculated results revealed that the LD 5 model provided the closest agreement.

In three spacetime dimensions, Einstein gravity minimally coupled to a scalar field featuring a two-parameter Higgs-like self-interaction is reformulated using a Chern-Simons form associated with the algebra $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$. Depending on the sign of the self-interaction couplings, the components $g^{\pm}$ correspond to $so(2,2)$, $so(3,1)$, or $iso(2,1)$. The field equations are expressed via the field strength of non-flat composite gauge fields, allowing conserved charges to be derived from boundary terms in the action. These charges align with standard pure gravity Chern-Simons theory but utilize non-flat connections. Field regularity is ensured by requiring trivial holonomy of the connections along contractible cycles; this condition is naturally satisfied by scalar solitons. Consequently, the Hawking temperature and chemical potential for rotating hairy black holes can be recovered, and their entropy is calculated using the same formula applicable to pure Chern-Simons theory. Additionally, within the conformal (Jordan) frame, the theory represents General Relativity with a cosmological constant conformally coupled to a self-interacting scalar field, and its description via a Chern-Simons form for appropriately constructed composite gauge fields is also briefly discussed.

Generalized parton distributions (GPDs) characterize the interplay between a nucleon's quarks and gluons in terms of their longitudinal momentum and transverse spatial location. These distributions can be restricted by analyzing photon leptoproduction observables generated through the interference of Bethe-Heitler and Deeply Virtual Compton Scattering (DVCS) processes. At leading twist and order, the DVCS amplitude is expressed via complex integrals of the GPD set {H, E, \~H, \~E}. While existing data from unpolarized or longitudinally polarized targets effectively constrain H and \~H, the GPD E remains poorly understood because extracting it demands measurements on transversely polarized targets—a significant challenge for fixed-target setups. Previous attempts to address this limitation have relied on DVCS on neutrons using deuterium targets, contingent upon assumptions of isospin symmetry and negligible final-state interactions. Currently, we propose the polarization of the recoil proton as a novel DVCS observable that offers high sensitivity to E, presenting a viable prospect for investigation at high-luminosity facilities like Jefferson Lab.

The distributed subgradient method (DSG) is a prominent algorithm for addressing large-scale distributed optimization in machine learning. While most existing DSG research assumes ideal communication among cooperative agents with exact and perfect information exchange, this assumption raises privacy issues and is impractical in scenarios with poor wireless link quality. To mitigate these challenges, a standard strategy involves locally quantizing data before transmission, thereby preventing raw data exposure and reducing data volume. However, compared to perfect data, quantization introduces fundamental challenges regarding accuracy loss, which adversely affects algorithmic convergence. To address this, we propose a generalized distributed subgradient method incorporating random quantization, interpretable as a two-time-scale stochastic approximation approach. We establish comprehensive convergence results for the proposed algorithm and derive upper bounds on convergence rates based on quantization bits, step sizes, and the number of network agents. These findings extend prior work, which often addressed only special cases without generalizing convergence rate conclusions. Finally, numerical simulations on linear regression tasks are performed to validate our theoretical findings.

Given the abundance of high-dimensional genetic biomarkers, it is crucial to discern their heterogeneous impacts on patient survival alongside robust statistical inference. Censored quantile regression has proven to be an effective method for uncovering how covariates influence survival outcomes. However, to our knowledge, few studies have addressed inference regarding the effects of high-dimensional predictors within this framework. This paper introduces a novel approach to perform inference on all predictors under a global censored quantile regression model, which examines covariate-response relationships across a continuous range of quantile levels rather than isolated discrete points. The proposed estimator integrates a series of low-dimensional model estimates derived from multi-sample splitting and variable selection techniques. We demonstrate that, subject to specific regularity conditions, the estimator is consistent and asymptotically converges to a Gaussian process indexed by the quantile level. Simulation results confirm that our procedure accurately quantifies estimation uncertainty in high-dimensional contexts. Furthermore, we apply this method to evaluate the heterogeneous effects of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) within lung cancer pathways on patient survival, utilizing data from the Boston Lung Cancer Survival Cohort, an epidemiological study focused on the molecular mechanisms of lung cancer.

Neural dependency parsing has demonstrated significant effectiveness, attaining state-of-the-art performance across various domains and languages. However, it relies heavily on extensive labeled datasets, which are expensive and time-consuming to generate. To address this annotation challenge, this paper introduces a self-training algorithm that trains a parser using its own predictions. Our proposed Deep Contextualized Self-training (DCST) method leverages representation models trained on sequence labeling tasks derived from the parser's output on unlabeled data, integrating these models with the base parser via a gating mechanism. We evaluate DCST across multiple languages in both low-resource in-domain and cross-domain scenarios, showing that it significantly outperforms conventional self-training approaches and recent semi-supervised methods.

This paper serves as a practical guide for applying the general theory of approximate randomization tests from Canay, Romano, and Shaikh (2017) specifically to linear regression models involving clustered data. A key advantage of this approach is its effectiveness even when the number of clusters is minimal, such as five. We offer a detailed, step-by-step algorithm for conducting the test and generating confidence intervals for the relevant parameter. Furthermore, we introduce three new findings: the method can be equivalently executed using weighted scores; the test and resulting intervals remain invariant regardless of whether the statistic is studentized; and we demonstrate the convexity of confidence intervals for scalar parameters. The text also outlines the essential prerequisites for the test, highlighting common pitfalls researchers should avoid. Finally, we present two empirical applications to clarify these concepts. Supporting software packages for {\tt R} and {\tt Stata} are provided to assist with implementation and the replication of the study's examples.

Diffusion-driven phenomena play a crucial role in materials science, particularly within energy conversion and transmission sectors. In the transformation of chemical energy into electrical energy, species diffusion is inherently tied to exchange rates and, consequently, the performance of conversion devices. Conversely, as an electric field traverses a medium, it induces the diffusion of species. The outcomes of this interaction can be managed to optimize surface nano-patterns, whereas uncontrolled morphological changes can cause irreversible degradation in metallic conductors. Thus, comprehending material behavior under the influence of diffusional driving forces holds significant scientific value. This dissertation aims to examine a specific instance of species diffusion in both energy conversion and transmission contexts. Specifically, the research investigates lithium insertion within the cathode electrode of lithium-ion batteries and the morphological evolution of inclusions driven by electromigration in metallic conductors. The study demonstrates that phase-field methods effectively capture the fundamental physics of these diffusion-driven phenomena.

We examine representations of the optical Dirac equation, with a specific focus on those featuring a purely real-valued Hamiltonian. For Maxwell's equations, this condition corresponds to the Majorana representation of the massless Dirac (Weyl) equation. By drawing parallels between the Dirac, chiral, and Majorana representations within both the standard and optical Dirac frameworks, we establish two novel optical Majorana representations. While the Dirac and chiral representations correspond to optical spin and helicity states, respectively, these newly derived Majorana representations are linked to the linear polarization of light. Consequently, this approach facilitates a comparison between electron and electromagnetic wave equations within the realm of classical field theory.

Our earlier research [J. Math. Phys. 49, 033513 (2008)] left two critical issues unresolved: the absence of a minimal group to substitute GL(4,C) and the lack of a mass term in the fermion Equation of Motion (EoM). Through detailed analysis, we determined that these challenges are interconnected via the conformal group, a subgroup of GL(4,C). While the Weyl group, a subset of the conformal group, facilitates the evolution of mass and charge and governs interaction vertex transformations, generating the mass term in the EoM necessitates the full conformal group. In this broader context, the $K_\mu$ generators are essential for shifting the vacuum from space-like (or light-cone-like) to time-like configurations. Building on our prior findings—that $\vec E^2-\vec B^2\neq 0$ for massive bosons and that two-photon processes produce $e^+ e^-$ pairs—we conclude that the mass term in strong interactions is linearly proportional to both (chromo-)magnetic flux and angular momentum.

This paper outlines the reconstruction of electrons and photons using the ATLAS detector for analyses based on the full LHC Run 2 dataset. It details an enhanced energy clustering algorithm and examines its impact on electron and photon identification and measurement. Using up to 81 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data acquired at $\sqrt{s}=$ 13 TeV from 2015 to 2017, the study determines corrections and calibrations influencing performance, including energy calibration, identification and isolation efficiencies, and the charge measurement of reconstructed electron candidates.

We examine a tripod atom light coupling configuration where two dark states function as quasi-spin states. By appropriately adjusting the coupling laser fields, it is shown that one can generate a lattice featuring spin-dependent sub-wavelength barriers. This capability enables flexible manipulation of atomic motion, transitioning from dynamics within an effective brick-wall lattice to free movement of atoms in one dark state and a tight-binding lattice with double the periodicity for atoms in the other. The spectrum shifts significantly between these regimes, governed by the laser fields. Current experimental methods are sufficient to produce such a tripod lattice. Furthermore, utilizing the tripod scheme to form a lattice of degenerate dark states introduces new avenues for spin ordering and symmetry breaking.

This paper examines the stable isotopy classes of a finite set of immersed circles on closed oriented surfaces that avoid triple or higher-order intersections, a framework serving as a planar counterpart to virtual knot theory and extending classical knot theory. While recent research has formulated Alexander and Markov theorems within this planar context, the algebraic structures differ: whereas twin groups (a specific class of right-angled Coxeter groups) govern the classical case, a newly introduced class of "virtual twin groups" fulfills this role in the virtual setting. The virtual twin group $VT_n$ encompasses the pure virtual twin group $PVT_n$, which functions as a planar analogue of the pure Artin braid group. In this work, we demonstrate that $PVT_n$ is an irreducible right-angled Artin group possessing a trivial center, providing its exact presentation. Furthermore, we reveal that $PVT_n$ decomposes into an iterated semi-direct product of infinite rank free groups. We offer a comprehensive characterization of the automorphism group of $PVT_n$ and confirm the splitting of natural exact sequences within these automorphism groups. As applications of these findings, we establish that $VT_n$ is residually finite and that $PVT_n$ exhibits the $R_\infty$-property.

If dark matter exists in a hidden sector that interacts minimally with the Standard Model, a distinct particle within that sector could temporarily dominate the early universe's energy density, triggering an Early Matter-Dominated Era (EMDE). During such an era, matter fluctuations grow faster than in radiation-dominated epochs, leading to the premature formation of microhalos compared to standard cosmological models. While these microhalos amplify dark matter annihilation signals, the magnitude of this boost is critically dependent on the small-scale cutoff in the matter power spectrum. For sufficiently cold dark matter, this cutoff is determined by the relativistic pressure of the hidden sector's dominant particle. This study tracks the evolution of dark matter density perturbations throughout this scenario to derive the final power spectrum. We examine how the relativistic pressure of the dominant hidden sector particle suppresses perturbations and express both the cutoff scale and the peak scale of the matter power spectrum as functions of that particle's properties. Furthermore, we provide transfer functions that connect the matter power spectrum with a pressure-induced cutoff to the spectrum arising from a cold hidden sector. These tools enable the rapid calculation of accurate matter power spectra for EMDE scenarios with initially hot hidden sectors and help identify specific models that significantly increase microhalo abundance.

To achieve generalization across unseen domains, known as domain generalization, models must learn domain-agnostic feature representations that capture the fundamental semantics of object categories. Recent progress in weakly supervised vision-language models demonstrates their capacity for semantic understanding by deriving holistic representations from inexpensive, noisy text annotations, thereby capturing object characteristics that transfer across domains. However, involving multiple source domains significantly increases the cost of curating textual annotations for every image, rendering the process tedious and often infeasible. This barrier prevents the direct application of these supervised vision-language methods to achieve optimal generalization on unseen domains. Driven by this challenge, we investigate how to leverage multimodal information from existing pre-trained networks in an "intrinsic" manner to improve generalization. Consequently, we introduce IntriNsic multimodality for DomaIn GeneralizatiOn (INDIGO), a streamlined approach that combines the intrinsic modality within pre-trained multimodal networks with visual data to enhance test-time generalization. Experiments across various Domain Generalization settings—ClosedDG, OpenDG, and Limited sources—demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on unseen domains, accompanied by a comprehensive analysis to elucidate INDIGO's holistic effectiveness.

Although the bag model achieved significant success in explaining mass spectra, its reputation has been tarnished by the issue of center-of-mass motion, which causes severe theoretical inconsistencies. For example, this problem renders meson masses and decay constants dependent on momentum rather than independent. This study presents a systematic method to address these difficulties, allowing for the consistent calculation of meson decay constants and baryon transition form factors within our framework. Specifically, the form factors for neutron $\beta$ decays are determined without any free parameters, yielding $F^V_1 = 1$ and $F^A_1 = 1.31$ (or a ratio $F_1^A/F_1^V = 1.31$), which closely matches the experimental result of $F^A_1/F^V_1 = 1.27$. Furthermore, we calculate the branching ratio for ${\cal B}(\Lambda_b \to \Lambda \gamma)$ as $(6.8 \pm 3.3) \times 10^{-6}$, a value that aligns well with the experimental measurement of $(7.1 \pm 1.7) \times 10^{-6}$.

Literature currently lacks experimental data on the viscosity of the radioactive hydrogen isotopologue tritium. Existing ab initio calculations neglect quantum mechanical effects, limiting their accuracy to temperatures at or above room temperature. To address this gap, a measurement apparatus was developed to determine the viscosity of gaseous hydrogen and its isotopologues (H$_2$, HD, HT, D$_2$, DT, T$_2$) under cryogenic conditions. This paper presents the initial findings from the Cryogenic Viscosity Measurement Apparatus (Cryo-ViMA), reporting viscosity measurements for gaseous hydrogen in the range of 200 K to 300 K.

This study introduces a novel class of dynamical systems defined by interval maps arising from symbolic actions of erasing substitution rules. We achieve this by providing a detailed examination of the geometric, analytical, dynamical, and arithmetic characteristics of a specific example. This example is notable for being arguably the simplest case that simultaneously yields intriguing properties and presents new, challenging problems.

This study examines how swelling-induced structural instabilities drive pattern transformations in periodic hydrogel systems. Our analysis encompasses single-phase and two-phase voided hydrogels, as well as reinforced hydrogel thin films. While the pattern evolution in single-phase structures aligns well with experimental data, the two-phase materials exhibit novel patterns resulting from the wrinkling of internal surfaces. Additionally, a comprehensive parametric investigation of reinforced hydrogel thin films uncovers new possibilities for designing complex out-of-plane surface modes driven by swelling instabilities. Beyond these buckling-type instabilities, we also observed the formation of micro-creases at the internal surfaces of periodic media prior to the loss of strong ellipticity in the effective moduli.

This study examines the transition form factors $f_+(q^2)$ and $f_-(q^2)$ (or $f_0(q^2)$) for exclusive semileptonic $B	o D\ell
u_\ell$ decays ($\ell=e, \mu, 	au$) using the standard light-front quark model (LFQM) grounded in light-front quantization. It is widely assumed that $f_+(q^2)$ avoids problematic contributions like zero modes and instantaneous effects, whereas $f_-(q^2)$ typically requires them because it involves multiple current components, such as $(J^+, J^-)$ or $(J^+, { f J}_\perp)$. However, contrary to this prevailing view, we demonstrate within the Drell-Yan ($q^+=0$) frame that $f_-(q^2)$ derived from either $(J^+, J^-)$ or $(J^+, { f J}_\perp)$ yields identical results without necessitating such treacherous contributions in the standard LFQM. Through numerical analysis, we calculate the form factors and branching ratios for $B	o D\ell
u_\ell$ across all lepton flavors, comparing our findings with experimental measurements and other theoretical predictions. Our computed branching ratios agree reasonably well with experimental data, except for the semitauonic $B^0	o D^-	au
u_	au$ channel. Additionally, we estimate the ratio ${\cal R}(D)= rac{{m Br}(B	o D	au
u_	au)}{{m Br}(B	o D\ell'
u_{\ell'})}$ (where $\ell'=e,\mu$) and compare it against both experimental results and other theoretical models.

Person re-identification has gained significant importance due to its extensive applications, yet it remains a difficult task in practice because of challenges such as varying poses, inconsistent lighting, occlusions, misalignments, and cluttered backgrounds. To address these issues, this paper introduces the Multi-Scale Body-Part Mask Guided Attention Network (MMGA), a framework that jointly learns attention mechanisms for both the entire body and specific body parts to simultaneously extract global and local features. Within MMGA, body-part masks are utilized to guide the training of corresponding attention modules. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively mitigates the negative impacts of pose variations, misalignments, and background clutter. On the Market1501 dataset, the proposed approach achieves a rank-1 accuracy of 95.0% and an mAP of 87.2%, while attaining 89.5% rank-1 and 78.1% mAP on the DukeMTMC-reID dataset, thereby surpassing existing state-of-the-art techniques.

We employ two complementary *ab initio* methods to investigate the electronic structure and derive effective spin models for the honeycomb material BaCo$_2$(AsO$_4$)$_2$, which is a proposed candidate for Kitaev physics. Both approaches indicate that the dominant direct hopping renders the bond-dependent Kitaev term negligible, thereby preventing the system from entering the desired spin-liquid phase. Consequently, we propose a concise three-parameter exchange model to characterize the interactions within the lowest doublet of this cobaltate. Notably, the distinctive double-zigzag ground state of BaCo$_2$(AsO$_4$)$_2$, which is stabilized by quantum fluctuations, arises primarily from third-neighbor interactions, encompassing both isotropic and anisotropic components. Furthermore, the significant third-nearest neighbor hopping identified in our *ab initio* calculations underscores the critical role these third-neighbor interactions play in stabilizing the material's unique ground state.

This article introduces a metric variation of the C^0-version of the Zimmer program tailored for three-dimensional manifolds. Following a re-evaluation of isometry groups in geometric three-manifolds, we examine homomorphisms from higher rank lattices to these groups, proving a dichotomy between finite image and infinite volume quotients. In the process, we compile existing classification results for finite group actions on three-manifolds and provide a response to a metric variation of the topological Zimmer program for aspherical three-manifolds, as requested by Weinberger and Ye; this answer relies on the established dichotomy and known topological rigidity phenomena in dimension three. Leveraging findings by John Pardon and Galaz-García-Guijarro, our dichotomy for homomorphisms of higher rank lattices into the isometry groups of three-manifolds extends the validity of a C^0-isometric Zimmer program to closely related singular geodesic spaces, specifically three-dimensional geometric orbifolds and Alexandrov spaces. Furthermore, utilizing Pardon's insights, we demonstrate that a topological version of the Zimmer Program holds in dimension three for Alexandrov spaces.

The study demonstrates that the well-known Allen--Dynes asymptotic limit for the superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) in the very strong coupling regime ($\lambda \gg 1$) is superseded within the antiadiabatic limit of Eliashberg equations ($\Omega_0/D \gg 1$). Specifically, the condition $T_c > \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\lambda}\Omega_0$ is replaced by $T_c > (2\pi^4)^{-1/3}(\lambda D\Omega_0^2)^{1/3}$, while the upper bound for $T_c$ is established as $T_c < \frac{2}{\pi^2}\lambda D$. In these expressions, $\lambda$ represents the Eliashberg--McMillan electron-phonon coupling constant and $\Omega_0$ denotes the characteristic phonon frequency, with $D$ (approximately equal to the Fermi energy $E_F$) serving as the conduction band half-width.

This study examines a randomness model for self-similar Cantor sets that possess finite, positive $1$-Hausdorff measure. We determine the precise rate at which the probability of a Buffon needle landing within distance $\delta$ of such a set decays. Both the models proposed by Peres and Solomyak and by Shiwen Zhang exhibit the same decay order for this probability: $\frac{c}{\log\frac{1}{\delta}}$. In this note, we demonstrate that a third randomness model shares this identical rate of decay. This model aligns with the intuition that any "reasonable" random Cantor set with finite, positive length will have a Favard length of order $\frac{c}{\log\frac{1}{\delta}}$ for its $\delta$-neighbourhood. A lower bound estimate was previously established by Mattila.

This study addresses the inductive construction, via vertex splitting, of triangulated spheres containing a fixed number of additional edges, termed braces. We demonstrate that for every positive integer $b$, an inductive method exists to generate such triangulations with $b$ braces, relying on a finite set of base graphs. Specifically, we prove that the maximum size of a base graph with $b$ braces is bounded linearly by $b$. For the specific cases where $b=1$ or $b=2$, we explicitly identify the corresponding base graphs. Leveraging these findings, we establish that doubly braced triangulations are generically minimally rigid within two distinct geometric settings: one derived from a hypercylinder in $\mathbb{R}^4$ and the other from a specific class of mixed norms on $\mathbb{R}^3$.

This study examines measurement-induced phase transitions within a Quantum Ising chain interacting with a monitoring environment. We contrast two distinct regimes of the measurement problem: the stochastic quantum-state diffusion protocol, representing infinite small jumps per unit time, and the no-click limit, which involves post-selection and is governed by a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. In both scenarios, increasing the measurement strength $\gamma$ yields remarkably similar phenomenology: a sharp transition from a critical phase characterized by logarithmic entanglement scaling to an area-law phase. This transition occurs at an identical measurement rate for both protocols. An effective central charge, derived from the logarithmic entanglement scaling, vanishes continuously at this shared transition point, albeit with differing critical behaviors that may indicate separate universality classes for each protocol. We attribute the discrepancy in central charge near the transition to noise-induced disentanglement, a hypothesis supported by entanglement statistics showing emergent bimodality as the critical point is approached. Furthermore, the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and its linked subradiance spectral transition offer a coherent framework for explaining both the extended critical phase—observed here in a model lacking continuous symmetry—and the transition into the area-law entanglement regime.

This paper details the design, implementation, and deployment of Lepton, a fault-tolerant system capable of losslessly compressing JPEG images to approximately 77% of their original size. By substituting the Huffman coding layer in standard JPEG compression with a parallelized arithmetic code, Lepton enables the rapid recovery of the exact original file bytes. The system achieves compression efficiency comparable to the best existing methods while decoding more than nine times faster in a streaming format. Released as open-source software, Lepton has been integrated into Dropbox's file-storage backend for one year. As of February 2017, it had compressed over 203 PiB of user JPEG files, resulting in storage savings exceeding 46 PiB.

This study utilizes a multi-decade archive of ground-based mid-infrared imagery (7–25 $\mu$m) of Saturn to investigate thermal emission variability, both seasonal and non-seasonal, spanning over one Saturnian year (1984–2022). Measurements from 3-meter and 8-meter class telescopes align well with synthetic images derived from Cassini temperature data and radiative climate model predictions. Specifically, 8-meter facilities can resolve thermal contrasts associated with Saturn's belts, zones, polar hexagon, and cyclones, all set against a backdrop of large-scale seasonal asymmetries. The research identifies seasonal shifts in brightness temperatures of approximately 30 K in the stratosphere and 10 K in the upper troposphere, corresponding to the formation of the northern and southern polar stratospheric vortices (NPSV and SPSV) in spring and their dissipation in autumn. Radiative climate models successfully replicate the timing of the first appearance of these warm polar vortices, confirming their radiative nature, though they occur within sharp boundaries shaped by dynamics. Axisymmetric thermal bands (4–5 per hemisphere) exhibit temperature gradients strongly linked to Saturn's zonal winds, suggesting winds that weaken with altitude and meridional circulation cells that generate the system of cool zones and warm belts. While Saturn's thermal structure shows high repeatability year-to-year (as seen when comparing images from 1989 and 2018), except at low latitudes, evidence of inter-annual variations emerges in the equatorial banding at 7.9 $\mu$m, which does not strictly follow a ~15-year equatorial stratospheric oscillation period. Furthermore, observations from 2017–2022 extend the Cassini mission's legacy by documenting the continued warming of the NPSV during northern summer.

Topologically interlocked materials, composed of unbonded, interlocking components, represent a promising avenue for diverse structural applications. These systems exhibit remarkable mechanical properties, such as superior combinations of stiffness, strength, and toughness, surpassing those of conventional engineering materials. While recent research has defined the theoretical upper bounds for the strength and toughness of beam-like topologically interlocked structures, these limits are only attainable with unrealistically high friction coefficients, leaving their practical feasibility in real-world structures uncertain. Drawing inspiration from biological systems, we propose a hierarchical approach to topological interlocking that bypasses these constraints and paves the way for optimized mechanical performance. By designing surface morphologies on beam-like structures, we enhance the effective frictional strength of interfaces, thereby enabling the achievement of theoretical limits with realistic friction values. Through numerical simulations, we investigate how sinusoidal surface geometries with adjustable amplitude and wavelength influence the maximum load-bearing capacity of these structures. Our study analyzes the impacts of architecting surface morphology in beam-like topologically interlocked structures, notably demonstrating its capacity to significantly boost mechanical performance.

To prepare for the photometric classification of transients from the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), we conducted tests using various training datasets. Leveraging depth estimates for the 4-metre Multi-Object Spectroscopic Telescope's (4MOST) Time Domain Extragalactic Survey (TiDES), we simulated a magnitude-limited sample extending to $r_{\textrm{AB}} \approx$ 22.5 mag using the machine learning pipeline `snmachine`. Our simulations revealed that machine-learning algorithms perform poorly in classifying supernovae when trained on magnitude-limited data compared to representative samples. However, performance significantly improved by combining the magnitude-limited training set with a simulated realistic sample of faint, high-redshift supernovae from larger spectroscopic facilities; this boosted the average area under the ROC curve (AUC) across 10 runs from 0.547–0.628 to 0.946–0.969, achieving 95% purity for two of the four algorithms. Furthermore, generating new artificial light curves via the `avocado` augmentation software yielded 95% purity across all 10 runs for every algorithm tested, with the artificial neural network reaching a peak average AUC of 0.986. While having authentic faint supernovae to complement magnitude-limited samples is essential for optimizing 4MOST spectroscopic selections, our findings demonstrate that data augmentation is also a necessary step to achieve optimal classification results.

We demonstrate that a complete power counting analysis of the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) requires accounting for both canonical dimensions and loop orders. Through specific examples, we show that relying solely on canonical dimensions can yield inconsistent outcomes. By incorporating both metrics, a definitive hierarchy of SMEFT terms is established, which practically aids in identifying and prioritizing the dominant effects within any high-energy process. Furthermore, this dual-counting approach ensures a consistent restriction on free parameters when applying SMEFT.

This study employs density functional theory, utilizing the generalized gradient approximation within Quantum Espresso and VASP software, to examine the lattice dynamics and elastic properties of Ti$_2$AlC, Ti$_2$AlN, Ti$_2$GaC, Ti$_2$GaN, Ti$_2$PbC, Ti$_2$CdC, and Ti$_2$SnC. The calculated lattice parameters align well with existing experimental data and prior theoretical investigations. Analysis of elastic anisotropy, Young's modulus, Poisson ratio, and shear modulus indicates that these MAX phases are stable and ductile, with Ti$_2$PbC and Ti$_2$CdC exhibiting superior stability compared to the others, suggesting potential for industrial use. Furthermore, the phonon spectra confirm dynamic stability across all seven compounds due to the lack of imaginary modes. Lattice thermal conductivity dependent on temperature was assessed using Slack's Debye theory, with the calculated $\kappa_{ph}$ for Ti$_2$AlC at 1300 K matching experimental results within 9%. Finally, applying Clarke's empirical formula to estimate minimum thermal conductivities ($\kappa_{min}$) reveals that Ti$_2$PbC has the lowest value among the studied phases.
