This work addresses the challenge of identifying a policy that maximizes expected cumulative reward for an agent navigating an unknown environment, a domain commonly known as Reinforcement Learning. A primary limitation of this framework is its dependence on large sample volumes at every learning step. To mitigate this, we introduce the parameter critic, a formulation that preserves sample validity even as policy parameters evolve. Specifically, we propose employing a function approximator to directly model the relationship between policy parameters and expected cumulative reward. Convergence analysis indicates that the parameter critic surpasses gradient-free parameter space exploration methods due to its robustness against noise. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach successfully solves the cartpole problem, validating our assertion that the agent can effectively learn an optimal policy while simultaneously establishing the link between parameters and cumulative reward.

To foster engagement, platforms like YouTube increasingly rely on personalized recommendation algorithms that narrow users' exposure to diverse content and reduce opportunities for self-reflection regarding their interests relative to others. This study explores how swapping recommendations with strangers can facilitate the discovery of new content and encourage reflection. We tested this concept by creating OtherTube, a browser extension for YouTube that showcases personalized recommendations from strangers. OtherTube enables users to (i) establish an anonymized profile for social comparison, (ii) share their own recommended videos, and (iii) browse the recommendations of others. We carried out a 10-day user study involving 41 participants, followed by interviews with 11 of them. Our findings indicate that viewing OtherTube recommendations helped users uncover and cultivate new interests. We also identified specific user and content traits influencing engagement with these exchanges; for instance, younger participants interacted more frequently, whereas perceived irrelevance of certain videos deterred viewing. Additionally, users reflected on both their own and others' interests, noting areas of similarity and difference. These results suggest promising avenues for designs that leverage the exchange of personalized recommendations among strangers.

How can we improve speech representations for end-to-end speech-to-text translation when labeled data is scarce? While current methods often try to leverage powerful machine translation capabilities for speech translation, they frequently overlook the representational gap between different modalities. This paper introduces the Speech-TExt Manifold Mixup (STEMM) approach to address this discrepancy. Specifically, STEMM mixes representation sequences from different modalities and feeds both unimodal speech and multimodal mixed sequences into the translation model simultaneously, utilizing a self-learning framework to regularize their predictions. Experiments on the MuST-C benchmark and additional analyses demonstrate that our method effectively reduces cross-modal representation gaps and yields significant performance gains over a strong baseline across eight translation directions.

Building on Paper I, where we employed the CUSP formalism to analytically derive the precise abundance and radial profiles of diffuse dark matter (dDM) and accreted subhaloes across all prior epochs without any free parameters, this work utilizes those findings as initial conditions to track the subsequent evolution of subhaloes and dDM within host haloes. By ignoring dynamical friction, we rigorously compute the impacts of iterative tidal stripping and heating on subhaloes orbiting inside their host haloes, thereby determining the quantity of dDM and sub-subhaloes they deposit into the intra-halo medium. We subsequently calculate the resulting abundance and spatial distribution of these stripped components. This analysis elucidates the influence of halo concentration on substructure and explains several prominent simulation features, such as the correlation between substructure and host halo mass. Furthermore, it isolates the distinct effects of dynamical friction on substructure. While these results apply strictly to purely accreting haloes, Paper III extends the investigation to low-mass subhaloes that are immune to dynamical friction within typical haloes that have undergone significant mergers.

Machine learning (ML), particularly neural networks, has achieved remarkable success in handling image and language data. This efficacy stems from the frequent absence of formal models for visual and auditory inputs, allowing neural networks to leverage their capabilities by learning directly from data. Conversely, physics often relies on robust formal models describing natural processes; however, ML has recently become valuable in this domain by accelerating numerical simulations and enhancing accuracy. A significant, unresolved challenge in classical physics involves comprehending turbulent fluid motion. This study addresses this by constructing a highly simplified turbulence representation using the Gledzer-Ohkitani-Yamada (GOY) shell model to explore the potential of physics-constrained, ML-assisted small-scale turbulence modeling. Rather than employing standard supervised learning, we propose a method designed to reconstruct key statistical properties of turbulence, such as self-similar inertial-range scaling, yielding promising experimental outcomes. Additionally, we examine the challenges and pitfalls associated with integrating machine learning with differential equations.

The future evolution of human-computer interfaces will introduce immersive digital environments that fully immerse users in 3D spaces, enabling interaction with virtual or digital twin objects. Consequently, collaborative extended reality (XR) applications are anticipated to arise, demanding rigorous performance standards from the supporting wireless connectivity infrastructure. This paper investigates how innovative multi-antenna coded caching (CC) methods can enable high-speed, low-latency communication and enhance user quality of experience (QoE) within a envisioned multi-user XR context. Specifically, we explain how these techniques allow for the prioritization of content destined for wireless bottleneck zones while leveraging the aggregate cache memory of users as an extra communication asset. To this end, we first examine recent progress in multi-antenna CC that optimizes the utilization of distributed in-device memory. Next, we analyze how XR application needs are accommodated within the 3GPP framework and how our proposed XR scenario aligns with expected use cases. Finally, we pinpoint emerging challenges associated with integrating CC techniques into multi-user XR environments and suggest novel practical solutions to overcome them.

Rapid urbanization, fueled by a growing global population, necessitates a critical examination of how to create livable cities. As modern smart cities increasingly integrate data-driven artificial intelligence, it is essential to recognize that while technology can promote prosperity, well-being, livability, and social justice, it requires supportive analog elements—such as thoughtful policies, established institutions, and responsible governance—to succeed. The primary goal of these smart cities must remain the enhancement of human welfare and social flourishing. However, research indicates that various technological business models and features can inadvertently exacerbate social issues like extremism, polarization, misinformation, and internet addiction. Consequently, addressing the philosophical and ethical dimensions of ensuring the security, safety, and interpretability of AI algorithms—which will serve as the foundation of future cities—is of paramount importance. There is a global demand for technology to become more humane and human-centered. This paper investigates key challenges, including security, robustness, interpretability, and ethical concerns regarding data and algorithms, with a specific focus on how these issues converge. We provide a comprehensive review of existing literature, analyzing how one challenge may trigger or resolve others. Additionally, the paper outlines current limitations and pitfalls, offering guidance on future research directions to bridge existing gaps and develop superior solutions. We believe this rigorous analysis will establish a foundational baseline for future research in this field.

Equivariant networks embed the symmetries inherent in a learning task directly into their architecture. This paper investigates the connection between equivariance and generalization error by applying PAC-Bayesian analysis to these networks, where feature space transformations are defined by group representations. Through perturbation analysis of equivariant networks in the Fourier domain across each layer, we establish norm-based PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds. These bounds quantify how group size, as well as the multiplicity and degree of irreducible representations, influence generalization error, offering guidance for their selection. Generally, the results suggest that employing a larger group size enhances generalization performance, a finding supported by extensive numerical experiments.

This study examines type II second harmonic generation in III-V-on-insulator wire waveguides through both theoretical analysis and experimental validation. Our findings demonstrate that the propagation direction is critical, as exploiting longitudinal field components enables robust and efficient conversion. We predict that, for comparable waveguide dimensions, the maximum theoretical conversion efficiency for type II processes exceeds that of type II processes. Additionally, we achieve an experimental conversion efficiency of 12 %/W, a result constrained by propagation losses.

Collaborative tasks are pervasive activities that necessitate communication to achieve shared objectives, with collaborative building being a prime example. Our objective is to create an intelligent builder agent within a simulated Minecraft environment that constructs user-specified structures solely through verbal interaction. To accomplish this, the agent must proactively seek clarification when additional information is required. Current research utilizing the Minecraft Corpus Dataset focuses primarily on executing instructions, often overlooking the critical role of asking clarifying questions. In this paper, we expand the Minecraft Corpus Dataset by categorizing all builder utterances into eight distinct types, including clarification questions, and introduce a novel agent model capable of deciding whether to ask for clarification or execute commands. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our model attains state-of-the-art performance on collaborative building tasks, marking a significant improvement. Furthermore, we define two new tasks: the "learning to ask" task and the "joint learning" task, the latter involving the simultaneous optimization of both collaborative building and learning to ask.

Recent photometric studies of Trans-Neptunian Objects (TNOs) have identified that cold classical TNOs possess unique z-band color signatures, indicating they belong to a distinct surface class. This observation implied the existence of an absorption feature in their reflectance spectra at wavelengths exceeding 0.8 microns. In this study, we present reflectance spectra ranging from 0.55 to 1.0 microns for six TNOs situated on dynamically cold orbits with semimajor axes near 44 au. Five of these spectra exhibit a clear and consistent decrease in spectral gradient above 0.8 microns, deviating from their linear red optical continuum and aligning with previously reported photometric color data. Contrary to predictions, we find no evidence that this spectral flattening results from an absorption band centered near 1.0 micron. Instead, we hypothesize that the uniform shape of these five spectra stems from the presence of similar refractory organics on their surfaces and/or comparable physical characteristics, such as porosity or grain size distribution. This spectral consistency supports the prediction that cold classicals share a common formation history and surface evolution. The sixth target, previously ambiguously classified as either hot or cold, displays a spectrum that remains nearly linear across the entire observed range. This suggests that this object is a hot classical interloper within the cold classical dynamical zone and implies that other interlopers can be identified by their linear reflectance spectra between 0.8 and 1.0 microns.

All Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are prone to errors that are often unexpected and distinct from typical human mistakes, termed "non-human" errors. These errors must be rectified without compromising existing capabilities or necessitating direct human intervention. This paper offers a preliminary report on a project employing a systematic method to enhance the intellectual efficacy of individual AIs through AI communities. We integrate concepts from learning within heterogeneous multiagent systems with novel mathematical frameworks designed for non-iterative error correction in legacy AI systems. The study outlines the mathematical underpinnings of non-destructive AI correction and establishes a series of new stochastic separation theorems. These theorems offer a fresh tool for developing, analyzing, and evaluating machine learning algorithms and methods in high-dimensional spaces. They demonstrate that, even with exponentially large datasets, classical linear classifiers in Fisher's form possess sufficient power to probabilistically separate errors from correct responses, thereby providing an efficient solution to the non-destructive correction problem. Specifically, we validate hypotheses from our 2017 paper, "Stochastic Separation Theorems," and address a general problem previously posed by Donoho and Tanner in 2009.

Hierarchically nanostructured porous electrodes are ubiquitous across diverse electrochemical energy applications, ranging from batteries and supercapacitors to sensors and electrocatalysis. Accurately modeling macroscopic transport and relaxation at the system level, despite the electrodes' intricate microscopic geometry, is crucial for understanding device performance. Specifically, the discharge behavior of capacitive porous electrodes often deviates from the traditional exponential decay typical of standard electrodes, where the rate of change of a dynamic quantity is directly proportional to the quantity itself. Instead, systems like electric double-layer capacitors (EDLCs) display power-law-like discharge profiles that are most effectively modeled using differential equations incorporating non-integer derivatives. By employing fractional-order integrals in the Riemann-Liouville sense alongside superstatistics, this study offers a framework for analyzing the macroscopic response of these electrode systems based on the mesoscopic behavior of their constituent parts. Depending on the physical assumptions regarding initial charge and characteristic time, the solutions may take the form of power-law-like functions or the Mittag-Leffler (ML) function. Ultimately, a generalized three-parameter Mittag-Leffler function is identified as the optimal model for describing experimental discharge data from commercial EDLCs across various time scales.

Approximating a signal with the optimal K-sparse representation in a redundant dictionary is an NP-hard challenge, typically addressed using suboptimal greedy Matching Pursuit (MP) algorithms. This paper introduces an acceleration method and an implementation of MP designed for a multi-Gabor dictionary, which combines multiple Gabor-type time-frequency dictionaries. Each dictionary in this concatenation consists of translations and modulations of a potentially distinct window, along with specific time and frequency shift parameters. The proposed speed-up relies on pre-calculating and thresholding inner products between atoms and performing residual updates directly in the coefficient domain, thereby eliminating the need to revert to the signal domain. Because this acceleration employs an approximate update step, the study provides both theoretical and experimental evidence of the algorithm's convergence. The software is coded in C (adhering to C99 and C++11 standards) and includes interfaces for Matlab and GNU Octave. Under certain configurations, this implementation achieves speeds up to 70 times faster than the standard Matching Pursuit Toolkit (MPTK).

This study examines resonant electron-plasmon interactions within a drifting electron gas of arbitrary degeneracy. By transforming the kinetic-corrected quantum hydrodynamic model into an effective Schrödinger-Poisson framework, we derive a driven coupled pseudoforce system through variable separation applied to a linearized system. We note that in the low phase-speed kinetic regime, the characteristic particle-like plasmon branch is significantly altered by a correction dependent on electron number density and temperature. Additionally, we offer an alternative interpretation of quantum wave-particle duality as a direct result of resonant electron-plasmon interactions (referred to as electron murmuration), wherein drifting electrons undergo resonant scattering by spatial electrostatic energy distributions, defined by de Broglie oscillations. We derive the phase shift and amplitude of excitations within the damped driven pseudoforce system, analyzing their variations relative to normalized chemical potential and electron temperature. Specifically, we detail the impact of kinetic corrections on the energy dispersion relation of the electron gas. Results indicate that only the low phase-speed branch of the dispersion curve is substantially influenced by these corrections. Furthermore, we observe that increasing electron number density raises the effective mass and reduces electron mobility, whereas increasing electron temperature produces the opposite effect. The kinetic correction also notably lowers the plasmon conduction band. Future elaborations of this model could explore beam-plasmon interactions and energy exchange in multispecies quantum plasmas.

This paper introduces a secure key exchange algorithm that leverages channel reciprocity in wireless environments to generate a shared secret between nodes $A$ and $B$. Reciprocity ensures that the phase characteristics of the links connecting $A$ to $B$ and $B$ to $A$ are identical. Nodes $A$ and $B$ measure multiple instances of these reciprocal phases, referred to as shared phase values. Each value is employed to mask points within a Phase Shift Keying (PSK) constellation by rotating it; this rotation corresponds to adding phases modulo-$2\pi$. Since channel phases are uniformly distributed across $[0,2\pi)$, the summation process yields a result that reveals no information about the individual components. To increase key capacity over static or slowly fading channels, the RF propagation path is intentionally perturbed to generate multiple independent multi-path fading realizations, each providing a new phase value. Attempting to intercept these shared phases leaves an eavesdropper (Eve) with an under-determined system of linear equations, preventing the recovery of any meaningful solution. This security property enables the establishment of a robust key between the two legitimate users.

This study introduces a methodological framework for estimating and simulating high-dimensional dynamical systems, including atmospheric and oceanic flows, using ensemble-based approaches. The system is embedded within a family of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces defined by kernel functions derived from the system's dynamics, a concept termed "Wonderland" due to its advantageous characteristics. Within this framework, both the Koopman and Perron-Frobenius operators are unitary and uniformly continuous, allowing them to be represented as exponential series of diagonalizable, bounded infinitesimal generators. Consequently, exact ensemble formulations for tangent linear dynamics and direct access to Lyapunov exponents become available. Wonderland facilitates the development of remarkably straightforward ensemble data assimilation techniques for trajectory reconstruction, relying on constant-in-time linear combinations of trajectory samples. This "embarrassingly simple" strategy is enabled by a rigorously justified superposition principle grounded in several fundamental theorems.

$\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theories featuring an $\mathfrak{so}(4N)$ algebra and specific global structures exhibit non-invertible symmetries. By identifying the holographically dual branes associated with these symmetries, we derive their fusion rules based on the branes' worldvolume dynamics.

Diffusion stands as the most fundamental stochastic transport mechanism. As the archetypal model for diffusion, Brownian motion has significantly advanced scientific disciplines including physics, chemistry, biology, and finance. Nevertheless, over the last few decades, experimental observations across numerous fields have revealed transport processes that deviate from diffusion and lack Brownian statistics. Such non-diffusive phenomena are observed in human mobility, intracellular dynamics, solar surface bright point motion, charge carrier transport in amorphous semiconductors, contaminant propagation in groundwater, foraging animal search patterns, and energetic particle transport in turbulent plasmas. These instances demonstrate that the classical diffusion paradigm—which relies on the assumptions of an uncorrelated (Markovian), Gaussian stochastic process—must be adapted to account for transport characterized by non-locality and long-range correlations.

Rather than providing a comprehensive review of non-diffusive transport, this article serves as an introductory overview for those new to the subject; readers seeking deeper insights are directed to the referenced literature. The text begins by reviewing the fundamentals of the classical diffusion model, followed by an examination of two potential generalizations: the Continuous-Time Random Walk (CTRW) and fractional Lévy motion (fLm).

The 2013 Dengue outbreak in Fiji caused a significant number of fatalities and remains a critical public health concern. Dengue fever, transmitted primarily through mosquito bites, is caused by one of four viral serotypes. Currently, diagnosis in Fiji is limited to hospitals, where the process is slow and inefficient; therefore, effective monitoring of the disease's spread is essential. With the rising availability of affordable smartphones and improved internet connectivity, there is a viable opportunity to develop a mobile application for Dengue surveillance. This paper proposes a GPS-enabled mobile app designed to track Dengue cases and provide a network visualization of the disease's spread, enabling health authorities to rapidly identify infected regions. A functional prototype has been developed and tested, with recommendations provided for future testing and full-scale implementation.

This work investigates planning and query-efficient algorithms utilizing linear function approximation alongside a simulator. We operate under the constraint that the agent possesses only local access to the simulator, restricting queries to previously visited states; this approach is more practical than many prior reinforcement learning studies involving generative models. We introduce two algorithms, Confident Monte Carlo Least Square Policy Iteration (Confident MC-LSPI) and Confident Monte Carlo Politex (Confident MC-Politex), tailored for this specific environment. Assuming that Q-functions for all policies are linear with respect to known state-action features, we demonstrate that these algorithms exhibit polynomial query and computational complexities regarding feature dimension, effective planning horizon, and desired sub-optimality, while remaining independent of the state space size. A key technical contribution is a novel proof technique employing a virtual policy iteration algorithm. This method allows us to apply existing results on $\ell_\infty$-bounded approximate policy iteration, proving that our algorithms can learn the optimal policy for a given initial state despite having only local simulator access. We anticipate that this technique can be generalized to broader contexts beyond the scope of this study.

As attribution-based techniques become essential for verifying model reliability in high-stakes contexts, guaranteeing the stability of these explanations—specifically their resilience to minute input changes—is paramount. Despite this need, prior research indicates that current state-of-the-art methods often produce unstable outputs. This work introduces metrics to quantify explanation stability, confirming the instability of several widely used approaches. We specifically propose new Relative Stability metrics that assess how explanations vary in response to alterations in the input, model representation, or the underlying predictor's output. Furthermore, experimental evaluations across three real-world datasets reveal significant insights regarding the performance of seven explanation methods under various stability metrics.

This study explores a Kohn-Luttinger-like mechanism driving superconductivity in Bernal bilayer and rhombohedral trilayer graphene. Using a continuum model, we demonstrate that the screened long-range Coulomb interaction alone is sufficient to generate superconductivity with critical temperatures matching experimental observations. In bilayer graphene, the order parameter exhibits a sign change between valleys, identifying the system as a valley-singlet, spin-triplet superconductor. Conversely, despite repulsive short-range interactions, the trilayer's complex Fermi surface results in a spin-singlet state. Introducing Ising spin-orbit coupling significantly boosts the critical temperature, aligning with experimental data, while causing the superconducting order parameter to lock between spin and valley degrees of freedom.

The application of information technology to analyze human behavior has become a significant area of scientific inquiry. Cultural and personality traits play a crucial role in shaping interpersonal interactions within crowds. This study outlines a methodology for identifying cultural characteristics in crowd dynamics using video data. By detecting, tracking, and characterizing pedestrians in recorded footage, the research leverages the Big Five personality model to uncover cultural distinctions. The results demonstrate that, when compared with existing literature, this model produces consistent and coherent insights regarding cultural differences across various countries.

The critical role of comprehending SARS-CoV-2 evolution cannot be overstated. Recent research confirms that natural selection is the primary driver of this evolution, favoring mutations that enhance viral infectivity. Our findings introduce a novel evolutionary mechanism: vaccine-breakthrough or antibody-resistant mutations. Specifically, the Y449S mutation in the spike protein's receptor-binding domain (RBD), which appears alongside N501Y, exhibits reduced infectivity relative to the original virus but effectively evades neutralizing antibodies. By analyzing evolutionary pathways across more than 1.9 million SARS-CoV-2 genomes, we identified a strong correlation between the frequency of these vaccine-resistant mutations and vaccination rates in Europe and America. We anticipate that, as a complementary transmission route, these mutations will become a dominant force in SARS-CoV-2 evolution once the majority of the global population is vaccinated. Ultimately, this study illuminates SARS-CoV-2 evolution and transmission, facilitating the development of next-generation vaccines and antibody therapies designed to resist mutations.

Modeling power plant outages is a critical component of power system planning. This study develops unavailability models for the fleets of eight nations in Northwest Europe and compares them with empirical distributions obtained from the open-access ENTSO-e Transparency Platform. Analysis of non-sequential models reveals limitations in empirical modeling, characterized by highly variable results across different countries. Furthermore, examining time-sequential models indicates a distinct requirement for fleet-specific analytic parameters. Although empirical distributions present several challenges and ambiguities, the authors suggest that comparing these two complementary approaches offers valuable qualitative and quantitative insights into generator unavailabilities.

Most landslide susceptibility research assumes slope instability is time-invariant, relying on the principle that past and present data predict the future. While this assumption is often reasonable, triggers such as rainfall or earthquakes inherently vary temporally; yet, this temporal dimension is seldom integrated into susceptibility models, appearing primarily in hazard assessments. This study examines landslides triggered by the 2017 Jiuzhaigou earthquake ($M_w = 6.5$), incorporating associated ground motion analyses at the Slope Unit (SU) level. We apply a Bayesian Generalized Additive Model, treating slope instability within SUs as following a Bernoulli distribution. Although this approach typically yields a susceptibility map specific to a single trigger event—limiting its utility for land-use planning—we utilize it first to accurately quantify the effects and distribution of ground motion on unstable SUs. By treating the impact of ground motion as time-invariant, we enable statistical simulations for various ground motion scenarios occurring between 1933 and 2017. Consequently, we derive the full range of potential susceptibility patterns over the last century, condensing this data into a comprehensive model representing all possible ground motion patterns since 1933. Furthermore, this backward statistical simulation framework can be applied in reverse: by accounting for specific ground motion scenarios, it can also project forward to estimate future unstable slopes.

Conventional machine learning operates within centralized cloud infrastructure, but growing security concerns alongside the availability of extensive data and computational power in wireless networks are driving the shift of learning algorithms to the network edge. This trend has given rise to federated learning (FL), a rapidly expanding field that unifies wireless communication and machine learning. This paper offers an in-depth examination of FL applications within sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks. We begin by outlining the essential requirements for deploying FL in wireless communications, followed by a discussion of its primary motivating applications. Furthermore, we pinpoint key issues and challenges, providing a thorough analysis of implementing FL techniques for wireless communication systems.

The mathematical models and numerical simulations presented in this work are inspired by satellite data revealing horizontal gradients in sea surface temperature and salinity that align closely with the slowly varying envelopes of rapidly oscillating waves. Such alignment between fluid property gradients and wave envelopes typically arises in regions with strong horizontal buoyancy gradients. The nonlinear models introduced here may offer future avenues for optimizing satellite imagery to simultaneously capture the dynamics of both waves and currents. The derived model operates at two levels of approximation: first addressing rapidly oscillating waves, and subsequently applying the slowly varying envelope (SVE) approximation via the WKB method. This WKB-based model of wave-current-buoyancy interaction, applicable to free surfaces with significant horizontal buoyancy gradients, identifies the ponderomotive force of the slowly varying wave envelope acting on surface currents through the horizontal buoyancy gradient as the mechanism behind these correlations. Within this framework, the buoyancy gradient appears explicitly in the WKB wave momentum, generating density-weighted potential vorticity whenever the buoyancy gradient is not parallel to the wave-envelope gradient.

Topological quantum computing relies on two fundamental operations: maintaining logical observables over time and transporting them across space. While memory experiments serve as a standard benchmark for temporal preservation, there is currently no equivalent established test for spatial movement. This paper addresses that absence by introducing "stability experiments," which evaluate a quantum error correction system's ability to calculate the product of stabilizers within a large area. These experiments function by assessing the system on a region that appears locally as a standard code but possesses a globally defined stabilizer product.
These lectures provide a concise overview of the primary research areas in particle physics that extend beyond the Standard Model.

Neural machine translation (NMT) faces a limitation where the computational expense of the softmax layer in the output layer restricts generation to high-frequency words only. In the context of Japanese-English NMT, the extensive vocabulary size is exacerbated by Japanese predicate conjugation, which can yield up to 19 surface forms for a single verb. This study targets predicate conjugation to compress the vocabulary. The current vocabulary list is saturated with various verb forms, prompting the proposal of methods that leverage conjugation information without discarding essential linguistic data. These approaches enable the generation of low-frequency words and handle out-of-vocabulary terms. Two specific strategies for integrating conjugation information were explored: treating it as a discrete token or embedding it as a vector feature. Experimental results indicate that vocabulary size can be reduced by approximately 86.1% (based on the Tanaka corpus) while allowing models to generate words absent from the training data. Additionally, BLEU scores improved by 0.91 points for Japanese-to-English translation and by 0.32 points for English-to-Japanese translation when using ASPEC.

We examine the thermal properties of a Bose-Hubbard model incorporating Rashba spin-orbit coupling, beginning with a strong coupling mean-field ground state. The spin-orbit coupling parameter ($\gamma$) plays a crucial role in inducing bosonic condensation at a finite wavevector $k_0$. Our findings indicate that the bosons can form either homogeneous, phase-twisted, or orbital-ordered superfluid phases, contingent upon the values of $\gamma$ and the inter-species interaction strength $\lambda$. We demonstrate that increasing $\gamma$ suppresses the critical interaction $U_c$ required for the superfluid-to-Mott insulator transition in the ground state and lowers the critical temperature $T_c$ for the superfluid-to-Bose-liquid transition at a constant interaction. Furthermore, we account for thermal broadening in the momentum distribution and characterize real-space profiles of thermally disordered magnetic textures, noting their homogenization when $T \gtrsim T_c$. Finally, we present a Landau theory-based framework for describing ground state phase boundaries and thermal transition scales, alongside proposed experiments to validate our theoretical predictions.
It has been proven that every homeomorphism mapping between any two closed, negligible subsets of $D^\tau$ can be extended to an autohomeomorphism of $D^\tau$.

This paper examines a one-dimensional Bresse system with finite memory, subject to homogeneous Dirichlet-Neumann-Neumann boundary conditions. We establish general decay properties for the system's energy, addressing scenarios where wave propagation speeds are either equal or distinct, provided the relaxation function satisfies specific criteria. Furthermore, through a specific example, we demonstrate that when wave speeds are equal and the relaxation function decays polynomially, our findings yield an optimal decay rate; specifically, the system's decay rate matches exactly that of the relaxation function.

The presence of monopoles serves as a defining hallmark of Kaluza-Klein multidimensional theories, featuring notably complex topological structures. Central to this study is the dipole solution, interpreted as a bound state of a monopole and an anti-monopole. In its ground state, termed monopolium, this entity is electromagnetically neutral in free space, interacting solely via gravity. However, when exposed to time-varying magnetic fields, monopolium develops an induced magnetic moment that fluctuates over time, leading to radiation. Our analysis of the most promising astrophysical conditions for such radiative monopolium reveals that the emitted radiation is negligible and undetectable by standard instrumentation. These results indicate that, should it exist, Kaluza-Klein monopolium could constitute a component of primordial dark matter.

This study introduces a lab-on-chip setup designed to precisely quantify losses in superconducting microstrip lines across microwave and sub-millimeter wavelengths. The microstrips consist of NbTiN, created via reactive magnetron sputtering, and amorphous silicon, deposited through plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD). Loss measurements at sub-mm frequencies were conducted using on-chip Fabry-P{\'e}rot resonators (FPR) functioning near 350 GHz, while microwave losses were assessed with shunted half-wave resonators sharing the same geometry on the identical chip. Our findings reveal an amorphous silicon loss tangent of $\tan\delta = 3.7\pm0.5\times10^{-5}$ at 6 GHz and $\tan\delta = 2.1\pm 0.1\times10^{-4}$ at 350 GHz. Although these values indicate exceptionally low losses for deposited dielectrics, the sub-mm wave losses are markedly greater than the microwave losses, a discrepancy that the conventional two-level system loss model fails to explain.

Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) remains the sole logical framework currently believed to capture PTIME, as it resides within PTIME without being proven distinct from it. A notable PTIME decision problem that lacks a known CPT definition is the isomorphism problem on unordered Cai-F\"urer-Immerman (CFI) graphs, often referred to as the CFI-query. This study investigates the expressive capacity of CPT concerning this problem and establishes a partial characterization of solvable instances based on the properties of symmetric XOR-circuits defined over CFI-graphs. Specifically, the CFI-query is definable in CPT for a given graph class only if, for every graph $G$, there exists an XOR-circuit $C$ with input gates corresponding to edges of $G$, which exhibits sufficient symmetry relative to $G$'s automorphisms and meets additional circuit criteria. Furthermore, we provide a sufficient condition for the CFI-query's solvability in CPT and introduce a novel CPT-algorithm that accepts structures comprising a CFI-graph alongside an XOR-circuit possessing the requisite properties. While the strongest existing CPT-algorithm handles instances with preorders featuring logarithmic-sized colour classes, our result implicitly generalizes this capability to preorders with polylogarithmic-sized colour classes, including certain unordered additional structures. Additionally, our findings offer new perspectives on the broader issue of solving unordered linear equation systems $A \cdot x = b$ over finite fields; such systems are CPT-definable if matrix $A$ has a rank of at most logarithmic relative to the size of the encoding structure. This outcome further demonstrates a separation between CPT and fixed-point logic with counting.

Cross-sectional strategies represent a traditional and widely adopted trading approach, with modern iterations leveraging advanced neural networks to achieve high returns. Although these methods excel in data-abundant environments featuring mature assets with extensive histories, they often result in overfitted models with diminished performance when applied to instruments lacking sufficient historical data. To address this, we present Fused Encoder Networks, a novel hybrid transfer ranking model that shares parameters. This architecture integrates information from an encoder-attention module trained on a source dataset with a parallel module designed for a smaller target dataset, thereby enhancing generalizability in scenarios with scarce data. Furthermore, the self-attention mechanism captures interactions between instruments not only during the training loss calculation but also at the inference stage. Demonstrating the model's efficacy using momentum strategies on the top ten cryptocurrencies by market capitalization, Fused Encoder Networks surpassed reference benchmarks across most metrics. It achieved a three-fold increase in the Sharpe ratio compared to classical momentum and improved performance by approximately 50% relative to the best benchmark model before transaction costs. Notably, the model maintained its superiority over baselines even after factoring in the substantial transaction costs inherent to cryptocurrency trading.

We introduce a unified optimization framework that integrates neural networks with dictionary learning to capture intricate relationships between resting-state functional MRI and behavioral data. Within this approach, the dictionary learning component decomposes patient correlation matrices into shared basis networks alongside subject-specific loadings. These personalized features are then fed simultaneously into a neural network to forecast multidimensional clinical metrics. Our innovative framework merges gradient information from the neural network with that of a standard matrix factorization objective. This combined procedure jointly estimates the basis networks, subject loadings, and neural network weights that best inform clinical severity. We assessed our integrated model on a multi-score prediction task involving 52 individuals diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). In a ten-fold cross-validation setup, our framework surpassed state-of-the-art methods in predicting three distinct measures of clinical severity.

This study investigates how the carrier-envelope phase influences electron-positron pair production within a spatially inhomogeneous electric field featuring symmetrical frequency chirping. We observe that, regardless of whether the initial frequency is high or low and whether chirping is present or absent, the interference strength in the momentum spectrum and the reduction in particle number fluctuate periodically with the phase. These periodic variations are notably more sensitive to applied parameters in low-frequency regimes. Specifically, under small chirping conditions, the reduction in particle number varies by over an order of magnitude across different phases at small spatial scales. While distinct optimal phases emerge for the reduced particle number at varying spatial scales, increasing the chirping magnitude consistently yields a higher number of created pairs. Furthermore, the momentum spectrum reveals various symmetry types, including mutual mirror/coincidence symmetry between two correlated phases and individual self-symmetry for a single phase. We provide a detailed analytical examination of the physical mechanisms underlying both the mutual symmetry between correlated phases and the individual symmetry at specific fixed phases. Finally, we anticipate that the combined effects of phase and chirping on the periodic and symmetrical behaviors of the momentum spectrum and particle number reduction may be extended to more complex fields, such as those involving multidimensional spatial coordinates.

Wind farms function as intricate systems that are simultaneously governed by the nonlinear, stochastic nature of weather patterns and heavily shaped by supervisory control protocols. A primary challenge in this domain is forecasting wind energy, an intermittent renewable source characterized by non-stationary dynamics. Addressing this, we examine one year of power time series data from an offshore wind farm, recorded at 10-minute intervals. Utilizing detrended fluctuation analysis, we assessed the autocorrelation of these series and identified a persistent regime exhibiting cross-over behavior. To enhance the modeling framework for large-scale complex wind energy systems, we constructed a stochastic reduced-form model for the power time series. This model captures the transitions between two dominant generation phases through a bistable deterministic component, while correlated stochastic fluctuations account for the observed persistence. Consequently, the model successfully replicates key empirical features, including the autocorrelation function and the bimodal probability density function.

Ramsey Theory focuses on preventing specific patterns, yet the act of avoiding one often causes others to appear. For instance, avoiding arithmetic progressions leads to repetition (Van der Waerden numbers), whereas avoiding monochromatic solutions to $a+b=c$ results in reflection (Schur numbers). We leverage these emerging patterns when coloring grids to prevent monochromatic rectangles. Like many challenges in this field, the problem's search space expands rapidly, complicating computational searches. While Steinbach et al. achieved an 18x18 grid solution with 4 colors by imposing rotation symmetry, this approach does not extend to 5 colors. In this paper, we formulate the problem using propositional logic and enforce internal symmetries to maintain satisfiability while guiding SAT solvers. By analyzing patterns with 2 and 3 colors, we identify a "shift pattern" that is both easily generalizable and efficiently encodable. Utilizing this pattern, we discover a novel 18x18 grid solution with 4 colors that is non-isomorphic to the previously known one. We also examine the pattern to derive necessary conditions that further reduce the search space. Finally, we discuss our efforts to find a 5-coloring for a 26x26 grid and outline additional open questions regarding the shift pattern.

This work presents a spinorial framework for Sasakian and 3-Sasakian structures across all dimensions, extending earlier findings specific to dimensions 5 and 7 [FK88, FK89, FK90]. Furthermore, we provide a full characterization of the invariant spinor space on a homogeneous 3-Sasakian manifold, demonstrating that it is generated by Clifford products of invariant differential forms with a specific invariant Killing spinor. Additionally, we establish a basis for the space of Riemannian Killing spinors on such a homogeneous 3-Sasakian space and identify which elements within this basis give rise to the homogeneous 3-Sasakian structure.

Since the 1990s, group III-nitrides (AlN, GaN, and InN) in the wurtzite phase have garnered significant attention for their successful optoelectronic applications. This paper presents a comprehensive investigation into the structural elastic and electronic properties of these three materials using both conventional and hybrid Density Functional Theory, offering a comparative analysis of their characteristics. We directly compare their electronic structures, specifically addressing the inversion of the top valence band caused by negative crystal field splitting and its implications for acceptor-doping challenges in AlN. By calculating elastic constants and the Young modulus, we establish a simplified model linking the deformation energy associated with parameter $u$ to the effective crystal-field splitting, thereby demonstrating a direct relationship between internal strain and crystal-field splitting.

We provide explicit formulas for a specific family of parametric binomial sums that include harmonic numbers, defined for $p=0,1,2$ and $|t|\leq1$:
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{H_{k-1}t^k}{k^p\binom{n+k}{k}}\quad \mbox{and}\quad
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{t^k}{k^p\binom{n+k}{k}}.
$$
Furthermore, we extend a known relationship between Stirling numbers of the first kind and the Riemann zeta function to involve the polygamma function, accompanied by several applications:
$$
\zeta(n+1)=\sum_{k=n}^{\infty}\frac{s(k,n)}{kk!}, \quad n=1,2,3,... .
$$
Illustrative examples include:
\begin{equation*}
\zeta(3)=\frac{1}{7}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{H_{k-1}4^k}{k^2\binom{2k}{k}},\quad
\mbox{and}\quad
\zeta(3)=\frac{8}{7}+\frac{1}{7}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{H_{k-1}4^k}{k^2(2k+1)\binom{2k}{k}},
\end{equation*}
which constitute novel series representations for the Apéry constant $\zeta(3)$.

Recent advancements in networking technology have drastically improved interpersonal connectivity, facilitating interactions among individuals with diverse ideologies and backgrounds. However, these social networks often foster severe opinion polarization and disagreement. While numerous reviews exist on modeling opinion formation, less focus has been placed specifically on polarization and disagreement. This paper reviews recent progress in these areas, emphasizing their evaluation and control. Current literature typically employs three metrics—polarization, disagreement, and the polarization-disagreement index (PDI)—noting a tradeoff between polarization and disagreement. Various strategies have been proposed to effectively manage these phenomena based on such metrics. This review is vital for summarizing existing work and enhancing the understanding and control of opinion polarization and disagreement.

Riboswitches are cis-acting regulatory RNA motifs commonly found within the leader sequences of bacterial mRNAs. Specifically, an adenine-sensing riboswitch regulates the *add* gene encoding adeninosine deaminase in *Vibrio vulnificus*. While the structural basis for its conformational shifts upon ligand binding remains largely unclear, existing hypotheses suggest that the ligand stabilizes the distal "kissing loop" complex. By employing full-atom molecular dynamics with explicit solvent, enhanced sampling, and sophisticated analysis, researchers aim to gain deeper insights into the formation of these tertiary contacts. This study utilized umbrella sampling simulations to investigate the thermodynamics of the kissing loop complex both with and without the cognate ligand. The researchers enforced the breaking and formation of the loop-loop interaction by restraining the distance between the two loops and validated result convergence using two distinct initialization protocols. A novel method for analyzing base contacts was applied to the structural data. Simulations qualitatively indicated that the ligand stabilizes the kissing loop complex, a finding consistent with previous simulation studies and available experimental data. However, the observed dependence of the stabilization value on the initialization protocol raises concerns regarding the quantitative interpretation of the results, highlighting the need for better-converged enhanced sampling simulations.

The ability of switching control strategies to harmonize safety with efficiency by combining high-performance uncertified controllers with conservative stabilizing ones has been recognized, yet their application under partial state observation remains underexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce a switching control strategy tailored for partially observed linear-Gaussian systems that offers provable performance guarantees. Our analysis demonstrates that this strategy achieves both safety and efficiency: first, it ensures the linear-quadratic cost remains bounded even when the uncertified controller is destabilizing; second, if the uncertified controller is stabilizing, the performance degradation caused by the strategy's conservativeness diminishes super-exponentially toward zero. Furthermore, numerical simulations on the Tennessee Eastman Process validate the efficacy of this switching approach.

Calibrating sensitive parameters that heavily impact forecasts can significantly boost the predictive capability of numerical models. This study aims to enhance simulations of surface wind speed and precipitation by optimizing Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model parameters specifically for tropical cyclones in the Bay of Bengal. The research focuses on ten cyclones spanning various intensity levels between 2011 and 2017. Using a multiobjective adaptive surrogate model-based optimization (MO-ASMO) framework, eight key parameters were adjusted to minimize errors in 10m wind speed and precipitation. The study compares outputs generated with default settings against those with calibrated parameters. Results indicate that calibration improved 10m wind speed predictions by 17.62% and precipitation by 8.20%. Furthermore, the impact of these adjustments on additional variables, including cyclone tracks, intensities, and 500 hPa wind fields, was analyzed. To validate the findings, eight further cyclones from 2011 to 2018 were used to test the calibrated parameters. Additionally, the robustness of these parameters under varying boundary conditions and grid resolutions was assessed. These findings hold substantial promise for enhancing tropical cyclone predictability, thereby facilitating better adaptation and mitigation planning to reduce societal risks.

Following the experimental confirmation of Bell-CHSH inequality violations, significant debate has arisen regarding the non-local and contextual nature of the systems involved. However, the specific hypotheses underlying Bell's inequalities vary depending on the probability space employed in their formulation. The observed violations can alternatively be interpreted in several ways: either hidden variables do not exist, or they exist but lack simultaneously assignable values, or while values can be assigned, joint probabilities are ill-defined, or averages across different contexts cannot be combined. Each of these perspectives remains valid, as different research communities adopt them to support their respective theoretical frameworks.

Recent technological progress has allowed for a thorough exploration of the link between molecular architecture and tumor heterogeneity by combining radiological imaging with genomic (radiogenomic) data. This study utilizes radiogenomic data from patients with lower grade gliomas (LGG), a form of brain cancer, to create a regression framework named RADIOHEAD (RADIOgenomic analysis incorporating tumor HEterogeneity in imAging through Densities) aimed at detecting radiogenomic associations. Imaging features are characterized by voxel intensity probability density functions of tumor sub-regions derived from multimodal MRI, while genomic information is represented by molecular signatures in the form of pathway enrichment scores linked to gene expression profiles. Using a Riemannian-geometric approach for principal component analysis on these probability density functions, each function is mapped to a vector of principal component scores, which serve as predictors in a Bayesian regression model where pathway enrichment scores act as the response variable. Variable selection is performed using a group spike-and-slab prior to accommodate the grouping structure among predictors induced by tumor sub-regions. Subsequently, a Bayesian false discovery rate mechanism infers significant associations based on the posterior distribution of the regression coefficients. The analysis identifies several pathways relevant to LGG etiology, including synaptic transmission, nerve impulse, and neurotransmitter pathways, as having significant associations with their corresponding imaging-based predictors.

Extracting meaningful insights from data frequently necessitates model fitting, particularly when the underlying functional form cannot be derived from first principles. In such scenarios, one must select among various potential models. A prevalent strategy involves minimizing information loss by reducing the number of fit variables—or model flexibility—as much as possible while maintaining an adequate fit to the data. This approach, implemented through the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), embodies the principle of Occam's razor. We contend that these same principles can optimize the penalty strength in penalized maximum-likelihood models. However, unlike typical AIC applications that choose from a finite set of maximum-likelihood models, penalty optimization requires selecting from a continuous range of candidates that inherently violate the maximum-likelihood condition. Consequently, we derive a generalized information criterion, AICp, to address this. This criterion incorporates the concept of effective free parameters, offering a flexible framework applicable to any model type, whether linear or non-linear, parametric or non-parametric, and regardless of parameter constraints. We demonstrate that AICp enables the optimization of any penalty strength without requiring separate Monte-Carlo simulations. As an illustrative application, we examine the optimization of smoothing in non-parametric models, a technique with widespread use in astrophysics, including dynamical modeling, spectral fitting, and gravitational lensing.

This work investigates the relationship between pseudo-differential and Wick operators using the Bargmann transform. We derive an expression for the Wick symbol based on the short-time Fourier transform of the Weyl symbol. This approach yields characterizations of Wick symbols for Shubin-type and infinite-order pseudo-differential operators, alongside findings on their composition. Furthermore, we establish a series expansion of Wick operators in terms of anti-Wick operators, which facilitates a sharp G{\aa}rding inequality and the transfer of hypoellipticity between Wick and Shubin symbols. Finally, we demonstrate continuity properties for anti-Wick operators and provide estimates for the Wick symbols associated with them.

The preferential attachment (PA) model serves as a widely used framework for representing dynamic social networks, including collaboration networks. Under the assumption that the PA function follows a parametric structure, we introduce and analyze the maximum likelihood estimator for the associated parameter. By employing a supercritical continuous-time branching process framework, we establish the almost sure consistency and asymptotic normality of this estimator. Furthermore, we present an alternative estimator relying solely on the network's final snapshot, demonstrating its consistency and asymptotic normality under broad conditions. Finally, we evaluate the performance of these estimators against a nonparametric approach through a limited simulation study.

Digital image correlation (DIC) and crystal plasticity simulations were employed to investigate cold dwell behavior in a coarse-grained Ti-6Al alloy across three temperatures, reaching up to 230°C. Creep strains within large volume grains, measured via DIC, served to calibrate the crystal plasticity model, allowing for the determination of critical resolved shear stresses (CRSS) for the two primary slip systems (basal and prismatic) as a function of temperature. Stress distributions along paths traversing the boundaries of two grain pairs—a "rogue" pair and a "non-rogue" pair—were analyzed at various temperatures. Load shedding was identified in the "rogue" grain pair, characterized by a stress increase in the "hard" grain during the creep phase. At elevated temperatures, 120°C emerged as the critical scenario, exhibiting the maximum stress difference at the grain boundaries between the two pairs. This phenomenon is attributed to the peak strain rate sensitivity of both prismatic and basal slip systems occurring at this specific temperature.

This study investigates the amplitude (Higgs) mode in the vicinity of the two-dimensional superfluid-Mott glass quantum phase transition. By mapping the Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonian for disordered interacting bosons onto an equivalent classical XY model in (2+1) dimensions, we calculate the scalar susceptibility of the order parameter amplitude using Monte Carlo simulations. To derive spectral densities, we apply a modified maximum entropy technique to analytically continue these scalar susceptibilities from imaginary to real frequencies. Our findings reveal that introducing disorder induces unconventional dynamical behavior in the Higgs mode that defies naive scaling, even though the transition's underlying thermodynamics follows a conventional power-law pattern. The resulting spectral densities display a broad, non-critical response across all energies and a momentum-independent dispersion for long wavelengths, providing strong evidence for the localization of the Higgs mode at all levels of dilution.

This study addresses the path guarding challenge within dynamic Defender-Attacker Blotto games (dDAB), focusing on how a robotic team can protect a graph path from adversarial agents. Given that multi-robot systems have proven effective in similar domains like perimeter defense and surveillance, they are ideal for this task. While a defender policy can guarantee path security regardless of information, possessing knowledge about the adversary and the environment can minimize the resources required for adequate security. In this work, we define the exact number of assets necessary to secure the shortest path between two nodes in dDAB games, specifically when the defender's detection range is limited to $k$-hops along that path. By analyzing the link between sensing range and resource requirements, we demonstrate that enhancing the defender's sensing capabilities significantly lowers the number of assets needed to maintain path defense.

Ultrasound elastography is a developing noninvasive method that visualizes pathological changes by assessing tissue mechanics. Accurate mechanical property estimation requires determining tissue displacement in all directions. Although elastography can measure displacement both axially and laterally, axial estimates are superior due to higher sampling rates, resolution, and the propagation of the carrier signal along the axial axis. While Synthetic Aperture (SA) imaging offers better lateral resolution than other ultrasound techniques, its limited depth of field restricts its use in elastography. Virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) addresses this by applying synthetic aperture beamforming to focused transmitted data, thereby retaining SA's high lateral resolution while extending the depth of field. Furthermore, VSSA enhances lateral sampling frequency without the need for interpolation. This study employs VSSA for beamforming to achieve improved lateral resolution and sampling density, followed by processing with our recently introduced OVERWIND elastography technique [1]. Simulation and experimental outcomes demonstrate significant improvements in the accuracy of lateral displacement estimation.

Let $G_1$ and $G_2$ be two groups. If a homomorphism $\phi$ exists from $G_1$ to $G_2$ mapping $a$ to $b$, then $G_1$ is said to degenerate into $G_2$. This paper investigates graph degeneration, demonstrating that group degeneration is a specific instance of graph degeneration. We highlight several notable properties of graph degeneration and apply this concept to provide a visual representation of graphs realized by finite abelian groups. Furthermore, we examine partial orders defined on the set $T_{p_1 \cdots p_n}$, which comprises all graphs realized by finite abelian $p_r$-groups for primes $p_r$ where $1 \leq r \leq n$. We establish that every finite abelian $p_r$-group of rank $n$ corresponds to a saturated chain of Young diagrams within the poset $T_{p_1 \cdots p_n}$. Additionally, we introduce a combinatorial formula representing the degree of a projective representation of a symmetric group; this formula calculates both the count of distinct saturated chains in $T_{p_1 \cdots p_n}$ and the number of finite abelian groups of various orders.

Shape displays are haptic devices designed for whole-hand exploration of three-dimensional surfaces, yet their scalability is often constrained by the mechanical intricacy and expense of conventional actuator arrays. This paper introduces the use of electroadhesive auxetic skins as a strain-limiting layer to achieve programmable shape deformation in a continuous "formable crust" display. These auxetic skins are fabricated as flexible printed circuit boards featuring dielectric-laminated electrodes on each auxetic unit cell (AUC), utilizing monolithic manufacturing to reduce costs and assembly duration. By stacking multiple sheets and applying voltage between electrodes on adjacent layers, electroadhesion secures individual AUCs, yielding a maximum in-plane stiffness variation of 7.6 times with a power consumption of 50 μW per AUC. We first characterize a single AUC and benchmark its performance against a kinematic model. Subsequently, we validate the capacity of a 5x5 AUC array to actively adjust its axial and transverse stiffness. Finally, we demonstrate this array functioning as a strain-limiting skin within a continuous shape display to programmatically regulate the shape output of an inflatable LDPE pouch. The integration of electroadhesion with auxetics facilitates novel capabilities for scalable, low-profile, and low-power control of flexible robotic systems.

A graph is defined as 2-factor Hamiltonian (2FH) when every one of its 2-factors constitutes a Hamiltonian cycle. A related, yet weaker, characteristic is the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian (PMH) property, which holds if each perfect matching (1-factor) of a graph can be extended into a Hamiltonian cycle. In their 2003 paper published in *Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B*, Funk et al. introduced the star product, demonstrating that for bipartite graphs with a 3-edge-cut, the existence of a 2FH structure is both necessary and sufficient if and only if the graph is formed via the star product of two bipartite 2FH graphs. However, this specific condition does not apply to the PMH property. Consequently, this paper explores utilizing star products to construct graphs—potentially non-bipartite, non-regular, and non-2FH—that satisfy the PMH property by employing a newly defined concept: malleable vertices. While the inclusion of a malleable vertex guarantees the PMH property, it does not ensure the graph is 2FH. Furthermore, while Funk et al. conjectured that bipartite cubic 2FH graphs can only be derived from $K_{3,3}$ and the Heawood graph through star products, this study reveals that a cubic graph is 2FH if and only if all its vertices are malleable. Additionally, the paper establishes that the aforementioned conjecture is equivalent to the assertion that every bipartite cyclically 4-edge-connected cubic graph with the PMH property (excluding the Heawood graph) possesses a perfect matching that extends to a Hamiltonian cycle in exactly one manner. Finally, necessary and sufficient conditions are provided for graphs containing a 2-edge-cut to exhibit either the 2FH or PMH property.

The origin of iPTF14hls, a luminous Type II supernova characterized by an irregular light curve, remains a subject of debate. Since its discovery, the event has maintained a nearly constant effective temperature and luminosity for approximately 600 days before entering a gradual decline; around 1000 days post-discovery, the light curve shifts to a steep drop, during which a spectrum reveals clear evidence of shock interaction with a dense circumstellar medium (CSM). This study investigates iPTF14hls as an interaction-powered supernova, demonstrating that its light curve can be modeled using wind-like CSMs. Analytic modeling suggests the progenitor underwent six mass-loss episodes over the last two centuries. If the 1954 eruption initiated the final mass-loss event, the stellar-wind velocity is estimated between 40 and 70 km/s across various models, with mass-loss rates ranging from 0.4 to 3.3 $M_{\odot }$ yr$^{-1}$. The derived total mass of ejecta and CSM ($M_{\mathrm{ej}}+M_{\mathrm{CSMs}}\simeq 245M_{\odot }$) aligns with iPTF14hls being a candidate for a (pulsational) pair-instability supernova. Further discovery and observation of similar stellar explosions are essential to understanding these unique supernovae.

The Coulomb Branch Formula is conjectured to represent the refined Witten index for $N=4$ Quiver Quantum Mechanics as a summation over multi-centered collinear black hole configurations, weighted by `single-centered' or `pure-Higgs' indices, with specific adjustments for quivers containing oriented cycles. Conversely, localization techniques express this index as an integral over the complexified Cartan torus and auxiliary fields, which, via Stokes' theorem, yields the renowned Jeffrey-Kirwan residue formula. In this work, we evaluate the identical integral using steepest descent methods, demonstrating that the index corresponds to a sum over deformed multi-centered collinear solutions, covering both regular and scaling types. Consequently, we verify the Coulomb Branch Formula for Abelian quivers with oriented cycles and pinpoint the source of pure-Higgs and minimal modification terms to collinear scaling solutions. Furthermore, for cyclic Abelian quivers, we note that certain scaling contributions replicate stacky invariants under trivial stability, a mathematically rigorous concept whose physical relevance was previously unclear.

Suspensions of self-propelled entities create a distinct mechanical stress driven by their motility, which significantly influences their large-scale collective dynamics. For microswimmers in fluids with negligible particle inertia, the virial "swim stress" has proven essential for understanding the rheology and nonequilibrium properties of active soft matter. However, the impact of finite particle inertia on stress generation and collective motion in larger organisms, such as fish, remains unclear. This study examines how finite particle inertia affects the mechanical pressure produced by suspensions of self-propelled bodies. Our findings indicate that swimmers across all scales generate both a unique "swim stress" and a "Reynolds stress," both of which shape collective motion. We observe that particle inertia functions similarly to confinement in overdamped active Brownian systems; specifically, a reduced swimmer run length diminishes swim stress and alters phase behavior. While the individual components of swim and Reynolds stresses vary with the magnitude of particle inertia, their sum remains independent of it. This reveals a critical principle for computing stresses in simulations of nonequilibrium systems: both Reynolds and virial stresses must be calculated to accurately determine the total stress generated by the system.

Skeleton-based Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have demonstrated high accuracy in action recognition; however, their large size and computational complexity, exemplified by models like 2s-AGCN, result in poor power efficiency and throughput on GPUs. Consequently, the need for model reduction and hardware acceleration in low-power GCN applications is growing. To overcome these challenges, this paper introduces RFC-HyPGCN, a runtime sparse feature compression accelerator utilizing a hybrid pruning strategy. This approach reorganizes multiplication orders to skip both graph and spatial convolution operations. It employs a coarse-grained pruning method for temporal filters following a channel-pruning dataflow for spatial convolutions, complemented by sampling-like fine-grained pruning in the time dimension. Additionally, the proposed architecture maps all convolutional layers to the chip to maximize throughput. To minimize storage usage, an online sparse feature compression format is implemented, dividing and encoding features into multiple banks with depth-variable mini-banks. The system further accelerates processing through quantization, input-skipping, and intra-PE dynamic data scheduling. Experimental results on 2s-AGCN show a model compression ratio of 3.0x to 8.4x and 73.20% graph-skipping efficiency with balanced weight pruning. When implemented on a Xilinx XCKU-115 FPGA, the architecture achieves a peak performance of 1142 GOP/s, delivering up to 9.19x and 3.91x speedups compared to the NVIDIA 2080Ti and V100 GPUs, respectively. Compared to recent accelerators for GCN-based action recognition, this design achieves a 22.9x speedup and improves DSP efficiency by 28.93%.

We present a comprehensive framework for counting walks on directed graphs where backtracking steps are penalized by a specific factor. By deriving the corresponding generating functions, we establish linear systems for calculating centrality metrics within this context. Specifically, we demonstrate that Katz-style network centrality incorporating backtracking penalties can be computed with the same efficiency as standard Katz centrality. Furthermore, analyzing the limit of this measure at its radius of convergence yields a novel formula for backtrack-downweighted eigenvector centrality, extending prior research to scenarios involving directed edges. This new theoretical approach integrates the strengths of both standard and nonbacktracking methods, effectively avoiding localization while accommodating tree-like structures. Finally, we examine the behavior of this backtrack-downweighted centrality measure using both synthetic and real-world networks.

Star formation efficiency (SFE) is known to fluctuate depending on the environment, notably in galactic starbursts and deep within galactic bulges, where quenching mechanisms such as AGN feedback and galactic dynamics play significant roles. This study investigates the SFE in the bulge of the AGN-host galaxy NGC 3169 by utilizing spatially-resolved observations of warm ionised gas from the CFHT's SITELLE spectrograph and cold molecular gas (CO(2-1)) from ALMA. Following the separation of AGN-ionised regions from star-forming areas via emission-line diagnostics, we calculated spatially-resolved molecular gas depletion times ($\tau_{dep} = 1/\text{SFE}$) with a resolution of approximately 100 pc within a galactocentric radius of 1.8 kpc. Our results reveal a star-forming ring between 1.25 $\pm$ 0.6 kpc, characterized by an average $\tau_{dep}$ of 0.3 Gyr. Conversely, inside 0.9 kpc, both molecular gas surface densities and depletion times rise as the radius decreases, with $\tau_{dep}$ reaching roughly 2.3 Gyr near 500 pc. By analyzing gas kinematics and comparing findings with simulations, we attribute the observed radial SFE profile in NGC 3169's central region to AGN feedback, bulge morphology, and dynamics.

This work introduces a novel potential energy surface (PES) and dynamical analysis of the reaction between H2CO and OH, leading to the formation of HCO + H2O and HCOOH + H. A critical issue regarding spurious long-range interactions in symmetry-adapted neural network (NN) models is identified, which hinders their direct use in low-temperature dynamics. To address this, the PES was constructed using a partitioning strategy combining a diabatic matrix with a many-body NN term, optimized via a new NN approach that eliminates these artificial asymptotic interactions. Quasi-classical trajectory and ring polymer molecular dynamics (RPMD) simulations were performed on this surface to determine the temperature-dependent rate constants for the various reaction pathways, demonstrating strong alignment with experimental results. Notably, the study examines a previously noted trapping mechanism within the RPMD framework, attributing it to spurious resonances caused by excitations of the ring polymer's normal modes.

This study introduces optimal quantum circuits designed to convert $k$ applications of an arbitrary $d$-dimensional unitary operator $U_d$ into its complex conjugate $\bar{U_d}$. These circuits support parallel execution and are mathematically proven to be optimal for all values of $k$ and $d$, achieving an average fidelity of $\left\langle{F}\right\rangle =\frac{k+1}{d(d-k)}$. Their optimality is established across multiple metrics, including average fidelity, noise robustness, and other standard performance indicators. While prior research focused solely on single-call scenarios ($k=1$) or the specific case of $k=d-1$, this work generalizes those findings. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach covers optimal transformations from $k$ calls of $U_d$ to any $f(U_d)$, where $f$ is an arbitrary homomorphism from the group of $d$-dimensional unitary operators to itself, given that complex conjugation is the sole non-trivial automorphism in this group. Finally, we utilize this optimal complex conjugation scheme to construct a probabilistic circuit capable of reversing arbitrary quantum evolutions.

Ultrashort optical pulses initiate diverse non-equilibrium phenomena in magnetic thin films, influencing electrons and spins within femtoseconds. To simultaneously investigate charge and magnetic degrees of freedom, we created an x-ray streaking method that offers a jitter-free visualization of absorption cross-section variations. This study details an experiment utilizing five photon energies at the Ni $M_{2,3}$-edges, enabling the extraction of absorption and magnetic circular dichroism time traces. These data provide comprehensive insights into transient alterations of electron and spin populations near the Fermi level. Our results indicate that both charge and magnetic dynamics are wavelength-dependent and can be qualitatively explained by ultrafast energy shifts in electronic and magnetic elemental absorption resonances, consistent with recent findings. Nevertheless, our analysis also suggests more intricate changes, underscoring the necessity for additional experimental and theoretical investigation to fully comprehend the interplay between electronic and spin degrees of freedom in optically excited magnetic thin films.

Anomaly detection remains a critical challenge in computer vision, primarily due to the limited availability of anomalous samples, which complicates the task. Consequently, recent approaches rely exclusively on normal images containing no defects for training. This study introduces a robust anomaly detection framework based on Student-Teacher Feature Pyramid Matching (STPM), utilizing a student and teacher network architecture. While generative models also address this issue by reconstructing normal inputs and calculating the discrepancy between the reconstruction and the original, standard STPM lacks image generation capabilities. To enhance STPM's performance, this work employs a student network to reconstruct normal features, mimicking the generative approach. Although this boosts accuracy, the resulting anomaly maps for normal images remain noisy because STPM was not trained on anomalous data, thereby hindering image-level detection precision. To further refine accuracy, the proposed method incorporates a discriminative network trained on pseudo-anomalies derived from these maps. The final architecture comprises two student-teacher pairs alongside the discriminative network, demonstrating high performance on the MVTec anomaly detection dataset.
