This study presents the initial measurements of balance functions (BFs) for all identified charged hadron combinations ($\pi$, $\rm K$, $\rm p$) in Pb$-$Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 2.76$ TeV, utilizing data from the ALICE detector. The BFs were analyzed as two-dimensional differential correlators across relative rapidity ($\Delta y$) and azimuthal angle ($\Delta\varphi$), with results examined across varying collision centralities. The $\Delta\varphi$ dependence of these functions is anticipated to reflect light quark diffusivity within the quark$-$gluon plasma. Observations show that while the azimuthal widths of all pair types significantly narrow from peripheral to central collisions, the longitudinal widths display divergent trends: $\pi\pi$ and cross-species pairs exhibit marked narrowing in central collisions, whereas $\rm KK$ and $\rm pp$ pairs remain unaffected by centrality. This dichotomy aligns qualitatively with strong radial flow effects and a two-stage quark production mechanism in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Furthermore, the first analysis of collision centrality evolution in BF integrals reveals that charge balancing fractions are nearly constant across different centrality classes in Pb$-$Pb collisions. Collectively, these findings offer novel and stringent constraints for theoretical models concerning hadron production and transport in relativistic heavy-ion environments.

Proofs, utilizing frameworks like sequent calculus and natural deduction, coexist alongside well-established imperative algorithms expressed through pseudocode. The relationship between these two concepts can be defined by the equation: imperative algorithms equal proofs with cuts. This insight motivates a broader generalization of pseudocode, termed *logical pseudocodes*, which parallels natural deduction proofs within computability logic \cite{Jap03,Jap08}. In this system, every statement maps directly to a specific step in a natural deduction proof. Consequently, the primary advantage of logical pseudocodes over traditional pseudocode is the assurance that each statement adheres to correctness and safety relative to the initial specifications. Furthermore, this approach represents an extension of the computability logic web (\colw) that incorporates forward reasoning capabilities.

Implicit solvation serves as a highly efficient, coarse-grained strategy within atomic-scale simulations to model the surrounding liquid electrolyte as a continuous polarizable medium. While originally developed for molecular chemistry involving finite solutes, these techniques are increasingly applied to first-principles studies of electrochemistry and electrocatalysis at extended, often metallic, electrodes. However, the common practice of representing these electrodes and their reactive surface chemistry via slabs in periodic supercells introduces distinct challenges. Primarily, it is difficult to capture the entirety of the double layer forming at the electrified solid-liquid interface (SLI) within supercell dimensions manageable by standard density-functional theory (DFT). This review examines liquid solvation methodologies from this specific application perspective, with a focus on their role in the widely used *ab initio* thermodynamics framework for surface catalysis. Importantly, implicit solvation can simulate the polarization of an electrode's electronic density under applied potential and the resulting capacitive charging of the full double layer, overcoming constraints imposed by the limited DFT supercell size. A critical barrier to further advancing this effective methodology for SLI applications remains the scarcity of relevant experimental or high-level theoretical reference data required for parametrization.

Oysters serve as a critical component of the bay's living ecosystem, functioning as natural ocean filters. However, commercial over-harvesting has recently caused severe damage to oyster reefs, necessitating preservation efforts to sustain ecological equilibrium. A fundamental step in this preservation is estimating oyster density, which depends on precise detection capabilities. Yet, developing accurate detection systems typically demands extensive datasets, a process that is costly and labor-intensive in underwater settings. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach that mathematically models oysters to generate synthetic images, thereby enhancing detection performance with minimal reliance on real-world data. By combining our synthetic data with actual data for training the OysterNet network, we achieved a performance improvement of up to 35.1% compared to using only real data, and advanced the state-of-the-art by 12.7%. These results demonstrate that leveraging the underlying geometric properties of objects can effectively boost recognition accuracy on limited datasets, encouraging researchers to adopt this strategy for other difficult-to-acquire data scenarios.

Recently, imperceptible dataset poisoning has been promoted as a data privacy safeguard, yet early-stopping emerges as a straightforward and potent defense among various countermeasures. To assess the susceptibility of poisons to this technique, we benchmarked error-minimizing, error-maximizing, and synthetic poisons by tracking peak test accuracy across 100 epochs, yielding several unexpected insights. First, poisons that achieve low training loss more rapidly exhibit reduced peak test accuracy. Second, a state-of-the-art error-maximizing poison demonstrates a seven-fold decrease in effectiveness when training halts at epoch 8. Third, our findings indicate that more robust and transferable adversarial attacks do not necessarily result in stronger poisons. Consequently, we recommend evaluating poisons based on their peak test accuracy.

We present a general framework for calculating photometric variations caused by the oblique rotation of stars featuring axisymmetric, inhomogeneous surfaces. Applying this framework to white dwarf lightcurves using two simplified surface inhomogeneity models, we demonstrate that, depending on the specific model and observer position, the resulting lightcurves deviate from the purely sinusoidal patterns seen in some white dwarfs. As a specific case, we fitted our model to the phase-folded lightcurve of the rapidly rotating white dwarf ZTF J190132.9+145808.7 (rotation period: 419s). Our analysis indicates that the spot driving these variations has a size of approximately 60° and an obliquity angle of roughly 60° or 90°, providing significant constraints on the distribution of magnetic fields on white dwarf surfaces.

Software sandboxing, also known as software-based fault isolation (SFI), offers a lightweight method for constructing secure systems from untrusted components. For instance, Mozilla leverages SFI to secure the Firefox browser by isolating third-party libraries, while companies such as Fastly and Cloudflare utilize it to safely host untrusted tenants within their edge cloud infrastructures. Despite substantial progress in optimizing and verifying SFI enforcement, the topic of context switching in SFI systems remains underexplored; nearly all existing SFI implementations rely on \emph{heavyweight transitions}, which are prone to errors and impose significant performance penalties due to the need to save, clear, and restore registers during switches. We identify a set of \emph{zero-cost conditions} that determine when sandboxed code possesses sufficient structure to ensure security through lightweight \emph{zero-cost} transitions, implemented as simple function calls. By adapting the Lucet WebAssembly (Wasm) compiler and its runtime to employ these zero-cost transitions, we eliminate unnecessary performance overhead for systems depending on Lucet for sandboxing; for example, image and font rendering speeds in Firefox improve by up to 29.7\% and 10\%, respectively. To reduce the trusted computing base by removing the Lucet compiler and its Wasm specification implementation, we (1) created \emph{VeriZero}, a \emph{static binary verifier} that confirms whether binaries generated by Lucet meet our zero-cost conditions within seconds, and (2) established the soundness of VeriZero by formulating a logical relation that defines when a compiled Wasm function adheres to these conditions regarding semantic behavior. Furthermore, we demonstrate the broader applicability of our model beyond Wasm by introducing \emph{SegmentZero32}, a custom-built SFI system utilizing x86 segmentation and LLVM with largely standard passes to enforce our zero-cost conditions; our prototype achieves performance comparable to the state-of-the-art Native Client SFI system.

This memoir, submitted for the "Habilitation à Diriger des Recherches," investigates the quantum geometric and algebraic dimensions of supersymmetric gauge theory that arise from the non-perturbative vacuum structure created by instantons. After providing a concise overview of the equivariant localization of the instanton moduli space, the work derives the instanton partition function—along with its extensions to quiver and supergroup gauge theories—using three distinct methods: the equivariant index formula, the contour integral formula, and the combinatorial formula. The text subsequently examines the geometric framework of $\mathcal{N} = 2$ gauge theory via Seiberg-Witten geometry and its connections to string and M-theory. Leveraging the theory's relationship with integrable systems, it demonstrates the quantization of this geometric structure through the $\Omega$-deformation of gauge theory and explores the quantum algebraic structures inherent in supersymmetric vacua. Furthermore, it introduces the concept of the quiver W-algebra, formed by the double quantization of Seiberg-Witten geometry, highlighting its unique characteristics, including affine and fractional quiver W-algebras as well as their elliptic deformations.

To collaborate with humans both safely and efficiently, industrial robots must be capable of rapidly adjusting their movements to respond to sudden environmental changes, such as unexpected obstacles blocking a planned path. In real-time motion planning, a vision system detects these obstacles, allowing the system to generate new trajectories based on current positions and execute them immediately. However, existing real-time planners often omit the smoothing post-processing step essential to sampling-based approaches, leading to jerky paths that are inefficient and less suitable for human interaction. To address this, we introduce a Realtime Trajectory Smoother utilizing a shortcutting technique. By leveraging fast clearance inference from a novel neural network, our method consistently smooths trajectories for a 6-DOF industrial robot arm within 200 ms on a standard commercial GPU. We have integrated this smoother into a complete Vision-Motion Planning-Execution loop, demonstrating real-time, smooth performance in an industrial robot operating under dynamic obstacle conditions.

The online advertising sector faces a constant requirement to update ad creatives—such as images and copy—to prevent user fatigue and integrate lessons from successful campaigns in similar product areas. For creative strategists, generating new ad themes for a specific brand is traditionally a laborious and time-intensive endeavor. Typically, strategists derive inspiration from historical ad campaigns and general brand knowledge. To automate the inference of ad themes from these multimodal historical sources, we introduce a theme (keyphrase) recommender system designed for creative strategists. This recommender aggregates outputs from a Visual Question Answering (VQA) task that processes: (i) ad images, (ii) associated ad text alongside brand Wikipedia pages, and (iii) queries regarding the ads. We utilize transformer-based cross-modality encoders to develop visual-linguistic representations for this VQA task. By evaluating two VQA formulations based on classification and ranking, our experiments on a public dataset demonstrate that cross-modal representations yield significantly superior classification accuracy and ranking precision-recall metrics compared to separate image and text representations. Furthermore, incorporating multimodal data provides a substantial performance boost over relying solely on textual or visual information.

Scenario-based question answering (SQA) has garnered growing research attention. Unlike the extensively studied machine reading comprehension (MRC), SQA presents greater challenges, particularly when it involves structured data like tables alongside textual passages, a subfield known as tabular scenario-based question answering (TSQA). Real-world AI applications of TSQA, such as answering high-school exam multiple-choice questions, demand the synthesis of data across multiple cells, the integration of tables with text and domain knowledge, and the inference of answers. To facilitate research in this area, we introduce GeoTSQA, a dataset comprising 1,000 real geography questions contextualized within tabular scenarios. To address this task, we enhance state-of-the-art MRC methods using TTGen, a new table-to-text generator. TTGen creates sentences from synthesized tabular data and provides the downstream MRC model with the most relevant ones, while its sentence ranking model combines information from the scenario, the question, and domain knowledge. Our method surpasses various strong baseline approaches on the GeoTSQA benchmark.

Extensive network logs, which capture multivariate time series from diverse devices and sensors, frequently contain critical insights into anomalous behaviors like intrusions and hardware failures. Current machine learning techniques for detecting anomalies in such time series generally rely on two assumptions: either that normal sequences exhibit consistent patterns for unsupervised training, or that a substantial volume of labeled normal and abnormal data is available for supervised training. In real-world scenarios, however, normal network activity often displays highly variable patterns (for instance, due to traffic rerouting), and abnormal events are typically rare. This paper introduces a novel semi-supervised approach that effectively models dependencies across network time series and temporal points to create meaningful activity representations for anomaly prediction. By utilizing limited labeled data to learn a separable embedding space distinguishing normal from abnormal samples, and by leveraging unlabeled data to address data scarcity, the method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in detecting events within a large-scale real-world network log.
This paper investigates the moments of central values of quartic Dirichlet $L$-functions and proves a quantitative non-vanishing result for these $L$-values.

Lately, Transformer-based methods have gained significant traction for long-term time series forecasting (LTSF). Although their performance has improved considerably, this paper challenges the fundamental validity of this research direction. While Transformers excel at capturing semantic correlations within long sequences, time series modeling specifically requires extracting temporal relationships among ordered, continuous data points. Although positional encoding and token-based sub-series embedding help retain some order, the inherent permutation-invariance of self-attention mechanisms inevitably causes a loss of temporal information. To substantiate this claim, we propose LTSF-Linear, a set of straightforward one-layer linear models. Experiments across nine real-world datasets reveal that LTSF-Linear surprisingly outperforms all existing sophisticated Transformer-based LTSF models, often by a substantial margin. Furthermore, we perform extensive empirical analyses to examine how various design choices in LTSF models affect their ability to capture temporal relations. We hope these unexpected results inspire new research avenues for LTSF and encourage a re-evaluation of Transformer-based approaches for other time series tasks, such as anomaly detection. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/cure-lab/LTSF-Linear.

We investigate turbulent Rayleigh-Bénard convection across a Rayleigh number range spanning four decades ($4 \times 10^8 < \text{Ra} < 2 \times 10^{12}$) within a cylindrical cell, employing harmonic modulation of the plate temperatures. Utilizing temperature sensors positioned both within the cell's interior and embedded in the highly conductive copper plates, we detect thermal waves propagating at the modulation frequency through the bulk convective flow. Our results confirm the recent numerical prediction [PRL 125, 154502 (2020)] regarding the substantial enhancement of the Nusselt number and detail its dependence on the frequency and amplitude of the applied temperature modulation.

Conformal symmetry may be spontaneously broken by defects or other background fields, which induce non-zero vacuum expectation values (VEVs) for certain scalar operators. This work examines the effective field theory of fluctuations around such backgrounds, demonstrating that it structures itself as a series expansion in powers of the inverse VEV, with calculations provided for leading-order corrections. The study specifically targets space-like defects within a four-dimensional Lorentzian framework pertinent to the pseudo-conformal universe model, though these findings generalize to other defect types and scenarios involving the reduction of conformal symmetry to Poincaré symmetry.

When exceptional points of a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian permeate the entire Brillouin zone, the vacuum of a band system regarding particles or holes can exhibit topological nontriviality. This process eliminates the geometric multiplicity of the Hamiltonian's eigenstates through coalescence, thereby placing the remaining bands on a topological foundation. We identify several distinct phenomena within these systems: a single-band topological model, a two-band Chern insulator where the topological number of the lower band fails to compensate for that of the upper band, a topologically protected boundary state that exhibits reduced damping under stronger dissipative forces, and topologically protected in-gap extended states. These findings are illustrated through the vibrational spectrum of a classical lattice, where active constraints serve as the essential mechanism for collapsing the otherwise demanding Hilbert subspace.

On August 14, 2019, the LIGO/Virgo collaboration detected a compact object with a mass of approximately $2.59_{-0.09}^{+0.08}~M_{\odot}$, which was part of a binary system containing a primary black hole of roughly $23~M_{\odot}$. This discovery sparked scientific debate regarding the identity of the lower-mass component, as its mass lies within the neutron star–black hole mass gap. Resolving the nature of the GW190814 event could provide crucial insights into open questions, such as the speed of sound and potential phase transitions into other degrees of freedom. In this study, we investigated the nuclear equation of state in relation to GW190814. First, we assessed constraints on the equation of state by considering scenarios where the low-mass companion is either a slowly or rapidly rotating neutron star, highlighting the significance of upper bounds on the speed of sound regarding dense nuclear matter properties. Second, we systematically analyzed the tidal deformability of a potential high-mass candidate, whether existing as an isolated star or within a binary neutron star system. Since tidal deformability and radius are highly sensitive to the neutron star equation of state, they serve as effective probes of dense matter characteristics. We hypothesize that similar isolated neutron stars or systems may exist in the universe, and their future detection could clarify the maximum mass limit of neutron stars.

This paper examines recent progress in the low-dimensional AdS/CFT correspondence, specifically targeting AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ and AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ dualities within massive Type IIA string theory. We begin by analyzing $\text{AdS}_3\times S^2\times \text{CY}_2\times I$ solutions to massive IIA supergravity that exhibit $\mathcal{N}=(0,4)$ supersymmetry, originally derived in 1908.09851. Our review covers the dual 2d conformal field theories associated with these geometries, alongside their interpretation as surface defects in 5d fixed-point theories residing on D4-D8 bound states. Subsequently, we explore $\text{AdS}_2\times S^3\times \text{CY}_2\times I$ solutions possessing $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetry from 2011.13932. We examine the superconformal quantum mechanics dual to these configurations, framing them as line defects manifesting as D0-D4 baryon vertices within 5d Sp(N) fixed-point theories. Finally, we highlight a specific instance of this solution class generated via non-Abelian T-duality acting on a non-compact isometry group, and we consider the potential inclusion of a 3d black hole geometry, previously constructed through similar T-duality methods, into this framework.

Let $K$ be a compact convex body in $\mathbb{R}^n$. For any affine line $L$, we define $\widehat{\chi}_K(L) = \int_L \chi_K(x) \, dl(x)$, where $dl$ represents the arc length measure; this quantity corresponds to the $X$-ray transform of the characteristic function $\chi_K$, or equivalently, the length of the chord $K \cap L$. We establish that if the boundary $\partial K$ is a $C^\infty$ real algebraic hypersurface and the $X$-ray transform $\widehat{\chi}_K(L)$ scales as the $m$-th root of a polynomial in $t$ under small parallel translations of $L$ by a distance $t$ (for some fixed $m \in \mathbb{N}$), then $\partial K$ must be an ellipsoid.

It is well established that stressors, such as X-rays, exert a more lethal influence on cells during rapid exponential growth compared to the stationary phase; this phenomenon underpins the efficacy of radiotherapy in cancer treatment. This effect can be interpreted through two distinct lenses: (a) heightened vulnerability during growth, or (b) enhanced protective and repair mechanisms in the stationary phase. While these explanations are not mutually exclusive, they differ fundamentally, as (a) represents a universal mechanism whereas (b) is contingent upon specific strains and stressors. This paper focuses on exploring the major aspects of explanation (a). First, we demonstrate that (a) aligns with existing experimental evidence regarding stress factors. Second, we note that (a) correctly anticipates that slow exponential growth (with doubling times of several hours) yields a lower mortality rate than fast exponential growth (with doubling times under an hour), a distinction the (b) framework cannot explain because both populations remain in the same phase. Third, we hypothesize that this stress effect extends to chronic stress caused by suboptimal environmental conditions. If this hypothesis holds, it suggests that even under standard culture conditions, the natural death rate in the stationary phase remains lower than in the growth phase. The paper concludes by outlining several open questions and proposing specific experiments to investigate them.

This thesis investigates the large-scale dynamics of flows governed by rotational effects, weak compressibility, and stratification, quantified by the Rossby, Mach, and Froude numbers. The initial section analyzes a three-dimensional, multi-scale problem involving the full Navier-Stokes-Fourier system, incorporating density and temperature variations alongside Coriolis, centrifugal, and gravitational forces. Within the framework of weak solutions, we examine the combined limits of incompressibility and fast rotation under small Mach, Froude, and Rossby numbers with general, ill-prepared initial data. When the Mach number is of a higher order than the Rossby number, we demonstrate that the limit dynamics follow an incompressible Oberbeck-Boussinesq type system. Conversely, if the Mach and Rossby numbers are of the same order, convergence is shown toward a quasi-geostrophic equation. Continuing this asymptotic analysis, the second part explores the impact of high rotation on the two-dimensional incompressible Euler system with density dependence. The primary objective here is to execute a singular limit in the fast rotation regime, establishing convergence of the Euler equations to a quasi-homogeneous system. The proofs of convergence for both primitive problems rely on compensated compactness arguments, specifically leveraging the structure of Poincaré waves to identify compactness properties for relevant quantities. Compared to prior work, our approach allows for the treatment of the entire parameter range in the multi-scale problem and extends results beyond the critical threshold where $Fr=\sqrt{Ma}$.

Topological insulators, Chern insulators, and Quantum Hall insulator phases serve as foundational models for symmetry-protected topological states of matter. This study details the experimental achievement of time-reversal invariant helical edge modes within bilayer graphene/monolayer WSe$_2$ heterostructures, a state often viewed as a precursor to generic topological insulators. Detecting this previously elusive phase required the fabrication of mesoscopic devices featuring both a moiré superlattice potential and strong spin-orbit coupling, enabling the electronic band structure to be switched between trivial and topological regimes via an external displacement field. The resulting topological phase is defined by a bulk bandgap and helical edge modes exhibiting electrical conductance precisely quantized to $2e^2/h$ in the absence of an external magnetic field. The existence of these helical edge modes is corroborated by experiments validating the Landauer-Büttiker model for quantum transport in multi-terminal mesoscopic systems. Non-local transport measurements further confirm that these modes are dissipationless and equilibrate at contact probes. By utilizing electric and magnetic fields, we demonstrated the tunability of various topological phases, facilitating transitions between trivial states and multiple distinct topological phases. Additionally, we provide theoretical analysis of a realistic model that not only replicates our experimental findings but also elucidates the origins of the topological insulating bulk and helical edge modes. Collectively, our experimental and theoretical findings establish a robust pathway to realizing the time-reversal invariant $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological phase of matter.

We demonstrate a proof-of-concept for free-space quantum key distribution (QKD) utilizing single photons emitted by an isolated defect in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). Operating at room temperature with 10% brightness, the source was integrated into a B92 protocol, achieving a secure key rate (SKR) of 238 bps and a quantum bit error rate (QBER) of 8.95% at a 1 MHz clock rate. Additionally, we investigated how temporal filtering of detected photons influences QKD performance. We anticipate that these findings will advance efforts to enhance the capabilities of optically active defects in hBN for practical, high-performance QKD applications.

Knowledge graph technology serves as a robust, semantically driven method for connecting entities, enabling users to generate new insights through data reasoning based on various rules. However, current knowledge graph construction often restricts event modeling—such as disaster scenarios—to isolated incidents, frequently overlooking the connections between cascading events. This paper presents our GeoAI (Geospatial Artificial Intelligence) approach to determine causality among events, specifically disasters, utilizing a framework of spatially and temporally grounded semantic rules. Through a case study on causal disaster event modeling, we illustrate how defined rules—including theme-based correlation identification, spatiotemporal co-occurrence constraints, and text mining of event metadata—facilitate the automatic extraction of causal links between distinct events. By enriching the event knowledge base and enabling the investigation of linked cascading sequences within large-scale knowledge graphs, our solution enhances both knowledge querying and discovery capabilities.

Let $\mathbf{P}_1, \mathbf{P}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{P}_k$ be partially ordered sets (posets). The {\em Boolean Ramsey number}, denoted $R(\mathbf{P}_1, \mathbf{P}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{P}_k)$, is defined as the smallest integer $n$ such that any $k$-coloring of the elements in the Boolean lattice $\mathbf{B}_n$ guarantees the existence of a monochromatic copy of some $\mathbf{P}_i$. This concept was originally proposed by Axenovich and Walzer~\cite{AW}. While recent literature has focused on determining $R(\mathbf{B}_m, \mathbf{B}_n)$, this paper investigates the function $R(\mathbf{P}_1, \mathbf{P}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{P}_k)$ specifically when each $\mathbf{P}_i$ is a $V$-shaped poset, formed by merging the minimal elements of two chains. A key contribution of the work is identifying the minimal posets $\mathbf{Q}$ that exist within $\mathbf{B}_n$ once the value of $R(\mathbf{P}_1, \mathbf{P}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{P}_k)=n$ is established, which satisfy the Ramsey property described above. Furthermore, we introduce the {\em Boolean rainbow Ramsey number}, $RR(\mathbf{P}, \mathbf{Q})$, defined as the minimum $n$ ensuring that an arbitrary coloring of $\mathbf{B}_n$ yields either a monochromatic $\mathbf{P}$ or a rainbow-colored $\mathbf{Q}$. Previous work by Chang, Li, Gerbner, Methuku, Nagy, Patkos, and Vizer provided an upper bound for $RR(\mathbf{P}, \mathbf{A}_k)$, where $\mathbf{P}$ is any poset and $\mathbf{A}_k$ is a $k$-element antichain; this paper extends that study to cases where $\mathbf{P}$ is a $V$-shaped poset.

In the era of big data and the Internet of Things (IoT), data owners must distribute vast amounts of information to intended recipients within insecure environments, creating a dilemma between preserving user privacy and maintaining data utility. While a privacy funnel based on mutual information was previously used to manage this trade-off, accurately characterizing mutual information remains difficult when sample sizes are small or distribution functions are unknown. This article introduces a privacy funnel utilizing a Mutual Information Neural Estimator (MINE) to refine the balance between privacy and utility. Rather than calculating mutual information through traditional methods, the proposed approach estimates it via a trained MINE to achieve high-precision results. By using estimated mutual information as a metric for both privacy and utility, the study formulates an optimization problem that trains a neural network to maximize data utility while ensuring the estimator's privacy leakage remains below a specific threshold. Simulation results confirm that MINE effectively approximates mutual information even with limited data samples, successfully quantifying privacy leakage and data utility retention to optimize the overall privacy-utility trade-off.

Within CAT(k) spaces, standard fixed point iterations utilizing proximal mappings—such as prox-prox, Krasnoselsky-Mann relaxations, and nonlinear projected gradients—achieve local linear convergence when linear metric subregularity is assumed. Since linear metric subregularity is a fundamental requirement for any linearly convergent fixed point sequence, this finding is optimal. To demonstrate this, we establish a framework for fixed point mappings that do not adhere to typical nonexpansiveness or firm nonexpansiveness conditions within p-uniformly convex spaces.

We present a unified framework designed for generic video annotation using bounding boxes. Addressing the well-known issue that video annotation is tedious and time-intensive, our work targets two key challenges: (1) automatically interpolating and extrapolating bounding boxes for frames not annotated by humans, and (2) automatically determining which frames require manual annotation. Our contributions are twofold: first, we introduce a model capable of both interpolation and extrapolation; second, we develop a guiding mechanism that sequentially suggests the next frame to annotate based on prior work. We extensively evaluate our approach on various challenging datasets in a simulated environment, demonstrating a 60% reduction in the number of manually drawn bounding boxes compared to linear interpolation and a 35% reduction over an off-the-shelf tracker. Additionally, we achieve a 10% improvement in annotation time compared to a state-of-the-art method [25]. Finally, through human annotation experiments and detailed analysis, we show that our approach cuts actual measured annotation time by 50% relative to commonly used linear interpolation.

Selecting the most suitable kernel is vital for numerous Machine Learning tasks, particularly in Gaussian Processes (GP), a leading method for regression and classification that depends extensively on kernel functions. Traditionally, GP research has limited kernels to ad hoc designs, predefined selections, or searches within a priori defined compositional spaces. This paper introduces a Genetic Programming approach that models kernel functions as trees of elementary mathematical expressions. This representation enables the modeling of a broader kernel set, potentially yielding superior solutions despite introducing new challenges. The proposed algorithm successfully addresses these issues to discover kernels that accurately capture data characteristics. Tested on various real-world time-series extrapolation tasks, this method outperforms state-of-the-art results while simultaneously reducing kernel complexity.

Staying current with evolving trends, technologies, and best practices in visualization and data analysis is growing increasingly challenging, particularly for novice data scientists. To address this, we introduce Lodestar, an interactive computational notebook that enables users to swiftly explore and build new data science workflows by choosing from a curated list of automated analysis suggestions. These recommendations are generated from directed graphs representing known analysis states, sourced from both manually curated online tutorials and a semi-automatic analysis of a corpus containing over 6,000 Jupyter notebooks. We assessed Lodestar through a formative study to inform future tool enhancements. Our findings indicate that users perceive Lodestar as a valuable resource for rapidly developing data science workflows.

Recent studies have concentrated on enhancing the efficiency of image classification training and inference, typically by targeting theoretical metrics such as ImageNet validation accuracy per FLOP. However, realizing these theoretical gains in practice remains difficult, especially when using high-performance training accelerators. This paper addresses the practical efficiency of state-of-the-art EfficientNet models on Graphcore IPU accelerators through three key extensions: (i) adapting depthwise convolutions to group convolutions; (ii) incorporating proxy-normalized activations to align batch normalization performance with batch-independent statistics; and (iii) minimizing compute by training at lower resolutions and performing cost-effective fine-tuning at higher resolutions. Our results demonstrate that these approaches significantly boost practical efficiency for both training and inference. The code is accessible at https://github.com/graphcore/graphcore-research/tree/main/Making_EfficientNet_More_Efficient.

Starting with a random map consisting of four transformations ($T_1, T_2, T_3, T_4$) and four parameters ($p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4$), we construct a random billiard map on a surface of constant curvature, which may be the Euclidean plane, the hyperbolic plane, or the sphere. For this billiard map, the Liouville measure remains invariant. Finally, we examine specific dynamical characteristics of circular billiards, including their ergodicity.

Federated learning (FL) enhances data privacy and efficiency in magnetic resonance (MR) image reconstruction by facilitating collaboration among multiple institutions without aggregating local data. However, performance often degrades due to domain shifts arising from varying MR imaging protocols. While recent FL approaches address this by improving global model generalization, they often overlook domain-specific features that hold critical information regarding device characteristics and local reconstruction needs. This paper introduces FedMRI, a specificity-preserving FL algorithm for MR reconstruction. The core strategy involves splitting the reconstruction model into a globally shared encoder to capture generalized representations and a client-specific decoder to maintain unique domain properties essential for reconstruction across clients with distinct distributions. This approach operates in both frequency and image spaces, enabling the simultaneous exploration of generalized features and client-specific attributes in different domains. Additionally, to accelerate the convergence of the global encoder under domain shift conditions, a weighted contrastive regularization is employed to directly rectify deviations between client and server during optimization. Extensive experiments confirm that FedMRI produces reconstructed images closest to the ground truth for multi-institutional data, surpassing existing state-of-the-art FL methods.

Determining the precise computational complexity of solving parity games remains a significant open question. While various researchers have investigated efficient algorithms for specific graph classes, Obdr\v{z}\'{a}lek previously demonstrated that the problem belongs to $\mathrm{P}$ for graphs with bounded tree-width or clique-width. Ganardi later refined this result, proving membership in $\mathrm{LOGCFL}$ for bounded tree-width graphs and establishing an additional assumption for the clique-width case. This work advances that research trajectory by proving that solving parity games on graphs of bounded tree-depth resides in logspace uniform $\text{AC}^0$. Our approach relies on first defining a modified version of clique-width termed "shallow clique-width," followed by a suitable reduction.

This study examines a sonic black-hole setup in which an atom condensate traverses a transition from subsonic to supersonic flow. We outline several criteria demonstrating the presence of nonclassical correlations arising from the quantum nature of spontaneous Hawking radiation. By synthesizing prior general work on Hawking radiation analogs, we analyze the detectability of these indicators and conclude that, among various detection methods, only the violation of quadratic Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities can be observed. Furthermore, numerical results presented herein substantiate the feasibility of measuring deep quantum correlations in specific, concrete scenarios.

This study investigates the cosmological properties of a recently proposed four-dimensional Gauss-Bonnet gravity framework via two distinct models that incorporate a varying cosmological constant. The construction of these models adheres to observational limits, including cosmic transit data and flat curvature constraints. Unlike conventional approaches, the current analysis derives cosmological parameters from a predefined scale factor reflecting specific cosmic behaviors, effectively reversing the standard methodology. Furthermore, the stability and cosmographic characteristics of both models have been examined.

Pure Yang-Mills theory in two spacetime dimensions exhibits exact Casimir scaling, implying an infinite spectrum of string tensions. This phenomenon is attributed to the non-propagating nature of gluons in 2D. However, standard symmetry arguments find this rich spectrum puzzling. Although center symmetry is conventionally thought to classify string tensions, its finiteness fails to account for an infinite number of confining strings. This note resolves the conflict between dynamical and kinematic perspectives by identifying a non-invertible 1-form symmetry capable of distinguishing Wilson loops across various representations. We also offer speculation regarding the potential implications of this finding for Yang-Mills theories in three and four dimensions.

This paper offers a concise review of existing literature that employs game theory to model decision-making scenarios pertinent to defense applications. Proven effective for simulating the decision processes of intelligent agents and players, game theory has already been applied across diverse fields such as economics, evolutionary biology, and computer science. In the defense sector, there is a specific need to model and forecast the actions of hostile actors, particularly in situations where players attempt to outmaneuver one another; this dynamic of competitive interaction is precisely what game theory excels at modeling. Over recent decades, numerous studies have utilized various branches of game theory to represent a wide array of defense-related situations. This paper delivers a structured review of these efforts, categorizing current literature based on the warfare types modeled, the specific game classifications used, and the participants involved. The resulting analysis summarizes the current state-of-the-art regarding game theory in defense contexts and outlines both the advantages and limitations of applying this framework to such scenarios.

We provide an exact analytical solution for the steady states of a broad class of driven-dissipative bosonic models in any number of dimensions. These models involve modes experiencing arbitrary two-photon driving, single-photon dissipation, and global Hubbard (or Kerr-type) interactions. Our findings uncover rich physical phenomena, such as dissipative phase transitions, complex mode competition, symmetry breaking, and the stabilization of many-body $SU(1,1)$ pair coherent states. Furthermore, our exact solutions allow for the characterization of spatial correlations and remain valid in regimes where conventional mean-field and semiclassical methods fail.

We address the $k$-means clustering problem within the dynamic streaming framework, where points from a discrete Euclidean space $\{1, 2, \ldots, \Delta\}^d$ are subject to dynamic insertions and deletions. For this scenario, we introduce a one-pass coreset construction algorithm that operates within $\tilde{O}(k\cdot \mathrm{poly}(d, \log\Delta))$ space, with $k$ denoting the target number of centers. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the inaugural dynamic geometric data stream algorithm for $k$-means that utilizes space polynomial in the dimension and achieves nearly optimal (linear) complexity with respect to $k$.

Annually, the number of objects launched into space continues to grow. As these items orbit at varying altitudes, those at lower levels reenter the atmosphere, largely disintegrating and depositing material into the upper layers. The expansion of space programs across nations, the acceleration of commercialization, and ambitious satellite constellation initiatives heighten concerns regarding future space debris and will steadily increase the mass flux entering the atmosphere. This study compares the influx of human-made (anthropogenic) debris to the natural mass influx caused by meteoroids from solar system bodies such as asteroids and comets. We evaluate the current and near-future significance of anthropogenic sources, taking into account both planned and partially deployed large satellite constellations. By reviewing relevant literature, we provide detailed insights into the mass, composition, and ablation characteristics of both natural and human-made materials. Currently, anthropogenic material accounts for approximately 2.8% of the annual injected mass compared to natural origins; however, future satellite constellations could raise this proportion to nearly 40%. In such a scenario, the injection of various metals from human sources would vastly exceed that of natural sources. Furthermore, we observe that the anthropogenic injection of aerosols into the atmosphere increases disproportionately. These developments may lead to previously unknown effects on Earth's atmosphere and its habitability.

Eu2Ir2O7, a potential Weyl semimetal, undergoes an insulator-to-metal transition dependent on Bi substitution at the Eu site. This study examines the (Eu_1-xBi_x)2Ir2O7 series using Hard X-ray Photoemission Spectroscopy (HAXPES). It is noted that replacing Eu3+ with the larger Bi3+ ion causes an anomalous 20% lattice contraction even at low Bi doping levels (3.5%). HAXPES data confirm that all cations maintain their nominal valence states across the series. Furthermore, the asymmetric character of Bi core-level spectra in metallic compositions suggests that Bi contributes to the density of states at the Fermi energy within this doping range. Valence band spectra reveal that the Bi 6s peak remains unchanged throughout the series and resides deep within the valence band. Based on these findings, we propose that Bi 6p - Ir 5d hybridization is the driving force behind the insulator-to-metal transition.

This report from the RF2 Topical Group for Snowmass 2021 outlines the physics motivation for investigating weak decays of strange and light quarks. Current and planned high-precision studies of kaon, hyperon, pion, and $\eta^{(\prime)}$ meson decays offer distinctive opportunities to test the Standard Model (SM). These investigations include precise determinations of the CKM quark-mixing matrix elements for rigorous unitarity checks, symmetry tests covering lepton flavor and number conservation, and tests of lepton flavor universality. Furthermore, within the framework of physics beyond the SM, experiments on strange and light quark decays are sensitive to new physics at the PeV mass scale and provide leading constraints on scenarios with feebly interacting hidden sectors below the GeV mass scale.

Controlling the stability of smart emulsions and foams through external stimuli is highly valuable for both fundamental research and practical applications. Microgels, defined as three-dimensional polymer networks swollen by a good solvent at the nano- and micro-scale, represent an emerging class of smart stabilizers. While previous studies have examined how external stimuli affect the two-dimensional phase behavior of microgels at air- and oil-water interfaces, the specific influence of the top-phase has largely been overlooked. This study presents findings that directly investigate how the top-phase impacts microgel properties at interfaces. We measured the dimensions of pNIPAM microgels following deposition from two distinct interfaces: air and decane-water. Results indicate that while the total in-plane size of the microgels grows with increasing interfacial tension, the fraction of the microgel located in the aqueous phase remains unchanged. By correlating the occupied area with interface surface tensions, we estimated an elastic modulus, which was found to be larger than values obtained via nanoindentation. Furthermore, combining compression, deposition, and visualization techniques reveals that the two-dimensional phase behavior of microgel monolayers remains unaltered, despite the increase in total in-plane size at higher interfacial tensions. A peer-reviewed, extended version of this preprint and the electronic supplementary information are available at S.~Bochenek, A.~Scotti, W.~Richtering, *Soft Matter*, 2020, DOI: 10.1039/d0sm01774d.

Software Product Lines (SPLs) represent families of related systems differentiated by their specific feature sets. Feature Models have become the industry standard for modeling SPL variability as they define features, their relationships, and valid feature combinations, placing them at the heart of SPL engineering tasks. This study presents an empirical investigation into how practitioners comprehend Feature Models specifically for validating configurations. We examined the relationship between the count of features and cross-tree constraints against the accuracy of validity checks, utilizing eye-tracking data to assess the difficulty of interpreting specific model sections and the associated cognitive load. Our findings indicate that neither the number of features nor the number of cross-tree constraints independently correlates with answer accuracy; rather, these factors interact to influence accuracy. Furthermore, the study revealed that Feature Models containing cross-tree constraints elicited differences in both the number and duration of eye fixations, whereas models without such constraints showed no such differences.

Solving underdetermined linear systems ($y=Ax$) for sparse solutions has gained significant attention recently. Among the various methods available, iterative thresholding algorithms are considered highly efficient and vital, largely because of their low computational costs, which make them ideal for large-scale applications. This paper aims to establish global convergence guarantees for a broad category of iterative thresholding algorithms. Because the thresholds in these methods are adjusted adaptively at every iteration, we refer to them as adaptively iterative thresholding (AIT) algorithms. Our primary result demonstrates that if matrix $A$ meets specific coherence conditions, AIT algorithms can identify the correct support set within a finite number of steps and subsequently converge exponentially fast to the true sparse solution once that set is found. Furthermore, we show that AIT algorithms are robust regarding their parameter choices. Additionally, we note that many existing iterative thresholding techniques, including hard, soft, half, and smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD) methods, fall within the scope of AIT algorithms analyzed in this study.

This study introduces a hierarchical framework designed to address discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games (PEGs) within extensive grid environments. By segmenting the grid into superstates, such as "rooms," the method establishes a dual-resolution decision-making system comprising local PEGs at the granular state level and an aggregated PEG at the superstate level. Due to their reduced state space size, both the local and aggregated games can be efficiently solved to reach a Nash equilibrium. To bridge these two levels of decision-making, the Nash values derived from the local PEGs serve as rewards for the aggregated game. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this hierarchical approach substantially lowers computational costs while preserving performance comparable to flat Nash policies during competition.

Future muon collider detectors will face significant Beam-Induced Backgrounds (BIB) caused by in-flight muon decays along the beam line, which can hinder the reconstruction of collision products by both the detector hardware and data analysis pipelines. This study investigates geometric strategies to mitigate these backgrounds for the readout, triggering, and analysis phases of upcoming experiments. Focusing on a 1.5~TeV collision energy scenario with a tungsten nozzle designed to block most BIB, we explore additional detector approaches to further suppress these effects, particularly within the densest innermost tracker layers. Furthermore, we present a conceptual design for a calorimeter specifically engineered to reject BIB.

Fashion recommendation is frequently defined as identifying complementary items for a specific garment or assembling outfits suitable for a particular user. This study tackles the challenge by introducing an additional semantic layer focused on the style of the suggested attire. We define style through two key dimensions: the mood and emotions implied by color combinations, and the suitability of selected garments for specific social occasions. To address the former, we utilize Shigenobu Kobayashi's color image scale, which maps emotional states and moods to color triples. The latter is handled by extracting garments from images depicting social events. In total, we incorporate a style classifier and an event classifier into a state-of-the-art garment recommendation framework to condition recommendations based on the query.

While conventional superconductors universally exhibit a single discontinuity in electronic specific heat at their critical transition temperature, many unconventional superconductors display an additional second-order jump at a lower temperature. This secondary feature often arises from a stabilized component of the order parameter linked to the spontaneous breaking of time-reversal symmetry. The separation between these two specific heat discontinuities can be modulated through external perturbations, including chemical substitution, hydrostatic pressure, and uniaxial strain. This study introduces a quantitative, multi-band theoretical framework to calculate the ratio of these heat capacity jumps based on the material's band structure and the momentum configuration of the order parameter. We analyze the specific gap profiles that dictate the magnitude of the second jump. Applying this formalism to Sr$_2$RuO$_4$ using gap functions derived from microscopic random phase approximation calculations, we demonstrate that recently proposed accidentally degenerate order parameters could result in a significantly suppressed second heat capacity jump. We explore the underlying causes of this suppression and examine the influence of spatial inhomogeneity on specific heat measurements. Our findings offer a plausible explanation for the historical absence of experimental detection of a second heat capacity jump in Sr$_2$RuO$_4$.

We investigate the implications of unique dispersive characteristics in linear fast sausage modes (FSMs) within pressureless magnetohydrodynamics, focusing on one-dimensional cylindrical equilibria featuring a continuous radial density profile ($\rho_0(r)$). Recent rigorous mathematical findings indicate that cutoff axial wavenumbers can be absent for FSMs if $\rho_0(r)$ changes gradually enough outside the nominal cylinder. Consequently, trapped modes could theoretically exist for any axial wavenumber and density contrast, with their long-wavelength axial phase speeds closely matching the external Alfvén speed. If such trapped modes emerge in the solutions to the associated initial value problem (IVP), FSMs would be far more likely to be observed than classical theory predicts, potentially explaining a wider array of periodicities. However, using axial fundamentals in active region loops as a case study, our finite-difference solutions to the IVP fail to exhibit this long-wavelength expectation. By superposing the required eigenmodes to re-solve the IVP, we explore this discrepancy and find that, for the parameters studied, trapped mode eigenfunctions span a spatial extent far exceeding the observationally plausible range of initial perturbations. This implies that trapped modes can absorb a negligible fraction of energy. We conclude that the lack of cutoff wavenumbers for FSMs in the examined equilibrium does not ensure a distinct temporal behavior.

While Margin Infused Relaxed Algorithms (MIRAs) are the dominant approach for tuning models in large-scale statistical machine translation, they are well-known for their implementation complexity. We propose a novel method that treats the N-best list as a permutation and optimizes by minimizing the Plackett-Luce loss against ground-truth permutations. Experiments using large-scale features show that this new approach is more robust than MERT; although it achieves performance comparable to MIRAs, it offers a distinct advantage through significantly easier implementation.

This study examines the parameterized complexity of recognizing proper $H$-graphs. Defined as intersection graphs of connected subgraphs within a subdivision of a multigraph $H$, proper $H$-graphs forbid containment relationships between vertex representations. Originally introduced by Biró, Hujter, and Tuza in 1992 as a parameterized extension of interval and circular-arc graphs, the concept of proper $H$-graphs was later formalized by Chaplick et al. in 2019 to generalize proper interval and circular-arc graphs. In these classes, $H$ serves as a structural parameter indicating the distance to a (proper) interval graph, making it valuable for designing efficient algorithms. Our findings are as follows:

*   When $H$ is a tree $T$ with $t$ nodes, we can determine in $2^{\mathcal{O}(t^2 \log t)} \cdot n^3$ time whether an $n$-vertex graph $G$ is a proper $T$-graph; for affirmative cases, the algorithm constructs a proper $T$-representation. This establishes that recognizing proper $H$-graphs where $H$ is a tree is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the size of $T$, resolving a previous open question where only NP-completeness was known.
*   In contrast, if $H$ is not restricted to being a tree, the recognition problem becomes significantly more difficult. We demonstrate the existence of a multigraph $H$ with 4 vertices and 5 edges such that deciding whether $G$ is a proper $H$-graph is NP-complete.

A recently proposed and examined storage ring operation method relies on steady-state microbunching, utilizing a laser cavity modulator to achieve longitudinal focusing of circulating microbunches. This study investigates how coherent undulator radiation influences the longitudinal multi-turn collective dynamics of single bunches, potentially revealing a novel instability mechanism. We derive multi-turn equations of motion for individual microbunches as two sets of difference equations: one for the modulator and another for the rest of the ring. By introducing undulator-averaged phase space coordinates, we obtain the dispersion equation. The predicted instability growth rate aligns reasonably well with numerical turn-by-turn tracking simulations, confirming the validity of the underlying assumptions. This analysis offers insights into coherent undulator radiation-driven multi-turn instabilities within the cavity modulator and compares this new mechanism with the Robinson instability found in conventional radio-frequency storage rings.

In nonholonomic mechanics, velocity-based constraints disrupt the standard connection between symmetries and conserved quantities established by Noether's Theorem for holonomic systems. Nevertheless, a specific subset of conserved quantities in nonholonomic systems, known as {\it horizontal gauge momenta}, arises from vector fields tangent to group orbits, implying that a modified version of this relationship may persist. This paper demonstrates that, provided specific conditions on the symmetry Lie group are met, the (nonholonomic) momentum map remains invariant along nonholonomic trajectories, thereby generalizing Noether's Theorem to the nonholonomic context. Our analysis yields a constructive approach with significant implications for the integrability and Hamiltonian formulation of certain nonholonomic systems. We illustrate these findings using three classic examples: the snakeboard, a solid of revolution rolling without slipping on a plane, and a heavy homogeneous sphere rolling without slipping within a convex surface of revolution. Notably, for the snakeboard, we identify a novel horizontal gauge momentum that uncovers previously unknown facets of its integrability.

This work examines the defocusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation in three spatial dimensions. We demonstrate that any radial solution staying bounded within the critical Sobolev space is necessarily global and exhibits scattering behavior. For the energy-supercritical case, we utilize a space-localized Lin–Strauss Morawetz inequality developed by Bourgain. In the inter-critical regime, we establish long-time Strichartz estimates alongside frequency-localized Lin–Strauss Morawetz inequalities.

On June 14, 2022, the EHT collaboration (EHTC) launched a webpage titled "Imaging Reanalyses of EHT Data" (https://eventhorizontelescope.org/blog/imaging-reanalyses-eht-data), addressing our recent publication in the Astrophysical Journal by Miyoshi et al. Upon reviewing the EHTC's comments, we determined that all five points raised are merely subjective and unsupported assertions; consequently, they fail to validate the EHTC's findings. We sincerely urge the EHTC to publish a discussion grounded in scientific reasoning rather than a compilation of unsubstantiated claims.

This paper examines contrastive explanations within formal argumentation, specifically addressing why one argument (the fact) is accepted while another (the foil) is rejected under different extension-based semantics. While recent research has primarily concentrated on generating minimal explanations for the acceptance or non-acceptance of arguments, there remains a gap in developing a proper argumentation-based framework for interpreting contrastive explanations. We demonstrate the conditions under which contrastive explanations hold meaning in both abstract and structured argumentation and illustrate how argumentation frameworks can render implicit foils explicit.

We introduce Spartan, a framework for training sparse neural networks with a fixed sparsity target. Spartan integrates two core techniques: (1) soft top-k masking of low-magnitude parameters solved through a regularized optimal transportation problem, and (2) dual averaging-based parameter updates that apply hard sparsification during the forward pass. This approach balances exploration and exploitation; initially, the model explores diverse sparsity configurations, but as the soft top-k approximation sharpens throughout training, the focus shifts to optimizing parameters against a stable sparsity mask. Spartan is versatile enough to support various sparsity allocation strategies, including unstructured and block-structured sparsity, as well as cost-sensitive allocation guided by linear models of per-parameter costs. In ImageNet-1K classification tasks, Spartan achieves 95% sparsity in ResNet-50 models and 90% block sparsity in ViT-B/16 models, with top-1 accuracy drops of less than 1% relative to fully dense training.

The effectiveness of fine-tuning pre-trained language models is heavily reliant on hyperparameter configuration. This paper examines how modern hyperparameter optimization (HPO) methods perform in this context. Initially, we evaluate three HPO algorithms on two state-of-the-art language models using the GLUE dataset. Our findings indicate that, given an equivalent time budget, HPO frequently fails to surpass grid search due to constraints in available time and issues with overfitting. To address these failures, we introduce two general strategies and a systematic experimental procedure. When applied, this approach demonstrates that HPO can succeed with better-tailored search spaces and time allocations, though overfitting persists in some scenarios. We conclude with recommendations for future research. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/microsoft/FLAML/tree/main/flaml/nlp/.

Identifying informative variables in information systems often relies on simple one-dimensional filtering methods that overlook interactions among variables, potentially discarding relevant ones. We introduce the MDFS (MultiDimensional Feature Selection) R package, which identifies informative variables by accounting for synergistic interactions between multiple descriptors and the decision variable. Built on an information-theory-based algorithm, MDFS features a C++ computational kernel and includes a high-performance CUDA C implementation. The package's effectiveness is demonstrated using the Madelon dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, which contains variables designed with synergistic properties. Results indicate that multidimensional analysis is more sensitive than one-dimensional tests, yielding more reliable variable importance rankings.

The issue of jointly recovering sparse signals in a distributed manner has gained significant recent interest. We consider a scenario where network nodes observe distinct sparse signals sharing a common support; utilizing linear compressed measurements and network communication, each node seeks to recover both the support and non-zero values of its specific signal. While distributed greedy algorithms have been suggested for this task, the most robust existing methods demand substantial data transmission, making them ill-suited for realistic network constraints. This paper addresses the problem using a reweighted $\ell_1$ soft thresholding approach, where the threshold is iteratively adjusted according to the current support estimate. The proposed method is designed for constrained networks, requiring only local communication between neighbors and transmitting indices from a finite set. We provide an analytical proof of the algorithm's convergence and demonstrate that it surpasses current state-of-the-art greedy methods by offering a superior balance between recovery accuracy and communication overhead.

A wide range of issues in causal inference and economics can be expressed using conditional moment models, which define target functions via sets of conditional moment restrictions. In nonparametric versions of these models, achieving efficient estimation typically depends on pre-set constraints regarding the ill-posedness measures of the hypothesis space, constraints that are difficult to verify when employing flexible models. This study tackles that challenge by introducing a procedure that automatically learns representations with regulated ill-posedness measures. The proposed method approximates a linear representation derived from the spectral decomposition of a conditional expectation operator, a technique applicable to kernelized estimators and recognized for supporting minimax optimal estimation in specific contexts. We demonstrate that this representation can be efficiently estimated from data and prove $L_2$ consistency for the resulting estimator. Finally, we assess the method on proximal causal inference tasks, showing promising results on high-dimensional, semi-synthetic datasets.

Recent self-supervised frameworks for visual representation learning frequently rely on Siamese network architectures. Although these networks are theoretically symmetric with two parallel encoders, they are often practically asymmetric due to various mechanisms introduced to disrupt this symmetry. This work formally investigates the significance of such asymmetry by explicitly differentiating the two encoders, assigning one to generate source representations and the other to produce targets. Our primary finding is that maintaining lower variance in the target compared to the source generally enhances learning. We empirically validate this insight through five case studies examining different variance-focused designs, supported by preliminary theoretical analysis of the baseline. Furthermore, we observe that improvements from asymmetric configurations generalize effectively across longer training schedules, diverse frameworks, and modern backbone architectures. Ultimately, combining multiple asymmetric designs yields state-of-the-art accuracy on ImageNet linear probing and competitive performance in downstream transfer tasks. We hope this investigation encourages further research into leveraging asymmetry for Siamese representation learning.

We investigate two-to-two scattering processes ($e^- \mu^+ \to f \bar{f}, \gamma \gamma$) within the context of a proposed electron-muon collider, focusing on contributions from dimension-6 and dimension-8 operators. This study contrasts the sensitivity to effective couplings achievable at the collider against that of recent low-energy measurements of muon decays and conversion processes ($\mu \to e \gamma$, $\mu \to e \bar{e} e$, and $\mu \to e$ conversion). While the collider offers significantly weaker sensitivity for first-generation fermion production, its reach for second- and third-generation fermions is comparable to or exceeds that of low-energy experiments. Notably, for the process $e^- \mu^+ \to \gamma \gamma$, the sensitivity to a dimension-8 contact interaction emerges as the most robust among the cases examined.

Flux-corrected transport (FCT) represents a category of flux limiter techniques. Unlike total variation diminishing (TVD) methods, deriving the standard FCT formulas for flux limiters lacks clarity, and adapting them when the underlying differential operator changes is not straightforward. We introduce a new mathematical framework based on linear programming to develop flux correction strategies for weighted hybrid difference schemes. These hybrid schemes combine a monotone scheme with a high-order scheme. Determining the maximal antidiffusive fluxes is formulated as an optimization problem featuring a linear objective function. Constraints for this optimization are established by applying inequalities valid for the monotone difference scheme to the hybrid difference scheme. Solving the resulting nonlinear optimization problem is achieved through the iterative resolution of linear programming tasks. A nontrivial approximate solution to these linear programming problems serves as the necessary flux limiters. We provide flux correction formulas applicable to scalar hyperbolic conservation laws and convection-diffusion equations. Specifically, the proposed FCT method for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws generates entropy solutions. Numerical results are included to demonstrate the approach.

Research indicates a strong correlation between human fixation patterns and Transformer-based attention, yet these analyses often overlook individual participant differences and rely primarily on monolingual datasets, limiting the generalizability of their findings. This study examines eye-tracking data from speakers of 13 languages reading in both their native language (L1) and as English language learners (L2). Our results reveal significant variations across languages, alongside the discovery that individual reading behaviors—such as skipping rates, total reading duration, and vocabulary proficiency (measured by LexTALE)—substantially impact the alignment between human and model attention, a factor that warrants consideration in future research.

Consider a metric space ${\mathfrak M}=({\mathcal M},\rho)$ and a Banach space $X$. Let $F$ denote a set-valued mapping from ${\mathcal M}$ to ${\mathcal K}_m(X)$, the collection of all compact, convex subsets of $X$ with dimension no greater than $m$. Our recent collaborative work with Charles Fefferman, titled "Finiteness Principle for Lipschitz selections," establishes efficient criteria for the existence of a Lipschitz selection $f:{\mathcal M}\to X$ satisfying $f(x)\in F(x)$ for all $x\in{\mathcal M}$. This paper offers fresh, alternative proofs of that result for two specific scenarios: when $m=1$ and $X$ is any Banach space, and when $m=2$ and $X$ is the plane ${\bf R}^{2}$. Both approaches rely on a straightforward reiteration formula concerning the "core" of a set-valued mapping $G:{\mathcal M}\to{\mathcal K}_m(X)$, where $G$ is Lipschitz with respect to the Hausdorff distance and satisfies $G(x)\subset F(x)$ for every $x\in{\mathcal M}$. Additionally, we provide multiple constructive criteria for determining the existence of Lipschitz selections for mappings from ${\mathcal M}$ into the family of all closed half-planes within ${\bf R}^{2}$.

**Context.** Establishing the metallicities and ages of M31 clusters is essential for understanding the galaxy's formation and evolution. The Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST) has conducted a comprehensive spectroscopic survey of clusters and candidates within M31.

**Aims.** We created a catalogue comprising 346 M31 clusters observed by LAMOST. By integrating LAMOST spectral data with multi-band photometry, we developed a novel algorithm to determine the metallicities and ages of these clusters.

**Methods.** We employed random forest classifiers trained on empirical literature data to distinguish between young and old clusters. For young clusters, ages were determined via spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting of multi-band photometry, while metallicities were estimated by matching observed spectral principal components from LAMOST spectra with those from young, metal-rich single stellar population (SSP) models. For old clusters, we constructed non-parametric random forest models linking spectral principal components and/or multi-band colours to cluster parameters using a training set derived from SSP models. The ages and metallicities of old clusters were subsequently estimated by fitting their observed spectral principal components and photometric colours against these models.

**Results.** We derived parameters for 53 young and 293 old clusters in our catalogue. Our results align well with existing literature. Additionally, we obtained age estimates for approximately 30 clusters and metallicities for about 40 sources for the first time.

Although V.I. Arnol'd introduced the concept of versal normal form, its systematic application has lagged behind the semidirect structure of formal transformations acting on formal vector fields; specifically, the linear component should be fully resolved before addressing nonlinear terms. This paper addresses that gap by providing a comprehensive first-order analysis for two- and three-dimensional irreducible nilpotent scenarios. Subsequently, we present an explicit nearly symplectic calculation to derive the transformation to versal normal form, applying it to specific problems in fluid dynamics and the celestial mechanics \(L_4\) case.

Using the MeerKAT telescope, we identified two new Black Widow millisecond pulsars within the globular cluster M28. PSR J1824$-$2452M (M28M) exhibits a 4.78-ms period and a 5.82-hour orbit, while PSR J1824$-$2452N (M28N) has a 3.35-ms period and a 4.76-hour orbit. Both systems display dispersion measures close to $119.30\,$pc$\,$cm$^{-3}$ and host low-mass companions ($\sim$$0.01-0.03\,$M$_\odot$) that fail to induce significant radio eclipses or orbital changes. With these additions, M28 now contains five confirmed black widow pulsars. These detections resulted from an initial stage of MeerKAT's globular cluster census under the TRAPUM Large Survey Project. The faint nature of these discoveries highlights MeerKAT's superior survey sensitivity compared to prior efforts, suggesting that further observations of this cluster will likely yield additional pulsar finds.

The notion of random processes has recently been generalized to graph signals, defining random graph processes as a class of multivariate stochastic processes where coefficients are matrices possessing a \textit{graph-topological} structure. Consequently, system identification for these processes focuses on uncovering their underlying topology, mathematically represented as graph shift operators (GSOs), such as adjacency or Laplacian matrices. In the seminal work introducing random graph processes, a \textit{batch} optimization approach was proposed to estimate GSOs for processes based on a \textit{causal} vertex-time autoregressive model. Building on this, an online version of the optimization was developed using adaptive filtering frameworks. Specifically, a modified stochastic gradient projection method was applied to a regularized least squares objective to construct the filter. This recursion was decomposed into three regularized sub-problems to handle challenges including multi-convexity, sparsity, commutativity, and bias, accompanied by a convergence analysis. Furthermore, experiments were performed to demonstrate the algorithm's performance, ranging from traditional mean squared error (MSE) metrics to successful recovery rates, thereby illuminating the method's potential, limitations, and avenues for future research.

Predictive maintenance is employed in industrial settings to enhance equipment availability and minimize costs associated with unexpected repairs. Typically, these applications rely on sensor data capturing physical indicators like vibration or temperature that correlate directly with machine degradation. However, when sensor data is unavailable, systems instead utilize event logs generated by the machinery. This work examines existing literature on predictive maintenance solutions and introduces a new public dataset comprising event logs from 156 machines. Furthermore, we establish an evaluation framework for predictive maintenance systems that incorporates business constraints and conduct experiments to identify effective solutions, offering guidance for future research utilizing this dataset.

A fundamental challenge in creating and maintaining crowd-sourced filter lists is the maintainers' inability to confidently foresee whether a new rule will disrupt websites or identify where such disruptions might occur. Due to the sheer scale of the Web, authors cannot broadly assess the impact of a proposed blocking rule before deploying it to millions of users. This lack of pre-deployment compatibility evaluation significantly diminishes the efficacy of filter-list-based content blocking, resulting in lists that are both overly cautious (with narrowly tailored rules to minimize breakage) and error-prone (still causing significant site failures). To effectively scale to the Web's vast scope, authors require an automated mechanism to detect when a new filter rule causes breakage before it reaches end users. This study presents the design and implementation of the first automated system capable of predicting when a filter list rule will break a website. By training a classifier on a dataset derived from EasyList compatibility data and novel browser instrumentation, we achieved practical accuracy levels (AUC 0.88). Our open-source system operates without human intervention to assess the compatibility risk of proposed privacy interventions. Additionally, we identify the 40 specific webpage behaviors that most strongly predict observed breakage.

The growing demand for cost-effective, high-quality experiences in expanding 3D vision applications has heightened the focus on point cloud visual quality. A review of existing Point Cloud Quality Assessment (PCQA) methods reveals that quality is typically evaluated using single-modal data, derived either from 2D projections or 3D point clouds. While 2D projections offer rich texture and semantic details but vary significantly with viewpoint, 3D point clouds are more robust to viewpoint changes but highly sensitive to geometric distortions. To combine the strengths of both modalities, we introduce a novel no-reference PCQA (NR-PCQA) metric based on multi-modal analysis. Specifically, we decompose point clouds into sub-models to capture local geometry distortions like point displacement and down-sampling, while simultaneously rendering 2D projections to extract texture features. These sub-models and projected images are then encoded using point-based and image-based neural networks, respectively. Finally, symmetric cross-modal attention mechanisms are utilized to integrate multi-modal quality information. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses all compared state-of-the-art methods and significantly outperforms previous NR-PCQA techniques, underscoring the effectiveness of our proposed method.
