Furthermore, we examine the distinct physical characteristics of timelike orbits in black hole versus naked singularity spacetimes and discuss the resulting implications. Our findings reveal several notable differences, most significantly that while particle bound orbits in Schwarzschild spacetime cannot precess opposite to their direction of motion, such reverse precession is possible within naked singularity spacetimes.

Measurements of $K^{*}$(892)$^{0}$ and $\phi$(1020) meson production in p-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}$ = 5.02 TeV have been conducted using the ALICE detector, focusing on the rapidity interval $-0.5 < y <0$. These mesons were identified through their decays into charged hadrons. The study presents transverse momentum spectra across a multiplicity-dependent range of 0–15 GeV/$c$ for $K^{*0}$ and 0.3–21 GeV/$c$ for $\phi$. Reported integrated yields, average transverse momenta, and particle ratios are benchmarked against data from pp collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 7 TeV and Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}$ = 2.76 TeV. In both p-Pb and Pb-Pb systems, these particles serve as probes for the hadronic phase, aiding the investigation of hadronization mechanisms when compared to other identified species. Specifically, the mean transverse momenta and the differential proton-to-$\phi$ ratio are analyzed in relation to event multiplicity. Furthermore, the short-lived $K^{*0}$ is examined to assess re-scattering effects, which are linked to the system's size and the duration of the hadronic phase.

By drawing an analogy to critical phenomena, it was demonstrated that Nikuradse's measurements of the turbulent friction factor ($f_t$) in pipes with radius $R$ and wall roughness $r$ can be unified into a single curve defined by the conveyance law $f_t Re^{1/4}=g_o(\chi)$. In this equation, $Re$ denotes the bulk Reynolds number and $\chi =Re^{3/4}\left({r}/{R}\right)$. Although the implicit function $g_o(.)$ was previously conjectured by aligning two asymptotic limits of $f_t$, the link between this function and the underlying turbulent eddy dynamics remained unclear. This study addresses that gap by utilizing models for the wall-normal velocity spectrum and pressure-strain return-to-isotropy to close a co-spectral density budget, thereby deriving $g_o(.)$. The proposed approach not only explicitly solves the conveyance law but also interprets $\chi$ as a dimensionless length scale representing the balance between viscous sublayer thickness and the characteristic height of roughness elements. Furthermore, the applicability of this method to published data extending beyond Nikuradse's original range in terms of roughness and Reynolds numbers is examined.

We obtain all-order formulas for perturbations of the Einstein-Hilbert action and Einstein equations, explicitly deriving the general $n$-th order terms of the perturbative series. We examine these perturbations across three distinct formulations of General Relativity, distinguished by their fundamental fields. Notably, we identify minimal building blocks capable of generating the complete set of perturbations within a specific metric perturbation convention for each formulation. We demonstrate that the number of perturbation terms increases linearly with the order of perturbation. Treating this convention as a reference point, we discuss extending these findings to other metric perturbation conventions. As a consistency verification, we calculate graviton scattering amplitudes using the perturbiner method grounded in the perturbative Einstein equation. Finally, we address the extension of these results to curved backgrounds and the inclusion of additional matter.

C*-algebra bundles provide a framework for representing the limits of physical theories where the algebraic structure varies with a specific parameter. A key instance involves the $\hbar\to 0$ limit within the C*-algebras of physical quantities in quantum theories, situated under strict deformation quantization. This paper analyzes such limiting processes by extending a bundle of C*-algebras to a specific parameter value, establishing both existence and uniqueness theorems for these extensions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these extensions are functorial with respect to the C*-product, dynamical automorphisms, and the Lie bracket (specifically in the $\hbar\to 0$ scenario) defined on the fiber C*-algebras.

An independent ethical evaluation of an artificial intelligence system entails an unbiased review of its development, deployment, and application to ensure alignment with ethical principles. Although system-level qualitative frameworks outlining high-level requirements and component-level quantitative metrics for measuring specific ethical dimensions have emerged in recent years, a significant gap remains between them, obstructing the practical execution of such assessments. This study addresses that disparity by designing a comprehensive independent ethical assessment process tailored for a text classification model, with a specific emphasis on hate speech detection. To strengthen bias evaluation, the assessment incorporates protected attributes mining and counterfactual-based analysis. It encompasses evaluations of technical performance, data bias, embedding bias, classification bias, and interpretability. The proposed methodology is illustrated through the assessment of a deep learning model designed for hate speech detection.

Although manually optimizing Register Transfer Level (RTL) datapaths is standard in the industry, it often impedes progress due to its high time consumption. We leverage the principle that complex RTL-to-RTL transformations can be decomposed into sequences of smaller, localized changes. By modeling RTL as a graph and applying contemporary graph rewriting methods, we automate circuit design space exploration to uncover functionally equivalent yet optimized architectures. Our results show that modern rewriting frameworks effectively replicate the diverse, complex optimizations performed by human engineers on bit-vector code, including nuanced, error-prone details regarding transformation validity under intricate bitwidth interactions. The proposed automated approach matches typical industrial manual optimization outcomes, achieving circuit area reductions of up to 71%. Beyond generating optimized RTL, our tool correctly determines that the optimal architecture for a specific arithmetic expression may vary based on operand widths, thereby producing a library of optimized designs instead of the single design point usually yielded by manual efforts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that previous academic research on maximizing carry-save representation and multiple constant multiplication is generalized and extended within this work, emerging as special cases of our broader approach.

This work investigates the resonant prescribed T-curvature problem on a compact 4-dimensional Riemannian manifold with boundary. We establish sharp energy and gradient estimates for the corresponding Euler-Lagrange functional to identify the critical points at infinity of the variational problem, assuming non-degeneracy of an associated Hamiltonian function. Leveraging these estimates, we formulate a Morse-type lemma in the vicinity of these critical points at infinity. Based on this lemma, we demonstrate new existence results derived from Morse theory. Furthermore, by integrating the Morse lemma at infinity with the Liouville variant of the Barycenter technique originally developed by Bahri and Coron [13] (as detailed in [46]), we prove novel existence theorems under specific topological constraints on the manifold's boundary and the entry and exit sets at infinity.

We present and analyze a one-parameter deformation of the $(1+1)$-dimensional polynuclear growth (PNG) model, termed the $t$-PNG model. This model is characterized by the condition that whenever two expanding islands coalesce, a new island sprouts at the merging site with probability $t$. When $t=0$, the system reduces to the standard PNG model; within droplet geometry, this corresponds to the length of the longest increasing subsequence of a uniformly random permutation or, equivalently, the outcome of patience sorting. In this framework, the $t$-PNG model introduces errors into the sorting algorithm with probability $t$. We demonstrate that for any fixed $t \in [0,1)$, the $t$-PNG model displays one-point Tracy-Widom GUE asymptotics at large times, while converging to the narrow wedge solution of the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) equation as $t \to 1$. Additionally, we define external source distributions likely to trigger Baik-Ben Arous-Peche type phase transitions. Our proofs rely on solvable stochastic vertex models and their relationship to determinantal point processes derived from Schur measures on partitions.

This study proposes a viable design for an integrated photonic circuit capable of single-qubit preparation and rotations via the third-order nonlinear process of difference frequency generation (DFG), defined within the temporal mode basis. The circuit's initial stage generates heralded single photons using spontaneous four-wave mixing in a micro-ring cavity specifically engineered to deliver a single-photon state in a distinct temporal mode. The subsequent stage implements DFG within a spiral waveguide featuring controlled dispersion characteristics to achieve color qubit preparation fidelity approaching unity. Furthermore, we introduce the generalized rotation operator associated with the DFG process, outline the methodology for device design, and present qubit preparation fidelity results as a function of user-accessible parameters.
This paper examines the KPZ equation on a torus and establishes that Gaussian fluctuations occur over long time scales.

Blockchains are sustained by a network of participants executing algorithms that create a distributed system resilient to Byzantine failures. For users, these systems mimic centralized computers capable of performing trustworthy, verifiable computations characterized by determinism and the immutability of results. Smart contracts are coded in specialized languages with deterministic semantics, initiated by external user invocations. These contracts possess local storage, can interact with one another, and facilitate the storage and transfer of cryptocurrency. Ensuring code correctness prior to deployment is critical, as contracts cannot be altered once live. However, verifying program correctness is challenging within this ecosystem due to the risk of malicious users or contracts designed to exploit others. Many vulnerabilities stem from unforeseen interactions between multiple contracts and the unknown code executing exploits. Furthermore, intense competition among blockchains to grow their user bases drives rapid implementation of new features and ideas. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a formal, extensible environment designed to reason about multi-contract interactions and verify properties before features are integrated into production blockchains. We present a computational model that simulates the execution platform, abstracts individual contract internals, and concentrates on interaction dynamics, demonstrating how various existing and proposed features can facilitate this reasoning process.

Let $G$ and $N$ be finite groups of order $2n$, where $n$ is odd. The pair $(G,N)$ is termed Hopf-Galois realizable if $G$ acts as a regular subgroup within the holomorph of $N$, denoted $\h(N)=N\rtimes\au(N)$. This article establishes necessary conditions for $G$ (and analogously for $N$) when one of the groups takes the structure $\mathbb{Z}_n\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_2$. We further demonstrate that these conditions are sufficient provided the radical of $n$ is a Burnside number. Consequently, this result classifies all skew braces whose additive or multiplicative group is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}_n\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_2$ under these circumstances.

This work introduces a general theoretical framework for the formation of skyrmion crystals (SkX) in chiral magnetic thin films and explores their intriguing thermodynamic properties. When the parameter $\kappa$, representing the relative strength of the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI), exceeds a certain threshold, these films can exhibit numerous metastable states with variable skyrmion densities, reaching a maximum limit. In an infinite film without an external magnetic field, the ground state consists of a long, zig-zagged ramified stripe skyrmion that spans the entire material. However, applying a perpendicular magnetic field of intermediate strength results in a ground state with a finite skyrmion density. Consequently, for $\kappa$ above a critical value, chiral magnetic films typically display a stripy phase at low fields and a skyrmion crystal only near an optimal field strength. Conversely, if $\kappa$ remains below this critical threshold, the lowest energy state persists as a stripy helical state regardless of the presence or absence of a magnetic field. The existence of these multiple metastable states accounts for the thermodynamic path dependence observed in various film states. Furthermore, the reduction of the $\kappa$ value as temperature increases clarifies why skyrmions often become metastable at lower temperatures in many systems. These insights provide a novel pathway for manipulating skyrmions and advancing applications based on skyrmion technology.

Since Lightning Network (LN) transactions are neither broadcast nor publicly recorded, LN is regarded as a scalability and privacy enhancement for Bitcoin. The protocol ensures that only the final channel state is confirmed upon closure, while nodes gossip regarding available routing channels and their aggregate capacities. To execute a multi-hop payment, a sender constructs a route using its local view of the network graph. Because channel balances remain private, payments frequently fail if an intermediary lacks sufficient funds; consequently, the system attempts multiple routes until success, creating a tradeoff between privacy and routing efficiency where hidden balances enhance privacy but reduce efficiency. This research demonstrates that an attacker can readily deduce channel balances through probing, a process requiring under a minute per channel with minimal capital and no operational costs. We detail the algorithm and validate our proof-of-concept on Bitcoin's testnet, arguing that LN's current balance between privacy and efficiency is suboptimal, leaving channel balances neither adequately protected nor effectively utilized. We propose two evolutionary paths: first, to bolster privacy, we suggest modifying error handling to obscure details of failed channels from the sender, which would neutralize our probing technique but increase routing failures by preventing the sender from identifying specific bottlenecks. Second, to enhance efficiency, we propose a new API allowing senders to query balances of channels they do not control. We contend that integrating these approaches enables LN to optimize both privacy and efficiency by concealing private data when possible while leveraging public data to improve routing performance.

This study introduces a low-complexity detector for MIMO systems utilizing the recently developed OTFS modulation scheme. The proposed approach linearly combines symbol-vector copies received across various diversity branches (including propagation paths and receive antennas) using maximum ratio combining (MRC) to iteratively enhance the signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) at the combiner output. To mitigate performance loss caused by spatial correlation among receiver antennas, we propose a sample-based estimation method that determines the correlation matrix and derives optimized MRC weights. Consequently, the detector achieves superior performance and reduced complexity compared to existing linear minimum mean square error (LMMSE) and message passing (MP) detectors for MIMO-OTFS systems.

NLP models have been shown to exhibit discriminatory tendencies toward groups defined by social identities like race and gender. In response to the harmful impacts of these biases, researchers have dedicated significant effort to developing promising mitigation strategies. Despite their practical significance, existing algorithmic fairness research lacks a deep comprehension of the relationships between various bias types. Social bias is inherently complex; social psychology studies frequently identify "generalized prejudice," where negative sentiments toward one group extend to others. For instance, individuals who demean ethnic minorities often also devalue women and LGBTQ+ people. Consequently, this work offers the first systematic investigation into bias correlations within mitigation efforts. Specifically, we analyze bias mitigation in two prevalent NLP tasks—toxicity detection and word embeddings—across three social identities: race, gender, and religion. Our results indicate that biases are interconnected, revealing scenarios where the independent debiasing methods currently favored in literature may be inadequate. We further explore whether jointly addressing correlated biases is preferable to isolated, individual debiasing approaches. Additionally, we examine the inherent trade-off between debiasing and accuracy. Ultimately, this study aims to encourage future research on joint bias mitigation that explicitly accounts for these correlations.

Expanding edge experiments offer a promising avenue for exploring new physical regimes within quantum Hall systems. While static edges exhibit gapless excitations described by free fields decoupled from the bulk, maintaining conformal symmetry, these properties may not hold when the edge expands. We develop a quantum field theory framework in 1+1 dimensional curved spacetime to investigate this expanding edge dynamics. Utilizing edge waveforms from the expansion region, we propose methods to address key questions: whether conformal symmetry persists, if edge expansion induces nonlinear interactions among edge excitations, and if these edge modes couple with bulk excitations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that expanding edges can serve as simulators for two-dimensional dilaton-gravity models, such as Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity. As a practical application, our theoretical setup suggests the potential to simulate the emission of analog Hawking radiation, characterized by the Gibbons-Hawking temperature, from the future de Sitter horizon generated in the expanding edge region.

We investigate radiative standing shocks within advective accretion flows around stellar-mass black holes using 2D radiation hydrodynamic simulations, specifically targeting super-Eddington accretion. Under conditions conducive to standing shocks, simulations reveal that the shock position on the equator migrates closer to the event horizon as the accretion rate increases. In the narrow, optically thin, and hot funnel along the rotational axis, the gas gradually transitions into a dense, optically thick state due to material flowing from the base of the radiative shock near the equator. Consequently, luminosity reaches approximately $10^{40}$ erg $s^{-1}$, exhibiting a strongly anisotropic distribution around the axis and dropping to very low edge-on values of roughly $10^{36}$ erg $s^{-1}$. Mass outflow rates from the outer boundary are substantial, ranging from $\sim 10^{-5}$ to $10^{-4} M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$, with most outflow originating through the radial boundary and potentially observable across a broad wind region. The models produce approximately black body spectra with temperatures between $5 \times 10^{6}$ and $3 \times 10^{7}$ K at the vertical outer boundary. Furthermore, these super-Eddington radiative shock models offer a plausible explanation for superaccretors such as SS 433 and Ultraluminous X-ray sources powered by stellar-mass black holes.

Latent knowledge embedded in the emotions and opinions of individuals expressed through social networks is vital for various applications, such as social management, dynamical processes, and public security. Affective computing, an interdisciplinary field connecting artificial intelligence with cognitive inference, offers the capability to extract emotion-focused insights from short text. These texts convey concealed information regarding an author's personality and cognition, which can establish both correlations and variations among users. Consequently, emotion recognition in brief content must account for authorial contrasts, allowing differences in personality and cognition to be identified within emotional expressions. To address this, we propose a framework that, on one hand, infers latent individual traits from short texts and, on the other, introduces a novel ensemble classifier featuring dynamic dropout convnets to extract emotions from textual contexts. Our method categorizes short text by jointly utilizing cognitive factors and hidden information. We employ outcome vectors in a new embedding model to enhance emotion-specific features, which are collectively assembled through lexicon inductions. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared to other methods, our proposed model achieves superior performance in recognizing emotions from noisy content.

Let $X$ be a K3 surface defined over a number field. We demonstrate that $X$ possesses infinitely many specializations exhibiting a jump in Picard rank, thereby generalizing our earlier collaboration with Shankar, Shankar, and Tang to include cases where $X$ may have potentially bad reduction. Additionally, we establish a comparable result for generically ordinary, non-isotrivial families of K3 surfaces over curves over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$, extending prior findings by Maulik, Shankar, and Tang. As a consequence, we provide a novel proof of the ordinary Hecke orbit conjecture for both orthogonal and unitary Shimura varieties.

This paper investigates a control system comprising a single major agent and a large number of identical minor agents, specifically analyzing the limit as the agent count approaches infinity. The mean field approach is employed to study this limiting system. We first establish the existence and uniqueness of motion for systems composed of finite-dimensional and mean-field-type subsystems. The primary contribution of this work is the demonstration of motion stability with respect to perturbations in dynamics, initial conditions, and controls. To exemplify the general theory, we analyze a Stackelberg game where the leader governs the major agent and the follower influences the minor agents. Applying the developed framework, we prove the existence of a solution.

It is established that canonical recurrent neural networks (RNNs) struggle with long-term dependencies, a challenge mitigated by the memory mechanisms in Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. Neural Turing Machines (NTMs) represent a new class of RNNs that function as programmable computers controlled by neural networks, capable of learning basic algorithmic tasks. Matrix neural networks utilize a matrix-based representation that inherently maintains the spatial structure of data, offering an advantage over canonical vector-based networks, and potentially providing superior memory capacity. In this paper, we introduce and examine a probabilistic definition of memory capacity for matrix-based RNNs using Fisher information. We derive bounds on this capacity under different hypotheses and compare them to those of vector-based counterparts. Specifically, we demonstrate that the memory capacity of these networks is limited by $N^2$ for an $N \times N$ state matrix, generalizing the known limit for vector networks. Furthermore, we analyze and confirm the increase in memory capacity achieved when incorporating external state memory, such as in NTMs. This insight motivates the construction of NTMs with matrix-based external memory, leading to the development of Matrix NTMs. We evaluate the performance of this new class of memory networks on algorithmic tasks like copying and recall, comparing them against Matrix RNNs. Our results show that adding external memory significantly enhances the performance of Matrix NTMs.

An orbit-like foliation refers to a singular foliation defined on a complete Riemannian manifold $M$ where the leaves are locally equidistant (constituting a singular Riemannian foliation) and infinitesimally homogeneous in the transverse direction. This category encompasses not only partitions of space into orbits of isometric actions but also numerous non-homogeneous examples, including partitions of $M$ into orbits of a proper groupoid. In this paper, we establish a version of the Kondrakov Embedding Theorem and an analogous Principle of Symmetric Criticality by Palais for basic functions associated with orbit-like foliations. As a demonstration of these concepts, we examine the corresponding Yamabe problem within this framework, as well as the case of fiber bundles with homogeneous fibers, aiming to find metrics with constant scalar curvature that respect the underlying Riemannian foliation structure. Additionally, we present an application concerning the existence of positive constant scalar curvature on exotic spheres. In a forthcoming revision, we plan to extend these findings to address the corresponding Kazdan–Warner problem.

This paper introduces HUMBI, a novel large-scale multiview dataset designed to capture human body expressions while wearing natural clothing. The primary objective of HUMBI is to enable the modeling of view-specific appearance and geometry for five key body signals: gaze, face, hands, body, and garments, across a diverse range of individuals. Data was collected using 107 synchronized HD cameras to record 772 unique subjects varying in gender, ethnicity, age, and style. Leveraging these multiview image streams, the study reconstructs high-fidelity 3D mesh models of body expressions, facilitating the representation of view-specific visual details. The results demonstrate that HUMBI is highly effective for learning and reconstructing complete human models, serving as a valuable complement to existing limited-view and subject datasets such as MPII-Gaze, Multi-PIE, Human3.6M, and Panoptic Studio. Building on HUMBI, we propose a new benchmark challenge focused on pose-guided appearance rendering, aiming to significantly enhance photorealism in 3D modeling of diverse human expressions—a critical factor for authentic social telepresence. The dataset is publicly accessible at http://humbi-data.net.

Let $s(n)$ represent the count of nonzero bits in the binary representation of an integer $n$. This work examines the Diophantine system $s(ab)=k$, $s(a)=\ell$, and $s(b)=m$ within the domain of odd integers $a$ and $b$, for fixed parameters $k$, $\ell$, and $m$. We derive an upper bound for the product $ab$ dependent on $\ell$ and $m$ when $k$ equals 2 or 3. Although no such bound exists for $k=4$, we provide an upper limit for the smaller of the two variables, $\min\{a,b\}$, expressed in terms of $\ell$ and $m$.

No single clustering algorithm is or will ever be universally superior; however, the goal remains to identify high-performing methods for specific tasks and eliminate those that consistently underperform. Traditionally, clustering is assessed via internal or external validity metrics. Internal measures evaluate properties of the resulting partitions, such as compactness or separability, but their reliability is often doubted because they may favor semantically meaningless groupings. External measures instead compare algorithm outputs against expert-defined ground truth labels. While classical similarity scores like Normalized Mutual Information, Fowlkes-Mallows, and the Adjusted Rand Index are common, they lack desirable properties, such as correctly handling pathological edge cases. Additionally, these scores are difficult to interpret (e.g., the meaning of a 0.8 score is unclear), and their values can fluctuate depending on the number of true clusters, complicating cross-dataset comparisons. To address these limitations, we introduce and analyze a novel metric: an asymmetric optimal set-matching accuracy that accounts for chance and imbalanced cluster sizes.

The study of symmetry within Boolean functions $f:\{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ is a well-established area in complexity theory. Symmetric functions, which remain invariant under the action of the symmetric group $S_n$, form a particularly significant class in this domain. A function is termed transitive (or weakly-symmetric) if there exists a transitive subgroup $G$ of $S_n$ such that $f$ is invariant under $G$'s action; essentially, the function's output does not change when the input bits are permuted according to some $\sigma \in G$. Over the last few decades, analyzing the complexity measures of such transitive functions has been a vibrant field of research.

This work investigates transitive functions through the lens of various combinatorial measures, specifically focusing on the maximum separation between different pairs of these measures. While similar investigations for general Boolean functions have been ongoing for years—with notable results compiled by Aaronson et al. (STOC, 2021)—the methods used to demonstrate separations often rely on non-transitive functions. For instance, celebrated constructions like the "pointer functions" by Ambainis et al. (JACM, 2017) and "cheat-sheet functions" by Aaronson et al. (STOC, 2016) do not possess transitivity. Consequently, separations between combinatorial measures for transitive functions have remained unproven.

In this paper, we demonstrate how to adapt certain existing functions to create transitive variants. These modified functions successfully exhibit separations between pairs of combinatorial measures analogous to those found in the broader context of general Boolean functions.

As the daily proliferation of classification models increases, so does the variety of tools available for interpreting and comparing them. Solutions like LIME and SHAP allow users to understand which input features drive a classifier's predictions, while numerical metrics such as accuracy facilitate straightforward comparisons between models. However, existing literature rarely addresses how to interpret a specific data feature's contribution relative to its impact on another classifier. This comparative analysis is crucial for revealing fundamental differences between models, selecting the appropriate classifier under varying feature conditions, and improving ensemble strategies. To address this gap, we introduce a Learning-from-Disagreement (LFD) framework designed to visually compare two classification models. LFD focuses on data instances where the two models produce conflicting predictions and trains a discriminator to learn from these discrepancies. Since the original training features may be inaccessible, the discriminator is trained using a set of meta-features derived from specific hypotheses about the classifiers' behaviors. By applying SHAP values to interpret the trained discriminator across these meta-features, we generate actionable insights into the compared models. Additionally, we propose multiple metrics to profile meta-feature importance from various angles. These metrics enable users to easily identify meta-features exhibiting the most complementary behaviors between the two classifiers, thereby enhancing ensemble performance. We validate the efficacy of our framework and visualizations using binary classification models within the financial services and advertising sectors.

In 1913, Niels Bohr successfully calculated the energy levels of the hydrogen atom by applying specific quantization rules to classical periodic orbits, inspiring many physicists to attempt similar approaches for other atoms. In a notable 1921 paper, I.~Langmuir numerically demonstrated the existence of a periodic orbit within the helium atom, treating it as a classical three-body problem. This paper provides an analytic proof confirming the existence of Langmuir's periodic orbit.

This paper introduces the NiuTrans system for the WMT21 translation efficiency challenge (http://statmt.org/wmt21/efficiency-task.html). Building on prior work, we examine diverse methods to enhance efficiency without compromising translation quality, specifically focusing on combining lightweight Transformer architectures with knowledge distillation. Furthermore, we boost translation speed through graph optimization, low-precision computation, dynamic batching, and parallel pre- and post-processing. On an NVIDIA A100 GPU, our system achieves a throughput of 247,000 words per second, representing a threefold increase over last year's performance. It currently holds the top position for both speed and lowest memory usage on the GPU-throughput track. The associated code, models, and pipeline can be accessed at NiuTrans.NMT (https://github.com/NiuTrans/NiuTrans.NMT).

Idiomatic expressions are a fundamental component of natural language that are continually evolving. Due to their non-compositional nature and capacity to convey either figurative or literal meanings based on context, they present a longstanding challenge for Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems. To tackle this, we investigate the task of detecting idiomatic expressions within sentences and pinpointing their locations. Previous research on this topic has focused on specific categories of idioms, resulting in limited generalizability to novel expressions. We introduce a multi-stage neural architecture incorporating an attention flow mechanism to identify these expressions. The network effectively integrates contextual and lexical information across various levels by utilizing both word and sub-word representations. Empirical evaluations across three of the largest benchmark datasets, featuring idioms with diverse syntactic patterns and varying degrees of non-compositionality, demonstrate that our model achieves new state-of-the-art performance. A key advantage of this model is its capacity to recognize idioms encountered during testing that were not present in the training data, yielding improvements of 1.4% to 30.8% over competitive baselines on the largest dataset.

This study derives the precise one-loop beta functions for four-derivative terms—specifically the Weyl tensor squared, Ricci scalar squared, and Gauss-Bonnet—in a minimal six-derivative quantum gravity framework within four spacetime dimensions, utilizing the Barvinsky and Vilkovisky generalized Schwinger-DeWitt method. For the first time, this yields the complete set of beta functions for a super-renormalizable quantum gravity model. The authors explicitly solve the full system of renormalization group (RG) equations, covering both Newton and cosmological constants, for the general case and for the six-derivative Lee-Wick (LW) quantum gravity model previously proposed by two of the authors. In the ultraviolet limit, the minimal theory demonstrates asymptotic freedom, describing free gravitons in Minkowski or (anti-)de Sitter ((A)dS) backgrounds contingent on initial RG conditions. Consistent with the LW prescription, ghostlike states emerge as complex conjugate pairs across all energy scales; however, due to renormalization group running, these ghosts can evolve into tachyons. The authors propose that extending the theory to include operators cubic in the Riemann tensor could alter the beta functions, potentially resolving this instability.

A new and intriguing category of scalar-tensor gravity theories involves constraints on field dynamics, where the scalar field either settles into a constant acceleration or ceases to accelerate, moving instead at a constant velocity. By integrating these constraints with mechanisms to dynamically neutralize a high-energy cosmological constant—such as via well-tempered or self-tuning methods—it becomes possible to achieve a cosmic expansion history featuring a matter-dominated era followed by late-time acceleration, even in the presence of a large cosmological constant, though the resulting late-time de Sitter limit may prove unstable. Models involving poles, such as those found in Dirac-Born-Infeld actions, are especially significant for establishing a cosmic speed limit.

We present \textit{Nocturne}, a novel 2D driving simulator designed to study multi-agent coordination under partial observability. Nocturne aims to facilitate research on inference and theory of mind within real-world multi-agent scenarios, eliminating the computational burden associated with computer vision and image-based feature extraction. In this environment, agents perceive only a blocked view of the scene, simulating human visual limitations. Unlike current benchmarks that rely on camera inputs to render human-like observations, Nocturne employs efficient intersection techniques to calculate a vectorized set of visible features within a C++ backend, achieving a performance of over $2000$ steps per second. Leveraging open-source trajectory and map data, the simulator supports the loading and replay of arbitrary real-world driving scenes. Utilizing this platform, we evaluated reinforcement-learning and imitation-learning agents, revealing that their coordination capabilities fall significantly short of human levels and diverge markedly from expert trajectories.

Twin-width is a newly defined graph parameter. This article calculates the twin-width for several finite graphs, specifically proving that graphs with 4 and 5 vertices have twin-widths no greater than 1 and 2, respectively. Furthermore, we demonstrate that neither dual graphs nor line graphs maintain their twin-width, and we provide upper bounds for the twin-width of King's and Rook's graphs.

This study introduces a new discrete-time multi-virus SIR (susceptible-infected-recovered) framework designed to model the propagation of competing epidemics across a networked population. Initially, we establish a sufficient condition ensuring that the infection levels of all viruses on the networked system decay to zero exponentially. Subsequently, we develop an observation model that aggregates the total infection levels at each node, reflecting individuals infected by multiple viruses with similar symptoms. We derive a sufficient condition for the model's local observability and introduce a Luenberger observer for estimating system states. Simulations demonstrate that the estimation error of this observer converges to zero prior to the extinction of the viruses.

We examine modifications of general relativity defined by a specific noncovariant restriction on metric components, which induces a perfect-fluid-like stress-energy tensor within the Einstein equations. This category encompasses recently proposed generalized unimodular gravity (GUMG) and its fundamental variant, unimodular gravity (UMG). By incorporating four Stueckelberg fields, we render these gravity models covariant and demonstrate that in GUMG, three of these fields dynamically decouple. Consequently, the covariant formulation of GUMG is dynamically equivalent to k-essence theory featuring a specific Lagrangian derivable from GUMG parameters. We present explicit examples of such reconstruction and briefly explore theories extending beyond GUMG, particularly those involving self-gravitating media. Furthermore, we contrast GUMG k-inflation with cuscuton models of dynamically inert k-essence fields and address the motivations for GUMG derived from effective field theory considerations.

Many datasets contain essential components alongside non-critical ones and noise. Specifically, for network-structured data, various techniques have been developed to isolate a "network backbone," defined as the collection of most significant links. Nevertheless, the potential applications of these compressed data representations remain largely unexplored. This study addresses that gap by introducing and investigating systematic methods to construct surrogate data from diverse types of temporal network backbones. We specifically examine the extent of original information required to be preserved with the backbone to enable data-driven numerical simulations of spreading dynamics. Our findings are demonstrated using empirical temporal networks exhibiting a wide range of structural characteristics and properties.

Optimizing the expected values of probabilistic processes is a core challenge in computer science, impacting areas from artificial intelligence to operations research and statistical computing. Regrettably, standard automatic differentiation methods designed for deterministic programs generally fail to calculate the accurate gradients required by gradient-based optimization techniques. In this paper, we introduce ADEV, an extension to forward-mode automatic differentiation that correctly computes the derivatives of expectations for probabilistic programs involving random choices. Our approach applies a source-to-source transformation to a high-level language supporting both discrete and continuous probability distributions. The transformed program yields a new probabilistic version where the expected return value represents the derivative of the original program's expectation. This output enables the generation of unbiased Monte Carlo estimates for the desired gradient, suitable for use within stochastic gradient descent loops. We establish the correctness of ADEV through logical relations defined over the denotations of the source and target programs. Given its modular extension of forward-mode AD, the algorithm allows for a compact implementation; we leveraged this to create a prototype in approximately a dozen lines of Haskell (https://github.com/probcomp/adev).

Inspired by the recent successful synthesis of the MoSi2N4 monolayer [Hong et al., Sci. 369, 670 (2020)], this study presents the first investigation into the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of MoSi2N4 nanoribbons (NRs). Band structure analyses reveal spin-polarization at zigzag edges, whereas armchair edges exhibit non-magnetic semiconducting behavior. For armchair configurations, an indirect-to-direct band gap transition is observed relative to the monolayer, with the energy gap widening as the ribbon width increases. Calculations also highlight anisotropic electrical and magnetic properties across both edge types; notably, a specific zigzag-edge configuration displays a Dirac-semimetal character. The emergence of magnetism and Dirac-semimetal features in these MoSi2N4 ribbons suggests novel physical properties that could be advantageous for next-generation electronic applications.

This study conducts a comprehensive analysis of systems designed to classify affective vocal expressions. It compares state-of-the-art acoustic features against two new vocal print metrics for detecting emotional states: the Hilbert-Huang-Hurst Coefficients (HHHC) and the Vector of Index of Non-stationarity (INS). The HHHC is introduced as a nonlinear feature vector representing affective states through their impact on the speech production mechanism. By leveraging Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) to capture non-stationary acoustic variations, the method extracts Hurst coefficients—closely tied to the excitation source—to construct this feature vector. The INS vector is further incorporated to provide dynamic information alongside the HHHC. These proposed features were evaluated across three German and English speech emotion databases using three established acoustic features as baselines. Additionally, the $\alpha$-integrated Gaussian model ($\alpha$-GMM) was implemented for emotion representation and classification, with its performance benchmarked against other stochastic and machine learning classifiers. The results indicate that HHHC yields significant improvements in classification accuracy compared to baseline features, while $\alpha$-GMM surpasses competing classification methods. Finally, the study assesses HHHC and INS as complementary features when paired with the GeMAPS and eGeMAPS feature sets.

This study introduces a novel approach for identifying key terms within patent claims, a critical step in retrieving patents with analogous claims for prior art analysis. The proposed technique integrates an examination of the distinctive writing style of legal claims with natural language processing (NLP) to decompose the text, ultimately modeling it as a specialized term hierarchy. When evaluated by the quality of search results generated from these extracted keywords, this method outperforms conventional approaches like TF-IDF. The system's effectiveness is assessed based on the relevance of the patents returned in response to queries built from the identified keywords.

The Neutrinos Angra Experiment utilizes a water-based Cherenkov detector situated at the Angra dos Reis nuclear power plant. The project has successfully concluded the commissioning of both the detector and its data acquisition system on-site. Designed to identify electron antineutrinos generated by the reactor, its primary objective is to validate the feasibility of monitoring reactor activity via antineutrino detection. This initiative aligns with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) program, which seeks to identify novel technologies for non-proliferation safeguards. Operating at the surface presents significant challenges, including high noise levels and the necessity for highly sensitive, compact detectors; consequently, the Angra experiment serves as an ideal platform for advancing these applications and mastering new analytical techniques and technologies. This report details the detector's primary characteristics and its electronics chain, covering both front-end and data acquisition components. Additionally, it presents preliminary physics results derived from the commissioning phase data. Finally, the report outlines future perspectives aimed at sustaining the program, emphasizing its critical role in integrating Latin American scientists and engineers into a global, cutting-edge scientific initiative.

The recent report detailing the creation of a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) composed of G-wave molecules—formed by bound pairs of Cesium bosons—is unexpected. These molecules are generated at a 19.87G resonance; typically, such resonances cause severe three-body loss, but this is markedly reduced when the gas density is lowered in a quasi-two-dimensional environment. The resulting G-wave molecules possess non-zero angular momentum projections, marking the first BEC with macroscopic intrinsic angular momentum. This study demonstrates that such intrinsic angular momentum will generate numerous novel quantum phenomena, including the splitting of collective modes without vortices, an orientation-dependent energy shift caused by the molecules' moment of inertia, and a contribution to angular momentum in non-uniform magnetic fields that differs from Berry phase currents. Furthermore, this intrinsic angular momentum offers a method to investigate half-vortices, excitations unique to bosonic molecular condensates, and the wavefunction responsible for the angular momentum can be reconstructed through noise correlations.

The concept of a semibiproduct, a generalization of the categorical biproduct that encompasses classical semidirect products within the context of groups, has recently been examined in the category of monoids, yielding surprising insights into the classification of weakly Schreier extensions. This paper aims to broaden the investigation of semibiproducts to include the category of semigroups. However, a comprehensive understanding of the subject necessitates a deeper analysis within the category of magmas. Indeed, while there exists a subclass of magma-actions, termed "representable," which classify all semibiproducts of magmas and exhibit behavior akin to semigroups, this subclass is nonetheless more general than the subset of associative magma-actions.

Current cyber security defenses often rely heavily on heuristics, standard procedure catalogs, and best practices. Focusing on data backup strategies, we propose mathematically modeling the associated threat landscapes and decision-making challenges. By expressing backup strategies through stochastic processes, we convert the search for optimal defenses into a reinforcement learning task. This approach allows for the training of autonomous agents capable of optimizing defense planning. Specifically, we address finding an optimal backup scheme in an adversarial environment where an attacker can initially infect data and subsequently destroy or encrypt it at a later stage, potentially corrupting multiple intermediate backups. In this scenario, traditional round-robin methods, which simply replace the oldest backup, are no longer optimal for minimizing exposure. Consequently, we formulate the problem as a hybrid discrete-continuous action space Markov decision process and solve it using deep deterministic policy gradients. Our results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm can identify storage update schemes that match or surpass existing methods across various exposure metrics.

A recent study by the PHENIX collaboration analyzed direct photon data from Au+Au, Cu+Cu, and Pb+Pb collisions across beam energies of 39 to 2760 GeV. The findings indicate a universal scaling of multiplicity, where direct photon $p_{T}$-spectra (up to 2 GeV/$c$) align with the charged hadron pseudorapidity density at midrapidity raised to a power of $\alpha=1.25$, within experimental error margins. Additionally, these spectra demonstrate geometrical scaling over the same $p_{T}$ range. By assuming a power-law dependence for the scaled spectra under both scaling laws, we derived two independent constraints for the exponent $\alpha$, which deviate from experimental data by approximately 10% on average. We also explore potential factors that could refine this estimate.

We establish two bounds regarding the discrete moments of Weyl sums. The initial bound derives from a conventional methodology, whereas the second utilizes a refinement of this technique to achieve a tighter estimate within particular ranges. Both demonstrations rely on the recently established main conjecture for Vinogradov's mean value theorem. Furthermore, we highlight two specific applications: first, we introduce a novel $k$-th derivative test for counting integer points near a curve using exponential sums, which surpasses existing geometric bounds though it applies only to certain functions; second, we demonstrate an enhanced polynomial large sieve inequality for univariate polynomials with a degree $k \geq 4$.

This study introduces a simulation-based deep learning Bayesian framework designed for estimating macroeconomic models. The method successfully derives posterior distributions even when the likelihood function is intractable; since the likelihood is unnecessary for this estimation process, filtering steps are also eliminated. Consequently, the approach facilitates Bayesian estimation of HANK models containing over 800 latent states and representative agent models solved via methods that do not produce a likelihood, such as projection and value function iteration. The validity of this framework is demonstrated by estimating a 10-parameter HANK model solved through the Reiter method, which generates 812 covariates per time step (with 810 being latent variables), proving its capacity to manage a vast latent space without requiring model reduction. Additionally, the algorithm is applied to an 11-parameter model solved via value function iteration, a scenario where traditional Metropolis-Hastings or standard maximum likelihood estimators fail. Furthermore, the posteriors derived from the Smets-Wouters (2007) model exhibit both superior quality and faster computation times using simulation-based inference compared to Metropolis-Hastings. Ultimately, this approach mitigates the computational burdens associated with Metropolis-Hastings and enables the estimation of solution methods that do not yield a tractable likelihood.

This study integrates mobile edge computing (MEC) with Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) to optimize the Age of Information (AoI) within communication-computing systems. By jointly processing tasks on both UAVs and Base Stations (BS), we aim to improve edge performance despite constraints in connectivity and computational resources. This collaborative approach leverages the strengths of both UAVs and BS to minimize network AoI. To ensure task freshness, we formulate an AoI minimization problem within a two-hop communication framework, where the first hop occurs at the UAVs and the second at the BS. To address these challenges, we employ a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) approach known as Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL). Our network comprises two agent types with distinct states and actions but sharing a unified policy. This FRL framework effectively manages the dual objectives of two-step AoI minimization and UAV trajectory optimization. Furthermore, we evaluate our proposed algorithm, which utilizes a centralized unit for weight updates, against a fully decentralized multi-agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG) method to enhance agent performance. Consequently, our suggested algorithm achieves approximately a 38% improvement over the MADDPG baseline.

Physics laboratories offer a distinctive setting for students to cultivate both their specific physics identities and broader science identities, largely because they allow for hands-on experimentation and data analysis within a low-pressure atmosphere. However, it is crucial to guarantee that every student benefits equally from these labs and follows a positive developmental path. By conducting interviews and reflexive ethnographic observations, we have identified and examined two prevalent work patterns that can hinder female students in introductory physics labs. Students adopting the "Secretary" archetype are confined to data recording and analysis, thereby missing the chance to fully engage with experimental work and develop their identities. Conversely, students in the "Hermione" mode undertake a disproportionate share of managerial tasks, leaving them with insufficient opportunities to interact with the various aspects of experimental work essential for identity growth. Utilizing a physics identity framework, we analyzed interview and observational data to explore how these work modes can lead to stalled development in students' physics and science identity trajectories within the lab course. This stagnation subsequently reinforces and perpetuates societal stereotypes and biases regarding who belongs in physics. This classification provides a vocabulary for discussing equity in the laboratory and serves as a valuable reference point for those aiming to prioritize equity when transforming physics instruction.

This study measures the transverse energy ($E_\mathrm{T}^{\gamma}$) spectra of isolated photons using data from proton-proton (pp) and lead-lead (PbPb) collisions at the LHC, recorded at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_\mathrm{NN}} =$ 5.02 TeV. The datasets comprise integrated luminosities of 27.4 pb$^{-1}$ for pp and 404 $\mu$b$^{-1}$ for PbPb events. Results are reported for photons with transverse energies between 25 and 200 GeV within the pseudorapidity range $|\eta|$ $<$ 1.44, covering various centrality classes for PbPb collisions. In PbPb collisions, photon production aligns with expectations from scaling pp results by the number of binary nucleon-nucleon collisions, indicating that photons do not interact with the quark-gluon plasma. Consequently, isolated photons serve as a probe for the initial energy of the associated parton in photon+jet analyses. These findings are compared with next-to-leading-order predictions from the JETPHOX generator across different parton distribution functions (PDFs) and nuclear PDFs (nPDFs), offering constraints to improve global nPDF fits.

We present a methodology for density-based topology optimization of non-Fourier thermal transport in nanostructures, utilizing adjoint-based sensitivity analysis of the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) alongside a new material interpolation technique called the "transmission interpolation model" (TIM). The primary challenge in BTE optimization lies in managing the interaction between real- and momentum-resolved material properties. By parameterizing material density through an interfacial transmission coefficient, TIM successfully recovers both the hard-wall and no-interface limits while ensuring a smooth transition between void and solid regions. Initially, we apply this approach to customize the effective thermal-conductivity tensor of a periodic nanomaterial; subsequently, we maximize classical phonon size effects under constrained diffusive transport, yielding a novel thermoelectric material design. Our method facilitates the systematic optimization of materials for heat management and conversion, as well as the broader design of devices where diffusive transport assumptions do not hold.

Most platforms currently employ content moderation strategies to mitigate interpersonal harms like harassment, relying primarily on punitive, offender-focused methods such as bans and content removals. This paper explores an alternative framework known as restorative justice, which prioritizes victim healing, offender rehabilitation, and collective community engagement to resolve harm. To evaluate the potential of restorative justice in addressing online harm, we conducted interviews with 23 participants from Overwatch gaming communities, representing moderators, victims, and offenders. By viewing current harm-resolution practices through the lens of restorative justice, we identified user attitudes toward adopting these processes. Our findings indicate that while online communities possess both the need for and existing infrastructure to support restorative justice, significant structural, cultural, and resource-based barriers hinder its implementation within the prevailing punitive systems. Finally, we examine the opportunities and challenges associated with applying restorative justice principles in digital environments.

Bubbles subjected to vibration can exhibit anomalous behavior, such as moving downward against buoyancy. Although bubble descent driven by the Bjerknes force is well-documented near acoustic resonance, these experiments show that such effects also occur at relatively low frequencies. The study utilized a thin, quasi-2D rectangular acrylic container partially filled with 20-cSt PDMS silicone oil and topped with ambient air. Sinusoidal axial vibrations caused the gas-liquid interface to rupture, generating liquid jets that broke into droplets, which then impacted the liquid to create gas cavities and transport bubbles below the interface. The experimental conditions featured a 280 Hz frequency, 15 g acceleration, and a 94-micron peak-to-peak displacement. Observed behaviors include: 1) free surface fragmentation into jets and droplets, forming bubbles beneath the surface; 2) downward migration of these bubbles within the cell; 3) attraction of bubbles to a deeper bubble, leading to their merger into a large bubble at the cell's base; 4) further merging of base bubbles into a larger, levitated bubble below the free surface that dampens surface breakup; and 5) a levitated bubble interface exhibiting breakup similar to the free surface, but with jets directed downward. Sandia National Laboratories is a multi-program laboratory managed and operated by Sandia Corporation, a wholly owned subsidiary of Lockheed Martin Corporation, for the U.S. Department of Energy's National Nuclear Security Administration under contract DE-AC04-94AL85000.

These notes present a reformulation of the classical Hilbert-Mumford criterion for GIT stability within the framework of algebraic stacks, a result previously achieved independently by Halpern-Leinster. Additionally, we provide a geometric condition ensuring that the substack of stable objects admits separated coarse moduli spaces. This approach is subsequently utilized to construct coarse moduli spaces for torsors under parahoric group schemes over curves.

Severe geomagnetic storms exhibit a clear ordering related to the solar cycle, occurring more often near solar maximum and during its declining phase, being more frequent in larger cycles, and displaying distinct patterns in odd versus even-numbered cycles. However, our understanding of the most extreme space weather events relies on spikes in cosmogenic-isotope records ($^{14}$C, $^{10}$Be, and $^{36}$Cl), which are linked to significantly more intense solar energetic particle (SEP) events than those recorded since the space age. Although both storms and SEPs originate from solar eruptions, the correlation between individual extreme storms and extreme SEPs is weak. Consequently, one cannot assume that the solar cycle trends observed in storms automatically apply to SEPs and isotope events. This study examines solar cycle trends in the timing and intensity of 67 SEP ground-level enhancements (GLEs) detected by neutron monitors from the mid-1950s onward. By applying various GLE occurrence probability models, we demonstrate that GLEs are approximately four times more likely during solar maximum than minimum and occur preferentially earlier in even-numbered cycles. Current data are insufficient to definitively conclude whether larger solar cycles generate more GLEs. We discuss the implications for potential space weather events recorded in cosmogenic-isotope data, finding that GLEs tend to cluster within a few tens of days, likely driven by highly productive active regions, and are separated by roughly 11 years due to solar cycle dynamics. Nevertheless, these temporal patterns fail to explain cosmogenic-isotope spikes, which necessitate multiple extreme SEP events occurring consecutively over several years.

We define a space consisting of pairs of distinct $\mathbb{C}{\rm P}^1$-structures sharing the same holonomy, where the quasi-Fuchsian space represents one connected component. According to the uniformization theorem for Riemann surfaces, each connected component of this space maps holomorphically to the product of the associated Teichm\"uller spaces (when applicable) with its diagonal removed. In this paper, we demonstrate that this uniformization map constitutes a complete local branched covering, thereby extending Bers' simultaneous uniformization theorem in a partial manner. Consequently, we provide a new proof of Bers' theorem that does not rely on the measurable Riemann mapping theorem.

This paper addresses the dynamics of gravitating Skyrmions within the Einstein-Skyrme system, specifically in Bondi coordinates and without a potential term. By assuming spherical symmetry, we establish that both the metric functions and the Skyrme ansatz rely on radial and retarded time coordinates, rendering the system dynamic. We demonstrate that unique solutions are guaranteed over a specific time interval, while global existence is rigorously proven only for small initial data using the proposed approach. Additionally, we examine potential configurations in the Einstein-Skyrme system that lead to singularities at the coordinate origin.

This study conducts a comprehensive high-dimensional analysis of \emph{centered kernel ridge regression} (CKRR), a variant of kernel ridge regression also referred to as kernel ridge regression with an offset. This approach addresses the bias inherent in standard kernel ridge regression by employing \emph{centered} kernels. The theoretical investigation assumes data drawn from a Gaussian distribution and extensively utilizes random matrix theory (RMT). In the asymptotic regime where both data dimension and training sample size grow to infinity with a fixed ratio, and subject to mild constraints on data statistics, we demonstrate that both empirical and prediction risks converge to deterministic quantities that explicitly characterize CKRR performance based on data statistics and dimensions. Building on these findings, we develop a consistent estimator for the prediction risk derived from training data, enabling the optimal tuning of design parameters. A central insight of this analysis is that, asymptotically, a broad class of kernels yield identical minimum prediction risks, a conclusion supported by experiments on both synthetic and real datasets.

Dependency networks, as proposed by Heckerman et al. (2000), offer a probabilistic graphical modeling approach suitable for systems with extensive variable sets. Similar to Bayesian networks, they utilize directed graphs where each node corresponds to a conditional probability table. Because learning and inference operate locally at the node level, these networks maintain computational efficiency even when scaling to a large number of variables. Nevertheless, the distribution learned by dependency networks lacks a closed-form expression; instead, it represents the stationary distribution of a Markov chain known as pseudo-Gibbs sampling. This limitation has historically hindered their advancement. This paper addresses the issue by associating a specific manifold with each node, allowing pseudo-Gibbs sampling to be interpreted as iterative m-projections onto these manifolds. This perspective establishes a theoretical bound for the existence of the stationary distribution within distribution space and reframes both structural and parameter learning as optimization problems. Additionally, experimental comparisons between dependency networks and Bayesian networks reveal that both achieve comparable accuracy in learning distributions. However, the results further indicate that dependency networks can learn significantly faster than Bayesian networks.

Individuals with blindness or low vision (pBLV) face substantial difficulties in identifying final destinations or targeting specific objects within unfamiliar settings. Beyond the initial task of locating and orienting toward a target, the approach phase is often fraught with frustration, particularly when deviations from the planned route occur to circumvent obstacles. This paper introduces a novel wearable navigation system designed to offer real-time guidance, enabling users to reach target objects efficiently and effectively in unknown environments. The system relies on two core visual computing capabilities: three-dimensional localization of the target object and continuous estimation of the user's trajectory, both derived from 2D video footage captured by an inexpensive monocular camera mounted on the user's chest. These functions allow the system to propose an initial route, dynamically update it as the user moves, and provide timely corrections. Experimental results indicate that the system maintains an accuracy error of under 0.5 meters in both indoor and outdoor settings. Entirely vision-based and independent of additional sensors, the system's computations are executed on a Jetson processor within the wearable device to ensure real-time navigation support.

We introduce novel perspectives on the propagation, attenuation, and dissipation of two-fluid torsional Alfvén waves regarding the heating of the lower solar atmosphere. Utilizing numerical simulations of partially ionized plasma, we solve two-fluid equations governing ions, electrons, and neutrals within a three-dimensional Cartesian framework. Our setup begins with a current-free magnetic field representing a flux tube anchored in the photosphere and expanding into the chromosphere and corona. The simulation's lower boundary is placed in the low chromosphere, the region where ion-neutral decoupling initiates; here, a monochromatic driver generates Alfvén waves with a 30-second period. As ion-neutral drift intensifies with altitude, two-fluid effects become prominent, allowing energy from both Alfvén and magneto-acoustic waves to be thermalized via ion-neutral collisions. Consequently, we detect a marked rise in plasma temperature along the magnetic flux tube. Ultimately, two-fluid torsional Alfvén waves may contribute significantly to solar chromospheric heating.

According to Einstein's theory of gravity, any compact object exceeding a few solar masses must be a black hole. Observations contradicting this rule would suggest either new physics beyond General Relativity or exotic matter fields outside the Standard Model, potentially offering insights into unresolved black hole mysteries. This paper provides a brief overview of current and future gravitational-wave tests designed to determine the nature of dark compact objects. These tests include analyzing the multipolar structure and tidal deformability during inspiral, examining ringdown signatures, and searching for near-horizon structures via gravitational-wave echoes.

This work examines the variety of features acquired by a two-layer neural network trained using least squares loss. We quantify this diversity by calculating the average $L_2$-distance between hidden-layer representations and theoretically explore how the learning of non-redundant, distinct features influences network performance. To achieve this, we establish new generalization bounds grounded in Rademacher complexity, which depend on feature diversity for such architectures. Our analysis demonstrates that greater distinctness among features at the hidden units correlates with improved generalization. Furthermore, we illustrate how these findings can be extended to deeper networks and alternative loss functions.

The time-dependent exchange-correlation potential undertakes the unique role of guiding fictitious non-interacting electrons to replicate the precise probability density of real interacting electrons. This function carries fascinating consequences for its architecture, particularly within the non-perturbative regime, where it generates step and peak characteristics that standard ground-state functional approximations fail to reproduce. This review examines insights gained over the last decade regarding these exact features in time-dependent density functional theory and explores their impact on simulation accuracy when electrons are driven significantly away from ground states.

This report details our strategy for the EPIC-KITCHENS-100 Multi-Instance Retrieval Challenge 2022. We begin by parsing sentences into semantic roles associated with verbs and nouns, then leverage self-attention mechanisms to incorporate contextualized video and textual features through triplet losses across various embedding spaces. Our approach surpasses the strong baseline in normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (nDCG), a metric better suited for evaluating semantic similarity. Consequently, our submission achieved 3rd place in nDCG and 4th place in mean Average Precision (mAP).

Facial Beauty Prediction (FBP) seeks to create automated systems for evaluating facial attractiveness. Historically, these results closely aligned with human ratings, thereby inheriting human annotators' biases. Given that artificial intelligence can exhibit racist and discriminatory tendencies, it is essential to identify the root causes of data skewness. Consequently, developing training datasets and AI algorithms that resist biased information presents a new challenge for researchers. Since aesthetic judgment is inherently prone to bias, this work advances the field by proposing an Unbiased Convolutional Neural Network for FBP. Although creating high-accuracy models for rating face attractiveness is feasible, ensuring ethical unbiasedness is equally critical. In this study, we present AestheticNet, a state-of-the-art prediction network that significantly surpasses existing competitors with a Pearson Correlation of 0.9601. Furthermore, we introduce a novel method for generating bias-free CNNs to enhance fairness in machine learning.

Natural language processing remains predominantly focused on English, despite an increasing global demand for models capable of handling other languages. However, transferring models across languages is often costly regarding annotation expenses, engineering time, and effort. This paper introduces a general framework designed to facilitate the efficient and effective transfer of neural models from English to other languages. By utilizing task representations as a form of weak supervision, this model- and task-agnostic approach allows numerous existing neural architectures to be adapted to new languages with minimal difficulty. The method requires only unlabeled parallel data and a loss function defined over task representations. We validate the framework by transferring an English sentiment classifier to three distinct languages. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses several strong baselines and competes with state-of-the-art methods that depend on more complex techniques and significantly greater resources. Furthermore, our framework successfully captures semantically rich and meaningful cross-lingual representations even without direct supervision.

Chirality and topology are foundational concepts deeply linked to the development of spin-textures as candidates for magnetic bits in information technology. However, progress is hindered because conventional perpendicular-to-plane (CPP) sensing devices make electrical detection of chiral properties highly complex. In this work, we utilize extensive first-principles simulations and multiple scattering expansions to reveal the emergence of chiral spin-mixing magnetoresistance (C-XMR). This effect facilitates efficient, all-electrical readout of the chirality and helicity in one- and two-dimensional magnetic states. Unlike the quadratic dependence seen in the recently discovered non-local spin-mixing anisotropic magnetoresistance (X-AMR), C-XMR scales linearly with spin-orbit coupling. We systematically analyze these transport phenomena across various non-collinear magnetic configurations, including spin-spirals and skyrmions, contrasting them with spin-orbit-independent multi-site magnetoresistances. Due to their straightforward integration into existing readout hardware, these magnetoresistances provide crucial tools for investigating the rich physics of topological and chiral magnetic objects using purely electrical methods.

The phenomenon of oscillation synchronization is commonly seen in natural systems, particularly within biological neural networks, where it manifests through frequency-modulated signals. While frequency modulation is a cornerstone technology in engineering, decades of literature on synchronization mechanisms have largely simplified oscillations into unmodulated, sinusoidal-like waves due to technical complexities. Consequently, there is a lack of mathematical frameworks—specifically within systems and control theories—to address frequency-modulated multi-agent systems. This paper introduces a novel formulation for synchronizing such systems. It develops new methodologies to resolve synchronization challenges by tackling three key issues: frequency observation in nonlinear oscillators influenced by network dynamics, achieving frequency consensus through network interaction despite observation errors, and establishing a robust small-gain condition linking these elements. The paper's structure comprises a new problem definition, rigorous theoretical analysis, and numerical validation.

We conduct a three-dimensional lattice simulation of electroweak symmetry breaking occurring via a two-step phase transition, one of which is first-order. Our findings indicate that: 1) if the breaking is driven by a Beyond Standard Model sector at energy scales around $\sim \mathcal{O}(10^{2-3})$ GeV, the resulting gravitational wave spectra exhibit broken power-law double-peak profiles; 2) if the breaking arises from a first-order phase transition in a high-scale global U(1) theory, cosmic strings form and subsequently decay via particle radiation, producing plateau-shaped gravitational wave spectra. These two scenarios can be differentiated by analyzing their respective gravitational wave signatures. Our research demonstrates that stochastic gravitational waves offer a viable alternative method for probing the Beyond Standard Model sector relevant to the electroweak symmetry breaking pattern in the early Universe.

While differential forms in Minkowski spacetime are a well-established topic, their application in Galilean and Carrollian spacetimes appears less developed, likely due to the lack of a standard Hodge star operator. Nevertheless, functional analogs of the Hodge star exist in these two spacetimes in the form of intertwining operators that map between corresponding representations on forms. Leveraging these operators could render differential forms a valuable instrument for formulating Galilean and Carrollian invariant equations, mirroring the utility they possess for constructing and manipulating Poincaré invariant equations in Minkowski spacetime.

In spaces with more than two dimensions ($d>2$), the configurations of four bodies can be mapped to the vertices of a tetrahedron. The system's volume variables are defined by the square of the tetrahedron's volume, along with weighted sums of the squared areas of its four faces and squared edge lengths. This study examines a family of translation-invariant potentials that rely exclusively on these volume variables, as well as solutions to Newton's equations dependent only on them. For systems with zero angular momentum ($L=0$), the corresponding Hamiltonian governing these solutions is derived. The analysis focuses on three detailed examples: (I) a (super)integrable four-body closed chain of harmonic oscillators in $d>2$ (referred to as the harmonic molecule); (II) a generic potential dependent on two volume variables where trajectories maintain a constant moment of inertia (valid for $d>1$); and (III) a four-body anharmonic oscillator for $d \geq 1$. This paper serves as the sequel to a previous study [IJMPA 36, No. 18 (2021)], which addressed the three-body classical problem using volume variables.

This study presents steady-state models for radiation-driven super-Eddington winds and static, expanded neutron star envelopes triggered by the high luminosities of Type I X-ray bursts. Employing flux-limited diffusion to simulate the shift from optically thick to thin regions, and incorporating general relativity, we examine how the photospheric radius near the star changes as the hydrostatic atmosphere transitions into a wind. Our results indicate that the photospheric radius increases monotonically from static envelopes ($r_{\rm ph}\lesssim 50-70$ km) to winds ($r_{\rm ph}\approx 100-1000$ km). While static envelopes can account for observed photospheric radii below $100$ km in most radius expansion bursts, this occurs only within a limited luminosity range; in the majority of cases, luminosity is expected to rise further, producing winds with radii exceeding $100$ km. During the contraction phase, our expanded envelope solutions reveal that the photosphere remains approximately $1$ km above the surface even when the effective temperature is just $3\%$ below its peak, representing a potential systematic error in interpreting measured Eddington fluxes at touchdown.
