Furthermore, clinical classification faces inherent ambiguities, as radiologists often provide varying diagnoses for difficult cases. To address these challenges, we introduce a controllable and explainable {\em Probabilistic Radiomics} framework that integrates radiomics with probabilistic deep learning. This framework extracts 3D CNN features exclusively from the lesion region, encoding them into a lesion representation via a controllable Non-local Shape Analysis Module (NSAM) utilizing self-attention. Drawing inspiration from variational auto-encoders (VAEs), an Ambiguity PriorNet approximates the distribution of ambiguity among human experts. The final diagnosis is generated by combining the lesion representation with sampled ambiguity priors, resulting in an end-to-end trainable network named $DenseSharp^{+}$. We validated the effectiveness of this method by applying it to lung nodule diagnosis using the LIDC-IDRI database.

This paper introduces a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) approach designed to enhance the resolution and segment retinal layers within optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans. OCT is recognized as an affordable, non-invasive imaging technique capable of identifying potential biomarkers for diagnosing and monitoring neurodegenerative conditions, such as Alzheimer's Disease, by analyzing retinal layer thickness. Addressing this, our study focuses initially on the complex challenges of retinal layer segmentation and super-resolution to achieve greater clarity and precision. We propose a GAN-based segmentation framework that integrates established architectures like U-Net and ResNet, augmented with transposed and sub-pixel convolution blocks to upscale OCT images by a factor of four. Furthermore, we utilize Dice loss as an auxiliary reconstruction term to optimize this joint task. Empirical results demonstrate that our top-performing configuration attained a Dice coefficient of 0.867 and an mIOU of 0.765.

This study addresses the output feedback exponential stabilization of a flexible beam equipped with a tip mass. In the absence of disturbances, it demonstrates that a single non-collocated measurement suffices to achieve exponential stabilization of the original system. This is accomplished by designing an infinite-dimensional Luenberger state observer to estimate the state and formulating an output feedback control law based on these estimates. This finding enhances previous existence results by F. Conrad and O. M\"{o}rg\"{u}l (SIAM J. Control Optim., 36 (1998), 1962-1986), which required two collocated measurements alongside high-order feedback. When accounting for boundary internal uncertainties and external disturbances, an infinite-dimensional disturbance estimator is developed to simultaneously estimate the state and total disturbance in real time. Utilizing these estimates, an output feedback control law is synthesized to ensure the exponential stabilization of the system while maintaining the boundedness of the closed-loop dynamics. Several illustrative simulations are provided to support these findings.

Recent experiments reveal that a soluble object immersed in a fluid spontaneously develops a dissolution pinnacle—a thin, upward-pointing form akin to the karst pinnacles seen in natural stone forests. This distinctive morphology arises from the interaction between interface movement and convective flows generated by the sinking of denser solute. While earlier studies linked these structures to shock formation in evolutionary equations, requiring the Gibbs-Thomson effect to ensure finite tip curvature, this research identifies a class of exact solutions that serve as attractors for shape dynamics in both two and three dimensions. Remarkably, these solutions display large yet finite tip curvature without any regularization and align closely with experimental data. Furthermore, the correlation between the initial dimensions of the shape and its final dissolved state could provide a principle for estimating the age and environmental conditions of geological formations.

Modulation recognition is a critical component of radio signal processing, yet existing research predominantly relies on supervised learning. This approach often proves impractical in real-world scenarios where acquiring signal labels is both difficult and expensive. This letter addresses the more challenging unsupervised challenge: can modulation types be clustered using a vast amount of unlabeled radio data? Solving this would enable modulation recognition through the manual labeling of only a minimal sample set. To tackle this, we introduce a Deep Transfer Clustering (DTC) model. DTC seamlessly combines feature learning with deep clustering and employs a transfer learning mechanism to enhance the feature extraction capabilities of an embedded Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). Experimental results demonstrate that our DTC model significantly surpasses various baselines, achieving state-of-the-art performance in clustering radio signals for modulation recognition.

We introduce DIY-IPS, a real-time, open-source mobile application for indoor positioning that utilizes dual-band RSSI fingerprinting of available WiFi access points to determine user locations without incurring additional infrastructure costs. By releasing the app as open source, we aim to save researchers the time required to recreate similar tools. DIY-IPS empowers researchers and users to (1) gather indoor positioning datasets with ground truth labels, (2) customize the application for enhanced accuracy or specific research needs, and (3) validate the performance of modified methods through live testing against ground truth data. Preliminary experiments have been conducted to demonstrate the app's effectiveness.

Deep Metric Learning algorithms strive to construct an efficient embedding space that maintains similarity relationships within input data. Although these methods have yielded substantial performance improvements across numerous tasks, they often overlook comprehensive similarity constraints, resulting in sub-optimal metrics within the embedding space. Furthermore, existing research has largely neglected their performance under noisy label conditions. To address the challenge of learning a discriminative deep embedding space, we propose a novel and effective Deep Class-wise Discrepancy Loss (DCDL) function. This approach segregates the underlying similarity distributions of embedding points across different classes by introducing class-wise discrepancies. Our empirical evaluations on three standard image classification datasets and two fine-grained image recognition datasets, conducted both with and without label noise, clearly demonstrate the necessity of integrating such class-wise similarity relationships alongside traditional algorithms when training discriminative embedding spaces.

Evaluating intervention impacts across multiple units and outcomes using time-series observational data is a common challenge in scientific research. This paper introduces a new method for estimating such effects by extending factor analysis-based approaches and implementing a Bayesian inference algorithm. Among the limited options available, our method uniquely handles mixed outcome types (continuous, binomial, and count), boosts the efficiency of causal effect estimates by jointly modeling multiple outcomes, and readily provides uncertainty quantification for all relevant causal parameters. We apply this approach to assess how Local Tracing Partnerships (LTP) influenced the efficacy of England's COVID-19 Test and Trace programme. Our findings indicate that, overall, LTPs exerted a modest positive effect on the programme, though there is significant heterogeneity in causal effect estimates across different units and time periods.

Thermal transport characteristics are critical for determining the performance of phase change memory (PCM) devices, which rely on rapid and reversible transitions between amorphous and crystalline states. This study presents a comprehensive experimental and theoretical investigation into the high-temperature thermal conductivity of GeTe, specifically during the fast amorphous-to-crystalline phase transition induced by heating. We utilized modulated photothermal radiometry (MPTR) to measure the thermal conductivity of GeTe in both phases at elevated temperatures, ensuring that thermal boundary resistances were accurately incorporated into the analysis. To elucidate the underlying physical mechanisms, we conducted rigorous theoretical calculations employing first-principles density functional theory and linearized Boltzmann transport equations (LBTE) via both direct and relaxation time approximation (RTA) methods, comparing results against the phenomenological Slack model. The experimental data for the amorphous phase were successfully described using the minimal thermal conductivity model with high precision. While theoretical estimates using direct solutions and the RTA method correctly captured the high-temperature trends of crystalline GeTe's thermal conductivity, they slightly overestimated and underestimated the experimental values, respectively. However, incorporating a rough estimate of vacancy contributions into the direct solution method yielded excellent agreement with experimental results. Furthermore, Umklapp scattering was identified as the dominant phonon-phonon scattering mechanism. We successfully determined the Umklapp scattering parameter for GeTe across the entire temperature range, providing a unique metric to compare and analyze Umklapp scattering processes in various materials.

Processing in memory (PiM) is an emerging computing paradigm with significant potential to boost performance and energy efficiency for data-heavy applications. While PiM architectures inherit the reliability risks of their underlying memory, relying on existing Error Correction Codes (ECC) is often insufficient because they fail to address errors generated during in-place computation. Although numerous established memory ECCs exist and are sometimes applied to PiM, they typically overlook computation-induced faults. This paper re-examines the ECC design landscape for PiM by accounting for both memory and computation errors. Based on these insights, we introduce an efficient error detection and correction pipeline and evaluate the trade-offs between performance, area, and coverage across three representative PiM technologies.
This paper categorizes finite-dimensional nilpotent Lie superalgebras with a superbreadth of no more than two.

We establish a complete Liouville-type theorem for the classical subcritical semilinear elliptic equation on the Heisenberg group, alongside a pointwise estimate near an isolated singularity. The core of our methodology relies on an a priori integral estimate derived from a generalized formula originally discovered by Jerison and Lee.

To explore how long-range van der Waals forces influence static friction, we develop an analytical formula for the static friction coefficient ($\mu_s$) between two thin layers of polarizable substances under zero load. We simplify the surface roughness by modeling it as sinusoidal corrugations and compute the interaction energy using perturbation theory up to the second order in the corrugation amplitude. The static friction coefficient is defined as the ratio of the maximum lateral Casimir force to the normal Casimir force; our findings indicate that this ratio does not depend on the materials' dielectric properties. Instead, it relies on geometric factors such as the interlayer distance, corrugation amplitude, and corrugation wavelength. As a proof of concept, our predicted $\mu_s$ values for graphene and hexagonal boron nitride align reasonably well with existing literature. This simplified framework can be extended to include other forces, including frequency-dependent van der Waals contributions and electrostatic interactions.

This study measures the transverse-momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) spectra and coalescence parameters ($B_2$) for (anti)deuterons in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV, distinguishing between events inside and outside jets. The jet axis is approximated by the direction of the leading particle with the highest $p_{\rm T}$ ($p_{\rm T}^{\rm{ lead}} > 5$ GeV/$c$). Events are then categorized into three azimuthal regions: the "Toward" region, which includes both jet fragmentation products and the underlying event (UE), and the "Transverse" region, which is primarily dominated by the UE. The jet signal is derived by subtracting the Transverse region from the Toward region. Results indicate that the coalescence parameter within the jet is roughly ten times larger than that of the underlying event. This finding aligns with the coalescence model, suggesting a smaller average phase-space distance between nucleons within the jet cone compared to the UE. These results are compared against predictions from a simple nucleon coalescence model (using PYTHIA 8 with the Monash 2013 tuning for nucleon phase space) and a deuteron production model based on ordinary nuclear reactions with energy-dependent cross sections tuned to data (implemented in PYTHIA 8.3). Both models successfully reproduce the significant disparity observed between in-jet and out-of-jet coalescence parameters.

In the context of multivariant Wright-Fisher models within population genetics, we propose defining equilibrium states through variations in the probability ratio, differing from the conventional approach that relies on deviations between the current process value and its equilibrium level. Consequently, the drift component of the gene frequency dynamics—originally formulated as a ratio of two quadratic forms—is converted into a cubic parabola adjusted by a specific normalization factor.

We contend that Wigner's friend thought experiment fails to justify the observer dependence of quantum states. Instead, an analysis using history vectors indicates that quantum collapse should be interpreted as a collapse of histories, not of states.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, agents typically gain advantages by training on related tasks, leveraging their shared characteristics to solve a broader spectrum of problems. Although this benefit is well-established for model-free approaches, we show that using a single learned dynamics model across multiple tasks can have a detrimental impact. This study investigates the core question of whether model-based multi-task RL yields similar gains from shared dynamics models as model-free methods do from shared policy networks. Our experiments reveal that a unified dynamics model leads to significant task confusion and degraded performance. To mitigate this, we propose imposing an internal structure on the model by training isolated sub-networks for each task, which substantially enhances performance without increasing the parameter count. We validate these findings through comparisons on both a basic gridworld and a more intricate VizDoom multi-task environment.

In 2020, the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST) concluded its commissioning and initiated the Commensal Radio Astronomy FasT Survey (CRAFTS), a multi-year project designed to map 60% of the sky. This study provides predictions regarding the detection of radio-flaring ultracool dwarfs (UCDs) via CRAFTS. Utilizing data on observed flaring UCDs from various unbiased, targeted radio surveys, we establish a detection rate of at least 3%. By assuming a flat radio spectrum for UCD flares ($

u}\propto 
u^{ eta+1}$ with $ eta$ = -1.0), we construct a flare luminosity function of $d N/d L \propto L^{-1.96 \pm 0.45}$, where $L=
u L_
u$. Our analysis indicates that CRAFTS is sufficiently sensitive to detect UCD flares out to approximately 180 pc. Through a 3D Monte Carlo simulation of the UCD population within the Galactic thin disk, which was processed through mock CRAFTS observations, we estimate that roughly 170 flaring UCDs could be identified via transient searches in circular polarization. While these results are only marginally dependent on the assumed scale height of UCDs, they are highly sensitive to the spectral index $ eta$; varying $ eta$ from 0 to -2.5 causes the expected number of detections to surge from about 20 to nearly 3,460. Furthermore, we explore follow-up strategies for flaring UCD candidates and discuss how these survey outcomes can enhance our understanding of UCD dynamics and behavior at $L$ band.

Pretraining is a widely adopted deep learning strategy designed to enhance performance and shorten training durations, showing significant promise in deep reinforcement learning (RL). However, its efficacy depends on the availability of a relevant dataset. This study assesses pretraining for RL tasks both with and without distracting backgrounds, utilizing large-scale public datasets with low relevance alongside custom-generated datasets labeled through self-supervision. Findings indicate that pretraining becomes ineffective when filters are learned from irrelevant datasets, whereas filters trained on in-distribution data consistently reduce RL training time and boost performance after 80,000 steps. Additionally, we explore how to optimally allocate a limited number of environment steps between pretraining and RL training to maximize outcomes. The project code is hosted on GitHub.

Video captioning represents a complex challenge at the nexus of vision and language, offering diverse real-world applications such as video retrieval, surveillance, aiding the visually impaired, and enhancing human-machine interfaces. Although recent deep learning approaches have yielded promising outcomes, they lag behind other vision tasks like image classification and object detection. A primary limitation of current methods is their reliance on cross-entropy loss, which lacks correlation with standard evaluation metrics like BLEU, METEOR, CIDER, and ROUGE; consequently, cross-entropy serves as an inadequate proxy for the true loss function in this domain. While techniques such as REINFORCE, Actor-Critic, and Minimum Risk Training (MRT) have been attempted to address this gap, they suffer from significant limitations and limited effectiveness. To overcome these issues, this paper introduces a Dynamic Loss Network (DLN), an alternative solution that generates feedback signals directly reflecting evaluation metrics. The proposed method demonstrates superior efficiency compared to existing solutions and is readily adaptable to similar tasks. Experimental results on the MSVD and MSRVTT datasets confirm that our approach outperforms previous methods.

This work investigates germs of holomorphic distributions characterized by "separated variables." A prominent instance of such a distribution in codimension one is the standard contact structure on $\mathbb{P}^{2m+1}$, alongside the Darboux distribution, which represents the local normal form for any contact structure. For a germ $D$ of a holomorphic distribution with separated variables at $(\mathbb{C}^n,0)$, we demonstrate the existence of a non-negative integer $\kappa$, determined by the Taylor coefficients of $D$, and a holomorphic submersion $H_{D}: (\mathbb{C}^n,0) \rightarrow (\mathbb{C}^{\kappa},0)$. On every level set of $H_{D}$, the distribution $D$ exhibits complete non-integrability. Additionally, we establish the existence of a holomorphic vector field $Z$ tangent to $D$, where each level set of $H_{D}$ contains a leaf of $Z$ that is somewhere dense within that level. Consequently, the field of meromorphic first integrals associated with $Z$ coincides with that of $D$.

Determining the primary parameters of star clusters is crucial for astrophysical research. The Gaia DR2 survey's greatest value stems from its provision of homogeneous photometry alongside precise positions, parallaxes, and proper motions for cluster stars, which enables highly accurate determination of membership probabilities. Leveraging the Gaia DR2 database, this study analyzes the open cluster Melotte 72, which is situated at a distance of 2345+/-108 pc and has an age of 1.0+/-0.5 Gyr. Analysis of the radial density profile yields a radius of 5.0+/-0.15 arcmin. Furthermore, the study estimates the cluster's reddening, luminosity and mass functions, total mass, galactic coordinates (X_Sun, Y_Sun, Z_Sun), and distance from the galactic center (R_g). Our findings indicate that Melotte 72 exhibits dynamical relaxation.

We report findings on the differential 2-jettiness distribution for boosted top quark pairs generated in $e^+e^-$ collisions within the peak region. These results incorporate QCD large-logarithm resummation at next-to-next-to-next-to-leading logarithmic (N$^3$LL) accuracy alongside next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) fixed-order corrections to matrix elements, computed using soft-collinear effective theory and boosted heavy quark effective theory. Leading-order electroweak and finite-width effects are also included. Our analysis examines the perturbative convergence of the cross section in both pole and MSR mass schemes, considering scenarios with and without soft gap subtractions. We observe a partial cancellation between renormalons associated with the pole mass and the soft function. However, when renormalon subtractions for both the top mass and the soft function are applied, perturbative uncertainties decrease systematically, and the stability of the peak position improves. Furthermore, we determine that the top MSR mass can be extracted from the 2-jettiness distribution peak with perturbative uncertainties significantly below 100 MeV, a finding with significant implications for Monte Carlo top quark mass calibrations.

Excitons play a central role in the optical properties of atomically thin transition metal dichalcogenides and 2D van der Waals heterostructures. In these systems, interlayer excitons—where an electron and a hole occupy separate layers—form quickly through direct charge transfer or Coulomb-mediated energy exchange. This study highlights significant intertube excitonic phenomena in quasi-1D van der Waals heterostructures composed of C/BN/MoS$_2$ core/shell/skin nanotubes. Notably, pulsed infrared excitation of excitons within the semiconducting carbon nanotubes (CNTs) triggered a rapid (sub-picosecond) response in the visible spectrum from the MoS$_2$ skin, which we ascribe to intertube biexcitons facilitated by dipole-dipole Coulomb interactions under coherent conditions. At longer timescales (>100 ps), hole migration from the CNT core to the MoS$_2$ skin further altered the MoS$_2$ absorption characteristics. This direct evidence of intertube excitonic coupling and charge transfer in 1D van der Waals heterostructures points toward potential applications in infrared and visible optoelectronics utilizing these radial heterojunctions.

The surge in informatics and technology has generated vast datasets with complex management and analytical challenges. Big Data analytics aims to uncover hidden insights and draw inferences from these volumes. While efficient algorithms and systems can handle storage and retrieval, the specific nature of Big Data raises concerns regarding statistical consistency that must be resolved. Because Big Data defies standard analytics, existing statistical theories and tools require significant adaptation. This paper proposes a general statistical framework and an algorithmic principle, illustrated with examples, designed to ensure the statistical accuracy of conclusions drawn from Big Data. This proposed approach has the potential to guide the advancement of Big Data analytics effectively. Furthermore, the suggested partition-repetition method is sufficiently broad to address all practical data analytic issues.

This paper establishes Li-Yau gradient estimates and Souplet-Zhang type estimates for the equation $ u_t = \Delta_\xi p + \lambda u + A(u) $ defined on a complete, noncompact metric measure space $ (M, g, e^{-\xi}dv_g) $ featuring a compact boundary. Additionally, we provide local gradient estimates for the equation $ \Delta_\xi(u^p) + \lambda u + A(u) = 0 $ on a complete, noncompact manifold with a compact boundary.

In grammar-based Genetic Programming (GP), the choice of grammar significantly influences solution quality by constraining the search space to valid syntax. This study introduces Probabilistic Structured Grammatical Evolution (PSGE), a novel method that integrates the representation and mapping strategies of both Structured Grammatical Evolution (SGE) and Probabilistic Grammatical Evolution (PGE). In PSGE, the genotype consists of dynamic lists—one for each grammar non-terminal—where each item represents a probability for selecting the next Probabilistic Context-Free Grammar (PCFG) derivation rule. Experimental results demonstrate that PSGE statistically surpassed Grammatical Evolution (GE) across all six benchmark problems evaluated. Furthermore, when compared to PGE, PSGE achieved superior performance on four out of the six analyzed problems.

This study examines the large-time asymptotic behavior of solutions to the Cauchy problem for the nonlocal focusing modified Korteweg-de Vries (MKdV) equation, utilizing step-like initial data where $u_0(x)$ approaches 0 as $x\rightarrow-\infty$ and a positive constant $A$ as $x\rightarrow+\infty$. Initially, we construct the fundamental Riemann-Hilbert (RH) problem linked to this step-like data by developing direct scattering theory. Leveraging the symmetries of the nonlocal MKdV equation under $x\rightarrow-x$ and $t\rightarrow-t$, we analyze the asymptotics for both $t\rightarrow-\infty$ and $t\rightarrow+\infty$. Our primary method involves applying steepest descent analysis to deform the original matrix-valued RH problem into a regular RH problem that admits an explicit solution. Ultimately, we derive the distinct large-time asymptotic behaviors of the Cauchy problem's solution across the four space-time sectors ($\mathcal{R}_{I}$, $\mathcal{R}_{II}$, $\mathcal{R}_{III}$, and $\mathcal{R}_{IV}$) covering the entire $(x,t)$-plane.

Private Information Retrieval (PIR) ensures user privacy when interacting with databases by allowing the download of a specific message without revealing its identity. Although recent studies have explored the advantages of relaxing privacy requirements, the precise definition of weak privacy remains underdeveloped. This paper quantifies information leakage in weak privacy scenarios using Rényi divergence, which extends the Kullback-Leibler divergence. By applying Rényi divergence to standard PIR problems, we characterize the trade-off between privacy leakage and download cost through convex optimization. Additionally, we introduce a novel PIR scheme that utilizes smaller message sizes than the Tian-Sun-Chen (TSC) approach. While this new scheme cannot match the PIR capacity of perfect privacy—since the TSC scheme already achieves minimum message size for that capacity—we demonstrate that it outperforms the TSC scheme in weak privacy settings, particularly when download costs are low.

This study introduces a novel dark energy framework derived from the holographic principle combined with Barrow entropy, utilizing a time scale as the infrared cutoff. By investigating both conformal time and cosmic age as infrared cut-offs, we assess the cosmological implications of this proposed dark energy model within a universe containing pressure-less matter. Our analysis reveals that the equation of state, deceleration parameter, and density parameters exhibit adequate behavior, suggesting these models can account for late-time acceleration, although stability is only achieved for specific values of the Barrow exponent $\Delta$. Additionally, we discuss the effects arising from interactions between different sectors of the universe.

Although multi-modal pre-training holds significant promise for extracting highly discriminative features from diverse data sources, its advancement is currently hindered by a scarcity of large-scale, modality-rich datasets. Capitalizing on the inherent advantages of e-commerce, where various modalities convey complementary semantic details, we introduce M5Product, a substantial multi-modal pre-training dataset. This resource encompasses five modalities—image, text, table, video, and audio—spanning more than 6,000 categories and 5,000 attributes. It is notably 500% larger than the biggest existing public dataset with a comparable modal count. Moreover, M5Product realistically mirrors real-world challenges by including incomplete modality pairs, noisy data, and a long-tailed distribution. To address these complexities, we propose SCALE (Self-harmonized ContrAstive LEarning), an innovative pre-training framework that unifies diverse modalities within a single model. SCALE employs an adaptive feature fusion mechanism where modality importance is dynamically learned from embeddings, influencing both inter-modality contrastive learning and masked tasks within a multi-modal transformer. We assess current state-of-the-art approaches on unlabeled data using the extensive modality count of M5Product and perform comprehensive experiments across four downstream tasks. These results demonstrate the superior performance of our SCALE model and highlight the critical roles of dataset scale and diversity.

Under the weakly guiding approximation, this study investigates orbital angular momentum (OAM) mode mixing caused by fiber ellipticity, deriving a comprehensive set of analytic formulas for spatial crosstalk via scalar perturbation theory. This approach fully accounts for the existing degeneracy between an OAM mode and its counterpart with an opposite topological charge. Consequently, the derived expressions provide an explicit equation for the $2\pi$ walk-off length, which defines the distance required for an input OAM mode to transform into its degenerate partner and revert to its original state. We also examine the validity of these expressions in scenarios involving spin-orbit interaction. Serving as a valuable mathematical resource for the analysis and design of fibers for spatially multiplexed transmission, the utility of these formulas is illustrated through applications to both few-mode and multimode step-index fibers.

In a graph $G$, a dominating set $S$ consists of vertices where each vertex outside $S$ is adjacent to at least one vertex in $S$. The domination number, denoted $\gamma(G)$, represents the smallest size of such a set. The common independence number, $\alpha_c(G)$, is defined as the largest integer $r$ ensuring that every vertex in $G$ is part of an independent set with cardinality at least $r$. This value lies between the independent domination number $i(G)$ and the standard independence number $\alpha(G)$, satisfying the inequality $\gamma(G) \le i(G) \le \alpha_c(G) \le \alpha(G)$. A graph $G$ is termed domination perfect if $\gamma(H) = i(H)$ holds for all induced subgraphs $H$ of $G$. Conversely, $G$ is called common domination perfect if $\gamma(H) = \alpha_c(H)$ for every induced subgraph $H$. We present a characterization of common domination perfect graphs based on ten specific forbidden induced subgraphs.

Optical cat states are fundamental to quantum computing and metrology. In this study, we experimentally measure the quantum coherence of these states using the relative entropy and l₁-norm of coherence within the Fock basis, based on cat states prepared at the rubidium D1 line. By passing the optical cat state through a lossy channel, we demonstrate that its quantum coherence remains robust despite losses, a property that distinguishes it from the decoherence behaviors observed in fidelity and Wigner function negativity. These findings confirm the resilience of optical cat state coherence against loss and facilitate their practical applications.

We introduce a technique for estimating the depth of dynamic scenes with arbitrary moving objects using ordinary video recorded by a moving camera. Our goal is to achieve a solution that is both geometrically and temporally consistent, ensuring that depth estimates for corresponding points across frames generate plausible, smooth 3D motion. We address this underconstrained problem using a novel test-time training framework where a depth-prediction CNN is trained simultaneously with an auxiliary scene-flow prediction MLP across the entire input video. By recursively unrolling the scene-flow MLP over varying time steps, we calculate short-range scene flow to enforce local smooth motion priors directly in 3D, and long-range scene flow to apply multi-view consistency constraints over wide baselines. We demonstrate accurate and temporally coherent results on diverse, challenging videos featuring various moving objects (pets, people, cars) and camera motion. The resulting depth maps enable several depth-and-motion-aware video editing effects, including object and lighting insertion.

This paper introduces a novel statistical approach to evaluate the dissimilarity between two random sets using a single realization for each. The methodology emphasizes the geometric characteristics of the set components, specifically analyzing the curvature of their boundaries alongside the ratios of their perimeters and areas. The study provides a theoretical foundation, outlines the method, validates it through a simulation study, and applies it to real-world data comparing two tissue types: mammary cancer and mastopathy.

We optimize finite-time stochastic heat engines featuring a periodically scaled Hamiltonian, subject to experimental constraints on bath temperature $T$ and the scaling parameter $\lambda$. A general geometric proof demonstrates that protocols maximizing efficiency for $T$ and $\lambda$ are piecewise constant, switching alternately between their permitted maximum and minimum values. Furthermore, when $\lambda$ is confined to a narrow range and the system remains near equilibrium at the isotherm endpoints, a comparable argument indicates this protocol also maximizes output power. These findings apply to arbitrary dynamics and are illustrated using an overdamped Brownian heat engine, which can be experimentally implemented via optical tweezers with stiffness $\lambda$.

We bring together Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem (1931), Tarski's Undefinability Theorem (1933), Godel-Carnap's Diagonal Lemma (1934), and Rosser's Incompleteness Theorem (1936), which strengthens Godel's first result. These proofs share significant similarities and employ nearly identical techniques.

Using Density Functional Theory, we examined the merging dynamics of two superfluid helium nanodroplets containing vortex lines with varying relative orientations, driven together by Van der Waals attraction. Our findings reveal a complex phenomenology heavily dependent on the initial vortex alignment. Specifically, when merging droplets contain a vortex and an anti-vortex, a dark soliton forms at the contact zone, eventually breaking down into vortex rings. We observed reconnection events between these vortices or rings, resulting in the generation of additional vortices. Simulations highlight the interplay between vortex creation and reconnection, alongside the critical role of the droplet surface, which pins vortex endpoints and reflects short-wavelength excitations from vortex interactions, thereby significantly influencing the final state. Furthermore, extra vorticity is nucleated near surface indentations formed during the dynamics, interacting with existing vortices. These surface-specific effects, absent in bulk liquid helium, demonstrate that the droplet surface can amplify vortex reconnections. Finally, energy spectrum analysis indicates that both vortex-antivortex ring annihilation and reconnections produce roton bursts of varying intensities.

Mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) are linked to both serious congenital disorders and the process of healthy aging. Because mtDNA is replicated and degraded randomly within organelles that constantly fuse and divide, the impact of these resulting mitochondrial networks on the temporal evolution of mutated mtDNA proportions (heteroplasmy) and cell-to-cell variability in these proportions remains poorly understood. This variability is crucial as it influences the count of diseased cells within a tissue. In this study, we present the first comprehensive theoretical framework connecting mitochondrial network dynamics with genetic states. Our results demonstrate that, across various conditions, the physical fraction of unfused mitochondria proportionally regulates both the rate of heteroplasmy variance increase and new mutations, regardless of the absolute fission-fusion frequency. Furthermore, under selective fusion scenarios, intermediate fusion-to-fission ratios prove optimal for eliminating mutant mtDNA. These findings suggest that therapeutically adjusting the network state, mitophagy rates, and copy numbers to decelerate heteroplasmy dynamics when mean heteroplasmy is low could offer benefits for treating mitochondrial diseases and promoting healthy aging.

The Minimal Geometric Deformation (MGD) method, a recent theoretical development, has sparked renewed interest in exploring higher-order curvature effects within relativistic astrophysics. This study employs the MGD technique to model strange stars under the framework of Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity. By combining the Tolman metric ansatz with the MIT Bag model equation of state for hadronic matter, anisotropy is incorporated through the superposition of a seed source and a decoupled energy-momentum tensor. The resulting system of equations yields two distinct solutions: one where the $\theta$ sector mimics the seed's radial pressure and energy density, and another representing a regular fluid model. Both solutions describe self-gravitating, static, compact objects exteriorized by the vacuum Boulware-Deser metric. Using observational data for three stellar candidates—PSR J1614-2230, PSR J1903+317, and LMC X-4—the solutions undergo rigorous viability testing regarding regularity and stability. Our findings indicate that the Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet parameter and the decoupling constant interact competitively to ensure physically viable stellar structures. A key novelty of this work is the demonstration of stable compact objects with masses exceeding $2 M_{\odot}$ without invoking exotic matter, thereby offering new insights into the physical implications and evolution of ultra-compact astrophysical entities.

As speech synthesis tools gain traction, the industry demands more personalized capabilities, specifically: (1) cloning a voice using low-resource, accessible data, and (2) cloning a voice while independently controlling style and prosody. To address these challenges, we introduce the Hieratron framework, which separates prosody and timbre into two distinct modules. This architecture enables the generation of speech with independent control over timbre and other audio characteristics. Experimental results demonstrate that Hieratron outperforms traditional methods even with very limited wild target speaker data. Furthermore, while offering control over speech style and language, the model improves the mean opinion score for speech quality by over 0.2 points.

The pursuit of batteries that charge quickly, remain safe, last longer, and perform well drives both the search for novel energy storage materials and the re-examination of those already in common use. Currently, there is renewed focus on anode materials, specifically graphite electrodes in lithium-ion batteries. This study examines the maximum limit of lithium intercalation in highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG), which features a quasi-ideal morphology and a LiC$_6$ stoichiometry representing a 100% state of charge (SOC). By immersing a sample in liquid lithium at ambient pressure and analyzing it via static $^7$Li nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), we identified unexpected indicators of superdense intercalation compounds, LiC$_{6-x}$. These compounds have been dismissed for decades, as the highest geometrically feasible composition, LiC$_2$, was thought to require high pressure. Consequently, we question the prevailing belief that further intercalation beyond LiC$_6$ is impossible under ambient conditions. Through monitoring the sample's aging over time and utilizing *ab initio* calculations to interpret the NMR data, we found that computed relative stabilities of various superdense configurations indicate that significant overintercalation occurs spontaneously, surpassing the currently accepted capacity limit.

Since the inception of artificial intelligence, researchers have long envisioned creating dialogue agents capable of engaging with humans in a natural manner. The Turing Test, a renowned benchmark, was designed to evaluate the ultimate validity of AI by determining if its conversations are indistinguishable from those of humans. It is unsurprising that constructing human-level dialogue systems remains a formidable challenge. While early rule-based approaches achieved only limited success, the advent of deep learning has driven significant progress in this field. This thesis concentrates on strategies designed to bridge the gap between current conversational agents and human-level interlocutors. These methods were developed and tested using inspiration from general state-of-the-art AI methodologies, while simultaneously addressing the unique characteristics inherent to dialogue systems.

Numerous dynamical systems feature hidden states possessing inherent orderings, exemplified by hierarchical relationships like "ally," "neutral," and "enemy" in international relations. These latent states are reflected in the ordered nature of entities' interactions, ranging from cooperation to conflict. Standard models for such systems typically utilize state-to-action emission and state-to-state transition matrices, often assuming that the rows of these stochastic matrices are independently drawn from a Dirichlet distribution. This conventional approach, however, ignores ordinal data by incorrectly treating states and actions as order-invariant categories, thereby impeding both interpretation and evaluation. To resolve this, we introduce the Ordered Matrix Dirichlet (OMD), a method where rows are sampled with conditional dependence, shifting probability mass toward the right as one moves down the rows. This mechanism establishes a well-ordered correspondence between latent states and observed action types. We assess the OMD across two contexts: a Hidden Markov Model and a newly developed Bayesian Dynamic Poisson Tucker Model designed for political event data. Models incorporating the OMD successfully recover interpretable latent states and demonstrate enhanced forecasting capabilities in few-shot scenarios. Furthermore, we outline the broad utility of the OMD in other fields where Dirichlet-sampled matrices are prevalent, such as topic modeling, and provide accessible code for implementation.

We examine both classical and quantum algorithms possessing a duality property: essentially, either the algorithm yields a meaningful improvement over random performance, or a vast number of solutions exist that are significantly inferior to random ones. This duality allows for guarantees that a nontrivial improvement will be found; specifically, if solutions much worse than random are scarce, such an improvement is assured. The quantum approach relies on a sudden change in a Hamiltonian. Although the method is general, we evaluate it within the specific framework of MAX-$K$-LIN$2$, covering both even and odd values of $K$. The classical algorithm represents a "dequantization" of this quantum method, achieving identical guarantees (and even proving results that remain conjectures in the quantum realm). Nevertheless, the quantum perspective aids in analyzing the classical algorithm's performance and may offer superior results in certain scenarios.

This work examines the quantum vacuum zero-point energy within Schwarzschild black holes and the Nariai limit of dS-Schwarzschild backgrounds. We demonstrate that the regularized vacuum energy density near the black hole and in the Nariai configuration matches the flat background value precisely, scaling with the fourth power of the quantum field's mass. A new length scale emerges from the de Sitter horizon radius generated by this vacuum zero-point energy, which must be compared against the black hole's horizon radius. Furthermore, we identify an upper mass limit for a black hole immersed in this energy, defined by the mass of the Nariai metric linked to the de Sitter background constructed from zero-point energy. Finally, we compute the variance in the vacuum zero-point energy distribution and the density contrast, revealing the development of significant inhomogeneities at sub-horizon scales.

This work introduces a probabilistic framework for modeling brittle and ductile fracture in phase-field theory, incorporating random variations in both material and geometric properties. While macroscopic failure mechanics traditionally assume homogeneous and deterministic material properties and precise spatial distributions, this approach acknowledges the strong fluctuations found at lower scales by introducing uncertainty into the model. The study establishes a mathematical basis for analyzing uncertainty through stochastic methods applied to microstructures experiencing brittle or ductile failure. The proposed model utilizes representative volume elements featuring randomly distributed stiff inclusions and voids within composite structures. An allocation strategy is developed to assign these heterogeneities and generate corresponding meshes in both two and three dimensions. The stochastic partial differential equation-based model is then solved using the Monte Carlo finite element technique, which approximates the expectation and variance of the failure solution field by evaluating numerous samples. For predicting failure mechanisms, the phase-field approach is employed, a widely accepted method for simulating fracture in solids. Furthermore, incremental perturbed minimization principles for gradient-type dissipative materials are utilized to derive perturbed governing equations, enabling the analysis of highly heterogeneous microstructures and the monitoring of uncertainty in failure mechanics. Finally, several numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed methodology.

This correspondence presents a new speech enhancement technique operating within the Hilbert-Huang Transform domain to counteract acoustic impulsive noise. Noise component estimation and selection rely on the impulsiveness index of decomposition modes. Experimental evaluations were performed across five types of acoustic noise, varying in impulsiveness index and non-stationarity, under different signal-to-noise ratios. Three existing algorithms served as baselines for the comparative analysis, assessing performance in both spectral and temporal domains. The proposed method yielded superior results according to objective quality metrics and demonstrated speech intelligibility rates comparable to those of competitive approaches.

Open dynamical systems serve as mathematical frameworks for machines that accept inputs, update their internal states, and generate outputs, applicable to entities ranging from neurons to robots. These systems can be interconnected through series, parallel, or feedback configurations to create new dynamical systems—a principle known as compositionality—which can be iterated in a fractal pattern to construct increasingly complex systems of systems. However, expanding system size leads to an exponential expansion of the state space. This paper introduces a method for determining the steady states of interconnected system-of-systems based on the steady states of their individual components. These states are structured into "steady state matrices" that extend the concept of bifurcation diagrams. The study demonstrates that the compositionality of dynamical systems aligns with the standard monoidal structure of these matrices, where serial, parallel, and feedback compositions of matrices map to multiplication, Kronecker products, and partial trace operations, respectively. Consequently, steady state matrices adhere to this compositional framework, exponentially lowering the complexity associated with analyzing the steady states of composite dynamical systems.

Random field excursions have become a crucial subject in data analysis across fields such as medicine, cosmology, and materials science. This research presents the first comprehensive investigation of their Betti numbers within the "sparse" regime. We examine a piecewise constant Gaussian field characterized by a positive covariance function that adheres to specific conditions regarding locality, boundedness, and decay rates. The excursion set of this field is modeled using a Čech complex. We establish several limit theorems for the complex's Betti numbers as both the window size and excursion level increase toward infinity. These findings encompass asymptotic estimates for the mean and variance, a phase transition from vanishing to non-vanishing values with a precise threshold calculation, and a weak law applicable in the non-vanishing regime. Additionally, we derive a Poisson approximation and a central limit theorem near the transition threshold. The proofs integrate techniques from extreme value theory with tools from combinatorial topology.

This paper utilizes the human perception process, specifically the interaction between vision and language, to create coherent paragraph descriptions for untrimmed videos. We introduce vision-language (VL) features comprising two modalities: a vision modality designed to capture global visual content of the entire scene, and a language modality intended to extract descriptions of scene elements involving both human and non-human objects (such as animals and vehicles) as well as visual and non-visual components (such as relations and activities). Additionally, we train our proposed VLCap model using a contrastive learning vision-language loss function. Experimental and ablation studies conducted on the ActivityNet Captions and YouCookII datasets demonstrate that our VLCap surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and diversity metrics.

Understanding spin-isospin transitions in nuclei located away from the valley of stability is crucial for modeling weak interaction processes relevant to astrophysics. Since these phenomena largely remain inaccessible to experimental observation, theoretical frameworks are essential for elucidating their characteristics. To capture the spin-isospin response, the proton-neutron relativistic quasiparticle random phase approximation (PN-RQRPA) has been developed, incorporating the relativistic density-dependent point coupling interaction alongside separable pairing forces within both $T=1$ and $T=0$ channels. By utilizing the recently refined DD-PCX interaction, which offers superior isovector properties for handling neutron-proton asymmetry, researchers have examined isobaric analog resonances (IAR) and Gamow-Teller resonances (GTR). Unlike other models that typically predict IAR excitation energies too low for the tin isotope chain, this approach successfully matches experimental data, whereas GTR characteristics are sensitive to the strength of the isoscalar pairing interaction. Consequently, this framework enhances the description of spin-isospin responses and facilitates future extensive calculations of charge-exchange excitations and weak interaction mechanisms within stellar environments.

Anomalies serve as a highly effective instrument for restricting theories that extend beyond the standard model. This work provides an instructional survey of key topics highlighting the critical function of spacetime anomalies within string theory. Following a general examination of anomaly cancellation in quantum field theory, the discussion centers on how type-I string theory achieves anomaly cancellation via the Green-Schwarz mechanism. The review also covers the concept of anomaly inflow and its utility in assessing anomalous couplings on D-branes. Finally, we offer a brief overview of recent advancements regarding the recasting of anomalies using category theory.

Activation functions are critical in shaping training dynamics and the overall performance of neural networks. While the widely used ReLU function is simple and effective, it suffers from drawbacks such as the "Dying ReLU" issue. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel activation function named Serf, which is characterized by being nonmonotonic and self-regularized. Similar to Mish, Serf is part of the Swish family of functions. Extensive experiments across computer vision tasks (image classification and object detection) and natural language processing tasks (machine translation, sentiment classification, and multimodal entailment), utilizing various state-of-the-art architectures, demonstrate that Serf significantly outperforms ReLU (the baseline) and other functions like Swish and Mish, particularly in deeper networks. Ablation studies confirm that Serf-based architectures excel over Swish and Mish across diverse scenarios, validating Serf's effectiveness and compatibility with different depths, complexities, optimizers, learning rates, batch sizes, initializers, and dropout rates. Furthermore, we analyze the mathematical relationship between Swish and Serf, revealing that a preconditioner function embedded in Serf's first derivative provides a regularization effect that smooths gradients and accelerates optimization.

Machine learning models often exhibit biases that lead to unfair treatment across various populations. Existing methods for assessing individual-level fairness typically depend on domain expertise to select metrics or rely on input transformations that may produce out-of-domain samples. We introduce a novel approach that eliminates both of these constraints. This method proposes a new criterion for evaluating individual fairness and utilizes a practical testing framework called fAux (pronounced fox). fAux operates by comparing the derivatives of the target model's predictions against those of an auxiliary model, which predicts the protected variable from the observed data. Our results demonstrate that this approach effectively detects discrimination on both synthetic and real-world datasets, offering both quantitative and qualitative improvements over current methods.

Next-generation techniques for tracking planets, including interplanetary laser ranging (ILR) and same-beam interferometry (SBI), are expected to boost the precision of solar system dynamics measurements by orders of magnitude. Achieving this demands a reevaluation of modeling approaches for the translational and rotational dynamics of natural celestial bodies, ensuring that model errors remain significantly smaller than measurement uncertainties. For specific future missions, it will be necessary to incorporate "figure-figure effects," which arise from the gravitational interactions between the complete mass distributions of celestial bodies. While the mathematical description of these effects to arbitrary degrees is often presented elegantly and compactly, it is not easily aligned with the formulations standard in space geodesy and ephemeris generation, thereby hindering robust implementation in operational software. We address this by formulating the problem in a way that aligns directly with typical dynamical modeling codes, utilizing spherical harmonic coefficients and Legendre polynomials. Furthermore, we derive an analytical formulation for the variational equations associated with both translational and rotational motion. We apply this methodology to Phobos and the KW4 binary asteroid system to evaluate the impact of figure-figure effects on estimations derived from next-generation tracking data. In the case of Phobos, neglecting these effects during estimation yields relative errors of $0.42\%$ and $0.065\%$ for the $\bar{C}_{20}$ and $\bar{C}_{22}$ spherical harmonic gravity field coefficients, respectively. Although these figures fall within current uncertainty margins, they are orders of magnitude larger than the errors achieved in previous simulations designed for accurately tracking a future Phobos lander.

This study investigates the structural, electronic, and vibrational characteristics of amorphous graphite [R. Thapa $\textit{et. al.}$, Phys. Rev. Lett. 128, 236402 (2022)]. The degree of structural ordering in amorphous graphite is examined and contrasted with that of crystalline graphite and amorphous carbon. Furthermore, the electronic density of states and localization across these phases were evaluated. Spatial projections of charge densities within the $\pi$ bands reveal significant charge accumulation on atoms involved in connecting hexagons. A vibrational density of states was calculated, offering a potential experimental signature for the material. Additionally, vibrational modes were analyzed using the phase quotient and mode stretching characteristics. The computed average thermal conductivity for aG was found to be 0.85 Wcm$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$ at room temperature and 0.96 Wcm$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$ at 1000 K.

This study investigates the optimal method for transmitting information over time to shape an agent's beliefs and subsequent actions within a framework featuring a binary state evolving via a Markov process and a finite set of actions. We define the sender's ideal messaging strategy in the limit as the time interval approaches zero. This optimal approach is non-myopic; based on the agent's current beliefs, it may involve revealing no information or dividing the agent's belief into two strategically selected posterior states.

This study investigates the out-of-time-order correlation (OTOC) within the Floquet transverse Ising model to validate its phase diagram. Initially, we derive an exact analytical solution for the transverse magnetization OTOC via the Jordan-Wigner transformation, computing the correlation propagation speed and examining how revival time varies with observable separation. To determine the system's phase structure, we utilize the longitudinal magnetization OTOC, which acts as an order parameter. By calculating the long-time average of this longitudinal OTOC, we numerically map the phase diagram of the Floquet transverse Ising system. Our analysis of both open and closed chains reveals distinct phases, identifying two paramagnetic states (0-paramagnetic and $\pi$-paramagnetic) and two ferromagnetic states (0-ferromagnetic and $\pi$-ferromagnetic), consistent with existing literature.

We demonstrate that, in certain cases, quantum state tomography relying on perfect knowledge of the measurement device performs worse than approaches that disregard such details, such as data pattern tomography. In these situations, the increased uncertainty regarding the measurement is exchanged for reduced uncertainty in the reconstructed signal. This phenomenon is particularly significant for minimal or nearly minimal informationally complete measurement configurations, which are of critical practical value.

The performance of suction cups in grasping and manipulation is enhanced by their capacity to conform to uneven and angular surfaces. However, this adaptation often compromises the necessary stiffness for subsequent manipulation, creating an ideal scenario where the device remains compliant during surface approach but becomes stiff upon attachment. While existing stiffness modulation methods typically demand extra actuation, this article introduces a novel stiffness-tunable suction cup designed for steep angular surfaces. By utilizing vacuum-driven granular jamming for sensorless stiffness modulation, the design integrates a conventional active suction pad with a granular stalk that mimics a hinge, ensuring compliance during adaptation and high stiffness after attachment. Experimental results demonstrate that the suction cup can accommodate angles up to 85 degrees with an actuation force under 0.5 N. Furthermore, the study examines how the length of the granular stalk influences adaptation and compares the performance of this active design against passive adaptation methods lacking stiffness modulation.

This study reports a search for a new heavy $W^{\prime}$ boson in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV, utilizing the complete Run 2 dataset from the ATLAS detector. The analysis targets the $W^{\prime}$ decay into a hadronic top quark and a bottom quark, employing DNN-based boosted-object techniques to identify the hadronic top. Background estimation relies on a data-driven approach with minimal systematic uncertainties. Upper limits on the product of the production cross-section and decay branching ratio are established for right-handed $W^{\prime}$ couplings decaying to top-bottom pairs, covering mass ranges from 1.5 to 5 TeV.

Many quantitative attack tree analysis techniques have been developed to calculate security metrics, such as the most probable, least expensive, or most harmful attacks. However, current approaches are often limited to specific metrics or cannot handle general attack trees. This paper categorizes attack trees based on two dimensions: proper trees versus directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) with shared subtrees, and static versus dynamic gates. We introduce novel algorithms for three of these four categories that operate within a generic attribute domain, accommodating a wide range of security metrics defined by attack tree semantics. Dynamic attack trees structured as DAGs remain an open challenge. Additionally, we evaluate the computational complexity of our proposed methods.

This study presents the first systematic application of covariant density functional theory (CDFT) to examine the ground states and fission characteristics of even-even actinides and superheavy nuclei ($Z=90-120$) spanning from the two-proton to the two-neutron drip lines, with a rigorous evaluation of theoretical systematic uncertainties. These findings offer essential theoretical data for modeling the r-process in heavy nuclei, specifically regarding fission recycling. The research utilizes four advanced, globally validated covariant energy density functionals (CEDFs)—DD-PC1, DD-ME2, NL3*, and PC-PK1—which represent the primary categories of CDFT models. Calculations were conducted for all these nuclei to determine ground state deformations, binding energies, two-neutron separation energies, $\alpha$-decay $Q_{\alpha}$ values and half-lives, and fission barrier heights. Furthermore, the study quantifies theoretical uncertainties in these observables and tracks their variation across proton and neutron numbers, identifying their primary origins. Two key contributors to these uncertainties are the spherical shell closures at $Z=120$, $N=184$, and $N=258$ (along with the structure of single-particle, particularly high-$j$, states near them) and the nuclear matter properties inherent to the employed CEDFs. Notably, these two factors influence different physical observables in distinct ways; for instance, uncertainties in ground state deformations are predominantly driven by shell structure, whereas uncertainties in fission barriers rely on both factors.

Animals can quickly deduce from minimal experience when different sets of state-action pairs share identical reward and transition dynamics. In contrast, modern reinforcement learning systems must laboriously learn through trial and error that these pairs are value-equivalent, often necessitating a prohibitively large number of environmental samples. MDP homomorphisms have been introduced to compress an observed MDP into an abstract representation, potentially enabling more sample-efficient policy learning. Consequently, significant gains in sample efficiency have been realized when a suitable homomorphism is constructed beforehand, typically by leveraging practitioner knowledge of environmental symmetries. We introduce a novel approach for constructing homomorphisms in discrete action spaces that utilizes a partial model of environment dynamics to identify state-action pairs resulting in the same state, thereby reducing the state-action space size by a factor equal to the action space cardinality. We term this method equivalent effect abstraction. In a gridworld environment, we empirically demonstrate that equivalent effect abstraction enhances sample efficiency in model-free settings and improves planning efficiency for model-based approaches. Additionally, on the cartpole task, we show that our method outperforms existing homomorphism learning techniques while requiring 33 times less training data.

In their seminal 2008 work, Green and Tao demonstrated the existence of arithmetic progressions of primes with any desired length. Shortly thereafter, Tao extended this result to the ring of Gaussian integers, while L\^e achieved a similar outcome for polynomial rings over finite fields. By 2020, Kai-Mimura, Munemasa, Seki, and Yoshino had generalized the theorem to orders within arbitrary number fields. This paper addresses the case of coordinate rings for affine curves defined over finite fields. The primary contribution lies in the careful selection of a polynomial subring within the target ring, which serves an analogous function to $\mathbb Z$ in the context of number fields. The validity of this selection and the demonstration of its favorable properties ultimately rely on the Riemann-Roch formula.

This study examines an adaptive network where connection weights evolve alongside the dynamical states of local nodes under external influence, mimicking the adaptive synaptic plasticity found in neuronal systems. When subjected to external forcing, this adaptive network exhibits exotic dynamical regimes absent in unforced counterparts, such as itinerant chimeras—where coherent and incoherent domains co-evolve with synaptic connections—as well as bump states and bump frequency cluster states. Furthermore, the system displays partial synchronization patterns, including phase and frequency clusters, forced entrainment, and incoherent states. To classify these emergent states and their transitions, we introduce two metrics for incoherence strength based on the standard deviation of temporally averaged frequency and the mean frequency itself. We present a two-parameter phase diagram illustrating the diversity of these dynamical states and derive the stability conditions for frequency-entrained states. The analysis utilizes the paradigmatic Kuramoto model of phase oscillators, a widely used generic framework for uncovering cooperative phenomena in both natural and engineered systems.

This study addresses the maximum weight $b$-matching problem within the random-order semi-streaming framework. Under the assumption that weights are small integers in the range $[1,W]$, we introduce an approximation algorithm achieving a ratio of $2 - \frac{1}{2W} + \varepsilon$. This algorithm operates with $O(\max(|M_G|, n) \cdot poly(\log(m),W,1/\varepsilon))$ memory, where $|M_G|$ represents the size of the optimal matching. Our approach extends Bernstein's 2015 work, which provided a $3/2 + \varepsilon$ approximation for maximum cardinality simple matchings. Furthermore, when $W$ is small, our method surpasses the $2 - \delta$ approximation achieved by Gamlath et al. in 2019 for maximum weight simple matching. Specifically, for the weighted $b$-matching problem, this is the first result to exceed an approximation ratio of $2$. Our methodology relies on a generalized weighted version of edge-degree constrained subgraphs, originally proposed by Bernstein and Stein in 2015. These subgraphs feature bounded vertex degrees, ensuring minimal edge usage and ease of computation. The proof that such a subgraph yields a $2 - \frac{1}{2W} + \varepsilon$ approximation of the maximum weight matching utilizes the classical König-Egerváry duality theorem.

This study evaluates the performance, energy efficiency, and usability of Python when developing HPC applications for GPUs. We analyze the portability of both performance and energy efficiency across CUDA and OpenCL, various GPU generations, and devices ranging from low-end to high-end. Our results indicate that the overhead of using Python is negligible for our applications, and CUDA and OpenCL implementations, when tuned to a comparable level, often achieve identical computational performance. Furthermore, our experiments reveal that performance differences vary significantly more between different GPU models than between the CUDA and OpenCL frameworks. Additionally, we demonstrate that while performance tuning effectively improves energy efficiency, specific adjustments are required to achieve optimal energy efficiency.

Given a Fano manifold $(M, J_0)$ that supports a Kähler-Ricci soliton, we examine the dynamics of the Kähler-Ricci flow under deformations of the complex structure $J_0$. Initially, we derive a Lojasiewicz-type inequality concerning Perelman's entropy along the flow. Subsequently, we demonstrate the convergence of the Kähler-Ricci flow when the initial complex structure belongs to the kernel $Z$ or the negative component of the second variation operator of Perelman's entropy. As applications, we resolve the Yau-Tian-Donaldson conjecture regarding the existence of Kähler-Ricci solitons within the moduli space of complex structures near $J_0$, and we establish that the kernel $Z$ represents the local moduli space of Fano manifolds exhibiting modified $K$-semistability. Furthermore, we prove a uniqueness theorem for Kähler-Ricci solitons.

Building upon previous research with Cris Negron regarding the cohomology of Drinfeld doubles $D(\mathbb G_{(r)})$, we establish a "geometric theory" of support varieties for "extended Drinfeld doubles" $\tilde D(\mathbb G_{(r)})$ associated with Frobenius kernels $\mathbb G_{(r)}$ of smooth linear algebraic groups $\mathbb G$ defined over a field $k$ of characteristic $p > 0$. For any $\tilde D(\mathbb G_{(r)})$-module $M$, we define the space $\Pi(\tilde D(\mathbb G_{(r)}))_M$ consisting of equivalence classes of "pairs of $\pi$-points" and demonstrate that the mapping $M \mapsto \Pi(\tilde D(\mathbb G_{(r)}))_M$ satisfies the majority of expected properties. Specifically, this association fulfills the "tensor product property" and features a natural continuous map $\Psi_{\tilde D}$ into cohomological support theory. Furthermore, when $M$ is finite dimensional and $\mathbb G_{(r)}$ meets certain conditions, this mapping serves as a "projectivity test," $\Psi_{\tilde D}$ becomes a homeomorphism, and $\Pi(\tilde D(\mathbb G_{(r)}))_M$ corresponds to the cohomological support variety of $M$ for various classes of $\tilde D(\mathbb G_{(r)})$-modules.

This study investigates baryon-number-violating oscillations of $\Xi_b^0$ particles using $pp$ collision data collected by the LHCb experiment, which corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 3 fb$^{-1}$. To determine the baryon number at production, the analysis requires the $\Xi_b^0$ to originate from the decays of resonances, specifically $\Xi_b^{*-} \to \Xi_b^0 \pi^-$ or $\Xi_b^{\prime-} \to \Xi_b^0 \pi^-$, while the baryon number at decay is identified through the final states resulting from $\Xi_b^0 \to \Xi_c^+ \pi^-$ followed by $\Xi_c^+ \to p K^- \pi^+$. No evidence for baryon number violation was observed, leading to a 95% confidence level upper limit on the oscillation rate of $\omega < 0.08$ ps$^{-1}$, where $\omega$ represents the associated angular frequency.

By utilizing $\mathcal{P}$-canonical forms for matrices, we establish the minimal polynomial of the Kronecker product of a set of matrices based on the minimal polynomials of the individual matrices. This approach enables us to demonstrate that the product $\prod\limits_{i=1}^{m}L(P_{i})$—where $L(P_{i})$ denotes the set of linear recurrence sequences over a field $F$ having $P_{i}$ as their characteristic polynomial—coincides with $L(P)$. In this context, $P$ represents the minimal polynomial of the Kronecker product of the companion matrices corresponding to $P_{i}$ for $1\leq i\leq m$. Furthermore, we illustrate how the $\mathcal{P}$-canonical form of an arbitrary complex matrix $A$ can be employed to determine the $\mathcal{P}$-canonical forms of both the matrix function $e^{tA}$ and a logarithm of $A$.
We expand upon a study by Lempp and Hirst regarding infinite analogues of certain finite complexity theory problems, employing intuitionistic reverse mathematics and Weihrauch analysis techniques.

Direct numerical simulations resolving individual pores are conducted to analyze turbulent open-channel flow over smooth, impermeable walls, impermeable rough walls, and a porous sediment bed characterized by a permeability Reynolds number ($Re_K$) of 2.6, typical of aquatic environments. The study examines four setups: (i) a permeable bed with randomly arranged sediment grains, (ii) an impermeable wall fully covered with roughness elements matching the top sediment layer, (iii) an impermeable wall with only half the roughness layer, and (iv) a smooth wall. Utilizing a double-averaging approach, researchers calculated mean velocity, Reynolds stresses, form-induced stresses, and the turbulent kinetic energy budget. Results indicate that the permeable bed and the impermeable full-layer wall produce similar magnitudes for mean velocity, Reynolds stresses, and form-induced pressure-velocity correlations associated with upwelling and downwelling fluxes. Conversely, the impermeable half-layer configuration exhibits a wall-blocking effect, leading to elevated streamwise stresses but reduced wall-normal stresses compared to the permeable bed. While bed roughness amplifies Reynolds shear stress with minimal impact from permeability, bed permeability exerts a substantial influence on form-induced shear stress, unlike its effect on Reynolds stresses. Furthermore, bed shear stress statistics reveal a higher probability of extreme events in permeable and rough-wall scenarios relative to smooth walls. These findings imply that bed permeability significantly affects hyporheic exchange modeling, and accurately capturing bed shear and pressure fluctuations requires accounting for at least the top layer of sediment.

The significance of uncertainty quantification (UQ) has recently driven the popularity of Bayesian methods for solving inverse problems across applied mathematics, physics, and engineering. Nevertheless, conventional Bayesian inference techniques relying on Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) often suffer from high computational costs and inefficiency when addressing high-dimensional challenges. To mitigate this, various surrogate model-based approaches have been introduced to accelerate inference, with the calibration-emulation-sampling (CES) framework notably demonstrating success in large-scale UQ scenarios. This study introduces a novel CES strategy for Bayesian inference that employs deep neural networks for the emulation stage. The proposed algorithm offers superior computational efficiency and enhanced robustness regarding training set variations. Additionally, integrating an autoencoder (AE) for dimensionality reduction accelerates the Bayesian inference process by up to three orders of magnitude. Consequently, our method, designated as the \emph{Dimension-Reduced Emulative Autoencoder Monte Carlo (DREAMC)} algorithm, enables Bayesian UQ to scale effectively to thousands of dimensions for inverse problems. We validate this approach using two low-dimensional inverse problems (linear and nonlinear) and further demonstrate its computational superiority over existing algorithms through two high-dimensional numerical examples involving elliptic and advection-diffusion equations.

This paper introduces Mixer-TTS, a non-autoregressive architecture designed for generating mel-spectrograms, which adapts the MLP-Mixer framework for speech synthesis. The foundational model incorporates pitch and duration predictors, where the latter is trained using an unsupervised alignment method. We also present an extended variant that integrates token embeddings from a pre-trained language model. Both the basic and extended versions achieve Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) of 4.05 and 4.11, respectively, compared to the original LJSpeech samples' MOS of 4.27. These models feature a compact parameter count and deliver significantly faster synthesis speeds than comparable quality systems.

This study introduces a spatiotemporal probabilistic framework to evaluate and quantify how hurricanes and storm surges compound their impact on the bulk power grid. Synthetic hurricane paths are created from historical records, while storm surge conditions are derived from observed hurricane parameters. System losses are assessed using a metric that measures total load loss. The simulations are conducted on a synthetic Texas 2000-bus system, mapped to the state's geographical area. Findings indicate that storm surge-induced inundation of power substations results in additional load losses as hurricanes move inland.

This study focuses on the rapid and precise calculation of exterior wave equations, which are truncated using exact circular or spherical nonreflecting boundary conditions (NRBCs)—conditions recognized for being nonlocal in both space and time. Initially, we establish analytic formulas for the associated convolution kernels, facilitating swift and accurate convolution evaluation requiring only $O(N_t)$ operations across $N_t$ time steps. To address spatial nonlocality, we implement a boundary perturbation approach, allowing the solution of wave equations for general bounded scatterers within a regular domain by solving a sequence of such equations. Furthermore, we develop an efficient spectral-Galerkin solver combined with Newmark's time integration method for the wave equation in this regular domain. Finally, extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the high-order accuracy of the NRBCs and the computational efficiency of the proposed methodology.

Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) serves as a versatile modeling framework for combinatorial optimization and is essential for gate array and quantum annealing systems. Both QUBO annealers and alternative solution methods gain advantages from initiating with a diverse collection of locally optimal solutions. This paper introduces a novel approach utilizing constraint programming to generate a set of one-flip local optima. Additionally, experimental results demonstrate that analyzing this solution set enables the creation of soft constraints to effectively guide the optimization process.

As the sensitivity of the global network of ground-based gravitational wave detectors has increased, leading to a higher detection rate for compact binary mergers, robust automation has become essential. Low-latency automated algorithms have been created to issue alerts upon detecting candidate signals, providing sky maps to aid electromagnetic follow-up observations, along with probabilities indicating the presence of neutron stars and the likelihood of electromagnetic counterparts. However, data quality problems, such as loud noise transients (glitches), can disrupt these low-latency algorithms, resulting in false alarms and skewed parameter estimates.
