This paper introduces a new analysis method that is resilient to glitches and capable of delivering fully Bayesian parameter inference—including sky maps and mass estimates—within minutes. The method relies on key components: wavelet-based denoising, penalized likelihood maximization during the initial search, rapid sky localization via pre-computed inner products, and heterodyned likelihoods for comprehensive Bayesian inference.

The recent triumph of Transformers in language processing has inspired their adaptation to multimodal environments, typically involving the joint training of a new visual model with a pretrained language model. However, the substantial memory demands of Transformers have led existing approaches to freeze the language model and train only the vision component, thereby restricting end-to-end cross-modal learning. This study addresses parameter reduction in multimodal Transformers specifically for audio-visual video representation learning. We mitigate high memory consumption by sharing Transformer parameters across layers and modalities; by decomposing the architecture into modality-specific and shared components, the model captures both individual and joint dynamics. Furthermore, we introduce a novel parameter-sharing strategy utilizing low-rank approximation. Our method achieves up to a 97% reduction in Transformer parameters, enabling end-to-end training from scratch. Additionally, we propose a negative sampling technique based on instance similarity within the CNN embedding space learned concurrently with the Transformers. To validate our approach, we pretrain the model on 30-second clips (480 frames) from Kinetics-700 and subsequently transfer it to audio-visual classification tasks.

This paper proves the three balls theorem for functions $u$ satisfying $Du=\lambda u$ within the framework of Clifford analysis. As an application, we extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}.$

Multimodal MRI offers clinically valuable, complementary data for assessing tissue health and diagnosing various conditions; however, obtaining a sufficient number of modalities from a single subject is often challenging due to study design constraints, despite the high demand for quantitative analysis. This study introduces a unified conditional disentanglement framework capable of synthesizing any arbitrary MRI modality from a given input. The proposed method relies on a cycle-constrained conditional adversarial training strategy, utilizing a modality-agnostic encoder to isolate modality-invariant anatomical features and a conditioned decoder to generate the target modality. Evaluated on four MRI types—T1-weighted, T1 contrast-enhanced, T2-weighted, and FLAIR—from the BraTS'18 dataset, the framework demonstrates superior synthesis quality compared to existing methods. Furthermore, experiments conducted on tumor segmentation using the synthesized data yield reported results.

Analyzing cell images is vital for Alzheimer's research, specifically for identifying A$\beta$ protein accumulation that impairs cellular function. Deep learning accelerates this workflow by enabling effective analysis with minimal low-level data. Through a comparison of multi-class semantic segmentation performance, we determined that U-Net is the most appropriate architecture for augmented microscopy. We developed an augmented microscopy approach to isolate nuclei in brightfield images and integrated a transformer based on the U-Net model to transform input images into sequences of topological information. The Intersection-over-Union performance remained stable regardless of the specific image preprocessing or ground-truth generation methods used. Furthermore, training on data from a specific cell type suggests that transfer learning offers limited applicability in this context. The proposed topological transformer extracts persistence silhouettes or landscape signatures, capturing the geometric properties of cell images. This feature extraction allows images to be treated as one-dimensional data collections, significantly lowering computational expenses. By relying solely on these topological features, we attempted to classify cell images by type. While the performance of transformers paired with SVM, XGBoost, LGBM, and basic convolutional neural network classifiers lagged behind conventional image classification methods, this study introduces a novel perspective in biomedical research by merging deep learning with topology. We hypothesize that future investigations will strengthen the validity of this approach.

The study explores mathematical models for street traffic designed to evaluate the significance of individual segments within the broader street system. Drawing upon cooperative game theory and reliability theory, a specific metric is developed to achieve this. The primary objective is to analyze techniques for ranking road sections and their functional roles, with a focus on determining how these elements contribute to the overall accessibility and efficiency of the entire network.

End-to-end optimization using Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in the complex time-frequency or time domains has demonstrated significant promise for monaural speech separation. However, recent research frequently optimizes loss functions defined exclusively in the time or complex domains, omitting a magnitude-based loss. While these approaches often yield superior scores on objective time-domain metrics, they tend to underperform in terms of speech quality, intelligibility, and automatic speech recognition (ASR) compared to methods that include magnitude loss. Although numerous studies have empirically observed this discrepancy, the underlying fundamental causes remain poorly understood and lack a thorough explanation. This paper introduces a novel perspective based on the implicit compensation between estimated magnitude and phase. Analytical findings from monaural speech separation and robust ASR tasks conducted in noisy and reverberant environments validate this viewpoint.

Core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) have the potential to generate substantial amounts of dust, with compelling evidence indicating that ejecta dust masses can accumulate significantly over time. We utilized the Monte Carlo radiative transfer code DAMOCLES to model red-blue asymmetries in the broad emission lines of CCSNe for the purpose of calculating ejecta dust masses. To improve accessibility, we developed and implemented a Tkinter graphical user interface (GUI) for DAMOCLES. This tool was evaluated by high school students participating in the Original Research By Young Twinkle Students (ORBYTS) programme, who employed it to determine dust masses at two distinct epochs for Type IIP CCSNe SN 2012aw and iPTF14hls, illustrating that individuals from diverse backgrounds can make meaningful contributions to scientific progress. Uncertainties in our model parameters were quantified using Bayesian methods. Analysis of the day 1863 H$\alpha$ profile of SN 2012aw, which exhibited a red scattering wing, constrained the dust composition to large silicate grains (radius $>0.1 \mu$m) with a mass of $6.0^{+21.9}_{-3.6}\times10^{-4} M_\odot$. A dust mass of $3.0^{+14}_{-2.5}\times10^{-4} M_\odot$ was derived from the day 1158 H$\alpha$ profile of the same supernova. For iPTF14hls, a dust mass of $8.1^{+81}_{-7.6}\times10^{-5} M_\odot$ was identified at day 1170, assuming a composition of 50% amorphous carbon and 50% astronomical silicate. Comparisons indicate that at 1000 days post-explosion, SN 2012aw and iPTF14hls produced less dust than SN 1987A, suggesting that SN 1987A may form larger dust masses than other Type IIP supernovae.

This paper addresses testing for the two-sample location problem in scenarios where the dimensionality exceeds the sample size. Conventional multivariate rank-based methods fail in high-dimensional contexts due to the unavailability of the sample scatter matrix. We introduce a new high-dimensional spatial rank test for this purpose and establish its asymptotic normality. The proposed method accommodates dimensions that grow at an exponential rate relative to the sample sizes. Simulation studies indicate that the test exhibits strong robustness and efficiency across a broad spectrum of distributions.

In their foundational research, Alon, Matias, and Szegedy developed various sketching methods, notably demonstrating that 4-wise independence suffices for accurate estimation of the second frequency moment. This paper extends their approach to product domains $[n]^k$ by leveraging products of 4-wise independent functions defined on $[n]$. We generalize the findings of Indyk and McGregor, who established this result specifically for $k = 2$. Their original focus was on detecting correlations within data streams. In their framework, a sequence of pairs $(i,j) \in [n]^2$ arrives, representing a joint distribution $(X,Y)$, and they devised approximation algorithms to measure the proximity of this joint distribution to the product of its marginals under different metrics—a task equivalent to assessing the independence between $X$ and $Y$. By applying our methodology, we derive a novel result for approximating the $\ell_2$ distance between a joint distribution and the product of its marginals for $k$-ary vectors, rather than merely pairs, achievable in a single pass. Our analysis yields a randomized algorithm offering a $(1 \pm \epsilon)$ approximation (with probability $1-\delta$) that utilizes space logarithmic in both $n$ and $m$, while scaling proportionally to $3^k$.

This paper outlines three methodological enhancements to the "SCK CEN approach" for Bayesian inference of radionuclide inventories in radioactive waste drums based on radiological data. First, we adopt the Dirichlet distribution as the prior for the isotopic vector, leveraging its property that sample elements naturally sum to one. Second, we show that Dirichlet priors can be integrated into a hierarchical model of prior uncertainty when existing isotopic composition data is available. Our Bayesian hierarchical framework utilizes this prior information while simultaneously allowing indirect measurement data (gamma and neutron counts) to influence the actual prior distribution within controlled limits, thereby accounting for uncertainty in that prior knowledge. Third, we propose regularizing the Bayesian inversion using Gaussian process (GP) priors for inferring 1D spatially distributed quantities. Regarding efficiency uncertainties, we retain the stylized drum modeling approach from our previous work to address source distribution uncertainty along the drum's vertical axis. Synthetic tests and application to a real waste drum demonstrate that combining hierarchical modeling of isotopic composition uncertainty with GP modeling of the vertical plutonium profile yields effective results. Furthermore, our GP prior successfully handles both spatially correlated and uncorrelated scenarios. The computational cost of our proposed method is approximately a few hours (around two hours) to generate uncertainty estimates for all variables of interest in the inverse problem, suggesting a need for further research to accelerate the inference process.

Myocardial motion and deformation serve as powerful indicators of cardiac function. While image registration is the predominant technique for tracking these movements, it constitutes an ill-posed inverse problem that typically necessitates prior assumptions about the solution space. Unlike existing methods that rely on explicit, generic regularizations like smoothness, this study introduces a novel approach capable of implicitly learning a biomechanics-informed prior tailored to the application and integrating it into a neural network-parameterized transformation model. Specifically, the method employs a variational autoencoder-based generative model to construct a manifold representing biomechanically plausible deformations. Motion tracking is subsequently achieved by traversing this learned manifold to identify optimal transformations while incorporating sequence information. Validated across three public cardiac cine MRI datasets with extensive evaluations, the results show that this approach surpasses other methods, delivering superior motion tracking accuracy, reasonable volume preservation, and enhanced generalizability across varying data distributions. Furthermore, it facilitates more accurate estimation of myocardial strains, highlighting its potential for characterizing spatiotemporal signatures to better understand cardiovascular diseases.

Crowd counting has emerged as a critical challenge in computer vision. Most existing approaches generate density maps by convolving ground-truth dot maps, placed at the center of human heads, with a Gaussian kernel. However, the rigid geometric structures of CNNs and ambiguous head-scale information often lead to incomplete extraction of head features. To address this, deformable convolution was introduced to enhance scale adaptability in CNN features by learning coordinate offsets for sampling points, thereby expanding the receptive field. Despite this, deformable convolution fails to uniformly cover heads with sampling points, causing information loss. This paper proposes an improved Normed-Deformable Convolution (NDConv), driven by a Normed-Deformable loss (NDloss), to mitigate non-uniform sampling. By constraining sampling point offsets to be more evenly distributed, NDConv ensures more complete feature extraction from heads, resulting in superior performance. Notably, NDConv is a lightweight module with a computational cost comparable to standard deformable convolution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on the ShanghaiTech A, ShanghaiTech B, UCF_QNRF, and UCF_CC_50 datasets, achieving Mean Absolute Errors (MAE) of 61.4, 7.8, 91.2, and 167.2, respectively. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/bingshuangzhuzi/NDConv.

The strong lottery ticket hypothesis suggests that pruning randomly initialized deep neural networks could serve as a computationally efficient alternative to deep learning using stochastic gradient descent. However, common parameter initialization methods and existence proofs typically assume zero biases, thereby neglecting the potential universal approximation capabilities of pruning. To address this limitation, we generalize various initialization schemes and existence proofs to accommodate nonzero biases, including explicit "looks-linear" approaches for ReLU activation functions. These methods not only facilitate truly orthogonal parameter initialization but also mitigate potential pruning errors. Furthermore, experiments on standard benchmark datasets demonstrate the practical advantages of nonzero bias initialization, while we introduce theoretically grounded extensions for state-of-the-art strong lottery ticket pruning techniques.

The swift advancement of information technology has generated vast amounts of textual data on online platforms. As a specialized subset of Information Extraction, Event Extraction has become increasingly prominent for its capacity to automatically identify events within human language. Despite this, comprehensive literature surveys on the topic remain scarce; existing reviews either delve deeply into specific technical details or concentrate narrowly on particular domains. This study offers a holistic overview of state-of-the-art event extraction techniques and their applications across both closed and open domains. A defining feature of this survey is its moderate complexity, which avoids excessive elaboration on individual methodological details. Instead, the focus is placed on analyzing the common characteristics, application areas, strengths, and limitations of representative works. Finally, the paper summarizes prevailing challenges, current solutions, and future research trajectories, aiming to assist researchers and practitioners in quickly grasping the current landscape of event extraction.

Delta Scuti variables are stars characterized by periodic luminosity variations driven by both radial and non-radial pulsations. Internally, these stars possess relatively small convective cores, where convective overshoot plays a significant role in determining their size. Recent modeling of radial pulsation in these stars revealed a strong correlation between the pulsation constant (Q) as a function of effective temperature and the extent of internal convective overshoot. However, prior studies were limited to models with a metallicity of Z = 0.02, leaving the influence of chemical composition on this relationship unexplored. This study extends the analysis of pulsation properties using the GYRE code by varying mass, rotation rate, convective overshoot, and metallicity to examine Q behavior at low temperatures. Our results indicate that the updated convective boundary treatment in MESA alters the previously identified overshoot dependence, with the resulting slope depending on both rotation and overshoot. Furthermore, we identified a metallicity dependence in Q values. The lowest metallicity models in our grid achieved higher temperatures than those in previous studies, uncovering a parabolic relationship between log Q and log Teff.

This study investigates undecidability within theories of function fields of positive characteristic, utilizing the geometric ring language $\mathcal{L}_F = \{0, 1, +, \cdot, F\}$, where $F$ serves as a unary predicate for nonconstant elements. Driven by Fehm's inquiry into the decidability of $\mbox{Th}_{\exists}(\mathbb{F}_p(t); \mathcal{L}_F)$—or equivalently, $\mbox{Th}_{\exists}(\mathbb{F}_p(t); \mathcal{L}_r)$ without parameters—we outline how to extend current methods to demonstrate the undecidability of $\mbox{Th}_{\forall^1\exists}(K; \mathcal{L}_F)$ without parameters. Here, $K$ represents the function field of a curve over an algebraic extension of $\mathbb{F}_p$ that is not algebraically closed. Additionally, we elaborate on the associated problem and its geometric consequences within this framework.

This research investigates the continuous multi-reference alignment problem, which involves estimating a periodic function on a circle from noisy, circularly-rotated data. Drawing inspiration from similar high-dimensional challenges in cryo-electron microscopy, we derive minimax estimation rates for general signals that are explicitly dependent on the dimension $K$. In a high-noise setting where the noise variance $\sigma^2$ is greater than or approximately equal to $K$, the estimation rate scales as $\sigma^6$ without additional dependence on $K$; this performance is attained via a bispectrum inversion method, accompanied by novel stability bounds for this procedure. Conversely, in a low-noise regime where $\sigma^2$ is less than or approximately equal to $K/\log K$, the rate scales as $K\sigma^2$, a result proven through a precise analysis of the maximum likelihood estimator that accounts for latent rotations. Furthermore, a complementary lower bound that bridges these two regimes is derived using Assouad's hypercube lemma.

Pre-trained language models (PLMs), such as BERT, have significantly advanced natural language processing. Since news articles are typically rich in textual content, PLMs offer substantial potential to enhance modeling for various intelligent news applications, including recommendation and retrieval systems. However, most current PLMs are extremely large, containing hundreds of millions of parameters. This scale presents significant challenges for online news platforms that must serve millions of users with strict low-latency requirements. Knowledge distillation offers a solution by compressing large models into smaller, more efficient versions while maintaining performance. Yet, existing models are typically pre-trained and distilled on general corpora like Wikipedia, which may not fully align with the specific nuances of the news domain, leading to suboptimal results for news intelligence. To address this, we introduce NewsBERT, a framework designed to distill PLMs specifically for efficient and effective news intelligence. Our approach utilizes a teacher-student joint learning and distillation framework where the student model collaboratively learns alongside the teacher, leveraging the teacher's learning experience. Furthermore, we propose a momentum distillation method that incorporates the teacher model's gradients into the student's parameter updates, facilitating better knowledge transfer. Extensive experiments across two real-world datasets and three tasks demonstrate that NewsBERT effectively boosts performance in diverse intelligent news applications while utilizing significantly smaller models.

This paper addresses a linearized Calderón problem for polyharmonic operators of order $2m$ (where $m \ge 2$), following the approach of Calderón's foundational work [Cal80]. We establish a uniqueness theorem for identifying coefficients of order $\leq 2m-1$ modulo gauge transformations, achieved by inverting momentum ray transforms.

A primary objective of the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST) is to chart Solar System small bodies to gain critical insights into the system's formation and evolution, a task particularly vital for the Outer Solar System populations located beyond Neptune ($r > 30$ AU). This whitepaper suggests a minimal adjustment to the LSST observing cadence designed to significantly boost the discovery rate of faint, distant Solar System objects throughout the entire Wide-Fast-Deep (WFD) survey region. Specifically, we recommend constraining the WFD cadence to ensure at least one sequence of approximately 10 or more visits per year, occurring within a $\sim 10$-day window in any combination of $g$, $r$, and $i$ bands. When paired with advanced shift-and-stack techniques (Whidden et al. 2019), this modification would facilitate a nearly comprehensive census of the outer Solar System down to $\sim 25.5$ magnitude. This approach would result in a 4–8-fold increase in Kuiper Belt Object (KBO) discoveries compared to single-epoch baselines and allow for the rapid identification and follow-up of anomalous distant objects in a volume of space roughly 5 times greater. These improvements would strengthen the scientific cases outlined in Schwamb et al. (2018), such as investigating Neptune's historical migration and detecting or placing stringent constraints on hypothetical planets beyond Neptune's orbit.

Irregularly sampled time series data frequently arise across diverse domains, yet standard analytical techniques often struggle to extract meaningful insights from them. This study aims to extend trajectory clustering methods to handle such irregular and sparse data. We begin by generating synthetic datasets and then introduce and evaluate four distinct data alignment strategies to facilitate spectral clustering. The same experimental framework is applied to real-world medical records from patients with sickle cell disease, whose pain levels were monitored over several months using a mobile application. Our findings indicate that various alignment methods for sparse, irregular datasets can yield different optimal cluster counts, even when the synthetic data's ground truth is known. Regarding the sickle cell cohort, a three-cluster solution appears most appropriate, corresponding to: (1) a low-pain group with occasional acute episodes, (2) a group experiencing moderate mean pain that fluctuates frequently between low and high states, and (3) a group suffering from persistent high pain. These results offer potential benefits for clinicians and patients in understanding and managing pain trajectories over time, and the developed methods are expected to be applicable to a broad spectrum of data sources within medicine and other fields.

Semi-supervised video object segmentation (semi-VOS) is extensively applied across numerous domains, focusing on tracking class-agnostic objects starting from an initial target mask. While existing solutions leveraging online-learning, memory networks, and optical flow achieve high accuracy, their computational complexity and slow inference rates hinder practical deployment. Conversely, earlier template matching approaches offer rapid processing but suffer from significant performance degradation. We present a new semi-VOS framework that combines template matching with a temporal consistency loss to bridge the accuracy gap of heavy models while drastically accelerating inference. Our approach employs both short-term and long-term matching: short-term matching refines target localization, whereas long-term matching enhances fine details and manages shape variations via an adaptive template attention module. To address error propagation caused by incorporating past estimates during template updates, we introduce a temporal consistency loss utilizing a transition matrix to ensure coherence between adjacent frames. On the DAVIS16 benchmark, our model achieves a J&F score of 79.5% at 73.8 FPS. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/HYOJINPARK/TTVOS.

Over recent years, the research and industrial sectors have increasingly focused on Microservices Architecture (MSA) due to its significant advantages. However, there remains a scarcity of comprehensive, evidence-based insights regarding the specific types of problems (such as faults, errors, failures, and mistakes) encountered by developers and the root causes triggering these issues. Such an understanding is crucial for advancing high-quality, impactful, and sustainable research and practice in MSA. To address this gap, we performed an empirical analysis of 1,345 issue discussions from five open-source microservices projects hosted on GitHub. Our findings established the first taxonomy of issues within open-source microservices, revealing that Technical debt (321 instances, 23.86%), Build issues (145 instances, 10.78%), Security concerns (137 instances, 10.18%), and Service execution/communication problems (119 instances, 8.84%) are the most prevalent categories. We further identified that "General programming errors," "Poor security management," "Invalid configuration and communication," and "Legacy versions, compatibility, and dependency" are the primary drivers behind these top four issue types. These results provide a structured taxonomy of issues linked to their underlying causes, offering empirical data to support future research and development of next-generation microservices systems.

Circadian clocks are essential for coordinating many physiological and developmental processes. The shapes of protein abundance oscillations offer insights into the biochemical mechanisms driving these clocks. We developed a mathematical framework demonstrating that these waveforms expose hidden aspects of circadian timekeeping. Our findings indicate that rhythmic variations in protein half-lives significantly lower the energetic cost of synthesizing proteins with specific waveforms, a conclusion supported by data from plants and mammals as well as our own seedling experiments. Additionally, we discovered that the previously puzzling cyclic expression of positive arm components in mammalian and insect clocks enables both diverse peak-time offsets and symmetrical waveform structures around those peaks. These varying peak-time differences may support tissue-specific or developmentally stage-specific multicellular functions. Furthermore, our waveform-guided methodology is applicable to other biological oscillators, such as those governing the cell cycle and synthetic genetic systems.

Sequential sampling is employed when the total population is unknown beforehand, and information is collected either individually or in batches. This manuscript introduces a novel algorithm designed to sequentially choose a balanced sample that accommodates both equal and unequal inclusion probabilities. Furthermore, the method is applicable for generating spatially balanced samples when the target population includes spatial coordinates. A simulation study was conducted, demonstrating that the proposed approach surpasses existing methods in performance.

We examine a moving vortex within a two-dimensional superconductor positioned at a distance $d$ from an adjacent metallic layer. By beginning with the microscopic imaginary time action and integrating out the electronic degrees of freedom, we derive a low-energy, long-wavelength effective action specific to the vortex. Our analysis centers on the vortex's kinetic energy to establish a general formula for its mass. We observe that as $d\to \infty$, Coulomb screening of density fluctuations induced by vortex motion leads to a minimal vortex mass, consistent with prior research. Conversely, in the limit where $d\ll \xi$ ($\xi$ being the superconductor's coherence length), the vortex mass diverges logarithmically with system size; this occurs because the proximity to the metal renders the screening mechanisms—typically responsible for reducing the mass—ineffective. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for recent experiments demonstrating a sharp decrease in resistance when a metallic gate is introduced near a superconducting film under a magnetic field at low temperatures.

A core objective of precision medicine is the discovery of predictive biomarkers, which identify patient subgroups that will derive the greatest or least benefit from specific treatments. Often, finding these biomarkers is a secondary outcome of the distinct task of estimating treatment rules. However, applying treatment rule estimation methods to clinical trials with more covariates than participants frequently leads to elevated false discovery rates. The resulting excess of false positives causes wasted resources during follow-up experiments for drug target identification and diagnostic assay development, ultimately harming patient outcomes. To address this, we introduce a variable importance parameter for directly evaluating the predictive significance of biomarkers and develop a flexible nonparametric inference procedure for this estimand. We demonstrate that our estimator is double-robust and asymptotically linear under lenient assumptions regarding the data-generating process, enabling valid statistical inference. These guarantees are confirmed through an extensive simulation study modeling randomized control trials with moderate to high-dimensional covariates. We subsequently apply this procedure to identify predictive biomarkers within tumor gene expression data from metastatic renal cell carcinoma patients in recently concluded clinical trials. Our results indicate that this approach more effectively distinguishes predictive from non-predictive biomarkers compared to methods primarily designed for treatment rule estimation. Finally, we briefly present an open-source software implementation of this methodology, the uniCATE R package.

Eye-in-hand camera calibration remains a cornerstone challenge in robotics that has been extensively investigated. This study explores learning-based techniques capable of solving this problem online using a single RGB image, with models trained exclusively on synthetic data. We evaluate three primary strategies: a direct regression model that predicts the extrinsic matrix directly from an image, a sparse correspondence approach that regresses 2D keypoints followed by PnP estimation, and a dense correspondence method utilizing regressed depth and segmentation maps to facilitate ICP-based pose estimation. Our experiments benchmark these techniques against one another and against established classical methods, revealing the unexpected finding that direct regression surpasses the other approaches. Additionally, we conduct a noise-sensitivity analysis to provide deeper insights into these outcomes.

Compact U(1) gauge theory in 3+1 dimensions features a confining phase, defined by a linear increase in the potential between oppositely charged particles at large separations. This confinement arises from the condensation of Abelian monopoles under strong gauge coupling. We investigate monopole properties and the deconfining order parameter in a zero-temperature setting with perfectly conducting parallel metallic plates, a setup typically linked to the Casimir effect. Through first-principles numerical simulations of compact U(1) lattice gauge theory, we demonstrate that reducing the gap between the plates induces a deconfining transition within the intervening vacuum. Consequently, we derive the phase diagram mapping gauge coupling against inter-plate distance.

Community search aims to identify cohesive, connected subgraphs within a network that adhere to specific topological constraints, such as degree limits. While most prior research concentrates solely on these structural properties, neglecting the impact of individual nodes, influential community search was introduced to address this oversight by incorporating node influence. In this framework, each node possesses a weight representing its influence, and a community's total influence is derived through an aggregation function—such as sum, average, minimum, or maximum—applied to the influence values of its constituent nodes. The primary goal is to retrieve the top-r communities with the maximum aggregate influence while respecting the given topological restrictions. However, current studies on influential community search face two key limitations: (i) they rely mainly on simple aggregation functions like minimum, which often fail to meet diverse real-world needs, and (ii) they typically lack constraints on community size, contrary to practical scenarios. To bridge this gap, this study investigates the identification of top-r influential communities, both with and without size limits, utilizing more complex aggregation functions like sum or average. We provide a theoretical analysis establishing the computational hardness of these problems and develop efficient, effective heuristic algorithms. Extensive experiments on large-scale real-world graphs confirm that our proposed approach is substantially more efficient than existing baseline methods.

Analyzing the marginal impact of antidepressants on body mass index (BMI) via electronic health records presents significant hurdles. Patient traits can act as confounders influencing both drug exposure and the timing of routine visits, while these traits may shift after a visit, creating dependencies between BMI monitoring and the stochastic evolution of the disease over time. This dynamic can induce a selection bias that skews the estimated effect of the medication. Although inverse visit intensity weights have been suggested to correct such imbalances, no existing methods address complex scenarios where covariates and monitoring processes mutually influence each other over time, a situation common in electronic health records. We examine how selection bias arises from outcome-dependent follow-up times and introduce a novel cumulated weight designed to model the entire monitoring trajectory, thereby overcoming these challenges and yielding a reliable estimate of antidepressant impact on BMI. Specifically, utilizing data from the United Kingdom's Clinical Practice Research Datalink, we compare the marginal effects of two prevalent antidepressants, citalopram and fluoxetine, on BMI. These findings are contrasted with results from simpler approaches that fail to account for endogeneity arising from covariate processes.

We propose the notion of temporal seeding in crystallization by analyzing the dynamics of an ensemble of coupled continuous time crystals. Our findings show that a single subsystem within a broken-symmetry phase, functioning as a nucleation site, can trigger time-translation symmetry breaking throughout the entire ensemble. This seeding phenomenon occurs under both coherent and dissipative coupling conditions across a wide spectrum of parameter regimes. Drawing parallels to mutual synchronization, we examine the scenario where all subsystems reside in the broken-symmetry phase. We find that more broadly detuned time crystals necessitate weaker coupling strengths to achieve synchronization, a result that contrasts with established principles in both classical and quantum synchronization theory. We attribute this unexpected observation directly to the seeding effect.

This study examines the feasibility of constructing a quantum memory resilient to thermal noise through large $N$ matrix quantum mechanics frameworks. Initially, we analyze the gauged $SU(N)$ matrix harmonic oscillator and various encoding strategies for quantum information. By computing the mutual information between the system and a reference that purifies the encoded data, we determine a critical temperature, $T_c$. Below this threshold, the encoded information remains shielded from thermal noise for a duration scaling with $N^2$, whereas above it, thermal noise rapidly degrades the information. Subsequently, we remove the gauge invariance constraint to investigate a matrix harmonic oscillator model possessing only global symmetry. Finally, we further eliminate symmetry requirements, proposing a model comprising $N^2$ qubits with interactions based on an approximate $SU(N)$ symmetry. In these ungauge scenarios, we observe that the benefits of gauging can be replicated via an energy penalty, yielding comparable memory times. Additionally, the proposed final qubit model offers promising prospects for experimental realization.

This study presents the initial measurement of ${\rm e}^{+}{\rm e}^{-}$ pair production at low transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T,ee}$) and low invariant mass ($m_{\rm ee}$) in non-central Pb$-$Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV using the ALICE detector at the LHC. Data were collected at midrapidity ($|\eta_{\rm e}| < 0.8$) across two centrality classes (50$-$70% and 70$-$90%$) for $p_{\rm T,ee} < 0.1$ GeV/$c$ and invariant masses between 0.4 and 2.7 GeV/$c^2$, as well as across three mass intervals for the most peripheral collisions. An excess of dielectron pairs is observed below $p_{\rm T,ee} = 0.1$ GeV/$c$, surpassing expectations from known hadronic sources and thermal radiation models. These excess $m_{\rm ee}$ spectra align with predictions of dielectron production via photon$-$photon interactions, where photons stem from the intense electromagnetic fields of the highly Lorentz-contracted lead nuclei. Furthermore, lowest-order QED calculations and a model incorporating the impact-parameter dependence of photon transverse momentum accurately describe the $p_{\rm T,ee}$ spectra. The measured $\sqrt{\langle p_{\rm T,ee}^{2} \rangle}$ for the excess spectrum in peripheral collisions matches values previously recorded at RHIC in a comparable phase-space region.

NectarCAM serves as the camera system for the medium-sized telescopes within the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA), operating across an energy spectrum from 100 GeV to 30 TeV. The instrument features 265 focal plane modules (FPMs), where each module contains seven pixels. Every pixel is equipped with a photo-multiplier tube, a preamplifier, an independently managed power supply, and a shared control system. To verify the quality of industrial FPM manufacturing and assess individual module performance in a dark environment prior to camera integration, we constructed a specialized test bench. This report details the performance metrics of 61 FPM prototypes evaluated using this setup. Our findings confirm that the photo-multiplier tube gains remain stable and that pulse widths, transit time spreads, afterpulse rates, and charge resolutions all meet the NectarCAM specifications.

The partial transpose serves as a fundamental diagnostic for entanglement in mixed quantum states, giving rise to the logarithmic negativity as its associated measure. While this measure has proven highly effective for characterizing bosonic many-body systems, extending the partial transpose to fermionic systems was a longstanding technical hurdle until a recent definition incorporating Fermi statistics was introduced. In this work, we propose a generalization of the partial transpose applicable to anyons exhibiting (non-Abelian) fractional statistics, leveraging the conceptual resemblance between partial transposition and braiding operations. Subsequently, we define an anyonic counterpart to the logarithmic negativity and demonstrate that it adheres to standard criteria, such as monotonicity, required of an entanglement measure. Specifically, we analyze the properties of anyonic logarithmic negativity by calculating it for a toy density matrix representing a pair of anyons across various categories. Furthermore, we conjecture that, unlike in ordinary qubit systems where the subspace of states with zero logarithmic negativity occupies a finite volume, this subspace constitutes a set of measure zero within the full space of anyonic states. We provide a proof for this conjecture within multiplicity-free categories.

We demonstrate that placing a massive object into a quantum superposition of spatially separated states leads to the eventual destruction of its coherence if a black hole is nearby. This phenomenon arises because the object's gravitational field emits soft gravitons into the black hole, enabling the latter to gain "which path" information regarding the superposition. An analogous effect occurs with quantum superpositions of electrically charged objects. We offer estimates for the decoherence times associated with these scenarios. We posit that the inevitability of black holes decohering any quantum superposition holds fundamental importance for understanding black holes within a quantum theory of gravity.

This study details the synthesis, structural characterization, and magnetic behavior of the single crystal bis(4-aminopyridinium) bis(oxalato)cuprate(II) dihydrate, (C₅H₇N₂)₂[Cu(C₂O₄)₂]·2H₂O, a facile spin 1/2 one-dimensional Heisenberg antiferromagnet. High-quality single crystals of the title compound were successfully produced via liquid-liquid or layer diffusion techniques with a 100% yield. Single crystal X-ray diffraction confirmed the excellent quality of the grown crystals, yielding a goodness of fit R value of 1.058. The structure consists of corner-sharing CuO₆ octahedra forming isolated Cu-Cu chains along the a-direction, well-separated in the b and c directions. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations using three distinct basis sets (B3LYP/6-311++G(d,p); B3LYP/LanL2DZ; and B3LYP/6-311++G(d,p) combined with B3LYP/LanL2DZ) optimized the monomeric unit's geometry and vibrational spectra. Experimental IR spectra showed a vibrational frequency for the CuO₆ octahedron that closely matched theoretical predictions using the mixed basis. Temperature-dependent DC magnetic susceptibility exhibited a low-temperature peak indicative of low-dimensional magnetism. A Bonner-Fisher fit validated the one-dimensional magnetic interaction, determining an exchange coupling constant of 1.23 K. Furthermore, magnetization measurements supported by Quantum Monte Carlo simulations confirm that this metal-organic crystal functions as an effective spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet, characterized by a low saturation field (Hs) of 1.75 T.

Information-Centric Networking represents a promising research domain that enables advancements in various areas, including forwarding strategies, caching policies, and applications like video streaming and instant messaging. This paper examines the mobility challenges within ICN and evaluates its performance in tactical wireless ad hoc networks. Specifically, we present simulation results analyzing Named Data Networking (NDN), an ICN implementation, across diverse mobility scenarios using the ndnSIM simulator. Our findings indicate that consumers can achieve superior file retrieval even during short-term producer unavailability when caching is employed. To enhance cache diversity and optimize Content Store utilization, we investigate probabilistic Least Recently Used (LRU) algorithms. Additionally, we compare the performance of our NDN network against a TCP-based approach utilizing the OLSR routing protocol, highlighting the respective strengths and weaknesses of each method.

Achieving seamless Quality of Service (QoS) requires all stakeholders—including hosts, applications, access networks, routers, and middleboxes—to adhere to a unified protocol and maintain mutual trust. This article examines the roles of these entities in delivering QoS over wireless networks within the context of the Differentiated Services (DiffServ) architecture. Our investigation begins by analyzing traces from WiFi and Cellular networks, which motivate a comprehensive empirical study of these participants. Our key findings are as follows: (i) Contemporary mobile VoIP applications actively request QoS from the network. (ii) While operating systems provide basic APIs for QoS requests, application developers often remain unaware of these needs or misapply the architecture in pursuit of enhanced QoS. (iii) Wireless access networks modify QoS requirements at the network edge, compelling subsequent routers to provide best-effort service instead. (iv) Secure tunnels also negate QoS requests. (v) Despite access networks nullifying QoS requests, network performance can still differentiate traffic. Furthermore, we highlight that while the latest 5G networks adopt the DiffServ framework, they struggle with challenges arising from privacy-focused applications, a difficulty that network neutrality is likely to exacerbate.

This work addresses a dual objective: first, classifying solution-generating techniques within (modified) supergravity, and second, categorizing canonical transformations of 2D $\sigma$-models that yield integrable-preserving mappings. Under a generalized Scherk-Schwarz ansatz, these two challenges share an identical algebraic structure derived from an underlying double Lie algebra $\mathfrak d$. Following our derivation of this classification, we examine its connection to modified supergravity and outline the specific requirements needed to revert to standard (unmodified) supergravity. Utilizing our master equation, which encapsulates all permissible continuous deformations within the solution-generating family, we demonstrate that these deformations are governed by the Lie algebra cohomologies $H^2(\mathfrak h,\mathbb R)$ and $H^3(\mathfrak h,\mathbb R)$ of the maximally isotropic subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ contained in the double Lie algebra $\mathfrak d$. We substantiate these findings with a non-trivial case study involving the bi-Yang-Baxter-Wess-Zumino model.

This study examines gravitational particle production in the presence of a chemical potential. By employing the uniformly smoothed Stokes-line technique alongside Borel summation, we elucidate the detailed temporal evolution of amplified particle generation. We derive analytic and semi-analytic expressions for the production quantity, duration, and width of both spin-1 and spin-1/2 particles across different Friedmann-Robertson-Walker (FRW) spacetimes. Furthermore, our research provides a practical validation of the uniformly smoothed Stokes-line method within the context of cosmology.

Using the AstroSat orbital observatory, we report observations of the active M-dwarf binary system AT Mic (dM4.5e+dM4.5e). Over a 20 ks exposure in the far ultraviolet ($130-180$ nm) and soft X-ray ($0.3-7$ keV) bands, we identified quiescent emission alongside at least five flares originating from various components of the binary. The X-ray flares were generally longer and lagged behind their UV counterparts by $5-6$ minutes, consistent with the Neupert effect. Spectral fitting of the X-ray data allowed us to derive plasma parameters, revealing a hot, multi-thermal corona with average temperatures between $\sim 7-15$ MK and an emission measure of $\sim (2.9-4.5)\times 10^{52}$ $\textrm{cm}^{-3}$; both metrics rose during flaring events. The heavy element abundance in AT Mic's corona is significantly lower than solar values ($\sim 0.18-0.34$ of the solar photosphere), but this abundance increased during flares as a result of chromospheric evaporation. The detected flares possessed energies of $\sim 10^{31}-10^{32}$ erg, and their energy-duration relationships suggest magnetic field strengths exceeding those found in typical solar flares.

Cross-entropy loss is extensively utilized for its robust theoretical foundation and efficacy; however, as training advances, its tendency to prioritize hard-to-classify instances can hinder further performance improvements. While existing research typically focuses on strategies to classify hard negatives, we propose instead to strategically set them aside to concentrate on misclassified samples with higher probabilities. By incorporating the expectation loss—a superior approximation of the zero-one loss—into the optimization objective, we demonstrate that the network achieves enhanced accuracy. Consequently, we introduce a training protocol that shifts between the two loss functions, gradually increasing reliance on the expectation loss in later stages. Our experiments confirm that this approach boosts performance across a wide range of classification domains, including computer vision, natural language processing, tabular data, and sequences. Our code and scripts are available in the supplementary materials.

Coherent coupling between a double quantum dot and an electromagnetic resonator allows single-electron tunneling events to trigger a lasing state. This study investigates the noise characteristics of the transport current within this lasing regime, examining both the zero-frequency shot noise and the full noise spectrum. As the system nears the lasing transition, the shot noise exhibits significant super-Poissonian behavior, shifting to sub-Poissonian behavior once deep within the lasing state. The noise spectrum reveals details regarding the coherent dynamics of the coupled system, displaying distinct features at the resonator's frequency caused by photon excitation. Furthermore, under conditions of strong interdot Coulomb interaction, we observe asymmetries in the auto-correlation noise spectra of the left and right junctions, attributing these differences to imbalances in the incoherent tunneling channels.

Concurrent multi-player games featuring $\omega$-regular objectives serve as a standard framework for modeling systems composed of multiple interacting components, each pursuing its own goal. The canonical solution concept for such games is the Nash Equilibrium (NE), representing a stable strategy profile. However, in many scenarios where the system is only partially observable—often due to internal variables—interactions are modeled as partial information games. Unfortunately, it remains an open question whether the existence of an NE in these games is decidable. A specific instance of partial information occurs when system-assigned process IDs are unknown to the processes themselves; in this case, processes possess full knowledge of the system state but remain uncertain regarding the impact of their actions on state transitions. We extend this framework by introducing Multi-Topology Games (MTGs), which are concurrent games involving multiple potential topologies where players are unaware of the actual topology in use. We demonstrate that generalizing the NE concept to MTGs can manifest in various ways. Accordingly, we propose two distinct definitions of NE: Conservative NE, where a player deviates only if they can strictly expand their winning set by adding topologies, and Greedy NE, where deviation occurs if a player can win in a topology they previously could not. We analyze the properties of these equilibria and prove that determining whether a game admits either is decidable.

Understanding visual relationships is fundamental to human interpretation of the visual world, yet it remains a significant challenge for current deep learning algorithms due to three interrelated technical hurdles: 1) detecting object entities and their attributes, 2) deducing semantic relationships between entity pairs, and 3) achieving systematic generalization to new object-relation combinations. This study employs Vision Transformers (ViTs) as the foundational model for visual reasoning, enhancing their capabilities by more effectively leveraging concepts defined as objects and their relations. We propose a novel concept-feature dictionary that enables flexible image feature retrieval during training using concept keys. This framework supports two new auxiliary tasks guided by concepts: a global task designed to enhance relational reasoning and a local task aimed at facilitating semantic, object-centric correspondence learning. To rigorously test the systematic generalization of visual reasoning models, we introduce systematic splits for the standard HICO and GQA benchmarks. Our proposed model, the Concept-guided Vision Transformer (RelViT), significantly surpasses previous methods, improving performance by 16% and 13% on the original splits of HICO and GQA, respectively, and by 43% and 18% on the systematic splits. Furthermore, ablation studies demonstrate the model's adaptability across various ViT variants and its robustness to hyper-parameter variations.

It is widely recognized that current numerical methods for solving time-fractional partial differential equations (PDEs) rely on all previous time steps. Consequently, the memory requirement increases linearly with the number of time steps, presenting a significant challenge, particularly for high-dimensional problems. To the best of our knowledge, addressing this issue remains an open question in the field of time-fractional PDEs. In this paper, we introduce an efficient, memory-free algorithm to resolve this challenge by utilizing incremental Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Numerical experiments demonstrate that our proposed algorithm is not only memory-free but also more efficient than standard solvers.

We present two parametrized families of piecewise affine maps defined on $[0,1]^2$ and $[0,1]^3$, extending the heterochaos baker maps originally proposed and studied in [Y. Saiki, H. Takahasi, J. A. Yorke, Nonlinearity, 34 (2021), 5744--5761] as minimal representations of unstable dimension variability in multidimensional dynamical systems. We demonstrate that the natural coding spaces associated with these maps correspond to the Dyck system arising from language theory. Leveraging this correspondence, we initiate a complementary investigation into their invariant measures. As an initial step, we establish the existence of two ergodic measures of maximal entropy for the generalized heterochaos baker maps and elucidate the mechanism underlying the failure of entropy approachability.

GQA~\citep{hudson2019gqa} serves as a dataset designed for real-world visual reasoning and compositional question answering. Our analysis reveals that top-performing vision-language models often generate answers on the GQA dataset that, while not matching the single ground-truth label, remain semantically valid and contextually correct. This issue is prevalent across most existing visual question answering (VQA) datasets, which typically enforce only one ground-truth answer per question. To overcome this constraint, we introduce Alternative Answer Sets (AAS), automatically generated ground-truth collections using standard NLP tools. We propose a semantic evaluation metric based on AAS and adapt leading VQA solvers to accommodate multiple plausible answers. Applying this method to the GQA dataset demonstrates measurable performance gains. The corresponding code and data can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/luomancs/alternative_answer_set.git}.

Following the 2012 discovery of the Higgs boson, particle physics has entered a thrilling new phase. A key inquiry remains whether the Standard Model accurately describes nature's scalar sector or if it is merely a component of a broader framework containing additional particles. A primary method for investigating this involves exploring extended scalar sector models at upcoming collider facilities. This discussion examines such models within the context of the high-luminosity LHC, potential proton-proton colliders with center-of-mass energies of 27 and 100 TeV, and future lepton colliders operating at various energy levels.

This study examines the thermal correction to the hyperfine interaction within hydrogen, deuterium, and the $^3$He$^+$ ion. Such corrections are accurately modeled using one-loop Feynman diagrams within quantum electrodynamics for bound states at finite temperatures. A straightforward analysis highlights the significance of these findings for future measurements of hyperfine splitting. Furthermore, the potential application of these results in testing the temporal variation of fundamental constants is briefly explored.

Ground-based observations suggest that Ultra High Energy Cosmic Rays (UHECR) with energies exceeding $10^{18.7}$ eV are composed of heavy particles, a conclusion supported by both shower depth and muon production data. Conversely, the arrival directions of cosmic rays above $10^{18.9}$ eV display a dipole anisotropy, which contradicts a heavy composition because high-Z nuclei would be significantly deflected by the Galactic magnetic field, thereby suppressing anisotropy; this discrepancy defines the UHECR composition problem. One potential resolution involves undiscovered effects in proton interactions at center-of-mass (CM) energies of 50 TeV, which could modify interaction cross-sections and product multiplicities to mimic heavy primaries. We utilize Extensive Air-Shower (EAS) simulations to assess how such modifications affect cosmic-ray observables, aiming to constrain the phenomenology of new high-energy proton interaction effects probed by $\sqrt{s}>50$ TeV collisions. Using the modified CORSIKA code, we simulate showers for primaries ranging from $10^{17}$ to $10^{20}$ eV, incorporating a possible increase in cross-section and multiplicity for hadronic collisions above the 50 TeV CM threshold. Our analysis examines composition-sensitive observables, including shower depth and muons, as functions of cross-section, multiplicity, and primary energy. Results indicate that to reconcile Auger shower depth measurements solely through new hadronic collision effects (assuming extragalactic UHECR are entirely protons even at the highest energies), the proton-air interaction cross-section must reach 800 mb at 140 TeV CM energy, accompanied by a 2-3 fold increase in secondary particles. We further investigate muon production within this specific scenario.

**Background.** Empirical Software Engineering (SE) research relies heavily on human subject experiments, necessitating well-defined samples to guarantee external validity. However, current sampling methods are often driven by convenience or specific purpose, which restricts the generalizability of findings. **Objective.** This study aims to map the current landscape of participant selection in empirical SE, pinpoint primary threats, and explore existing mitigation strategies, ultimately proposing a robust selection framework. **Method.** We conducted a review of existing SE guidelines for participant selection and performed a preliminary literature analysis to determine practical selection practices. **Results.** We introduce a novel selection methodology comprising three steps: defining the target population's characteristics, identifying accessible sampling sources, and minimizing the discrepancy between the selected sample and the target population. **Conclusion.** We present a roadmap for the development and empirical validation of this selection methodology.

The collective behaviors of motile active matter are significantly influenced by the interactions among autonomous microswimmers. We examine this phenomenon specifically in two-faced Janus spheres, a prevalent microswimmer design featuring hemispheres composed of distinct materials. By customizing the chemical and physical surface characteristics of these spheres, their mutual interactions—ranging from attraction and repulsion to alignment—can be precisely adjusted. To systematically analyze these effects, we track the dynamics of a single gold-capped Janus particle within the external temperature gradient generated by an optically heated metal nanoparticle. We quantify the resulting orientation-dependent repulsion and alignment, explaining these observations through a simplified theoretical model of induced thermoosmotic surface fluxes. This model demonstrates that the particle's angular velocity is exclusively governed by the temperature distribution along the equator between the hemispheres and the contrast in their phoretic mobilities. Furthermore, we show that the distortion of the external temperature field caused by the particles' heterogeneous heat conductivity disrupts the apparent symmetry of the system.

We present the discovery of a new, very low-mass binary system, 2MASS J10274572+0629104, utilizing Gaia DR2 astrometry and Kepler K2 photometry. The K2 light curve exhibits a beat pattern composed of two periodic signals; analysis via the Lomb-Scargle periodogram reveals rotation periods of 0.2114 ± 0.0002 days and 0.2199 ± 0.0003 days. We attribute these periods to two M6 spectral type stars with nearly equal luminosities, marking the first identification of an ultracool binary system through light curve beat patterns. Near-infrared spectroscopy determined the system's parameters to be: RV = -9.8 ± 0.6 km s^-1, v sin i = 21.5 ± 1.1 km s^-1, T_eff = 3110 ± 40 K, and log g = 5.2 ± 0.2. While the rotational periods and kinematic motions suggest a young age, the object does not belong to any known moving group. Additionally, we observed three significant white light flares in the K2 data, with estimated total bolometric energies (UV/optical/IR) of 2.6 × 10^33, 5.0 × 10^33, and 3.5 × 10^33 erg, respectively.

Quantum annealing technologies are designed to address optimization and sampling challenges in computation. Systems like the D-Wave Quantum Processing Unit (QPU) leverage the Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) framework to define model optimization tasks, utilizing quantum phenomena to accelerate processing beyond the capabilities of classical computers. This study proposes a vehicle routing problem formulated within the QUBO model as a combinatorial issue, generating exponentially possible route solutions. The primary objective is to optimize vehicle journeys to their destinations, specifically targeting traffic congestion on specific roads. The research presents a QUBO formulation that selects optimal routes by optimizing the distribution of vehicle flow across alternative roads, weighted by road segment characteristics. Constraints are established based on road density levels, where road weight parameters influence the cost function for each route option. Simulations conducted on the D-Wave quantum annealer demonstrate optimal results in deploying routes for multiple vehicles, enabling each to access various road options to accurately reduce congestion. Consequently, this solution offers a pathway to advance QUBO modeling for increasingly complex vehicle routing and traffic congestion scenarios.

Grading programming assignments is often burdensome for instructors and unfeasible in large-scale Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) with thousands of enrollees. Prior studies have indicated that program repair methodologies could facilitate feedback generation in educational contexts. This paper introduces a new, fully automated program repair algorithm tailored for introductory programming tasks. The core mechanism driving its automation and scalability involves leveraging existing correct student submissions to fix erroneous ones. The methodology was assessed through two experiments: (I) An analysis of 4,293 flawed student attempts from a pre-existing MOOC, measuring the volume, scope, and caliber of generated fixes. Results show the approach successfully repaired 97% of attempts, with 81% of those being high-quality, minor corrections. (II) A preliminary user study within an interactive teaching environment to assess performance and the utility of the repairs. The study yielded encouraging initial outcomes, with an average usefulness rating of 3.4 out of 5, suggesting the approach is viable for interactive educational settings.

Inverse problems involve reconstructing images from partial or corrupted data, a task common in MRI, computed tomography, deblurring, superresolution, and inpainting. Since numerous image hypotheses often align with both the measurements and prior knowledge, the objective shifts from identifying a single optimal solution to exploring the range of probable hypotheses by sampling the posterior distribution. This paper introduces a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN capable of generating dozens of high-fidelity posterior samples every second. Using quantitative metrics such as the conditional Fréchet inception distance, we show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art results for posterior sampling in both multicoil MRI and inpainting scenarios.

Electrons at a helium surface exhibit distinct resonant absorption lines corresponding to transitions between quantized subbands moving perpendicular to the surface. A magnetic field oriented parallel to this surface significantly alters the absorption spectrum. We demonstrate that this phenomenon arises from the coupling of out-of-plane motion to the in-plane quantum dynamics of a strongly correlated electron liquid or Wigner crystal. This mechanism mirrors the mixing of electron transitions with phonons in color centers. Consequently, the spectrum allows for a direct analysis of many-electron dynamics and provides a means to test color center theory within a system featuring controllable coupling.

This study examines the application of large-scale, pre-trained models (CLIP and HuBERT) to multilingual speech-image retrieval. In non-English scenarios, training distinct models for each language yields results that significantly surpass the current state-of-the-art, whereas a single model handling three languages also achieves performance comparable to prior benchmarks. We highlight critical distinctions in model behavior and efficacy between English and non-English contexts, likely stemming from the English-only nature of CLIP and HuBERT's pre-training. Furthermore, our models demonstrate capability in mono- and cross-lingual speech-text and speech-speech retrieval, even though they were never exposed to any parallel speech-text or speech-speech data during training.

This work examines the long-term dynamics of interfaces in two-component systems. Each component follows a one-dimensional Allen-Cahn equation subject to Neumann boundary conditions, small space-time white noise, and a symmetric double-well potential defined on the interval $[-\epsilon^{-1},\epsilon^{-1}]$, with the components coupled via an attractive linear force. Instantons are characterized as noise-free stationary solutions connecting two pure phases. We demonstrate that at time $t=\epsilon^{-1}$, as $\epsilon \rightarrow 0$, if the initial states are near an instanton, both components remain proximal to the same instanton, the center of which undergoes Brownian motion.

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) offer significant advantages for cosmic exploration due to their immense energy output, luminosity, and high redshifts. Several luminosity correlations within GRBs have already served as tools for testing cosmological models. Notably, a specific subset of long GRBs characterized by known redshifts and a plateau phase in their afterglow light curves exhibits a correlation between the rest-frame end time of this plateau and the corresponding X-ray luminosity. In this study, we re-examine this subsample and discover that the correlation becomes markedly tighter when a third parameter—the isotropic $\gamma$-ray energy release—is included. Furthermore, both long and intermediate-duration GRBs adhere to the same three-parameter correlation equation. We propose that this refined correlation supports the hypothesis that GRBs with afterglow plateaus originate from rapidly rotating magnetars, with the plateau phase resulting from continuous energy injection by the magnetar. Consequently, the newly formed millisecond magnetars associated with these GRBs may serve as effective standard candles for measuring cosmic distances.

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) is a Markov chain method designed to sample from a high-dimensional distribution defined by the density $e^{-f(x)}$, provided the gradient of $f$ is available. A key focus is the $d$-dimensional Gaussian distribution with covariance matrix $\Sigma$, where $f(x) = x^\top \Sigma^{-1} x$. We demonstrate that HMC can achieve a distribution $\varepsilon$-close in total variation distance using $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\kappa} d^{1/4} \log(1/\varepsilon))$ gradient queries, with $\kappa$ representing the condition number of $\Sigma$. Our approach employs Hamiltonian dynamics with long, random integration times. This strategy stands in contrast to, and was inspired by, recent findings establishing an $\widetilde\Omega(\kappa d^{1/2})$ query lower bound for HMC when using fixed integration times, even within the Gaussian setting.

This paper investigates the processes $e^+e^- \to J/\Psi \eta_c$, $J/\Psi \eta_c'$, $\psi' \eta_c$, and $\psi' \eta_c'$ using the light-cone formalism. The study demonstrates that, neglecting higher Fock state contributions, the required twist-3 distribution amplitudes can be uniquely derived from twist-2 distribution amplitudes via equations of motion. By employing models for these twist-2 amplitudes, the cross sections for the aforementioned processes were computed, yielding results consistent with Belle and BaBar experimental data. The analysis further reveals that relativistic and radiative corrections are essential for aligning theoretical predictions with experimental observations. A comparison with previous studies indicates that results from papers applying NRQCD to calculate these corrections are overestimated by approximately a factor of 1.5.

This research investigates a reaction-diffusion-convection system featuring nonlinear drift within a domain containing periodically distributed obstacles. The drift's nonlinearity arises from the hydrodynamic limit of a totally asymmetric simple exclusion process (TASEP), which models a population of interacting particles traversing an obstacle-filled region. Due to a large imposed drift scaling, this nonlinearity is anticipated to diverge as the scaling parameter approaches zero. To derive the upscaled model equations and determine the structure of effective transport tensors, we utilize two-scale formal homogenization asymptotics incorporating drift. Furthermore, we apply Schauder's fixed point theorem alongside monotonicity arguments to establish the weak solvability of the resulting upscaled model in an unbounded domain. Ultimately, this work aims to provide the theoretical insights necessary for designing thin composite materials capable of withstanding high-velocity impacts.

Gravitational microlensing offers a potential method for identifying low-amplitude pulsational variations. The transient brightness amplification during a microlensing event enhances the signal-to-noise ratio, thereby improving the detectability of pulsational features within light curves. This study investigates two main scenarios: first, the standard case where the point-source and point-lens approximation holds, and second, situations involving transit events (single lens) or caustic crossings (binary lens) where this approximation fails. In the first scenario, dividing the observed light curve by the best-fitted microlensing model yields residuals that reveal pulsational features with reduced uncertainties. In the second, residuals relative to a simple best-fit model exhibit more complex behavior. We utilize Monte-Carlo simulations of microlensing for pulsating variables directed toward the Galactic bulge to analyze surveys conducted by OGLE and KMTNet. Our results demonstrate that the efficiency for detecting pulsational signatures with intrinsic amplitudes less than 0.25 mag—specifically during single and binary microlensing events with a significance of $\Delta \chi^{2} > 350$—ranges from approximately 50% to 60%. This maximum efficiency is observed for pulsational periods of roughly 0.1 to 0.3 days. Furthermore, we examine the risk of misinterpreting high-magnification microlensing events of non-radially pulsating stars (NRPs) as planetary or binary microlensing events. We conclude that small asymmetric features near lightcurve peaks, caused by stellar pulsations, may be incorrectly diagnosed as crossings or close approaches to small caustic curves.

This paper builds upon our investigation into the geometry of the $p$-adic eigencurve at a point corresponding to a weight $1$ cuspform $f$ that is irregular at $p$ and possesses complex multiplication, along with its ramifications for Iwasawa and Hida theories. The study presents new findings, specifically by expressing the Fourier coefficients of specific non-classical $p$-adic modular forms within the generalized eigenspace of $f$ using $p$-adic logarithms of algebraic numbers. Furthermore, we calculate the enigmatic cross-ratios associated with the $p$-ordinary filtrations of the Hida families that include $f$.

The Heisenberg representation offers a potent method for analyzing quantum circuits, specifically those limited to the non-universal Clifford gates (H, S, and CNOT), a capability confirmed by the Gottesman-Knill theorem which enables efficient simulation of such circuits. We demonstrate that Gottesman's semantics for quantum programs can function as a type system, facilitating the efficient characterization of a standard subset of these programs. Furthermore, we show that this approach extends beyond the Clifford set to partially describe a wide array of programs. Finally, we utilize these types to analyze separable states and the superdense coding protocol.

Although the search for higher $P$-wave charmonium states remains an open question even after the identification of $2P$ charmonia, this work utilizes an unquenched quark model to demonstrate the spectroscopic properties of the $3P$, $4P$, and $5P$ families. For the $3P$ states, predicted masses near 4.2 GeV and their two-body open-charm decay patterns suggest that these states could be detected via open-charm channels arising from $\gamma\gamma$ fusion and $B$ decays at upcoming experiments such as LHCb and Belle II. Furthermore, we calculate the masses for the $4P$ and $5P$ charmonia. By combining these results, we observe that coupled-channel effects become increasingly significant as the radial quantum number rises, a trend well-explained by the modified Godfrey-Isgur model incorporating a screened potential.

This study introduces a control strategy designed to approach and fully reveal a partially occluded target object. The method relies exclusively on classified point cloud data captured by an in-hand camera mounted on the robot's end effector. Results demonstrate that the proposed controller progressively moves the robot into close proximity with the object, systematically exposing the neighborhood of every visible point, thereby enabling potential complete unveiling. The efficacy of this control scheme was validated through both simulations and physical experiments utilizing a UR5e robot equipped with an in-hand RealSense camera, testing its ability to uncover the stem of a grape within a mock-up vine environment.

This research examines the allocation of bailouts and subsidies to individuals within a financial network who face income shocks. Building upon the Eisenberg and Noe financial clearing framework, we integrate a bailout policy modeled after the discrete stimulus checks distributed globally during the COVID-19 economic relief efforts. We demonstrate that optimally distributing these bailouts across a financial network to maximize various social welfare objectives is computationally intractable. Consequently, we devise approximation algorithms to optimize these goals and prove guarantees regarding their approximation ratios. Furthermore, we incorporate multiple fairness constraints into the optimization models and determine the relative bounds of solutions with and without these constraints. Finally, we apply our methodology to diverse datasets, including real-world data on large financial institutions and semi-artificial data reflecting realistic societal interactions between people and businesses derived from mobility patterns. Our findings indicate that the proposed algorithms yield practical, reasonable results and surpass other network-based heuristics. We argue that viewing this problem from a societal perspective can assist policymakers in making well-informed decisions regarding subsidy issuance.

The performance of reinforcement learning (RL) agents is fundamentally tied to the variety of learning scenarios produced by their environments and the extent to which these environments mirror real-world conditions. Yet, current simulators fail to offer systematic support for modeling distributions regarding initial states and transition dynamics. Moreover, in intricate domains like soccer, the infinite scope of potential scenarios renders it impossible for any single research team to curate a complete collection for training, testing, and benchmarking RL algorithms. To resolve this challenge, we introduce, for the first time, the use of the formal scenario specification language SCENIC to intuitively model and generate interactive scenarios. By integrating SCENIC with the Google Research Soccer environment, we developed a platform named SCENIC4RL. Leveraging this platform, we present a dataset comprising 36 SCENIC-encoded scenario programs alongside demonstration data derived from a selected subset. We report experimental findings that validate the efficacy of our dataset and platform for training, testing, and evaluating RL algorithms. Crucially, we have open-sourced the platform to facilitate collective contributions from the RL community toward building a comprehensive scenario library.

It is a well-established fact that eavesdroppers can compromise quantum communication security by altering the angle of incoming light. Randomizing detector roles has been suggested as an effective defense against this specific attack. However, we demonstrate that this countermeasure can be circumvented if the attack is generalized to include additional variables. Leveraging experimental data from prior studies, we illustrate how randomization successfully thwarts the original attack but fails when Eve expands her strategy. Our findings and methodology offer a means to certify the security of free-space quantum communication receivers against all forms of detector-efficiency-mismatch attacks.

Retinal vessel networks, observable via fundus imaging, play a crucial role in diagnosing various systemic diseases beyond ocular conditions. Segmenting this vascular system facilitates specialized image analysis by enabling the quantification of morphological features. Consequently, numerous Deep Learning architectures have been investigated to automate this task.
