To overcome this, the study proposes architected electrodes featuring unit cells with spatially varying geometries optimized through computational methods. A resolved simulation approach is utilized to create a homogenized representation of these unit cells, providing effective properties that feed into a continuum model for the negative half-cell of a vanadium redox flow battery. Computational design optimization is then applied to identify porosity distributions that minimize power loss, resulting in architected porosity electrodes. When compared to conventional electrodes with uniform bulk porosity, these architected designs demonstrate enhanced power efficiency across a range of flow rates and current densities. Furthermore, the proposed design methodology was applied to scale up an electrode, achieving power efficiency comparable to bench-scale systems. Consequently, the variable porosity architecture and associated computational design framework presented here offer a new route for automatically generating spatially engineered electrode structures with improved power performance.

Pseudo-Boolean Optimization (PBO) and Maximum Satisfiability (MaxSAT) serve as natural optimization extensions of Boolean Satisfiability (SAT). Although straightforward mappings exist between PBO and MaxSAT, various algorithms have been developed specifically for each in recent years. This paper introduces Weighted Boolean Optimization (WBO), a unified framework that integrates and expands upon both PBO and MaxSAT. Furthermore, it presents a novel unsatisfiability-based algorithm for WBO, derived from recent MaxSAT approaches. Beyond standard MaxSAT, this algorithm solves weighted MaxSAT and PBO, supporting pseudo-Boolean constraints either natively or through translation into clausal form. Experimental findings demonstrate that unsatisfiability-based MaxSAT algorithms can be orders of magnitude more efficient than existing specialized methods. Finally, the study shows how algorithms designed for PBO or MaxSAT can be adapted to operate within the WBO framework.

How can embodied agents, which must both perceive and move, acquire visual representations? Current approaches typically rely on *tabula rasa* learning, where visual representations and locomotion are learned simultaneously from scratch, often aided by auxiliary tasks like predicting actions between observations. This paper demonstrates that a two-stage strategy is significantly more effective: (1) offline pretraining of visual representations using self-supervised learning (SSL) on large-scale pre-rendered indoor datasets (Omnidata), and (2) online finetuning of visuomotor representations for specific tasks using image augmentations over extended training schedules. We term this approach Offline Visual Representation Learning (OVRL). Through extensive experiments across three 3D datasets (Gibson, HM3D, MP3D), two navigation tasks (ImageNav, ObjectNav), and two policy algorithms (Reinforcement Learning and Imitation Learning), we found that OVRL representations yield substantial improvements over the state of the art. Specifically, performance on ImageNav increased from 29.2% to 54.2% (a 25% absolute, 86% relative gain), and on ObjectNav from 18.1% to 23.2% (a 5.1% absolute, 28% relative gain). Notably, the same visual encoder achieved these results while generalizing to datasets unseen during pretraining. Although pretraining benefits may wane or vanish with very long finetuning schedules, OVRL's performance gains continue to grow rather than diminish as the agent accumulates up to 2 billion frames of experience.

Radio interferometry enables astronomers to investigate minute spatial scales that single-dish telescopes often cannot access. Nevertheless, reconstructing the radio sky from interferometric data remains an ill-posed deconvolution challenge that has occupied researchers for fifty years. An even greater hurdle is achieving super-resolution imaging, which resolves details finer than the array's diffraction limit. To address this, we introduced a novel learning-based method for radio interferometric imaging, drawing upon recent breakthroughs in classical computer vision tasks such as single-image super-resolution (SISR) and deconvolution. We trained a high dynamic range residual neural network to map dirty images to the true radio sky, designating this procedure as POLISH, which contrasts with the conventional CLEAN algorithm. The feed-forward architecture of learning-based methods like POLISH is essential for processing data from the upcoming Deep Synoptic Array (DSA-2000). Our results demonstrate that POLISH achieves super-resolution and successfully deconvolves actual observations from the Very Large Array (VLA). Super-resolution capabilities on DSA-2000 will facilitate the measurement of shapes and orientations for hundreds of millions of star-forming radio galaxies, establishing it as a potent cosmological weak lensing survey and tool for probing dark energy. Furthermore, we project that it will effectively constrain the lensing power spectrum, offering a complementary approach to next-generation optical missions like Euclid.

Extreme Population A quasars, which accrete matter at exceptionally high rates and may involve super-Eddington massive black holes, could serve as a novel class of distance indicators spanning cosmic epochs from the present back to less than one billion years after the Big Bang. Beyond their utility in cosmology, these xA quasars hold fundamental significance for understanding active galactic nucleus (AGN) physics and host galaxy evolution, although their observational characteristics remain largely unexplored. Leveraging selection criteria derived from systematic variations along the quasar main sequence, researchers can identify xA quasars in substantial numbers across a wide redshift range using major optical surveys. Currently, a sample of approximately 250 quasars exists at low and intermediate redshifts, with larger samples readily obtainable from recent Sloan Digital Sky Survey data releases. Expanding this sample will clarify the intrinsic properties of xA quasars, which are expected to exhibit an extreme, well-defined Eddington ratio with minimal scatter compared to the general quasar population. Consequently, we propose a method to determine key cosmological parameters using redshift-independent "virial luminosity" estimates derived from emission line widths, a technique analogous to luminosity estimations in early and late-type galaxies. A critical challenge in applying xA quasar luminosity estimates to cosmology is identifying emission lines that show predominantly virial broadening across diverse redshifts and luminosities. This report outlines preliminary progress utilizing the AlIII 1860 intermediate ionization line and the Hydrogen Balmer line H-beta as virial broadening indicators, alongside a brief discussion of the method's future prospects based on xA quasars.

Spectre attacks and their numerous variants represent a novel class of vulnerabilities impacting modern processors by exploiting branch prediction structures to misdirect speculative execution. This paper introduces a defense mechanism utilizing Control-Flow Integrity (CFI)—a technique designed to prevent control-flow hijacking—applied to the committed execution path to mitigate the most severe Spectre variants, specifically Spectre-BTB and Spectre-RSB. CFI operates by restricting the destinations of indirect branches to a predefined set of legal targets derived from a control-flow graph (CFG). As CFI is increasingly integrated into both mainstream software (such as Windows and Android) and hardware (including Intel's CET and ARM's BTI), the necessary CFI data is now accessible via hardware extensions. Leveraging this information, our proposed solution, SPECCFI, extends CFI principles to constrain illegal control flow during speculation. It ensures that control flow instructions only target valid destinations to limit dangerous speculation on forward paths (indirect calls and branches). Additionally, we enhance this protection with a precise, speculation-aware hardware stack to restrict speculation on backward control-flow edges (returns). By integrating SPECCFI with existing defenses against branch target predictor attacks (Spectre-PHT), we address all known non-vendor-specific Spectre vulnerabilities. Our evaluation demonstrates that SPECCFI incurs minimal overhead regarding both performance and hardware complexity.

It has been proposed that type IIA string theory orientifold vacua containing fluxes can stabilize moduli and allow arbitrary decoupling between the AdS and Kaluza-Klein scales by taking specific unconstrained RR-flux quanta to infinity. In this study, we identify a new scalar field within the open-string sector that enables interpolation between such IIA vacua differing in flux quanta. We demonstrate that the limit of large fluxes aligns well with the distance conjecture. This indicates that massive IIA vacua satisfy a crucial Swampland criterion and implies that scale-separated AdS vacua may not belong to the Swampland. Furthermore, our analysis naturally points to a flux-based analogue of "Reid's fantasy," suggesting that flux vacua with distinct quantized flux numbers can be connected via trajectories in open-string field space rather than solely through singular domain walls.

We introduce a method to differentiate between zero-energy peaks arising from Majorana modes and those caused by other phenomena at finite temperatures. This approach involves substituting the standard metallic lead with a resistive lead (large $R$ in k$\Omega$) during tunneling spectroscopy. The significant dissipation effects introduced by the high resistance alter the tunneling conductance in distinct manners. Specifically, the Majorana peak continues to increase as temperature drops, following a $G \propto T^{2r-1}$ scaling for $r = e^2R/h < 1/2$. In contrast, zero-energy peaks originating from other effects split into two at finite temperatures, with the conductance at zero voltage bias exhibiting a power-law dependence on temperature. Furthermore, dissipative tunneling involving a Majorana mode falls into the same universal class as the unstable critical point observed in cases without a Majorana mode.

Recent advancements in natural language processing have led to state-of-the-art models and datasets of massive scale, posing significant challenges to sample-based explanation methods regarding interpretability, efficiency, and faithfulness. This study introduces a novel approach that enhances explanation interpretability by utilizing arbitrary text sequences as the unit of explanation. Furthermore, we implement a Hessian-free method that ensures model faithfulness. To facilitate a fair comparison with existing techniques, we propose a semantic-based evaluation metric that aligns more closely with human judgment than traditional diagnostic or re-training measures. Empirical results across multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms popular explanation techniques, such as Influence Functions and TracIn, on semantic evaluations.

Dark matter halo density profiles are typically modeled using fitting functions like NFW or Einasto; however, these approximations fail in the transition zone where halos are dominated by recently accreted material. In Paper I, we dynamically separated simulation particles into orbiting and infalling populations to analyze their distinct profiles. This work introduces simple yet precise fitting functions to capture the asymptotic behaviors of both components at large and small radii. The orbiting component is represented by a truncated Einasto profile, $\rho_{\rm orb} \propto \exp \left[-2/\alpha\ (r / r_{\rm s})^\alpha - 1/\beta\ (r / r_{\rm t})^\beta \right]$, featuring a five-parameter space that includes normalization, distinct physical scale and truncation radii, and exponents $\alpha$ and $\beta$ governing the steepening rate. The infalling component is modeled as a power law in overdensity that smoothly approaches a constant at the halo center. We demonstrate that these formulas reproduce averaged total profiles from simulations with approximately 5% accuracy across a vast parameter space encompassing halo mass, redshift, cosmology, and accretion rate. Furthermore, when fixing $\alpha = 0.18$ and $\beta = 3$, the orbiting term reduces to a three-parameter model that, on average, fits individual halos more effectively than the standard Einasto profile.

Let $N = \binom{n}{2}$ and $s \geq 2$. Consider $s$ independent permutations of the edge set $E(K_n)$ of the complete graph $K_n$, denoted as $e_{i,j}$ for $i=1,2,\ldots,N$ and $j=1,2,\ldots,s$. A {\em MultiTree} is defined as a subset $I \subseteq [N]$ such that the edge sets $E_{I,j}$ form spanning trees for each $j=1,2,\ldots,s$. This paper investigates the minimal value $m=m(n)$ for which the interval $[m]$ almost surely contains a MultiTree. We establish a hitting time result for the case $s=2$ and provide an upper bound of $O(n\log n)$ for $s \geq 3$.

There is a significant demand for spatial AI capable of executing complex visual tasks and collaborating effectively with humans. To meet this requirement, a visual SLAM system is needed that can rapidly adapt to novel scenes without pre-training and produce dense maps for subsequent tasks in real-time. Existing learning-based and non-learning-based visual SLAMs fail to fulfill these criteria due to inherent component limitations. This paper introduces Orbeez-SLAM, a visual SLAM that integrates implicit neural representation (NeRF) and visual odometry to achieve these objectives. Furthermore, Orbeez-SLAM operates using only RGB input from a monocular camera, ensuring broad applicability in real-world scenarios. We evaluate its performance across various challenging benchmarks, demonstrating that it is up to 800 times faster than strong baselines while delivering superior rendering results.

Diffusion models have earned widespread acclaim for their state-of-the-art ability to synthesize realistic objects from highly complex data distributions, even when conditioned on specific labels. However, their iterative sampling process is inherently computationally inefficient. To address this in multi-class conditional generation, we introduce a novel, structurally distinct framework where diffusion models are hierarchically branched based on intrinsic class relationships. We demonstrate that these branched models significantly enhance sampling efficiency across multiple classes. Additionally, we highlight other benefits, such as the ease of integrating new classes within a continual-learning environment and a unique interpretability that provides deeper insights into the generative process. Representing an alternative to traditional linear architectures, branched diffusion models offer transformative potential for efficient generation, online learning, and scientific discovery.

Program slicing condenses a program into a minimal version that preserves a specific computation, known as the slicing criterion. A recent multi-lingual approach called observation-based slicing (ORBS) speculatively removes code segments and then executes the program; if the behavior regarding the slicing criterion remains unchanged, the deletion is finalized. Although this method makes ORBS language-independent, it can generate unintuitive slices, particularly when the execution environment influences the outcome. For instance, ORBS might remove the statement "a = 0" if the variable 'a' already holds a zero value, as the deletion does not alter the slicing criterion's result. Consequently, slices may vary across different environments due to factors like initialization and call stack reuse. The proposed technique, nVORBS, addresses this issue by validating candidate slices across multiple distinct execution environments. An empirical study was conducted to gather initial insights into the frequency of such environment-induced slice variations, specifically comparing slices generated by seven different nVORBS configurations. Looking ahead, nVORBS represents a variation of metamorphic testing, suggesting that concepts from metamorphic testing could enhance dynamic program analysis.

The first author's dense lattice sphere packings, derived from orders within $\mathbb{Q}$-division rings, are now presented in algorithmically effective forms. These lattices arise by lifting appropriate codes from prime characteristic to orders $\mathcal{O}$ in such rings, and we establish a Minkowski--Hlawka type theorem for these lifts. By utilizing the extra symmetries provided by finite subgroups of units in $\mathcal{O}$, we demonstrate that this approach yields effective constructions of lattices that approach the best-known lower bounds for packing density $\Delta_n$ across several new dimensions $n$. Furthermore, this work unifies and broadens numerous earlier constructions.

Statistical relational AI and probabilistic logic programming have predominantly centered on discrete probabilistic models, primarily to facilitate the succinct modeling of independencies and to ensure efficient inference. For scalable inference within hybrid models, three specific types of independencies are crucial: conditional independencies elegantly captured by Bayesian networks, context-specific independencies naturally expressed through logical rules, and relational independencies among attributes of related objects succinctly modeled by combining rules. This paper presents DC#, a hybrid probabilistic logic programming language that merges the syntax and semantics of distributional clauses with those of Bayesian logic programs to qualitatively represent these three independence types. Furthermore, we introduce FO-CS-LW, a scalable inference algorithm for DC#. This method extends the context-specific likelihood weighting algorithm (CS-LW)—a novel sampling technique that leverages conditional and context-specific independencies in ground models—to the first-order domain by incorporating unification and combining rules.

Amorphous silicon films created via electron beam evaporation exhibit significantly higher atomic densities when grown at greater thicknesses, elevated temperatures, and slower deposition rates. These films approach crystalline silicon density when exceeding ~300 nm in thickness at 425 °C with deposition rates below 1 Å/sec. A suite of spectroscopic methods reveals details regarding atomic disorder, local strain, dangling bonds, and nanovoids. While electron diffraction indicates that short-range order remains consistent across all growth temperatures, fluctuation electron microscopy uncovers a previously unobserved form of medium-range order in films grown above room temperature. Raman spectroscopy data show that atomic disorder and local strain diminish as growth temperature rises and display a non-monotonic relationship with thickness. Dangling bond density drops with higher growth temperatures but varies only slightly with thickness. Analysis via positron annihilation Doppler broadening spectroscopy and electron energy loss spectroscopy confirms that reduced atomic density stems from nanovoids rather than density fluctuations within the network. Furthermore, specific heat and mechanical loss measurements, which assess the density of tunneling two-level systems alongside structural data, indicate that these systems in amorphous silicon films are linked to nanovoids and their immediate surroundings—essentially loosely bonded regions where atomic constraints are minimal.

This work examines global solutions for multidimensional Riemann problems associated with nonlinear hyperbolic conservation systems, emphasizing their overall configurations and internal structures. We highlight recent rigorous advancements in analyzing two-dimensional Riemann problems featuring transonic shock waves across various prototype hyperbolic conservation systems, while also addressing broader multidimensional Riemann issues and related nonlinear partial differential equations. Specifically, we illustrate four distinct two-dimensional Riemann problems using these prototypes, demonstrating how they can be recast and resolved as free boundary problems. In this formulation, the transonic shock waves serve as the free boundaries for the corresponding nonlinear conservation laws of mixed elliptic-hyperbolic type and associated nonlinear partial differential equations.

This paper demonstrates that gravity can arise as an effective field theory derived from an interacting quantum field theory by integrating out the fermionic degrees of freedom, provided the field equations satisfy Cauchy predictability. The gravitational source is identified with the quantum interactions inherent in the original QFT. This relationship closely mirrors the ER=EPR conjecture and underscores how the emergence of classical theories depends fundamentally on underlying quantum processes and interactions. We examine two specific scenarios to illustrate these findings: one where gravity is initially absent and another where it is present. The latter scenario yields first-order corrections to Einstein's equations, successfully reproducing established phenomena such as effective event horizons and gravitational birefringence.

Geometrical frustration gives rise to exotic quantum phenomena, including the spin-liquid phase, particularly in triangular and Kagom\'e lattices. According to the principle that the superconducting (SC) gap must change sign across a nesting wavevector, both intra-band and inter-band Fermi surface (FS) nesting can induce unique SC ground states characterized by $d$-wave and $s^{\pm}$ symmetries, respectively. In systems with an odd number of FSs, comparable strengths in multiple inter-band nestings can create frustration regarding the sign-reversal criterion between different FS sheets, thereby fostering novel SC order parameters. This study reports the experimental detection of a time-reversal symmetry breaking pairing state in Re$_2$Hf driven by FS nesting frustration. Additionally, electronic specific heat and transverse-field $\mu$SR measurements indicate a fully gaped pairing symmetry. First-principles electronic structure calculations confirm multiple FS sheets with similar inter-band nesting strengths. Utilizing {\it ab-initio} band structures, we calculated the spin-fluctuation mediated SC pairing symmetry, identifying an $s+is'$-pairing state that aligns with experimental findings. Our work highlights a new SC state, offering a valuable platform for both applied and fundamental research.

This study presents the design and performance evaluation of a 100 cm$^2$ SiPM-based photodetector intended as a PMT alternative. By aggregating signals from 94 SiPMs, the device achieves an output with a dark count rate below 100 cps across its entire surface when cooled with liquid nitrogen, alongside a signal-to-noise ratio exceeding 13 and a timing resolution superior to 5.5 ns. Operating on a 100 $\Omega$ differential line, the module delivers approximately 360 mW at 5 V and supports a dynamic range surpassing 500 photo-electrons. Additionally, the unit functions at room temperature, though its dark count rate increases by roughly six orders of magnitude under these conditions.

We introduce a novel operational meaning for nonclassicality in estimating nonequilibrium temperatures of bosonic baths under Gaussian dynamics and Gaussian state probing. We establish a bound on thermometry performance when utilizing classical probe states. Subsequently, we demonstrate that employing nonclassical probes, specifically single-mode and two-mode squeezed vacuum states, allows for a significant surpassing of this classical limit. Notably, we find that this enhancement is also attainable through Gaussian measurements. Consequently, we propose a fully Gaussian protocol for improved thermometry that is straightforward to implement within quantum optics platforms.

This study introduces a generalized model designed to investigate the growth of dislocation loops in irradiated binary Zr-based alloys. The framework incorporates temperature variations, loop-size-dependent efficiencies for absorbing point defects, the localized strength of grain boundary sinks, and the concentration of alloying elements. Applied to zirconium-niobium alloys under reactor neutron irradiation, the model simulates the dynamics of loop radius expansion. It examines how loop radii and strain evolve across different grain sizes, distances from grain boundaries, and niobium concentrations. Results indicate that the localized nature of grain boundary sinks causes non-uniform deformation within the grains. Furthermore, adding niobium as an alloying element reduces loop radii while simultaneously enhancing the growth of local strains inside the grains.

The capacity to manipulate multiple degrees of freedom within a high-dimensional Hilbert space, alongside the ability to entangle photons, has facilitated novel quantum protocols for diverse information processing tasks. This work introduces a method for generating and controlling polarization-path-frequency entanglement using components essential for executing a polarization-controlled quantum walk in both position and frequency domains. Hyperentangled states are realized through controlled dynamics within an interferometric configuration employing half-wave plates, beam splitters, and frequency shifters (such as electro-optic devices) to independently manipulate polarization, path, and frequency. The primary focus is on leveraging polarization to direct movement to specific values in frequency and position spaces. Furthermore, negativity calculations across subspaces are performed to validate the controllability of entanglement between them. Recent experimental advancements in realizing quantum walks using photonic states underscore the viability of this approach for generating hyperentangled states.

Deeply-inelastic scattering (DIS) is poised for a transformative era, driven by the anticipated precision initiatives at the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) and the Large Hadron-electron Collider (LHeC). Although these endeavors are critical for addressing persistent challenges in (non)perturbative QCD and understanding hadronic and nuclear structures, they also offer significant benefits across broader physics domains at the Energy and Intensity Frontiers, such as the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) and upcoming $\nu A$ experiments. This plenary talk outlines key instances of the potential High Energy Physics (HEP) impact arising from the synergistic EIC and LHeC programs, drawing insights from their respective Yellow Report and Whitepaper. Readers are invited to explore the comprehensive studies and literature referenced herein for further details.

We present a new deep-learning framework designed for significant image upscaling (e.g., 4x, 8x) by leveraging pristine high-resolution examples. The goal is to reconstruct high-resolution images from their downsampled counterparts. This system employs a multi-level progressive strategy, beginning with a 2x upscale and refining the result for higher magnifications (4x and 8x). The architecture is recursive, repeating the same process at each stage, and residual, as the network refines the output of a conventional upscaler. These network residuals are enhanced via Iterative Back-Projections (IBP) calculated within the feature space of a convolutional network. To support multi-level operations, we extend the standard back-projection algorithm using a recursion similar to Multi-Grid methods typically used to solve large systems of linear equations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the network can be viewed as a standard upsampling-and-filter approach utilizing a space-variant filter that adapts to geometric structures, providing insight into how the network learns to upscale. Ultimately, our system achieves state-of-the-art quality even with a relatively small number of parameters.

This study examines a general model of self-propelling agents interacting via pairwise potentials under noisy conditions with communication time delays. Building on previous findings [Phys. Rev. E 77, 035203(R) (2008)] that link coupling amplitude to pattern bifurcations induced by time delays, we expand these results by fully mapping the bifurcation structure within the mean field approximation. Our analysis establishes a direct correlation between dynamical behaviors in various regions of the coupling-time delay plane and the corresponding coherent swarm patterns observed in simulations. We calculate the spatio-temporal scales of these structures and illustrate how the complex interplay of coupling strength, time delay, noise intensity, and initial conditions influences the swarm. Specifically, we demonstrate that sufficiently high coupling strength or time delay creates a noise intensity threshold that drives the swarm from a misaligned to an aligned state. Furthermore, we show that when noise intensity varies over time, this alignment transition displays hysteresis.

We establish a non-asymptotic lower bound for the eigenspectrum of the design matrix in any linear bandit algorithm exhibiting sub-linear regret, provided the action set possesses well-behaved curvature. Specifically, we demonstrate that the minimum eigenvalue of the expected design matrix scales as $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ whenever the expected cumulative regret is $O(\sqrt{n})$, with $n$ representing the learning horizon, assuming the action space maintains a constant Hessian near the optimal arm. This finding indicates that such action spaces necessitate a polynomial lower bound, contrasting with the logarithmic lower bound established by \cite{lattimore2017end} for discrete (well-separated) action spaces. Moreover, whereas prior results are limited to the asymptotic regime ($n \to \infty$), our analysis for these "locally rich" action spaces yields an any-time guarantee. Under a mild technical condition, we also derive a comparable high-probability lower bound on the minimum eigenvalue. We apply these findings to two practical contexts: \emph{model selection} and \emph{clustering} within linear bandits. Regarding model selection, we prove that an epoch-based linear bandit algorithm adapts to true model complexity at an exponential rate relative to the number of epochs, utilizing our new spectral bound. For clustering, we examine a multi-agent framework where we show, by exploiting the spectral result, that forced exploration is unnecessary; agents can simultaneously execute a linear bandit algorithm and estimate their underlying parameters, thereby achieving low regret.

Contemporary analog computers excel at rapidly solving extensive systems of ordinary differential equations while maintaining low energy usage and restricted precision. This paper reviews N-body physics applied to a straightforward water model based on force fields commonly used in molecular dynamics. We present a configuration that simulates the temporal evolution of a single water molecule. To our knowledge, this is the first such simulation executed on an analog computer. Key implementation considerations, including scaling, data range, and circuit architecture, are emphasized. Furthermore, we evaluate the system's performance and contrast the results with a numerical method.

This paper introduces a novel concept formation method capable of incrementally learning and predicting labels for visual images. It combines convolutional image processing techniques from computer vision with a concept formation framework derived from psychological studies on how humans gradually develop and utilize concepts. The approach is experimentally assessed through an incremental adaptation of the MNIST digit recognition task. Performance is benchmarked against Cobweb, a concept formation model lacking convolutional capabilities, as well as two convolutional neural networks with varying levels of processing complexity. This research marks an initial step toward integrating modern computer vision principles with classical concept formation theories.

This study introduces a rapid, accurate, and informative ranking algorithm for pairwise comparisons by utilizing a generative data model that accounts for comparison noise. The algorithm outputs a confidence metric for each comparison and addresses the challenge of ranking numerous items from sparse, noisy data in various contexts, such as online gaming, document retrieval, and human perception analysis. While existing algorithms exist, there is a specific need for fast, large-scale solutions that maintain accuracy even when comparison data is limited. Our proposed model involves solving a non-convex optimization problem, which we approximate tightly using a sum of quasi-convex functions and a regularization term. By applying iterative reweighted minimization combined with the Primal-Dual Hybrid Gradient method, we developed PD-Rank. In simulated data matching our model—even with 10% erroneous comparisons—PD-Rank outperforms all comparable methods by 0.1 in Kendall tau, and it leads in accuracy when data follows the Bradley-Terry model. In both scenarios, PD-Rank is approximately ten times faster, completing tasks in seconds. Furthermore, on real-world data, PD-Rank achieves the same Kendall tau as active learning methods with significantly reduced computational time.

The Hoffman program for any real or complex square matrix $M$ linked to a graph $G$ originates from Hoffman's foundational research on the limit points for the spectral radius of adjacency matrices, noting that this radius does not exceed $\sqrt{2+\sqrt{5}}$. A signed graph $\dot{G}=(G,\sigma)$ consists of a simple graph $G=(V,E)$ and a sign function $\sigma: E(G)\rightarrow \{+1,-1\}$. This paper investigates the Hoffman program specifically for signed graphs, with the goal of identifying all such graphs whose spectral radius remains within the bound of $\sqrt{2+\sqrt{5}}$.

We demonstrate that the three-dimensional Thurston geometries satisfy the equations of motion for 3D new massive gravity as vacuum solutions. Furthermore, we examine their corresponding Lorentzian forms.

This research investigates $D^+\pi^-$, $D^0 \pi^+$, and $D^{*+}\pi^-$ final states utilizing 1.0 $fb^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data recorded at a 7 TeV center-of-mass energy by the LHCb detector. The $D_1(2420)^0$ resonance is detected within the $D^{*+}\pi^-$ channel, whereas the $D^*_2(2460)$ resonance appears in the $D^+\pi^-$, $D^0 \pi^+$, and $D^{*+}\pi^-$ channels; spin-parity assignments and properties are determined for both. Additionally, four resonances are identified between 2500 and 2800 MeV, comprising two with natural parity and two with unnatural parity. Furthermore, extra structures are noted near 3000 MeV across all three final states.

Time reversal invariant (TRI) topological superconductors (TSCs) and superfluids (TSFs) represent robust, symmetry-protected, gapped topological phases. This study investigates how these states evolve when subjected to time reversal symmetry breaking (TRB) fields and/or strong TRI fields, where TRB fields physically manifest as internal spin exchange fields arising from background magnetic order. Our findings indicate that fully gapped TSFs and TSCs are generally distinct from nodal states, separated by zero-temperature quantum critical points defined by generalized quantum Lifshitz fields with unique scaling behaviors. These emergent Lifshitz fields further govern the system's properties in the quantum critical regime at finite temperatures. Additionally, for specific subsets of TRB fields, we observe a precursor to bulk transitions where surface states display quantum critical behavior near zero field. Finally, we examine the possibility of a fully gapped TSF or TSC smoothly transitioning into a topologically trivial state without undergoing a phase transition.

This work investigates and demonstrates ranked sparsity, a natural phenomenon in modeling that arises when feature sets exhibit varying levels of information quality. Traditional and modern model selection techniques often fail in this context because they assume "covariate equipoise"—the idea that every potential parameter has an equal chance of inclusion. However, this assumption frequently breaks down, particularly with derived variables. For example, considering all possible interactions as candidates often violates covariate equipoise, leading to over-specified, opaque models. The sheer volume of additional candidates drastically increases false discoveries in interactions, creating unnecessarily complex and hard-to-interpret structures filled with spurious effects. We propose a strategy that demands stronger evidence before allowing specific variables, such as interactions, to enter the final model. This ranked sparsity approach can be executed using the sparsity-ranked lasso (SRL). Simulation studies comparing SRL against competing methods reveal that it is a highly effective technique due to its speed, accuracy, and ability to generate more transparent models with fewer false interactions. We further demonstrate its practical value by applying it to predict lung cancer survival using gene expression data and clinical covariates, with a specific focus on identifying gene-environment interactions.

Magnetars, which are isolated neutron stars characterized by magnetic fields typically exceeding $10^{14}$ G, display unique outburst periods lasting several months. During these events, researchers frequently observe the evolution of soft X-ray pulse profiles alongside nonthermal magnetospheric emissions. By utilizing near-daily NICER data covering the first 37 days of a recent outburst decay from SGR 1830-0645, we clearly detected a phase migration of pulse peaks. This migration caused the pulse morphology to shift from an initial triple-peaked structure to a single-peaked one; such merging of peaks has not previously been recorded in magnetars. Our high-resolution, phase-resolved spectroscopic analysis indicates that while the initial pulse shape was complex, there was no significant temperature evolution. However, the inferred surface hot spots contracted during both the peak migration and the overall outburst decay. We propose two potential mechanisms for this evolution: first, internal surface heating driven by crustal tectonic motion, with an inferred speed of $\lesssim100$ m day$^{-1}$, constraining the driving region's density to $\rho\sim10^{10}$ g cm$^{-3}$ at a depth of approximately 200 m. Second, the hot spots may be heated by particle bombardment from a twisted magnetosphere containing flux tubes or ropes, analogous to solar coronal loops, which untwist and dissipate over a 30-40 day timescale. Consequently, the peak migration could result from a combination of field-line footpoint motion (driven by crustal activity) and evolving surface radiation beaming. This novel dataset vividly illustrates the dynamics of magnetar outbursts while underscoring the necessity for a more comprehensive theoretical framework that integrates both the magnetosphere and the crust.

Quantum phase transitions are fundamental to explaining how matter displays drastically different behaviors at extremely low temperatures when microscopic parameters shift slightly. However, pinpointing these transitions remains a significant challenge both theoretically and experimentally. This study demonstrates that deliberately driving systems out of equilibrium through sudden quenches offers a viable method for identifying quantum phase transitions. We find that these transitions leave unique signatures in the intermediate-time dynamics and post-equilibration outcomes of local observables within quantum-chaotic spin chains. Additionally, we reveal that the effective temperature of the resulting thermal-like states can display minima near quantum critical points. Finally, we outline experimental verification using Rydberg atoms and investigate nonequilibrium indicators of quantum criticality in models featuring topological transitions.

We present nuclear spin-lattice relaxation rate measurements for $^{63}$Cu and $^{65}$Cu in cuprous oxide (Cu$_2$O), conducted using zero-field Cu nuclear quadrupole resonance at temperatures ranging from 77 to 325 K. Based on these detailed isotopic data, we determined a finite magnetic relaxation rate, $^{63}W_M$, alongside a dominant nuclear quadrupole relaxation rate, $^{63}W_Q$. The temperature dependence of $^{63}W_Q$ followed a $T^{2.1}$ trend, whereas $^{63}W_M$ varied as either $T^{1.6}$ or $T^{\beta}\mathrm{exp}(-\it\Delta/T)$, with $\beta$ = 0.6(3) and $\it\Delta$ = 190(62) K. We further explored the nuclear spin scattering mechanism arising from a non-degenerate Fermi gas as a potential source for the observed magnetic relaxation.

In an economy driven by data, datasets hold substantial economic worth. Consequently, creators who invest resources in gathering and refining data are motivated to prevent unauthorized usage, necessitating technical proof of ownership when misuse occurs. Dataset watermarking offers a solution for this verification and can discourage illicit use. This paper examines a recently proposed method called "radioactive data" to determine its viability for proving ownership of image datasets utilized in training machine learning (ML) models. While the original study indicated that radioactive data works well in white-box environments, our findings reveal that its effectiveness diminishes in scenarios with a low number of classes ($\leq 30$) or few samples per class ($\leq 500$). Conversely, we demonstrate that black-box verification remains effective across all tested datasets, even when white-box verification fails. Based on this, we propose enhancing white-box verification confidence by incorporating watermarked samples directly into the process. Additionally, we emphasize the critical need to evaluate the robustness of radioactive data for ownership demonstration, noting that this constitutes an adversarial context distinct from standard provenance identification.

Compared to the more widely studied field of ML model watermarking, which is often vulnerable to model extraction attacks, radioactive data shows resilience against such threats. This suggests its potential utility in verifying ML model ownership in a manner robust to extraction attacks.

We demonstrate that for any family $\mathcal{T}$ of distinct triangles defined on $n$ vertices, the absence of a rainbow triangle—comprising three edges from different members of $\mathcal{T}$ that collectively form a triangle—implies that $|\mathcal{T}| \le \frac{n^2}{8}$. We further establish the sharpness of this bound and identify the extremal configurations. Additionally, we examine a variant where triangles need not be distinct, proving that the same asymptotic limit applies. Following the initial release of this paper on arXiv, we discovered that the sharp upper bound of $\frac{n^2}{8}$ was established earlier by Gy\H{o}ri (2006) and independently by Frankl, F\"uredi, and Simonyi (unpublished). Notably, Gy\H{o}ri also derived a stronger result for scenarios allowing repetitions.

Graph-based collaborative filtering has garnered growing research attention due to its ability to extract rich collaborative signals from high-order interactions. Traditionally, user and item embeddings are constructed within Euclidean spaces via graph propagation. However, recent studies highlight that high-order interactions often exhibit tree-like structures, a domain where hyperbolic geometry excels. Despite this, interaction graphs inherently possess hybrid and nested geometric properties that single-geometry models fail to capture effectively. To address this limitation, we introduce a hybrid geometric space that leverages the strengths of both Euclidean and hyperbolic geometries to learn more expressive representations of user-item interactions. Experiments on public datasets confirm the efficacy of our approach.

Predicting protein structures rapidly and accurately remains a central challenge in structural biology, biotechnology, and molecular medicine, as three-dimensional models are essential for the rational design of proteins with enhanced or new functionalities. While X-ray crystallography remains the predominant method despite its limitations, NMR-based techniques are increasingly favored. Typically, structure prediction relies on distance restraints, yet simple NMR triple-resonance experiments often suffice for determining the structures of small proteins. Historically, protein folding simulations incorporating experimental data have assigned weights to experimental information and physical force fields in an arbitrary manner, limiting the method's generalizability to novel proteins. Moreover, these approaches necessitate a complete and nearly error-free assignment of chemical shifts derived from NMR due to their deterministic nature. This thesis introduces Chemshift, a component within the Phaistos protein structure determination software designed to manage chemical shift assignments. Implemented within a probabilistic framework, Chemshift handles both the assignment of experimental data and the weighting relative to physical terms without discarding any data. Given a partial assignment of NMR peaks, the module refines these assignments to facilitate protein folding with minimal bias.

This study presents a geometrically rigorous nonlinear analysis of elastic shells within the framework of finite, albeit small, strain theory. The primary focus lies in introducing the full shell metric and assessing its impact on nonlinear structural behavior. By utilizing the precise relationship between reference and equidistant strains, a comprehensive analytic elastic constitutive relation is derived via the reciprocal shift tensor, linking energetically conjugated forces and strains. Using these strict relations, the geometric stiffness matrix is explicitly formulated through the variation of the unknown metric, with a compact representation also provided. Although the Kirchhoff-Love hypothesis assumes linear displacement distribution, a nonlinear strain distribution emerges along the shell thickness; this aspect is frequently overlooked in thin shell analyses based on initial geometry, neglecting the shell's increasing curvature in subsequent configurations. The research demonstrates that the shell's curvature at any given configuration dictates the appropriate formulation. For shells that develop significant curvature during deformation, accounting for the nonlinear strain distribution through the thickness is essential for accuracy. Four computational models were evaluated: one relying on the full analytical constitutive relation and three simplified variants. Selected numerical experiments assessed the robustness, efficiency, and accuracy of the proposed formulation. The key finding is that employing the full metric is often necessary to capture the complete response of shells, even those initially thin. Finally, a simplified model offering the optimal balance between efficiency and accuracy is recommended for the nonlinear analysis of strongly curved shells.

Augmented Reality represents a promising avenue for human-machine interaction, particularly within robotics where systems operate within specific environments. It is advantageous to present visualizations and solicit user input directly within these surroundings. This study investigates the concept using the Microsoft HoloLens to capture indoor spaces and render interaction cues for recognized object categories. As the user navigates, the 3D mesh recorded by the device is annotated in real-time with semantic classes via a projective method, enabling the application of advanced 2D semantic segmentation techniques. These results are integrated onto the mesh, where significant object segments are identified and projected in 3D for the user to view. Furthermore, users can initiate actions by gesturing toward the objects. The paper provides qualitative findings and offers a detailed analysis of the method's accuracy and performance using an indoor dataset.

Quantum secret sharing (QSS) serves as a fundamental building block for the emerging quantum internet, enabling secure communication among multiple parties. Nevertheless, constructing a large-scale QSS network remains a formidable challenge because of channel attenuation and the necessity for multiphoton interference or high-fidelity multipartite entanglement distribution. In this work, we introduce a three-user QSS protocol that operates without monitoring signal disturbance while guaranteeing unconditional security. We demonstrate that the final key rate of our protocol surpasses the Pirandola-Laurenza-Ottaviani-Banchi bound for quantum channels, with simulated transmission distances exceeding 600 km using existing technologies. These findings provide a pathway toward implementing high-rate, large-scale QSS networks.

In 1983, Borowiecki and Jóźwiak introduced an open problem regarding the characterization of graphs with purely imaginary per-spectra. The most comprehensive result to date, a partial solution from 2004 by Yan and Zhang, established that graphs devoid of an even subdivision of $K_{2,3}$ possess a purely imaginary per-spectrum. Subsequently, Zhang and Li demonstrated in 2012 that such graphs are planar and admit a Pfaffian orientation. This paper details the construction of graphs with purely imaginary per-spectra that do contain an even subdivision of $K_{2,3}$, encompassing both planar and nonplanar cases, through the coalescence of rooted graphs.

The non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE), a defining characteristic of non-Hermitian systems, describes the accumulation of bulk-band eigenstates at the boundaries when open boundary conditions are applied. This study examines how NHSE behaves under electric fields through analytical calculations of the dynamical evolution of initial bulk states and numerical computations of spectral winding numbers, eigenstate distributions, and dynamical trajectories. We demonstrate that both DC and AC fields exert significant control over NHSE, driven by the interplay among Stark localization, dynamic localization, and the NHSE itself. Furthermore, finite-size analysis of non-Hermitian systems subjected to a pure DC field reveals a size-dependent NHSE phenomenon. We also propose an electronic circuit scheme to implement the discussed model. These findings aim to enhance the comprehension of NHSE and its manipulation.

The light-cone gauge method applied to $T\overline{T}$ deformed models yields the $T\overline{T}$ deformed matrix nonlinear Schrödinger equation, the Landau--Lifshitz equation, and the Gardner equation. This work provides a detailed analysis of one-soliton solutions for the $T\overline{T}$ deformed nonlinear Schrödinger and Korteweg--de Vries equations. Specifically, the deformed NLS soliton demonstrates the phenomenon of particle width widening or narrowing; whether the soliton expands or contracts relies not merely on the sign of the deformation parameter but also on specific soliton and potential parameters. Furthermore, the $T\overline{T}$ deformed KdV equation supports a one-parameter family of one-soliton solutions beyond the standard velocity parameter. This additional parameter alters soliton characteristics, notably by influencing the dispersion relation.

To examine dust characteristics within the nuclear regions of quasars, we analyzed the extinction curves of the FeLoBAL quasar SDSS J163004.29+311957.6 along with two analogous objects. The parameterized curves reveal a 2175 \AA~ bump in the underlying extinction, a feature consistent with observations in the Local Group and a subset of high-redshift star-forming galaxies. Compared to the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), the bumps detected here align much more closely with those found in the Milky Way (MW). These features, alongside similar 2175 \AA~ bumps in high- and low-ionization BAL quasars identified by Zhang et al., likely represent counterparts to the 2175 \AA~ bump in quasar environments. Generally, the dust grains responsible for these features are small, susceptible to disruption by high-energy photons, and struggle to survive the intense radiation fields of active galactic nuclei (AGN). Nevertheless, the 2175 \AA~ bump appears frequently in BAL quasars due to absorption-line outflows. The shielding provided by outflow clouds likely facilitates the assembly of MW-like dust grains or prolongs their survival in the quasar nucleus. Further observational studies are required to understand the physical and chemical conditions governing this process.

Underwater experiments at ultrasonic frequencies demonstrate the negative refraction of acoustic waves using a three-dimensional locally resonant acoustic metafluid composed of soft porous silicone-rubber micro-beads suspended in a yield-stress fluid. By measuring the refraction angle of an acoustic beam passing through a prism-shaped metafluid and applying Snell's law, the acoustic index relative to water is determined. These experimental results align excellently with calculations based on Multiple Scattering Theory, confirming that negative refraction is contingent upon the volume fraction ($\Phi$) of the resonant micro-beads. While only positive refraction is observed in a diluted metafluid ($\Phi=3\%$), negative refraction is successfully demonstrated across a wide frequency band in a concentrated metafluid ($\Phi=17\%$).

Machine learning encompasses a vast array of techniques, each with unique benefits and use cases. This paper focuses on one such approach: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). As deep neural networks utilizing a specialized linear operation known as convolution, CNNs rely on this mechanism as their defining feature, making it the central topic of this study. The analysis begins with the theoretical underpinnings of convolutions and CNNs, then explores enhancements and augmentations designed to expand the method's ability to estimate diverse function classes. Specifically, the paper examines two improvement strategies: the use of locally connected layers to reduce translation invariance, and tiled convolution to learn more complex invariances than standard convolution allows. Additionally, the application of the Fast Fourier Transform is highlighted for boosting computational efficiency. The discussion subsequently covers two highly effective practical applications: the YOLO architecture, a state-of-the-art model for image object classification that precisely identifies bounding boxes, and tumor detection in mammography, where CNNs achieve 7.2% higher specificity than human doctors with only 0.3% lower sensitivity. Finally, the paper briefly addresses the ethical and regulatory concerns arising from technologies that surpass human performance across various domains.

Tidal disruption events (TDEs) are typically identified via their transient activity in optical or X-ray bands. A defining characteristic of X-ray-detected TDEs is "supersoft" X-ray emission, a feature unique to this class among extragalactic sources, except for a few rapidly variable hyper-luminous X-ray sources (HLXs) or supersoft active galactic nuclei (AGN), which can be distinguished by their optical signatures. Our objective is to identify extragalactic supersoft sources linked to galactic centers, a category expected to contain overlooked TDEs, supersoft AGN, and nuclear HLXs. Detecting these sources would enable the investigation of accretion in extreme regimes across various black hole mass scales. To achieve this, we conducted a blind search for supersoft X-ray sources (SSS) by cross-correlating optical and X-ray catalogs to isolate extragalactic near-nuclear candidates, subsequently filtering for steep spectra (photon index $\Gamma>3$) and high luminosities ($L_X>10^{41}$~erg~s$^{-1}$). This approach yielded approximately 60 sources, including 15 previously identified supersoft AGN or TDEs, thereby validating our selection method. Among the remaining 36 sources, which exhibit unusually steep spectra, optical classification confirms them as AGN. The final group consists of nine previously unknown sources displaying spectral properties consistent with either extremely soft-excess dominated AGN (five sources) or TDEs (four sources). Follow-up observations with {\it XMM-Newton} on one of these candidates confirmed its likely TDE nature. This study represents the first effort to discover TDEs based on spectral characteristics rather than variability, successfully retrieving known TDEs and identifying new extreme ultrasoft sources, including four new TDE candidates, one of which has been verified through follow-up data.

Observational data strongly indicate active meteorology within brown dwarf atmospheres, evidenced by near-infrared brightness fluctuations. Clouds play a pivotal role in defining these atmospheres' thermal structures and spectral characteristics; however, the underlying mechanisms driving variability remain uncertain. Existing one-dimensional and global circulation models are limited by resolution and cannot fully address this complexity. To overcome these constraints, this study employs a convectively resolving model coupled with grey-band radiative transfer to examine the interaction between convective dynamics and cloud variability across a broad temperature range and a spatial domain spanning hundreds of kilometers. The model incorporates six cloud types with microphysics that include settling processes, utilizing Rosseland mean coefficients for radiative activity. For the first time in three dimensions, the study demonstrates how radiative cloud feedback can spontaneously induce variability in both temperature and cloud structure. Among the cloud types, silicates exert the most significant influence on thermal structure, occasionally generating secondary convective layers depending on particle size, while iron and aluminum clouds also substantially impact the atmosphere. Computed thermal spectra reveal that clouds primarily smooth spectral features at optical wavelengths. When compared to observed L and T dwarfs on the color-magnitude diagram, most simulated atmospheres appear redder, though simulations including cloud holes align more closely with actual observations.

The Standard Model (SM), often regarded as the pinnacle of particle physics, has successfully passed many experimental tests. Yet, it fails to account for certain observations, such as dark matter and the universe's matter-antimatter asymmetry. To address these gaps, the SM can be expanded by introducing new particles and interactions, a concept collectively known as "new physics" (NP). The findings presented in this article offer a significant potential avenue for discovering these new elements.

This study investigates the cosmic infrared background (CIB) as a large-scale structure tracer for cross-correlating with the CMB to leverage the Integrated Sachs-Wolfe (ISW) effect. Utilizing the refined linear CIB model by Maniyar et al. (2018), we derive theoretical CIB-ISW cross-correlations for Planck HFI frequencies (217, 353, 545, and 857 GHz) and IRAS 3000 GHz. Our predictions indicate a positive cross-correlation between the CIB and CMB that diminishes rapidly at small scales. A signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) analysis reveals that, in an ideal scenario covering 70% (or 40%) of the sky free from residual contaminants like galactic dust, the SNR ranges from 4.2 to 5.6 (or 3.2 to 4.3), peaking at 857 GHz. Fisher matrix analysis suggests that detecting an ISW signal with such high SNR over 40% of the sky would significantly tighten cosmological parameter constraints, improving dark energy equation-of-state limits by 80%. However, a more realistic assessment incorporating residual galactic dust contamination shows that dust power spectra, which dominate at the lower multipoles of interest, drastically reduce the SNR, rendering ISW detection challenging. Even with conservative 10% residual dust levels in the CIB power spectra, the SNR drops sufficiently to make detection difficult. Testing the method's feasibility on current maps, we measured the cross-correlation between CIB and CMB Planck maps over the 11% GASS field in the southern hemisphere. Given the limited sky coverage and existing dust residuals, we found no detectable ISW signal, with results consistent with zero. To limit SNR degradation to no more than 10% over a 40% sky area, we conclude that galactic dust must be cleaned down to a 0.01% level on the power spectrum.

In recent years, Economic Model Predictive Control (EMPC) has garnered substantial interest as a leading advanced control strategy for future smart manufacturing. While EMPC enhances economic outcomes, it also substantially increases computational demands, making model approximation a standard technique for mitigating this complexity. This study evaluates three representative approximation methods applied to EMPC: first-principle-based model reduction (such as proper orthogonal decomposition), system identification from input-output data (yielding explicit mathematical models via subspace identification), and neural network approaches also based on input-output data. A representative algorithm was selected for each method. To assess computational complexity and economic performance, two benchmark processes with distinct dynamic characteristics and complexities were chosen: an alkylation process and a wastewater treatment plant (WWTP). Based on simulation results, the advantages and limitations of each approach are summarized, concluding with proposed directions for future research in control-oriented model approximation.

Machine learning algorithms derive their efficacy from extracting meaningful features within vast datasets. As both models and data scales grow, methods capable of distilling large datasets into compact yet highly effective subsets will become increasingly valuable for enhancing training efficiency and feature extraction. To this end, we introduce a novel distributed kernel-based meta-learning framework that achieves state-of-the-art performance in dataset distillation using infinitely wide convolutional neural networks. For example, by utilizing merely 10 data points (representing 0.02% of the original dataset), we achieved over 65% test accuracy on the CIFAR-10 image classification task, a substantial leap from the previous best result of 40%. Our state-of-the-art findings generalize across multiple configurations for MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN. Additionally, we conduct preliminary analyses of our distilled datasets to investigate how they diverge from naturally occurring data.

Social recommender systems are theoretically designed to boost recommendation accuracy by leveraging social data, particularly when user-item interaction records are sparse. Despite this promise, industry observations indicate that these systems often underperform in real-world applications. Research identifies three primary causes for this failure: (1) most users possess only a few social connections, rendering social relations ineffective for them; (2) social ties are inherently noisy yet are often applied indiscriminately; and (3) the assumption that social relations are universally applicable across contexts is flawed, as they actually exhibit heterogeneous strengths depending on the scenario. Current models typically focus solely on homophily while ignoring these critical limitations. To address these issues, we introduce a deep adversarial framework built upon Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). Specifically, to tackle the first two challenges, we develop a GCN-based autoencoder that enriches relational data by encoding high-order and complex connectivity patterns, while enforcing a reconstruction constraint on social profiles to ensure the validity of identified neighborhoods. Once purified social relations are established for each user, we employ a GCN-based attentive social recommendation module to handle the third challenge by capturing the varying strengths of these relations. Finally, adversarial training is utilized to integrate all components through a Minimax game, ensuring coordinated optimization to enhance overall recommendation performance. Comprehensive experiments across multiple open datasets demonstrate the framework's superiority, and ablation studies validate the significance and efficacy of each proposed component.

Extracting keyphrases that effectively represent a document remains a difficult challenge. Over recent years, numerous keyword detection strategies have been developed, ranging from statistical frequency analyses of tokens to specialized neural language models and graph-based structures derived from the document itself. Among these, graph-based methods stand out for their computational efficiency while sustaining high retrieval performance. A defining characteristic of such methods is their immediate transformation of token space into graphs before further processing. This paper introduces a novel unsupervised approach that merges document segments into a sequential format prior to graph construction. Additionally, by utilizing Personalized PageRank—which factors in both the frequencies of these sub-phrases and token lengths during node ranking—we demonstrate state-of-the-art retrieval capabilities. This method achieves results up to two orders of magnitude faster than leading unsupervised detectors like YAKE and MultiPartiteRank. Furthermore, the approach's scalability was validated by generating keyphrases for a biomedical corpus containing 14 million documents in under a minute.

Current video conferencing systems struggle with degraded user experiences when network conditions worsen, as existing codecs fail to function effectively at extremely low bitrates. While recent neural approaches attempt to reconstruct talking-head videos at such bitrates using sparse frame representations like facial landmarks, they often fail during significant movement or occlusions and do not scale to higher resolutions. To address this, we introduce Gemino, a novel neural compression system for video conferencing built upon a high-frequency-conditional super-resolution pipeline. Gemino upscales a very low-resolution target frame by enhancing high-frequency details—such as skin texture and hair—using information derived from a single high-resolution reference image. By employing a multi-scale architecture that processes model components at varying resolutions, Gemino scales to resolutions comparable to 720p. Additionally, the system is personalized to learn individual-specific details, significantly improving fidelity at low bitrates. Implemented atop aiortc, an open-source Python WebRTC library, Gemino operates in real-time on 1024x1024 videos using an A100 GPU, delivering 2.9 times lower bitrate than traditional codecs while maintaining equivalent perceptual quality.

Gapped graphene has been suggested as an ideal system for observing the valley Hall effect, a transport phenomenon involving electron flow characterized by distinct valley indices. However, this study demonstrates that the effect is more accurately understood as a manifestation of the orbital Hall effect. In this framework, the ambiguous "valley" indices are substituted with the orbital magnetic moment, a physical quantity defined consistently across the entire Brillouin zone. This reformulation eliminates the arbitrariness associated with selecting cut-off values for valley-restricted integrals in valley Hall conductivity; instead, the orbital Hall conductivity is defined as a Brillouin zone integral of a newly introduced quantity known as the orbital Berry curvature. Furthermore, expressing the phenomenon in terms of the orbital Hall effect offers a direct explanation for the accumulation of opposite orbital moments at sample edges, a feature previously detected in Kerr rotation measurements.

We present an alternative approach to applying the Maurey-Nikishin-Pisier factorisation within Fourier restriction theory. Utilizing an induction-on-scales technique, our relatively straightforward method is applicable to any compact quadratic surface, including compact sections of the paraboloid and the hyperbolic paraboloid. This is accomplished by constructing near-extremisers with substantial "mass," a construction that may hold independent interest.

In the semileptonic decays of heavy baryons and mesons, the lepton-mass dependence isolates into the quadratic $\cos^2	heta$ term of the differential $\cos	heta$ distribution; we refer to this normalized coefficient as the convexity parameter. This insight enables a test of lepton universality in heavy hadron decays that remains independent of form-factor effects. By extracting the quadratic rate coefficient, removing the lepton-mass factor, and limiting the phase space integration to the $	au$ lepton region, one can define optimized partial rates that are identical across all three $(e,\mu,	au)$ channels within a specific semileptonic decay according to the Standard Model. We examine how New Physics can disrupt this equality. Furthermore, we analyze semileptonic decays of heavy mesons, including $ ar{B}^0 	o D^{(\ast)+} \ell^-  ar
u_\ell$ and $B_c^- 	o J/\psi (\eta_c)\ell^-  ar
u_\ell$, as well as heavy baryon decays such as $\Lambda_b 	o \Lambda_c \ell^-  ar
u_\ell$, for each lepton flavor $\ell=e,\mu,	au$.

The Mpemba effect refers to the phenomenon where a hot system cools more rapidly than an identical one starting at a lower temperature. While experimental studies, such as those involving water and clathrate hydrates, typically define this effect by the timing of phase transitions, existing theoretical research has not accounted for such timing, and most abstract models lack phase transitions entirely. This work employs phenomenological Landau theory to pinpoint the time of second-order phase transitions and provides a concrete demonstration that the Mpemba effect can indeed occur within such models.

Reinforcement learning (RL) often struggles with high-dimensional observations, a challenge that data augmentation has recently addressed by encoding invariances directly from raw pixels. However, our empirical findings reveal that not all samples hold equal value, and indiscriminately adding more augmented inputs can actually destabilize Q-learning. To address this, we propose a model-agnostic Contrastive-Curiosity-Driven Learning Framework (CCLF), designed to fully leverage sample importance and enhance learning efficiency through self-supervised methods. Powered by our contrastive curiosity mechanism, CCLF prioritizes experience replay by selecting the most informative augmented inputs and, crucially, regularizes both the Q-function and the encoder to focus on under-learned data. Additionally, it incentivizes exploration via a curiosity-based reward. Consequently, agents utilizing CCLF can concentrate on high-value samples and learn representation invariances more effectively, even with significantly fewer augmented inputs. We tested CCLF across several base RL algorithms on the DeepMind Control Suite, Atari, and MiniGrid benchmarks, demonstrating superior sample efficiency and learning performance compared to other state-of-the-art approaches.

Investigating user interests represents a critical yet difficult challenge in recommender systems, one that mitigates the closed-loop feedback between models and user interactions. While contextual bandit (CB) algorithms aim to balance exploration and exploitation to reveal latent user preferences, traditional CB methods are restricted to small, sampled item sets (typically hundreds). This limitation confines their application to specific scenarios such as post-ranking, homepage top-item selection, ad creative choice, or online A/B testing. This paper presents two straightforward yet effective hierarchical CB algorithms that enable classical models like LinUCB and Thompson Sampling to explore the entire item space rather than just a limited subset. First, we build a hierarchical item tree using a bottom-up clustering approach to structure items from coarse to fine granularity. Second, we introduce the Hierarchical CB (HCB) algorithm, which treats exploration as a sequence of decisions aimed at finding a path from the root to a leaf node, with feedback propagated backward along that path. Furthermore, we propose the Progressive Hierarchical CB (pHCB) algorithm, which gradually expands visible nodes once they meet a specific confidence threshold, thereby preventing misleading decisions at higher levels during the sequential process. Extensive experiments on two public recommendation datasets validate the effectiveness and flexibility of these proposed methods.

The Nona-Bayer colour filter array (CFA) pattern stands as a leading alternative to conventional Bayer patterns. However, despite its significant benefits, these non-Bayer configurations are prone to generating visual artefacts when reconstructing RGB images from noisy sensor data. This research comprehensively tackles the challenge of learning RGB reconstruction from noisy Nona-Bayer CFA data. We introduce a novel spatial-asymmetric attention module that jointly learns bi-directional transformations and large-kernel global attention to mitigate visual artefacts. By integrating this module with adversarial learning, we generate realistic images from Nona-Bayer CFA inputs. The proposed method's effectiveness has been validated and benchmarked against state-of-the-art reconstruction techniques. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach successfully reconstructs RGB images from noisy Nona-Bayer CFA without introducing visually disturbing artefacts, outperforming existing methods in both qualitative and quantitative assessments. Source code is available at: https://github.com/sharif-apu/SAGAN_BMVC21.

This paper details the WLV-RIT submission for the 2020 HASOC shared task on identifying hate speech and offensive content in Indo-European languages. The HASOC 2020 organizers supplied participants with annotated datasets comprising social media posts in code-mixed Dravidian languages, specifically Malayalam-English and Tamil-English. We focused on Task 1, which involved identifying offensive comments in code-mixed Malayalam from YouTube. Our approach leveraged existing English data by employing cross-lingual contextual word embeddings and transfer learning to generate predictions for Malayalam text, with further performance gains achieved through various fine-tuning strategies. Ultimately, our system attained a weighted average F1 score of 0.89 on the test set, securing 5th place among 12 participants.

This study searches for pairs of light pseudoscalar bosons with masses between 4 and 15 GeV, produced via the decay of the 125 GeV Higgs boson. The analysis examines final states where one pseudoscalar decays into two tau leptons, and the other decays into either two tau leptons or two muons. Data were collected by the CMS experiment from 2016 proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. By combining the 4$\tau$ and 2$\mu$2$\tau$ channels, the search constrains the product of the Higgs boson production cross section and its branching fraction into the 4$\tau$ final state ($\sigma\mathcal{B}$), utilizing the linear relationship between the fermionic coupling strength of pseudoscalar bosons and fermion mass. No significant excess above standard model expectations is observed. Consequently, observed and expected upper limits on $\sigma\mathcal{B}$, normalized to the standard model Higgs production cross section, are established at 95% confidence level in the range of 0.022 to 0.23 and 0.027 to 0.19, respectively, across the analyzed mass spectrum.

Tchebycheffian splines represent smooth, piecewise functions where each segment originates from a potentially distinct Tchebycheff space, serving as a natural extension of algebraic polynomial spaces. Under appropriate conditions, they retain most properties of polynomial splines and can be expressed using Tchebycheffian B-splines (TB-splines), which mirror the structure of polynomial B-splines. A notable subclass comprises splines whose segments reside in the null-spaces of constant-coefficient linear differential operators. These allow for the flexible combination of polynomials, exponentials, and trigonometric functions with multiple shape parameters, supported by recent advancements in efficient evaluation and manipulation techniques. This paper explores the application of such TB-splines as a compelling alternative to standard polynomial B-splines and rational NURBS within isogeometric Galerkin methods. We examine strategies for leveraging the extensive geometrical and analytical flexibility of the underlying Tchebycheff spaces based on specific problem requirements. Ultimately, TB-splines provide a robust and versatile framework for the isogeometric paradigm, extending capabilities well beyond the constraints of the rational NURBS model.

We investigate the breaking of time-reversal invariance (TRI) induced by a magnetic field within the quantum kicked rotor (QKR) framework, utilizing Izrailev's finite-dimensional model. Our findings reveal a continuous crossover from TRI to time-reversal non-invariance (TRNI) observed in both spectral and eigenvector fluctuations of the QKR. We demonstrate that the characteristics of this $\text{TRI} \rightarrow \text{TRNI}$ transition are governed by the ratio $\alpha^2/N$, where $\alpha$ represents the chaos parameter and $N$ denotes the dimensionality of the evolution operator matrix. Specifically, when $\alpha^2/N \gtrsim N$, the transition aligns with predictions from random matrix theory; however, for $\alpha^2/N < N$, the transition exhibits significant deviations from such theory. Additionally, as $\alpha^2/N$ decreases, the rate of this transition with respect to the magnetic field increases substantially.

Although two-dimensional convolutional neural networks (2D-CNNs) allow for domain manipulation via channel statistics in image processing—where instance normalization effectively yields domain-invariant features—our analysis reveals that audio features rely primarily on frequency statistics rather than channel statistics for domain-relevant information. Guided by this insight, we propose Relaxed Instance Frequency-wise Normalization (RFN), a plug-and-play module that explicitly normalizes along the frequency axis. This approach eliminates instance-specific domain discrepancies in audio features while mitigating the loss of discriminative information. Empirical results demonstrate that integrating RFN into networks outperforms previous domain generalization methods on acoustic scene classification, offering enhanced robustness across various audio devices. Notably, RFN secured first place in the DCASE2021 TASK1A challenge for low-complexity acoustic scene classification with multiple devices, achieving a significant margin of improvement. This work extends our earlier technical report.

This study investigates the magnetic response of interacting electrons within a spatially non-uniform disordered system, characterized by impurities confined to one region while leaving the other pristine.
