We model electron interactions using the standard Hubbard Hamiltonian, which reveals anomalous characteristics in energy spectra and flux-driven circular currents that vary with the concentration of up and down spins. For small systems with few electrons, we provide exact solutions that clarify fundamental mechanisms, whereas large systems with higher electron counts are analyzed using mean-field approximations. The impact of disorder is particularly notable; beyond a critical threshold, the system exhibits signatures completely opposite to those of uniform disordered systems, a phenomenon that becomes even more significant when Hubbard interactions are included. Additionally, we identify unusual half-flux-quantum periodic currents in specific cases and offer a suitable explanation for them. Our comprehensive analysis serves as a framework for studying the magnetic response of interacting electrons in other analogous non-uniform disordered systems.

This study received partial funding from the Department of Physics and Astronomy of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine's Fundamental Research Program, titled "Mathematical models of non equilibrium processes in open systems" (N 0120U100857).

Quantum vortices serve as the optical and condensed-matter equivalents found in superconductors, superfluids, Bose-Einstein condensates, and nonlinear optics, acting as the fundamental carriers of orbital angular momentum and rotation. Although they facilitate critical pair interactions and phase transitions within nonlinear fluids, their linear dynamics are equally valuable for engineering complex light structures and topological entities like full Bloch beams in multi-component systems. In this study, we induce directional motion of a quantum vortex within an open-dissipative microcavity polariton fluid, observing the packet's self-splitting and the trembling of its center of mass. Simultaneously, the vortex core exhibits ultrafast spiraling along diverging and converging circles with sub-picosecond precession. This unique behavior involves the creation and annihilation of vortex-antivortex pairs and a periodically varying topological charge. The observed spiraling and branching mechanics directly manifest the underlying Bloch pseudospin space, which is shown to rotate and split. This reshaping results from three simultaneous drives—differential group velocities, Rabi frequency, and dissipation rates—acting along distinct momentum and complex frequency directions, leveraging natural properties of coupled polariton fields. This state, characterized by linear momentum coupled with oscillating angular momentum, underscores the complexity of multi-component open quantum fluids and their inherent capacity to generate sophisticated, dynamic topological light textures.

This study examines nonnegative solutions to the nonlinear integral inequality $u \ge I_{\alpha}\ast\big((I_\beta \ast u^p)u^q\big)$ almost everywhere in $\mathbb{R}^N$, where $\alpha, \beta\in (0,N)$, $p, q>0$, and $I_\alpha$, $I_\beta$ represent the Riesz potentials of orders $\alpha$ and $\beta$, respectively. Our methodology employs a nonlocal positivity principle to determine the optimal parameter ranges for $\alpha$, $\beta$, $p$, and $q$ regarding the existence and nonexistence of solutions. Additionally, we analyze the optimal decay behavior of these solutions at infinity.

Universal Dependencies (UD) provide a standardized cross-lingual syntactic framework designed to enhance multilingual applications. While recent studies demonstrate that converting syntactic dependencies into logical forms enables semantic parsing, these approaches are restricted to English and fail to process dependency graphs necessary for handling complex phenomena like control. To address this, we present UDepLambda, a semantic interface for UD that translates natural language into logical forms in a nearly language-agnostic manner and supports dependency graph processing. We evaluate the system using question answering tasks against Freebase, releasing German and Spanish translations of the WebQuestions and GraphQuestions datasets to enable multilingual assessment. Experimental results indicate that UDepLambda surpasses strong baselines across various languages and datasets. Specifically, for English, it achieves a 4.9 F1 point gain over the state-of-the-art on GraphQuestions. The code and data are available for download at https://github.com/sivareddyg/udeplambda.

This research investigates cosmological perturbations within k-essence and kinetic gravity braiding models under the framework of two-field measure theory (TMT). By examining scalar perturbations in the uniform field gauge, we derive the field sound speeds and conduct a stability analysis using the kinetic matrix and mass eigenvalues. In k-essence models, the introduction of the new measure field in TMT completely alters the field's propagation speed, creating significant distinctions from scenarios without this measure, ultimately yielding a physically viable model for the Universe. Conversely, for kinetic gravity braiding models within TMT, the perturbation speed generally equals the speed of light due to the specific properties of the new measure field. This scenario invariably introduces a ghost field. Additionally, we derive general expressions for the mass eigenvalues and identify, through a specific example, the presence of tachyonic instabilities.

This work identifies the necessary conditions and structures on categories and semigroups that allow for the construction of pseudo-products and trace products, respectively, aiming to establish their relationship with maximal precision. Drawing inspiration from the ESN Theorem and its extension to ample semigroups, this approach is self-dual (two-sided) and relaxes the requirement for commuting projections. Furthermore, it demonstrates that the condition of projections forming a band (being closed under multiplication) is inherently natural. The study also examines one-sided reducts in comparison to (generalized) D-semigroups and analyzes the specific scenario where the category functions as a groupoid.

We introduce a collection of exactly solvable quantum impurity models featuring inverse-square interactions, which characterize a single spin-$1/2$ Kondo impurity within a Luttinger liquid, applicable to both continuum and lattice settings. These model wave functions are structured as Jastrow products and may correspond to either fermionic or bosonic baths, contingent upon the exponents of the Jastrow factors. We demonstrate that they constitute exact ground states for an open-boundary, two-component Calogero-Sutherland model in the continuum (or a long-range interacting $t-J$ model on the lattice) coupled to a localized spin-$1/2$ impurity. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between these wave functions and the chiral correlators of specific conformal field theories.

Predicting language varieties and dialects is a critical natural language processing task with diverse applications. For Arabic, spoken by approximately 300 million people, the majority of dialects currently lack support. To alleviate this limitation, we introduce a large-scale dataset encompassing 319 cities across all 21 Arab nations. We propose a Hierarchical Attention Multi-Task Learning (HA-MTL) method for dialect identification that leverages data at the city, state, and country levels. Additionally, we assess the performance of BERT on these three tasks in comparison to the proposed MTL approach. Finally, we release and benchmark both our dataset and the developed models.

This study categorizes irreducible modules for loop extended Witt algebras that possess finite-dimensional weight spaces, identifying them as either modules with uniformly bounded weight spaces or highest weight modules. Furthermore, we demonstrate that all such modules are single-point evaluation modules for $n \geq 2$, thereby establishing them as irreducible modules for extended Witt algebras.

The Mu3e experiment, located at the Paul Scherrer Institute, is investigating the charged lepton flavor violating decay $\mu^+ \rightarrow e^+ e^+ e^-$ with a target sensitivity of one in $10^{16}$ muon decays. The first phase, currently being built, is designed to achieve a branching ratio sensitivity of $2.5\times10^{-15}$ by recording $10^{8}$ muon decays per second for one year. To handle the high particle rates, the experiment employs a highly granular detector composed of thin high-voltage monolithic active pixel sensors (HV-MAPS) and scintillating timing detectors, generating approximately 100 GB/s of data. A Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) based Data Acquisition System manages this influx, utilizing a farm of graphics processing units to filter for interesting events and reduce the output rate to 100 MB/s. This paper details the current status of the DAQ system and presents initial results from the 2021 integration run, which marked the first operation of a detector slice at the $\pi$E5 muon beam line at PSI.

Over the past 155 years, we have analyzed support for women and migrants within German political discourse. Our approach involves (1) establishing a gold-standard dataset of 1,205 contextual text snippets annotated for support toward these groups, (2) training a BERT model using this annotated data, and (3) utilizing the model to identify large-scale trends. Our findings reveal that support for women exceeds support for migrants, yet both have risen consistently over time. While direct opposition toward women is virtually absent, debates surrounding migrants exhibit greater polarization. Additionally, we address the challenges of annotation caused by ambiguity and indirectness in political language, particularly politicians' tendency to attribute stances to opponents. Overall, our results suggest that, as reflected by the political elite, German society has become progressively fairer.

We introduce a comprehensive framework for developing posterior sampling techniques within model-based reinforcement learning. Our analysis demonstrates that the regret of these algorithms can be bounded by the Hellinger distance in conditional probability estimation. Furthermore, we establish that optimistic posterior sampling effectively manages this Hellinger distance when model error is quantified using data likelihood. This approach enables the creation and rigorous analysis of unified posterior sampling algorithms that achieve state-of-the-art sample complexity across numerous model-based RL scenarios. By applying our general findings to various specific instances, we highlight the adaptability and broad applicability of our framework.

This work investigates the persistence characteristics of solutions to a broad class of generalized wave equations, encompassing models for elastic rod vibrations and shallow water dynamics, such as the BBM, Dai, Camassa-Holm, and Dullin-Gottwald-Holm equations, alongside recent formulations incorporating the Coriolis effect. We derive unique continuation theorems and characterize the asymptotic profiles of solutions within this general framework. Leveraging these findings, we demonstrate that no non-trivial solutions with spatially compact support exist for the equation. Consequently, we apply these general results to analyze the specific equations previously mentioned.

This study addresses the bound state problem for a Hamiltonian incorporating both spin-orbit and Raman coupling, perturbed by a one-dimensional short-range potential $V$ that models impurity scattering. Beyond deriving bound states via weak solutions using Fourier transforms or by directly solving the eigenvalue equation on an appropriate domain, the analysis demonstrates that standard point-interaction formulations of $V$ give rise to additional states induced by spin-orbit coupling.

Driven by the swift advancement of deep learning-based intelligent detection algorithms, significant strides have been achieved in the automatic recognition of road defects and the parsing of road markings. This progress effectively mitigates the challenges associated with the high cost and time consumption of manual street inspections by professionals. To achieve this, we introduce RoadAtlas, a new end-to-end integrated system designed to facilitate: 1) the detection of road defects, 2) the parsing of road markings, 3) a user-friendly web dashboard for data presentation and input, and 4) a backend infrastructure featuring a well-organized database and developed APIs.

A class $ \mathcal{F} $ of analytic functions defined as $ f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_nz^n $ within the unit disc $ \mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\} $ exhibits a Bohr phenomenon if there exists a radius $ r_f>0 $ such that for all $ f\in\mathcal{F} $ and $ |z|=r\leq r_f $, the inequality $ I_f(r):=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|a_n|r^n\leq{d}\left(f(0),\partial \mathbb{D}\right) $ holds, where $ d $ denotes Euclidean distance. This largest possible radius $ r_f $ is termed the Bohr radius, and the corresponding inequality is known as the Bohr inequality for $ \mathcal{F} $. If a positive real number $ r_0 $ exists such that $ I_f(r)\leq {d}\left(f(0),\partial \mathbb{D}\right) $ is valid for every $ f\in\mathcal{F} $ when $ 0\leq r<r_0 $ but fails for $ r>r_0 $, then $ r_0 $ is defined as the sharp bound for the inequality relative to the class $ \mathcal{F} $. This paper establishes a sharp refinement of the Bohr-Rogosinski inequality for specific classes of harmonic mappings.

Modern risk assessment frequently demands the estimation of extremal behaviors in sums of random variables across various fields. This study establishes the first-order upper-tail characteristics of weighted sums involving bivariate random variables, relying on minimal assumptions regarding their marginal distributions and copulas. The extremal properties of the marginal variables are modeled using the generalized Pareto distribution, with their dependence structures defined through specific subclasses of limiting representations by Ledford and Tawn (1997) and Heffernan and Tawn (2004). Our analysis reveals that the upper-tail behavior of the aggregate sum is influenced by distinct factors contingent upon the signs of the marginal shape parameters: when both parameters are negative, the aggregate's extremal behavior depends on both shape parameters and the coefficient of asymptotic independence (Ledford and Tawn, 1996); however, if both are positive or possess differing signs, the upper-tail behavior is governed exclusively by the largest marginal shape. Additionally, we derive the aggregate upper-tail behavior for several well-known copulas, providing deeper insight into tail structures when the copula does not fit within the conditions of the aforementioned limiting dependence subclasses.

All-optical spin switching (AOS) marks a promising new direction in magnetic storage by enabling spin manipulation without magnetic fields, yet its fundamental mechanisms remain poorly defined. While many AOS ferrimagnets like GdFeCo are amorphous, making high-level first-principles analysis impractical, the crystalline half-metallic Heusler alloy Mn$_2$RuGa offers a viable alternative. This study presents the most comprehensive density functional theory investigation to date on Mn$_2$RuGa, introducing two key concepts—the spin anchor site and the optical active site—as foundational pillars for AOS in ferrimagnets. In Mn$_2$RuGa, the Mn$(4a)$ atom functions as the spin anchor, characterized by a band structure situated below the Fermi level and a robust spin moment, whereas the Mn$(4c)$ atom acts as the optical active site with bands crossing the Fermi level. Joint analysis of magneto-optical Kerr spectra and band structure calculations indicates that the interplay between Ru-$4d$ and Ga-$4p$ states drives the formation of these distinct sites. These findings provide a unified framework for understanding both Mn$_2$RuGa and GdFeCo and pave the way for future applications. Specifically, we propose a Mn$_2$Ru$_x$Ga-based magnetic tunnel junction capable of controlling magnetoresistance with a single laser pulse.

We briefly investigate the classical dynamics of the Carrollian limit, characterized by a vanishing speed of light and an inability to propagate signals, using a simple effective action in flat space where the open string tachyon serves as a scalar field. The canonical analysis reveals that the resulting equation of motion is of Dirac type, contrasting with the Schrödinger-type equation found in non-relativistic cases. The ultimate goal is to analyze this latter scenario in the presence of electromagnetic fluxes, demonstrating that the open string tachyon cannot be interpreted as time in this context.

This study investigates the nuclear modification factors of single and dihadron production at high transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) within high-energy heavy-ion collisions using a next-to-leading-order (NLO) perturbative QCD framework. In these $A+A$ collisions, parton fragmentation functions are altered by jet energy loss, which scales with the jet transport coefficient $\hat{q}$, representing the interaction strength between the parton jet and the created medium. By performing a global fit to experimental data regarding single hadron and dihadron suppression across six existing sets of NLO parton fragmentation functions, we quantitatively determine $\hat{q}$. The results yield $\hat{q}/T^3 = 4.74 - 6.72$ at a temperature of $T = 370$ MeV for central $Au+Au$ collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=200$ GeV, and $\hat{q}/T^3 = 3.07 - 3.98$ at $T = 480$ MeV for central $Pb+Pb$ collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=2.76$ TeV. Numerical analysis indicates that the uncertainties in extracting $\hat{q}$ arise from varying contributions of gluon-to-hadron fragmentation among the six FF sets, driven by the fact that gluon energy loss is $9/4$ times greater than quark energy loss.

Automating the manipulation of garments is difficult primarily because of the vast variability in how these objects are configured. To mitigate this inherent diversity, we introduce "canonicalized-alignment," a task designed to simplify downstream applications by narrowing the range of possible garment states. This process functions as a "cloth state funnel," transforming arbitrarily arranged clothing into a specific, predefined deformable state (canonicalization) while simultaneously positioning it at a suitable rigid orientation (alignment). Ultimately, this results in a compact collection of structured and highly visible configurations, which are ideal for subsequent manipulation skills. To facilitate this, we propose a novel canonicalized-alignment objective that effectively steers the learning process away from detrimental local minima. Leveraging this objective, we develop a multi-arm, multi-primitive policy that strategically selects between dynamic flings and quasi-static pick-and-place actions to achieve efficient canonicalized-alignment. We validate this approach on a real-world system for ironing and folding, utilizing the learned policy as a foundational initial step. Empirical results show that our task-agnostic canonicalized-alignment enables even simple, manually designed policies to perform effectively in scenarios where they previously failed, thereby bridging the divide between automated non-deformable manufacturing and deformable manipulation. The code and qualitative visualizations are accessible at https://clothfunnels.cs.columbia.edu/, and a video demonstration is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TkUn0b7mbj0.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic, bicategorical structure that extends topological Hochschild homology (THH) and maintains key properties like Morita invariance. By leveraging Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, we establish an equivalence between functors originating from the THH of a bicategory and shadows defined on that same bicategory. This result enables a novel, conceptual demonstration of the Morita invariance of shadows.

This study examines the shadows of static black holes, both those carrying magnetic monopoles and those immersed in magnetic fields, by incorporating QED effects via numerical backward ray-tracing. For static black holes with magnetic monopoles, we establish the relationship between the shadow radius and the coupling constant. In the case of neutral black holes within uniform magnetic fields, we observe that shadow contours deviate only minimally from ellipses for equatorial observers, revealing a linear correlation between eccentricity and the coupling constant. When the observer angle $\theta_o$ differs from $\pi/2$, the shadow curves remain well-approximated by ellipses in most scenarios, with exceptions occurring only under extremely strong magnetic fields when the observer is positioned near $\theta_o=\pi/4$ or $3\pi/4$. Furthermore, our analysis is extended to a neutral static black hole encircled by a current loop.

Physics-based forecasts of the solar cycle serve as a valuable method to validate our comprehension of solar dynamics. Prior to the onset of cycle 25, numerous such predictions were formulated utilizing flux transport dynamo (FTD) models, surface flux transport (SFT) models, or hybrid approaches. The underlying physical principle shared by these forecasts is that the surface poloidal field existing near cycle minimum largely dictates the intensity of the following cycle. This review begins with brief overviews of SFT and FTD models. Subsequently, it compares seven physics-based prediction models across four dimensions: the predictor itself, the derivation method, the application process, and the specific target of prediction. Furthermore, we illustrate the significant impact of assimilated magnetograms on forecasting outcomes through two SFT numerical experiments. We recommend that uncertainties regarding both initial magnetograms and sunspot emergence be incorporated into these physics-based predictions, given their substantial influence on results. Additionally, this review emphasizes the insights derivable from diverse predictions rather than evaluating the accuracy of the prediction outcomes themselves.

Scalar fields interacting non-minimally with gravity via the term $\xi |\phi|^2 R$ could significantly impact early universe physics. Although much existing research addresses the dynamics of such coupled scalars within the Einstein frame—where gravity follows the standard Einstein-Hilbert action—we introduce a method to solve these dynamics directly in the original Jordan frame, retaining explicit non-minimal couplings. This algorithm accommodates scenarios featuring both minimally and an arbitrary number of non-minimally coupled scalars, with cosmic expansion driven by all present fields. Its applicability extends to cases involving complete inhomogeneity, full non-linearity (arising from effects like backreaction or mode rescattering), and regimes where the universe's expansion is dominated by non-minimally coupled species. As a demonstration, we examine geometric preheating involving a non-minimally coupled spectator field while the inflaton oscillates post-inflation. Future applications of this technique may help clarify quantum-level aspects of the equivalence between the Jordan and Einstein frames.

The collective mode spectrum of a symmetry-broken state, like a superconductor, offers essential insights into the order parameter's nature. Within this framework, we introduce a microscopic weak-coupling theory describing collective modes in a generic multi-component superconductor that breaks time-reversal symmetry. We demonstrate that fluctuations in both the relative phase and amplitude of the two order parameter components manifest as well-defined underdamped collective modes, even when nodal quasiparticles are present. Furthermore, we show that these "generalized clapping modes" are accessible through various experimental methods, including ac electronic compressibility, electron energy loss spectroscopy, microwave spectroscopy, and ultrafast THz spectroscopy. Finally, we explore the implications of this work as a novel form of "collective mode spectroscopy," significantly broadening the range of experimental probes available for detecting time-reversal symmetry breaking in unconventional superconductors such as Sr$_{2}$RuO$_{4}$, UTe$_{2}$, and moiré heterostructures.

Quantum phase estimation stands as a fundamental element in designing quantum algorithms, enabling the determination of eigenvalues for exponentially large, sparse matrices. The speed at which these eigenvalues can be extracted, termed the Heisenberg limit, is bounded by the circuit complexity needed to simulate general Hamiltonians. Recently, single-qubit control versions of quantum phase estimation that avoid inter-experiment coherence have attracted attention for their shallow circuit depth and minimal qubit requirements. This study demonstrates that such methods can reach the Heisenberg limit even when preparing eigenstates of the system is not feasible. Given a quantum subroutine that yields samples of a phase function $g(k)=\sum_j A_j e^{i \phi_j k}$ with unknown eigenphases $\phi_j$ and overlaps $A_j$ at a cost of $O(k)$, we propose a method to estimate the phases $\{\phi_j\}$ with a root-mean-square error $\delta$ using a total quantum cost of $T=O(\delta^{-1})$. Our approach merges the concept of Heisenberg-limited multi-order quantum phase estimation for individual eigenvalues [Higgins et al (2009); Kimmel et al (2015)] with dense quantum phase estimation subroutines that employ classical time-series analysis for QEEP [Somma (2019)] or the matrix pencil method. We prove that our adaptive algorithm achieves Heisenberg-limited scaling when utilizing the time-series/QEEP subroutine, while numerical results suggest that the matrix pencil technique also supports this scaling.

Rational approximation has recently become a powerful numerical method for solving exterior wave propagation issues, though it was previously restricted to media invariant along the primary propagation direction. This paper introduces a novel model order reduction technique designed to compress unbounded waveguides containing layered inclusions. The approach solves a nonlinear rational least squares problem via the RKFIT algorithm. We demonstrate that these approximants can be transformed into precise finite difference representations within a rational Krylov framework. Numerical results reveal that RKFIT generates more accurate grids than prior analytic methods and remains effective even with strong scattering resonances. Furthermore, spectral adaptation enables finite difference grids with dimensions at or below the Nyquist limit.

Driven by globalization and accelerating technological advancements, production volumes and the accessibility of counterfeit goods have reached unprecedented levels. Consequently, manufacturers and distributors across all sectors—from food and pharmaceuticals to luxury goods—are increasingly demanding greater supply chain transparency to combat counterfeiting. This paper presents a decentralized application (DApp) built on Blockchain technology designed to identify fake products within supply chains. Leveraging the inherent immutability and security of Blockchain records, the proposed system manages product ownership transfers. Consumers can verify a product's distribution history and ownership details by scanning a unique Quick Response (QR) code generated by the DApp for each item linked to the Blockchain.

Magic windows, also known as magic mirrors, are optical systems engineered with specific surface deformations or thickness profiles to generate targeted images. Research indicates that the resulting image intensity distribution correlates with the Laplacian of the surface relief's height. We have experimentally demonstrated these devices using flat optics that leverage optical spin-to-orbital angular momentum coupling, establishing a novel approach to light manipulation. To design these flat optics, a reconfigurable spatial light modulator served as the magic mirror to define the required patterns and experimental parameters. Subsequently, the flat plate and spin-to-orbital angular momentum coupler were fabricated by spatially structuring nematic liquid crystals. This setup successfully illustrates a polarization-switchable magic window, where the displayed image depends on the input circular polarization's handedness: one circular polarization reveals the desired image, while the opposite polarization displays the image corresponding to the negative of the window's phase.

As V2X technology advances, cooperative control of multiple vehicles has become a prominent research area; however, field testing remains infrequent due to financial and safety constraints. To address this challenge, this study introduces a digital twin approach for multi-vehicle experimentation, integrating both physical and virtual vehicles to execute coordination tasks. A prototype system was developed to validate the method's efficacy, comprising a sand table testbed, its corresponding digital twin, and a cloud infrastructure. System performance was evaluated across several metrics, including time delay and localization accuracy. Furthermore, a vehicle-level experiment within a platoon scenario was conducted, and the results substantiate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

We present MINER, a novel neural signal model engineered for the efficient high-resolution encoding of extensive signals. The core advancement of our multiscale implicit neural representation lies in its utilization of a Laplacian pyramid for internal modeling, facilitating a sparse multiscale decomposition that isolates orthogonal signal components across various scales. By employing small multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) to represent disjoint patches within the pyramid at each scale, we allow the network's capacity to grow adaptively from coarse to fine resolutions, ensuring that only regions with significant signal energy are encoded. Optimizing MLP parameters in a coarse-to-fine sequence accelerates approximations at broader scales, leading to an exceptionally rapid training process. When applied to large-scale signal tasks, such as gigapixel imagery and massive point clouds, MINER achieves representation accuracy comparable to competing methods like ACORN while utilizing fewer than 25% of the parameters, 33% of the memory footprint, and just 10% of the computational time.

The convergence of modern production demands and sophisticated robotic capabilities has driven the formation of collaborative teams integrating humans and autonomous robots. While this integration offers significant advantages, it also raises the challenge of effectively managing such teams given the distinct characteristics of their members. To address this, the paper introduces a task allocation framework designed for human-robot collaborative scenarios. The proposed approach merges optimal offline allocation with an online reallocation strategy that adapts to plan inaccuracies and unforeseen events. This strategy also incorporates human subjective preferences and task-switching costs to enhance both team efficiency and human satisfaction. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments involving two manipulators cooperating with a human operator to complete a box-filling task.

Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) technology is poised to emerge soon. While quantum machines with 50 to 100 qubits might soon outperform current classical digital systems, gate noise will restrict the reliability of the circuit sizes they can execute. These NISQ devices will serve as valuable instruments for investigating many-body quantum physics and hold other potential applications; however, a 100-qubit computer will not immediately revolutionize the world. Instead, it should be viewed as a major milestone on the path to more advanced quantum technologies. Consequently, quantum technologists must continue working toward more precise quantum gates and, ultimately, achieve fully fault-tolerant quantum computing.

We introduce the Hida-Mat\'ern kernels, a canonical family of covariance functions defined over the entire space of stationary Gauss-Markov Processes. This class extends standard Mat\'ern kernels by enabling the flexible construction of priors for processes containing oscillatory components. We demonstrate the generality of this framework by showing that any stationary kernel—including widely utilized squared-exponential and spectral mixture kernels—is either directly included within this class or serves as an appropriate asymptotic limit. Leveraging the Markovian nature of these processes, we derive state space model representations using solely the kernel and its derivatives. This approach facilitates more efficient Gaussian Process inference, bypassing typical computational constraints. Furthermore, we illustrate how exploiting the unique properties of this state space representation enhances numerical stability while significantly reducing computational complexity.

Thermodynamic conventions struggle to capture dynamical distinctions, particularly when structural and energetic shifts caused by localized rare events are negligible. By applying ensemble theory within trajectory space, we propose a statistical framework to resolve this issue. While thermodynamics is primarily governed by spatial particle interactions, dynamics are dominated by the temporal correlations of events. In this context, the zeros of the dynamic partition function signify phase transitions in space-time—known as dynamic phase transitions (DPTs)—analogous to how Yang and Lee described traditional phase transitions, thereby defining dynamic phases on either side of these zeros. Just as temperature and pressure serve as thermal and mechanical potentials, we interpret the controlling variable of DPT, the dynamic field, as the dynamical potential. These insights pave the way for a unified understanding of phases and phase transitions.

Although formal verification methods are commonly employed to establish the functional correctness of software, analyzing nonfunctional attributes like time complexity typically relies on manual reasoning. Such inefficiencies can lead to severe performance issues within large-scale, intricate systems. This paper introduces a proof-of-concept demonstrating how the Dafny verification tool can be utilized to specify and verify the worst-case time complexity of binary search. Furthermore, this methodology offers a novel pedagogical approach for teaching algorithms and complexity in academic settings.

The increasing prevalence of social media has heightened concerns regarding child safety online, particularly concerning interactions between minors and adults with predatory intent. While previous research on online sexual grooming has depended on domain experts to manually annotate dialogues—thereby restricting both the scale and scope of such studies—this work evaluates the efficacy of automated methods in detecting conversational patterns as a substitute for human annotators. Grounded in psychological theories of online grooming, we categorized $6772$ chat messages from child-sex offenders into one of eleven distinct predatory behaviors. We then trained bag-of-words and natural language inference models to classify these behaviors, demonstrating that while the top-performing models achieve results consistent with human annotation, they do not yet match human-level accuracy.

When initiating a joint venture, it is essential to comprehend partners' preferences and the degree of their dedication to shared objectives. Creating an upfront agreement regarding future rewards and repercussions serves as a vital mechanism for securing cooperation. Drawing on Evolutionary Game Theory (EGT), this study examines how prior commitments can function as a tool to improve coordination, particularly in scenarios with asymmetric payoffs, across both pairwise and multi-party interactions. Coordination is often more intricate than cooperation because, unlike cooperation dilemmas which have a single desirable outcome, coordination problems may involve multiple viable collective goals. Our analytical and numerical findings indicate that the viability of prior commitments as an evolutionary strategy for boosting coordination and social welfare relies heavily on the collective benefit, the intensity of competition, and critically, how asymmetric gains are settled within the commitment. Furthermore, in multi-party settings, prior commitments are essential when high group diversity is necessary for optimal alignment. These results remain consistent across varying selection intensities. Ultimately, our analysis offers fresh perspectives on the intricacies of behavioral evolution driven by human commitment capabilities and informs the design of self-organized, distributed multi-agent systems to ensure coordination among autonomous entities.

Over the past few years, two distinct yet connected advances have emerged in the research of irrelevant deformations within two-dimensional quantum field theories (QFTs). The first involves deforming a 2D QFT using the determinant of the energy-momentum tensor, known as the $T\bar{T}$ deformation. The second pertains to two-dimensional holographic field theories dual to string theory in asymptotically Anti-de Sitter (AdS) spacetimes, where the deformation is termed the single-trace $T\bar{T}$ deformation. This single-trace variant maps to a bulk string background that transitions from AdS geometry in the infrared (IR) to a linear dilaton spacetime—the vacuum of little string theory (LST)—in the ultraviolet (UV). It acts as a valuable instrument for investigating holography in both asymptotically AdS and non-AdS settings under controlled conditions, offering specific insights into flat spacetime holography.

This dissertation focuses on the single-trace $T\bar{T}$ deformation and its extensions involving $U(1)$ currents, specifically $J\bar{T}$ and $T\bar{J}$ deformations, within the framework of gauge/gravity duality. The work presents novel findings regarding holography in asymptotically non-AdS spacetimes. Additionally, it examines two-point correlation functions in single-trace $T\bar{T}$ deformations, as well as entanglement entropy and the entropic $c$-function across single-trace $T\bar{T}$, $J\bar{T}$, and $T\bar{J}$ deformations.

Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) connectivity analysis is a widely used method for distinguishing between clinical and healthy populations. Prior to constructing functional brain networks, fMRI time series require multiple preprocessing steps to mitigate artifacts and enhance data quality; however, these procedures can inadvertently distort results. For instance, spatial smoothing is recognized for altering functional network architecture, yet its impact on group-level network differences remains unclear. This study examines how spatial smoothing influences distinctions between patients and controls in autism spectrum disorder and bipolar disorder, utilizing fMRI data smoothed with Gaussian kernels ranging from 0 to 32 mm. Our findings indicate that smoothing significantly impacts inter-group network differences. Specifically, for weighted networks, increasing the smoothing kernel heightens these differences, whereas for thresholded networks, larger kernels tend to reduce differences, though this outcome varies based on network density. Additionally, smoothing modifies the effect sizes of individual link differences, a phenomenon independent of region-of-interest (ROI) size but dependent on link length. The effects of spatial smoothing are complex, non-trivial, and difficult to anticipate, carrying significant implications: the selection of a smoothing kernel directly influences observed network differences.

This study explores random-shift representations for $\alpha$-homogeneous shift-invariant classes of random fields, denoted as $K_{\alpha}[Z]$, originally defined in \cite{hashorva2021shiftinvariant}. In this context, $Z(t)$ represents a stochastically continuous $\mathbb{R}^d$-valued random field defined on either $T=\mathbb{R}^l$ or $T=\mathbb{Z}^l$. We demonstrate that the relevant random-shift representations arise from constructing cluster random fields, which are fundamental to analyzing the extremes of stationary regularly varying random fields. A key consequence of these representations is their strong connection to Rosiński (or mixed moving maxima) representations of max-stable random fields. Furthermore, we establish that multiple distinct cluster random fields can be derived for a specific $K_{\alpha}[Z]$, a flexibility that facilitates the development of new representations for extremal functional indices, Rosiński representations of max-stable random fields, and random-shift representations of shift-invariant tail measures.

Communication within and between intricate systems is a fundamental aspect of natural sciences and domains like graph neural networks. The brain exemplifies such a complex system, characterized by the continuous orchestration of interactions among its various regions. To study this communication, the brain is typically partitioned into anatomical areas responsible for specific computations; these areas must collaborate to execute tasks and facilitate higher-order cognition. At the macroscopic level, interaction occurs via signal propagation along the cortical surface and through white matter tracts across extended distances. Determining when and what specific signals are exchanged over time remains an unsolved challenge, often investigated using functional or structural data. This paper introduces a non-linear generative framework for analyzing communication derived from functional data. We resolve three limitations of conventional connectivity methods by explicitly modeling communication directionality, identifying interactions at every timestep, and promoting sparsity. To validate our model, we simulate temporal data featuring sparse node communication, demonstrating its ability to recover expected dynamics. Furthermore, we apply the model to temporal neural data from diverse tasks, revealing that it captures communication patterns highly specific to each task. This specificity suggests potential applications in understanding psychiatric disorders, which are hypothesized to involve distinct communication deficits between brain regions compared to controls. In conclusion, we present a generalizable model for dynamic communication learning on graphs, demonstrating its relevance to a specific subfield of natural sciences with broad scientific implications.

Landsat-8 (NASA) and Sentinel-2 (ESA) represent two major satellite initiatives offering accessible multi-spectral imagery. Their sensors capture Earth's surface across visible and infrared wavelengths; however, frequent cloud cover, which blocks these wavelengths, often renders images data-poor. To enhance the availability of cloud-free imagery for specific regions, researchers can merge observations from multiple satellites. Yet, sensor disparities can render these images incompatible. This study investigates using a transformer-based model to bridge spectral and spatial gaps between the two satellite datasets. Results are benchmarked against a fully convolutional UNet architecture. Contrary to expectations, although deep learning models generally surpass classical methods, the UNet significantly outperformed the transformer in our experimental evaluations.

Because tetraquark operators can be decomposed into mesonic clusters, there is a significant interaction between compact and molecular configurations within tetraquarks. This phenomenon is investigated using an effective field theory framework, which models the compact tetraquark as an elementary particle. Through the coupling to mesonic clusters, an initially formed compact tetraquark bound state undergoes deformation, evolving into a molecular-type structure characterized as a shallow bound state.

To achieve robust GPS-vision navigation in urban environments, we introduce an Integrity-driven Landmark Attention (ILA) method grounded in stochastic reachability. Drawing inspiration from human cognitive attention, we employ convex optimization to identify a subset of landmarks derived from both GPS and vision data, thereby optimizing integrity-driven performance. Utilizing known measurement error bounds under non-faulty conditions, our ILA adopts a unified strategy capable of handling faults in both GPS and vision systems while remaining compatible with any standard off-the-shelf estimator. We evaluate measurement deviations to determine the stochastic reachable set of expected positions for each landmark, parameterized by probabilistic zonotopes (p-Zonotopes). By applying set union operations, we construct a p-Zonotopic cost function that quantifies position bound sizes based on landmark inclusion or exclusion. Through convex relaxation, we jointly minimize this cost and maximize the count of selected landmarks. Validation on an urban dataset confirms enhanced localization accuracy and robust predicted availability relative to a predefined alert limit.

While deep learning can generate control policies, verifying their safety remains difficult due to the resulting networks' nonlinearity and substantial size. To address this, we introduce OVERT, a sound algorithm for verifying the safety of nonlinear discrete-time closed-loop dynamical systems governed by neural network controllers. OVERT's innovation stems from merging concepts from classical formal methods with those from modern neural network verification. Its core mechanism involves approximating nonlinear functions with optimally tight piecewise linear bounds, which are specifically engineered for smooth integration into ReLU neural network verification tools. This approach enables the proof of bounded-time safety properties through either reachable set computation or direct feasibility query solving. We validate OVERT using several classical benchmark examples, demonstrating that it outperforms existing methods in both computational efficiency and the tightness of the resulting reachable sets.

Plastic deformation in metal alloys often localizes into distinct bands via the Portevin--Le Chatelier effect, including propagating "A" bands defined by their width and speed. Although this instability stems from the collective interaction between mobile solute atoms and dislocations, the underlying reasons for its strain-rate sensitivity remain unclear. By utilizing high-resolution imaging during tensile tests on an aluminum alloy, we demonstrate that band velocities undergo significant fluctuations. Each band generates a velocity signal akin to crackling noise bursts seen in various driven avalanche systems, ranging from fracture cracks to the Barkhausen effect in ferromagnets. The statistical properties of these velocity bursts, including their average shapes and size distributions, align with predictions from a simple mean-field model of critical avalanche dynamics. Consequently, these findings unveil a new paradigm of criticality governing deformation localization.

We introduce an architecture designed for continual learning in highly challenging scenarios where task boundaries are undefined or unknown, and classes must be learned online with each example appearing only once. To achieve strong performance under these strict constraints while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, we leverage recent advancements in contrastive, self-supervised learning. This approach utilizes a pre-trained, general-purpose image encoder with frozen weights, thereby eliminating forgetting. Additionally, the pre-trained encoder significantly streamlines the downstream classification task, which is handled by an ensemble of simple classifiers. Collectively, this ensemble demonstrates superior performance compared to any single classifier, a benefit further enhanced through specialization and competitive selection. We evaluate the encoder-and-ensemble architecture on standard continual learning benchmarks, where it surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin on the most difficult tasks, as well as in less common settings involving gradual data distribution shifts or sequential class presentation.

We introduce Mixture of Contrastive Experts (MiCE), a unified probabilistic clustering framework that integrates discriminative representations from contrastive learning with semantic structures derived from a latent mixture model. Inspired by the mixture of experts paradigm, MiCE utilizes a gating function to segment an unlabeled dataset into subsets based on latent semantics, while employing multiple experts to perform contrastive learning on the distinct instances assigned to each subset. To address the challenging inference and learning issues arising from latent variables, we have developed a scalable Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm variant for MiCE and provided convergence proofs. In our empirical evaluation across four standard natural image datasets, MiCE demonstrates significantly superior clustering performance compared to various prior methods and a robust contrastive learning baseline.

This study adapts a training methodology modeled after the original AlphaGo system to tackle the imperfect information game of Reconnaissance Blind Chess (RBC). By relying solely on observable information rather than a complete game state description, we initially train a supervised agent using publicly available game data. Performance is then enhanced through self-play utilizing the on-policy reinforcement learning technique, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). To circumvent issues arising from partial observability, we omit any search mechanisms, relying exclusively on the policy network to generate moves during gameplay. This strategy yields an ELO of 1330 on the RBC leaderboard, securing the 27th position as of this writing. Our results demonstrate that self-play substantially boosts performance and that the agent competes acceptably well without employing search or making assumptions regarding the hidden aspects of the game state.

Building on the work of Antieau and Bhatt-Morrow-Scholze, we establish a filtration on topological Hochschild homology, along with its variants $TP$ and $TC^-$, for quasi-lci rings possessing bounded torsion. This filtration aligns with the BMS-filtration upon $p$-adic completion. We then calculate the graded components of this filtration using Hodge completed derived de Rham cohomology relative to the base ring $\mathbb{Z}$. The cofiber of the natural map from $\mathrm{gr}^{n}TC^-(-)$ to $\mathrm{gr}^{n}TP(-)$ is denoted as $L\Omega^{<n}_{-/\mathbb{S}}[2n]$. For a regular, connected scheme $\mathcal{X}$ of dimension $d$ that is proper over $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})$, and for any integer $n$, the complex $L\Omega^{<n}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{S}}$ is anticipated to yield the Zeta-value $\pm\zeta^*(\mathcal{X},n)$ exactly when paired with Weil-\'etale cohomology with compact support, $R\Gamma_{W,c}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{Z}(n))$. By integrating these findings with a recent theorem developed jointly with Flach, we derive a formula connecting $L\Omega^{<n}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{S}}$ and $L\Omega^{<d-n}_{\mathcal{X}/\mathbb{S}}$ to the Weil-\'etale cohomology of the archimedean fiber $\mathcal{X}_{\infty}$ with Tate twists $n$ and $d-n$, the Bloch conductor $A(\mathcal{X})$, and the special values of the archimedean Euler factor of the Zeta-function $\zeta(\mathcal{X},s)$ at $s=n$ and $s=d-n$. This relationship serves as an analogue to the functional equation of Zeta-functions.

This paper applies the modular method, building on recent work by Freitas and Siksek, to investigate non-trivial, primitive solutions $(x,y,z) \in \mathcal{O}_K^3$ of the equation $x^r+y^r=z^p$ with signature $(r,r,p)$, where $K$ is a totally real field and $r \geq 5$ is a fixed prime. An adapted version of the modular method is employed, following Freitas's approach to constructing Frey curves over totally real subfields of $K(\zeta_r)$. In the case where $K=\mathbb{Q}$, it is shown that no non-trivial, primitive integer solutions exist with $2|z$ for signatures $(r,r,p)$ when $r$ belongs to the set $\{5,7,11,13,19,23,37,47,53,59,61,67,71,79,83,101,103,107,131,139,149\}$ and $p$ is sufficiently large. Analogous findings apply to quadratic fields; for instance, when $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$, there are no non-trivial, primitive solutions in $\mathcal{O}_K^3$ with $\sqrt{2}|z$ for signatures $(5,5,p), (7,7,p), (11,11,p), (13,13,p)$ and large enough $p$.

We examine single graviton loop corrections to the effective field equation governing a massless, minimally coupled scalar field on a de Sitter background, utilizing the simplest gauge. Our analysis reveals a significant temporal logarithm during the late-time freeze-in process, though it yields no correction to the freeze-in amplitude itself. Furthermore, we identify a prominent spatial logarithm (at large distances) within the scalar potential induced by a point source; this phenomenon can be accounted for via renormalization group methods by treating one of the higher-derivative counterterms as a curvature-dependent field strength renormalization. Finally, we outline how these findings pave the way for a project aimed at eliminating gauge dependence by incorporating quantum gravitational corrections to both the source that perturbs the effective field and the observer measuring it.

This paper provides a comprehensive description and validation of a discontinuous Galerkin (DG) finite element method tailored for multi-component, chemically reacting compressible Navier-Stokes equations. The approach preserves key DG advantages, specifically discrete conservation and high-order accuracy within smooth flow regions. To ensure pressure equilibrium across adjacent elements, the method employs a consistent thermodynamic model, weak formulation, and nodal basis selection, thereby preventing unphysical pressure oscillations in smooth areas and at interfaces where temperature remains continuous. Furthermore, an hp-adaptive DG method named DGODE is introduced to solve the stiff systems of ordinary differential equations governing temporal species concentration changes. This coupled solver is tested on demanding scenarios, including multi-component shocked flows and chemically reacting detonations, deflagrations, and shear flows with detailed kinetics. Results confirm the absence of spurious pressure oscillations and verify discrete conservation where applicable. The solver accurately reproduces expected temperature and species profiles in detonations, including two-dimensional cellular structures, and generates stable, high-order approximations of these profiles in one-dimensional pre-mixed flames without artificial stabilization. Additionally, high-order solutions for two- and three-dimensional multi-component reacting shear flows are presented, all computed without any extra stabilization.

This study introduces a model of the FLRW universe containing matter and dark energy fluids, based on the assumption that the deceleration parameter varies linearly with the Hubble constant. This approach yields a time-dependent deceleration parameter that captures the universe's transition from deceleration to acceleration. The framework describes a quintessence scenario where the equation of state satisfies $\omega_{(de)}\geq -1$, with this phase persisting within the redshift range $0 \leq z \leq 0.5806$. The model is demonstrated to align with current observational data, and various cosmological parameters concerning the universe's evolution have been examined.

Modeling biological soft tissues is complicated largely because of material heterogeneity. The microstructural patterns that dictate these tissues' mechanical responses are both hard to characterize and to simulate. Recently, machine learning (ML) techniques have enabled a more comprehensive exploration of the vast parameter space associated with heterogeneous material blocks by predicting their mechanical behavior. Specifically, ML models can be trained on datasets of simulations to approximate computationally intensive heterogeneous material simulations, effectively capturing the range of spatial heterogeneity in the material of interest. However, applying these methods broadly to biological tissue faces a significant limitation: obtaining and analyzing the relevant microstructural patterns is difficult, which restricts the number of useful examples available to define the input domain. This study investigates the effectiveness of ML-based generative models and procedural methods for augmenting limited input pattern datasets. Our findings indicate that a Style-based Generative Adversarial Network (StyleGAN) with adaptive discriminator augmentation can successfully generate highly authentic patterns using only 1,000 examples. Generally, diverse generated patterns that closely resemble real ones can serve as inputs for finite element simulations, thereby meaningfully expanding training datasets. To support this methodological advancement, we have developed an open-access dataset of Finite Element Analysis simulations based on Cahn-Hilliard patterns, which we anticipate will allow future researchers to build upon the work presented here.

We introduce a method for automatically extracting measured values from astrophysical literature, utilizing the Hubble constant as a pilot case. Our rules-based model, a traditional natural language processing technique, successfully retrieved 298 Hubble constant measurements complete with uncertainties from a corpus of 208,541 arXiv astrophysics papers. Additionally, we developed an artificial neural network classifier to pinpoint arXiv papers reporting novel measurements. Our analysis reveals that reporting measurements with proper uncertainties and units is essential for identifying new findings within free text. These results accurately reflect the current tension in Hubble constant measurements and recover the $3.5\sigma$ discrepancy, demonstrating the tool's utility for meta-analyses of astrophysical data drawn from extensive publication sets.

Common methods for measuring predictive uncertainty in deep neural networks, such as ensembling or Monte Carlo Dropout, typically rely on multiple models or weights, incurring computational overhead or yielding limited prediction diversity. This survey introduces an alternative framework based on Evidential Deep Learning, which enables models to express uncertainty regarding unfamiliar data by reverting to prior beliefs. Unlike traditional techniques, this approach estimates uncertainty within a single model and during a single forward pass by parameterizing distributions over distributions. The review summarizes existing literature with a primary focus on classification tasks and extends to regression applications. Additionally, it offers a critical comparison of the strengths and weaknesses of these methods against current approaches and outlines key theoretical results to guide future research.

Utility functions, along with their equivalents such as value, objective, loss, reward functions, and preference orderings, serve as a foundational component in most contemporary machine learning architectures. However, these mechanisms for establishing goals and directing optimization encounter significant practical and conceptual hurdles when tasked with simultaneously pursuing independent, multi-dimensional objectives that cannot be reduced to one another. Ethicists have established several impossibility theorems arising from this context; these findings suggest that it is impossible to formally define an outcome as beneficial for a population without contravening strong human ethical intuitions (specifically regarding social welfare functions). We contend that this constitutes a critical practical issue for any machine learning system—such as medical decision support tools or autonomous weaponry—or for rigid, rule-based bureaucracies responsible for high-stakes decisions concerning human lives: such systems ought to avoid employing objective functions in their strict mathematical form. Instead, we investigate the alternative of utilizing uncertain objectives, which can be represented as partially ordered preferences or as probability distributions over total orders. We demonstrate that existing impossibility theorems can be recast as uncertainty theorems within both of these frameworks and derive lower bounds on the uncertainty necessitated by these impossibility results. Finally, we propose two conjectures concerning the link between uncertainty in objectives and the occurrence of severe unintended consequences in AI systems.

We introduce and evaluate both centralized and distributed algorithms designed for device-to-device video scheduling and streaming. These methods simultaneously tackle the challenges of link scheduling and video quality adaptation during streaming. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed algorithms substantially outperform traditional approaches that handle these issues separately.

We present the fundamental theorem of projective geometry for semimodules over semirings, building upon recent advancements regarding bases in semimodules defined over semirings. This work involves a detailed examination of linear algebra structures within the semiring framework. Furthermore, we offer more explicit findings to clarify the implications of our primary theorem concerning mappings between tropical lines in the tropical plane. In addition, we investigate the geometric relationships linking these concepts to the extensive theory of tropical geometry.

In galaxy clusters with intermediate temperatures (T = 2.5 - 4.5 keV), iron abundance determinations rely nearly equally on Fe K transitions at ~6.7 keV and Fe L transitions between 0.9 and 1.3 keV. Although measurements based on K-shell data are regarded as reliable, the limitations of current instrumental resolution and incomplete knowledge of atomic physics make modeling the complex Fe L-line profile difficult, potentially introducing biases. This study investigates the systematics arising from Fe L-line modeling that could affect iron abundance estimates in this temperature regime. We analyze a sample of three luminous galaxy clusters with extensive XMM-Newton observations falling within the 2.5 - 4.5 keV temperature range. By fitting spectra from concentric rings using APEC and APEC+APEC models while alternatively excluding L and K bands, we calculate the fractional difference in metal abundances ($\Delta Z/Z$) to assess the consistency between K- and L-shell-derived results. We examine how the $\Delta Z/Z$ distribution varies with cluster radius, ring temperature, and X-ray flux. Systematics induced by the L lines, determined through individual fits of MOS and pn spectra, remain constant at 5 - 6% across the entire temperature range. In contrast, joint fitting of MOS and pn data yields a slightly higher estimate of 1 - 2%. No significant dependence on X-ray flux is observed. The measured 5 - 8% value suggests that these systematics contribute modestly to derived iron abundances, bolstering confidence in future measurements. Currently, these results offer the most accurate estimate of such systematics, though upcoming microcalorimeters are expected to significantly enhance our understanding of the atomic processes driving Fe L emissions.

This paper investigates the bifurcation from a line soliton for a stationary nonlinear Schrödinger equation defined on the product space $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{T}$. We broaden previous findings by extending them to a wider class of nonlinearities. The core of our analysis depends on establishing a lower bound for the solution to the associated "auxiliary equation," followed by the application of the Crandall-Rabinowitz theorem.

Adversarial Machine Learning has become a significant area of Computer Science, driven by the inherent fragility of trained models and crowdsourcing methods that facilitate data manipulation. While interest in adversarial attacks on graphs has exploded over the past two years, the Graph Classification domain remains largely unexplored. Because Graph Classification datasets comprise discrete graphs with class labels, previous studies have bypassed direct gradient optimization, opting instead for indirect Reinforcement Learning techniques. This work investigates the novel challenge of Data Poisoning attacks—occurring during the training phase—against Neural Networks for Graph Classification, employing Reinforcement Learning Agents.

Hybrid Knowledge Bases (HKBs) utilizing Lifschitz's logic of Minimal Knowledge with Negation as Failure effectively integrate the expressiveness of Description Logics and Logic Programming. Although Motik and Rosati's syntax for these systems excludes function symbols, Knorr et al. established an alternating fixpoint partition to define a well-founded semantics for function-free HKBs. This paper introduces an iterated fixpoint semantics capable of handling HKBs that include function symbols. We demonstrate that this new semantics generalizes the approach by Knorr et al., as it aligns with the alternating fixpoint partition when no function symbols are present. Furthermore, the proposed framework is well-suited for future probabilistic extensions using a distribution semantic approach.

High-resolution (1 km) monthly precipitation climatologies for the Norwegian mainland, covering the period 1981–2010, were generated using Multi-linear Local Regression Kriging (MLRK). This statistical technique interpolates observed station normals onto a regular grid by modeling the impact of key geographical factors—latitude, longitude, elevation, and proximity to the sea—at a local scale. The MLRK process involves two stages: first, a background precipitation field is estimated via multi-linear local regression using geographical data; second, kriging interpolation refines this field to align more closely with station residuals (the difference between observed normals and the background field). Accuracy was assessed using a leave-one-out cross-validation method to reconstruct station normals and benchmark performance against other interpolation techniques. Due to sparse observational coverage in remote and mountainous areas of Norway, numerical model outputs were also incorporated. These models provide a station-density-independent reference field for evaluating MLRK, although they are less precise than direct observations. Specifically, a 2.5 km resolution regional climate simulation (2003–2016), derived from the dynamical downscaling of the ERA-Interim global reanalysis, was utilized. Beyond validating MLRK, the study examined the integration of numerical model data with observed climatologies, revealing that this hybrid approach yields more accurate high-resolution climatologies for the country. In this combined framework, numerical models supply critical data for remote and rugged terrains, while in-situ observations correct for model biases.

Using 1.0 fb⁻¹ of proton-proton collision data collected by the LHCb experiment at a center-of-mass energy of √s = 7 TeV, the ratio of branching fractions for the radiative B decays B⁰ → K*⁰γ and Bₛ⁰ → φγ has been determined. The result is BR(B⁰ → K*⁰γ)/BR(Bₛ⁰ → φγ) = 1.23 ± 0.06(stat.) ± 0.04(syst.) ± 0.10(fₛ/fₑ), where the uncertainties correspond to statistical, experimental systematic, and fragmentation fraction ratio (fₛ/fₑ) contributions, respectively. By applying the world average for BR(B⁰ → K*⁰γ), the branching fraction for Bₛ⁰ → φγ is derived as (3.5 ± 0.4) × 10⁻⁵. Additionally, the direct CP asymmetry in B⁰ → K*⁰γ decays was measured with the same dataset, yielding A_CP(B⁰ → K*⁰γ) = (0.8 ± 1.7(stat.) ± 0.9(syst.))%. These findings represent the most precise measurements to date and are consistent with prior experimental data and theoretical predictions.

We employ the experimentally determined difference in $\Lambda$ separation energies between the mirror hypernuclei ${^4_\Lambda \rm He}$ and ${^4_\Lambda \rm H}$ to restrict the $\Lambda$-neutron interaction. Our hyperon-nucleon interaction, derived using chiral effective field theory at next-to-leading order, incorporates the dominant charge-symmetry breaking (CSB) component. Specifically, we calibrate the strengths of the two resulting CSB contact terms by fitting them to the separation energy differences observed in the $0^+$ and $1^+$ states of these hypernuclei. By design, this interaction accurately reproduces all low-energy hyperon-nucleon scattering data, as well as the properties of the hypertriton and the CSB effects in ${^4_\Lambda \rm He}$-${^4_\Lambda \rm H}$. Consequently, we can generate the first predictions for $\Lambda$n scattering lengths, relying exclusively on existing hypernuclear data.

Due to the characteristics of mobile devices and their unlocking mechanisms, authentication credentials are highly susceptible to shoulder surfing, a type of observation-based attack. Although existing research has explored methods to mitigate this threat, the actual effectiveness of shoulder surfing on contemporary systems remains poorly understood. This paper presents a large-scale online study (n=1173) designed to establish a baseline for the vulnerability of current unlock authentication systems. By analyzing controlled video recordings of victims entering 4- and 6-digit PINs and 6-length Android unlock patterns on various devices from different angles, we recruited participants to act as attackers attempting to deduce the inputs through observation. Our findings indicate that 6-digit PINs are the most resistant to this attack, with a success rate of only 10.8% for a single observation, rising to 26.5% with multiple observations. In contrast, 6-length Android patterns are significantly more vulnerable, suffering attack rates of 64.2% and 79.9% for single and multiple observations, respectively. Disabling the feedback lines for patterns reduces these rates to 35.3% and 52.1% for single and multiple observations. Additionally, data regarding hand position, phone size, and viewing angles provide insights into the best and worst-case scenarios for shoulder surfing vulnerability, offering guidance for users to enhance their security and establishing benchmarks for future research.

I demonstrate that the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) quadrupole evolves more quickly than anticipated due to the Sun's acceleration toward the Galactic center. Recent measurements from Gaia EDR3 indicate this acceleration causes a fractional quadrupole change of approximately 10^{-9} per year, which is ten times greater than the expected evolution from the CMB's last scattering surface.

Sampling initiates the transformation of an analog optical signal into a digital electrical one, which can subsequently be analyzed using established electrical signal processing techniques. While mode-locked lasers are frequently employed for all-optical sampling, they present several limitations. A new, straightforward all-optical sampling technique leverages the frequency-time coherence of the signal itself. This approach relies on just two coupled modulators driven by an electrical sine wave, facilitating easy integration into suitable platforms like Silicon Photonics. The proposed method enables all-optical sampling with electrically adjustable bandwidth, repetition rate, and time shift.

Technologies, applications, and services spanning from sensors to big data analytics and artificial intelligence are fundamentally reshaping the automotive sector. This paper introduces our multidisciplinary effort to develop a publicly accessible dataset aimed at advancing visual marketing research and applications within the automotive industry, including areas such as exterior design, consumer analytics, and sales modeling. Our motivation stems from the increasing focus on product aesthetics, coupled with the absence of a large-scale dataset encompassing diverse variables and information. By conducting a user survey, we identified common challenges faced by both marketing researchers and computer scientists, and we designed our dataset specifically to address these issues. The collection comprises 1.4 million images from 899 car models, paired with corresponding vehicle specifications and sales data spanning over a decade in the UK market. To our knowledge, this represents the inaugural large-scale automotive dataset integrating images, text, and sales information from multiple sources across an extended timeframe. We detail the data structure and preparation methodology, contributing methodologically to multi-source data fusion and sharing, while also presenting three application examples to demonstrate the dataset's utility.

Any proposed Peccei-Quinn (PQ) symmetry is susceptible to various forms of explicit breaking, which are well-known to potentially undermine the axion's resolution of the strong CP problem. Furthermore, it has been proposed that under specific conditions, such breaking could result in an unexpectedly large axion mass. Two primary corrections to this calculation have been extensively studied: higher-dimensional symmetry-breaking operators in theories involving a complex field for spontaneous PQ breaking, and small instantons. Inspired by scenarios where small instantons dominate the $\theta$ potential in non-abelian gauge theories, we frame the issue of axion quality as constraints on a Wilsonian effective action at energy scales just above those of QCD. Within this framework, the conventional axion mass calculation presumes a nearly exact PQ symmetry in the action, while higher-dimensional operators and small instantons act as symmetry-breaking terms. This approach allows for a unified analysis of axion quality. If one posits order-one CP violation at high energies, the requirement to solve the strong CP problem imposes strict constraints on the axion potential within this Wilsonian action, necessitating that the axion mass remain extremely close to its standard value.

Driven by the early-time dynamics of quark-gluon plasma in high-energy heavy-ion collisions, we utilize classical-statistical lattice simulations combined with linear response theory to derive gluonic spectral functions for overoccupied gauge theories far from equilibrium. Our analysis in 3+1 dimensions reveals that the spectral function displays quasiparticle excitations across all momenta, which largely align with perturbative hard-thermal loop predictions, though some nonperturbative deviations are also observed. Conversely, excitation structures in 2+1 dimensions are inherently nontrivial and nonperturbative. These nonperturbative interactions result in broad peaks within the spectral function, indicating a lack of soft quasiparticles in such theories. Furthermore, this implies that systems exhibiting large momentum anisotropy may experience substantial nonperturbative corrections, a factor with important implications for phenomenological applications in heavy-ion collision studies.

Automatically pinpointing software bugs to the specific code changes that caused them holds the promise of boosting developer productivity and enhancing software quality. Achieving this automation requires effectively aligning bug reports with source code modifications, even when a substantial vocabulary gap separates the natural language of the reports from the identifiers used in the code. To overcome this challenge, methods must capture semantics unique to software engineering and specific projects to identify relationships between these documents beyond simple word matching. While transformer-based deep learning models like BERT are highly effective at utilizing contextual information, their high computational cost often makes them unsuitable for time-sensitive environments. This paper outlines a method to accelerate BERT for use in changeset-based bug localization. We also examine key design choices, such as optimal changeset encoding and strategies for matching bug reports to individual changes to maximize accuracy. Our study compares our model's performance and accuracy against non-contextual baselines (e.g., vector space models) and prior BERT-based approaches in software engineering. Evaluation results indicate that our proposed BERT model offers distinct advantages over these baselines, particularly for bug reports that provide no explicit clues about related code elements.

Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) serves as a comprehensive framework for modeling diverse problems. Because commercial solvers are specifically designed to handle QUBO, and the formulation is inherently quadratic, it is essential to convert higher-degree pseudo-Boolean problems into this format. Traditional conversion methods introduce extra auxiliary variables and penalty terms for each high-order term. This paper enhances the standard cubic-to-quadratic transformation by reducing both the count of auxiliary variables and the magnitude of penalty coefficients. Comprehensive experiments on Max 3-SAT, modeled as QUBO, demonstrate a reduction in the subproblem size for minimizing auxiliary variables approaching 100%.

Addressing the critical challenge of missing data in machine learning, we propose a regularization framework based on the principle that imputation techniques must maintain the data's causal structure. This approach, named MIRACLE (Causally-Aware Imputation Algorithm), enhances baseline imputation methods by iteratively refining them through simultaneous modeling of the missingness mechanism and enforcing consistency with the underlying causal data generation process. Extensive evaluations on both synthetic and real-world public datasets demonstrate that MIRACLE consistently outperforms various benchmark methods across all missingness scenarios: missing at random, completely at random, and not at random.

This paper extends the Difference in Differences (DiD) literature by demonstrating that both additive and multiplicative standard and coarse Structural Nested Mean Models (SNMMs), as defined by Robins (1994–2004), Lok and Degruttola (2012), and Vansteelandt and Joffe (2014), are identifiable under parallel trends assumptions. Our approach facilitates adjustments for time-varying covariates, allows for the identification of effect heterogeneity based on these covariates, and supports the estimation of additional causal contrasts, including "blip" effects and controlled direct effects. Furthermore, we estimate treatment effects across a broad spectrum of treatment patterns, avoiding restrictions to "staggered adoption" scenarios and accommodating multidimensional treatments with mixed categorical and continuous components. Importantly, these enhancements require no stronger parallel trends assumption than those typically used in DiD studies, and we offer a sensitivity analysis method for potential violations of this assumption. Unlike much of the existing DiD work, our framework focuses exclusively on panel data rather than repeated cross-sectional data. Additionally, we outline how to estimate optimal treatment regimes using optimal regime SNMMs under parallel trends and an extra, stringent assumption of no effect modification by unobserved confounders.
