We conclude by applying our methods to real-world datasets to assess the impact of bank deregulation on housing prices and the influence of floods on flood insurance uptake.

By integrating three concepts—port-Hamiltonian energy-based modeling, structural analysis from circuit theory, and the structural analysis of general differential-algebraic equations—we have developed a novel representation for electrical circuits known as compact port-Hamiltonian equations. These equations are distinguished by their remarkable simplicity and symmetry, guaranteeing an index of at most 1 alongside other favorable numerical characteristics. The approach has been realized in Matlab, accompanied by formal proofs and numerical demonstrations.

With the expanding use of Natural Language Processing (NLP) in sensitive domains such as political profiling and educational essay evaluation, there is a critical demand for greater model transparency to foster stakeholder trust and detect biases. Although significant research in Explainable AI has produced methods that translate complex NLP model predictions into human-readable insights, how individuals interpret these explanations remains largely unexamined. Inherent human biases can hinder the comprehension of such explanations, potentially leading to flawed assessments of model outputs. To investigate the efficacy of saliency-based post-hoc explainability methods in NLP, we conducted a randomized survey experiment. The findings reveal that humans tend to accept these explanations with insufficient critical scrutiny.

This paper establishes criteria for the boundedness of fractional integral operators within vanishing generalized weighted Morrey spaces and examines the associated commutators generated by BMO functions.

Self-organized criticality (SOC) has been suggested as a universal driver for scale-free dynamics across numerous complex systems, potentially including the brain. Although experimental data across diverse neural recordings have confirmed these scale-free patterns, the underlying biological mechanisms remained unclear. Drawing on experimental evidence and employing various network models, synaptic plasticity was identified as a potential mechanism that could drive brain dynamics toward a critical state. This review examines how biologically plausible plasticity rules, functioning across multiple timescales, are integrated into models and how they shift network dynamics by altering the number and strength of neuronal connections. While some rules facilitate the stabilization of criticality, others require supplementary mechanisms to avoid diverging from this state. We propose that plasticity rules capable of inducing criticality can be categorized based on the duration of near-critical dynamics that persist after the rules are deactivated. Furthermore, we explore the role of self-organization and criticality in computation. Ultimately, while criticality offers valuable insights into brain function and self-organization, living neural networks appear to utilize not only criticality for computational purposes but also deviations from it.

Lithium (Li), which originates from multiple sources including the Big Bang, stars, and cosmic rays, holds significant interest because it is heavily depleted during stellar lifetimes and its chemical evolution within the Milky Way remains poorly understood. To effectively constrain models of stellar and galactic chemical evolution, there is a critical need for precise lithium abundance measurements across a wide spectrum of evolutionary stages, metallicities, and galactic volumes. While industrial-parameterization era spectroscopic surveys like APOGEE, GALAH, RAVE, and LAMOST have successfully employed data-driven methods to rapidly derive stellar labels (atmospheric parameters and abundances), we aim to advance this field by applying machine-learning techniques specifically for lithium analysis in preparation for upcoming surveys such as 4MOST and WEAVE. We developed a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) trained on Gaia-ESO Survey iDR6 stellar labels ($\mathrm{T_{eff}}$, log(g), [Fe/H], and A(Li)) combined with GIRAFFE HR15N spectra to infer these parameters and abundances for approximately 40,000 stars. Our results demonstrate that the CNN accurately learns the underlying physics of stellar labels by identifying relevant spectral features across diverse evolutionary stages and parameters. Notably, the network successfully isolates the lithium absorption line at 6707.8 Å amidst thousands of other spectral lines in the GIRAFFE HR15N configuration, enabling the discovery of rare objects such as lithium-rich giants. These high-performance outcomes are attributable to a meticulously constructed, high-quality, and homogeneous training dataset. This CNN methodology is exceptionally well-suited for next-generation spectroscopic surveys targeting lithium and other elements, including the 4MIDABLE-LR/HR (4MOST Milky Way disk and bulge low- and high-resolution) projects. In this context, it is essential to thoroughly investigate the caveats of machine-learning applications alongside realistic uncertainties in labels and upper limits for abundances.

Despite the rapid expansion of literature on dynamic connectivity methods, current approaches predominantly focus on estimating networks independently for each individual, thereby missing opportunities to utilize shared information patterns. We introduce novel graph-theoretic methods for estimating population-level dynamic networks that borrow information across heterogeneous samples in an unsupervised way, guided by covariate data. Specifically, we propose a Bayesian product mixture model that applies independent mixture priors at every time scan and employs covariates to determine mixture weights, creating time-varying sample clusters designed to pool information. This computation is executed via an efficient Expectation-Maximization algorithm. Comprehensive simulation studies demonstrate significant improvements in recovering true dynamic networks compared to existing methods. Furthermore, an analysis of fMRI block task data involving behavioral interventions identifies subgroups with similar dynamic connectivity and reveals intervention-related changes concentrated in biologically meaningful brain regions. Conversely, traditional dynamic connectivity approaches detect little to no temporal changes, a result that appears biologically implausible and underscores the difficulties caused by the inability to systematically share information across samples.

We calculate the total Stiefel-Whitney class for a real representation $\pi$ of $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)$ (with $q$ being odd) by utilizing character values of $\pi$ evaluated on order $2$ diagonal elements. Additionally, we determine the total Stiefel-Whitney class for real representations of both $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ and $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$.

This study demonstrates high qubit coherence, minimal crosstalk, and low single-qubit gate errors within a superconducting circuit architecture designed for scalability to two-dimensional qubit lattices. The design incorporates an inductively shunted cavity enclosure, combining non-galvanic out-of-plane control wiring with qubits and resonators fabricated on opposite sides of a substrate. The proof-of-principle device, comprising four uncoupled transmon qubits, achieves average energy relaxation times of $T_1=149(38)~\mu$s, pure echoed dephasing times of $T_{\phi,e}=189(34)~\mu$s, and single-qubit gate fidelities of $F=99.982(4)\%$ via simultaneous randomized benchmarking. Due to the three-dimensional integration of the control wiring, qubits remain individually addressable as the architecture scales into larger lattices. Furthermore, band structure simulations indicate that the tiled enclosure will maintain a clean electromagnetic environment for enclosed qubits at any scale.

Tafazzul Husain Khan (c. 1727–1800), who initially served in the Awadh court, spent his final twenty years as a loyal associate of the East India Company. His unique distinction among court officials lay less in his intellectual depth, political skill, or negotiation abilities, and more in his passion for mathematics and astronomy. Interactions with Company staff, who possessed knowledge of Oriental languages and modern science, allowed him to refresh his mathematical skills and motivated him to undertake—and allegedly complete—the translation of several significant mathematical works, including Newton's *Principia*. However, Campbell's 1804 obituary, which claimed Khan translated the *Principia* directly from Latin into Arabic, is supported by insufficient evidence. An examination of the three posthumously published tracts attributed to Khan reveals that none are translations of Newton's work. Consequently, until concrete proof emerges, assertions regarding his translations of the *Principia* and other Western texts remain mere rumors, subject to the distortions inherent in collective memory.

Signal transmission is a fundamental phenomenon throughout the living world, ranging from molecules initiating complex metabolic pathways to animals warning their groups of predators. When communication serves a shared interest, simple sender-receiver models demonstrate how reliable signaling can evolve. While these games have been widely studied, particularly regarding static network effects on information transfer, no prior research has addressed the coevolution of strategy and network structure. This study demonstrates that such coevolution drives the spontaneous formation of distinct groups from a uniform population. Furthermore, it enables the emergence of novel "hybrid" signaling groups—combinations of complementary behaviors that depend on evolved network structures for effective communication, which would otherwise fail. These findings apply broadly to common interest signaling games, remain robust across various parameters, and address known issues of communication inefficiency. Our results offer fresh perspectives on adaptive behavior, signaling, and group formation in both natural and social systems where network structures frequently change, with implications for research involving metabolic networks, neural and protein interactions, and social organisms.

Parametrized motion planning algorithms are highly versatile and universal, capable of operating under diverse external conditions treated as input parameters. This paper investigates the parameterized motion planning problem within sphere bundles. Our primary findings establish upper and lower bounds for parametrized topological complexity: upper bounds generally rely on the sectional categories of the corresponding fibrations, while lower bounds are derived from characteristic classes and their attributes. We explicitly calculate the parametrized topological complexity across numerous examples, demonstrating that it can attain arbitrarily large values.

Numerous image enhancement and editing tasks, including forward and inverse tone mapping or color grading, lack a singular solution and instead offer a spectrum of options, each embodying a distinct style. However, current learning-based approaches often strive to identify a single mapping, effectively ignoring stylistic variations. This paper demonstrates that stylistic information can be extracted from collections of image pairs and compressed into a 2- or 3-dimensional vector. This approach provides both an efficient representation and an interpretable latent space for modifying image styles. Specifically, the global color transformation between image pairs is modeled using a custom normalizing flow conditioned on a polynomial basis of pixel colors. We demonstrate that this architecture outperforms PCA and VAE methods in encoding image style within low-dimensional spaces, achieving an accuracy near 40 dB. This represents a significant improvement of approximately 7–10 dB over existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Relativistic gravitational anomalies give rise to anomalous transport coefficients that become active at finite temperatures in condensed matter systems featuring gapless fermions. The chiral vortical effect (CVE) manifests as an anomalous chiral current along a rotation axis, derived from a gravimagnetic field and gravitational anomaly. Similarly, the chiral torsional effect (CTE) originates from hydrodynamically independent frame fields and connections. We examine the relationship between CVE, CTE, and gravitational anomalies for relativistic fermions through the lens of torsion and the Nieh-Yan anomaly. Our analysis reveals that the DC transport coefficients of these two anomalies are intimately linked, contingent on whether torsion is non-zero within the hydrodynamic framework. When torsion is considered, the relativistic anomaly from torsion is well-defined, replacing ultraviolet divergent terms with dependencies on chemical potential or temperature. This anomaly term is second-order in gradients and contributes to linear response for CTE, implying the same for CVE. As a case study, we consider chiral $p+ip$ Weyl superfluids or conductors. At low energies, the system behaves effectively relativistically along a specific anisotropy axis, with hydrodynamics governed by two velocities: the normal velocity $\boldsymbol{v}_n$ and the superfluid velocity $\boldsymbol{v}_s$. These two anomalies arise from the rotation of the normal component and the dependence of momentum density on the superfluid velocity (the order parameter). Specifically, in the CVE, a chiral current is generated by the solid-body rotation of the normal component with angular velocity $\boldsymbol{v}_n = \boldsymbol\Omega \times \boldsymbol{r}$. Conversely, in the CTE, a chiral current is produced by the vorticity $\nabla \times \boldsymbol{v}_s$, which corresponds to torsion in the low-energy effective theory. In equilibrium, the average $\langle\langle \nabla \times \boldsymbol{v_s}\rangle\rangle$ equals $2\boldsymbol\Omega$, causing the two anomaly currents to cancel each other out.

We introduce PSFormer, a highly effective point transformer designed for 3D salient object detection. Functioning as an encoder-decoder architecture, PSFormer leverages transformers to model contextual information across multiple scales, addressing both point-level and scene-level perspectives. Within the encoder, we implement a Point Context Transformer (PCT) module that captures region-specific contextual features at the point level by utilizing two distinct transformers to uncover inter-point relationships. In the decoder, a Scene Context Transformer (SCT) module learns scene-level context representations; it combines Upsampling-and-Transformer blocks with Multi-context Aggregation units to synthesize global semantic and multi-level features from the encoder into a comprehensive global scene context. Experimental results demonstrate that PSFormer outperforms existing methods, confirming its superior robustness in challenging scenarios involving small objects, multiple objects, and those with complex structures.

During the Galaxy's first billion years, it experienced multiple mergers with dwarf satellites of varying masses. The debris from the Gaia-Sausage/Enceladus (GSE) event, which caused the Milky Way's most recent major merger, currently dominates the inner halo and has been proposed as the origin of both the Hercules-Aquila Cloud (HAC) and the Virgo Overdensity (VOD). By integrating data from SEGUE, APOGEE, Gaia, and StarHorse to analyze chemodynamical properties, we confirm the connection between HAC, VOD, and GSE. Our results show that the orbital eccentricity distributions of these stellar overdensities match those of GSE. Additionally, they exhibit similar, sharply peaked metallicity distribution functions, which supports the theory of a shared origin. Furthermore, within all examined chemical-abundance spaces, HAC and VOD are indistinguishable from the characteristic GSE population. Collectively, these findings provide definitive proof that the GSE merger is the primary source of the stellar populations residing in these halo overdensities.

Multimodal speech recognition seeks to enhance automatic speech recognition (ASR) performance by utilizing associated visual cues alongside audio inputs. Although prior methods heavily rely on robust visual representations, often through fine-tuning pretrained image models, the speech component has received comparatively little focus. This study explores improving the foundational speech recognition system using analogous techniques applied to visual encoders, specifically representation transfer and data augmentation. First, we demonstrate that initializing with a pretrained ASR model boosts state-of-the-art results; notably, incorporating visual information yields gains even when starting from a powerful unimodal system. Second, we implement speech data augmentation to steer the multimodal system toward attending to visual stimuli, a method that supersedes previous word masking strategies by offering conceptual simplicity and consistent performance improvements in multimodal contexts. We present empirical findings across three multimodal datasets, featuring the newly introduced Localized Narratives.

This study extends the Polyakov-Nambu-Jona-Lasinio (PNJL) model to the zero-temperature regime to describe the confinement/deconfinement transition. By modifying the scalar and vector interaction strengths of the original PNJL model to depend on the traced Polyakov loop, the effective interactions become contingent upon the quark phase, thereby enabling a backreaction of quarks on the gluonic sector even at $T=0$, a feature anticipated by quantum chromodynamics. A detailed thermodynamic analysis of this extended model, designated PNJL0, reveals that, with an appropriate Polyakov potential, it exhibits a first-order confined/deconfined quark phase transition at zero temperature. Additionally, we demonstrate that the vector channel is crucial for permitting non-zero $\Phi$ solutions within the PNJL0 framework. Finally, by examining the sensitivity of the combined quarkyonic and deconfinement phases to the vector interaction strength and the proposed zero-temperature Polyakov-loop potential parametrization, we establish a viable parameter window for the bulk values of the relevant constants.

The study investigates the impact of quenched disorder on frustrated systems by introducing random fluctuations into antiferromagnetic (AF) interactions on a checkerboard lattice. Utilizing a cluster mean-field approach within the replica framework yields an effective single-cluster model, which is analyzed using one-step replica symmetry breaking (RSB) with precise calculations of all intracluster interactions. By adjusting the ratio of second-neighbor to first-neighbor interactions ($J_2/J_1$), competing forces are generated; as $J_2/J_1$ approaches 1, the system becomes highly frustrated, triggering a phase transition between AF orders even without disorder. In the clean limit, AF order emerges at lower $J_2/J_1$ values, with the Néel temperature dropping as frustration intensifies. However, quenched disorder alters this behavior by inducing a replica symmetry breaking (RSB) spin glass phase when the disorder strength $J$ is sufficiently high. Specifically, in the region of maximum frustration, a mixed phase characterized by staggered magnetization arises under weak disorder conditions. This indicates that systems with competing interactions are susceptible to exhibiting glassy dynamics rather than conventional ordering when subjected to weak quenched disorder.

We present a theory of unipotent morphisms for algebraic stacks. This framework enables two applications: first, a unipotent counterpart to Gabber's Theorem concerning torsion $\mathbf{G}_m$-gerbes, and second, the demonstration that smooth Deligne-Mumford stacks with quasi-projective coarse spaces possess the resolution property in positive characteristic. Central to our approach is a descent theorem for flags, established through the work of Schappi.

This study examines the Cohen-Macaulay compactification of twisted cubics within projective n-space, which serves as the fine moduli scheme for CM-curves possessing the Hilbert polynomial 3t+1. We demonstrate that for projective 3-space, the moduli scheme of these CM-curves is isomorphic to the twisted cubic component of the Hilbert scheme. Furthermore, we provide a description of this compactification for twisted cubics in n-space.

The basin of attraction comprises all initial points that eventually converge to an attracting set, making its understanding vital for analyzing the dynamics of specific systems. This study tackles the challenge of reconstructing basins of attraction in multistable systems using solely labeled data. We frame this issue as a classification problem, employing a deep neural network to predict the attractor associated with any given initial condition. Furthermore, we present a technique to approximate the basin boundaries based on the trained classifier. Additionally, we establish a connection between basin structure complexity and reconstruction quality through the metric of basin entropy. Finally, we validate the proposed approach by applying it to the Lorenz system within a bistable regime.

Current object detectors for environmental perception lack an inherent safety layer within their model architecture, raising significant concerns regarding the trustworthiness of their predictions. Recent adversarial attacks demonstrate that most existing detection networks are susceptible to input manipulation, a vulnerability that could jeopardize the safety of autonomous vehicles in real-world scenarios. This issue is further exacerbated when uncertainty errors cannot propagate through submodules that are not integrated into an end-to-end design. To mitigate these risks, a parallel verification module is necessary to validate object proposals generated by Deep Neural Networks. This study aims to verify 3D object proposals from the MonoRUn model by introducing a plausibility framework that utilizes cross-sensor data to minimize false positives. The proposed verification metric incorporates prior knowledge through four distinct energy functions, each applying a specific prior to generate an energy value that provides a plausibility assessment for the hypothesis. Additionally, we implement a novel two-step approach to enhance the optimization of the composite energy function used in the energy model.

By integrating Bayesian change-point detection with latent variable models, we can segment high-dimensional time-series data, assuming that change-points reside on a lower-dimensional manifold where discrete latent variables are inferred. Although full inference for this model is computationally prohibitive, current approaches rely on pseudo-observations derived from point-estimates, which can compromise detection accuracy if the estimates lack certainty. To address this limitation, we introduce a multinomial sampling methodology that enhances detection rates and minimizes delay without increasing computational complexity or sacrificing analytical tractability. Experimental results demonstrate superior performance compared to baseline methods, and we include an application example focused on human behavior analysis.

Extracting information from scientific literature presents significant challenges due to its specialized nature. This paper outlines the entity recognition techniques we developed for the DEAL (Detecting Entities in the Astrophysics Literature) shared task, which aims to create a system capable of identifying named entities within a dataset of astrophysics scholarly articles. Our participation strategy was designed to facilitate an empirical comparison between word-based tagging and span-based classification approaches. When evaluated on two hidden test sets provided by the organizers, our top-performing submission attained F1 scores of 0.8307 during the validation phase and 0.7990 during the testing phase.

Let $p$ denote a prime number and $m$ an integer coprime to $p$. Drawing inspiration from arithmetic topology, we define the twisted Iwasawa invariants $\lambda, \mu, \nu$ for ${\rm GL}_N$-representations and covers of knots associated with the group $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z}_p$. Among other results, we demonstrate that the collection of these Iwasawa invariants uniquely determines both the genus and the fibered nature of a knot, thereby establishing their profinite rigidity. We provide several illustrative examples to clarify these concepts and further prove the $\mu=0$ theorem for ${\rm SL}_2$-representations of twist knot groups, accompanied by additional remarks.

Strategic behaviors like "click framing" have frequently emerged in real-world recommendation systems targeting sequential learning methods. Inspired by this, we investigate combinatorial multi-armed bandits (CMAB) under strategic reward manipulation, where each arm alters its emitted reward signals to serve its own interests. This model of adversarial behavior relaxes earlier frameworks such as adversarial attacks and corruption. We introduce a strategic variant of the combinatorial UCB algorithm that achieves a regret of at most $O(m\log T + m B_{max})$ under such manipulations, with $T$ representing the time horizon, $m$ the number of arms, and $B_{max}$ the maximum budget per arm. Furthermore, we establish lower bounds on the budgets required for arms to induce specific regret levels in the bandit algorithm. Comprehensive experiments on online worker selection for crowdsourcing, online influence maximization, and online recommendations—utilizing both synthetic and real datasets—validate our theoretical results regarding robustness and regret bounds across various manipulation budget scenarios.

We establish Taylor's Formula within the context of conformable fractional derivatives. This formulation is subsequently utilized to generalize several recent and classical integral inequalities to conformable fractional calculus, specifically those of Steffensen, Chebychev, Hermite-Hadamard, Ostrowski, and Gruss.

This study re-examines the evolution of the scale factor within a flat FRW spacetime by introducing a novel generalized decay law for the dynamic $\Lambda$-term under modified gravity theories. The analysis investigates specific cosmological parameters and their behavior across a generalized framework that encompasses multiple decay laws previously found in the literature. Additionally, we derive observational constraints on the model parameters and calculate the current values of $\{\Omega_{m_0}$, $\Omega_{\Lambda_0}$, $q_{0}$, $t_{0}$, $\omega_{0}\}$, comparing these results with various observational data. The discussion also covers the occurrence of finite-time singularities in both the past and future within this model.

We introduce two advancements for numerically integrating functions across the Brillouin zone. First, we propose a nonuniform grid known as the Farey grid, which extends the capabilities of regular grids. Second, we develop symmetry-adapted Voronoi tessellation, a versatile method for assigning weights to points within any arbitrary grid. By merging these innovations, we present a strategy for Brillouin zone integration and interpolation that offers substantial computational efficiency compared to traditional approaches relying on uniform regular grids. We validate this methodology through first-principles studies of Kohn anomalies in the phonon dispersions of graphene and MgB2, as well as in assessing electron-phonon driven band gap renormalization in diamond and bismuthene. In phonon calculations, our approach yields speedups of 3 to 4 times when using density functional perturbation theory and 6 to 7 times when employing finite differences with supercells, effectively equating the computational cost of these two methods. Furthermore, electron-phonon coupling calculations exhibit even greater performance gains. Finally, we demonstrate that the Farey grid can be constructed as a combination of standard regular grids, which should ease the integration of this technique.

It is widely accepted that a conductivity platform typically requires an insulator with topologically non-trivial bulk states, a principle observed in the two-dimensional quantum (anomalous) Hall effect, quantum spin Hall effect, and three-dimensional topological insulators. In this study, we introduce a spin Hall conductivity (SHC) platform within a specific class of three-dimensional metallic materials featuring triply degenerate points near the Fermi level. Utilizing a four-band **k**·**p** model, we demonstrate that an SHC platform emerges between the $|\frac{3}{2},\pm\frac{3}{2}\rangle$ and $|\frac{1}{2},\pm\frac{1}{2}\rangle$ states in such metallic systems. Furthermore, our *ab initio* calculations predict that an experimentally synthesized TaN exhibits a nearly ideal SHC platform with a width of 0.56 eV, suggesting viability for high-temperature applications. The electrical conductivity tensor of TaN reveals a spin Hall angle of -0.62, surpassing many previously reported materials and positioning it as a superior candidate for generating stable spin currents.

This study examines a flat FLRW cosmological model incorporating a perfect fluid of variable Chaplygin gas within $f(R; T)$ gravity and particle creation. The analyzed scale factors indicate that the universe undergoes accelerated expansion driven by effective negative pressure generated during its evolution. The impact of particle creation pressure on various cosmological parameters is discussed in detail. Using established values for free parameters, the research investigates the late-time expansion of the universe alongside energy conditions. Furthermore, state-finder diagnostics are applied to the considered scenarios, and the time evolution of the source function suggests that particle production remains nearly constant at late times.

Quantum key distribution (QKD) leverages fundamental quantum mechanics to enable the exchange of unconditionally secure keys between remote users. While earlier studies utilizing the "Micius" quantum science satellite initially proved the viability of a global QKD network, practical implementation of space-based QKD has historically been hindered by technical challenges, particularly the substantial size and weight of ground stations needed to capture quantum signals. This study reports successful space-to-ground QKD demonstrations utilizing portable receiving ground stations. These portable units weigh under 100 kg, occupy less than 1 cubic meter, and can be installed within 12 hours, representing reductions of approximately two orders of magnitude in weight, spatial footprint, and deployment time compared to prior systems. Furthermore, the equipment is user-friendly and can be situated on building rooftops in urban environments. Secure keys were successfully generated from the "Micius" satellite to these portable stations at six distinct locations in China, yielding an average final secure key length of about 50 kb per satellite pass. These findings significantly expedite and facilitate the practical deployment of space-based QKD.

Novel states of matter can be stabilized through the interplay of diverging electronic density of states, strong interactions, and spin-orbit coupling. Recent studies on magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) have revealed numerous new phases driven by interaction-induced spin-valley polarization. This work investigates correlated phases arising from the synergy between spin-orbit coupling-enhanced valley polarization and a large density of states below half-filling ($\nu \lesssim 2$) in a TBG device coupled with tungsten diselenide. We observe an anomalous Hall effect accompanied by a sequence of highly tunable Lifshitz transitions, which vary with carrier density and magnetic field. Notably, magnetization exhibits an abrupt sign reversal near half-filling, confirming its orbital character. The reported coercive fields are roughly ten times larger than those in previous graphene-based moiré systems, likely due to a Stoner instability facilitated by van Hove singularities in the flexible bands. Although Hall resistance lacks quantization at zero magnetic field—suggesting a ground state with partial valley polarization—perfect quantization and complete valley polarization emerge at finite fields. These results demonstrate that band singularities within flat bands, when combined with spin-orbit coupling, can stabilize ordered phases even at non-integer fillings of the moiré band.

This note re-examines the Rankin-Selberg integral of Shimura type for generic representations of $\mathrm{SL}_2\times \mathrm{GL}_2$, originally developed by Ginzburg, Rallis, and Soudry. We present a distinct and more "intrinsic" approach to the unramified computation. Unlike their method, which relies on a local functional equation for general linear groups, our approach utilizes the Casselman-Shalika formulas for unramified Whittaker functions associated with $\mathrm{SL}_2$ and $\mathrm{GL}_2$.

Autonomous vehicles are poised to become the backbone of future connected transport systems, yet they face significant vulnerabilities to physical-proximity attacks, such as sensor saturation. This study investigates whether such attacks can disrupt swarms of autonomous vehicles operating in large fleets for taxi and delivery services. We analyze the strategic options available to both attackers and defenders (fleet operators) in these conflicts, concluding that attackers generally hold the advantage. By exploiting inherent weaknesses in road networks identified through graph analysis, they can execute debilitating denial-of-service attacks. Experimental results based on real-world courier data from ten cities indicate that most urban areas will require infrastructure upgrades to protect driverless vehicles from these threats. Furthermore, we identified several hidden costs for equipment designers and operators, most notably the necessity of redesigning road networks for attack robustness, which raises fundamental questions regarding the overall benefits of such systems.

Building on the rule-algebraic stochastic mechanics framework, we provide new findings regarding the connections between stochastic rewriting systems modeled by continuous-time Markov chains, their associated discrete-time embedded chains, and specific combinatorial generating function expressions. We propose several generating function methods that enable a unique form of static analysis for rewriting systems, achieved by marginalizing state distributions through pattern-counting observables.

We investigate ultrafast ionization dynamics using orthogonally polarized two-color (OTC) laser pulses based on the resonant "$\omega+2\omega$" scheme. Through numerical simulations of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation and analysis of photoelectron momentum distributions, we identify signatures of dynamic interference and the dynamic Autler-Townes effect, phenomena that cannot be characterized within the spectral domain. Leveraging the OTC approach, we demonstrate that these concurrent dynamical effects can be distinguished in momentum space by manipulating spatial quantum interference. Specifically, we show that by tailoring the control pulse via this scheme, one can enhance the ionization rate through the Autler-Townes effect while leaving dynamic interference unaffected. This enhancement arises from constructive interference between partial photoelectron waves of opposite parity, manifesting as a symmetry-breaking in the momentum distribution. We examine this scenario using a hydrogen atom prototype, noting its broad applicability to other systems. These findings suggest potential applications for photoelectron interferometers to regulate electron dynamics in both time and space, as well as for the precise temporal characterization of attosecond pulses.

Empirical research frequently employs subclassification and matching to control for observed covariates, though these techniques are predominantly limited to binary treatments and remain underdeveloped for continuous exposures. Matching by exposure dose proves especially valuable in instrumental variable frameworks and for elucidating dose-response relationships. This paper introduces two criteria for optimal subclassification based on within-subclass homogeneity tailored to continuous exposure doses. We also present an efficient polynomial-time algorithm that guarantees an optimal solution for one criterion and acts as a 2-approximation for the other. Furthermore, we explain how to integrate dose information and apply penalties to manage the number of resulting subclasses. Through extensive simulations, we systematically compare our proposed design against optimal non-bipartite pair matching, demonstrating that combining our subclassification method with regression adjustment reduces model dependence in parametric causal inference involving continuous doses. Finally, we apply this new design and its associated randomization-based inference to evaluate the impact of transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) monitoring during coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery on postoperative outcomes using Medicare and Medicaid data, providing evidence that TEE monitoring reduces the all-cause 30-day mortality rate.

Extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs), comprising a compact object orbiting a significantly more massive black hole (such as those found in galactic centers), serve as valuable tools for investigating galactic nuclear environments and performing high-precision tests of the Kerr metric. This study examines the influence of an external third-body perturbation on EMRI systems. The orbital dynamics are most profoundly altered when the inner body encounters a resonance with the outer body, leading to modifications in the system's conserved quantities—specifically energy, angular momentum, and the Carter constant—or equivalently, the actions. These changes induce a cumulative phase shift in the gravitational waveform over time. We introduce a general methodology for determining action variations during resonance crossings, applicable to generic orbits within Kerr spacetime. Our findings demonstrate that these action changes correlate with the gravitational waves emitted by the binary system, quantified by the amplitudes of the Weyl scalar $\psi_4$ at both the horizon and infinity, at the resonant frequency. Consequently, we can calculate action variable changes for each body without explicitly solving for metric perturbations, allowing us to utilize existing black hole perturbation theory codes. We verify that this approach effectively probes resonant interactions in both static and dynamical regimes. Future work will employ this technique to investigate third-body effects in EMRIs and assess their potential impact on waveforms for the LISA mission.

We offer a comprehensive overview of the various computational methods evolved over time to investigate supercooled liquids, glassy materials, and the physics governing the glass transition. These numerical strategies are categorized into four primary groups. For each category, we outline the fundamental concepts while omitting technical specifics. We also detail the specific questions each approach can resolve and summarize the key findings achieved to date. Finally, we highlight two critical avenues for future computational research on glassy systems.

This paper introduces three robust clustering methods for multivariate time series, designed from the perspective of underlying generating processes. These approaches represent robust adaptations of a fuzzy C-means model, utilizing either estimated quantile cross-spectral densities or classical principal component analysis. To ensure resilience against outliers, the study employs metric, noise, and trimmed strategies: the metric method integrates a distance measure into the objective function to counteract outlier influence; the noise method constructs an artificial cluster to absorb outlying series; and the trimmed method removes the most atypical series from the dataset. By leveraging the quantile cross-spectral density, these techniques effectively reveal general dependence structures. Extensive simulations involving multivariate linear, nonlinear, and GARCH processes demonstrate that the proposed algorithms are highly effective at handling outlying series with distinct dependence patterns, significantly outperforming existing alternatives. The practical value of these methods is further illustrated through two case studies applied to financial and environmental data.

In recent years, group IV hexagonal-diamond crystals have garnered significant interest within semiconductor physics due to the emergence of advanced and efficient growth techniques. Despite this progress, numerous questions regarding their extrinsic doping potential and how it stacks up against traditional diamond-like structures remain unanswered. This study addresses these issues through numerical simulations based on Density Functional Theory (DFT). The comparative analysis of group III and V dopants reveals three key findings: first, while doping maintains the bulk site symmetry ($T_d$) in diamond-type crystals, impurities in hexagonal crystals shift toward either higher ($T_d$) or lower ($C_{3v}$) symmetry configurations depending on the dopant's valence; second, for Si and Ge, group III impurities are more readily incorporated into the hexagonal-diamond phase, where the local $C_{3v}$ symmetry better accommodates the impurity's three-fold coordination, whereas n-type impurities show no distinct preference for either phase; third, for carbon, both n-type and p-type dopants exhibit greater stability in the hexagonal-diamond structure compared to the cubic form, a trend that is significantly more pronounced for n-type impurities.

It has been established that for the isospin $I=1/2$ $\pi$N scattering amplitude, $T^{I=1/2}(s,t)$, the values $s={(m_N^2-m_\pi^2)^2}/{m_N^2}$ and $s=m_N^2+2m_\pi^2$ serve as accumulation points of poles on the second sheet of the complex $s$ plane, thereby constituting accumulation points of singularities for $T^{I=1/2}(s,t)$. In contrast, for $T^{I=3/2}(s,t)$, only $s={(m_N^2-m_\pi^2)^2}/{m_N^2}$ acts as an accumulation point of poles on the second sheet of the complex $s$ plane. This result holds to all orders within chiral perturbation theory.

This paper defines Multiple Object Forecasting (MOF) as the task of predicting future bounding boxes for tracked objects. Unlike prior object trajectory forecasting research that focuses on a bird's-eye view, we approach the problem from an object-level perspective, aiming to forecast complete bounding boxes rather than just trajectories. To address this challenge, we present the Citywalks dataset, featuring over 200,000 high-resolution video frames. Recorded across 21 cities in 10 European countries under diverse weather conditions, Citywalks includes more than 3,500 unique pedestrian trajectories. For evaluation, we adapted established trajectory forecasting methods for MOF and demonstrated cross-dataset generalizability on the MOT-17 benchmark without fine-tuning. Additionally, we propose STED, a new encoder-decoder architecture for MOF that integrates visual and temporal features to model both object-motion and ego-motion, achieving superior performance over existing MOF approaches. Code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/olly-styles/Multiple-Object-Forecasting

Matching sources across photometric catalogues can erroneously link objects of different brightness as detections of the same source. Incorporating magnitude data enables the rejection of such unphysical matches. This study presents a method that utilizes photometric information from both catalogues to evaluate counterparts, yielding an approximate tenfold improvement in the Bayes' factor. By integrating this photometric data, the approach avoids reliance on prior astrophysical knowledge. Furthermore, it accommodates scenarios where sources have no counterparts or overlap multiple potential ones. The method formally calculates the probability that two sources represent the same astrometric object, accounting for systematic astrometric perturbations caused by contaminants. We apply this technique to two scenarios: first, testing IPHAS-Gaia matches to compare catalogues with similar wavelength coverage but different dynamic ranges; second, analyzing IPHAS-2MASS matches to demonstrate the method's robustness with catalogues of comparable astrometric precision. We discuss the significance of including magnitude information in both contexts and explore extending the approach to multi-catalogue matching via an iterative process. Ultimately, this method facilitates the selection of high-quality matches by providing an overall probability for each pairing, allowing users to confidently select known good matches.

Liang information flow serves as a widely adopted metric in classical network theory for quantifying causation, with extensive applications in fields such as finance and climate. A key feature of this method involves freezing or subtracting specific nodes to evaluate their causal impact on the rest of the network. This approach has not yet been extended to quantum network dynamics. In this work, we generalize Liang information flow to the quantum realm by employing von-Neumann entropy. We utilize this framework to determine the relative significance of different network nodes in causally influencing a target node, demonstrating the method through small-scale quantum networks.

For decades, numerical simulations of convective envelopes in solar-type stars have identified anti-solar differential rotation profiles, which feature slow equators and rapid poles—a reversal compared to the Sun. These profiles typically emerge in simulations of slow rotators with high Rossby numbers. While such rotation patterns have been observed in evolved stars, they have never been definitively detected in cool, main-sequence solar-type stars. Detecting this regime in main-sequence stars would significantly enhance our understanding of their magnetorotational evolution. This study aims to pinpoint the most promising cool main-sequence candidates for anti-solar differential rotation within the \textit{Kepler} dataset. We first present a novel theoretical formula to estimate the fluid Rossby number ($Ro_{\rm f}$) for these stars using observational data, while accounting for internal structure and metallicity effects. Based on this, we compiled a list of likely candidates, dividing them into two groups: 14 targets at solar metallicity and 8 at other metallicities. Our analysis indicates that stars with the highest $Ro_{\rm f}$ values are likely early-G or late-F stars with a surface gravity of approximately log$_{10}g=4.37$~dex. We conclude that cool main-sequence candidates for anti-solar differential rotation do exist in the \textit{Kepler} sample. The primary candidate is KIC~10907436, followed by the solar analog KIC~7189915 and the seismic target KIC~12117868 as particularly interesting cases. Future characterization of these 22 stars is anticipated to clarify how dynamics influence the magnetic and rotational evolution of old solar-type stars at high Rossby numbers.

This paper examines both the theoretical framework and experimental measurements concerning the magnetic moments of charm baryons. The $\Lambda_c^+$ baryon is of particular interest because its magnetic moment equals that of the charm quark. Additionally, measuring the magnetic moments of other charm baryons, such as $\Xi_c$, facilitates detailed spectroscopic analysis. While the $\Lambda_c$ magnetic moment can be derived from radiative charmonium decays, current results exhibit tension with most theoretical predictions. As recently noted, bent-crystal experiments at the LHC offer a direct method to measure these magnetic moments. However, achieving precise measurements requires accurate determination of polarisation and weak decay parameters. In this work, we revisit the formalism for the necessary angular analysis and provide a detailed evaluation of the initial polarisation of deflected $\Lambda_c$ baryons relative to crystal orientation. We identify a specific crystal orientation that enables the measurement of the $\Lambda_c$ dimensionless electric dipole moment with precision comparable to its $g$-factor, a significant improvement in efficiency over previous estimates. Ultimately, we emphasize the critical need for precise measurements of initial polarisation and weak decay parameters to effectively compare direct measurements with those derived from decays.

We introduce a method that integrates feature correlation and sequential processing for dense optical flow estimation from event cameras. While contemporary frame-based optical flow techniques predominantly depend on matching costs derived from feature correlation, current event camera methods lack explicit computation of such costs; instead, learning-based approaches typically utilize U-Net architectures to sparsely estimate flow. Our primary finding demonstrates that incorporating correlation features yields significant performance gains over prior methods relying exclusively on convolutional layers. Against the state-of-the-art, our approach achieves dense optical flow estimation and lowers the end-point error by 23% on the MVSEC dataset. Additionally, we observe that existing event camera optical flow methods have been evaluated only on datasets featuring minimal displacement fields, capped at a maximum flow magnitude of 10 pixels. In response, we present a new real-world dataset characterized by displacement magnitudes up to 210 pixels and a camera resolution three times higher. On this new dataset, our method reduces the end-point error by 66%.

Recent calculations utilizing the third quantization formalism within canonical quantum gravity have determined the entanglement entropy of a multiverse pair of universes emerging from the vacuum. This study investigates how treating a scalar field as either quantum or classical affects the entanglement entropy across three distinct scenarios: de-Sitter universes, flat universes dominated by stiff matter, and closed universes containing a scalar field. The results indicate that the entanglement entropy remains unchanged for the first case, is zero for the second, and depends on the scalar field's treatment in the third.

This research examines a specific category of elections characterized by trichotomous input formats that enable voters to explicitly express negative sentiments. Focusing on multiwinner elections with a strong emphasis on selecting proportionally representative committees, we develop various axioms to address these negative feelings and propose structural frameworks for such preferences to enhance preference aggregation. We introduce two distinct classes of axioms aimed at more efficiently aggregating trichotomous preferences, alongside trichotomous adaptations of established multiwinner voting rules. By evaluating these adapted rules against our proposed axioms and supporting our findings with simulation data, we leverage the social optimality of our proportionality-based axioms to assess the quality of voting rules for electing proportionally representative committees using trichotomous ballots.

This paper presents the construction of conformal scattering theories for tensorial wave equations, specifically the tensorial Fackerell-Ipser and spin $\pm 1$ Teukolsky equations on Schwarzschild spacetime. Our approach begins by establishing conformal scattering for the tensorial Fackerell-Ipser equations, which are derived from the Maxwell and spin $\pm 1$ Teukolsky equations. Our methodology integrates Penrose's conformal compactification with energy decay results for tensorial fields satisfying the Fackerell-Ipser equations to demonstrate energy equality across the conformal boundary ($\mathfrak{H}^+\cup \scri^+$ or $\mathfrak{H}^-\cup \scri^-$) and the initial Cauchy hypersurface $\Sigma_0 = \left\{ t=0 \right\}$. Furthermore, we prove the well-posedness of the Goursat problem by extending H\"ormander's results for tensorial wave equations. Finally, leveraging the findings regarding the tensorial Fackerell-Ipser equations, we establish the conformal scattering construction for the spin $\pm 1$ Teukolsky equations.

The quantum marginal problem focuses on determining which sets of quantum states across various subsystems are compatible, meaning they can serve as marginals of a single multipartite quantum state. This work introduces a countable set of inequalities that any compatible collection of states must satisfy. Furthermore, this family of inequalities is proven to be sufficient, as every incompatible set of states will violate at least one inequality within the family.

The integration of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for automatically segmenting organs-at-risk (OARs) in CT scans into radiotherapy workflows is gaining traction; however, these outputs still necessitate time-consuming manual review and correction by clinicians before clinical deployment. This study aimed to create a tool capable of automatically detecting errors in 3D OAR segmentations without relying on ground truth data. Our proposed solution employs a novel architecture that merges CNNs with graph neural networks (GNNs) to simultaneously utilize segmentation appearance and shape information. The model was trained via self-supervised learning on a synthetically generated dataset featuring parotid segmentations with realistic contouring errors. We evaluated the model's performance through ablation studies, assessing various architectural components and the efficacy of transfer learning from an unsupervised pretext task. Our top-performing model achieved a precision of 85.0% and 89.7% for internal and external errors, respectively, with recall rates of 66.5% and 68.6% for the parotid gland. This offline quality assurance tool has the potential to streamline the clinical workflow by identifying areas requiring clinician attention, thereby reducing the time spent on contour corrections. All source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/rrr-uom-projects/contour_auto_QATool.

Uncertainty relations define the minimum possible value for the product of the standard deviations of observables. By linking the standard deviations of quantum observables to the numerical radius of operators, we derive a universal uncertainty relation applicable to any $k$ observables, with its formulation varying based on whether $k$ is even or odd. This relation is tight for cases where $k=2n$ and $k=3$. Specifically, for two observables, the relation provides a streamlined reformulation of Schrödinger's uncertainty principle.

The significance of de Rham cohomology equipped with spacelike and timelike compact supports for elucidating the structure of classical and quantum Maxwell theory on curved spacetimes has recently been recognized. Analogously, causally restricted cohomologies of various differential complexes serve comparable functions within other gauge theories. This paper introduces a methodology for calculating these causally restricted cohomologies by expressing them in terms of cohomologies with either compact or unrestricted supports. The approach leverages the property that the de Rham-d'Alembert wave operator can be extended to a chain map homotopic to zero, alongside the fact that its causal Green function participates in a convenient exact sequence. As an initial application, the method is applied to the de Rham complex and subsequently to the Calabi (or Killing-Riemann-Bianchi) complex, which arises in linearized gravity on constant curvature backgrounds. Furthermore, the discussion extends to applications involving other complexes, generalized causal structures, and functoriality.

This paper identifies a hypergraph with its family of edges. A hypergraph $\mathcal E$ satisfies property $C(k,{\rho})$ if and only if the intersection of any sub-collection of $k$ edges has cardinality strictly less than ${\rho}$. A subset of vertices $Y$ is defined as a "vertex cover" if it intersects every edge $E$ in $\mathcal E$, and it is termed "minimal" if no proper subset of $Y$ retains this property. Given a set $A$ and a collection of cardinals $S$, the notation $[A]^{S}$ denotes the family of subsets of $A$ whose cardinalities belong to $S$. For cardinals ${\lambda}$ and ${\rho}$, a set of cardinals $S$, and a natural number $k$, the relation $\mathbf M({{\lambda}},{S},{k},{{\mu}})\to \mathbf{MinVC}$ holds if every hypergraph $\mathcal E$ contained within $[{\lambda}]^{S}$ that satisfies property $C({k},{{\rho}})$ possesses a minimal vertex cover. When $S$ is the singleton set $\{\kappa\}$, this is abbreviated as $\mathbf M({{\lambda}},{\kappa},{k},{{\mu}})\to \mathbf{MinVC}$. A set of cardinals $S$ is described as "nowhere stationary" if its intersection with any ordinal $\alpha$ having cofinality greater than ${\omega}$ is not stationary in $\alpha$; notably, countable sets and sets of successor cardinals are nowhere stationary. The paper establishes the following results:
(1) $\mathbf M({{\lambda}},{S},{2},{k})\to \mathbf{MinVC}$ for any nowhere stationary set $S$ of cardinals and any ${\lambda}\ge {\omega}$.
(2) $\mathbf M({{\lambda}},{{\kappa}} ,{2},{{\rho}})\to \mathbf{MinVC}$ whenever ${\rho}<\beth_{\omega}\le {\kappa}\le {\lambda}$.
(3) $\mathbf M({{\lambda}},{{\omega}},{r},{k})\to \mathbf{MinVC}$ given ${\lambda}\ge {\omega}$ and finite $k,r$.
(4) $\mathbf M({{\lambda}},{{\omega}_1},{3},{k})\to \mathbf{MinVC}$ given ${\lambda}\ge {\omega}_1$ and finite $k$.

Cash-refund and installment-refund income annuities (IAs) differ significantly from the life-only versions typically favored by economists. Unlike standard annuities, refundable IAs guarantee that the annuitant or their beneficiary will eventually receive the full principal amount back, albeit gradually over time. Despite refundable IAs now constituting the majority of annuity sales in the United States, they remain largely overlooked by insurance and pension economists. Although factors such as recursivity complicate their pricing, duration, and money's-worth ratios, this paper proposes a method to make refundable IAs analytically tractable. A primary finding concerns the market price of cash-refund IAs when adjusted for an insurance loading on their actuarial present value. The study proves that, counterintuitively, price is no longer a declining function of age, meaning older buyers may pay more than younger ones. Furthermore, there is a specific threshold valuation rate below which no viable price exists; this phenomenon may also explain the near-disappearance of inflation-adjusted IAs.

This study investigates scattering amplitudes involving the coupling of two-particle systems through a single external current insertion, denoted as $2+\mathcal{J}\to 2$. These amplitudes offer structural insights into the excited spectrum of QCD. We establish an exact analytic representation for these reactions and demonstrate how to rigorously define form-factors for both bound states and resonances derived from them. Additionally, we examine the implications of the narrow-width limit within these amplitudes and the function of the Ward-Takahashi identity for conserved vector currents. These findings are applicable to any number of two-body channels lacking intrinsic spin, provided the current possesses an arbitrary Lorentz structure and quantum numbers. Together with existing finite-volume formalisms, this work establishes a comprehensive framework for calculating this specific class of amplitudes using lattice QCD.

We introduce a catalog containing approximately 100,000 periodic variable stars found in TESS Full Frame Images, selected from members of widely dispersed moving groups identified by Gaia in earlier papers in this series. By integrating rotation periods from our catalog with previously established rotation periods for benchmark open clusters, we construct an empirical gyrochronology relation describing angular momentum evolution that holds for stars aged 10 to 1000 Myr. After excluding stars with rotation periods shorter than 2 days—most of which are binaries—we attain a typical age precision of ~0.2–0.3 dex, with accuracy improving at older ages. Significantly, these empirical relations extend beyond FGK-type stars to include M-type stars, owing to the angular momentum distribution's superior smoothness, simplicity, continuity, and monotonicity compared to the rotation period distribution. Consequently, we can now trace in fine detail the nature of angular momentum loss in low-mass stars as functions of both mass and age. We also characterize the variability amplitudes of cool stars across mass and age, which may correlate with starspot coverage fractions. Additionally, we identify pulsating variables among the hotter stars in the catalog, such as $\delta$ Scuti, $\gamma$ Dor, and SPB-type variables. These data mark a significant advancement in estimating precise ages for FGK- and M-type field stars, beginning from the pre-main-sequence evolutionary phase.

As quantum machines expand in size and intricacy, analyzing the computational burdens placed on them by classical control systems becomes essential. This study quantifies the overheads introduced by real-time graph traversal algorithms, which are required to identify computational routes through fragmented cluster states for executing one-qubit gates—a fundamental step in practical photonic measurement-based quantum computing. By evaluating two distinct approaches, a global breadth-first search covering the entire cluster and an incremental method navigating a limited sub-section, we examine the balance between path-finding accuracy and operational speed, a factor that limits the system's photonic clock cycle. Furthermore, we discuss the wider implications of these findings for deploying classical control systems within measurement-based photonic quantum architectures.

This paper introduces the concept of explainable face recognition, which focuses on clarifying why a facial matcher identifies specific faces. We present the inaugural comprehensive benchmark and baseline evaluation for this field by defining a novel assessment protocol known as the "inpainting game." This protocol consists of 3,648 triplets—comprising probe, mate, and nonmate images derived from 95 subjects—where the nonmate is created by synthetically inpainting specific facial features such as the nose, eyebrows, or mouth. The goal for an explainable face matcher is to generate an attention map that highlights the regions in the probe image responsible for matching the mate while excluding the inpainted nonmate. This approach establishes ground truth for measuring which image areas contribute to face matching. Additionally, we offer a thorough benchmark on this dataset that compares five leading network attention methods across three facial matchers. This evaluation features two newly proposed algorithms, subtree EBP and Density-based Input Sampling for Explanation (DISE), which significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art techniques. Finally, we provide qualitative visualizations of these attention mechanisms on new images and investigate how explainable face recognition models can enhance transparency and trust in facial matching systems.

Wide Field Small Aperture Telescopes (WFSATs) are ideal for time-domain astronomy due to their ability to capture celestial images with high frequency and cost efficiency. An automated data processing algorithm capable of identifying objects and determining their positions and magnitudes is essential for advancing scientific research. This study enhances a deep neural network-based target detection method by incorporating two new branches to enable photometry and astrometry. Since these neural networks rely on data-driven regression, limited and diverse training data can introduce epistemic uncertainty into the final results. Consequently, we investigated how discrepancies in background noise and point spread functions between training sets and real observations contribute to measurement uncertainty. To mitigate this, we implemented a transfer learning strategy to train the network using real data. The proposed algorithm achieves high accuracy in identifying object types, positions, and magnitudes, processing images of any size in approximately 0.125 seconds. It is designed to be integrated into WFSAT data pipelines to enhance response speed and detection capabilities for time-domain astronomical events.

Sunspots have been instrumental in advancing our comprehension of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) wave phenomena within the solar atmosphere, particularly regarding slow MHD modes. Recent research indicates that transverse wave modes are prevalent throughout most of the chromosphere. Leveraging high-resolution Ca II 8542 {\AA} data from the Swedish Solar Telescope, this study presents the first evidence that chromospheric super-penumbral fibrils extending from sunspots also exhibit widespread transverse motions. We interpret these movements as transverse waves, specifically the MHD kink mode. By analyzing the statistical characteristics of more than 2,000 transverse motions, we determined distributions for periods and amplitudes that align closely with prior observations of chromospheric transverse waves in quiet Sun fibrils. The existence of these waves in super-penumbral fibrils prompts significant inquiries regarding their generation mechanisms and may influence our understanding of MHD wave energy transport through a sunspot's atmosphere.

Bacteria swimming in bulk fluids exhibit remarkable collective behaviors. While three-dimensional collective motion is well-documented, the corresponding dynamics in confined two-dimensional environments, which better reflect natural bacterial habitats, remain largely unexplored. Through precise experiments using *Escherichia coli* within Hele-Shaw chambers, we demonstrate that minor adjustments in confinement levels result in profound shifts in collective swimming patterns. Specifically, when bacteria can pass one another during collisions, long-range nematic order arises; however, slightly reducing the chamber height to prevent crossing induces the formation of clusters characterized by short-range polar order. By analyzing the swimming kinetics of individual cells, we uncover the microscopic mechanisms driving these two distinct phases. This research offers significant insights into confined bacterial collective motion and illustrates a practical method for regulating the emergent symmetry of these collective states.

The paper derives Maclaurin series expansions and related identities for positive integer powers of the inverse sine and inverse hyperbolic sine functions, their compositions with incomplete gamma functions, and positive integer powers of the inverse tangent and inverse hyperbolic tangent functions, all expressed using first kind Stirling numbers and binomial coefficients. Utilizing the newly derived expansion for powers of the inverse sine function, the authors obtain a closed-form expression for specific partial Bell polynomials, generate a series representation for the generalized logsine function, and establish several combinatorial identities involving first kind Stirling numbers, with some results simplifying or unifying existing knowledge. Furthermore, these new expansions for powers of the inverse (hyperbolic) sine and tangent functions enable the derivation of infinite series representations for the constant Pi and its positive integer powers.

When spherical grains are discharged from a hole at the base of a vertical cylinder submerged entirely underwater, the discharge rate is observed to depend on the fill height, unlike the established behavior of dry, non-cohesive grains. Surprisingly, as the hopper empties and granular pressure decreases, the discharge rate initially rises by approximately 25%. In cases of deep filling where the rate stabilizes, we analyzed the relationship between the discharge rate and both the grain and hole diameters. The discharge rate scales with the product of the hole's cross-sectional area and the terminal velocity of isolated grains. However, a cutoff effect occurs for small holes with a diameter roughly 2.5 times that of a grain, which represents a larger threshold than the corresponding cutoff found in the Beverloo equation for dry granular flow.

A central challenge in contemporary physics is understanding dark matter (DM), for which various models have been proposed. Since the majority of DM cannot consist of Standard Model (SM) particles, we investigate brane world theory as a potential framework for identifying non-SM DM candidates. In flexible brane world models, the new degrees of freedom arising from brane fluctuations are termed branons; these exhibit behavior similar to weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs), a leading DM candidate. We report on a multi-target search for branon DM annihilation signals in dwarf spheroidal galaxies using the ground-based MAGIC gamma-ray telescope, establishing the most stringent constraints on branon DM within the TeV mass range.

We calculate the equilibrium state, fundamental oscillation eigenfrequencies, and quadrupolar tidal deformability for anisotropic polytropic spheres. These calculations involve numerically solving the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equation, Chandrasekhar radial oscillation equations, and a nonlinear first-order Riccati equation for tidal deformability, each adapted to account for anisotropic effects. Specifically, using a polytropic exponent of $\gamma=2$ and the Cattoen, Faber, and Visser anisotropic model, we demonstrate that anisotropy influences radial pressure, energy density, the speed of sound, radial stability, and tidal deformability.

Recent interest has focused on specialized accelerators as a means to lower the power usage of neural network inference. A particularly promising class employs nonvolatile memory arrays to store weights and execute *in situ* analog computation directly within the array. Although previous studies have investigated the design space of analog accelerators to enhance performance and energy efficiency, rigorous assessments of their inference accuracy have been scarce. This research demonstrates that architectural choices, especially regarding how neural network parameters are mapped to analog memory cells, significantly impact accuracy. When tested with ResNet50 on ImageNet, the system's ability to withstand analog non-idealities—such as cell programming errors, ADC resolution limits, and parasitic resistances—improves when hardware analog values are kept proportional to network weights. Contrary to prior assumptions, fully storing weights as analog quantities offers resilience to cell imprecision nearly equivalent to bit slicing methods, which distribute weight bits across multiple devices. By leveraging this proportionality, analog designers can align hardware precision with algorithmic requirements instead of forcing intermediate results to match the precision of digital accelerators. Consequently, this approach yields an analog accelerator that is more accurate, robust against analog errors, and energy-efficient.

Knowledge Graph (KG) embedding aims to derive vector representations for entities and relations. While traditional models reason over graph structures, they struggle with graph incompleteness and long-tail entities. Conversely, recent approaches leveraging pre-trained language models utilize textual data but fail to incorporate graph structures. We empirically demonstrate that these two feature types are complementary. Consequently, we introduce CoLE, a Co-distillation Learning framework for KG Embedding designed to harness the synergy between graph structures and text. The graph component employs a Transformer to reconstruct entity representations from their neighborhood subgraphs, while the text component utilizes a pre-trained language model to generate representations from soft prompts derived from entity names, descriptions, and relational neighbors. To facilitate mutual enhancement, we propose co-distillation learning, enabling each model to distill selective knowledge from the other's prediction logits. In this setup, every model functions as both teacher and student. Experimental results on benchmark datasets show that our models surpass related baselines, with the ensemble CoLE approach advancing the state-of-the-art in KG embedding.

This paper extends the concept of slice-torus invariants to links. We establish several properties of these newly defined invariants, including their behavior under crossing changes, a bound for slice genus, an obstruction to strong sliceness, and a combinatorial limit. Additionally, we demonstrate an application to calculating the splitting number. Finally, by combining slice-torus link invariants with Whitehead doubling, we define new strong concordance invariants for links that are proven to be independent of the corresponding slice-torus invariants.

This paper tackles the challenge of categorizing documents within the global network of open-access repositories by their type. We demonstrate that repository-provided metadata capable of distinguishing between research papers, theses, and slides is absent in more than 60% of instances. Although such document-type metadata is valuable for diverse applications—from research analytics to enhancing search and recommender (SR) systems—it has not been adequately addressed within the repositories' infrastructure. Consequently, we propose a novel supervised machine learning approach that classifies document types using exclusively text-specific features. Our experiments reveal that random forest and Adaboost classifiers achieve the highest performance with an F1-score of 0.96. Furthermore, an analysis of SR system logs from the CORE [1] digital library aggregator indicates that users are approximately ten times more likely to click on research papers and theses than on slides. This finding suggests that incorporating document types as a feature for ranking or filtering SR results in digital libraries could significantly enhance user experience.

It remains uncertain whether high-mass protostars originate from high-mass prestellar cores, akin to low-mass star formation, or from collapsing lower-mass fragments within pre-protostellar clusters. This ambiguity is partly due to a lack of envelope structure data for protostars with masses of several tens of solar masses, a critical range where a transition from intermediate to high-mass formation is expected. To address this, we analyzed eight Cygnus-X sources with literature mass estimates falling within this gap, aiming to determine their masses, luminosities, and envelope density profiles. By integrating these findings with data on similarly evolved sources, we conducted a meta-analysis of protostellar envelope parameters across a luminosity range spanning six decades. Using archival broadband photometric continuum data from 1.2 to 850 $\mu$m, we performed spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting to calculate bolometric luminosities for our eight targets, alongside initial mass and radius estimates required to model density and temperature profiles using the Transphere radiative transfer code. Our results show that envelope masses, densities at 1000 AU, outer radii, and density power law indices all align with established literature trends across the full luminosity spectrum. Since most of our sources fall within an intermediate to moderately high mass and luminosity range, these findings reinforce the continuity between low- and high-mass star formation mechanisms. Furthermore, our density power law indices match observed values showing no clear luminosity dependence. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the trends in all envelope parameters for high-mass protostars are statistically indistinguishable from those of low- and intermediate-mass protostars.

This brief survey paper examines recent progress regarding the regularity and potential singularity formation in solutions to the 3D Navier-Stokes equations. Key motivating inquiries include whether specific norms concentrate or accumulate at small scales as potential blow-up times approach, the rate at which scale-invariant norms diverge, the feasibility of deriving explicit quantitative regularity estimates, and whether the criticality barrier can be breached, even marginally. These questions are deeply interconnected. Furthermore, many recent breakthroughs in Navier-Stokes research draw directly upon results and methodologies from nonlinear dispersive equations.

This study examines the non-equilibrium dynamics of non-Gaussian fluctuations within relativistic hydrodynamics, a framework essential for investigating the QCD critical point in heavy-ion collision experiments. Leveraging the hierarchy of relaxation time scales that arises near the critical point, we concentrate on the slowest mode—specifically, specific entropy fluctuations—which exhibit increasing equilibrium magnitude, non-Gaussianity, and relaxation time as the critical point is approached. We derive evolution equations for the non-Gaussian correlators of this diffusive mode under arbitrary relativistic hydrodynamic flow conditions. Furthermore, we contrast these findings with the simpler scenario of stochastic diffusion on a static, homogeneous background, highlighting terms that are unique to full hydrodynamics, which incorporates both pressure fluctuations and flow.

The demand for single-camera 3D particle tracking is rising, particularly driven by biomedical research that frequently utilizes single-plane microscopy. Defocusing-based techniques are well-suited for widespread adoption because they depend on standard microscopy imaging instead of requiring specialized optics. However, their broader application has been hindered by a shortage of accessible, user-friendly software. DefocusTracker addresses this as an open-source toolbox grounded in the universal principles of General Defocusing Particle Tracking (GDPT). It utilizes only a reference look-up table and image recognition to map a particle's image to its corresponding out-of-plane depth. Designed with a modular architecture, the toolbox allows for the seamless integration of new image recognition methods without altering the workflow or external interface. Currently implemented in MATLAB, a parallel version in Python is under development.

The zero-energy astrophysical S-factors for the direct nuclear capture reactions $^{3}{\rm He}(\alpha, \gamma)^{7}{\rm Be}$, $^{3}{\rm H}(\alpha, \gamma)^{7}{\rm Li}$, and $^{7}{\rm Be}(p, \gamma)^{8}{\rm B}$ have been estimated using the two-body potential cluster model, based on the extranuclear capture approximation proposed by D. Baye and E. Brainis. Calculations of the S(0)-factors were performed with two distinct potential models for each reaction, calibrated to binding energies and empirical asymptotic normalization coefficients from existing literature. Consequently, new values for the S(0)-factors were derived.
