A causal structure defines the functional relationships among random variables, and a distribution is considered compatible with such a structure if it can be generated by a process adhering to these dependencies. Determining this compatibility is both practically and theoretically significant, though notoriously difficult. Recently, a broad class of algorithms known as inflation techniques has emerged; these methods associate a hierarchy of progressively stricter compatibility tests with any causal structure, where each test is solvable via efficient convex optimization. Notably, in classical settings, this hierarchy is proven complete, meaning it eventually detects every incompatible distribution. While a similar quantum inflation hierarchy exists for scenarios where classical observations stem from quantum measurements, its completeness remains unproven. This paper presents the first provably convergent version of the quantum inflation hierarchy. Our convergence proofs rely on de Finetti Theorems, which demonstrate that specific symmetries enforce random variable independence—a non-convex property—within convex optimization frameworks. A pivotal element of our approach is a Quantum de Finetti Theorem applicable to general tensor products of $C^*$-algebras, extending prior research limited to minimal tensor products.

This paper examines a massive multiple-input multiple-output (mMIMO) system aided by a simultaneous transmitting and reflecting reconfigurable intelligent surface (STAR-RIS). Specifically, we derive a closed-form expression for the coverage probability of such a system, incorporating correlated fading and phase-shift errors. Since the coverage probability relies on statistical channel state information (CSI) regarding large-scale statistics, phase configurations are optimized at intervals of several coherence periods. This approach significantly reduces the complexity and overhead associated with optimizing passive beamforming, contrasting with the higher demands of STAR-RIS networks using instantaneous CSI. Numerical results validate our analysis, highlighting key properties such as the influence of the number of RIS elements and phase errors, while confirming the advantages of STAR-RIS over reflective-only RIS.

Achieving rapid, autonomous navigation in complex, unstructured settings like forests is difficult because it demands that robots generate new plans in real-time on hardware with limited computing power. This paper presents a search-based planning framework that adjusts sampling density dynamically to ensure dynamically feasible plans while maintaining computational efficiency. A primary hurdle in such planning is that dense obstacles require larger graphs to ensure completeness, yet these larger graphs hinder search efficiency by reducing heuristic accuracy. To overcome this, we propose a two-part framework: one component maximizes planner completeness for a fixed graph size, while the other dynamically expands the graph size within computational limits. This approach relies on motion planning graphs defined by a single parameter, "dispersion," which measures the maximum trajectory cost to reach any arbitrary state from the graph. Real and simulated experiments demonstrate that adapting dispersion in real-time enables operation across environments with varying obstacle densities. Simulations show improved performance compared to baseline search-based algorithms, and real-world tests confirm flight speeds of up to 2.5 m/s in cluttered pine forests.

The decay $\Lambda_b^0\rightarrow\chi_{c1}p\pi^-$, which is suppressed by the Cabibbo factor, has been observed for the first time utilizing data from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. This analysis used an integrated luminosity of 6 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the LHCb detector. Additionally, evidence supporting the $\Lambda_b^0\rightarrow\chi_{c2}p\pi^-$ decay is reported. By employing the $\Lambda_b^0\rightarrow\chi_{c1}pK^-$ decay as a normalization reference, the following branching fraction ratios were determined:

$$
\begin{array}{rcl}
\frac{\mathcal{B} (\Lambda_b^0\rightarrow\chi_{c1}p\pi^-)}{\mathcal{B} (\Lambda_b^0\rightarrow\chi_{c1}pK^-)} & = & (6.59 \pm 1.01 \pm 0.22 ) \times 10^{-2} \,, \\
\frac{\mathcal{B} (\Lambda_b^0\rightarrow\chi_{c2}p\pi^-)}{\mathcal{B} (\Lambda_b^0\rightarrow\chi_{c1}p\pi^-)} & = & 0.95 \pm 0.30 \pm 0.04 \pm 0.04 \,, \\
\frac{\mathcal{B} (\Lambda_b^0\rightarrow\chi_{c2}pK^-)}{\mathcal{B} (\Lambda_b^0\rightarrow\chi_{c1}pK^-)} & = & 1.06 \pm 0.05 \pm 0.04 \pm 0.04 \,,
\end{array}
$$

where the first uncertainty corresponds to statistical variations, the second to systematic effects, and the third to uncertainties in the branching fractions of the $\chi_{c1,2}\rightarrow J/\psi\gamma$ decays.

We systematically investigated the temporal characteristics of biphotons—pairs of time-correlated single photons—generated through spontaneous four-wave mixing in a hot atomic vapor. The measured duration of the biphoton wave packet or two-photon correlation function was adjusted across a range of approximately 70 to 580 ns by varying the coupling power. We derived an analytical formula for the biphoton's spectral profile within a Doppler-broadened medium. This expression indicates that the spectral profile is primarily governed by electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT), exhibiting a Lorentzian shape with a linewidth comparable to that of the EIT resonance. Consequently, the Doppler-broadened influence results in an exponential-decay temporal profile for the biphotons, a finding that aligns with our experimental data. Using a weak classical light probe, we further measured the EIT spectra under identical conditions to those used for the biphoton measurements. Theoretical predictions for the biphoton wave packets, calculated using parameters derived from the classical-light EIT spectra, matched the experimental results. This agreement confirms that in a Doppler-broadened medium, the classical-light EIT spectrum serves as a reliable predictor of the biphoton's temporal profile. Additionally, the observed biphoton temporal widths closely matched the analytical formula's predictions based on the biphoton's EIT effect. Overall, this study offers an analytical framework for quantitatively understanding both the spectral and temporal profiles of biphotons in Doppler-broadened media.

We conducted a comprehensive X-ray spectral analysis of the unobscured Seyfert-1 galaxy MCG--02--58--22 to determine the characteristics of its X-ray reprocessing environment, utilizing data from Suzaku (2009) and simultaneous observations from XMM-Newton and NuSTAR (2016). Our investigation yielded the following key findings: 1. The primary X-ray emission from the corona remained stable across these observations, with no changes in either the power-law slope ($\Gamma=1.80$) or luminosity ($L_{2-10 \rm keV}= 2.55\times 10^{44} $ erg/s). 2. By 2016, the soft excess flux had halved, the Compton hump diminished or disappeared entirely, and the narrow FeK$\alpha$ emission line exhibited a marginal broadening ($\sigma=0.35\pm0.08$ keV) alongside a doubling of its flux. 3. Physical modeling indicates that while the normalization of the narrow FeK$\alpha$ line component remained constant between the two epochs, the Compton hump vanished during this period. Given the stability of the primary X-ray continuum, we infer that variations in the reprocessed emission must stem from changes within the reprocessing medium. Our main conclusions are: A. The disappearance of the Compton hump in 2016 is likely attributable to a dynamic, clumpy torus undergoing infall or outflow, or to a polar torus wind. B. The torus in this active galactic nucleus likely comprises two distinct structures: an equatorial toroidal disk responsible for the narrow FeK$\alpha$ emission and a polar component generating the variable Compton hump. C. The simultaneous halving of the soft-excess flux and doubling of the FeK$\alpha$ flux cannot be sufficiently accounted for by ionized disk reflection models alone.

This research offers a comprehensive large-scale benchmarking of cloud-based Speech-to-Text platforms, including Google Cloud Speech-to-Text, Microsoft Azure Cognitive Services, Amazon Transcribe, and IBM Watson Speech to Text. The evaluation involved approximately 101 hours of data comprising 40,158 clean and noisy audio files for each system, with an additional analysis of background noise impact across five Signal-to-Noise ratios ranging from 40dB to 0dB. Findings indicate that Microsoft Azure achieved the lowest transcription error rate at 9.09% on clean speech while demonstrating strong robustness in noisy environments. Google Cloud and Amazon Transcribe exhibited comparable performance, though Amazon Transcribe is noted as being highly restricted for time-sensitive applications. Although IBM Watson functions accurately in quiet settings, its high sensitivity to background noise significantly hampers its practical utility in real-world scenarios.

Existing laser-interferometric gravitational wave detectors face a fundamental precision barrier caused by displacement noise arising from various optical components. To address this, several Displacement-Noise-Free Interferometer (DFI) schemes have been proposed, operating on a principle analogous to decoherence-free subspaces in quantum sensing: specific modes encode gravitational wave information while remaining immune to displacement noise. This paper establishes quantum precision limits for general DFI configurations, determining both the optimal measurement basis and squeezing strategies. We propose a triangular cavity DFI architecture and apply our derived bounds to it. Our precision analysis, utilizing diverse noise models, demonstrates that the DFI characteristic yields unique sensitivity profiles and enhanced precision through noise suppression and increased squeezing gain. Additionally, we outline further extensions of this scheme.

The angular distributions for the decay $B^+ \to K^*(892)^+\mu^+\mu^-$ are investigated using data from the CMS detector in $\sqrt{s} = 8$ TeV proton-proton collisions at the LHC, which correspond to an integrated luminosity of 20.0 fb$^{-1}$. As a function of the squared dimuon invariant mass, the study determines the muon forward-backward asymmetry and the longitudinal polarization of the $K^*(892)^+$ meson. These findings represent the initial results for this exclusive decay channel and are consistent with standard model predictions.

Recently, Visual Transformers (ViT) and subsequent models have replaced convolutions with self-attention, achieving accuracy equal to or surpassing CNNs. More recently, MLP-Mixer eliminated both convolutions and self-attention, relying solely on Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) layers. To facilitate cross-patch communication, it introduced an additional token-mixing MLP alongside the standard channel-mixing MLP. While MLP-Mixer yields promising results on extremely large-scale datasets, it fails to match the performance of CNNs and ViTs on medium-scale datasets like ImageNet1K and ImageNet21K. This performance gap prompted a re-evaluation of the token-mixing MLP. We found that this component is essentially a depthwise convolution with a global reception field and spatial-specific configuration, properties that render it susceptible to overfitting. Consequently, this paper proposes a new pure MLP architecture called spatial-shift MLP (S²-MLP). Unlike MLP-Mixer, S²-MLP contains only channel-mixing MLPs, using a spatial-shift operation for patch communication. This approach features a local reception field and is spatial-agnostic, offering a parameter-free and computationally efficient solution. On the ImageNet-1K dataset, S²-MLP achieves higher recognition accuracy than MLP-Mixer and matches ViT's performance with a significantly simpler architecture and reduced FLOPs and parameters.

Successfully navigating the harsh Martian environment requires the delicate coordination of hundreds of specialists from varied backgrounds to maximize the scientific potential of rovers. This operations team comprises numerous individuals with independent yet overlapping goals, collaborating to determine surface activities for the upcoming planning cycle. They must collaborate within strict time limits to comprehend each other's constraints and objectives, a process that often demands frequent revisions. This study investigates the complexities of Mars surface operations, ranging from high-level scientific aims to creating valid, safe, and optimal activity plans ready for transmission to the rover. By analyzing these challenges, we seek to clarify how planning intent can be articulated and effectively conveyed to increasingly autonomous future spacecraft. Our results highlight the intricate human-to-human interactions necessary during plan formulation, which rely heavily on a diverse set of soft skills and core competencies to bridge communication between science and engineering teams. Furthermore, we identified significant difficulties in extracting planning intent from operators—a challenge that will grow more intense as ground-based operators increasingly cooperate asynchronously with on-board autonomy. While constructing sophisticated robots and landing them on Mars are extraordinary achievements, ensuring that scientists can fully leverage the mission remains a persistent and evolving challenge, especially as autonomy levels rise.

This study investigates the quantum entanglement dynamics within a one-dimensional anisotropic XXZ spin-1/2 chain using adaptive time-dependent density-matrix renormalization-group methods across two distinct quench scenarios: an anisotropic interaction quench and a maximum domain wall quench involving staggered magnetization. The analysis focuses on the pairwise entanglement between adjacent qubits in the spin chain. Results indicate that entanglement can be generated and exhibit oscillatory behavior in both quench cases, with the anisotropic interaction significantly affecting the frequency of these entanglement oscillations.

Many collective decision-making scenarios involve a strategic conflict between individual self-interest and the promotion of the common good, evident in contexts like pandemic masking, voting, and vaccination. Networked public goods games model this dynamic, using networks to represent strategic interdependence among agents. While traditional models assume agents act solely out of self-interest, altruism has long been recognized as a significant motivator. We propose a novel extension of public goods games that incorporates altruistic motivations by adding a utility term reflecting the perceived benefits an agent gains from others' welfare, mediated by an altruism graph. Crucially, we treat altruism not as fixed, but as a lever to foster the common good. Consequently, our primary algorithmic focus is determining the computational complexity of altering the altruism network to achieve specific investment profiles in public goods games. We demonstrate that this problem is solvable via linear programming when a principal can fractionally adjust the altruism network. However, if the principal's actions are restricted to all-or-nothing modifications, the problem generally becomes intractable, though we identify several tractable special cases.

Early Dark Energy (EDE) that transitions to subdominance near matter-radiation equality offers a potential solution to the Hubble tension. However, a theoretical challenge arises regarding why the EDE energy scale coincides with that of equality despite their distinct physical origins. Sakstein and Trodden [Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 161301 (2020)] addressed this coincidence issue using neutrinos with $\mathcal{O}({\rm eV})$ mass. In this study, we introduce a novel EDE scenario where both the initiation and termination of EDE are driven by the radiation-matter transition, specifically examining a $k$-essence model. By reformulating the cosmic evolution equations as a two-dimensional dynamical system, we analyzed its primary characteristics. Our findings indicate that $k$-essence cannot fully implement the proposed scenario; however, an alternative EDE model within $k$-essence exists where the transition's end is triggered by the radiation-matter shift, while its onset relies on scalar field initial conditions. Consequently, this model addresses only half of the coincidence problem. A complete resolution under our initial scenario framework warrants further investigation.

This paper presents the Label-Aware Ranked loss, a new metric loss function that leverages the ordinal nature of labels in regression tasks, offering an improvement over state-of-the-art Deep Metric Learning approaches. We demonstrate that this loss achieves minimization when data points with distinct labels are positioned at uniform angles relative to one another within the embedding space. To evaluate its effectiveness, we applied the method to a challenging short-range radar people-counting regression task inside a vehicle cabin. The results show that our approach boosts overall accuracy by 6.7% and neighboring label accuracy by 2.1%, achieving final performance levels of 83.0% and 99.9% respectively, which surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods.

Self-interference (SI) represents a primary obstacle in full-duplex (FD) systems, necessitating efficient SI cancelers to facilitate the widespread adoption of FD technology in beyond fifth-generation wireless networks. Current SI cancellation techniques predominantly rely on polynomial representations of the SI signal at the receiver; although these methods perform effectively in practice, they demand high computational complexity. Conversely, neural networks (NNs) are regarded as promising alternatives for modeling the SI signal with lower computational overhead. Accordingly, this paper introduces two novel, low-complexity NN architectures: the ladder-wise grid structure (LWGS) and the moving-window grid structure (MWGS). These structures are designed to replicate the non-linearity and memory effects inherent in the SI signal, thereby enabling effective cancellation while maintaining low complexity. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that both LWGS and MWGS-based cancelers achieve cancellation performance equivalent to polynomial-based approaches, while reducing computational complexity by 49.87% and 34.19%, respectively.

A branchwise-real tree order is defined as a partial order tree where each branch is isomorphic to a real interval. This paper presents constructions of such trees that are both rigid (lacking non-trivial order-automorphisms) and uniform in two distinct senses. Specifically, I demonstrate the existence of a rigid branchwise-real tree where every branching point shares the same degree; another where every point branches with a uniform degree; and a third where every point branches with a uniform degree while admitting no order-preserving mapping into the real numbers. These trees are constructed iteratively through stages, relying on a key technique: the creation, within $\mathrm{ZFC}$, of a family of "sufficiently generic" colorings of $(0,\infty)$, which guide the progression of the construction.

Simulating fermionic systems on quantum computers necessitates mapping anti-commuting variables onto operators within the qubit Hilbert space. While the Jordan-Wigner transformation is the most established method, it encodes fermionic operators as non-local qubit operators, which can impede simulation speed. Recent efforts have therefore sought local encoding schemes. This paper argues that strict locality may be overly restrictive, demonstrating that operator size can be minimized through quasi-local encoding. We present examples applicable to condensed matter lattice models and quantum gravity systems, such as SYK models. Additionally, we offer a general framework for constructing codes tailored to specific problems and resources, illustrating how certain quasi-local encodings can be derived by truncating the state preparation circuits of local encodings. The discussion concludes with considerations for designing codes under device connectivity constraints.

This study investigates the fine structure of nonlinear modal interactions across various one-dimensional Burgers and three-dimensional Navier-Stokes flows. The analysis centers on the preferential alignments of Fourier mode phases within triadic interactions, which are fundamental to understanding energy flux dynamics between scales. We introduce new diagnostic tools to assess the coherence levels of these triadic interactions across different flow scenarios. Our investigation encompasses extreme viscous Burgers flows and 3D Navier-Stokes flows, alongside singularity-forming inviscid Burgers flows and viscous or Navier-Stokes flows derived from generic turbulent and simple unimodal initial conditions, such as the Taylor-Green vortex. A primary finding is that although extreme viscous Burgers and Navier-Stokes flows exhibit identical relative levels of enstrophy amplification through nonlinear effects, this outcome arises from triadic interactions with markedly different coherence levels. Specifically, in viscous Burgers flows, flux-carrying triads achieve phase saturation that maximizes energy flux to small scales; conversely, in 3D Navier-Stokes flows with extreme initial data, this flux is mediated by a highly selective subset of helical triads. Furthermore, comparing flows generated from extreme versus generic initial conditions reveals striking similarities between these two categories, observed in both the 1D viscous Burgers equation and the 3D Navier-Stokes equation.

Network meta-analysis serves as a robust method for synthesizing evidence from independent studies and evaluating multiple treatments at once. A key component of this process is establishing ranks for all treatment options regarding a specific disease outcome. However, these estimated rankings often face significant challenges, including substantial uncertainty, multiplicity problems, and the frequent inability to account for ties, which complicates interpretation when rankings are viewed as absolute metrics. To overcome these limitations, we propose a ranking strategy designed for high-order uncertainty scenarios that yields more conservative outcomes, thereby enhancing interpretability while addressing multiple comparison issues. Additionally, to allow for ties between treatment effects, we introduce a Bayesian Nonparametric approach for network meta-analysis. This method leverages the inherent clustering properties of Bayesian Nonparametric techniques to assign a positive probability of equality between treatment effects. The effectiveness of this procedure is illustrated through numerical simulations and a practical application analyzing antidepressant treatments.

The widespread adoption of mobile devices has spurred the growth of mobile services that deliver personalized, context-aware content to users. These modern services operate as a distributed system, combining local end-devices like smartphones with remote cloud servers. Their success relies heavily on the capacity to anticipate future contexts—such as location—to pre-fetch data or generate specific recommendations. Machine learning (ML) models have become a prevalent tool for predicting these future contexts. Recent advancements in this field emphasize personalized ML models, where unique models are trained for each individual to align predictions with specific user behaviors. Although personalization enhances service effectiveness, it simultaneously elevates privacy risks because these models embed unique contextual behaviors of each user. To illustrate these dangers, we introduce several attribute inference-based privacy attacks, demonstrating that they can compromise privacy with up to 78% accuracy in top-3 prediction scenarios. In response, we propose Pelican, a privacy-preserving personalization framework for context-aware mobile services that utilizes both device and cloud resources to tailor ML models while minimizing privacy leakage. Evaluated using real-world location-aware mobile service traces, Pelican demonstrates the ability to significantly reduce privacy exposure by as much as 75%.

Building on the work of Conway and Lagarias, who demonstrated that specific roughly triangular areas within a hexagonal grid resist tiling by tribones—a term coined by Thurston—this study examines a two-parameter family of roughly hexagonal regions in the same grid. We establish that a valid tribone tiling for such a region exists precisely when its two defining parameters correspond to paired pentagonal numbers of the form $k(3k \pm 1)/2$.

Our earlier research, utilizing hydrodynamical simulations with a basic galaxy formation model that omitted feedback, demonstrated that dense, massive filaments at high redshift create potential wells capable of trapping and compressing gas, thereby influencing galaxy formation within their resident low-mass haloes. This study employs the Auriga simulations—a suite of high-resolution, zoom-in hydrodynamical models of Milky Way-like galaxies with a sophisticated galaxy formation framework—to determine if these findings remain valid. Consistent with our prior results, we observe that dwarf galaxies located in filaments exhibit higher baryonic and stellar fractions compared to field counterparts of similar halo mass. Furthermore, at a fixed parent halo mass, filament-hosted dwarfs display marginally elevated star formation rates relative to field dwarfs. However, no significant difference was detected in the g-r colors between the two populations. Additionally, we find that at high redshifts, the gas within dwarf galaxies tends to align its spin with the hosting filament. Collectively, these results support a scenario where massive high-redshift filaments facilitate gas accretion and boost star formation in dwarf-sized dark matter haloes.

Our prior research demonstrated that superluminal particles are permissible within general relativistic gravity, contingent upon the metric being locally Euclidean. In this study, we derive the temperature-dependent probability density function for a canonical ensemble of such particles across two scenarios: space-times invariant under Lorentz symmetry and those invariant under Euclidean symmetry. While Lorentzian metrics remain stable under normal matter density, Euclidean metrics can emerge under specific gravitational conditions, persisting briefly in the extremely dense and hot environment of the early universe. Furthermore, superluminal particles facilitate thermodynamic equilibrium more rapidly and drive a swift expansion of matter density, thereby rendering inflation mechanisms—which rely on ad-hoc scalar fields—unnecessary. This conclusion aligns with Occam's razor.

Human-object interaction (HOI) detection, functioning as a downstream task of object detection, involves identifying human-object pairs and determining their semantic relationships within an image. Recently, one-stage approaches have gained prominence due to their efficiency; however, these methods often overlook spatial scale variations by focusing solely on interaction points or filtering pairs. To mitigate this limitation, we introduce QAHOI (Query-Based Anchors for Human-Object Interaction detection), a transformer-based framework. This method employs a multi-scale architecture to capture features across varying spatial resolutions and utilizes query-based anchors to predict all components of an HOI instance. We further demonstrate that integrating a powerful backbone significantly boosts QAHOI's accuracy, allowing the transformer-based variant to surpass recent state-of-the-art methods by substantial margins on the HICO-DET benchmark. The source code is accessible at the provided link.

This technical report details the 2nd-ranked model developed for AQTC, a challenge recently added to the CVPR 2022 Long-form Video Understanding (LOVEU) competition. The task involves significant challenges related to multi-step responses, multi-modal data, and varied, evolving button representations within videos. To tackle these issues, we introduce a novel context-grounded attention mechanism designed to enhance feature mapping. Furthermore, we conduct an analysis of button quantities and perform ablation studies on various step networks and video features. Consequently, our approach secured 2nd overall place in the LOVEU competition's Track 3, achieving 1st place in two of the four evaluation metrics. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/jaykim9870/CVPR-22_LOVEU_unipyler.

Let $F_n(k)$ denote the generalized Fibonacci sequence defined by the recurrence $F_n = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2} + \dots + F_{n-k}$ for $n \geq k$, given initial values $(F_0, F_1, \dots, F_{k-1})$. Define $B_n(k,j)$ as the term $F_n(k)$ generated when the initial conditions are set such that $F_j = 1$, while $F_i = 0$ for all $i < j$ and $j < i < k$. This paper demonstrates that any $F_n(k)$ can be represented as a sum of terms $B_n(k,j)$. Furthermore, it provides finite sum expressions for both $B_n(k,j)$ and $F_n(k)$, derives various properties, and calculates their 2-adic orders across specific ranges of $k, j,$ and $n$, with particular evaluations for $B_n(3,j)$ and $B_n(4,j)$ covering most values of $j$ and $n$.

Early brain sensory systems quickly adjust to varying input statistics, a process necessitating recurrent neuronal communication. Mechanistically, this recurrent interaction is frequently indirect, facilitated by local interneurons. This study investigates the computational advantages of routing recurrent communication through interneurons versus establishing direct recurrent links. We examine two mathematically manageable recurrent neural networks designed to whiten their inputs: one utilizing direct recurrent connections and the other employing interneurons to mediate recurrence. Through analysis of continuous synaptic dynamics and numerical simulations, we demonstrate that the interneuron-based network exhibits superior robustness to initialization compared to the direct-recurrent network. Specifically, the convergence time for synaptic dynamics in the interneuron-mediated network scales logarithmically with the initialization spectrum, whereas it scales linearly in the direct-recurrent network. These findings indicate that interneurons provide a computational benefit for rapid adaptation to shifting input statistics. Notably, the interneuron network represents an overparameterized solution to the whitening objective of the direct-recurrent network, suggesting our results mirror the implicit acceleration phenomenon seen in overparameterized feedforward linear networks but within a recurrent context.

This study examines nonparametric regression estimation in the presence of both additive and multiplicative noise, developing adaptive thresholding estimators utilizing Laguerre series. When the unknown function resides within a Laguerre-Sobolev space, the proposed method attains asymptotically near-optimal convergence rates. The analysis addresses two distinct noise models: (1) independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) Gaussian errors and (2) long-memory Gaussian errors. Under the i.i.d. scenario, the achieved convergence rates align with established literature findings. Conversely, in the long-memory setting, convergence rates are influenced by long-memory parameters only when the memory effect is sufficiently strong in either noise component; otherwise, the rates remain identical to those observed under i.i.d. noise conditions.

This paper addresses the problem of reconstructing smooth complex-valued functions $f: [-\pi, \pi] \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$, subject to an unavoidable global phase ambiguity, using a finite collection of Short Time Fourier Transform (STFT) magnitude data. We propose two distinct algorithms designed to approximately invert these measurements, each supported by theoretical error bounds that confirm their validity. Furthermore, extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that both methods perform effectively in practical applications and exhibit robust numerical convergence.

Recently, massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems have garnered substantial attention for next-generation wireless networks. However, the extensive number of antennas employed in these systems renders channel state information (CSI) estimation particularly difficult, as accurate CSI is crucial for realizing the full benefits of massive MIMO technology. This study introduces the application of the Ensemble Square Root Filter (EnSRF) and its variant, the Particle-wise Update version of the Ensemble Square Root Filter (PUEnSRF), to estimate time-selective, frequency-flat fading channel coefficients within massive MIMO environments. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that PUEnSRF estimates achieve significantly superior accuracy and faster filter convergence compared to traditional particle filters.

This study introduces various techniques to enhance the precision of equation-driven thermal models for photovoltaic (PV) modules operating at minute-to-second intervals. It proposes an RC-equivalent conceptual framework that incorporates wind effects, demonstrating how the thermal time constant ($\tau$) can be derived from empirical data. This constant enables the transition from static to dynamic thermal modeling by applying the Exponential Weighted Mean (EWM) method to irradiance and wind inputs. For fixed-mount PV systems, the average $\tau$ is found to be $6.3 \pm 1$ minute. Building on this framework, a Filter-EWM-Mean Bias Error (FEM) correction methodology is established. Two proposed models, WM1 and WM2, are evaluated against the Ross, Sandia, and Faiman models across twenty-four datasets spanning fifteen sites, with temporal resolutions varying from 1 second to 1 hour, predominantly at 1-minute intervals. Results indicate that the FEM approach reduces average model errors (both RMSE and MAE) across all sites and models compared to standard steady-state equivalents by $-1.1$ K and $-0.75$ K, respectively.

Advances in deep learning have significantly enhanced the precision of dialogue response selection, primarily by employing complex neural architectures to model the intricate relationships between dialogue history and potential responses. Although highly effective, these sophisticated models incur substantial computational costs, limiting their practical application to re-ranking stages. This study introduces a solution for directly selecting appropriate responses from vast corpora, including non-parallel datasets comprising only unpaired sentences, utilizing a dense retrieval framework. To maximize the capabilities of dense retrieval, we incorporate a custom interaction layer and implement specialized learning strategies. Our model demonstrates superior performance compared to strong baselines in traditional re-ranking evaluations, a result particularly notable given its efficiency. Furthermore, we validate the approach in realistic settings through full-rank evaluation, aiming to select optimal responses from candidate pools containing millions of options and assessing them via human annotation. Our proposed model significantly outperforms pipeline systems that combine fast recall with expressive re-ranking modules. Additionally, human evaluation confirms that expanding the candidate pool with non-parallel corpora further enhances response quality.

With the ongoing expansion of the "Mobile AI" revolution, understanding the behavior of deep neural networks deployed at the edge has become increasingly critical. MobileNets remain the preferred architecture for mobile deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs), yet they frequently suffer from substantial accuracy loss when subjected to post-training quantization. Although research has proposed quantization-aware training and other techniques to address this issue, there remains a gap in understanding why MobileNets—and depthwise-separable CNNs (DWSCNNs) broadly—perform significantly worse during quantization compared to other CNN structures. Driven by the need for deeper insights into this phenomenon, we adopt a novel approach by examining the multi-scale distributional dynamics of MobileNet-V1, various smaller DWSCNNs, and standard CNNs. Our investigation focuses on how quantization affects weight and activation distributional dynamics as data flows through layers, alongside broader shifts in network-level distributional dynamics. This granular analysis uncovered pronounced fluctuations in dynamic range and a "distributional mismatch" between channel-wise and layer-wise distributions in DWSCNNs, factors that exacerbate quantized degradation and distributional shifts during information propagation. Additionally, our examination of activation quantization errors indicates that DWSCNNs accumulate significantly more quantization error than regular CNNs. We hope these findings will inspire new strategies to mitigate changes in distributional dynamics and enhance post-training quantization for mobile applications.

This paper investigates endomorphisms developed by Sarah Koch in her thesis, specifically analyzing the eigenvalues of their differentials at fixed points. Koch previously established that for every post-critically finite unicritical polynomial, there corresponds a post-critically algebraic endomorphism of $\mathbb{CP}^k$, and she demonstrated that the eigenvalues of the differentials along periodic cycles outside the post-critical sets possess a modulus strictly exceeding $1$. In this work, we prove that the eigenvalues at fixed points are either $0$ or have a modulus strictly greater than $1$, thereby validating a conjecture the author formulated in his own thesis. Furthermore, we offer a specific characterization of these values based on the multiplier of the associated unicritical polynomial.

We introduce a streamlined approach for accessing and controlling the topology of massive Dirac fermions by adjusting the scalar potential. We systematically demonstrate how a spatial distribution of this potential can alter the mass term and gap signature, as well as the dispersion relation, thereby inducing band inversion through inverse Klein tunnelling. In two dimensions, this emergent mechanism, termed the Scalar Hall Effect, enables the direct manipulation of non-trivial topological invariants such as the Chern number, thus creating new avenues for controlling physical phenomena rooted in non-trivial topology.

Quantum Bayesian AI (Q-B) represents a nascent domain that harnesses the computational advantages of quantum computing, promising exponential acceleration for numerous Bayesian algorithms. Our objective is to directly apply these techniques to statistical and machine learning challenges. We establish a duality between classical and quantum probability to compute relevant posterior quantities. Our framework unifies MCMC, Deep Learning, and Quantum Learning under the lens of von Neumann's principle of quantum measurement. Additionally, quantum embeddings and neural gates play a crucial role in data encoding and feature selection, exhibiting a natural duality with established kernel methods in statistical learning. We demonstrate the performance of quantum algorithms on two basic classification tasks and conclude by outlining directions for future research.

Modern machine learning heavily relies on efficient solvers for nonconvex optimization. This paper examines two straightforward accelerated gradient approaches—restarted accelerated gradient descent (AGD) and restarted heavy ball (HB)—applied to general nonconvex problems satisfying gradient and Hessian Lipschitz conditions. We demonstrate that both algorithms locate an $\epsilon$-approximate first-order stationary point using $O(\epsilon^{-7/4})$ gradient evaluations, supported by concise proofs. Our complexity bound includes no hidden polylogarithmic terms, thereby surpassing current state-of-the-art results by a factor of $O(\log\frac{1}{\epsilon})$. These methods are notably simple, comprising only Nesterov's classical AGD or Polyak's HB steps alongside a restart strategy, without requiring negative curvature exploitation or the minimization of regularized surrogate functions. Furthermore, our elementary analysis avoids the strong convexity assumptions typically invoked in existing studies for AGD or HB.

Composite quantum state ensembles can display nonlocal characteristics, meaning their optimal discrimination might necessitate global operations. However, an ensemble of $N$ pairwise orthogonal pure states can always be perfectly distinguished using an adaptive local scheme when $(N-1)$ copies of the state are available. In this letter, we present examples of orthonormal bases within a two-qubit Hilbert space where adaptive discrimination demands 3 copies. For this composite system, we comprehensively analyze the multi-copy adaptive local distinguishability of orthogonal ensembles, thereby assigning varying degrees of nonlocal strength to different ensembles. Additionally, we identify ensembles that require fewer copies for discrimination under an adaptive separable scheme compared to an adaptive local scheme. Our construction holds significant application in multipartite secret sharing and suggests an intriguing super-additivity phenomenon regarding locally accessible information.

Many real-world systems can be effectively modeled as multilayer networks, offering an efficient framework for characterizing their complexity. Evidence from system biology suggests that interactions between distinct molecular networks significantly influence global network functions. This study examines molecular multiplex networks formed by the coupling of transcriptional regulatory networks (TRN) and protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks, specifically investigating their controllability and energy requirements. Our results indicate that driver nodes typically avoid essential or pathogen-associated genes; however, applying external inputs to these specific genes substantially lowers energy costs, highlighting their critical importance in network control. Furthermore, we observe that a lower number of minimal driver nodes and reduced energy demands correlate with disassortative coupling between the TRN and PPI networks. These findings, validated across multiple species, provide a comprehensive understanding of gene roles in biological processes and network control.

The current COVID-19 pandemic has elevated science to the forefront of public conversation, highlighting the complexity of the subject and the difficulties involved in communicating it effectively. A particularly charged issue within this discourse concerns the recording and reporting of disease mortality; this topic is inherently emotional and central to the decision-making processes that have dictated lockdowns, social restrictions, and business closures. To address the significant controversy and public anger surrounding causality in mortality, the first section of this article examines the fundamental principles of attributing causes of death, outlines the statistical methods used for mortality estimation, and illustrates these concepts by analyzing reporting practices in England and their frequent misrepresentations. The second section is empirical, presenting data and an analysis of how COVID-19 mortality has been covered in the mainstream media of the UK and the USA, including a comparative study across both nations and various outlets. The results reveal a consistent and concerning lack of technical understanding regarding the subject matter in both countries. Notably, the analysis shows that with remarkable consistency ($\rho>0.998$), media outlets that published a higher volume of articles on COVID-19 mortality also exhibited a higher proportion of those articles that misrepresented mortality figures.

Let $\mathcal{L}$ denote the Schrödinger operator defined as $-\Delta+V$, under the assumption that the potential $V$ fulfills a reverse Hölder inequality. In this Schrödinger framework, we examine the weighted Morrey-Campanato spaces $BMO_{\mathcal L,w}^\alpha (\mathbb R^d)$ and $BLO_{L,w}^\alpha (\mathbb R^d)$. We demonstrate that the variation operator $V_\sigma(\{T_t\}_{t>0})$ for $\sigma>2$, and the oscillation operator $O(\{T_t\}_{t>0}, \{t_j\}_{j\in \mathbb Z})$—where the time sequence satisfies $t_j<t_{j+1}$, $\lim_{j\rightarrow +\infty}t_j=+\infty$, and $\lim_{j\rightarrow -\infty} t_j=0$—are bounded mappings from $BMO_{\mathcal L,w}^\alpha (\mathbb R^d)$ to $BLO_{\mathcal L,w}^\alpha (\mathbb R^d)$. Here, $T_t$ is given by $t^k\partial_t^k e^{-t\mathcal L}$ for $t>0$ and $k\in \mathbb N$. Furthermore, we prove that these boundedness properties also hold for the maximal operators associated with the family $\{t^k\partial_t^k e^{-t\mathcal L}\}_{t>0}$, where $k\in \mathbb N$.

For decades, it has remained unclear why scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) experiments showed buckled dimers on the Si(001) surface as symmetric at temperatures below 20 K. Although these symmetric images were previously attributed to an STM artifact, the specific mechanism behind this observation was unknown. Using first-principles density-functional theory calculations, we demonstrate that these symmetric images result from the flip-flop motion of buckled dimers driven by quantum tunneling (QT). We found that at low temperatures, tunneling-induced hole charging on the surface lowers the energy barrier for dimer flipping, resulting in a significant QT-driven flip-flop frequency. In contrast, this quantum tunneling effect becomes negligible when the surface charging involves electrons. Our findings offer an explanation for low-temperature STM data that displays apparent symmetric structures in both filled-state and empty-state images.

Strategic problems have revealed that Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) systems can master sophisticated solutions exceeding human limits, particularly within complex environments. Although this potential offers exciting prospects for intelligent assistance tools with revolutionary capabilities, deploying such technology in real-world contexts introduces substantial risks, necessitating confidence in their reliability and transparency. Since superhuman strategies are inherently opaque and intricate, and real-world scenarios often preclude rigorous performance validation, establishing trust in these systems proves challenging. While Explainable AI (XAI) has enhanced transparency across modern AI through various methods, current research lacks approaches that deliver domain-level insights to experts facing strategic situations. This paper examines the nature of superhuman DRL strategies, their characteristics, the hurdles involved in adapting them to real-world applications, and the role of explainability as a critical factor in fostering trust.

Grasping the noise within gravitational-wave detectors is fundamental to both identifying and interpreting gravitational-wave signals. Glitches represent transient, non-Gaussian noise artifacts stemming from various environmental and instrumental sources. The Gravity Spy initiative employs a machine-learning algorithm to categorize these glitches according to their time-frequency morphology. These classified glitches serve as input for detector-characterization efforts aimed at mitigation and data-analysis studies focused on reducing their impact. This work presents the Gravity Spy analysis of data collected up to the conclusion of the third observing run of Advanced LIGO, classifying 233,981 glitches from LIGO Hanford and 379,805 from LIGO Livingston into distinct morphological classes. Our findings reveal that glitch distributions vary between the two LIGO sites, underscoring the necessity for data-quality studies that are customized for each gravitational-wave observatory.

Recent advancements have enabled supervised training of Convolutional Object Detectors, such as Faster R-CNN, to identify threats in carry-on luggage via X-ray imagery, supporting the Transportation Security Administration's (TSA) goal of safeguarding U.S. air travelers. Although increasing training data with threat examples could enhance the reliability of these deep learning algorithms, acquiring such data through realistic staging is costly. Conversely, real-world data can be gathered rapidly and inexpensively. This paper introduces "Background Adaptive Faster R-CNN," a semi-supervised threat recognition framework designed for two-stage object detectors that leverages domain adaptation techniques from deep learning. The method utilizes two distinct data sources as "domains": a manually curated set containing threats and a real-world set presumed to be threat-free. To prevent the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) from encoding superficial domain-specific characteristics—which would allow it to minimize supervised loss without improving object recognition—two adversarially trained domain discriminators are employed: one for object proposals and another for image features. In the hand-collected domain, only background object proposals and image features are utilized. The losses generated by these domain-adaptive discriminators are integrated into the standard Faster R-CNN loss function for images from both domains. This strategy aims to lower threat detection false alarm rates by aligning the statistical properties of background features from curated data with those from real-world scenarios. The proposed approach demonstrates performance gains on two independently collected datasets of labeled threats.

This paper investigates deviation inequalities for sums of high-dimensional random matrices and operators, specifically addressing cases involving dependence and arbitrary heavy tails. Given the growing significance of estimating high-dimensional matrices, where data dependence and heavy-tail characteristics are paramount, we establish a dimension-free upper bound on the deviation. Unlike traditional bounds, this result relies on the effective rank of the matrices rather than their explicit dimension, thereby generalizing several existing studies on matrix sum deviations. Our proof utilizes two primary techniques: (i) variational approximation of the dual moment generating functions and (ii) robustification via the truncation of matrix eigenvalues. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these findings to various problems, including covariance matrix estimation, hidden Markov models, and overparameterized linear regression models.

This study explores communication-efficient split learning within a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) framework. Specifically, we mathematically break down the inter-layer connections of a neural network into a sequence of linear precoding and combining transformations that, when combined with over-the-air computation (OAC), effectively form a linear neural network layer. In this architecture, the precoding and combining matrices serve as trainable parameters, while the MIMO channel remains implicit. By leveraging channel reciprocity and appropriately adapting the backpropagation process, the proposed approach eliminates the need for implicit channel estimation, thereby reducing system costs and enhancing overall efficiency. Furthermore, practical constellation diagrams are employed as activation functions to prevent the transmission of arbitrary analog signals common in traditional OAC systems. Numerical results are provided to validate the efficacy of the proposed scheme.

Central massive black holes can generate sustained, wide-angle winds capable of stripping gas from galactic stellar bulges, potentially explaining the observed correlation between black hole mass and stellar velocity dispersion. As these winds traverse the galaxy, they collide with the interstellar medium to create strong shocks—akin to supernova explosions—that accelerate charged particles to high energies. This study utilizes Fermi Large Area Telescope data to investigate gamma-ray emission from galaxies exhibiting ultra-fast outflows (UFOs), defined as highly ionized, rapid outflows (v~0.1c) detected via hard X-ray absorption in nearby active galactic nuclei (AGN). Through a sensitive stacking analysis, we detect average gamma-ray emission from these systems and rule out alternative non-UFO origins. Our results indicate that gamma-ray luminosity correlates with AGN bolometric luminosity and that these outflows convert approximately 0.04% of their mechanical power into gamma rays. Interpreting this emission as a result of cosmic rays (CRs) accelerated at shock fronts, we conclude that the gamma-ray signal marks the beginning of wind-host interaction and demonstrates that these outflows can accelerate CRs within the transition zone between galactic and extragalactic populations.

OpenRefine is a widely used open-source utility for data cleaning that enables users to export their executed workflows in JSON format for potential reuse on different datasets. We have created or2yw, a new tool that converts OpenRefine's JSON-based operation history into a YesWorkflow (YW) model, allowing the workflow to be visualized and queried using the YW platform. Originally designed to help researchers annotate program scripts and expose implicit dataflow dependencies and workflow steps, the YW tool is now leveraged by or2yw to automatically generate YW models from OpenRefine histories. This process provides a "workflow view" of previously executed data cleaning sequences.

The or2yw tool supports the generation of various YW model types, including a linear model that reflects the sequential order of OpenRefine operations and a *parallel model* that identifies independent workflow branches. The parallel model is derived by analyzing dependencies between steps; for instance, if two operations do not share read or write columns, they are treated as parallel steps. These resulting YW models function as prospective provenance—queryable and visualizable knowledge artifacts that serve two main purposes: (i) assisting authors in documenting their data cleaning processes to enhance transparency, and (ii) helping other users better understand and reuse these workflows.

This study aims to localize visible sound sources within videos without relying on manual annotations. Our primary technical advancement demonstrates that training a network to explicitly distinguish challenging image fragments—even when the sound-emitting object is present—substantially enhances localization accuracy. We achieve this by introducing an elegant mechanism that automatically mines hard samples and integrates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our method attains state-of-the-art results on the widely recognized Flickr SoundNet dataset. Additionally, we present the VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS) benchmark, which offers new bounding box annotations for the recently released VGG-Sound dataset, explicitly marking visible sound sources in each video clip. This dataset is video-based, unlike Flickr SoundNet, and is 20 times larger than comparable existing resources, comprising 5,000 videos across over 200 categories. We further demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms various baselines on the VGG-SS benchmark.

Ontologies serve as formal models of concepts and their intricate interrelations, extensively utilized to encapsulate extensive domain knowledge in fields like biology and medicine, where ontologies often encompass hundreds of thousands of concepts. Given their substantial scale, visualization is essential for authoring, investigating, and comprehending the data within these structures. Current visualization tools predominantly emphasize hierarchical arrangements, often neglecting non-hierarchical associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, a new visualization method designed to enable the exploration of all concept relationships while simultaneously displaying the ontology's hierarchical framework. By integrating icicle plots, visual compression strategies, and interactive elements, this hybrid approach enhances space efficiency and mitigates visual structural complexity. A user study involving domain experts assessed OntoPlot's usability against the standard ontology editor Protégé. The findings validate that OntoPlot successfully meets its design objectives for association-focused tasks and is highly preferred by domain experts.

Although neural sequence-to-sequence automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems are theoretically capable of handling an open vocabulary with the right modeling units, they typically struggle to identify words absent from their training data, such as names, numbers, or technical terms. To address this, Huber et al. suggested enhancing end-to-end ASR with a word/phrase memory and an access mechanism to correctly recognize these unseen items. This paper investigates (a) dynamic methods for populating this memory with critical words and (b) the balance between improved recognition of new terms and the risk of false alarms for added vocabulary. Our results show that using an optimal set of new words significantly boosts the detection rate of unseen words with only a slight rise in false alarms (F1 score increasing from 0.30 to 0.80). Furthermore, we demonstrate that meaningful keywords can be successfully extracted from supporting documents and applied effectively.

This study addresses the initial boundary value problem for multi-dimensional Boussinesq equations lacking thermal diffusion, subject to either velocity damping or diffusion and stress-free conditions within a horizontally periodic strip. We establish the global existence of classical solutions in high-order Sobolev spaces, assuming high-order compatibility conditions near a linearly stratified equilibrium. Furthermore, we demonstrate the convergence of temperature to an asymptotic profile and derive sharp decay rates for both the velocity field and temperature fluctuations across all intermediate norms, utilizing spectral analysis alongside energy estimates. To our knowledge, these findings represent the first determination of sharp decay rates for temperature fluctuations and vertical velocity within all intermediate norms for the linearly stratified Boussinesq equations.
Assuming $G$ is a graph with edge ideal $I(G)$, we establish precise lower bounds for the depth of $I(G)^2$ expressed via the star packing number of $G$.

Preparing corpora for low-resource languages and developing human language technology to process them is a demanding endeavor, largely because of the scarcity of native-speaking expert linguists and the significant time and resources required. Bhojpuri, Magahi, and Maithili are low-resource Indo-Aryan languages spoken in India's Purvanchal region; due to their close relationship with Hindi—a relatively high-resource language—we conducted comparisons using Hindi. We gathered data for these three languages from diverse sources, cleaning the text as much as possible without altering its content. The collected material spans various domains and genres. We computed basic statistical metrics at character, word, syllable, and morpheme levels, both absolutely and relatively, to assess linguistic properties such as morphological, lexical, phonological, and syntactic complexity. These corpora were also manually annotated with parts-of-speech (POS) and chunk tags using the BIS tagset. The POS-tagged datasets comprise 16,067, 14,669, and 12,310 sentences for Bhojpuri, Magahi, and Maithili, respectively, while the chunking datasets contain 9,695 and 1,954 sentences for Bhojpuri and Maithili. We compared these statistical measures against a standard Hindi corpus. To mitigate the influence of corpus size, we attempted to equalize sizes across languages for most metrics, though in some instances, utilizing the full corpus proved superior despite size disparities. Although the findings are not entirely conclusive, we aimed to derive insights regarding the languages and their corpora.

Emerging dimming is a phenomenon observed in isolated solar active regions (ARs) during the initial phases of magnetic flux emergence. Detected by the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly, it is characterized by a swift drop in extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) brightness in the 171 Å channel alongside a concurrent rise in the 211 Å channel. This study investigates the physical mechanisms behind this event by examining coronal thermodynamic and magnetic characteristics. By calculating time-dependent differential emission measures for 18 events occurring between 2010 and 2012, we found a strong correlation between the emission measure (EM) decline in the 5.7 ≤ log₁₀T ≤ 5.9 temperature range and the EM increase in the 6.2 ≤ log₁₀T ≤ 6.4 range, spanning eight orders of magnitude. This correlation implies that coronal plasma is being heated from quiet-Sun, sub-MK temperatures up to 1–2 MK, which is characteristic of ARs. Furthermore, potential field extrapolations reveal substantial changes in local magnetic connectivity, as the dimming area becomes connected to the newly emerged flux through extended loops. Consequently, we conclude that emerging dimming is likely the result of coronal heating episodes driven by reconnection between emerging and ambient magnetic fields.

Drimbe and Vaes demonstrated an orbit equivalence superrigidity theorem for left-right wreath product actions within the measurable framework. In this work, we derive the corresponding result for the topological context concerning continuous orbit equivalence. Consequently, we identify minimal, topologically free actions that exhibit continuous orbit equivalence superrigidity. A key component of our proof involves establishing continuous cocycle superrigidity for specific generalized full shifts, thereby extending our earlier collaboration with Chung.

Deep learning has significantly enhanced 3D object detection accuracy for both LiDAR and stereo camera inputs in autonomous driving. However, while these networks excel at generalization, they are prone to overfitting on spurious artifacts like consistent variations in brightness, vehicle dimensions, and models. Most existing datasets are gathered from limited geographic regions within a single country under similar weather conditions. This paper addresses the challenge of adapting 3D object detectors between different datasets. We find that naive adaptation attempts lead to severe accuracy drops. Through extensive experimentation, we discovered that the primary obstacle is the variation in average car sizes across different locations. A straightforward correction based on these average sizes effectively bridges the adaptation gap. Our proposed method is simple and can be integrated into most existing 3D detection frameworks, offering a baseline for cross-country adaptation and suggesting that the problem is more solvable than previously thought. The code is available at https://github.com/cxy1997/3D_adapt_auto_driving.

Recent years have seen a surge in interest regarding efficient neural network architectures, with modern designs prioritizing not just accuracy but also inference speed and model compactness. This paper introduces FUN, a new family of Frequency-domain Utilization Networks. By leveraging the inherent efficiency of the frequency domain through the Discrete Cosine Transform, these networks operate directly within that domain. Employing contemporary techniques like compound scaling and inverted residual layers, we have developed a suite of models that allow for a tunable trade-off between size, latency, and accuracy, while surpassing competing RGB-based models. Comprehensive evaluations confirm that our approach offers robust alternatives to existing methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that operating in the frequency domain enables dynamic input compression during inference without requiring any architectural modifications.

The study introduces and examines discrete counterparts to index transforms based on Bessel and Lommel functions. Additionally, inversion theorems are formulated for appropriate function and sequence classes.

The Strip Packing (SP) problem involves placing $n$ axis-aligned rectangles, each with a width no greater than $W$, into a vertical half-strip $[0,W]\times[0,\infty)$ without overlap, aiming to minimize the total height. A common practical restriction limits solutions to those that are guillotine separable, meaning every rectangle can be isolated through a recursive series of edge-to-edge, axis-parallel cuts that avoid intersecting other items. This paper investigates approximation algorithms for the Guillotine Strip Packing (GSP) problem, which enforces this separability constraint. GSP extends both the classical Bin Packing problem and makespan minimization on identical machines, rendering it strongly NP-hard. Furthermore, via a reduction from the Partition problem, it is NP-hard to achieve a polynomial-time $(3/2-\varepsilon)$-approximation for GSP (mirroring the hardness of general SP) for any $\varepsilon > 0$. We introduce a polynomial-time $(3/2+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for GSP and a pseudo-polynomial-time $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm. The latter result is notable because achieving a $(5/4-\varepsilon)$-approximation for general SP in pseudo-polynomial time is NP-hard. Consequently, our findings effectively resolve the approximability of GSP in both polynomial and pseudo-polynomial contexts.

Video grounding focuses on identifying the specific time interval within an unedited video that matches a given textual query. Most current approaches operate under two main frameworks: top-down models, which define candidate segments beforehand and then classify and regress them, and bottom-up models, which directly predict frame-level probabilities for segment boundaries. Despite these variations, existing methods are not truly end-to-end, as they depend on computationally expensive post-processing to refine results. To address this, we reframe video grounding as a set prediction problem and introduce GTR, a novel end-to-end multi-modal Transformer. GTR comprises dedicated encoders for video and language inputs alongside a cross-modal decoder for grounding tasks. To enable efficient end-to-end training, we employ a Cubic Embedding layer to convert raw video data into visual tokens, while a newly designed Multi-head Cross-Modal Attention mechanism enhances modality fusion within the decoder. The model is optimized using a Many-to-One matching loss. Comprehensive experiments on various design choices, along with extensive evaluations across three benchmarks, demonstrate GTR's superior performance. Notably, all three typical variants of GTR achieve state-of-the-art results across every dataset and metric while offering inference speeds several times faster than previous methods.

This study addresses a general online stochastic optimization problem characterized by multiple budget constraints over a finite time horizon. During each period, a reward function and several cost functions are revealed; the decision-maker must select an action from a convex, compact set to maximize reward while adhering to budget limits, where each cost function represents the consumption of a specific budget. These reward and cost functions are drawn from an unknown distribution that varies non-stationarily over time. The primary goal is to maximize cumulative reward while satisfying all budget constraints, a framework applicable to diverse fields such as online linear programming and network revenue management. We examine two scenarios: (i) a data-driven setting where a prior estimate of the true distribution exists but may be imperfect, and (ii) an uninformative setting where the true distribution is entirely unknown. We introduce a unified measure based on Wasserstein distance to quantify both the inaccuracy of the prior in the first setting and the degree of non-stationarity in the second. We demonstrate that this measure provides a necessary and sufficient condition for achieving sublinear regret in both contexts. For the data-driven scenario, we propose a novel algorithm grounded in a primal-dual approach that incorporates prior distributional information into an online gradient descent procedure within the dual space, which also extends naturally to the uninformative setting. Under both conditions, the proposed algorithms achieve regret of an optimal order. Finally, numerical experiments illustrate how these algorithms can be effectively combined with re-solving techniques to enhance empirical performance.

Stellar variability poses a significant challenge to achieving the sensitivity needed to detect Earth-like exoplanets via the radial velocity (RV) method. To investigate activity signatures in Sun-like stars, we introduce SolAster, an open-source pipeline designed to compare space-based data with ground-based, disk-integrated RVs. Leveraging high-resolution Dopplergrams, magnetograms, and continuum filtergrams from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), we calculate 'Sun-as-a-star' disk-integrated RVs caused by rotationally modulated flux imbalances and suppressed convective blueshifts, alongside other metrics like unsigned magnetic flux. By comparing these SDO results with daily NEID ground-based solar RV measurements, we identified a robust link between magnetic activity indicators and RV variations, reinforcing the utility of unsigned magnetic flux as a proxy for stellar activity in slowly rotating stars. Removing the signal from measured unsigned magnetic flux improved NEID RV precision by approximately 20% (roughly 50 cm/s in quadrature), reducing the RMS scatter to about 60 cm/s over five months. Additionally, we analyzed correlations between individual and averaged spectral line shapes in NEID data and SDO-derived magnetic indicators to guide future research. Finally, applying SolAster to archival transit data for Venus and Mercury demonstrated the capability to recover sub-50 cm/s RV variations in SDO data by directly measuring Rossiter-McLaughlin (RM) signals.

Experimental design involves selecting samples from a specific set to generate the most accurate estimator for a chosen criterion. Within linear regression, various optimal designs have been established, each tied to a distinct metric such as mean square error or robustness. Typically, calculating these designs is an NP-hard task, prompting the use of convex relaxations that treat samples as probability distributions. While greedy approaches and rounding techniques have garnered significant attention, directly sampling from the optimal distribution has seen little investigation. This paper establishes theoretical bounds for randomized methods applied to E and G-optimal designs. To achieve this, we introduce a novel concentration inequality for the eigenvalues of random matrices, leveraging a refined concept of intrinsic dimension to measure the efficacy of these randomized strategies. Furthermore, we validate our theoretical findings through experiments, focusing specifically on G-optimal design in the context of identifying the best arm for linear bandits.

Research has demonstrated that multilingual language models facilitate significant transfer between different scripts and languages. This study investigates the internal representations responsible for such cross-lingual transfer, using gender distinctions as a practical case study to analyze how gender concepts are encoded within shared subspaces across various languages. Our findings reveal that gender representations comprise multiple prominent components common to all languages, alongside elements specific to individual languages. This distinction between language-independent and language-specific components offers an explanation for a notable empirical observation: while gender classification transfers effectively across languages, interventions designed to remove gender, when trained on a single language, do not readily generalize to others.

Structured light illumination is an active 3-D scanning method that projects and captures striped patterns to measure surface warping upon reflection. Specifically, phase measuring profilometry (PMP) utilizes time-multiplexed rolling sinusoidal waves, which necessitate either a stationary target or extremely rapid scanning to minimize motion artifacts. However, achieving high-speed scanning imposes a heavy demand on projector electronics to generate continuous-tone patterns within brief exposure windows. While binary patterns are highly valuable in this context, converting continuous-tone patterns to binary carries significant risks. Consequently, this paper presents a continuous-to-binary conversion algorithm designed to generate binary patterns that most accurately emulate their continuous-tone originals. Experimental results demonstrate a noise reduction of over three times compared to traditional halftoning methods.

This study introduces a lightweight approach to boost video engagement by delivering personalized artistic media, specifically static thumbnails and animated GIFs. The method leverages client-side computational resources to analyze Lightweight Thumbnail Containers (LTCs) within full-length sports footage, identifying personalized events. Rather than processing the entire video, the system focuses on small video segments to create these artistic assets, resulting in superior computational efficiency compared to baseline techniques that utilize full videos. By retrieving and utilizing only LTCs and specific video segments, the approach minimizes both transmission bandwidth and local storage requirements during generation. Experimental results on the Nvidia Jetson TX2 demonstrate that the proposed method reduces computational complexity by 3.57 times compared to the State-of-the-Art (SoA) approach. Qualitative evaluations further reveal that the generated GIFs achieved an average rating 1.02 points higher than those produced by the SoA method. To our knowledge, this represents the first technique to employ LTCs for artistic media generation, successfully delivering lightweight, high-performance services even on resource-constrained devices.

Persistence represents a key feature of numerous natural complex systems, defined by the duration a system stays in a specific state before transitioning to another. Investigating this phenomenon requires varied definitions and methodologies, contingent on whether the focus is short-term or long-term persistence. This paper examines the primary definitions, concepts, methods, existing literature, and recent advancements regarding persistence in complex systems. Initially, we outline the most prevalent definitions for both short-term and long-term scenarios. Subsequently, we analyze the most pertinent techniques for characterizing persistence in each context. Furthermore, a comprehensive literature review is conducted. We also present and evaluate significant findings on persistence, supported by empirical evidence from detailed case studies covering both temporal scales. Finally, the work concludes with an outlook on the future of research into persistence.

This paper presents a broad class of weighted spaces for holomorphic Dirichlet series featuring real frequencies, which are analytic within a specific half-plane, and investigates composition operators acting on these spaces. Specifically, when the symbol generating the composition operator is affine, we establish criteria for both boundedness and compactness. Additionally, we examine the cyclicity property and, as a secondary result, provide a sufficient condition ensuring that the direct sum of the identity operator and a weighted forward shift operator on the Hardy space $H^2$ is cyclic.

This chapter provides a general introduction and status review of the perturbative approach to quantum gravity (QG). It is a revised adaptation of chapters from Part II of a recent textbook on quantum field theory (QFT) and QG, co-authored with I.L. Buchbinder and published by Oxford University Press. The discussion covers the selection of starting actions in QG models, the degrees of freedom and propagators of metric perturbations, as well as power counting and renormalizability. We also examine issues associated with higher-derivative theories, including ghosts, quantum unitarity, and the stability of classical solutions within general relativity, along with potential solutions to these challenges. Using general QFT theorems from gauge theories, we detail gauge fixing and parametrization dependencies. Furthermore, we present a basic example of deriving one-loop divergences and discuss a significant application of the renormalization group in QG. The topic of gauge-invariant renormalizability in QG is addressed in a separate chapter of this Handbook, co-authored with P.M. Lavrov.

This research employs Shannon's formalism to examine the quantum information entropy of a particle subjected to an Aharonov-Bohm-type effect. Since quantum information studies require an analysis of the system's eigenstates—specifically its wave functions and energy levels—we modeled the particle as being confined within a cylindrical box under the influence of a dislocation defect that generates this effect. Our findings indicate that the dislocation alters the system's eigenstates, thereby impacting its overall quantum information.

This study establishes non-asymptotic bounds regarding the average convergence rate of the empirical measure within the law of large numbers, specifically using Wasserstein distance. We further examine occupation measures associated with ergodic Markov chains. A primary motivation for this work is the approximation of probability measures using finitely supported ones, known as the quantization problem. Our findings indicate that the convergence rates for empirical or occupation measures align with or closely approximate previously established optimal quantization rates in various scenarios, a point particularly emphasized in the context of infinite-dimensional Gaussian measures.

Boolean operations are a fundamental paradigm for creating and modifying digital shapes, yet computing mesh Booleans remains notoriously difficult. Although conceptually straightforward, these operations are plagued by numerical approximations that render the detection and processing of intersection points unreliable, causing implementations relying on floating-point arithmetic to frequently encounter degeneracies and failures. While methods based on rational numbers or exact geometric predicates offer the necessary robustness, they historically incurred such high computational costs that their use was limited to offline applications. We present the first algorithm for robust Boolean operations capable of achieving interactive frame rates on meshes containing up to 200,000 triangles. Our comprehensive evaluation covers interactive scenarios, batch processing of large mesh collections, handling of massive meshes with millions of elements, and variadic operations involving hundreds of shapes. In all these tests, we consistently outperform existing solutions by at least an order of magnitude.

This paper introduces a learning-based method for detecting Sparse Code Multiple Access (SCMA) signals by applying a deep neural network to the unfolded Message Passing Algorithm (MPA).
