To address this, the authors propose an alternative known as the Robust Density-Aware Distance (RDAD) filtration, which extends the persistence of small holes surrounded by dense areas. This is accomplished by weighting the distance function according to density estimates derived from Bell et al. Furthermore, the integration of distance-to-measure enhances stability and reduces noise associated with density estimation. The efficacy of this filtration in detecting small holes and its resilience to noise are validated through both analytical examples and comprehensive numerical experiments, alongside proofs of its fundamental mathematical properties.

Over the past decade, the surge in neural networks has driven major advancements in natural language processing (NLP), catalyzing parallel innovations in data-to-text generation (DTG). This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the neural DTG paradigm, systematically analyzing its methodologies, benchmark datasets, and evaluation frameworks. It clearly delineates DTG within the broader natural language generation (NLG) domain, offering a current synthesis of existing literature and tracing the trajectory of technological adoption both inside and beyond the NLG community. By presenting this holistic perspective, the survey identifies promising future research directions for DTG, emphasizing not only the development of linguistically proficient systems but also those that prioritize fairness and accountability.

We demonstrate that the space of transfinite words, specifically ordinal-indexed words over a Noetherian space, remains Noetherian under a natural topology termed the regular subword topology. Furthermore, we characterize both its sobrification and its specialization ordering, and we establish upper bounds for its dimension and stature.

Consider two groups, $G$ and $H$, acting on path-connected topological spaces $X$ and $Y$, respectively, where $H$ is a finite group of order $m$. Assuming the quotient maps $p:X\to X/G$ and $q:Y\to Y/H$ are regular coverings, it is established that the wreath product $G\wr H$ acts naturally on $W = X^m\times Y$, inducing a regular covering $r:W \to W/(G\wr H)$. This paper provides an explicit formulation of $\pi_1(W/(G\wr H))$ as a specific wreath product $\pi_1(X/G)\,\wr_{\partial_Y}\pi_1(Y/H)$, defined by a non-effective action of $\pi_1(Y/H)$ on the set of maps $H\to\pi_1(X/G)$. This action is mediated by the boundary homomorphism $\partial_{Y}:\pi_1(Y/H) \to H$ associated with the covering $q$. While this result is recognized, it is typically applied only when $X$ and $Y$ are contractible, rendering $W$ contractible and $W/(G\wr H)$ the classifying space for $G\wr H$. The study applies these findings to determine the homotopy types of orbits for generic smooth functions $f$ on orientable compact surfaces $M$, specifically regarding the natural right action of the diffeomorphism group $\mathcal{D}(M)$ on $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(M,\mathbb{R})$.

It is established that relatively pseudocomplemented lattices function as an algebraic semantics for intuitionistic logic. To broaden this concept to non-distributive lattices, the first author defined sectionally pseudocomplemented lattices: lattices with a top element 1 where every interval [y, 1], or section, is pseudocomplemented. We generalize this notion to partially ordered sets (posets) possessing a top element. Our objective is to demonstrate that such a poset can serve as an algebraic semantics for a specific type of more general intuitionistic logic, provided an implication is defined as presented in the paper. We establish several properties of this implication, which is characterized as "unsharp" because the resulting value for given inputs may be a subset of the poset rather than a unique element, yet all possible values are maximized. Furthermore, we show that this implication uniquely determines the poset; when a new operator \odot is introduced in an "unsharp" manner, the resulting structure constitutes an "unsharply" residuated poset.

Active automata learning, commonly known as model learning, is a powerful method for deriving black-box finite state models of software components. However, extending this approach to infinite state systems with data-carrying inputs and outputs has proven difficult. Current tools for such systems suffer from scalability issues and are limited to specific system classes, such as register automata with equality or inequality constraints. This paper demonstrates how to enhance model learning performance by extracting constraints on input and output parameters from execution traces and providing this grey-box information to the learner. Specifically, we present new implementations of the tree and equivalence oracles within RALib that leverage these derived constraints. Using an existing Python tainting library, we extract these constraints from program runs and compare our grey-box RALib against the traditional black-box version across various benchmarks, including data structures from Python's standard library. Our proof-of-concept implementation achieves nearly a two-order-of-magnitude reduction in the number of inputs required to test the software system. Furthermore, our generalizable approach allows RALib to learn models beyond the reach of black-box techniques, such as those for combination locks.

Reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-enabled communication represents a transformative technology that allows for the manipulation of wireless propagation environments through smart, low-cost reflective surfaces. However, achieving superior performance compared to traditional systems with purely passive RIS requires an impractically large surface area. To address this limitation, active RIS has been recently introduced, offering simultaneous signal amplification and reflection at the cost of increased power consumption. This paper proposes a novel over-the-air beamforming technique for RIS-assisted multi-user multiple-input single-output (MISO) systems, eliminating the need for pre- or post-processing hardware at both the transmitter and receiver. In this scheme, the reflection coefficients of the active RIS elements are tailored to maximize sum-rate gains. To solve the resulting non-convex quadratically constrained quadratic programming (QCQP) problem, we first apply semidefinite relaxation (SDR) to transform it into a convex feasibility problem, which is then efficiently resolved using the CVX optimization toolbox. Furthermore, drawing inspiration from this beamforming approach, we develop a new high-rate receive index modulation (IM) scheme equipped with a low-complexity sub-optimal detector. Finally, comprehensive simulations evaluate the sum-rate and bit error rate (BER) performance of the proposed designs.

We introduce a new resampling-based approach designed to create an asymptotically exact test for any subset of coefficient hypotheses within high-dimensional linear regression models. This method can be integrated into various multiple testing frameworks to generate confidence intervals for significant predictor variables. It generates permutation test statistics for individual hypotheses through repeated data splitting and variable selection, then defines tests for subsets by appropriately aggregating these individual statistics. The procedure is highly flexible, accommodating diverse selection techniques and multiple combining functions. We describe both an exact implementation and an approximate version that reduces memory requirements and computation time, enabling scalability to even higher dimensions. Finally, we demonstrate the method's efficacy using simulations and real-world gene expression data analysis.

Pre-trained transformer models like BERT have proven highly effective for Information Retrieval (IR), particularly when used to re-rank initial search results. Standard IR benchmarks assume a single query represents a user's information need; however, prior studies indicate that (I) user queries for the same need vary significantly and (II) neural models are often fragile, performing poorly with modified inputs. Guided by these findings, this work investigates the robustness of retrieval pipelines against semantically equivalent query variations. To capture the variability inherent in user queries, we developed a taxonomy based on manual annotations of transformations in the UQV100 dataset. For each syntax-altering category within this taxonomy, we implemented specific automatic methods to generate query variations. Experiments across two datasets and two IR tasks demonstrate that retrieval pipelines lack robustness to these variations, resulting in an average effectiveness drop of approximately 20%. The associated code and datasets can be accessed at https://github.com/Guzpenha/query_variation_generators.

This study evaluates the Krotov method for both open (non-unitary) and closed (unitary) quantum systems to determine optimal controls for qubits and qutrits interacting with an environment. In the unitary approach, controls are derived by ignoring environmental interactions and subsequently applied to the system under noisy conditions. We examine two scenarios: preparing a target state from an initial state and implementing quantum gates. Our results indicate that for state preparation, non-unitary optimization yields superior controls compared to the unitary method. Conversely, for quantum gate implementation, both methods achieve comparable mean fidelities. Given that unitary optimization is independent of decay rates and specific noise types, while also being computationally more efficient, we conclude that employing unitary optimization is the preferred current practice for implementing quantum gates in open quantum systems.

Anomaly detection seeks to distinguish anomalies from normal samples, where pretrained networks offer a promising solution. However, fine-tuning these networks on single-class data poses a risk of pattern collapse. To address this, we introduce CAP (Constrained Adaptive Projection with Pretrained Features). This framework utilizes a simple linear projection head that processes a specific input alongside its $k$ most similar pretrained normal representations for feature adaptation. Additionally, it employs a modified self-attention mechanism to uncover relationships within one-class semantic features. A specialized loss function is designed to prevent pattern collapse by measuring the similarity between specific data and its adaptive normal counterpart, while also incorporating a constraint term to gently align the pretrained and adaptive feature spaces. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on both semantic and sensory anomaly detection benchmarks, attaining 96.5% AUROC on CIFAR-100, 97.0% AUROC on CIFAR-10, and 89.9% AUROC on the MvTec dataset.

This research investigates the asymptotic behavior of the complex modified Korteweg-de Vries (mKdV) equation, given by $\partial_t u + \partial_x^3 u = \pm |u|^2 \partial_x u$. In the real-valued setting, solutions originating from small, localized initial data are known to display modified scattering in the region $|x| \geq t^{1/3}$ and self-similar behavior for $|x| \leq t^{1/3}$. We demonstrate that these same asymptotic properties apply to the complex mKdV equation. The primary challenge in the complex case arises because the nonlinearity cannot be formulated as a derivative, complicating the control of low-frequency dynamics. To address this, we decompose the solution as $u = S + w$, where $S$ represents a self-similar solution sharing the same mean as $u$, and $w$ is a remainder term with superior decay. Leveraging the explicit form of $S$, we achieve enhanced low-frequency behavior for $u$ that surpasses what can be obtained through dispersive estimates alone.

Linked Data Fragments (LDFs) serve as web-based gateways for accessing and querying Knowledge Graphs. Variations among these interfaces, such as SPARQL endpoints and Triple Pattern Fragment servers, exist regarding the SPARQL expressions they support and the metadata they expose. While client-side methods have been developed to handle queries on individual interfaces, prior federated query processing has largely focused on homogenous federations involving only one type of LDF, typically SPARQL endpoints. This study tackles the complexities of executing SPARQL queries across federations comprising heterogeneous LDF interfaces. To achieve this, we define the concept of federations of Linked Data Fragments and introduce a framework for querying such heterogeneous environments. This framework includes query decomposition, query planning, and physical operators customized to the specific characteristics of different LDF types. We propose specific approaches for each component of the framework and validate them through an experimental study using the FedBench benchmark. The findings demonstrate significant performance gains resulting from these interface-aware strategies that leverage the unique capabilities of diverse interfaces within federations.

We build a temporal network based on two-dimensional active particle systems governed by the Vicsek model, and we numerically examine the interevent time bursts between specific particle pairs. Our findings indicate that across various noise strengths, the interevent time distribution for a target edge exhibits a heavy tail, signaling strong burstiness. To further analyze this phenomenon, we compute the burstiness parameter and the memory coefficient. Results demonstrate that near the critical points of the Vicsek model, the burstiness parameter reaches its minimum value for each density, suggesting a link between the model's phase transition and the bursty signal characteristics. Additionally, the memory effect plays a negligible role in burstiness. Furthermore, by applying the susceptible-infected model to spreading dynamics on this temporal network, we observe a positive correlation between burstiness and information spreading.

The Security-Constrained Economic Dispatch (SCED) serves as a critical optimization framework for Transmission System Operators (TSOs) to clear real-time energy markets while maintaining grid reliability. Amidst rising operational uncertainties driven by the expanding integration of renewable generators and distributed energy resources, operators are required to continuously assess system risks in real-time, necessitating rapid evaluation of grid behavior under fluctuating loads and renewable outputs. However, solving an optimization problem for every possible scenario is impractical due to the stringent time constraints of real-time operations. To address this, the paper introduces a Machine Learning (ML) proxy for SCED capable of predicting optimal solutions within milliseconds. Drawing on a rigorous analysis of MISO market-clearing optimizations, the study proposes a new ML pipeline designed to tackle key challenges, including variability in load, renewable generation, and production costs, as well as the combinatorial nature of commitment decisions. Additionally, a novel Classification-Then-Regression architecture is introduced to better capture SCED solution dynamics. Numerical experiments conducted on the French transmission system demonstrate that this approach can generate accurate optimization proxies compatible with real-time operational timelines, achieving relative errors under 0.6%.

We construct the free field realization of the fundamental $W$-currents and screening currents for the deformed $W$-superalgebra ${\cal W}_{q,t}\bigl(A(M,N)\bigr)$, which corresponds to the Lie superalgebra of type $A(M,N)$. Leveraging this construction, we derive higher $W$-currents and establish a closed system of quadratic relations between them. While these relations remain invariant regardless of the specific Dynkin diagram chosen for the $A(M,N)$ Lie superalgebra, the screening currents do not share this property. Consequently, we are able to define ${\cal W}_{q,t}\bigl(A(M,N)\bigr)$ explicitly through generators and relations.

Modeling real-world audio is a core challenge in creative machine learning applications and domains such as speech processing and bioacoustics. While Transformer-based generative models and previous approaches like DDSP can generate realistic sounds, they often lack interpretability and offer limited control. As an alternative, this study explores using modular synthesizers—compositional, parametric electronic instruments—to model non-musical sounds. However, inferring the necessary synthesizer parameters for arbitrary sounds remains difficult, as prior research has largely concentrated on musical audio. In this work, we optimize a differentiable synthesizer from TorchSynth to emulate and creatively generate animal vocalizations. We evaluate various optimization techniques, ranging from gradient-based search to genetic algorithms, for parameter inference, and demonstrate how these parameters can be controlled and interpreted to effectively model non-musical sounds.

Chern-Simons modified gravity emerges as a low-energy effective framework derived from string theory, incorporating an anomaly-canceling correction to the Einstein-Hilbert action. This correction involves the term $\varphi R \tilde R$, which couples the Pontryagin density $R \tilde R$ with a scalar field $\varphi$ treated either as a dynamical or non-dynamical background field. While many standard solutions to Einstein's general relativity remain valid within this amended theory, the Kerr metric stands out as a special case, prompting a search for rotating black hole solutions. This study extends the solution originally published in Phys. Rev. D \textbf{77}, 064007 (2008) by permitting the potential $V$ to take non-zero values, specifically analyzing three scenarios: $V=\mathrm{const.}$, $V\propto \varphi$, and $V\propto \varphi^2$. For the first time, we present novel rotating black hole solutions within the dynamical Chern-Simons gravity framework that include a potential and generalize prior results. Derived in the slow-rotation limit (parameterized by $\varepsilon$), these axisymmetric and stationary solutions represent a distortion of the Kerr metric induced by a dipole scalar field. Furthermore, we observe that when $V\propto \varphi$, the metric's rectification scales inversely with the fourth power of the radial distance from the black hole's center, suggesting that these models can satisfy constraints from weak-field experiments.

We propose a straightforward framework for the formation of collective memory. Within neighborhoods, agents continuously exchange signals, where the prevalence of support determines which signals prevail locally. Through interactions across different neighborhoods, this influence propagates, occasionally resulting in the emergence of a collective signal. We introduce a logical system to analyze this process of memory emergence and present initial technical findings regarding the logic.

Neutrinos may undergo rapid flavor transitions in the dense cores of core-collapse supernovae and neutron star mergers due to the neutrino fast flavor instability (FFI). When this transformation is substantial, the FFI can profoundly influence supernova explosions and the production of heavy elements in the universe. Because many advanced simulations utilize neutrino transport methods based on angular moments, determining whether these distributions are unstable to the FFI remains challenging due to incomplete information. This study evaluates various moment-based instability tests proposed in existing literature. We apply time-independent, general relativistic neutrino transport to a snapshot from a 3D neutron star merger simulation to create realistic neutrino distributions and assess the accuracy of each criterion in predicting instability. Furthermore, we introduce a novel "maximum entropy" instability test; although more complex, it provides more detailed (though still approximate) estimates of the electron lepton number (ELN) crossing width and depth. Our findings indicate that the maximum entropy test and the resonant trajectory test are especially accurate in predicting instability for this snapshot, even though all tested methods correctly identify regions where significant flavor transformation is most probable.

This study introduces a new second-order cone relaxation for the semidefinite programming model of optimal power flow, one that avoids the "angle relaxation" assumption. Building on methods by Kim et al., we adapt the approach for complex matrices and apply it to 3x3 positive semidefinite matrices to create novel second-order cone constraints that complement the standard 2x2 principal-minor based ones. We then apply this framework to optimal power flow in meshed networks, accompanied by numerical examples.

We investigate $2 \to 2$ scattering amplitudes for a scalar particle with mass $m$, assuming $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry where the particle is odd under this transformation. Our analysis covers two categories of amplitudes: fully nonperturbative cases and effective field theory (EFT) scenarios characterized by a cut-off scale $M$. By employing a primal numerical approach that enforces complete non-linear unitarity, we derive new constraints on observables across space-time dimensions $2 \leq d \leq 4$ for both amplitude types. These bounds significantly outperform those derived from linearized unitarity or positivity conditions alone. We explore how these results can restrict EFTs and compare our findings with perturbative calculations in $\phi^4$ theory at weak coupling, demonstrating that the latter saturates the established limits.

We re-examine a representation of the Riemann zeta function $\zeta(s)$ formulated using normalized incomplete gamma functions, originally proposed by the author and S. Cang in Methods Appl. Anal. {\bf 4} (1997) 449--470. By applying the uniform asymptotics of the incomplete gamma function, we derive an asymptotic-like expansion for $\zeta(s)$ along the critical line $s=1/2+it$ as $t\to+\infty$. The leading term consists of the original Dirichlet series smoothed by a complementary error function with a suitable argument, accompanied by a sequence of correction terms. This work aims to present these correction terms in a more accessible form by expressing them as inverse powers of $\omega$ (where $\omega^2=\pi s/(2i)$) multiplied by coefficients that are trigonometric functions of $\omega$.

This study addresses initial value problems for semilinear wave equations of derivative type featuring spatial weights in one dimension. The lifespan estimates for classical solutions in this context differ significantly from those involving nonlinearities of the unknown function directly, as global-in-time existence can be achieved through spatial decay.

Using non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations, we examined the Soret effect in binary mixtures of dimers and monomers, specifically isolating the contribution of internal degrees of freedom in flexible molecules to this phenomenon. Our results indicate that as molecules become softer, the thermal diffusion factor decreases and may even reverse sign. We attribute these observations to two proposed mechanisms: first, temperature-induced structural changes that cause bulkier molecules to migrate toward hotter regions; and second, an asymmetry in restitution coefficients between rigid and flexible molecules, leading to larger restitution events for flexible molecules located in the hot zone.

This study reports the initial observation of $Z$ boson production in proton-lead collisions at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair of $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=5~\text{TeV}$. The analysis utilizes a dataset with an integrated luminosity of $1.6~\text{nb}^{-1}$ gathered by the LHCb detector. $Z$ boson candidates are identified through pairs of oppositely charged muons, selected within pseudorapidities from 2.0 to 4.5 and with transverse momenta exceeding $20~\text{GeV}/c$. The selection further restricts the invariant dimuon mass to the interval of $60-120~\text{GeV}/c^2$. The measured production cross-section for $Z \to \mu^+\mu^-$ is $13.5^{+5.4}_{-4.0}\text{(stat.)}\pm1.2\text{(syst.)}~\text{nb}$ in the forward direction (proton beam) and $10.7^{+8.4}_{-5.1}\text{(stat.)}\pm1.0\text{(syst.)}~\text{nb}$ in the backward direction (lead beam), where the uncertainties are listed as statistical and systematic, respectively.

This study investigates the impact of magnification within the Dark Energy Survey Year 3 analysis of galaxy clustering and galaxy-galaxy lensing, utilizing two distinct lens populations: Luminous red galaxies (redMaGiC) and a magnitude-limited sample with redshift-dependent cuts (MagLim). Using Balrog image simulations to model systematic effects, we account for magnification's influence on both galaxy flux and size selection. Our results indicate that magnification constitutes a significant systematic for the MagLim sample. We present cosmological constraints derived from galaxy clustering auto-correlations and galaxy-galaxy lensing signals under varying magnification priors, observing broad consistency in parameters for both $\Lambda$CDM and $w$CDM models. However, when treating the magnification bias amplitude as a free parameter, the two-point correlation functions favor a different amplitude than the fiducial value derived from simulations. We validate our magnification analysis by comparing cross-clustering between lens bins against predictions from a baseline analysis relying solely on lens auto-correlation, suggesting that non-magnification systematics may drive the observed discrepancy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating cross-clustering between lens redshift bins into the fit substantially enhances constraints on lens magnification parameters, enabling the use of uninformative priors on magnification coefficients without compromising constraining power or encountering prior volume issues.

Face anti-spoofing (FAS) is a critical and ubiquitous component of face recognition systems. Despite achieving high accuracy, FAS systems remain imperfect due to the dynamic nature of real-world environments and the continuous emergence of novel presentation attacks. Practically, the goal is to maintain strong performance on the original source domain while adapting effectively to a new target domain using only a limited number of labeled samples from that new scenario. This paper identifies and tackles this practical challenge, termed Few-Shot Domain Expansion for Face Anti-Spoofing (FSDE-FAS). This task is difficult because scarce target data can lead to overfitting on the new domain and catastrophic forgetting of the source domain knowledge. To overcome these issues, we introduce the Style transfer-based Augmentation for Semantic Alignment (SASA) framework. Our approach generates auxiliary target samples via photorealistic style transfer to augment the limited data. Furthermore, we design a mechanism to align the source and target domains at both the instance and distribution levels, while employing a constraint to minimize forgetting and stabilize source domain performance. We establish two benchmarks to simulate FSDE-FAS scenarios, and experimental results demonstrate that the proposed SASA method surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches.

We have constructed approximately two dozen exactly solvable Markov chains defined on one-dimensional finite and semi-infinite integer lattices, utilizing the convolutions of orthogonality measures associated with Krawtchouk, Hahn, Meixner, Charlier, $q$-Hahn, $q$-Meixner, and little $q$-Jacobi polynomials. These constructions yield stationary probability distributions, along with complete sets of eigenvalues and eigenvectors, directly through the polynomials and their respective orthogonality measures. Furthermore, an intriguing property known as "convolutional self-similarity" is exhibited by these stationary distributions.

Cost volume plays a critical role in contemporary deep learning models for optical flow estimation, typically formed by computing the inner product of two feature vectors. However, the conventional inner product used in standard cost volumes often restricts the representational capacity of flow models by ignoring correlations across different channel dimensions and assigning equal weights to each. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a learnable cost volume (LCV) based on an elliptical inner product, which extends the standard approach using a positive definite kernel matrix. To ensure positive definiteness, we apply spectral decomposition to the kernel matrix and re-parameterize it through the Cayley representation. This proposed LCV serves as a lightweight module that can be seamlessly integrated into existing architectures to replace traditional cost volumes. Experimental findings indicate that the LCV not only enhances the accuracy of state-of-the-art models on standard benchmarks but also strengthens their robustness against variations in illumination, noise, and adversarial perturbations in input data.

This study explores the explosive disruption of low-mass neutron stars using Newtonian hydrodynamic simulations enhanced by a nuclear reaction network encompassing approximately 4500 isotopes. Our analysis examines how nuclear processes—specifically neutron capture, $\beta$-decays, and spontaneous fission—influence the hydrodynamic instability evolution within these stars. We demonstrate that following surface mass ejection, low-mass neutron stars experience delayed explosions accompanied by an electron anti-neutrino burst peaking at roughly $3\times10^{50}$ erg s$^{-1}$, alongside ejecta heated to approximately $10^{9}$ K. Furthermore, the ejecta facilitate a robust r-process nucleosynthesis, producing heavy elements near the second and third r-process peaks as well as lanthanides. These findings indicate that the explosions of low-mass neutron stars may represent a significant source for solar chemical elements.

Building on a prior study by N. H. Tong [Phys. Rev. B 92, 165126 (2015)], which employed an equation-of-motion based series expansion to derive the second-order strong-coupling expansion for the Anderson impurity model's single-particle Green function, this paper presents two theoretical improvements. First, we adopt a more precise method for self-consistently computing the averages within G1. Second, during the resummation, we utilize updated coefficients for the continued fraction, informed by the formally exact Mori-Zwanzig framework. These enhancements yield a more accurate prediction for the impurity spin response to the bath's magnetic bias. Furthermore, when integrated with dynamical mean-field theory, our approach offers a superior description of the half-filled Hubbard model's antiferromagnetism.

This research addresses the challenge of identifying whether a heterogeneous dense subhypergraph exists. The null hypothesis assumes a heterogeneous Erdős-Rényi uniform random hypergraph, whereas the alternative posits a similar hypergraph containing a dense substructure. We derive detection thresholds under known edge probabilities and develop an asymptotically powerful test to differentiate between these scenarios. Additionally, we propose an adaptive test that operates without requiring knowledge of edge probabilities, offering greater practical utility.

Cross-domain cold-start recommendation has become a significant and growing challenge for recommender systems. While previous research primarily addresses either cross-domain user recommendation or cold-start item recommendation, this study highlights a specific scenario where a new domain, in its early stages, possesses users similar to those in a source domain but generates far fewer interactions. In such cases, it is essential to adapt user preferences from the source domain to the target domain, particularly for newly introduced content lacking sufficient feedback. To address this gap, we introduce COUPLE (Cross-dOmain User Preference LEarning), a self-trained framework designed for cold-start recommendation leveraging various semantic tags, such as item attributes or video genres. Specifically, COUPLE integrates three preference levels: user history, user content, and user group, to ensure reliable recommendations. User history is modeled using a domain-aware sequential approach, while a frequency encoder processes underlying tags to capture user content preferences. Furthermore, a hierarchical memory tree with orthogonal node representations is employed to generalize user group preferences across different domains. The entire framework utilizes a contrastive learning approach combined with a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queue to generate more distinctive representations. Extensive experiments on two datasets confirm COUPLE's effectiveness in both user and content cold-start scenarios. Additionally, a one-week online A/B test on the Taobao APP demonstrated that COUPLE achieves superior Click-Through-Rates (CTR) compared to other baselines. The method is currently deployed in production for cross-domain cold micro-video recommendation.

The gravitational-wave event GW190521 offers fresh perspectives on black hole mass distributions and astrophysical formation pathways. Given recent independent assertions that GW190521 possessed significant pre-merger eccentricity, this study examines the implications for dynamically formed binaries resembling GW190521. While the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) could detect such binaries if they originate from isolated formation channels with circular orbits, we demonstrate that dynamically formed analogues might bypass the LISA frequency band entirely. Through simulations of GW190521-like systems formed via post-Newtonian binary-single scattering, we find that these binaries can indeed enter the LIGO-Virgo band with substantial eccentricity, consistent with recent findings, though likely remaining below $e_{\rm 10Hz} \lesssim 0.7$. The existence of these eccentric binaries strengthens the scientific case for a decihertz gravitational-wave observatory, such as a kilometer-scale Midband Atomic Gravitational-wave Interferometric Sensor (MAGIS). Observations of such systems by a decihertz detector prior to merger would constrain their eccentricity more precisely than LIGO-Virgo alone could achieve, offering further insights into the specific environments where these binaries form.

This study establishes consistent compactifications for Einstein-Maxwell and Einstein-Maxwell-Lovelock theories on direct product spacetimes defined as $\mathcal{M}_D=\mathcal{M}_d\times\mathcal{K}^{p}$, where $\mathcal{K}^p$ represents a Euclidean internal manifold with constant curvature. Such compactifications necessitate a precise flux of $p$-forms distributed across the internal manifold. The dynamics of these $p$-forms are governed by two distinct interactions: specific couplings to the curvature tensor and a tailored interaction with the electromagnetic field of the $d$-dimensional brane, the latter regulated by an extension of the recently introduced Quasitopological Electromagnetism framework. We solve the resulting second-order field equations for these compactified theories and construct general homogeneous charged black p-branes. Specifically, we derive homogeneous Reissner-Nordstr\"om black strings and black p-branes within Einstein-Maxwell theory, as well as homogeneous charged Boulware-Deser black p-branes for quadratic and cubic Maxwell-Lovelock gravities.

In this study, $R$ represents a commutative ring with identity, and $M$ denotes a nonzero unital $R$-module. We extend the notion of semiannihilator small submodules to $T$-semiannihilator small submodules relative to an arbitrary submodule $T$ of $M$.

This study applies a novel gravity theory by Finzi, characterized by enhanced interactions at large scales, to examine the thermodynamics of galaxy clusters. Utilizing a statistical model, we derive various equations of state. Furthermore, we compare the clustering parameter's behavior against its standard Newtonian equivalent and investigate the general distribution function alongside its response to changes in the clustering parameter's strength. Additionally, we explore the potential for phase transitions, observing that such transitions can occur in a hierarchical manner.

The ALICE collaboration utilized Run 1 data from the LHC to measure the production of $\mathrm{K}^{*}(\mathrm{892})^{0}$ and $\mathrm{\phi(1020)}$ in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 8$ TeV. Differential yields, expressed as d$^{\rm 2}N$/d$y$d$p_{\rm{T}}$, were determined at midrapidity ($|y| < 0.5$) across transverse momentum ranges of $0 < p_{\rm{T}} < 20$ GeV/$c$ for $\rm{K}^{*0}$ and $0.4 < p_{\rm{T}} < 16$ GeV/$c$ for $\phi$. Additionally, this study presents refined measurements for these particles at $\sqrt{s} = 7$ TeV. The analysis investigates the dependence on collision energy for $p_{\rm{T}}$ distributions, integrated yields, and particle ratios within inelastic pp collisions, comparing findings across various collision systems. Results indicate that particle ratios remain consistent with measurements at other LHC energies. While an increase in collision energy leads to a hardening of particle spectra, the relative abundances of these particles show no dependence on energy. Finally, the $p_{\rm{T}}$-differential yields for $\rm{K}^{*0}$ and $\phi$ at 8 TeV are evaluated against predictions from multiple Monte Carlo event generators.

This study introduces new fixed point theorems for multivalued mappings within $\alpha$-complete metric spaces by utilizing a broader class of simulation functions. The findings extend and generalize several established fixed point results found in existing literature. Additionally, examples and consequences are provided to demonstrate the practical applicability of this theoretical framework.

We report the definitive orbit for the late-type spectroscopic binary HD 1, derived from 553 spectra collected over 13 years using our robotic STELLA facility and its high-resolution echelle spectrograph, SES. The system exhibits long-term radial-velocity stability of approximately 50 m/s, with a single radial velocity measurement achieving an rms residual of 63 m/s, nearing the anticipated precision. Spectral lines of HD 1 display rotational broadening with a $v\sin i$ value of 9.1$\pm$0.1 km/s. Although the spectrum appears single-lined, it yielded an orbit characterized by an eccentricity of 0.5056$\pm$0.0005 and a semi-amplitude of 4.44 km/s. By relying solely on the high-precision SES data, we refined the orbital period to 2318.70$\pm$0.32 days, an improvement over the 2317.8$\pm$1.1 days derived when combining older datasets from DAO and Cambridge/Coravel. To maintain solution integrity, we excluded the less precise older data. Furthermore, we re-evaluated the astrophysical parameters of HD 1 through spectrum synthesis and, incorporating the new *Gaia* DR-2 parallax, propose a higher luminosity than previously reported. We conclude that HD 1 is a slightly metal-deficient K0 III-II giant star, approximately 217 times more luminous than the Sun, while its companion remains undetectable in optical wavelengths. Additionally, we provide evidence for a third component within the system.

We introduce the inaugural data release of the Survey on extragALactic magnetiSm with SOFIA (SALSA Legacy Program), comprising resolved imaging polarimetric observations of 14 nearby galaxies ($<20$ Mpc) using HAWC+ across the $53$ to $214$ $\mu$m range. These observations achieve a resolution of $5$-$18$" ($90$ pc $-$ $1$ kpc). This work outlines the background on extragalactic magnetism, defines key terms, and details the program's scientific motivation and sample selection. Our primary focus is on general trends in emissive polarization fraction. Far-infrared polarimetric data trace the thermal polarized emission from magnetically aligned dust grains throughout galaxy disks, revealing polarization fractions ($P$) of $0$-$15$% in the cold ($T_{\rm d} = [19,48]$ K) and dense ($\log_{10}(N_{\rm HI+H_{2}}) = [19.96,22.91]$) interstellar medium. Spiral galaxies exhibit a median polarization fraction of $\langle P_{154\mu m} \rangle = 3.3\pm0.9$% across their disks. We report the first polarized spectrum for starburst galaxies, which displays a minimum between $89$-$154$ $\mu$m. The declining $53$-$154$ $\mu$m polarized spectrum likely results from reduced dust grain alignment efficiency caused by temperature variations along the line-of-sight within galactic outflows. Our findings indicate that starburst galaxies and star-forming regions in normal galaxies possess the lowest polarization fractions. Furthermore, 50% (7 of 14) of the galaxies require a broken power-law to describe the $P-N_{HI+H_{2}}$ and $P-T_{d}$ relations, revealing three distinct trends. Group 1 shows a relative increase in anisotropic random B-fields driven by compression or shear in galactic outflows, starburst rings, and inner bars; Groups 2 and 3 exhibit a relative increase in isotropic random B-fields driven by star-forming regions in spiral arms, and/or enhanced dust grain alignment efficiency due to shock-driven regions or specific evolutionary stages.

The manifold hypothesis posits that high-dimensional data resides on or close to a low-dimensional, nonlinear manifold. Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) attempt to model this by learning mappings from low-dimensional latent vectors to high-dimensional data, while enforcing global latent structure via a predefined prior distribution. However, if this prior diverges from the true data manifold's structure, the resulting model becomes less accurate. To address this discrepancy, we propose the Variational Autoencoder with Learned Latent Structure (VAELLS), which embeds a learnable manifold model within the VAE's latent space. This approach allows the model to discover the nonlinear manifold structure directly from the data and utilize it to define the latent prior. By integrating a latent manifold model, we ensure the prior aligns closely with the data and enable the definition of generative transformation paths in the latent space, allowing class manifolds to be described through transformations derived from class-specific examples. We validate the model using datasets with known latent structures and further demonstrate its effectiveness on real-world data.

This study concludes the investigation initiated in arXiv:1207.4867, which focused on deriving one-loop oblique corrections within the MSSM. Utilizing a novel two-component spinor formalism distinct from prior literature, we compute the contributions from fermion superpartners—specifically the neutralino and chargino sectors—to the self-energies of Standard Model electroweak gauge bosons. The corresponding $S$, $T$, and $U$ parameters are also derived. Our findings are validated through two distinct methods, followed by a comprehensive comparative analysis with existing results.

Research indicates that Augmented Reality (AR) learning games generally enhance student learning; however, their application in special education contexts, where accessibility is critical, remains underexplored. Consequently, this study aims to investigate AR games within accessible learning environments and elucidate their benefits compared to conventional methods. Through a systematic review of major databases over the last ten years, we analyzed user evaluations, student learning outcomes, and system features documented in existing literature. Our findings reveal that AR game applications foster student learning across three dimensions: cognitive, affective, and retention. Despite these positive impacts, significant design limitations persist in current AR games tailored for special needs. Drawing from these insights, we propose strategic design recommendations for future AR learning applications aimed at accessible education.

Recent work (ArXiv: 2007.03785) applied the established 2D celestial CFT (CCFT) method to derive the asymptotic symmetry algebra of $\mathcal{N}=1$ supergravity. This study extends that framework to the maximally supersymmetric, four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=8$ supergravity theory within asymptotically flat spacetimes, establishing a new extended asymptotic symmetry algebra designated as $\mathcal{N}=8$ $\mathfrak{sbms}_4$. By employing the CCFT technique, we identify the necessary currents to generalize the $\mathcal{N}=8$ super-Poincaré and $\mathrm{SU}(8)_R$ R-symmetry current algebras on the celestial sphere $\mathcal{CS}^2$. Furthermore, we expand the definition of shadow transformations and demonstrate that the global $\mathrm{SU}(8)_R$ algebra does not admit any infinite-dimensional extensions within this theory.

As intermittent renewable energy sources increasingly feed into electrical grids, Distribution System Operators (DSOs) must adapt network structures to incorporate new stakeholders while ensuring stability and flexibility. Segmenting the grid into logical clusters offers significant organizational and technical advantages to address these challenges, yet identifying the optimal partition remains complex due to its intricate nature. Concurrently, quantum computing has emerged as a promising technology over the last few decades for accelerating solutions to difficult combinatorial optimization problems. This study investigates the application of quantum computing in Graph Partitioning using electrical modularity. We evaluated various quantum annealing and hybrid approaches against standard IEEE test cases. Results from the IEEE 14-bus test case indicate that the D-WaveSampler quantum annealing method achieves solutions equal to or 1% better than optimal for specific partition counts. For larger test cases, hybrid quantum annealing demonstrated a relative error under 0.02% compared to classical benchmarks, with the IEEE 118-bus case exhibiting notable speed improvements. These performance gains could facilitate real-time planning and grid operations. Ultimately, this work aims to serve as an initial demonstration of quantum computing's potential in modernizing and adapting electrical grids for the decentralized future of energy systems.

Recent focus on the societal implications of AI has centered heavily on fairness concerns. While existing research has highlighted unfair AI systems and suggested debiasing approaches, significant challenges persist. Representation learning for Heterogeneous Information Networks (HINs), a core component of complex network mining, drives applications with social consequences, such as automated career counseling, yet few efforts have targeted the prevention of harmful bias amplification, like sexism in employment. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces a comprehensive suite of de-biasing methods for fair HIN representation learning, encompassing sampling-based, projection-based, and graph neural network (GNN)-based strategies. We systematically analyze these algorithms, particularly their ability to balance fairness against prediction accuracy. Our evaluation focuses on an automated career counseling scenario designed to reduce gender bias in job recommendations. Drawing on results from two datasets, we determine the most effective fair HIN representation learning techniques across varying conditions.

The Beam Instrumentation group at CERN has introduced a novel scintillating fibre beam monitor designed for measuring secondary particle beams within the CERN Experimental Areas. Distinguished by its straightforward design, the device offers a minimal material budget, vacuum compatibility, robust performance, cost-effectiveness, and ease of manufacture. By employing various read-out methods, the monitor can execute multiple tasks, including determining beam profile, position, and intensity, performing momentum spectrometry, generating rapid trigger signals, and measuring time-of-flight for particle identification. It has been successfully commissioned in the newly established test beams of the CERN Neutrino Platform, demonstrating excellent performance as detailed in the accompanying paper.

We demonstrate a method for calculating the degrees of the Deligne extension of Hodge bundles within a variation of Hodge structure over $\mathbb{P}^1$ characterized by Hodge numbers $(1,1,\dots,1)$, utilizing the local exponents of the associated Picard-Fuchs equation as outlined by Eskin-Kontsevich-Möller-Zorich. This approach enables the determination of Hodge numbers for Zucker's Hodge structure on the relevant parabolic cohomology groups. Furthermore, we apply these findings to families of elliptic curves, K3 surfaces, and Calabi-Yau threefolds.

Segmentation of Complete Renal Structures (CRS) in 3D aims to simultaneously identify kidneys, tumors, and associated arteries and veins within a single inference. Achieving this would significantly aid preoperative planning and intraoperative guidance for laparoscopic partial nephrectomy (LPN), thereby playing a pivotal role in renal cancer management. However, current efforts have failed due to the intricate shapes of renal anatomy, low image contrast, and substantial anatomical variability. This study introduces Ensemble Multi-condition GAN (EnMcGAN) for the first time, utilizing adversarial ensemble learning to address these challenges. The research offers three key contributions: first, a multi-windowing committee inspired by windowing techniques, which partitions CTA images into narrow windows with varying centers and widths to enhance contrast at salient boundaries and soft tissues, subsequently fusing segmentation results from these windows to improve overall quality. Second, a multi-condition GAN equipped with multiple discriminators that ensures segmented structures adhere to realistic shape conditions, thereby refining shape feature extraction. Third, an adversarial weighted ensemble module that employs trained discriminators to evaluate segmentation quality, normalizing these scores to determine ensemble weights specific to each input image and thus optimizing the final results. The study enrolled 122 patients, achieving a mean Dice coefficient of 84.6% for renal structures. Extensive experiments demonstrate powerful segmentation accuracy and significant clinical value for renal cancer treatment.

We contend that resonant friction significantly impacts a disc when its rotational direction is misaligned with that of the host nuclear star cluster. The disc's gravity perturbs the cluster, which in turn applies a powerful counter-torque to the disc. We suggest this torque explains the observed disruption of the clockwise young stellar disc in the Galactic Center, and numerical simulations confirm that it reproduces the observed distribution of the stars' angular momenta. More broadly, we hypothesize that the rotation of nuclear star clusters stabilizes the orientation of transient massive accretion discs around central supermassive black holes, thereby influencing both the direction and magnitude of the black holes' spins.

We define graded Lie-Rinehart algebras as a natural extension of graded Lie algebras. For an abelian group $G$, we demonstrate that if $L$ is a tight $G$-graded Lie-Rinehart algebra over an associative and commutative $G$-graded algebra $A$, then both $L$ and $A$ split into orthogonal direct sums: $L = \bigoplus_{i \in I}I_i$ and $A = \bigoplus_{j \in J}A_j$. In this decomposition, each $I_i$ represents a non-zero ideal of $L$ and each $A_j$ a non-zero ideal of $A$, with the property that for every $i \in I$, there exists a unique $j \in J$ such that $A_jI_i \neq 0$. Moreover, each $I_i$ constitutes a graded Lie-Rinehart algebra over $A_j$. Additionally, under mild assumptions, we establish that these decompositions of $L$ and $A$ are determined by their respective families of gr-simple ideals.

Addressing the dynamic characteristics of traffic, we examine a robust network design variant where link capacities must be reserved to ensure routability for any demand vector within a polyhedral set. The goals are to either minimize congestion or a linear cost, assuming fractional and dynamic routing dependent on the current traffic state. We first demonstrate that the minimum congestion version of this problem cannot be approximated within any constant factor. Furthermore, leveraging the ETH conjecture, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(\frac{\log n}{\log \log n})$ for its approximability, indicating that Räcke's 2008 $O(\log n)$ approximation ratio is tight. By employing Lagrange relaxation, we provide a novel proof of this $O(\log n)$ approximation. A significant implication of our Lagrange-based reduction and inapproximability findings is that the linear cost version of robust network design also resists constant-factor approximation, resolving a longstanding open question posed by Chekuri in 2007. Additionally, we offer an alternative proof of Goyal et al.'s (2009) result, which shows that the optimal cost under static routing can exceed the dynamic routing cost by a factor of $\Omega(\log n)$. Finally, we establish that even when restricted to only two paths per commodity, both the minimum congestion and linear cost versions of the robust network design problem remain hard to approximate within any constant factor.

Meta-learning has recently attracted significant interest within the fields of artificial intelligence and machine learning. This paper presents and analyzes an adaptive submodular meta-learning framework. The problem input consists of a collection of items, each possessing an initially unknown random state that can only be revealed by selecting the item. The goal is to adaptively choose a subset of items that maximizes performance across a variety of tasks, where each task is defined as an adaptive submodular function mapping item sets and their states to a real value. To balance computational efficiency with the need for personalized solutions for future tasks, our approach first identifies an initial solution set derived from previously observed tasks. Subsequently, when a new task emerges, the remaining items are adaptively added to this initial set. Unlike methods that compute a fresh solution for every new task, our meta-learning strategy reduces test-time computational costs because the initial set is pre-computed during training. To address this problem, we propose a two-phase greedy policy that guarantees a $1/2$ approximation ratio for monotone cases. For non-monotone scenarios, we introduce a two-phase randomized greedy policy that achieves a $1/32$ approximation ratio.

We introduce a fundamental method for constructing finite-mass Dirac monopoles within $U(1)$ gauge theories featuring a single scalar field with non-minimal interactions. Unlike typical monopoles where energy density clusters at the core, our solutions in the BPS limit demonstrate that this energy is instead distributed across a spherical shell. Our framework can be understood as a limit involving infinitely massive $W$ bosons interacting with the electromagnetic field through a dipole moment. By integrating our approach with concepts from Weinberg and Lee, we map out a broad spectrum of $U(1)$ gauge models capable of supporting finite-mass Dirac monopoles. Notably, established classical monopoles, including Wu-Yang, 't Hooft-Polyakov, and Cho-Maison configurations, appear as specific instances within this general landscape.

For the first time, event-by-event correlations among three flow amplitudes in Pb--Pb collisions have been quantified using higher-order Symmetric Cumulants. Our findings reveal that three-harmonic correlations evolve distinctly during the medium's collective dynamics compared to those present in the initial state. These results extend beyond the scope of prior lower-order flow measurements, as the new observables explicitly eliminate contributions from two-harmonic correlations. Furthermore, comparisons with Monte Carlo simulations yield novel, independent constraints on the initial conditions and properties of the nuclear matter generated in heavy-ion collisions.

We present findings that precisely measure the impact of data augmentation on convergence rates and estimation variance. These results yield surprising insights: contrary to prevailing intuition, data augmentation can sometimes increase, rather than decrease, the uncertainty of estimates, such as empirical prediction risk. Our primary theoretical instrument is a limit theorem concerning functions of randomly transformed, high-dimensional random vectors, with the proof leveraging research on the noise stability of functions involving many variables. The anomalous behavior we uncover does not stem from model complexity but can arise even in the most basic scenarios; for instance, we demonstrate this with a ridge regressor featuring only two parameters. Conversely, our analysis also confirms that data augmentation can deliver tangible, quantifiable advantages.

We introduce a scalable and resilient framework for quantum computing using two-dimensional qubit arrays with fixed longitudinal coupling. This method eliminates the need for tunable couplers, thereby reducing the hardware complexity typical of conventional quantum systems. Our strategy involves driving specific qubit subarrays so that the global multi-qubit Hamiltonian decomposes into a sum of commuting few-qubit blocks, followed by efficient optimization of unitary evolution within these blocks. Each driving pulse applies the desired gate to the targeted qubits while simultaneously applying identity operations to neighboring undriven qubits, effectively neutralizing unwanted evolution caused by constant qubit-qubit interactions. We demonstrate that a universal set of high-fidelity quantum gates can be implemented on these basis blocks; by shifting the driving pattern, arbitrary quantum circuits can be executed across the array. Accounting for imperfect Hamiltonian characterization, we employ robust optimal control to achieve fidelities near 99.99% despite 1% uncertainties in qubit-qubit and drive-qubit couplings, as well as a detuning uncertainty of 0.1% relative to the qubit-qubit coupling strength. This robustness is essential for scaling up, given that parameter uncertainties become significant in large-scale devices.

Human life is increasingly conducted within cyberspace, where the concept of privacy adapts to various online activities. This article examines three specific domains: securing information retrieval, ensuring privacy in large-scale distributed or parallel processing, and training machine learning models on decentralized user data (federated learning). For each area, the text outlines the underlying motivation, defines the problem, reviews historical breakthroughs, and highlights recent advancements and key concepts. Additionally, it explores shared techniques and interconnections among these fields, concluding with a discussion of open challenges and unresolved problems.

Driven by the rapid expansion of ubiquitous technologies, new pervasive approaches are emerging to introduce innovative features and advance research in human-computer interaction. This paper introduces a hand gesture recognition system that leverages a smartphone's integrated speakers and microphones. The proposed method emits an inaudible ultrasonic sonar signal through the device's stereo speakers, which is subsequently captured by the microphone and analyzed using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to identify gestures. To enhance detection accuracy, the study proposes data augmentation techniques and evaluates three dual-channel input fusion strategies: the first merges dual-channel audio into a single spectrogram image; the second employs early fusion by concatenating the spectrograms; and the third utilizes late fusion, where two convolutional branches process each channel independently before merging outputs at the final layers. Experimental results on a publicly available dataset containing six gestures demonstrate promising performance, achieving a baseline accuracy of 93.58%.

We have theoretically realized several hyperparallel optical components, such as a quantum single-photon transistor, router, and dynamic random access memory (DRAM). Our design accounts for unavoidable side leakage and the imperfect birefringence inherent in quantum dot (QD)-cavity mediators, enabling these optical elements to achieve unity fidelities. These hyperparallel architectures leverage both the polarization and spatial degrees of freedom of photons to enhance parallel processing efficiency, expand channel capacity, conserve quantum resources, shorten operation times, and mitigate environmental noise. Furthermore, the proposed practical schemes demonstrate robustness against side leakage and constraints on coupling strength within microcavities.

We build a first-order local model for Poisson manifolds near a broad category of Poisson submanifolds and specify the conditions required for this model to serve as a local normal form. This linearization theorem encompasses all established linearization theorems regarding fixed points and symplectic leaves as specific instances. Furthermore, the symplectic groupoid adaptation of these findings provides a resolution to the groupoid coisotropic embedding problem.

Several methods have been suggested to address the black hole information paradox, with a recent proposal utilizing a pseudo-density operator. While this approach has effectively resolved the issue for a single black hole using a two-qubit entangled system, this paper extends the investigation to a binary black hole system by employing a three-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state. Our findings demonstrate excellent alignment with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we examined the interaction between the two black holes by analyzing the correlations among the qubits within the binary system, with results showing complete consistency with the proposed model. Beyond verification, we suggest integrating modern gravitational wave detection into our optical setup as an input source. This strategy bridges the gap between observational gravitational wave resources and the study of black hole properties through the lenses of quantum information and entanglement.

This paper examines the infinite-depth limit of finite-width residual neural networks featuring random Gaussian weights. Under appropriate scaling, we demonstrate that as depth approaches infinity while width remains fixed, pre-activations converge in distribution to a zero-drift diffusion process. In contrast to the infinite-width limit, where pre-activations weakly converge to a Gaussian random variable, our findings indicate that the infinite-depth limit produces distinct distributions contingent on the specific activation function employed. We present two instances where these distributions admit closed-form expressions. Additionally, we identify a notable regime shift in post-activation norms as width transitions from 3 to 4. Finally, we analyze the sequential limit of infinite depth followed by infinite width and contrast it with the more conventional infinite-width-then-infinite-depth approach.

While graph embedding-based domain adaptation (DA) methods utilizing Laplace graphs effectively preserve data manifolds, they face two critical limitations. First, they focus solely on maintaining underlying data structures in the embedding, neglecting sub-domain adaptation which necessitates considering intra-class similarity and inter-class dissimilarity; this oversight can result in negative transfer. Second, existing approaches apply manifold learning separately across distinct feature and label spaces, preventing a unified and comprehensive learning process. To address these challenges, this paper builds upon our prior DGA-DA work to introduce Attention Regularized Laplace Graph-based Domain Adaptation (ARG-DA). Specifically, we develop an Attention Regularized Laplace Graph for class-aware DA by weighting the significance of various sub-domain adaptation tasks. Additionally, employing a custom-designed FEEL strategy, our method dynamically aligns manifold structures across different feature and label spaces, achieving comprehensive manifold learning. Extensive experiments confirm the efficacy of ARG-DA, which consistently surpasses state-of-the-art DA techniques across 7 standard benchmarks comprising 37 cross-domain image classification tasks involving objects, faces, and digits. Furthermore, the paper provides a detailed analysis of the proposed method, examining its sensitivity, convergence, and robustness.

Molecules are widely distributed in interstellar space and can be identified through spectroscopic observations. Currently, over 271 molecular species have been discovered within the interstellar medium or circumstellar envelopes. Laboratory-measured spectroscopic parameters enable the identification of new species and the derivation of physical properties. These parameters are systematically organized into databases, with the CDMS and JPL databases being the two most prevalent. Although new parameters are continually measured or calculated and added to these repositories, the existing spectroscopic data at any given moment ultimately restricts the identification of molecules in astronomical observations. This study performs a meta-analysis of the CDMS and JPL databases, presenting statistics on transition frequencies and their uncertainties while discussing the issue of line confusion in specific physical environments. Furthermore, we evaluate the potential for detecting molecules in typical interstellar medium environments using upcoming facilities. The findings indicate that CSST/HSTDM and SKA1-mid possess the capability to detect certain complex organic molecules, or even amino acids, provided reasonable assumptions regarding interstellar conditions.

While Virtual Personal Assistants like Siri hold significant promise, their development faces the core challenge of enabling computational devices to truly comprehend human speech. Natural language understanding remains one of AI's most underwhelming failures, suggesting that computer scientists may fundamentally misunderstand the nature of language. However, philosophers and linguists view language differently, and this paper details how we have integrated concepts from these other fields into our implementation. Our approach is grounded in the concept of language as action, utilizing Conversation Analysis to observe how people actually employ language. We observe that human communication involves not only the explicit exchange of information but also the implicit management of social relations. While recognizing this dynamic is one matter, implementing it requires a specific mechanism. This mechanism relies on the principles that language is intentional—we think, speak about, and recognize intentions in others—and cooperative, as we are driven to assist one another. This inherent compulsion offers a solution to the persistent issue of maintaining topic relevance. This methodology has recently yielded success by significantly enhancing user satisfaction, regardless of task completion rates. Furthermore, we propose Talk Markup Language (TalkML), a draft alternative to VoiceXML that streamlines interaction scripting by establishing default behaviors for scenarios involving no input or unrecognised speech.

The Cyber-Physical-Social System (CPSS) is an emerging paradigm born from the necessity to comprehend the reciprocal influence between Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) and human beings. This transition from CPS to CPSS stems primarily from the proliferation of sensor-equipped smart devices and their deep integration with users. Although the CPSS concept has existed for over ten years, it has garnered significant attention recently. Integrating human dimensions into CPS research has revealed numerous challenges, with human dynamics introducing complexities that remain largely unexplored. While some scientific literature has partially addressed the conceptualization of CPSS, it remains largely use-case dependent, resulting in a scarcity of generic frameworks as most studies focus on specific domains. Additionally, the connection between the system's core, its design principles, and systems theory remains tenuous. This study seeks to resolve these gaps by conducting a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) to analyze the full spectrum of CPSS, identifying current perspectives on definitions, fundamental principles, and application areas. Building on these findings, the paper proposes a domain-independent definition and a meta-model for CPSS grounded in Systems Theory. Finally, it outlines feasible future research directions based on this systemic perspective and the proposed meta-models.

The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) is developing modern network management frameworks built upon the NETCONF protocol and the YANG data modeling language. Two prominent open-source projects, netopeer (a NETCONF server) and ncclient (a NETCONF client), currently support the mandatory Secure Shell (SSH) transport for the latest NETCONF v1.1 protocol. We have recently extended both projects by implementing NETCONF over Transport Layer Security (TLS) and integrating NETCONF Call Home (CH) mechanisms using reverse TLS and SSH. The CH mechanism enables a NETCONF server (netopeer) located behind a Network Address Translation (NAT) device to establish a successful NETCONF session with a Network Management System (NMS) acting as a NETCONF client (ncclient). This article details how these standards facilitate the management of home routers and NAT boxes using these recent enhancements to the NETCONF protocol.

Using first-principles kinetic simulations, we demonstrate that a large-scale Alfvén wave (AW) traveling through an inhomogeneous medium decays into kinetic Alfvén waves (KAWs), which subsequently energize both ions and electrons. Our results show that these two species can absorb unequal portions of the initial AW energy, leading to differential heating. Furthermore, the electric fields associated with the KAWs generate non-Maxwellian characteristics in the particle velocity distribution functions (VDFs), consistent with observations from space. This mechanism relies exclusively on the interaction between a large-scale AW and magnetic shear, suggesting its relevance to various laboratory and astrophysical plasmas.

As crowd-sourced news curation becomes standard, it is crucial to examine not only how individuals consume information on social news platforms but also how they influence ranking mechanisms. This study introduces and provides a novel dataset comprising one year of activity logs from 309 Reddit users. Leveraging this data, we present findings that illuminate the browsing and voting patterns of participants. Our results indicate that the majority of users do not read the articles they vote on; specifically, 73% of posts received ratings (upvotes or downvotes) without prior content viewing. Additionally, we provide evidence of cognitive fatigue within the browsing sessions of users who are most prone to voting.

We address the challenge of best subset selection in linear regression, aiming to identify the optimal set of $k$ features for each model size. This task becomes especially difficult when the number of available features vastly exceeds the number of data samples. We introduce COMBSS, a new continuous optimization approach that generates a solution path comprising a compact set of models with varying sizes, serving as candidates for the best subset. COMBSS demonstrates high computational speed, enabling subset selection even when features number in the thousands. Simulation results compare COMBSS against established methods like Forward Stepwise, Lasso, and Mixed-Integer Optimization. Given its superior performance, formulating best subset selection as a continuous optimization problem suggests promising new research avenues for feature extraction across diverse regression models.

We propose a novel set of lattice models utilizing hexagonal $\sqrt{N}\times\sqrt{N}$ super-cells of the honeycomb lattice with a single-hole defect (HL-D-1/2N) to achieve nontrivial isolated flat-bands. By conducting both tight-binding and density functional theory calculations, we identify experimentally realized graphitic carbon nitride (specifically HL-D-1/8 based C$_4$N$_3$) as an ideal host for these flat bands. While the high-energy ferromagnetic P-6m2 C$_4$N$_3$ phase exhibits half-metallicity unrelated to the flat bands, it is dynamically unstable. Employing a structure search method grounded in group and graph theory, we discovered a new corrugated Pca21 C$_4$N$_3$ structure with the lowest energy among all known variants. This Pca21 phase is an intrinsic ferromagnetic half-semiconductor (with a Curie temperature $T_c \approx$ 241 K), featuring one semiconducting spin-channel (1.75 eV) and one insulating spin-channel (3.64 eV)—a rare property in 2D systems. The emergence of its ferromagnetic semiconducting nature stems from an isolated $p_z$-state flat band shifted upward to the Fermi level by the corrugation. Furthermore, the Pca21 C$_4$N$_3$ structure exhibits both piezoelectric and ferroelectric characteristics, establishing C$_4$N$_3$ as an unusual transition-metal-free 2D multiferroic.

This study introduces a deep learning framework based on a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) specifically designed for forecasting solar-wind conditions. The model is trained using 193 Å wavelength imagery from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) and solar-wind speed measurements from the Advanced Composition Explorer (ACE) at the L1 Lagrangian point. The custom CNN architecture was developed from the ground up to accommodate four years of historical data. To align the solar-wind observations with the source images, the wind was ballistically traced back to the Sun, assuming constant propagation speed, thereby extracting corresponding coronal intensity data from the AIA frames. For the year 2018, this forecasting approach achieved a root mean square error (RMSE) of 76.3 km/s and an overall correlation coefficient of 0.57 in predicting solar-wind speed, demonstrating significant superiority over benchmark models. Additionally, the model attained a threat score of approximately 0.46 in detecting High-Speed Ejections (HSEs) without generating any false alarms.

The advent of Transformer models has recently revolutionized natural language processing (NLP), with BERT emerging as a pioneering text encoder that leverages solely the attention mechanism—eliminating recurrent components—to achieve state-of-the-art performance across numerous NLP tasks. This paper presents a novel text classifier built upon topological data analysis, utilizing BERT's attention maps converted into attention graphs as its exclusive input. This architecture effectively handles tasks such as spam detection, grammatical correctness verification, and sentiment analysis of movie reviews. The model achieves performance comparable to the BERT baseline and surpasses it in specific areas. Furthermore, we introduce a technique to reduce the number of attention heads processed by the topological classifier, successfully pruning the count from 144 down to as few as ten without compromising performance. Our research also demonstrates that the topological model exhibits superior robustness against adversarial attacks compared to the original BERT, a property that persists even after pruning. To our knowledge, this study represents the first application of topological-based models to adversarial attacks within the NLP domain.

Few-shot learning (FSL) focuses on transferring knowledge from base categories with abundant labeled data to novel categories with limited information, a task of significant theoretical interest and practical value. Despite extensive prior research, most existing FSL methods fail to address the distributional shifts resulting from sample selection bias. This bias creates spurious correlations between semantic causal features—those intrinsically linked to class labels—and non-causal features. Ideally, causal features should remain invariant across distributional changes, be strongly tied to the target classes, and generalize well to new categories, whereas non-causal features lack this stability. To address this, we introduce PatchMix, a novel data augmentation strategy that disrupts these spurious dependencies by replacing patch-level information and supervision in query images with random gallery images from different classes. We theoretically demonstrate that this mechanism uniquely identifies causal features compared to existing approaches. To enhance the discriminability of these features for classification, we further propose Correlation-guided Reconstruction (CGR) and a Hardness-Aware module for distinguishing similar instances and classes. Additionally, our framework is adaptable to unsupervised FSL scenarios.

The Reionization Era Bright Emission Line Survey (REBELS) is a Cycle-7 ALMA Large Program designed to identify and characterize some of the most luminous star-forming galaxies in the universe beyond redshift 6.5. By systematically surveying 40 of the brightest UV-selected galaxies across a 7-square-degree region, REBELS detects bright [CII] and [OIII] emission lines at 158 and 88 microns, respectively, alongside dust-continuum radiation. The selection of these 40 targets combined multiple photometric criteria, each rigorously vetted using three independent sets of photometry and template-fitting software. Expanding on two prior pilot programs, this initiative increases the known population of massive interstellar medium reservoirs at z>6.5 by approximately four to five times, reaching over 30 objects. This manuscript outlines the program's observational strategy and presents initial findings. Analysis of 60.6 hours of ALMA data collected during the program's first year (November 2019 to January 2020) reveals the discovery of 18 highly significant (>7 sigma) [CII] lines; 13 of these also exhibit >3.3 sigma dust-continuum emission. These discoveries more than triple the count of known bright ISM-cooling lines in the z>6.5 universe, bringing ALMA-derived redshifts in this epoch to levels comparable to those from Lyman-alpha surveys. Furthermore, an analysis of search completeness relative to star formation rate (SFR) indicates a ~79% efficiency for detecting [CII] when the SFR (UV+IR) exceeds 28 solar masses per year. These results further underscore ALMA's effectiveness as a "redshift machine," particularly during the epoch of reionization.

The phase transition kinetics of aqueous hydroxypropyl cellulose solutions were investigated through turbidimetric monitoring and mathematical modeling. Phase separation was simulated on a one-dimensional Flory lattice using a nonlinear Cahn-Hilliard equation, where mobility varies with component concentration. For a specific range of interfacial energy parameters, the study tracked changes in average cluster size, mass, and concentration. Simulation results identified three distinct stages of spinodal decomposition: early, intermediate, and final.
