During the intermediate stage, cluster mass growth kinetics align with standard diffusion mass transfer, while the evolution of average cluster size follows a scaling function with an exponent near 1/3, characteristic of systems with a conserved scalar order parameter. Finally, it was demonstrated that the cluster concentration at the final stage is governed by the temperature dependence of the interfacial energy.

Automated Essay Scoring (AES) represents a multidisciplinary intersection of Education, Linguistics, and Natural Language Processing (NLP). The effectiveness of an NLP model in AES depends on its capacity to manage long-term dependencies and infer meaning, even from poorly written text. Although large, pretrained transformer-based models currently lead the state-of-the-art in many NLP applications, their high computational costs hinder practical deployment. This paper aims to challenge the prevailing NLP notion that larger models are superior for AES tasks. We assess various fine-tuned pretrained models with a relatively small parameter count on an AES dataset. Through model ensembling, we demonstrate excellent performance using fewer parameters than most existing pretrained transformer-based approaches.

This paper presents our system submitted for SemEval 2020 Task 9, focusing on Sentiment Analysis for Code-Mixed Social Media Text, alongside other related experiments. Our top-performing approach utilizes a Transfer Learning model that fine-tunes "XLM-RoBERTa," a transformer-based multilingual masked language model, using monolingual English and Spanish datasets as well as Spanish-English code-mixed data. This system surpassed the official task baseline, reaching a 70.1% average F1-Score on the official leaderboard with the test set. For subsequent submissions, we improved this result to a 75.9% average F1-Score on the test set under the CodaLab username "ahmed0sultan."

Adversarial training (AT) for robust representation and self-supervised learning (SSL) for unsupervised representation are both prominent research areas. Combining AT with SSL has enabled significant yet difficult progress in learning robust representations without labels. A common approach, adversarial contrastive learning, couples these methods, creating a complex optimization challenge. Inspired by a divide-and-conquer strategy, we hypothesize that the task can be simplified and enhanced by addressing two sub-problems separately: non-robust SSL and pseudo-supervised AT. This shift moves the focus from optimizing a coupled system to solving individual sub-problems. Consequently, this work abandons direct integration methods and introduces a two-stage framework called Decoupled Adversarial Contrastive Learning (DeACL). Extensive experiments show that DeACL achieves state-of-the-art adversarial robustness in self-supervised settings while substantially cutting training time, confirming its effectiveness and efficiency. Additionally, DeACL offers a more interpretable solution and helps bridge the gap between semi-supervised AT and the exploitation of unlabeled data for robust learning. The code is available at https://github.com/pantheon5100/DeACL.

Deep learning has demonstrated significant success in image classification and offers substantial potential for the rapid and dependable categorization of pollen grain aerial imagery. Nevertheless, when applied to natural images, these methods frequently encounter generalization challenges, resulting in suboptimal performance on unseen test distributions. This study introduces a robust deep learning framework designed to effectively generalize for pollen grain aerobiological imagery classification. We propose a convolutional neural network (CNN) approach that integrates established best practices to enhance generalization capabilities. Beyond standard techniques such as data augmentation and weight regularization, we employ implicit regularization strategies like manifold mixup to facilitate the learning of smoother decision boundaries. Furthermore, we leverage proven state-of-the-art architectures, specifically EfficientNet CNNs. Drawing inspiration from generative modeling using variational autoencoders, we train models with an enriched learning objective that enables the network to concentrate on relevant image regions. Additionally, we construct an ensemble of neural networks to ensure robustness in test set predictions. Experimental results indicate improved generalization performance, measured by a weighted F1-score, achieved through these combined approaches. The proposed method secured fourth place in the final rankings of the ICPR-2020 Pollen Grain Classification Challenge, attaining a weighted F1 score of 0.972578, a macro average F1 score of 0.950828, and a recognition accuracy of 0.972877.

For a Fell bundle $\mathcal{B}=\left\{B_{s}\right\}_{s \in G}$ over a discrete group $G$, we employ representation theory to define the Fourier and Fourier-Stieltjes spaces $A(\mathcal{B})$ and $B(\mathcal{B})$ of $\mathcal{B}$. We demonstrate that if $\mathcal{B}$ is saturated, then $B(\mathcal{B})$ is canonically isomorphic to the dual of the cross-sectional $C^*$-algebra $C^{*}(\mathcal{B})$. Furthermore, when the fibers admit a compatible family of co-multiplications, both $B(\mathcal{B})$ and $A(\mathcal{B})$ become Banach algebras. This condition is satisfied, for instance, when the identity fiber $B_e$ is a Hopf $C^*$-algebra or when $\mathcal{B}$ arises from a $C^*$-dynamical system. We establish that if $A(\mathcal{B})$ is a Banach algebra possessing a bounded approximate identity, then $B(\mathcal{B})$ serves as the multiplier algebra of $A(\mathcal{B})$. Additionally, we prove a Leptin-type theorem by showing that the amenability of $G$ guarantees a bounded approximate identity for $A(\mathcal{B})$ in bundles derived from a $C^*$-dynamical system $(A,G,\gamma)$, while the converse remains an open question.

Contrastive learning currently dominates the training of dense retrieval models, yet this work explores the frequently neglected influence of ranking context. Specifically, we analyze its key components: scoring numerous negatives simultaneously for each query, employing retrieved (query-specific) negatives rather than random ones, and utilizing a fully list-wise loss function. To integrate these elements, we propose Contextual Document Embedding Reranking (CODER), a highly efficient framework. During the reranking phase, CODER adds minimal computational cost to an initial retrieval stage (operating within milliseconds per query), making it compatible with any leading dual-encoder method. Following a lightweight fine-tuning process via CODER, the models function effectively as standalone retrievers. Extensive experiments on the MS MARCO and TripClick datasets demonstrate that contextual reranking of precomputed embeddings significantly boosts retrieval performance. This gain is particularly notable when greater relevance data is available per query; notably, on the TripClick collection, our approach establishes new state-of-the-art results by a substantial margin.

This paper derives explicit relationships connecting power losses caused by mode mismatches in Hermite-Gauss optical modes to those affecting the fundamental spatial mode. Results indicate that higher-order modes exhibit greater sensitivity to beam parameter discrepancies. This finding holds particular significance for gravitational-wave detectors, where proposals utilize higher-order optical modes in lasers to reduce thermal noise, yet quantum-enhanced systems remain highly vulnerable to such losses. Consequently, this study should guide the establishment of mode matching and squeezing specifications for both Advanced+ and Third Generation detectors.

A central promise of machine learning is aiding users with personal tasks; however, since the context needed for accurate predictions is often sensitive, privacy-protecting systems are essential. Ideally, a privacy-preserving system achieves perfect secrecy, ensuring that interactions reveal no additional private information to adversaries, even when multiple tasks are performed on the same data. Currently, privacy and quality appear to be in conflict in existing personal task systems. Neural models typically demand extensive training to perform well, yet individual users possess limited data, leading systems to learn from aggregated data across multiple users. This approach violates perfect secrecy; consequently, recent academic work has relied on statistical privacy notions, asserting that the probability of inferring private information about a user must remain low. Given the vulnerabilities of these statistical methods, we investigate whether strong perfect secrecy can be attained using recent zero-to-few sample adaptation techniques facilitated by foundation models. In response, we introduce FOCUS, a framework designed for personal tasks. Evaluation on standard privacy benchmarks reveals that our approach, which satisfies perfect secrecy, competes effectively with strong collaborative learning baselines on six out of seven tasks. Furthermore, we empirically analyze the proposal, highlighting its opportunities and limitations across various task types, model inductive biases, and sizes.

This paper introduces a strategy to address inefficient clustering performance by incorporating data augmentation as a supplementary plug-in. While classical methods like K-means, Gaussian mixture models, and spectral clustering remain fundamental to data-driven tasks, Deep Embedded Clustering (DEC)—which utilizes neural networks for simultaneous unsupervised feature learning and clustering—has recently gained significant traction. Existing deep clustering research primarily focuses on designing appropriate loss functions and selecting suitable neural architectures for feature extraction. However, a persistent challenge across these approaches is data sparsity, characterized by high intra-class and low inter-class variance, which often results in suboptimal clustering and incorrect cluster assignments. To overcome this, we apply data augmentation to enhance cluster density and boost overall performance. Specifically, we train a variant of the Convolutional Autoencoder (CAE) using augmented data to build an initial feature space, creating a novel model for deep clustering. Our proposed strategy is evaluated on a crowdsourced Indian Heritage dataset, where extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over current state-of-the-art methods.

Random Forests (RFs) represent one of the most prevalent machine learning classifiers. Despite their lack of interpretability, no dedicated non-heuristic methods currently exist for generating RF explanations. Given recent advancements in polynomial-time algorithms for explaining models like naive Bayes, a key inquiry arises: can RF explanations be computed in polynomial time? This paper provides a negative answer by establishing that finding a single PI-explanation for an RF is D^P-complete. Additionally, the authors introduce a propositional encoding for RF explanations, allowing them to be solved using SAT solvers. This differs from prior research on boosted trees and neural networks, which relies on SMT or MILP encodings. Experimental evaluations across various public datasets indicate that the proposed SAT-based method effectively scales to RF sizes typical in real-world applications. More significantly, the results show that for most test cases, this SAT-based approach substantially outperforms existing heuristic techniques.

We present a novel framework for single-channel target source separation that distinguishes sources of interest using non-mutually exclusive attributes such as loudness, gender, language, and spatial location. This proposed heterogeneous separation framework effectively utilizes datasets with significant distribution shifts to learn cross-domain representations across various conditioning concepts. Experimental results demonstrate that training separation models with heterogeneous conditions enhances generalization to new concepts using unseen out-of-domain data and significantly outperforms single-domain specialist models. Specifically, this approach facilitates more robust learning of challenging discriminative concepts and can surpass permutation invariant training even with oracle source selection. Furthermore, we examine the inherent behavior of source separation training with heterogeneous metadata and suggest strategies to mitigate issues arising from difficult separation conditions. Finally, we provide a comprehensive collection of preparation recipes for all utilized datasets to advance research in this demanding area.

Standard quasi-steady state approximations for reducing fast-slow chemical reaction networks fail when the fast subsystem possesses first integrals, which we term approximate conservation laws. Leveraging concepts from tropical geometry, we define these fast subsystems and identify such laws. We demonstrate that any approximate conservation law evolves more slowly than the species it encompasses, effectively acting as a supplementary slow variable within an extended system. By eliminating specific variables from this extended system, we derive networks devoid of approximate conservation laws, rendering them amenable to standard singular perturbation reduction techniques. This framework, applicable to the quasi-equilibrium approximation common in biochemistry, addresses both two-timescale reductions of fast-slow systems and multiple-timescale reductions of multiscale networks. Multiscale networks exhibit hierarchical relaxation; consequently, our multiple-timescale reduction method at any given scale partitions the system into three subsystems: (i) fast slaved variables governed by algebraic equations, (ii) slow driving variables described by reduced ordinary differential equations, and (iii) much slower quenched variables that remain constant. The algebraic constraints on the fast variables correspond to chains of nested, normally hyperbolic invariant manifolds, where faster manifolds possess higher dimensions and encompass the slower ones. We present these reduction methods algorithmically for networks featuring linear, monomial, or polynomial approximate conservation laws.

Keywords: Model order reduction, chemical reaction networks, singular perturbations, multiple timescales, tropical geometry.

Optical trapping of magnetic iron-oxide particles is notoriously challenging due to their high refractive indices and significant absorption at infrared trapping wavelengths. To address this, we synthesized ferromagnetic upconversion particles based on Fe co-doped NaYF4:Yb,Er. These particles feature refractive indices suitable for optical trapping and exhibit lower heat generation than hematite particles at off-resonant wavelengths. With hexagonal shapes measuring approximately 3 micrometers, they possess a high coercivity of 20 mT and a saturation magnetization of 1 Am²/kg. These properties enable the simultaneous application of optical and magnetic forces for micro-manipulation across all six degrees of freedom of a rigid body. Furthermore, when illuminated at the 975 nm absorption resonance, these particles generate significant heat while emitting visible light, suggesting potential applications in fluorescence microscopy and the photothermal therapy of cancer cells.

We demonstrate that, subject to specific orientation requirements relative to $R$, a Hamiltonian isotopy $\psi^1$ on a symplectic manifold $(M, \omega)$ which preserves a relatively exact Lagrangian $L$ as a set acts trivially on $R_*(L)$, where $R_*$ denotes a generalized homology theory. Our methodology draws inspiration from the work of Hu, Lalonde, and Leclercq (\cite{Hu-Lalonde-Leclercq}), who established a comparable result over $\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\mathbb{Z}$ under more restrictive orientation hypotheses. Nevertheless, our distinct approach allows us to conclude that if $L$ is a homotopy sphere, the restriction $\psi^1|_L$ is homotopic to the identity map. Our technical framework diverges from both theirs and that of Cohen, Jones, and Segal (\cite{Cohen-Jones-Segal, Cohen}).

Furthermore, under analogous conditions, we prove that $\psi^1|_L$ acts trivially on $R_*(\mathcal{L} L)$, where $\mathcal{L} L$ represents the free loop space of $L$. This finding implies that when $L$ is a surface or a $K(\pi, 1)$ space, $\psi^1|_L$ is homotopic to the identity. Additionally, employing techniques from \cite{Lalonde-McDuff}, we establish that for any family of Lagrangians Hamiltonian isotopic to $L$ over a sphere or torus, the corresponding fibre bundle cohomologically splits over $\mathbb{Z}/2$.

Although prior research demonstrates that machine learning (ML) can enhance the predictive accuracy of coarse-grid climate models, these ML-enhanced approaches are more susceptible to irregular inputs compared to traditional physics-based models. Since ML-generated corrections feed back into the model's underlying physics, the resulting ML-corrected simulations frequently generate out-of-sample data, leading to instability and frequent crashes. This study demonstrates that integrating semi-supervised novelty detection to identify such out-of-sample data and subsequently disabling the ML correction stabilizes simulations and significantly boosts prediction quality. We developed an augmented climate model incorporating a one-class support vector machine (OCSVM) novelty detector, which delivered superior temperature and precipitation forecasts over a year-long simulation compared to both a baseline (no-ML) and a standard ML-corrected run. By improving the accuracy of coarse-grid climate models, this work facilitates access to reliable climate modeling for researchers lacking massive computational resources.

We resolve the equivariant generalized Nash problem for all non-rational normal varieties admitting a torus action of complexity one. Specifically, we provide an explicit combinatorial characterization of the Nash order defined on the set of equivariant divisorial valuations for any such variety. Leveraging this description, we affirmatively address the classical Nash problem within this context, demonstrating that every essential valuation is indeed a Nash valuation. Furthermore, we characterize terminal valuations and apply our findings to refute a question posed by de Fernex and Docampo. By constructing examples of Nash valuations that are neither minimal nor terminal, we highlight a remarkable new property of the singularity class under study.

Accurate prediction of wildfire expansion is essential for effective land management and disaster preparedness. Addressing this need, we introduce "Next Day Wildfire Spread," a comprehensive, large-scale, multivariate dataset encompassing nearly ten years of remote-sensing records for historical wildfires across the United States. Unlike previous datasets relying solely on Earth observation satellites, our collection integrates two-dimensional fire data with various explanatory factors—such as topography, vegetation, weather conditions, drought indices, and population density—spatially aligned over 2D regions, creating a resource-rich environment for machine learning. To illustrate the dataset's utility, we developed a neural network leveraging its spatial attributes to forecast wildfire spread. We evaluated this model against other machine learning approaches, specifically logistic regression and random forest. This dataset serves as a benchmark for advancing wildfire propagation models based on remote sensing data with a one-day lead time.

Metric trees and metric tree arrangements serve as indexing structures for cones within the polyhedral fan of Dressians Dr(2, n) and Dr(3, n), respectively. This study examines cone adjacency in Dr(3, n) by introducing general Whitehead moves, which establish conditions for such adjacency based on the corresponding metric tree arrangements. Building on these findings, we define generalized metric tree arrangements that parameterize points in Dr(k, n), thereby extending established results to this broader context.

This paper presents a non-parametric memory framework for spatio-temporal segmentation that encapsulates the immediate spatial and temporal context of an autonomous vehicle (AV). The proposed representation is characterized by three core capabilities: (i) retaining historical observations, (ii) strengthening prior beliefs, and (iii) discarding outdated information based on incoming data. Strengthening beliefs is crucial for handling initial uncertainty, particularly when objects are heavily occluded or distant. Conversely, the ability to forget is essential to prevent erratic vehicle behavior caused by false positives. Our approach leverages 3D reasoning, which is vital for distinguishing between instances where an element should be remembered versus forgotten, especially regarding occlusion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this method serves as an online module that augments static world models, such as HD maps, by identifying and persisting dynamic changes that should be overlaid onto the static representation.

This study proposes a hybrid architecture combining a superconductivity-proximitized quantum spin Hall (QSH) insulator with a quantum anomalous Hall (QAH) insulator to facilitate the chiral injection of electrons into Majorana bound states (MBS). Furthermore, an unexplored phase space region is identified, leveraging an exchange-field-induced enhancement of the helical edge state for MBS detection. Two-dimensional transport simulations compare this proposed configuration against a setup lacking the QAH region, incorporating moderate disorder, a small finite bulk out-of-plane magnetic field, and a Rashba field. The striking contrast observed between the two scenarios highlights the potential for unprecedented resilience against disorder-induced masking of MBS signals in the proposed hybrid system.

Current automatic story evaluation techniques prioritize lexical coherence, which often diverges from human preferences. To address this, we propose **StoryER**, a novel **Story** **E**valuation framework designed to align with human judgment. This method comprises three sub-tasks: **R**anking, **R**ating, and **R**easoning. When presented with either machine-generated or human-written narratives, StoryER requires the system to produce: 1) a preference score reflecting human inclination, 2) specific ratings along with associated confidence levels, and 3) detailed comments on various story dimensions (e.g., introduction, character development). To facilitate these tasks, we have curated a well-annotated dataset containing (i) 100,000 ranked story pairs and (ii) 46,000 ratings and comments covering multiple story aspects. We fine-tuned the Longformer-Encoder-Decoder (LED) model on this dataset, assigning the encoder to predict preference scores and aspect ratings while the decoder generates comments. Extensive experiments establish a competitive benchmark for each task, demonstrating a strong correlation with human preferences. Furthermore, we observed that jointly learning preference scores, aspect ratings, and comments yields performance gains across all individual tasks. Our dataset and benchmarks are publicly released to advance research in story evaluation. \footnote{Dataset and pre-trained model demo are available at anonymous website \url{http://storytelling-lab.com/eval} and \url{https://github.com/sairin1202/StoryER}}

We apply the methodology from Moughal's doctoral thesis to examine the joint spike transition, uncovering new categories of worldlines that experience unique transitions and rectifying existing misunderstandings regarding spikes.

This work addresses the optimization of the minimum (weighted) component value of a vector within a polymatroid, which represents a specific instance of the lexicographically optimal base problem originally defined and resolved by Fujishige. We propose an alternative framework modeling this issue as a zero-sum game: a maximizing player with a mixed strategy set corresponding to the polymatroid's base faces off against a minimizing player with a mixed strategy set defined by a simplex. We demonstrate that this game, along with three related variations, unifies various problems in search, sequential testing, and queuing theory. Additionally, we provide a concise derivation of optimal strategies for both participants and an expression for the game's value. Finally, we characterize the set of optimal strategies for the minimizing player and examine specific scenarios where these strategies can be determined with particular ease.
We categorize maximal digraphs with a Hermitian spectral radius no greater than $2$.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have significantly expanded the capabilities of automatic computer vision, allowing users to directly query the content within images and videos. This paper investigates the foundational steps required for a future Visual Data Management System (VDMS) capable of storing, managing, indexing, and querying predictions generated by these deep learning models. We introduce a query and data model that separates the neural network architectures, query workloads, and data source semantics from the query processing layer. Our proposed system, DeepLens, utilizes dataflow query processing, and this research prototype provides initial experiments that highlight critical open research questions in visual analytics. A primary conclusion is that any future "declarative" VDMS must re-examine query optimization and automated physical design through a unified lens that balances performance and accuracy. Choices regarding physical design and query optimization can drastically alter system performance by orders of magnitude and may even impact the accuracy of the results.

Building upon our earlier study [2109.01110], we will calculate a novel $G_2$ instanton partition function. This effort completes the essential components required for the instanton partition function linked to a broad range of $G_2$ manifolds.

Integrating statistical (data-driven) and symbolic (knowledge-driven) approaches is broadly acknowledged as a primary challenge in contemporary artificial intelligence. While recent years have generated numerous publications on hybrid neuro-symbolic systems, the existing literature remains highly diverse, largely empirical, and lacks a cohesive framework to unify this wide array of systems. This paper analyzes a substantial corpus of recent work to propose a collection of modular design patterns for such hybrid architectures. By combining only a small set of elementary patterns as foundational blocks, we can characterize the architecture of a vast number of hybrid systems. The paper's principal contributions are: 1) a taxonomically structured vocabulary for describing both processes and data structures within hybrid systems; 2) a suite of over 15 design patterns, categorized into elementary and compositional types; and 3) the application of these patterns to two realistic use cases. These patterns uncover previously unrecognized similarities between systems and extend and refine Kautz's earlier categorization of neuro-symbolic architectures.

5G New Radio introduces Multi-connectivity (MC) with packet duplication as a reliability boost, where identical data packets are sent from multiple transmitters. However, this approach is resource-intensive because it consumes radio resources from several transmitters to serve a single user, making the balance between performance gains and resource usage a critical design challenge. To address this, the proposed work presents a heuristic, latency-aware, and resource-efficient dynamic MC algorithm that selectively activates MC for critical users, thereby maximizing benefits while minimizing resource consumption. Numerical results demonstrate that this algorithm achieves the same outage performance improvements as traditional MC schemes but utilizes up to 45% fewer resources.

Leveraging over ten years of expertise in academic research, technology creation, industry collaboration, postgraduate education, doctoral mentorship, and organizational consulting, we introduce the 'CDAC AI Life Cycle.' This comprehensive framework guides the design, development, and deployment of AI systems and solutions through three distinct phases: Design, Develop, and Deploy. Spanning from conception to production, these phases encompass 17 specific stages. The 'Design' phase emphasizes contextualizing problem descriptions by examining public literature and service-based resources on advanced AI applications, algorithms, pre-trained models, and, crucially, ethics guidelines and frameworks; this analysis subsequently directs data and Big Data acquisition and preparation. The 'Develop' phase is technique-focused, converting data and algorithms into AI models that undergo benchmarking, evaluation, and explanation. In the 'Deploy' phase, computational performance is assessed to refine pipelines for model operationalization, ultimately achieving the hyperautomation of a process or system as a complete AI solution. This solution is continuously monitored and evaluated to inform future iterations of the life cycle. Additionally, this article contributes an ontological mapping of AI algorithms to applications and establishes an organizational context for the AI life cycle.

This research investigates the cosmological particle production of Dirac fermions within a Friedman-Robertson-Walker spacetime, specifically examining a (1+1)-dimensional scenario where the scale factor's evolution is governed by Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity equations. To advance the quantum simulation of this phenomenon, we analyze two lattice regularization methods that facilitate an exploration of how particle production interacts with topological effects in bounded spacetimes. Notably, employing a Wilson-type discretization for the Dirac field reveals that asymptotic Minkowski vacua linked by intermediate expansion represent symmetry-protected topological ground states, characterized by boundary-localized zero-modes with exponential decay. We demonstrate that particle production can populate these zero modes, a result that stands in contrast to naive-fermion discretizations where conformal, zero-mass fields show no such production. Finally, we outline a framework for simulating this gravitational analogue using ultra-cold atoms in Raman optical lattices, necessitating real-time adjustment of Raman-beam detuning to match the simulated spacetime's scale factor, alongside band-mapping measurements.

This study examines an "up-the-gradient" model describing the creation of auxin transport channels, driven by auxin-mediated polarization of the PIN1 transporter. We demonstrate that this framework supports a family of traveling wave solutions defined by the height of the auxin pulse. Furthermore, we derive scaling laws governing the velocity and width of these waves and confirm these analytical findings through numerical simulations. Additionally, we present explicit formulas for the leading-order wave profiles, facilitating the identification of how biological parameters influence the system. Our proofs rely on extending the scaling principle originally formulated by Friesecke and Pego for constructing pulse solutions in the classic Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou model, which represents a one-dimensional chain of coupled nonlinear springs.

Developing code is challenging, yet demonstrating its correctness is significantly more difficult. As verified software projects expand, the need for efficient verification of large codebases becomes increasingly critical. This challenge is particularly acute in the realm of verified cryptographic libraries. To match the features and competitiveness of unverified alternatives, these libraries must verify a vast array of algorithms and APIs. However, this process is often repetitive, and extracting commonalities between algorithms has historically been difficult, necessitating substantial manual labor.

This paper demonstrates how a strategic blend of established functional programming techniques can achieve a tenfold increase in the volume of verified code within the popular HACL* cryptographic library, all while maintaining performance. We examine three interrelated techniques, presented in order of increasing complexity. First, we employ dependent types to precisely define the specification and state machine of block algorithms, a concept previously described only informally. Second, we utilize partial evaluation to create a higher-order, stateful functor that converts any unsafe block API into a safe version. Finally, we apply elaborator reflection to automate the creation of these functors via a code-rewriting tactic. The result is a programming style reminiscent of C++ templates, yet it relies on user-defined tactics and partial evaluation rather than native compiler support.

This paper adapts Fraenkel's generalization of Wythoff's game to handle non-monotonic scenarios. By doing so, we define a specific class of Wythoff games that encompasses all Beatty sequences. Furthermore, in the appendix, we demonstrate that if a solution set for a known Fraenkel generalized game follows a Beatty pattern, then that game is equivalent to a $t$-Wythoff game.

Utilizing a comprehensive longitudinal dataset spanning five years from a European nation, this study investigates specialization within criminal careers. By clustering crime categories based on their relative frequency of co-occurrence in individual criminal histories, we establish a natural, data-driven taxonomy of specialization. Defining specialists as active offenders who remain confined to a single category of criminal behavior, we analyze their socio-demographic characteristics, geographic scope, and roles within collaboration networks compared to generalists. Relative to generalists, specialists are typically older, more likely to be female, operate within a narrower geographic area, and participate in smaller, more tightly-knit local networks. Furthermore, we observe that specialists are more deeply embedded in criminal networks, providing evidence that specialization reflects a division of labor and organizational structure.

This study introduces a novel coupled generalized three-form dark energy framework, where dark energy is modeled as a three-form field and other components as ideal fluids. A dynamical analysis yields four fixed points: two saddle points corresponding to radiation- and matter-dominated universes, and two attractors representing distinct dark energy-dominated universes. Utilizing observational data from cosmic microwave background (CMB), baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO), and Type Ia supernovae (SN Ia), we constrain the model parameters. Comparative analysis with the coupled three-form, generalized three-form, and $\Lambda$CDM models reveals that only the coupled generalized three-form dark energy model significantly alleviates the $H_0$ tension, yielding $H_0=70.1_{-1.5}^{+1.4}$ km/s/Mpc, consistent with R19 at the $2.0\sigma$ confidence level. Furthermore, an investigation into the best-fit dynamical behavior demonstrates that this model is equivalent to a quintom dark energy scenario, exhibiting early dark energy characteristics with a small positive equation of state in the early universe.

Utilizing the edge states of topological magnon insulators offers a promising avenue for developing stable spintronic devices. Nevertheless, experimentally verifying the topology of magnon bands remains a significant challenge. In this work, we derive a fundamental connection between light-matter coupling and the quantum geometry of magnon states. This relationship enables the use of two-magnon Raman circular dichroism as an optical method to probe magnon topology in honeycomb magnets, specifically targeting the Chern number and topological gap. These findings open new possibilities for integrating light with topological magnons in functional quantum devices.

This study demonstrates that classical nonlinear systems can exhibit quantum-like characteristics, such as memory, when subjected to appropriate external perturbations. We employ the two-dimensional complex Ginzburg-Landau equation in its vortex glass phase as a model system. An external drive is introduced to simulate a quantum measurement protocol, defined by a "measurement rate" (the frequency of drive repetition) and a "mixing rate" (determined by the drive's intensity). Through various analytical measures, we observe that the system's ability to maintain coherence and statistically recover its initial glass state depends on the amplitude and periodicity of the perturbing field. We further discuss the relevant parametric regimes and the energy cascade mechanisms linked to the dynamics of vortex waveforms and domain boundaries.

Measuring moral narratives within user-generated content, news, and public discourse is essential for grasping individual concerns, averting violent protests, and mitigating social polarization. While Moral Foundation Theory (MFT) originally utilized a five-dimensional framework, recent advancements have introduced the Liberty Foundation as a sixth dimension. Due to its recent addition, existing linguistic tools are insufficient for detecting liberty-related themes in text corpora. Given the Liberty Foundation's relevance to pressing societal debates like vaccination, we propose two data-driven methods to generate candidate lexicons from aligned online news documents reflecting divergent worldviews. Following rigorous experimentation, we offer a novel lexicon that evaluates how individuals with opposing perspectives express the liberty moral foundation in written communication. The resulting LibertyMFD dictionary serves as a vital resource for policymakers to comprehend diverse, large-scale viewpoints on contentious issues such as uprisings, abortion, and vaccination in real time.

This study investigates the numerical simulation of periodic solids, known as phononic crystals, using the framework of couple stress elasticity. The inclusion of extra terms in the elastic potential energy induces dispersive behavior in shear waves, even without material periodicity. To analyze bulk wave propagation in these materials, we formulate an action principle in the frequency domain and develop a finite element method for couple stress theory under extended Bloch-periodic boundary conditions. A key distinction from traditional finite element approaches for phononic crystals is the presence of higher-order derivatives, which we address using a Lagrange-multiplier technique. Following the presentation of the variational principle and general finite element treatment, we specialize the method to determine dispersion relations in elastic bodies with periodic material properties. The resulting implementation calculates dispersion curves for both homogeneous and porous couple stress solids, revealing that the porous variants exhibit a notable bandgap structure.

Satellite-based backhaul services doubled in volume between 2012 and 2018, creating growing demand that traditional fixed resource allocation in satellite systems struggles to optimize efficiently. This research evaluates the effectiveness of dynamic resource allocation mechanisms for these satellite backhaul services. The study utilizes OpenSAND to emulate the satellite system, Amarisoft for the LTE network, and OpenBACH to orchestrate experiments. It assesses the benefits of applying TCP PEP mechanisms and dynamic resource allocation across various traffic types by measuring Quality of Experience (QoE) for web browsing, data transfer, and VoIP applications. Key findings indicate that neither PEP nor Layer-2 access mechanisms yield significant improvements under congested conditions. However, in non-congested scenarios, optimizing protocols and channel access mechanisms can substantially enhance data transfer performance. Additionally, tuning Constant Rate Assignment offers a way to reduce resource costs and improve QoE when network load is low.

False positives represent a critical challenge in agnostic domain shift for domain adaptive pedestrian detection. Since labeling every box across vast target domains is unfeasible, our focus shifts to suppressing false positives unsupervised. This paper innovatively frames object detection as a ranking task between positive and negative boxes, elegantly converting false positive suppression into a box re-ranking problem that eliminates the need for manual annotation. A key issue in box re-ranking is the lack of labeled validation data for selecting optimal candidates; to address this while preserving true positive detection, we introduce "box number alignment," a self-supervised metric that prevents model capacity degradation. Extensive experiments on cross-domain pedestrian datasets confirm the framework's effectiveness, and its successful extension to two general unsupervised domain adaptive object detection benchmarks further demonstrates its superiority over state-of-the-art methods.

This study introduces a stacked model designed to forecast cumulative fluid production for oil wells featuring multistage-fracture completions, utilizing a hybrid of Ridge Regression and CatBoost algorithms. Built upon an expanded digital database encompassing reservoir, well, and fracturing design parameters, the dataset currently aggregates data from over 5,000 wells across 23 oilfields in Western Siberia, Russia, totaling 6,687 fracturing operations. Although the initial dataset contained 387 parameters covering construction details, reservoir properties, fracturing designs, and production metrics, the model training process distills these down to 38 key input features. The resulting model generates physically interpretable plots illustrating the relationship between target production and design variables such as the number of stages, proppant mass, and both average and final proppant concentrations alongside fluid rates. Additionally, we established a suite of methods employing Euclidean distance and clustering to identify similar offset wells, aiding field engineers in analyzing historical treatments for comparable wells. These techniques are also leveraged to define optimization parameter boundaries for specific pilot wells during field testing. Furthermore, an inverse problem aimed at selecting optimal fracturing design parameters to maximize output is formulated by optimizing a high-dimensional black-box approximation function subject to constraints, solved via four distinct methods: surrogate-based optimization, sequential least squares programming, particle swarm optimization, and differential evolution. Finally, a comprehensive recommendation system integrating all these methods is created to guide production stimulation engineers toward optimized fracturing designs.

By employing the characterization of spin representations through exterior forms, we present a comprehensive classification of invariant spinors across the nine homogeneous realizations of the sphere $S^n$. For each instance, we establish the dimension of the corresponding spinor space, provide an explicit description, and analyze the associated geometric structures contingent upon the metric. This work recovers established findings within Sasaki and 3-Sasaki contexts while introducing several novel examples; notably, we supply the first known instances of generalized Killing spinors possessing four distinct eigenvalues.

This paper details the luminosity measurement for the ATLAS detector at the LHC during Run 2, utilizing $pp$ collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV. The absolute luminosity scale was established via van der Meer beam separation scans conducted during specific running periods each year, with results extrapolated to the physics data-taking phase using auxiliary data from multiple luminosity-sensitive detectors. Total uncertainties for the integrated luminosities across individual years span from 0.9% to 1.1%, with partial correlations existing between years. Following standard data-quality selections, the complete Run 2 $pp$ dataset amounts to an integrated luminosity of $140.1\pm 1.2$ fb$^{-1}$, representing a 0.83% uncertainty. Additionally, a specialized low-pileup dataset recorded between 2017 and 2018 for high-precision Standard Model analyses was evaluated separately, yielding an integrated luminosity of $338.1\pm 3.1$ pb$^{-1}$.

We examine the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov (KZ) equations over $\mathbb{C}$ specifically when hypergeometric solutions correspond to hyperelliptic integrals of genus $g$, resulting in a $2g$-dimensional complex solution space. Additionally, we analyze these equations modulo $p^s$ (where $p$ is an odd prime and $s$ is a positive integer) and over the $p$-adic field $\mathbb{Q}_p$. We construct polynomial solutions modulo $p^s$ to investigate the solution space $\mathcal{M}_{p^s}$. Our findings demonstrate that the $p$-adic limit of $\mathcal{M}_{p^s}$ as $s \to \infty$ yields a $g$-dimensional solution space over $\mathbb{Q}_p$, consisting of power series within a specific asymptotic region of the KZ equations.

In a joint appendix with Steven Sperber, we explore all asymptotic zones for the case $g=1$, involving elliptic integrals. In this scenario, the $p$-adic limit of $\mathcal{M}_{p^s}$ as $s \to \infty$ produces a one-dimensional solution space over $\mathbb{Q}_p$ at each asymptotic zone. Utilizing Dwork's theory, we prove that these solution germs over $\mathbb{Q}_p$, defined across different asymptotic zones, analytically continue into a single global invariant line subbundle of the associated KZ connection. Notably, while the corresponding KZ connection over $\mathbb{C}$ lacks proper nontrivial invariant subbundles, this invariant line subbundle represents a novel feature specific to the KZ equations over $\mathbb{Q}_p$. For $g=1$, we detail the Frobenius transformations of the solutions and subsequently recover the unit roots of the zeta functions for elliptic curves defined by $y^2 = \beta x(x-1)(x-\alpha)$ over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_p$, where $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times$ and $\alpha \neq 1$.

This research examines solutions to the generalized porous medium equation within the context of infinite graphs. We establish the existence and uniqueness of mild solutions for any graph when the integrable data are either nonnegative or nonpositive. Furthermore, for integrable data that change sign, we demonstrate existence and uniqueness provided additional constraints are met, such as local finiteness or a uniform lower bound on the node measure.

We introduce and analyze a novel automata-theoretic challenge called control improvisation. This problem involves creating an improviser—a probabilistic algorithm that generates words from a given automaton's language—while adhering to two specific constraints: satisfying an admissibility predicate and demonstrating a defined level of randomness. Applications of control improvisation are diverse; for instance, it can generate musical improvisations that meet rhythmic and melodic requirements, where admissibility is measured by a bounded deviation from a reference melody. Our analysis of the problem's complexity identifies scenarios where it can be solved efficiently, as well as instances where it is #P-hard or undecidable. Furthermore, we demonstrate that symbolic methods utilizing Boolean satisfiability (SAT) solvers can provide approximate solutions for certain intractable cases.

Recent discoveries of excited states have often been interpreted as hadronic bound states, prompting the question of whether such hadrons can also exist as resonant states. This study extends the complex scaling method (CSM) to consistently calculate both bound and resonant states within the $\Lambda_c D(\bar D)$ and $\Lambda_c \Lambda_c (\bar \Lambda_c)$ systems. In these systems, meson exchange contributions from $\pi, \eta, \rho$ are negligible, while intermediate- and short-range forces mediated by $\sigma/\omega$ exchange dominate. Our findings reveal that the $\Lambda_c D$ system fails to form either bound or resonant states. Conversely, resonant states are found across a broad parameter range for the $\Lambda_c \bar D$ and $\Lambda_c \Lambda_c (\bar \Lambda_c)$ systems, with higher bound state energies facilitating resonance formation. Among these resonances, P-wave states exhibit lower energies and narrower widths, making them the most stable and experimentally observable. In contrast, D-wave and F-wave resonances possess energies reaching tens of MeV and widths up to hundreds of MeV.

This study reports the first calculation of $\pi-N$ scattering in the iso-spin $I=3/2$ channel at the physical point. Utilizing $N_f=2+1+1$ twisted mass fermions with clover improvement at a physical pion mass, we computed energy levels for both stationary and moving frames, extending up to a total momentum of $|\vec{P}|=\sqrt{3} \,\frac{2\pi}{L}$ across all pertinent irreducible representations of the lattice symmetry groups. Through a phase-shift analysis incorporating $s\,(\ell=0)$ and $p\,(\ell=1)$ waves within a Breit-Wigner framework, we extracted the parameters characterizing the $\Delta$ resonance.

This study addresses the inverse problem of identifying a source term within a structural acoustic PDE model, which consists of a two- or three-dimensional interior acoustic wave equation linked to a Kirchhoff plate equation via a boundary interface. For this system, we establish uniqueness and derive stability estimates for the source term using a single boundary measurement of the "structure." The uniqueness proof relies on Carleman estimates, while the stability result is achieved through an observability inequality combined with a compactness/uniqueness argument. Finally, an operator theoretic approach provides the necessary regularity for the initial conditions to attain the desired stability estimate.

This study applies a symmetry-preserving regularization technique to address ultraviolet divergences within a vector-vector contact interaction model designed for low-energy QCD. In this framework, the contact interaction serves as a representation of the nonperturbative kernels required for Dyson-Schwinger and Bethe-Salpeter equations. The regularization approach relies on a subtraction scheme that bypasses conventional integral evaluation procedures which typically compromise symmetry. Focusing on heavy-light mesons, the method was implemented to analyze the pseudoscalar pion and kaon. We solved the Dyson-Schwinger equation for the propagators of u, d, and s quarks and derived the corresponding bound-state Bethe-Salpeter amplitudes. This process ensures that the Ward-Green-Takahashi identities, which embody the model's global symmetries, remain satisfied regardless of the momentum routing in loop integrals.

This paper details our experience in designing, prototyping, and empirically analyzing Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) based on RF switches. Our RIS architecture consists of patch antenna arrays, delay lines, and programmable radio-frequency switches, which facilitate passive 3D beamforming without requiring active RF components. Utilizing PCB technology and affordable electronic parts, we constructed this design and rigorously validated the prototype in a controlled setting using high spatial resolution codebooks. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive dataset characterizing our RIS and outline the costs involved in replicating the design.

Recent attention has shifted toward addressing Visual Question Answering (VQA) tasks that demand reasoning beyond the visual content itself. This study specifically targets questions requiring commonsense reasoning. Unlike prior approaches that rely on static knowledge bases, we explore the integration of contextualized knowledge via Commonsense Transformer (COMET), a model trained on human-curated data. We introduce a framework to generate, select, and encode external commonsense knowledge alongside visual and textual signals within a novel pre-trained Vision-Language-Commonsense transformer, termed VLC-BERT. Evaluation on the knowledge-intensive OK-VQA and A-OKVQA datasets demonstrates that VLC-BERT surpasses existing models utilizing static knowledge bases. Additionally, a comprehensive analysis elucidates which types of questions gain advantages from contextualized commonsense knowledge and which do not.

FreezeML introduces a novel method for first-class polymorphic type inference, utilizing term annotations to govern the instantiation and generalization of polymorphic types. Building conservatively upon Hindley-Milner inference, it initially extended Algorithm W. In contrast, contemporary techniques like HM(X) and OutsideIn($X$) leverage constraints to accommodate advanced features such as type classes, type families, and rows. This work marks the initial step in modernizing FreezeML by proposing a constraint-based type inference algorithm. Drawing inspiration from the Pottier/R\'emy formulation of HM(X), we define a new constraint language that enables the expression of FreezeML type inference problems as constraints. Furthermore, we introduce a deterministic stack machine designed to resolve these constraints, providing proofs for both its termination and correctness.

Since 1996, we have tracked meridional motions within the Sun's surface layers, revealing systematic and significant fluctuations. Generally, the meridional flow velocity is rapid during cycle minima and sluggish during cycle maxima. These variations are defined by a weakening of the flow on the poleward flanks of active latitudes, which can be understood as an inflow toward sunspot zones layered over a broader poleward flow pattern. Additionally, we observe cycle-to-cycle variability; specifically, the meridional flow was slower at both the minimum and maximum of cycle 23 compared to corresponding phases in cycles 21, 22, and 24. Models indicating that magnetic flux transport is modulated by variable meridional flows suggest this can substantially influence the magnitude and timing of subsequent sunspot cycles by affecting the Sun's polar magnetic fields. We propose that the meridional flow anomalies observed during cycle 23 led to the diminished polar fields at its conclusion, thereby resulting in the weak cycle 24 and the exceptionally long minimum between cycles 23 and 24.

Identifying the pair potential $v({\bf r})$ that reproduces a specific pair correlation function $g_2({\bf r})$ or structure factor $S({\bf k})$ at equilibrium in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ represents a significant inverse problem in statistical mechanics. Recently, Zhang and Torquato proposed that any realizable correlation function or structure factor from a translationally invariant nonequilibrium system can be replicated by a classical equilibrium ensemble using only effective pair interactions. Verifying this conjecture for both nonequilibrium and complex equilibrium scenarios demands more advanced inverse methods. We have developed a new optimization algorithm to derive effective pair potentials for the pair statistics of general translationally invariant disordered many-body systems, whether in equilibrium or nonequilibrium, at positive temperatures. This approach employs a parameterized set of pointwise basis functions for the potential, initialized with forms guided by small- and large-distance behaviors predicted by statistical mechanics. A nonlinear optimization technique then minimizes an objective function combining the target $g_2({\bf r})$ and $S({\bf k})$, ensuring highly accurate capture of correlations across all distance scales. To demonstrate the method's robustness, we successfully determined the effective pair interactions for four distinct target systems. Our results show that the optimized potentials reproduce the target pair statistics with exceptional accuracy, achieving total $L_2$-norm errors roughly ten times smaller than those obtained by prior methods.

This work presents a combinatorial investigation of split matroids, a class inspired by tropical geometry perspectives on matroid polytopes. Split matroids are notable for generalizing paving matroids while maintaining closure under duality and minor operations. Additionally, they have enabled precise asymptotic bounds for the dimension of the Dressian and yielded new insights into the rays of tropical Grassmannians. In this paper, we define elementary split matroids, a subclass encompassing all connected split matroids. We establish a hypergraph characterization of these matroids based on independent sets and demonstrate that the class remains closed under duality, minor formation, and truncation. Unlike the broader class of split matroids, elementary split matroids are defined by a single forbidden minor. As an application, we derive a complete enumeration of binary split matroids.

The Bilateral Filter (BF) serves as a rapid, lightweight, and effective method for image denoising, which has also been widely adapted for point cloud processing. However, its reliance on continuous manual parameter tuning hinders efficiency and user satisfaction. To address this, we introduce LBF, an end-to-end learnable bilateral filtering network for point cloud denoising; to our knowledge, this represents the first such approach. Unlike traditional BF methods that apply uniform parameters across an entire point cloud, LBF learns adaptive parameters for individual points based on their geometric properties (e.g., corners, edges, planes), thereby eliminating residual noise, preserving geometric details, and preventing shape distortion. Beyond this learnable paradigm, LBF incorporates two core innovations. First, unlike local BF, it leverages multi-scale patches to achieve global-scale feature perception. Second, it employs a geometry-aware bi-directional projection loss, ensuring denoised outputs remain faithful to the underlying surfaces. Consequently, users can achieve optimal denoising results without laborious parameter tuning. Experimental results demonstrate that LBF significantly outperforms competing methods on both synthetic and real-scanned datasets.

Assuming a smooth, free action of a compact, connected Lie group $G$ on a smooth, compact manifold $M$, we demonstrate that the set of $G$-invariant Riemannian metrics on $M$ having exactly $G$ as their automorphism group forms an open dense subset within the space of all $G$-invariant metrics, provided $M$'s dimension is sufficiently large relative to $G$'s. Consequently, every compact, connected Lie group can be realized as the automorphism group of some compact, connected Riemannian manifold; this result extends the prior findings of Bedford-Dadok and Saerens-Zame by relaxing the required dimension constraints. Furthermore, under less stringent conditions regarding both dimensions and actions, we establish that the space of $G$-invariant metrics whose automorphism groups preserve the $G$-orbits constitutes a dense $G_{\delta}$ set in the space of all $G$-invariant metrics.

The rapid surge in mobility has triggered significant challenges, including urbanization, expensive highway construction, and air pollution. To mitigate these issues, this master's thesis explores the deployment of a ridesharing system. Recognized as a highly efficient transportation solution, ridesharing addresses energy consumption, environmental degradation, and traffic congestion by reducing the volume of vehicles on the road, thereby minimizing traffic jams and greenhouse gas emissions. Beyond its environmental benefits, the core objective of ridesharing is to share travel costs, facilitate social interaction, and enhance the overall travel experience. Consequently, this dissertation presents the Stable Multi-Criteria Rideshare Matching (SMRM) system, an effective solution that (i) incorporates users' personal preferences when sharing private vehicles and (ii) ensures stable matching between drivers and passengers. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed system surpasses existing competitors in both stability quality and cost efficiency.

Keywords: Smart cities, Social sustainability, Ridesharing, Social preferences, TOPSIS, Stable marriage.

This work establishes two universal approximation theorems for a specific class of dropout neural networks. These feed-forward architectures assign a random $\{0,1\}$ filter to each edge, operating in two distinct modes: a random mode where edge outputs are multiplied by their respective filters, and a deterministic mode where outputs are multiplied by the expected value of those filters. Typically, the random mode is employed during training, while the deterministic mode is used for testing and prediction.

Both theorems follow a similar structure: for any target function and a threshold $\varepsilon > 0$, they guarantee the existence of a dropout network that is $\varepsilon$-close in probability and under the $L^q$ norm. The first theorem addresses networks in the random mode; it relies on minimal assumptions regarding activation functions, covers a broad spectrum of network architectures, and extends even to approximation schemes beyond neural networks. Its foundation lies in an algebraic property demonstrating that random networks can exactly match deterministic networks in expectation. The second theorem imposes stronger conditions to deliver a more robust result: it ensures the existence of a network capable of approximating a function in both modes simultaneously. The proofs for this theorem utilize recursive edge replacement with independent copies and a specialized first-layer replacement strategy that links the expanded network to the input.

The target functions belong to general normed spaces, with approximation quality measured by the corresponding norms, and the networks are constructed explicitly. Due to the distinct methodologies employed, the two results offer independent insights into the approximation capabilities of random dropout networks. Collectively, these findings confirm that dropout neural networks broadly satisfy the universal approximation property.

Contextual Language Models (CLMs) have significantly advanced NLP benchmarks, making the use of their word embeddings in downstream tasks like text classification standard practice. However, without intervention, CLMs often inherit intrinsic gender biases from their training data, causing downstream model predictions to fluctuate noticeably based on gendered terms (e.g., "he" vs. "she") or neutral words. This paper investigates these biases within BERT, a widely used CLM, specifically focusing on five downstream tasks involving emotion and sentiment intensity prediction. For each task, we trained a simple regressor using BERT's embeddings and evaluated the resulting gender bias against an equity corpus. Ideally, given the task design, models should ignore gender-specific input features; however, results reveal a strong dependency on gendered words and phrases. We argue that this bias can be mitigated by eliminating gender-specific features from the embeddings. Consequently, we identified directions within each BERT layer that primarily encode gender information, defining this region as the gender subspace in the semantic space. We propose an algorithm to pinpoint fine-grained gender directions—one primary direction per layer—avoiding the complexity of multi-dimensional subspace representation while preserving other critical information. Experimental results demonstrate that removing embedding components along these identified directions successfully reduces gender bias induced by BERT in downstream tasks.

Data-driven techniques, particularly deep learning, have emerged as potent instruments for prediction across numerous fields. A pertinent inquiry is whether these methods can effectively forecast global weather patterns several days ahead. Although early investigations offer hope, the absence of standardized datasets and evaluation metrics has hindered comparative analysis among studies. This work introduces a benchmark dataset specifically designed for data-driven medium-range weather forecasting, a subject of significant interest to both atmospheric and computer scientists. The data, sourced and processed from the ERA5 archive, is optimized for integration into machine learning models. Additionally, we establish straightforward evaluation metrics to facilitate direct comparisons between various methodologies. We also provide baseline performance scores derived from simple linear regression, deep learning architectures, and purely physical forecasting models. The dataset is accessible at https://github.com/pangeo-data/WeatherBench, accompanied by reproducible code and introductory tutorials. We anticipate that this resource will accelerate advancements in data-driven weather forecasting research.

This study introduces and critically evaluates a dynamic-Immersed Boundary method integrated with a BGK-Lattice Boltzmann technique. Fluid dynamics are simulated on a three-dimensional D3Q19 lattice, while the immersed body surface is represented by Lagrangian points subject to elastic potentials and bending resistance. Flow quantities and the necessary forcing field to satisfy boundary conditions are precisely interpolated using moving least squares reconstruction. The model's validity is extensively confirmed through benchmark data for both rigid and deformable bodies. Rigid transport is verified by simulating the gravitational settling of a sphere across five scenarios, followed by an analysis of tumbling inertial particles that recovers the Jeffery orbit for a prolate spheroid. Additionally, the revolution periods for oblate spheroids and disk-like particles are determined as functions of the Reynolds number, revealing a critical threshold beyond which revolution ceases for both shapes. Finally, the study examines deformable object transport, assessing steady membrane deformation under shear for three stiffness levels and systematically analyzing the tumbling of weakly deformable spheroids under shear with respect to strain stiffness, bending resistance, and membrane mass.

We introduce a novel boson expansion theory that eliminates the necessity of the closed-algebra approximation, a prerequisite for all previous formulations. This approach extends conventional practical boson expansion methods, which aim to clarify nuclear collective motion, by offering a framework where the closed-algebra approximation can be either omitted or applied judiciously. Consequently, this method simplifies the derivation of boson expansions and maps the fermion subspace onto the boson subspace with greater fidelity than existing practical techniques. A detailed examination of the two-phonon norm matrix, encompassing all phonon excitation modes, elucidates the fundamental mechanism for constructing the fermion subspace that is to be mapped from the entire fermion space. Previous practical methods have incorrectly utilized the closed-algebra approximation to inappropriately amplify the Pauli principle, an approach that must be superseded by methods that either discard this approximation or employ it correctly.

Linear and nonlinear electronic spectra serve as essential tools for investigating electronic energy absorption and transfer. This work introduces a pure-state Ehrenfest method capable of generating accurate linear and nonlinear spectra for systems featuring numerous excited states and intricate chemical environments. By expressing initial conditions as superpositions of pure states and transforming multi-time correlation functions into the Schrödinger picture, we demonstrate significant accuracy gains over the traditional projected Ehrenfest approach, particularly when the initial state involves coherence between excited states. Although such coherence is absent in standard linear spectrum calculations, it is crucial for modeling multidimensional spectroscopies. We validate the method's efficacy by showing its ability to quantitatively reproduce exact linear, 2DES, and pump-probe spectra for a Frenkel exciton model in slow bath regimes, while also capturing the primary spectral features observed in fast bath regimes.

The crank, a partition statistic introduced by Dyson in 1944 to offer a combinatorial proof for a Ramanujan congruence concerning Euler's partition function $p(n)$, is the subject of this paper, where we establish links between it and unimodal compositions. Additionally, we present a separate combinatorial proof of a newly discovered truncated Euler pentagonal number theorem attributed to Xia and Zhao.

We investigate (generalized) discrete symmetries within two-dimensional semisimple topological quantum field theories (TQFTs), defined as theories where fusion rules are diagonalizable. Our findings demonstrate that, within this specific basis, 0-form symmetries manifest as permutations, whereas 1-form symmetries operate via phase factors. Consequently, we provide an explicit framework for gauging these symmetries. A key application of our work extends the equivariant Verlinde formula to arbitrary Lie groups. This generalized formula yields numerous predictions regarding the geometry of Hitchin moduli spaces, which we validate in specific instances involving low genus and an SO(3) gauge group.

This work employs numerical simulations and linear stability analysis to investigate the sedimentation of circular, flexible loops within a viscous fluid. The numerical framework couples a local slender-body theory for fluid flow with Euler-Bernoulli elastic forces acting on an inextensible fiber. Beginning with an inclined circular configuration, the dynamics are simulated using truncated Fourier modes to reveal three distinct motion regimes—absolute stability, two-dimensional dynamics, and three-dimensional dynamics—determined by the relative magnitudes of gravitational and elastic forces. We determine the governing parameter and formulate a simple semi-analytic stability criterion, which is subsequently validated numerically. Across all scenarios, the sedimenting loops evolve toward stable, planar equilibrium shapes, characterized by a single free parameter that depends on the fiber's initial conditions and material properties.

This study presents the concept of the fractional quantum heat engine, using the space-fractional quantum Szilard engine as a case study to demonstrate that these systems can achieve greater efficiency than their conventional quantum counterparts.

This study investigates the potential of next-generation direct detection dark matter experiments to constrain light mediators using measurements from coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering (CE$
u$NS) and elastic neutrino-electron scattering (E$
u$ES). Incorporating realistic factors such as quenching corrections, atomic binding effects, background noise, detection efficiency, and energy resolution, we analyze two representative detector configurations. For both scenarios, we derive model-independent projected sensitivities across all Lorentz-invariant interaction types: scalar ($S$), pseudoscalar ($P$), vector ($V$), axial vector ($A$), and tensor ($T$). Specifically for vector interactions, we examine two established gauge symmetries: $U(1)_{B-L}$ and $U(1)_{L_\mu - L_	au}$. Our findings indicate that upcoming dark matter detectors could impose competitive constraints on these interactions, improving upon current limits from dedicated CE$
u$NS experiments, XENON1T, beam dump facilities, and collider searches by approximately an order of magnitude for all channels $X=\{S,P,V,A,T\}$.

Nuclear rings represent vigorous star-forming regions located at the centers of barred galaxies. To investigate the factors governing their structure and star formation rate (SFR; $\dot{M}_{\rm SF}$), we conducted semi-global hydrodynamic simulations of these rings under constant mass inflow rates ($\dot{M}_{\rm in}$). Utilizing the TIGRESS framework developed by Kim \& Ostriker, we modeled radiative heating and cooling, star formation, and associated supernova (SN) feedback. Our findings indicate that SN feedback is insufficient to either dismantle the ring or suppress star formation across its entirety. Subject to a steady $\dot{M}_{\rm in}$, star formation within the ring remains remarkably stable and continuous, showing only minor temporal variations. We observe a strong correlation between the ring SFR and the inflow rate, following the relation $\dot{M}_{\rm SF}\approx 0.8\dot{M}_{\rm in}$ across a range of $\dot{M}_{\rm in}=0.125-8\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$. Vertically, the ring maintains dynamical equilibrium where midplane pressure—driven by SN feedback—counterbalances the gravitational weight of the overlying gas. Consequently, the SFR surface density scales nearly linearly with midplane pressure, consistent with pressure-regulated, feedback-modulated star formation theory. Based on these results, we conclude that the ring SFR is causally driven by $\dot{M}_\text{in}$, whereas the ring's gas mass adjusts to the SFR to sustain vertical dynamical equilibrium within the gravitational potential generated by both gas and stars.

In common law, new case outcomes are primarily driven by precedent rather than statutes. Understanding the precise mechanism of this influence is vital for ensuring judicial consistency and fairness. For the first time, we address this question computationally by evaluating two established jurisprudential perspectives: Halsbury's view, which posits that precedent arguments determine outcomes, and Goodhart's view, which emphasizes the significance of precedent facts. Utilizing a corpus of European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) cases—which includes both the target cases and the cited precedents—we model the problem as a classification task from an information-theoretic standpoint. Our analysis reveals that precedent arguments share 0.38 nats of information with the case outcome, compared to only 0.18 nats for precedent facts (a 58% reduction), suggesting Halsbury's perspective aligns better with ECtHR decisions. However, our qualitative analysis indicates that Goodhart's view prevails in specific statutory contexts, particularly where the underlying legal concepts are less clear-cut.

This study demonstrates the viability of magnetoentropic mapping for swiftly identifying magnetic cycloid and skyrmion phases in uniaxial systems, utilizing the model hosts GaV$_4$S$_8$ (easy-axis anisotropy) and GaV$_4$Se$_8$ (easy-plane anisotropy). By employing a straightforward numerical model of the spin Hamiltonian, we interpret these measurements to achieve unambiguous characterization of both distinct phase regions and their boundaries. In both lacunar spinel chemistries, the observed magnetoentropic features align excellently with a minimal spin Hamiltonian incorporating Heisenberg exchange, single-ion anisotropy, and anisotropic Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions. Specifically, we detect characteristic high-entropy behavior within the cycloid phase, which acts as a precursor to skyrmion formation at higher temperatures and provides a clear experimental signature of this transition. These findings indicate that numerical modeling-guided magnetoentropic mapping is a powerful tool for deciphering the intricate magnetic phase diagrams typical of skyrmion hosts. However, a notable exception arises in the easy-plane system GaV$_4$Se$_8$, where an anomalous low-temperature high-entropy state is observed but not accounted for by the numerical model; potential origins for this state are explored.

This paper examines the Inönü-Wigner contraction of the conformal algebra. Beginning with the light-cone formulation of the Poincaré algebra, we extend it to derive the conformal algebra in $d$ dimensions. For simplicity and compactness, we select five dimensions and compactify the third transverse direction into a circle of radius $R$ using Kaluza-Klein dimensional reduction, designating the inverse radius $1/R$ as the contraction parameter. Following the contraction, the resulting representation corresponds to a continuous spin representation in four dimensions. While scaling symmetry persists through the contraction, the special conformal translation vector undergoes a transformation, behaving analogously to a four-momentum vector. Additionally, we address the generalization of this framework to arbitrary $d$ dimensions.

The free $\mathbb{Z}$-module formed by non-trivial homotopy classes of closed curves on an oriented surface carries a Lie bialgebra structure defined by the Goldman bracket and the Turaev cobracket. M. Chas previously provided a combinatorial reformulation of these operations by identifying surface curve homotopy classes with cyclic words composed of the fundamental group's generators and their inverses. In this work, we introduce novel definitions for both the Goldman bracket and the Turaev cobracket, derived from the partitions of these cyclic words.

This thesis investigates loop amplitudes with identical helicity within self-dual Yang-Mills and self-dual gravity theories. These amplitudes have long been hypothesized to represent an anomaly and are recently associated with ultraviolet divergences in two-loop quantum gravity. The first section examines loop amplitudes in self-dual Yang-Mills, demonstrating that the four-point one-loop amplitude reduces to a calculation of shifts, which strongly supports an anomaly-based interpretation. Subsequently, we introduce a novel formula for one-loop amplitudes across all multiplicities, expressed via Berends-Giele currents linked by an effective propagator. We validate this formula by noting that it naturally yields the correct collinear properties. To confirm its accuracy, we perform explicit calculations for three-, four-, and five-point cases, successfully reproducing established results. The region momentum variables are pivotal to our formula, suggesting connections to both worldsheet and momentum twistor frameworks. The second section analyzes the one-loop behavior of chiral Einstein-Cartan gravity alongside the one-loop amplitudes in self-dual gravity.

We present Swift observational results for the high-mass Be/X-ray binary system 1A 1118-615, covering an outburst in January 2009 and a flaring event in March 2009. By applying the epoch-folding technique, we identified pulsed periods of 407.69(2) seconds during the January outburst and 407.26(1) seconds following the March flare. The outburst spectrum is well-fitted by a high-temperature blackbody model (kT ~ 1-3 keV) with a small radius (R ~ 1 km), suggesting emission from the neutron star's polar cap. Conversely, post-outburst spectra require an additional low-temperature component (kT ~ 0.1-0.2 keV) with a larger radius (R ~ 10-500 km), indicative of emission from the inner accretion disk region. Our findings indicate that the hot spot on the accreting neutron star dominates the radiation during outbursts, while the presence of both the X-ray contribution and the soft component implies that polar cap and accretion disk emissions coexist after the outburst. The unique dual-blackbody signature observed at the flaring stage offers new insights into interpreting X-ray emission from accreting neutron stars.
