This second installment surveys current state-of-the-art transceiver architectures for OTFS systems, emphasizing cyclic prefix (CP) configuration, windowing, pulse shaping, channel estimation, and signal detection. Additionally, the study examines OTFS performance metrics such as diversity gain and achievable data rates. Comparative simulations are utilized to assess the error performance of various OTFS detection methods, while the benefits of coded OTFS systems relative to coded orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) are explored.

We demonstrate that interacting quark stars (IQSs), constructed from interacting quark matter (IQM) and incorporating strong interaction phenomena like perturbative QCD corrections and color superconductivity, can be sufficiently compact to possess a photon sphere, a critical feature for gravitational wave echo signatures. By employing an IQM equation of state that unifies all interacting phases through simple reparametrization and rescaling, we reduce the system's degrees of freedom to a single dimensionless parameter, $\bar{\lambda}$, which quantifies the magnitude of strong interaction effects. Our analysis reveals that gravitational wave echoes are feasible for IQSs where $\bar{\lambda}\gtrsim10$ under conditions of high central pressure. Upon rescaling back to dimensional parameters, we examine the implications for the effective bag constant $B_{\rm eff}$ and the superconducting gap $\Delta$ as functions of the perturbative QCD parameter $a_4$ and the strange quark mass $m_s$. Furthermore, we compute the rescaled gravitational wave echo frequencies $\bar{f}_\text{echo}$ for these stars, deriving a concise scaling relation for the minimum echo frequency: $f_\text{echo}^{\rm min}\approx 5.76 {\sqrt{B_{\rm eff}/\text{(100 MeV)}^4}} \,\,\, \rm kHz$ in the limit of large $\bar{\lambda}$.

Clinical research frequently necessitates longitudinal patient tracking, a process often hindered by patient drop-out, logistical hurdles, and funding constraints that can compromise data completeness and analytical validity. Conversely, abundant baseline data from individuals with comparable profiles but outside the study timeframe—often unlabeled—remains underutilized. This paper explores leveraging such unlabeled instances to enhance survival time prediction. Specifically, we introduce a third supervisory tier in survival analysis that complements fully observed and censored data with unlabeled cases. We propose three methods to address this novel scenario and evaluate them across fifteen real-world clinical and gene expression datasets. Our findings indicate that all proposed approaches improve predictive accuracy on independent test sets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a semi-supervised wrapper method effectively integrates partial supervision from censored data, consistently yielding superior results and significant performance gains compared to ignoring unlabeled data.

A positive integer $N$ is defined as a $\theta$-congruent number if it is the area of a rational $\theta$-triangle $(a,b,c)$, specifically $N \sqrt{r^2-s^2}$, where the angle between sides $a$ and $b$ is $\theta$. The parameters satisfy $\theta \in (0, \pi)$, $\cos(\theta)=s/r$, and $0 \leq |s|<r$ are coprime integers. Fujiwara \cite{fujw1} established that $N$ is a $\theta$-congruent number if and only if the associated elliptic curve $E_N^\theta: y^2=x (x+(r+s)N)(x-(r-s)N)$ possesses a rational point of order greater than 2. Furthermore, for any natural number $N \neq 1,2,3,6$, $N$ is a $\theta$-congruent number precisely when the rank of $E_N^\theta(\mathbb{Q})$ exceeds zero.

This paper provides an affirmative answer to a question regarding the generation of new rational $\theta$-triangles for a $\theta$-congruent number $N$ from existing ones. This is achieved by extending Fermat's algorithm—which constructs new rational right triangles from a known one—to any angle $\theta$ meeting the specified criteria. We demonstrate that this generalization mirrors the duplication formula on $E_N^\theta(\mathbb{Q})$. Additionally, by utilizing the addition of two distinct points in $E_N^\theta(\mathbb{Q})$, we outline a method to derive new rational $\theta$-triangles for $N$ from two given distinct ones. The study also offers an alternative proof for Fujiwara's Theorem 2.2 and one aspect of Theorem 2.3. Notably, we compile a complete list of all torsion points in $E_N^\theta(\mathbb{Q})$ along with their corresponding rational $\theta$-triangles.

In support of metaphor analysis, we present a statistical, data-driven study that empirically tests established hypotheses and offers the first quantitative examination of the systematic characteristics of metaphors. This approach also renders metaphor theory a foundation for meaning emergence that can be measured and incorporated into Natural Language Processing frameworks.

This paper investigates a Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (SIR) model incorporating asymptomatic cases, contact tracing, and isolation within a configuration network framework. By applying degree-based approximation, we formulate a system of differential equations that lacks an analytical solution. We conduct an early-time analysis to determine an epidemic threshold; below this threshold, the disease extinguishes rapidly, whereas above it, a substantial portion of the population becomes infected. This threshold relies solely on disease parameters, the network's mean access degree, and the proportion of asymptomatic individuals, remaining independent of the contact tracing and isolation parameters. Our approximate analysis significantly lowers computational complexity, yielding a nonlinear system that is not nearly linear, for which we provide a stability analysis. Finally, simulations of the SIR model with contact tracing and isolation across five real-world networks demonstrate that these interventions are effective in containing epidemics.

The accuracy of astrochemical models relies heavily on dependable binding energy (BE) values that account for the diverse morphological and energetic characteristics of binding sites on ice-grain mantle surfaces. In this work, we introduce the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP) and its associated database, which utilizes quantum chemical methods to generate comprehensive BE distributions for molecules attached to an amorphous solid water (ASW) surface model. Highly automated, BEEP enables the sampling of binding sites across a collection of water clusters and the calculation of precise BEs. Applying our protocol, we calculated 21 BE distributions for interstellar molecules and radicals on an amorphized ensemble of 15–18 water clusters, each containing 22 molecules, resulting in distributions with 225 to 250 unique binding sites. We employed Gaussian fitting to report the mean and standard deviation for each distribution. Comparisons with existing experimental data reveal that low- and high-coverage experimental BEs align well with the high BE tails and mean values of our distributions, respectively. While previously reported single BE theoretical values generally agree with ours, notable differences exist in some instances. Furthermore, we demonstrate how varying BE values influence typical astrophysical problems, such as calculating snow lines in protoplanetary discs. The BEEP database will be made publicly available to facilitate community-driven expansion to other molecules and ice models.

RapidSim is a lightweight tool designed for the swift simulation of phase space decays involving beauty and charm quark hadrons, facilitating rapid investigations into signal and background decay properties within particle physics analyses. Built upon ROOT's TGenPhaseSpace class, it incorporates externally supplied fixed-order next-to-leading-logarithm calculations to accelerate initial hadrons to the specific energies required for the target production environment. The framework supports user-defined momentum resolution functions to emulate imperfect track reconstruction and allows for the application of custom efficiency shapes during generation to replicate the impacts of geometric and kinematic selection criteria on final state particles, as well as decay dynamics. Mis-identification effects of final state particles can be readily configured through files, and the system is easily extensible to accommodate additional particle types. This paper outlines the RapidSim framework, its features, and presents several example use cases.

We utilize spatial dynamics and geometric singular perturbation theory to generate radially symmetric spot and gap solutions that are far from onset within a two-component dryland ecosystem model describing vegetation patterns on flat terrain. We establish links between the geometric properties of these spots and gaps and those of stationary and traveling front solutions in the same system. Specifically, we prove that spots with a large radius are unstable by deriving an asymptotic relationship between a critical eigenvalue of the spot and a coefficient representing the sideband instability of an adjacent stationary front. Additionally, we show that such spots are unstable to intermediate-wavelength angular perturbations, assuming the spot radius is sufficiently large. These findings are supported by numerical simulations and spectral calculations.

The class imbalance problem, a critical challenge in learning node representations, has garnered significant attention. While existing research attributes imbalance primarily to unequal quantities of labeled examples across classes (quantity imbalance), we contend that graph data present a distinct source of imbalance stemming from the asymmetric topological properties of labeled nodes; specifically, these nodes differ in their structural roles within the graph (topology imbalance). This work first investigates this previously unrecognized topology-imbalance issue, examining its characteristics, origins, and detrimental effects on semi-supervised node classification. We subsequently offer a unified framework for jointly analyzing both quantity and topology imbalances by considering the node influence shift phenomenon within the Label Propagation algorithm. Based on this analysis, we introduce Totoro, a metric grounded in influence conflict detection to quantify graph topology imbalance, and propose ReNode, a model-agnostic method that adaptively re-weights the influence of labeled nodes according to their relative positions to class boundaries to mitigate topology imbalance. Systematic experiments confirm the effectiveness and generalizability of our approach in alleviating topology imbalance and enhancing semi-supervised node classification. Furthermore, our analysis reveals varying sensitivities of different Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to topology imbalance, offering a novel perspective for evaluating GNN architectures.

Digital image watermarking aims to safeguard media content by embedding and extracting hidden messages from images, even when subjected to various processing steps like lossy compression and interactive editing that introduce noise or distortion. Conventional watermarking methods often struggle with robustness under specific constraints, whereas recent deep learning approaches fail to adequately address information loss across separate feature encoding and decoding pipelines. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a compact neural network solution called the Invertible Watermarking Network (IWN). Built upon a single Invertible Neural Network (INN), our bijective propagation framework treats message embedding and extraction as a pair of inverse problems, learning a stable invertible mapping to solve both challenges simultaneously. To further improve robustness, we incorporate a straightforward yet effective bit message normalization module to compress the embedded data, alongside a noise layer designed to simulate diverse practical attacks within the IWN framework. Extensive experiments confirm the superiority of our approach across a wide range of distortions.

The study of random walks on dynamic graphs has gained prominence due to their ability to adapt to the evolving structures of real-world networks. Generally, a significant disparity exists between static and dynamic graph settings regarding the lazy simple random walk: while the cover time for static graphs with $n$ vertices is bounded by $O(n^3)$, certain edge-changing dynamic graphs can exhibit exponential hitting times. Conversely, prior research suggests that random walks on dynamic graphs with a time-homogeneous stationary distribution behave nearly identically to those on static graphs. This paper strengthens that observation by deriving general and enhanced bounds. Specifically, we analyze random walks governed by a sequence $(P_t)_{t\geq 1}$ of irreducible and reversible transition matrices sharing a common stationary distribution. We establish bounds for mixing, hitting, and cover times based on the hitting and relaxation times of the walk defined by the worst-case fixed $P_t$. Furthermore, we present the first bounds for hitting and cover times involving multiple random walks and coalescing times on dynamic graphs, effectively extending well-known static graph results. Our findings generalize previous upper bounds for specific dynamic walks, such as lazy simple and $d_{\max}$-lazy walks, offering tighter and improved estimates in various scenarios. Notably, our generalization yields tight bounds for the lazy Metropolis walk on any dynamic graph: $O(n^2)$ for mixing and hitting times, and $O(n^2\log n)$ for cover time. Additionally, our bound on coalescing time implies a corresponding consensus time bound for pull voting on dynamic graphs.

To determine the charged-to-neutral pion mass difference, we apply the infinite volume reconstruction method. This approach combines a lattice QCD-computed hadronic tensor with an analytic photon propagator, yielding mass splitting results with exponentially suppressed finite-volume errors. The study utilizes six gauge ensembles created via $2+1$-flavor domain wall fermions, five of which correspond to the physical pion mass. Employing both Feynman and Coulomb gauges, the calculation demonstrates excellent agreement as the lattice spacing vanishes. Following continuum extrapolation and an analysis of remaining finite-volume effects, we derive a pion mass splitting of $\Delta m_\pi = 4.534(42)(43)~\mathrm{MeV}$, which aligns closely with experimental data.

Frustrated spin ladders exhibit the well-known Haldane (H) and rung-singlet (RS) phases, where the transition between them remains a subject of debate. This study addresses this problem by applying quantum information theory to frustrated mixed-spin-(1, 1/2) ladders featuring antiferromagnetic leg, rung, and diagonal interactions. By employing the infinite time-evolving block decimation (iTEBD) and density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) methods, we compute key metrics including entanglement entropy (EE), the Schmidt gap, and the degeneracy of levels within the entanglement spectrum (ES). Our findings reveal an intermediate phase characterized by ES levels that lack the distinct degeneracies associated with the H and RS phases. Further analysis of short-range spin correlations along legs, rungs, and diagonals indicates that this intermediate phase is driven by long-wavelength modulations similar to bond order waves.

The discussion of asymmetric heterotic orbifolds is approached from the worldsheet perspective. Beginning with Buscher's gauging of a theory involving D compact bosons, the duality-covariant description proposed by Tseytlin is derived following a non-Lorentz invariant gauge fixing. The residual gauge symmetry allows for the elimination of doubled constant zero modes, leaving D physical target space coordinates; this process mirrors the strong constraint of double field theory at the worldsheet level. Extending this framework to heterotic theory is direct, as all findings are expressed using invariant and generalized metrics. An explicit procedure is outlined for constructing a generalized metric that remains invariant under T-duality orbifold actions. Furthermore, the text demonstrates how shift orbifolds result in redefinitions of Narain moduli. Finally, several higher-dimensional T-folds are constructed, including a new asymmetric Z6 orbifold.

This demonstration introduces VirtualConductor, a system capable of creating conducting videos from any provided music track and a single user's photograph. The process begins by gathering and building a large-scale dataset of conductor movements. Next, we introduce the Audio Motion Correspondence Network (AMCNet) alongside adversarial-perceptual learning to capture cross-modal relationships, resulting in diverse, realistic motions that are synchronized with the music. Finally, by integrating 3D animation rendering with a pose transfer model, the system synthesizes conducting videos from a single user image, enabling anyone to virtually conduct.

Attention maps are a widely used heatmap technique for explaining Visual Question Answering (VQA) models, intended to help users identify the specific image or question elements the model relies on for its answers. However, current visualizations often mislead users by highlighting relevant regions even when the model generates incorrect answers. To address this, we introduce Error Maps, which clarify mistakes by pinpointing image areas where the model is likely to fail. These maps reveal instances where correctly attended regions are processed erroneously, thereby enhancing user comprehension of such failures. To assess these new explanations, we developed a metric that simulates user interpretation to gauge their potential utility in understanding model correctness. Furthermore, user studies demonstrate that our approach improves users' ability to discern model correctness by approximately 30% compared to baseline methods, and our proxy metrics exhibit a strong correlation ($\rho>0.97$) with users' actual ability to predict model accuracy.

Convolutional Neural Networks are now the standard for image classification, yet they suffer from a lack of translation invariance. This deficiency stems from the use of strides, which disregard the sampling theorem, and fully connected layers that fail to account for spatial relationships. We demonstrate that strides can significantly enhance translation invariance when paired with sufficient local homogeneity—meaning high similarity between adjacent pixels. Our findings indicate that local homogeneity is dataset-dependent and determines the necessary balance between pooling kernel size and stride to achieve invariance. Additionally, we identify a trade-off regarding pooling kernel size: while larger kernels improve invariance, they degrade generalization. Finally, we evaluate the effectiveness of alternative approaches, including global average pooling, anti-aliasing, and data augmentation, using both empirical results and the framework of local homogeneity.

This work addresses the challenge of automatically creating stories across various languages. Unlike previous research focused solely on monolingual generation, our cross-lingual approach facilitates broader investigations into story planning. We introduce a method that leverages Large Language Models guided by plans to identify the most effective planning strategy for story generation. By evaluating four distinct plan types, we systematically analyze how different planning approaches influence the resulting outputs. Our findings indicate that structuring plans as question-answer pairs enhances story coherence and provides story creators with greater control.

This study employs the cavity method from statistical physics to analyze how vaccination influences epidemic spread within structured networks. Unlike prior research that assumed vaccines completely block transmission, we allow vaccinated nodes to retain a small transmission probability, thereby extending the cavity method to accommodate heterogeneous node transmissibility. Our findings confirm that vaccination, even with partial transmission, can achieve herd immunity, with the required threshold varying based on the assortativity between nodes of differing transmissibility. Furthermore, we investigate social distancing using bond percolation, demonstrating that selectively removing links between highly transmissible nodes reduces epidemic risk more effectively than targeting high-degree nodes. Finally, by adapting recent techniques to calculate risk distribution equations for heterogeneous populations, we show that targeted social distancing can lower overall risk more than untargeted vaccination campaigns, as evidenced by a comparison of random versus targeted strategies for deleting nodes and links.

This study introduces a novel stochastic framework designed to identify optimal combination therapies for colon cancer-induced immune responses. The progression of colon cancer is modeled using an Itô stochastic process, with its probability density function evolution dictated by the Fokker-Planck equation. To determine the best therapeutic combinations, an open-loop control optimization problem is formulated. Numerical simulations involving a regimen of the chemotherapy agent Doxorubicin and the immunotherapy drug IL-2 confirm the validity of the proposed approach.

This paper introduces a gaze correction and animation approach designed for high-resolution, unconstrained portrait images, eliminating the need for gaze angle or head pose annotations during training. Conventional gaze-correction techniques typically depend on precise gaze and head pose labels for training data; however, applying unsupervised methods to high-resolution, real-world face images remains an unresolved challenge due to the difficulty of obtaining such labels. To tackle this, we introduce two new datasets: CelebGaze and high-resolution CelebHQGaze. We then frame gaze correction as an image inpainting task, utilizing a Gaze Correction Module (GCM) and a Gaze Animation Module (GAM). Furthermore, we develop an unsupervised training strategy called "Synthesis-As-Training" to capture the relationship between eye region features and gaze angles, enabling semantic interpolation within the learned latent space for gaze animation. Additionally, to reduce memory and computational demands during both training and inference, we integrate a Coarse-to-Fine Module (CFM) with the GCM and GAM. Extensive experiments across low- and high-resolution wild face datasets confirm the method's effectiveness in both gaze correction and animation, demonstrating its superiority over state-of-the-art approaches. The code is accessible at https://github.com/zhangqianhui/GazeAnimationV2.

Data imputation has long been utilized to address missing data challenges, yet the exponential growth in incomplete datasets often renders traditional imputation models computationally prohibitive for real-world applications. To tackle this, we introduce SCIS, a scalable imputation system designed to drastically accelerate the training of differentiable generative adversarial imputation models while maintaining accuracy guarantees for large-scale incomplete data. SCIS comprises two core modules: Differentiable Imputation Modeling (DIM) and Sample Size Estimation (SSE). DIM employs a novel masking Sinkhorn divergence function to render arbitrary generative adversarial imputation models differentiable, whereas SSE determines an optimal sample size to ensure the final model meets user-defined accuracy thresholds. Extensive experiments across multiple real-life large-scale datasets show that SCIS accelerates generative adversarial model training by a factor of 7.1x. By utilizing approximately 7.6% of the samples, SCIS achieves accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art imputation methods while requiring significantly less computation time.

Realistic hyperspectral image (HSI) super-resolution (SR) seeks to produce high-resolution (HR) HSIs with enhanced spectral and spatial fidelity from low-resolution (LR) inputs. While generative adversarial networks (GANs) have demonstrated effectiveness in image super-resolution, existing GAN-based approaches often struggle with mode collapse during optimization, which restricts their ability to perform invariant spectral-spatial reconstruction. This issue frequently results in spectral-spatial distortions, particularly when the upscaling factor is large. To address mode collapse, this study introduces a novel GAN architecture integrated with a latent encoder (LE-GAN). This model maps spectral-spatial features from image space into a latent space, generating a coupling component that regularizes the output samples. By conceptualizing an HSI as a high-dimensional manifold within a latent space, the optimization challenge is reframed as learning the distribution of high-resolution HSI samples in that latent space, thereby aligning the generated SR-HSI distributions more closely with those of the original HR counterparts. Experimental evaluations assessed the model's super-resolution performance and its efficacy in mitigating mode collapse. The proposed method was validated on two real HSI datasets from different sensors (AVIRIS and UHD-185) across various upscaling factors and noise levels, and compared against state-of-the-art SR models including HyCoNet, LTTR, BAGAN, SR-GAN, and WGAN.

Within the global economy, credit institutions are pivotal to development due to their lending functions. However, this role entails significant challenges, primarily the risk of borrower default. Consequently, Credit Risk Modeling (CRM)—the assessment of a debtor's likelihood of failing to repay—has become critical. While statistical methods have long been the dominant approach in CRM, recent applications of machine and deep learning techniques have demonstrated marked improvements in predictive accuracy and performance. Despite these advantages, such advanced models often lack reliable interpretability regarding their generated scores. This opacity frequently prevents them from adhering to regulatory frameworks in Western nations, such as the GDPR. To address this explainability gap, this paper proposes the use of LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations). We demonstrate its application on a real-world credit-risk dataset and evaluate its effectiveness, discussing the necessary refinements required to ensure its reliable adoption and regulatory compliance.

Software emerges from the dynamic and efficient communication among organizational members, a principle highlighted by Conway's Law, which posits that systems reflect an organization's communication architecture. Yet, because developers frequently belong to multiple entities—such as corporate and regional groups—the impact of affiliations outside their primary company on the development process remains ambiguous. This paper investigates the social influence of nationality by analyzing variations in software repositories linked to different countries. Leveraging a new dataset sourced from GitHub, we pinpoint characteristics that distinguish repositories based on their developers' countries. We introduce a novel method that models repository development sequences as embedding tasks, enhanced by repository profile features, achieving 79.2% accuracy in predicting a repository's country of origin. Furthermore, a case study on repositories from prominent corporations reveals that country provides a more accurate descriptor of development differences than company affiliation alone. These findings carry significant implications for software development, underscoring the necessity of accounting for the multiple groups developers associate with when forming and structuring teams.

A \emph{signed graph} $(G, \sigma)$ consists of a graph $G$ paired with a mapping $\sigma:E(G) \rightarrow \{+,-\}$. The theory of homomorphisms for signed graphs is a recent advancement that deepens the link between graph coloring and minor theories. Building on this, we explore the relationship via the concept of Extended Double Covers of signed graphs, introduced recently by Naserasr, Sopena, and Zaslavsky. Specifically, a signed graph $(B, \pi)$ is termed \emph{planar-complete} if every planar signed graph $(G, \sigma)$ satisfying the conditions of a fundamental no-homomorphism lemma relative to $(B,\pi)$ possesses a homomorphism to $(B, \pi)$. We propose the conjecture that if a connected signed graph $(B, \pi)$ containing no positive odd closed walk is planar-complete, then its Extended Double Cover ${\rm EDC}(B,\pi)$ is likewise planar-complete. This conjecture significantly generalizes the Four-Color Theorem and is closely tied to several conjectures extending this landmark result. A signed graph $(B,\pi)$ \emph{bounds} a class of graphs if every member of that class admits a homomorphism to $(B,\pi)$. Supporting our conjecture, we establish it for the subclass of signed $K_4$-minor free graphs. Motivated by this result, we examine the search for optimal homomorphism bounds within signed $K_4$-minor-free graphs subject to girth constraints, offering nearly optimal solutions. Additionally, our research contributes to the advancement of weighted signed graphs.

This paper introduces ResTv2, a streamlined, accelerated, and more robust multi-scale vision Transformer designed for visual recognition tasks. By simplifying the EMSA architecture from ResTv1—specifically by removing the multi-head interaction component—and utilizing an upsample operation to recover medium- and high-frequency details lost during downsampling, ResTv2 achieves improved efficiency. Furthermore, we investigate various techniques to optimize the deployment of ResTv2 backbones in downstream applications. Our analysis reveals that while combining EMSAv2 with window attention can substantially lower theoretical FLOPs, it may reduce computation density, thereby diminishing actual processing speed. We comprehensively evaluate ResTv2 across ImageNet classification, COCO object detection, and ADE20K semantic segmentation. Experimental results demonstrate that ResTv2 significantly outperforms recent state-of-the-art backbones, highlighting its potential as a reliable foundation model. The corresponding code and models will be made publicly available at \url{https://github.com/wofmanaf/ResT}.

We theoretically investigate the squeezing phenomenon arising from a three-wave mixing process in a nonlinear optical medium where the $a_{1}^{\dagger}$ mode couples with both the $a_{2}^{\dagger}$ and $a_{3}^{\dagger}$ modes, focusing on the operator $S_{3}\equiv \exp[\mu(a_{1}a_{2}-a_{1}^{\dagger}a_{2}^{\dagger})+\nu(a_{1}a_{3}-a_{1}^{\dagger}a_{3}^{\dagger})]$. The derivation yields a novel three-mode squeezed vacuum state within Fock space, accompanied by an analysis of its uncertainty relation, which reveals that $S_{3}$ can produce enhanced squeezing. Furthermore, utilizing the integration within an ordered product (IWOP) of operators technique, we obtain the normally ordered expansion of $S_{3}$. Finally, the Wigner function for this new three-mode squeezed vacuum state is computed by applying Weyl ordering invariance under analogous transformations.

The study examines a multiplicative stochastic process constrained by a lognormal lower bound. A model for this process is developed, deriving its distribution function—which relies on four parameters—and associated statistical characteristics. By calibrating these parameters, the analysis demonstrates that the theoretical distribution aligns with empirical distributions observed in specific real-world datasets.

Ionic gating has emerged as a widely used method for investigating and regulating electric charge transport and electronic ground states across diverse materials. Its popularity stems from the ability of the electric-double-layer field-effect transistor (EDL-FET) architecture to generate significant modulations in surface charge density, a capability that extends even to tuning the properties of metallic systems. This short review summarizes the primary advancements made in controlling the superconducting (SC) characteristics of thin films of conventional metallic superconductors using ionic gating. I examine how gate-induced charge doping, although restricted to a thin surface layer by electrostatic screening, produces a long-range "bulk" modification of SC properties. This phenomenon arises from the coherent nature of the SC condensate, as demonstrated by the suppression of critical temperatures in films significantly thicker than the electrostatic screening length and the marked thickness dependence of these effects. Furthermore, I explore how this behavior is modeled through the proximity effect between the charge-doped surface layer and the unperturbed bulk under varying degrees of approximation. I also discuss how first-principles calculations have been utilized to identify the cause of an anomalous increase in electrostatic screening length at ultrahigh electric fields, thereby fully validating the proximity effect model. Finally, I present a comprehensive framework that combines ab-initio Density Functional Theory with the Migdal-Eliashberg theory of superconductivity, enabling the determination of properties for any gated thin film of a conventional metallic superconductor purely from first principles.

Conventional theories define topological band properties as intrinsic bulk characteristics that remain independent of the reference frame, allowing the bulk-edge correspondence principle to predict edge states in regions between topologically distinct materials. In this study, we investigate a two-dimensional elastic phononic plate featuring an engraved Kekulé-distorted honeycomb pattern. Our analysis reveals that pseudospin and pseudospin-dependent Chern numbers lack invariance, rendering the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ number insufficient for determining the presence of edge states. Furthermore, we identify distinctive pseudospin textures and pseudomagnetic fields. Ultimately, we successfully design and experimentally realize synthetic helical edge states at a dislocation interface joining two subdomains with identical bulk patterns differing only by a relative translation, with the edge states visualized using laser vibrometry.

Segmenting individual objects within indoor settings is a critical hurdle for robots navigating cluttered spaces filled with numerous small items, a task often hampered by the constraints of 3D sensing technologies that limit object detection. Although deep learning offers potential solutions, the requirement for manual annotation of 3D data for supervised training is prohibitively time-consuming. This study investigates zero-shot instance segmentation (ZSIS) utilizing RGB-D data to recognize previously unseen objects in a category-agnostic framework. To facilitate this research, we propose a zero-shot split of the Tabletop Objects Dataset (TOD-Z) and introduce a method that leverages annotated objects to learn pixel-level "objectness," enabling generalization to novel categories in cluttered indoor scenes. Named SupeRGB-D, our approach clusters pixels into small regions based on geometric indicators and merges them using deep agglomerative clustering. SupeRGB-D surpasses current baselines in detecting unseen objects while maintaining comparable accuracy for known ones. Furthermore, it is exceptionally lightweight, requiring only 0.4 MB of memory, making it ideal for mobile and robotic deployment. The dataset split and source code will be released publicly upon acceptance.

Relying on apical growth and hyphal branching as the primary drivers of fungal network expansion, we introduce a two-dimensional simulation utilizing a binary-tree model to characterize the growth dynamics of a generic thallus. Our findings indicate that within a uniform environment, fungal growth optimizes both exploration and exploitation through a distinct angular distribution of apical branches. To validate these results, we employed two complementary methods to extract angle values, comparing the simulation outcomes with experimental data from the saprophytic filamentous fungus *Podospora anserina*. Ultimately, we present a validated, computationally efficient model capable of rapidly testing various conditions and constraints. This tool will facilitate future research by complementing laboratory experiments—which can be costly, time-consuming, or limited in scope—with enhanced characterization of fungal network growth dynamics.

This study investigates how clumpy accretion induces perturbations in the circumstellar disks of pre-main-sequence stars. We conducted 3D hydrodynamical smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations of disks disturbed by a recent clump accretion event, subsequently utilizing radiative transfer calculations to determine their observable characteristics. The results demonstrate that density waves form at the moment of the clump's infall; after multiple revolutions, these waves evolve into spiral and ring-like structures. The simulated millimeter-wavelength images closely resemble observations made by the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) in certain protoplanetary disks, leading us to propose that clumpy accretion is a likely origin for these features.

Predicting the growth of unruptured intracranial aneurysms (UIAs) is critical for assessing rupture risk and guiding surveillance and treatment strategies based on initial Time-of-Flight MRA (TOF-MRA) scans. Since aneurysm size and morphology are established predictors of growth and rupture, this study evaluates the feasibility of using a mesh convolutional neural network to forecast UIA expansion from baseline TOF-MRAs. The dataset comprises 151 TOF-MRAs containing 169 UIAs, categorized as either growing (49 cases, defined as >1 mm increase) or stable (120 cases). UIAs were segmented from the MRAs, and corresponding meshes were generated automatically. The research compares models utilizing only the UIA mesh against those incorporating region-of-interest (ROI) meshes that include both the aneurysm and adjacent parent vessels. A classification model was developed to distinguish between growing and stable UIAs, featuring a mesh convolutional neural network enhanced with novel edge features such as shape index and curvedness to capture surface topology. The study also examined whether including input edge mid-point coordinates improved performance. The optimal model, which achieved an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 63.8%, utilized UIA meshes augmented with edge mid-point coordinate features, yielding an average F1 score of 62.3%, accuracy of 66.9%, sensitivity of 57.3%, and specificity of 70.8%. These findings present a mesh-based convolutional neural network approach for predicting future UIA growth with promising results.

This study introduces a stochastic framework for modeling the temporal evolution of nanomagnet magnetization, bridging the gap between the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert and Landau-Lifshitz-Bloch regimes through modulation of noise intensity. The analysis incorporates the noise's finite autocorrelation time, treating it as colored rather than white, and examines the resulting impact on magnetization response scales. It demonstrates that the hierarchy of magnetization moments can be closed via an appropriate truncation scheme; the validity of this scheme is verified by directly solving the moment equations and comparing the results with averages derived from a numerical solution of the corresponding colored stochastic Langevin equation. These comparisons are conducted on magnetic systems subjected to both external uniform magnetic fields and internal uniaxial anisotropy at a single site.

This paper introduces REVEAL, an end-to-end Retrieval-Augmented Visual Language Model designed to encode world knowledge into a large-scale memory for answering knowledge-intensive queries. REVEAL comprises four core components: memory, encoder, retriever, and generator. The unified encoder processes diverse multimodal knowledge sources, such as image-text pairs, QA pairs, and knowledge graph triplets, to populate the large-scale memory. The retriever then identifies the most relevant entries within this memory, while the generator integrates the retrieved knowledge with the input query to generate responses. A primary innovation of our method is the end-to-end pre-training of the memory, encoder, retriever, and generator on vast datasets. Additionally, leveraging a variety of multimodal knowledge sources yields substantial performance improvements. Experimental results demonstrate that REVEAL achieves state-of-the-art performance on visual question answering and image captioning tasks.

Effective scheduling of Device-to-Device (D2D) links to mitigate excessive interference is vital for the success of wireless D2D communications. While most conventional scheduling schemes prioritize system throughput or fairness, they often overlook information freshness. This paper introduces a novel scheduling framework that jointly optimizes Age of Information (AoI) and throughput for D2D links operating under a last-come-first-serve policy with packet replacement (LCFS-PR). This approach is driven by the observation that maximizing throughput can suppress the activation of links with poor channel conditions, leading to degraded AoI performance. Specifically, we derive expressions for the network's overall average AoI and throughput by analyzing spatio-temporal interfering queue dynamics under a mean-field assumption. Furthermore, we propose a neural network architecture to learn the mapping from geographic locations to optimal scheduling parameters within a stationary randomized policy; once trained, this network enables scheduling decisions without requiring real-time Channel State Information (CSI) estimation. To address the challenge of back-propagating implicit loss functions, we derive a numerical solution for the gradient. Numerical results demonstrate that the deep learning approach achieves performance comparable to a computationally intensive local optimal algorithm. Additionally, we present an AoI-throughput trade-off curve, illustrating that AoI approaches infinity as throughput reaches its maximum.

Traditionally, the characteristic length of a superconducting condensate is linked to the spatial distribution of the gap function. However, since the condensate consists of Cooper pairs, the term "Cooper-pair wave function" is often more recognizable to a wider audience. In conventional single-band superconductors, the gap function aligns with the center-of-mass wave function of a Cooper pair (modulo the coupling constant), making their respective characteristic lengths identical. Surprisingly, in two-band superconductors, these lengths match only near the critical temperature. At lower temperatures, they can diverge significantly, raising the question of which length scale should be preferred when defining the spatial extent of the band-dependent condensate in multiband materials.

Reconstructing the three-dimensional distribution of the universe's most extreme sources is central to modeling extragalactic astroparticle skies. Full-sky near-infrared tomographic surveys have already allowed the astroparticle community to correlate astrophysical neutrino and ultra-high cosmic ray (UHECR) source densities, limit binary black-hole merger distributions, and pinpoint components of the extragalactic gamma-ray background. This work synthesizes efforts to refine and expand catalogs from gravitational-wave and near-infrared researchers, aiming to establish a cosmographic perspective on stellar mass ($M_*$) and star formation rates (SFR). A dataset of approximately 400,000 galaxies within 350 Mpc—comprising an equal split of spectroscopic and photometric distances—enables unprecedented cosmography, including $M_*$ and SFR calculations alongside corrections for incompleteness related to distance and Galactic latitude. The resulting 3D distribution of $M_*$ and SFR aligns with Cosmic Flows. Furthermore, densities of $M_*$ and SFR stabilize to values consistent with deep-field observations beyond 100 Mpc, indicating a nearly isotropic distribution for distant sources. Beyond applications for the four astroparticle communities, this study examines megaparsec-scale $B$-field distributions inferred from the 3D matter layout, a factor believed vital for shaping the ultra-high-energy sky. These advancements offer a fresh foundation for modeling UHECR anisotropies, holding promise for identifying their elusive sources.

Axion-gluon interactions generate quadratic couplings between axions and matter fields. When the axion is an ultralight dark matter candidate, these interactions cause slight oscillations in hadron masses and other nuclear properties, leading to corresponding oscillations in atomic energy levels. By applying existing atomic spectroscopy data, we constrain this axion-gluon coupling. Furthermore, we project the sensitivity of future experiments, including those utilizing molecular and nuclear clock transitions. Our analysis demonstrates that both current and near-future experiments restrict a finely tuned region of axion model parameter space. These constraints can rival or surpass existing limits derived from oscillating neutron electric dipole moments and supernova bounds, as well as anticipated results from upcoming magnetometer-based studies. Additionally, we briefly examine the potential reach of accelerometers and interferometers.

Mahjong, a multi-player imperfect-information game originating in China during the late 19th century, presents significant challenges for artificial intelligence research. Sanma, a three-player variant of the Japanese Riichi Mahjong, distinguishes itself with unique traits such as a reduced tile count, which fosters a more aggressive gameplay style. While Sanma offers its own complex challenges and research potential, it remains an unexplored domain. This paper introduces Meowjong, the first AI dedicated to Sanma, developed using deep reinforcement learning. We establish an informative and compact two-dimensional data structure to encode observable game states. Additionally, we pre-train five convolutional neural networks (CNNs) corresponding to Sanma's five actions: discard, Pon, Kan, Kita, and Riichi. The primary model, the discard model, is further refined through self-play reinforcement learning employing the Monte Carlo policy gradient method. Meowjong's models achieve supervised learning accuracies comparable to those of four-player Mahjong AIs, with significant performance gains realized after applying reinforcement learning. As the inaugural AI for Sanma, Meowjong establishes a new state-of-the-art benchmark for the game.

Accurate line-by-line modeling of molecular cross sections requires incorporating several physical processes "beyond Voigt," including the speed-dependent Voigt (SDV) and Rautian (SDR) profiles as well as the Hartmann-Tran profile. Calculating these profiles necessitates evaluating the difference between two complex error functions, $w(i z_-)-w(i z_+)$, where the arguments $z_\pm$ are derived from the sum and difference of two square roots. These square root terms can become extremely large, causing significant cancellation errors in the default implementation of their difference. We first demonstrate that these issues can be circumvented by a straightforward reformulation of $z_-$. Additionally, we show that utilizing a single rational approximation of the complex error function valid across the entire complex plane (such as those proposed by Humlicek, 1979, or Weideman, 1994) allows for the computation of SDV and SDR with at least four significant digits. Our benchmarks indicate that while SDV and SDR calculations are approximately 2.2 times slower than Voigt function evaluations, this overhead does not significantly extend overall program execution time because speed-dependent parameters are only applicable to a small fraction of strong spectral lines.

Density modelling involves inferring an unknown probability density function from data samples, representing a core challenge in unsupervised machine learning. This study demonstrates that, under standard cryptographic assumptions, there are specific density modelling scenarios where fault-tolerant quantum computers achieve a super-polynomial advantage over classical algorithms. Additionally, we present several insights and results relevant to establishing future distribution learning separations between quantum and classical methods. Specifically, (a) we outline the connections between hardness results in supervised and distribution learning, and (b) we prove that any weak pseudo-random function can generate a density modelling problem that is hard for classical algorithms to solve. This latter finding suggests that quantum-classical separations for density modelling might be provable using assumptions weaker than those required for pseudo-random functions.

This study evaluates the secrecy performance of a dual-hop RF-FSO decode-and-forward (DF) relaying system involving a source, relay, destination, and eavesdropper, where the eavesdropper is positioned near the destination to intercept the relay's optical transmission. Both the radio frequency and free-space optical links experience ($\alpha$-$\kappa$-$\mu$)-shadowed fading and unified Málaga turbulence combined with pointing errors. We derive closed-form analytical expressions for the secure outage probability (SOP), strictly positive secrecy capacity (SPSC), and intercept probability (IP) to assess the mixed system's security. Furthermore, asymptotic expressions for these metrics are obtained by expanding the Meijer's G function as the electrical signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the FSO link approaches infinity. Monte-Carlo simulations are conducted to validate the derived analytical results. The findings demonstrate that secrecy performance is significantly influenced by fading, shadowing, detection methods (specifically heterodyne detection versus intensity modulation/direct detection), atmospheric turbulence, and pointing errors. Additionally, the results indicate that heterodyne detection at the destination yields superior performance compared to intensity modulation/direct detection.

Solving reinforcement learning (RL) tasks is often difficult without well-structured rewards. While previous research on provably efficient RL typically addresses this through specific exploration techniques, an alternative approach involves reframing the challenge as a multi-task RL problem. In this formulation, the task space includes both the difficult target task and simpler tasks that serve as an implicit curriculum. This perspective allows existing multi-task RL algorithms to be leveraged as a more efficient solution compared to tackling the single challenging task from the beginning. This study presents a theoretical framework that converts a single-task RL problem into a multi-task problem defined by a curriculum. Under mild regularity assumptions regarding the curriculum, we demonstrate that sequentially solving the tasks in this multi-task setting is computationally more efficient than solving the original single-task problem, all without relying on explicit exploration bonuses or dedicated exploration strategies. Furthermore, we show that these theoretical findings can be applied to create a practical learning algorithm capable of accelerating curriculum learning in simulated robotic environments.

Vision Transformers (ViTs) are rapidly evolving and beginning to rival the dominance of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in computer vision. By substituting CNNs' fixed inductive biases with a general-purpose Transformer architecture, ViTs have achieved superior performance, particularly when abundant data is available. However, ViTs are susceptible to overfitting on small datasets, necessitating large-scale pre-training that consumes significant time. This paper aims to eliminate the reliance on pre-training by reintroducing CNN inductive biases into ViTs while maintaining their architectural potential for higher performance ceilings and establishing more effective optimization goals. First, an "agent CNN" is constructed based on the provided ViT to incorporate these inductive biases. Subsequently, a bootstrapping training algorithm is introduced to jointly optimize both the agent and the ViT through weight sharing, allowing the ViT to learn inductive biases from the agent's intermediate features. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-1k with limited training data demonstrate that these inductive biases enable ViTs to converge much faster and outperform standard CNNs even with fewer parameters. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhfeing/Bootstrapping-ViTs-pytorch.

Over the last few years, cross-modal image-text retrieval (ITR) has garnered significant attention from the research community owing to its substantial research potential and wide-ranging practical applications. This field addresses scenarios involving queries from one modality and retrieval galleries from another. The present paper offers a comprehensive and current survey of ITR methodologies, organized around four key dimensions. First, by decomposing an ITR system into feature extraction and feature alignment, we review recent advancements in these areas. Second, we introduce an efficiency-oriented analysis of ITR systems. Third, to remain current, we provide a pioneering overview of cross-modal pre-training techniques for ITR. Finally, we outline standard benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics, perform an accuracy comparison among representative approaches, and conclude by discussing several critical but under-explored issues.

This study introduces a novel error bound for solving the tensor complementarity problem TCP$(q, \mathcal{A})$, assuming $\mathcal{A}$ is a $P$-tensor and $q$ is a real vector. We demonstrate that this new bound offers greater sharpness compared to existing error bounds found in prior literature. Furthermore, we derive both absolute and relative error bounds specifically for TCP$(q, \mathcal{A})$ where $\mathcal{A}$ is an even-order positive diagonal tensor.

Keywords: Tensor complementarity problem, $P$-tensor, global error bound, positively homogeneous operator.

Using the nonrelativistic quark model, the study computes the decay constants for low-lying S-wave $B_c$ mesons, specifically $B_c(nS)$ and $B^*_c(nS)$ where $n\leq 3$. The calculations incorporate the running coupling of the strong interaction and meticulously address uncertainties arising from parameter variations and the loss of Lorentz covariance. Additionally, as a supplementary result, the appendixes provide the decay constants for low-lying S-wave charmonium and bottomium states.

This study examines Power Splitting-based Simultaneous Wireless Information and Power Transfer (PS-SWIPT) within Multiple Access Channels (MAC), incorporating decoding costs and non-linear energy harvesting (EH) constraints at receivers to address practical system limitations. Under these conditions, we formulate and analyze achievable rates and maximum departure regions for two established scenarios: a standard PS-SWIPT MAC and a PS-SWIPT MAC featuring user cooperation. For the classical PS-SWIPT MAC, we derive closed-form expressions for optimal power splitting factors using two fundamental decoding methods: simultaneous decoding and successive interference cancellation. In the cooperative scenario, we determine the joint optimal power allocation for users alongside the optimal PS factor. Our findings indicate that decoding performance in the classical setting depends on the specific decoding cost function, with one scheme outperforming the other. Furthermore, we demonstrate that user cooperation can enhance the performance of a PS-SWIPT MAC under decoding cost and non-linear EH constraints. Finally, the impact of decoding cost functions, the non-linear EH model, and inter-user channel quality is analyzed, accompanied by a discussion of the resulting system performance characteristics.

We offer practical and robust protocols for learning various properties of an unknown n-qubit quantum state using a minimal number of state copies. Specifically, we introduce a depth-modulated randomized measurement framework that bridges two established classical shadows approaches based on random Pauli and random Clifford measurements, treating these as special cases corresponding to zero and infinite depths, respectively. We concentrate on the regime where depth scales logarithmically with n, demonstrating that this approach maintains the advantageous traits of both extreme schemes while remaining experimentally viable, unlike the random Clifford method. We detail methods for two primary objectives: estimating expectation values of specific observables derived from generated classical shadows and calculating upper bounds on the depth-modulated shadow norm to ensure rigorous accuracy guarantees. Our analysis covers observables expressible as linear combinations of poly(n) Pauli operators and those representable as low bond dimension matrix product operators. For the Pauli class, both tasks are solved efficiently in n. For the matrix product operator class, while we do not guarantee efficiency, we provide a practical method involving the variational computation of heralded approximate inverses for tensor networks, enabling efficient execution of both tasks.

Numerous practical challenges require the numerical resolution of equations involving operator functions, or matrix functions. Specifically, over the past decade, mathematical models featuring fractional powers of elliptic operators and the numerical techniques used to analyze them have gained significant attention. Computational strategies for these non-standard issues rely on approximating the operator function. The most prevalent methods employ various forms of rational approximation, alongside techniques utilizing exponential sums. This paper highlights the potential of approximating via exponential products. Solving equations with operator functions involves transforming them into standard stationary or evolutionary problems. These general methodologies are demonstrated using a problem involving the fractional power of an operator. The first category of methods utilizes the integral representation of the operator function across rational approximation, exponential sums, and exponential products. The second category focuses on resolving an auxiliary Cauchy problem derived from a specific evolutionary equation.

The J-region asymptotic giant branch (JAGB) technique represents a novel standard candle derived from the stable intrinsic J-band magnitude of color-selected carbon stars, offering precision on par with other primary distance indicators like Cepheids and the Tip of the Red Giant Branch (TRGB). To evaluate the method's accuracy, we applied it to M33 within the Local Group, a galaxy chosen for its low metallicity, moderate inclination, and proximity, which make it an ideal environment for testing systematics in local distance measurements. Utilizing high-precision optical BVI and near-infrared JHK photometry, we analyzed three independent indicators: the JAGB method, the Cepheid Leavitt Law, and the TRGB. Our results yield the following distances: $\mu_0$ (TRGB I) = 24.72 +/- 0.02 (stat) +/- 0.07 (sys) mag, $\mu_0$ (TRGB NIR) = 24.72 +/- 0.04 (stat) +/- 0.10 (sys) mag, $\mu_0$ (JAGB) = 24.67 +/- 0.03 (stat) +/- 0.04 (sys) mag, and $\mu_0$ (Cepheid) = 24.71 +/- 0.04 (stat) +/- 0.01 (sys) mag. Notably, this study provides the first direct comparison of JAGB distances derived from both ground-based and space-based photometry. Using the (F814-F110W) color combination to isolate JAGB stars, we measured $\mu_0$ (JAGB F110W) = 24.71 +/- 0.06 (stat) +/- 0.05 (sys) mag. These findings establish a distance to M33 accurate to 2%, further confirming the JAGB method as a robust extragalactic distance indicator capable of constraining the local Hubble constant via space-based observations. We anticipate measuring the Hubble constant using the JAGB method in the near future with data from JWST.

This work examines the relationship between matter density and its tracers through the lens of the probability distribution function (PDF). A key component of this relationship is the conditional expectation value $\langle \delta_{\mathrm{tracer}}|\delta_m\rangle$, which involves averaging both tracer and matter densities across a specific scale. We introduce a novel approach to integrate a Lagrangian bias expansion of this expectation value into conventional frameworks for modeling the PDF of density fluctuations and counts-in-cells statistics. By utilizing N-body simulations and mock galaxy catalogs, we verify the precision of this expansion and contrast it with the more prevalent Eulerian parametrization. For halos containing typical luminous red galaxies, the Lagrangian model offers a substantially improved description of $\langle \delta_{\mathrm{tracer}}|\delta_m\rangle$ at second order in perturbations compared to the Eulerian method. Another critical aspect of the matter-tracer link is shot noise, defined as the dispersion of tracer density around the conditional mean. Since this noise is frequently significantly non-Poissonian, we demonstrate the effectiveness of a broader two-parameter shot-noise model across various tracers and simulations. Both components of our analysis are designed to facilitate future applications to observational survey data.

We establish a sharp estimate for the free energy of directed polymers in a one-dimensional random environment. While this estimate was previously known for Gaussian environments, we extend it to cases where the environment's law is infinitely divisible.

Dynamic heterogeneity is anticipated to be a fundamental concept for elucidating the origins of slow dynamics near the glass transition. Previous research has attempted quantitative assessments of this phenomenon through two distinct approaches: analyzing speckle patterns in scattering experiments or calculating four-body correlation functions from microscopic configuration data derived from molecular dynamics simulations or real-space observations via confocal microscopy. However, the physical link between dynamic heterogeneities identified by these different methods remains unclear. This study establishes a connection between dynamic heterogeneities defined by speckle patterns and those derived from four-body correlations, and it further validates the accuracy of this relationship.

Investigating bias is crucial for ensuring the transparency and applicability of deep learning systems in healthcare, yet this area remains severely underexplored. This study examines two distinct cohorts: Group H, for which high-resolution images and labels are available, and Group L, which relies solely on deprecated lower-resolution data. We analyze how this disparity in data resolution leads to systematic prediction biases against Group L when models are evaluated at higher resolutions. Our findings reveal that training on a single resolution causes a substantial loss of volumetric distinctions between groups, resulting in inaccurate segmentations (measured by DSC) and classification failures for the low-resolution cohort. Furthermore, we investigate multi-resolution strategies to mitigate this systematic bias. Specifically, we assess the impact of image resampling, scale augmentation, and resolution independence, demonstrating that multi-resolution approaches can effectively reduce such biases.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has gained significant traction in both academic and industrial sectors for the automated design of high-performance deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). However, the prohibitive computational cost of fully training CNNs via stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for evaluation renders most current NAS approaches impractical for real-world applications. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel, cost-effective performance estimation metric called Random-Weight Evaluation (RWE). Rather than training the entire network, RWE initializes all layers except the final one with random weights, enabling a single network assessment in mere seconds. Additionally, we incorporate a complexity metric within a multi-objective NAS framework to effectively balance model size and performance. Our method successfully generates a set of efficient models achieving state-of-the-art results across two real-world search spaces. We further validate the algorithm's practicality by transferring findings from the CIFAR-10 dataset to ImageNet. Finally, ablation studies conducted on the NAS-Bench-301 dataset demonstrate that our proposed RWE outperforms existing methods in accurately estimating model performance.

Classification methods that rely on directly estimating and analyzing posterior probabilities are vulnerable to degradation when the original class priors shift. We demonstrate that it is possible to uniquely determine the data likelihoods for a test instance (up to a scaling factor) by utilizing its original class posteriors alongside dataset priors. With these recovered likelihoods and a new set of priors, one can re-calculate the posteriors via Bayes' Rule to account for the updated priors. This approach is computationally straightforward and facilitates the dynamic adjustment of original posteriors.

This study examines the transport behavior of self-propelled ellipsoidal particles within a smooth, corrugated channel featuring a two-dimensional asymmetric potential and Gaussian colored noise. The analysis explores the impacts of the channel geometry, potential landscape, and colored noise characteristics. Results indicate that as the load force increases, the particle's motion direction shifts from the positive x-axis to the negative x-axis. An optimal pore size facilitates directional transport, whereas pores that are either excessively large or small hinder transport velocity. Furthermore, high noise intensity along the x-axis suppresses directional transport, while an appropriate level of noise along the y-axis enhances it. A transport reversal phenomenon is observed as the self-propelled speed (v0) increases. Additionally, perfect spherical particles demonstrate superior ease of directional transport compared to needle-like ellipsoidal particles.

Sarcopenia is a medical condition defined by the decline in both muscle mass and function. A quantitative diagnostic approach involves identifying the CT slice at the center of the third lumbar vertebra (L3) and segmenting the muscles at that level. This paper introduces a deep reinforcement learning method designed to accurately locate the L3 CT slice. We train a reinforcement learning agent by rewarding it for discovering the correct position, specifically utilizing a Deep Q-Network to determine the optimal policy for this task. Visualizations of the training process reveal that the agent effectively mimics the scrolling behavior of an experienced radiologist. Extensive experiments comparing our approach to other state-of-the-art deep learning methods for L3 localization demonstrate its superiority, showing robust performance even when data and annotations are limited.

In reference [25], Moffatt defined helicity within an inviscid fluid and investigated how smooth solutions to barotropic compressible flows maintain this property. This paper demonstrates that weak solutions to the aforementioned system, belonging to Onsager-type spaces $\dot{B}^{1/3}_{p,c(\mathbb{N})}$, ensure helicity conservation. Furthermore, analogous results are established for the homogeneous incompressible Euler equations and the surface quasi-geostrophic equation.

In load balancing, network nodes are assigned loads that must be evenly distributed through local exchanges. Although this problem has been widely examined in static environments, algorithms for dynamic networks with guaranteed convergence times were only recently introduced. This paper investigates the time complexity of load balancing within dynamic networks. First, we demonstrate that randomness is unnecessary by presenting a deterministic algorithm that marginally outperforms prior methods, albeit without relying on matching-based mechanisms. Next, we address integral loads, where values cannot be divided infinitely, and prove that no matching-based algorithm can achieve bounded convergence in this scenario. To overcome both this impossibility result and a known limitation for non-integral cases, we employ smoothed analysis, which involves random perturbations of worst-case network topologies. Our findings indicate that these impossibility results do not apply under smoothed analysis, implying that load balancing in practical systems may converge faster than theoretical lower bounds suggest.

The evolution of digital pathology has created a demand for Histopathology Image Retrieval (HIR) systems capable of searching biopsy image databases to locate cases similar to a query. These systems enable pathologists to efficiently access vast repositories of diagnosed cases to leverage insights from associated pathology reports. Given that HIR systems often manage millions of gigapixel images, it is essential to extract compact yet expressive image features to ensure both accuracy and efficiency in retrieval. This paper introduces the use of Gram barcodes as image features for HIR systems. Distinct from most feature generation methods, Gram barcodes rely on high-order statistics that characterize tissue texture by summarizing correlations between feature maps across layers of convolutional neural networks. We conducted HIR experiments on three public datasets using a pre-trained VGG19 network to generate Gram barcodes, demonstrating highly competitive performance.

Hasse diagrams offer a rigorous framework for visualizing the architecture of statistical designs formed by crossing and nesting experimental factors. While they have historically been utilized to automate the creation of linear models and their corresponding subspaces for intricate designs, this paper contends they should also serve as a core element in planning and teaching introductory or service-level experimental design courses. Specifically, we demonstrate how Hasse diagrams facilitate the construction of elementary designs and the identification of key properties, including degrees of freedom, error strata, experimental units, and denominators for F-tests. Because linear (mixed) models map directly onto these diagrams, the process of defining and specifying models in statistical software becomes more intuitive. We illustrate how instructors can effectively employ Hasse diagrams to build designs by merging simple unit and treatment structures, detect pseudo-replication, and explore topics such as randomization, unit-treatment versus treatment-treatment interactions, and complete confounding. These capabilities establish Hasse diagrams as a potent instrument for unifying diverse ideas and concepts.

Software-Defined Networking (SDN) has revolutionized modern networking through its flexible and programmable architecture. Backed by robust hardware and high-speed communication links, SDN enables the virtualization of control functions and allows for rapid network reconfiguration to meet dynamic application needs. However, attempts to apply SDN's centralized control model to the Internet of Things (IoT) have revealed significant hurdles stemming from the limitations of low-power embedded devices and networks located at the IoT edge. Specifically, depending on external SDN controllers situated in the backbone network creates performance bottlenecks, such as increased latency. Consequently, we argue for supporting Software-Defined IoT networks by deploying lightweight SDN controllers directly on embedded hardware. We first evaluate the performance of two prominent SDN implementations for IoT mesh networks, $\mu$SDN and SDN-WISE, demonstrating that $\mu$SDN offers substantial improvements over SDN-WISE. Subsequently, we utilize $\mu$SDN to investigate the performance differences between embedded and external controllers. Our analysis highlights how the benefits of an embedded controller diminish as the network scales, and we determine the threshold at which an external controller becomes preferable for larger networks.

This work rigorously defines weakly and weakly regularly persistent input trajectories, establishing their connection to the Observability Grammian and the existence and uniqueness of solutions in Moving Horizon Estimation (MHE) problems. Leveraging a novel time-uniform Implicit Function Theorem, the paper demonstrates that these concepts guarantee the stability of MHE solutions against small additive measurement perturbations, ensuring stability both uniformly and non-uniformly over time. Furthermore, the study provides illustrative examples and counter-examples of weakly and weakly regularly persistent input trajectories within the context of 2D bearing-only navigation.

Node embedding techniques represent network nodes as low-dimensional vectors, which are then utilized for various downstream prediction tasks. Despite their increasing popularity in recent years, the robustness of these methods against input data perturbations remains largely unexplored. This study empirically evaluates the resilience of node embedding models against both random and adversarial poisoning attacks. Our comprehensive assessment examines representative approaches based on Skip-Gram, matrix factorization, and deep neural networks. We analyze the impact of edge addition, deletion, and rewiring attacks, calculated using either network properties or node labels. Additionally, we explore the effectiveness of common node classification attack baselines that presume complete knowledge of node labels. The study presents both qualitative findings through embedding visualizations and quantitative metrics regarding downstream node classification and network reconstruction performance. Our results indicate that node classification outcomes are more susceptible than network reconstruction ones, that degree-based and label-based attacks are typically the most detrimental, and that label heterophily can significantly affect attack efficacy.

Conceived by N.G. de Bruijn in 1968, Automath, a "mathematical language," stands as the first functional theorem prover, having been employed to verify numerous mathematical specimens. Its objectives and syntactic concepts inspired Th. Coquand and G. Huet to create the Calculus of Constructions (CC), an early interactive theorem prover that underpins the widely adopted Coq system. While Automath's original syntax remains difficult to comprehend, it is fundamentally rooted in a derivation system akin to CC. Despite extensive references within the type theory community, a comprehensive description of the relationship between Automath's syntax and CC is still lacking. This paper examines the origins and unique syntactic features of Automath, presenting a generic Automath system that encapsulates most common variants within a modern syntactic framework. The resulting system utilizes $\lambda$D, a direct extension of CC that incorporates definitions.

This paper introduces a novel formulation of relativistic quantum mechanics applied to a free, massive, spin-zero elementary particle within Minkowski spacetime. The reformulation mandates equal treatment of time and space, as well as timelike and spacelike intervals, ensuring the theory is fully symmetric and consistent with Special Relativity. Within the path integral framework, the theory accurately recovers the classical action of a relativistic particle and permits the definition of a new quantity termed "vector-mass." The physical implications of this vector-mass regarding nonlocality, the uncertainty principle, and the quantum vacuum are subsequently detailed and analyzed.

This work examines top-quark physics at the ILC, emphasizing complete off-shell processes for $t\bar{t}$ and $t\bar{t}H$ production, alongside top-quark decays and leptonic $W$ boson decays. Particular attention is given to combining the resummed vNRQCD threshold calculation with the fixed-order NLO QCD continuum calculation, offering an updated validation of this matching procedure. All computations were executed using the \wz event generator framework.

Most current approaches for video text spotting rely on a three-stage pipeline involving text detection, recognition of localized text, and post-processing tracking to produce final outputs. These methods generally adhere to the tracking-by-matching paradigm and involve complex architectures. In contrast, this paper introduces TransDETR, a streamlined yet effective end-to-end framework based on Transformer sequence modeling that integrates Detection, Tracking, and Recognition. TransDETR offers two primary advantages: first, unlike traditional methods that explicitly match adjacent frames, it implicitly tracks and recognizes text across long-range temporal sequences (spanning more than seven frames) using distinct text queries; second, it represents the first fully end-to-end trainable video text spotting system capable of simultaneously handling detection, tracking, and recognition. Extensive experiments across four datasets—ICDAR2013 Video, ICDAR2015 Video, Minetto, and YouTube Video Text—demonstrate that TransDETR achieves state-of-the-art results, yielding up to an 8.0% improvement on video text spotting tasks. The project's code is available at https://github.com/weijiawu/TransDETR.

Let $X$ be a separated scheme of finite type and dimension $d$ defined over a perfect field $k$ with positive characteristic $p$. This paper establishes that Bloch's cycle complex $\mathbb{Z}^c_X$, representing zero cycles modulo $p^n$, is quasi-isomorphic to the fixed part of a specific dualizing complex derived from coherent duality theory via the Cartier operator. Consequently, we derive novel vanishing theorems for higher Chow groups of zero cycles with mod $p^n$ coefficients in the context of singular varieties.

Weyl-Wigner representations for canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states are derived for all quadratic Hamiltonians by applying a Wick rotation to the Weyl-Wigner symbols of Heisenberg and metaplectic operators. The Wick mapping reveals the behavior of classical structures linked to these unitaries, demonstrating that a thermal equilibrium state is entirely characterized by a complex symplectic matrix, which defines its thermodynamic properties. The study examines four categories of Hamiltonian dynamics: Parabolic, Elliptic, Hyperbolic, and Loxodromic. Furthermore, semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are developed and contrasted with classical and quadratic behaviors.

We detail both the prospects and obstacles for improving AI's role in scientific discovery. A conflict arises because the objectives of industrial AI differ from those of scientific AI, creating a tension between merely spotting patterns in data and uncovering genuine patterns in the world through data. By overcoming the core challenges of aligning domain-specific scientific models with data-driven AI systems, we anticipate that these models will revolutionize hypothesis formation, the discovery process, and the scientific method itself.
