This study employs machine learning techniques grounded in weak supervision to conduct these searches. By utilizing mixed samples, weak supervision enables the detection of resonances with minimal prior knowledge regarding production mechanisms and allows for effective background modeling using sidebands or control regions, thereby reducing dependence on simulations. However, weak supervision alone proves inefficient at isolating specific regions within the multi-dimensional space of interest. Consequently, we propose a new strategy for searching for resonances that utilizes a signature- and topology-based classification procedure, followed by the application of weak supervision combined with Deep Neural Network algorithms. The efficacy of this approach is assessed through the inclusive and exclusive production of Standard Model Higgs bosons decaying into photon pairs across tailored phase-space regions at the LHC. After confirming the method's capability to extract various Standard Model Higgs signal mechanisms, a search for new phenomena in high-mass final states is established for the LHC.

Non-cartesian Freyd categories, known as effectful categories, serve as a generalization of both premonoidal and Freyd categories. We develop string diagrams for effectful categories based on those of a monoidal category augmented with a freely added object. Furthermore, we demonstrate that effectful categories function as pseudomonoids within a monoidal bicategory of promonads, utilizing an appropriate tensor product.

Although interest in developing super-resolution (SR) algorithms to upscale low-resolution images has grown, automatically assessing the visual quality of these outputs remains difficult. This study examines Super-Resolution Image Quality Assessment (SR IQA) within a two-dimensional framework contrasting deterministic fidelity (DF) and statistical fidelity (SF). This approach clarifies the trade-offs among existing SR methods, which cluster differently across the DF-SF spectrum. We identify a notable trend: traditional SR algorithms typically prioritize DF at the expense of SF, whereas recent Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) based methods excel in SF but often struggle with DF. To address this, we introduce an uncertainty weighting scheme utilizing content-dependent sharpness and texture analysis to combine both metrics into a single Super Resolution Image Fidelity (SRIF) index. When evaluated on subject-rated datasets, the SRIF index outperforms current state-of-the-art IQA models.

This article defines the semigroup linked to a substitution. We utilize this to build a minimal automaton that produces the substitution sequence u in reverse order. Specifically, when the substitution possesses a coincidence, we demonstrate that this automaton fully characterizes the semicocycle discontinuities of u.

This study examines flat metric solutions within multigravity theory—a ghost-free framework involving $(N+1)$ rank-2 tensor fields, consisting of one massless and $N$ massive spin-2 components—specifically when arbitrary, including Planck-scale, cosmological constants are present. The results indicate that for any finite $N$, regardless of its magnitude, flat solutions are impossible without fine-tuning the potential parameters. However, in the case of an infinite number of fields, flat solutions become viable within an infinite-dimensional parameter space. This ground state represents a collective phenomenon that cannot be approximated by any finite $N$.

Determining treatment impacts and analyzing their heterogeneity is vital for optimization and decision-making across numerous scientific and engineering fields. While Machine Learning models like Random Forests and Neural Networks are commonly used, various meta-algorithms have emerged to estimate the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) in binary scenarios, offering the benefit of not being limited to a single supervised learning approach. However, estimating these effects becomes significantly more difficult when treatments are not binary. This paper examines the Rubin Causal Model within a multi-treatment framework, specifically targeting the estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects. We extend \textit{Meta-learning} techniques to derive CATE estimates for every potential treatment level. By evaluating these meta-learners on synthetic and semi-synthetic observational datasets, we assess their performance, with a particular emphasis on the efficacy of the X-learner.

Although recent advances have successfully integrated spike-based coding with error backpropagation, spiking neural networks remain predominantly focused on sensory processing tasks involving traditional data structures such as visual or auditory inputs. In contrast, knowledge graphs—a widely adopted graph-based representation where entities are nodes and their interconnections are edges—are extensively used in both industry and research. These graphs provide a unified framework for describing complex systems like molecules, social networks, and industrial facilities, enabling graph embedding algorithms to generate context-aware predictions within these data-rich environments. We introduce a spike-based algorithm in which graph nodes are encoded by the spike times of specific neuron populations, while edges are represented by the time differences between population spikes. Training such spike-based embeddings relies solely on spike times and their intervals, aligning with recent frameworks for spiking neural network training. This model can be readily implemented on existing neuromorphic hardware, positioning knowledge graph inference within an environment where these architectures excel and opening up significant industrial applications for this technology.

Mobile Crowdsensing (MCS) has revolutionized how service providers gather, process, and analyze data by leveraging user mobile devices to support advanced applications. However, MCS systems face significant security challenges, including data poisoning, task clogging, and the submission of fake sensing tasks, which degrade system performance and exhaust computational resources. Notably, fake tasks often mimic legitimate submissions to drain platform resources. This study proposes a two-stage detection approach: first, a Self-Organizing Feature Map (SOFM) is used in an unsupervised manner to pre-cluster legitimate data, thereby creating a new dataset with a more balanced ratio of legitimate to fake tasks to improve detection efficacy. Second, a Deep Neural Network (DeepNN) is trained on the remaining data. The final technique, termed pre-clustered DeepNN (PrecDeepNN), enhances performance by appending the pre-clustered legitimate tasks to the DeepNN's positive predictions. Experimental results demonstrate that this method significantly improves discrimination accuracy, raising the average rate from the baseline DeepNN performance to 0.9812.

Let $G$ be an additive abelian group and let $A=\{a_{0}, a_{1},\ldots, a_{k-1}\}$ be a nonempty finite subset of $G$. For a positive integer $h$ with $1\leq h\leq k$, the restricted signed sumset $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$ is defined as $\{\Sigma_{i=0}^{k-1}\lambda_{i} a_{i}: (\lambda_{0},\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{k-1}) \in \{-1,0,1\}^{k},~\Sigma_{i=0}^{k-1}|\lambda_{i}|=h \}$. The direct problem seeks to determine the minimum cardinality of $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$ as a function of $|A|$, whereas the inverse problem aims to identify the structural properties of $A$ that yield this minimum cardinality. This article addresses specific instances of both the direct and inverse problems for $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$ when $A$ consists of integers. Furthermore, we formulate several questions as conjectures for the unresolved cases.

This paper introduces a neural network-based energy management system (NN-EMS) designed for islanded AC microgrids powered by multiple distributed generators (DGs) that utilize PV-battery configurations. Variations in irradiation, which are both stochastic and uneven, lead to disparate PV outputs and consequently create unequal states-of-charge (SoC) among the DG batteries. Over time, this disparity can escalate significantly, causing certain batteries to hit their SoC limits and lose the ability to regulate the DC-link of hybrid grid-forming DGs. To address this, the proposed NN-EMS learns an optimal state-action mapping derived from optimal power flow (OPF) outputs. The training data was generated by running a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) based OPF on droop-controlled island microgrids under realistic generation and load profiles. By doing so, the resulting NN-EMS controller incorporates knowledge of optimal states and network dynamics. Unlike traditional centralized time-ahead methods, this approach eliminates the need for precise generation-load forecasting and can respond to near-real-time PV power fluctuations without solving an OPF. The effectiveness of the proposed NN-EMS controller was validated through case studies on a CIGRE LV microgrid featuring PV-battery hybrid DGs. Additionally, the proposed concept can be adapted to create decentralized controllers that collaborate to achieve global objectives without requiring communication.

Hand pose estimation serves as a critical component in numerous human-robot interaction systems. Yet, existing methods often struggle with inaccurate landmark predictions in real-world environments and impose significant computational costs. To address these challenges, this paper introduces "FastHand," a rapid and precise framework designed for hand pose estimation. By employing a lightweight encoder-decoder architecture, FastHand meets the demands of practical applications on embedded hardware. The encoder utilizes deep layers with minimal parameters, whereas the decoder leverages spatial location data to enhance result accuracy. Experiments conducted on two public datasets confirm that this pipeline outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques. FastHand achieves high accuracy while operating at a speed of 25 frames per second on an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 GPU.

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence has led to a heightened need for system explainability, as clear explanations reduce opacity, foster transparency, and build stakeholder trust. This position paper explores the synergies between requirements engineering (RE) and Explainable AI (XAI). We identify key challenges within XAI and propose a framework alongside research directions to demonstrate how RE practices can address these issues.

This paper introduces the Collaborative Pure Exploration in Kernel Bandit (CoPE-KB) problem, offering a new framework for multi-agent, multi-task decision-making under constraints of limited communication and general reward functions, with applications spanning recommendation systems and network scheduling. We examine two CoPE-KB scenarios, Fixed-Confidence (FC) and Fixed-Budget (FB), and propose two optimal algorithms: CoopKernelFC for FC and CoopKernelFB for FB. These algorithms utilize innovative, efficient kernelized estimators to jointly ensure computational and communication efficiency. We establish matching upper and lower bounds for both statistical and communication metrics to prove algorithmic optimality. Furthermore, these theoretical bounds effectively measure how task similarities accelerate learning, relying solely on the effective dimension of the kernelized feature space. Our analytical methods—including data dimension decomposition, linear structured instance transformation, and communication round-speedup induction—are novel and extendable to other bandit problems. Finally, empirical evaluations confirm our theoretical findings and highlight the superior performance of our proposed algorithms.

The photon, the primary carrier for observing the cosmos and the sole free massless particle within the Standard Model (SM), has been the subject of investigation regarding potential deviations from Ampère-Maxwell law. These deviations could stem from a genuine photon mass as described by de Broglie-Proca theory, or from effective mass arising from Lorentz-Poincaré Symmetry Violation (LSV) in SM extensions (SME). Utilizing six years of data from the Magnetospheric Multi-Scale (MMS) mission—a four-satellite constellation that predominantly traversed turbulent magnetic reconnection zones, capturing approximately 95% of observations outside the quieter solar wind—we analyzed 3.8 million data points across the solar wind, magnetosheath, and magnetosphere. While we report strict upper limits, a minority of cases exhibited deviations: 2.2% in modulus and 4.8% in Cartesian components for high-resolution burst data and optimal tetrahedral configurations across all regions, rising to 21% and 29.9% respectively within the solar wind. These anomalies may result from unaccounted experimental errors or non-Maxwellian terms, suggesting we might be approaching the limits of measurability for missions not specifically designed for this purpose. Finally, we compare our experimental findings against more rigorous, model-dependent constraints.

This study presents STAR's measurements of directed flow ($v_1$) for pions, charged and neutral kaons ($K_s^0$), protons, and antiprotons in Au + Au collisions at $\sqrtsNN = 200$ GeV. A negative slope in $v_1(y)$ is observed across pions, antiprotons, protons, and kaons, with the proton $v_1(y)$ slope at midrapidity being exceptionally small. A significant discrepancy exists between proton and antiproton $v_1$ values in 5-30% central collisions. While anti-flow accounts for the negative slope, it struggles to explain the centrality dependence of the difference between proton and antiproton $v_1(y)$ slopes. The $v_1$ excitation function is also reported, and comparisons with model calculations (RQMD, uRQMD, AMPT, and QGSM) reveal that none of the four models adequately describe the experimental data.

This study examines the influence of the laminar-turbulent interface on interscale energy transfer within a boundary layer experiencing bypass transition, utilizing the Karman-Howarth-Monin-Hill (KHMH) equation. By employing a local binary indicator function to identify this interface, we define two-point intermittencies to decompose standard-averaged interscale and interspace energy fluxes into conditionally-averaged components. Our analysis reveals that the streamwise inverse cascade previously reported stems from events occurring at the downstream (head) or upstream (tail) boundaries of a turbulent spot. However, three-dimensional energy flux maps highlight distinct differences between these regions: the downstream interface exhibits a stronger inverse cascade that dominates across a broader range of streamwise and spanwise separations. We attribute this observation to a propagating spot of simplified geometry crossing a fixed streamwise position. Additionally, we derive a conditionally-averaged KHMH equation, extending similar formulations for single-point statistics to two-point statistics. Comparing three-dimensional maps of conditionally-averaged production and total energy flux within turbulent spots against standard-averaged quantities in fully turbulent regions indicates remarkable dynamical similarities for two-point statistics. While such similarities were previously known only for single-point quantities, our findings demonstrate that they also apply to two-point statistics.

Fractional calculus serves as a potent instrument for modeling nonlinear systems, with the M derivative acting as a generalization of other fractional derivatives that adheres to integer calculus properties. This paper outlines a method for resolving M fractional sequential linear differential equations with constant coefficients, applicable where alpha ≥ 0 and beta > 0. Furthermore, it provides a detailed analysis of the existence and uniqueness of solutions for nth-order sequential linear M fractional differential equations, supported by illustrations covering both homogeneous and non-homogeneous scenarios.

We present a novel, general framework for superconductivity within Fermi systems characterized by strong repulsive interactions. In these systems, where kinetic energy is negligible compared to bare repulsion, charge carrier dynamics are heavily restricted by the proximity of other carriers. By treating kinetic terms as a perturbation relative to the atomic limit, we demonstrate that pairing arises from correlated multi-particle tunneling processes that encourage two itinerant carriers to remain close. Our analytically controlled theory yields a quantitative expression linking $T_c$ to microscopic parameters, with peak $T_c$ values reaching approximately 10% of the Fermi temperature. This work establishes a robust approach for investigating strong-coupling superconductivity featuring unconventional pairing symmetry and proposes a viable pathway for achieving finite angular momentum superfluidity of spin-polarized fermions in optical lattices.

This paper derives an exact black hole spacetime metric within the Einstein-Hilbert-Bumblebee (EHB) gravity framework surrounding a global monopole field. We investigate the black hole's horizon, temperature, and photon sphere. By applying the null geodesics equation, we determine the shadow of a Schwarzschild-like black hole containing a topological defect in bumblebee gravity. Notably, the shadow's radius expands as the global monopole parameter increases. Furthermore, we visualize the shadows and energy emission rates across various parameter values. Additionally, employing the Gauss-Bonnet theorem, we compute the deflection angle in the weak-field limit and explore the feasibility of testing the impacts of both global monopole and bumblebee fields on weak deflection. Our findings indicate that both the global monopole parameter and the Lorentz symmetry breaking parameter exert an increasing influence on the deflection angle.

At low Mach numbers, the Euler equations exhibit three asymptotic limits: purely convective, purely acoustic, and a mixed convective-acoustic regime. Standard collocated density-based schemes for compressible flow typically fail in this regime because their artificial diffusion scales incorrectly. While prior research has examined these schemes across various limits and offered design guidelines, such studies have largely concentrated on specific discretizations or solely on the convective limit.

This paper reviews low-Mach behavior by employing modified equations, which represent the continuous Euler equations augmented with artificial diffusion terms found in a broad class of schemes. By accounting for both convective and acoustic effects, we identify three natural diffusion scalings. Through single- and multiple-scale asymptotic analysis of these scalings, we demonstrate that many key low-Mach characteristics of this scheme class can be effectively reproduced within a continuous framework.

As an illustration, we show that numerous existing low-Mach Roe-type finite-volume schemes align with one of these three scalings. Our findings support previous analyses of these schemes and refine existing design guidelines by incorporating both convective and acoustic influences. Finally, discrete analysis and numerical examples illustrate the performance of minimal Roe-type schemes under each of the three scalings across convective, acoustic, and mixed flow conditions.

This study presents the initial magnetohydrodynamic simulations, conducted within full general relativity, of self-consistently rotating neutron stars (NSs) featuring ultrastrong mixed poloidal and toroidal magnetic fields. The initial uniformly rotating NS models were generated under assumptions of perfect conductivity, stationarity, and axisymmetry. While the specific geometry of the mixed field configuration may influence the timing of various instabilities identified in analytic perturbative studies, all simulated models ultimately succumb to them. Spontaneous differential rotation emerges within the cores of these magnetars, which eventually reverts to uniform rotation after a sufficient duration. Rapidly rotating magnetars exhibit substantial ejecta, potentially responsible for transient kilonova signatures; however, by the conclusion of the simulations, no highly collimated, helical magnetic fields or incipient jets—essential for gamma-ray bursts—have formed at the poles.

We document the discovery of long-lived Floquet prethermal states within a bulk solid featuring dipolar-coupled $^{13}$C nuclei in diamond at room temperature. By employing pulsed spin-lock Floquet control on nuclear spins initialized in a transverse state, we successfully inhibit their decay for durations exceeding several minutes. Specifically, we measure Floquet prethermal lifetimes of $T_2'\approx$90.9s, representing an extension of over 60,000 times compared to the nuclear free induction decay. During approximately 10 minutes of continuous spin interrogation, which involves roughly 5.8 million control pulses, the $^{13}$C nuclei are optically hyperpolarized by lattice Nitrogen Vacancy (NV) centers. This synergy between hyperpolarization and continuous readout provides substantial signal-to-noise ratios, enabling the examination of Floquet thermalization dynamics with exceptional precision. We distinguish four distinct regimes of the thermalization process, identifying short-term transient behaviors that establish the prethermal plateau and long-term system heating toward infinite temperature. These findings highlight novel possibilities for Floquet control in networks of dilute, randomly distributed, low-sensitivity nuclei. Notably, the combination of minute-scale prethermal lifetimes and continuous spin interrogation paves the way for quantum sensors based on hyperpolarized Floquet prethermal nuclei.

We have examined a Lagrangian where the Einstein-Hilbert term is modified by the Weyl cube operator, the lowest-dimensional non-vanishing on-shell operator that arises as a two-loop counterterm. We analyze in detail the tension between this operator and Schwarzschild de Sitter (SdS) spacetime.

This study explores prior-independent mechanism design, where a single mechanism is engineered to deliver near-optimal outcomes across all prior distributions within a specific class. While existing research predominantly examines mechanisms featuring truthtelling equilibria (truthful mechanisms), Feng and Hartline (2018) proposed the "revelation gap" to measure the performance loss incurred by restricting designs to truthful approaches. We address a primary open question from their work by demonstrating a non-trivial revelation gap for revenue maximization.

Our investigation centers on the standard problem of selling one item to one agent using only a single sample from the agent's valuation distribution. We introduce the sample-bid mechanism, a straightforward non-truthful approach, and establish that its prior-independent approximation ratio is bounded by 1.835 (or 1.296) for regular (respectively, MHR) distributions. Furthermore, we prove that no truthful mechanism can surpass an approximation ratio of 1.957 (or 1.543) for regular (respectively, MHR) distributions. These findings confirm a non-trivial revelation gap, as the sample-bid mechanism outperforms the best possible prior-independent truthful mechanism. Additionally, regarding computational hardness, we demonstrate that no mechanism, regardless of truthfulness, can achieve a prior-independent approximation ratio better than 1.073, even when dealing with uniform distributions.

Free-standing silicon nitride (SiN) mechanical resonators are pivotal for applications like temperature and mass sensing, as well as for fundamental optomechanical studies. To predict thermal noise, frequency fluctuations, and sensor responses to temperature variations, it is essential to understand the thermal coupling between a membrane resonator and its environment. This study presents closed-form expressions for intrinsic thermal coupling parameters in free-standing thin films, including total thermal conductance to the surroundings, thermal response time, and the relative impact of thermal radiation. While the model applies to any free-standing thin film anchored on all sides, we specifically highlight the SiN case, where spectral emissivity is rigorously analyzed across varying thicknesses and temperatures. Our findings indicate that radiative heat exchange can significantly contribute to, or even dominate, thermal coupling in membranes of dimensions typical for optomechanical experiments. We validate our model experimentally by measuring the radiative thermal coupling between a SiN mechanical resonator and a ceramic heater under high vacuum conditions.
This note calculates the cohomology of the elliptic tangent bundle, a Lie algebroid employed to characterize singular symplectic forms derived from generalized complex geometry.

This survey paper examines image-based graph neural networks and introduces a three-step classification method. First, the Quickshift algorithm segments images into superpixels to decrease input data volume by 30%. These superpixels then form a region adjacency graph, which is processed by a state-of-the-art graph convolutional neural network to yield classification scores. Additionally, the paper evaluates spatial and spectral convolution filtering techniques within graph neural networks, concluding that spectral-based models outperform both spatial-based models and classical CNNs with lower computational costs.

Model Predictive Control (MPC) is a highly effective strategy for managing systems subject to input and state constraints, yet its performance relies critically on the precision of open-loop predictions. In uncertain environments, this precision hinges on available knowledge regarding model properties and disturbance uncertainties. This work focuses on scenarios where such information is accessible only through observed system trajectories. We introduce a general scenario-based optimization framework for the stochastic control of linear systems with additive disturbances and approximately known dynamics. Our primary contribution is establishing an upper bound on the number of scenarios needed to ensure probabilistic guarantees on the quality of solutions for deterministic, finite-horizon, scenario-based optimal control problems. We offer a theoretical analysis of the method's sample complexity and validate its efficacy through a simulation example. By leveraging sampling, this approach eliminates the need for explicit knowledge of model or disturbance distributions, rendering it suitable for a broad range of applications.

This work presents the initial investigation into charm quark diffusion relative to the jet axis within heavy ion collisions. The analysis utilizes jets with $p_\mathrm{T}^\mathrm{jet}$ exceeding 60 GeV and D$^0$ mesons with $p_\mathrm{T}^\mathrm{D}$ greater than 4 GeV, collected by the CMS detector during lead-lead (PbPb) and proton-proton (pp) collisions at a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_\mathrm{NN}} = 5.02$ TeV at the LHC. The radial distribution of D$^0$ mesons concerning the jet axis provides insight into meson production mechanisms, as well as the energy loss and diffusion processes experienced by their parent partons within the strongly interacting medium formed in PbPb collisions. Comparisons with Monte Carlo event generators reveal that the pp radial distribution is well-modeled by PYTHIA, whereas SHERPA predicts a steeper slope than observed in the data. In PbPb collisions, the D$^0$ meson distribution for transverse momenta between 4 and 20 GeV suggests a greater average distance from the jet axis compared to pp results, indicating charm quark diffusion in the heavy ion medium. However, at higher $p_\mathrm{T}^\mathrm{D}$ values, the radial distributions for PbPb and pp collisions are found to be comparable.

A primary objective of Mode Division Multiplexing-Wavelength Division Multiplexing (MDM-WDM) networks is to ensure dependable communication across various channels and transmission modes. This reliability is quantified by the minimum Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) margin, which is influenced by launched power, Multimode-Erbium Doped Fiber Amplifier (MM-EDFA) gain, and Multimode Fiber (MMF) nonlinearity. This paper presents an analytical model for MMF nonlinearity derived from the Enhanced Gaussian Noise (EGN) framework, incorporating carrier phase estimation and the first four dispersion terms. The validity of this proposed EGN model is confirmed via split-step Fourier method simulations. Within a multi-node linear network framework, the study formulates a joint optimization problem for power and gain allocation aimed at maximizing the minimum SNR margin. Practical constraints, such as MM-EDFA saturation power and maximum gain limits, are integrated, and the problem is resolved using convex optimization techniques. Three distinct scenarios are evaluated: (1) equal power and equal MM-EDFA gain across all spans for every channel and mode, where gain matches span loss; (2) unequal power allocation among channels and modes while maintaining equal MM-EDFA gain across spans; and (3) a fully optimized approach where both the power assigned to each channel and mode and the MM-EDFA gain for each span are independently optimized.

We examined 39 ks of NuSTAR observations of the high-mass X-ray binary Cen X-3 to study spectral variations linked to orbital and spin phases. Covering an orbital phase range of $\Phi=0.199$–$0.414$ (with $\Phi=0$ marking mid-eclipse), our orbital-phase-resolved spectroscopy indicated that low-energy photons dominate the spectral fluctuations, suggesting that variability largely stems from absorption by stellar wind clumps. Conversely, spin-phase-resolved spectroscopy combined with energy-resolved pulse profiles revealed significant flux changes in high-energy bands, pointing to varying Comptonization efficiencies within the accretion column as the source of variability. Distinct variability was observed in energy bands containing Fe emission lines or cyclotron resonance scattering features (CRSF) compared to adjacent bands. Specifically, Fe lines exhibited low variability across the spin phase, implying their emission regions are distant from the neutron star. Additionally, both the central energy and strength of the CRSF showed a positive correlation with spin-phase-resolved flux, indicating that photons from high-flux regions traverse stronger magnetic fields and deeper absorption zones. Finally, our analysis of the independence between orbital and spin-phase variability found no correlation, suggesting that the accretion stream remained stable throughout the observation.

Fact verification using structured data is crucial for numerous real-world scenarios but remains a difficult research challenge, especially when it requires combining symbolic operations with informal inference derived from language understanding. This paper introduces Program-enhanced Verbalization and Graph Attention Network (ProgVGAT), a framework that integrates program execution into textual inference models. Specifically, we propose a verbalization model that incorporates program execution to gather evidence embedded within table operations. Building on this, we develop Graph Attention Verification Networks designed to synthesize diverse evidence sources—including those from verbalized program execution, program structures, and original statements and tables—to reach a final verification conclusion. To support this framework, we introduce a program selection module optimized with a novel margin loss-based training strategy to generate more precise programs, which has proven effective in improving verification outcomes. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework achieves new state-of-the-art performance on the TABFACT benchmark dataset, reaching an accuracy of 74.4%.

A linear dashpot model is used to analyze a single ball bouncing against a rigid surface. It is demonstrated that incorporating gravity causes the coefficient of restitution to vary with impact velocity, differing from earlier studies that neglected gravitational effects. This velocity dependence is most significant at low impact speeds and high damping levels. Previous analyses have varied in their definition of contact: some assume contact persists as long as compression is non-zero, while others end the collision earlier to avoid generating attractive forces. This study compares these differing approaches and suggests a hybrid model. This hybrid model effectively replicates experimental data regarding a cart bouncing repeatedly on a spring.

This study presents a second-order framework for bilevel optimization, a mathematical programming domain where the solution to a parameterized lower-level problem is optimized at an upper level. While current methods typically rely on first-order sensitivity analysis via the implicit function theorem (IFT) to compute gradients for the lower-level solution and apply first-order optimization techniques to the upper level, this paper extends such analysis to generate second-order derivative information (the IFT Hessian). This extension facilitates the application of faster-converging second-order optimization algorithms at the upper level. Our analysis demonstrates that (i) computations for the IFT gradient can largely be repurposed for the IFT Hessian, (ii) error bounds established for the IFT gradient are directly applicable to the IFT Hessian, and (iii) calculating IFT Hessians can substantially reduce total computational cost by extracting more information from each lower-level solve. We validate these results and illustrate the method's versatility through applications in least squares hyperparameter auto-tuning, multi-class SVM auto-tuning, and inverse optimal control.

In their 2006 work "Finite element exterior calculus, homological techniques, and applications," Arnold, Falk, and Winther demonstrated the geometric decomposition of both full and trimmed polynomial spaces on simplicial elements into direct sums of trace-free subspaces. Their 2009 paper, "Geometric decompositions and local bases for finite element differential forms," subsequently provided direct constructions of extension operators for these same spaces. Previously, these two families were addressed separately, utilizing distinct isomorphisms to map each to the other's trace-free subspaces and employing mutually incompatible extension operators. This new work introduces a unified operator, $\mathring{\star}_T$, that consolidates the two separate isomorphisms and establishes a weighted-$L^2$ norm suitable for creating well-conditioned basis and dual-basis functionals for geometric decomposition. Furthermore, it defines a single extension operator, $\dot{E}_{\sigma,T}$, capable of performing geometric decompositions for all differential forms, as well as for the full and trimmed polynomial spaces individually.

The Spitzer Survey of Stellar Structure in Galaxies (S$^{4}$G) is a comprehensive near-infrared investigation of more than 2300 nearby galaxies, significantly advancing our knowledge of their structural details. However, because the original sample relied solely on radio-derived velocities for selection, it exhibited a bias toward late-type disk galaxies, underrepresenting lenticular and elliptical systems. To address this, a subsequent Spitzer survey was launched, incorporating 465 early-type galaxies (ETGs) into the dataset for analysis consistent with the initial study. This release presents the ETG extension data up to the third processing pipeline (P3), focusing on surface photometry. Using reduced and masked Spitzer IRAC 3.6$\mu$m and 4.5$\mu$m images processed through Pipelines 1 and 2, respectively, we generated curves of growth and radial surface brightness profiles, applying both standard and inclination-corrected methods. From these profiles, we calculated integrated properties including total magnitudes, stellar masses, concentration indices, and size metrics, while also illustrating NIR scaling relations for ETGs. Our analysis explores trends across the entire S$^{4}$G and the ETG extension, emphasizing distinctions between early-type and late-type galaxies (LTGs). Results indicate that ETGs are, on average, more massive and concentrated than LTGs, with subtle variations observed among ETG morphological subtypes. Furthermore, we derived scaling relations for mass–size (half-light and isophotal), mass–concentration, mass–surface brightness (central, effective, and within 1 kpc), and mass–color, comparing them against prior visible light studies. We observe strong agreement with previous findings, although certain relationships, such as mass–central surface brightness, necessitate more rigorous multi-component decompositions for full interpretation.

Although deep residual networks consistently outperform traditional feed-forward networks in accuracy, the reasons for their efficacy remain unclear. This study conducts a spectral analysis of Residual Neural Tangent Kernels (ResNTK) within the context of massively over-parameterized, fully connected residual networks utilizing ReLU activations. We demonstrate that, similar to standard FC-NTK, when inputs are uniformly distributed on the hypersphere $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, the eigenfunctions of ResNTK correspond to spherical harmonics, while eigenvalues decrease polynomially with frequency $k$ at a rate of $k^{-d}$. These findings indicate that the Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space associated with ResNTK contains the same functions as both FC-NTK and the Laplace kernel. Furthermore, by leveraging the analogy to the Laplace kernel, we show that a specific hyper-parameter governing the balance between skip and residual connections determines whether ResNTK exhibits the depth-dependent spikiness observed in FC-NTK or retains a stable form.

Although classical control methods like PID and LQR are effective for maintaining system states, their implementation grows increasingly difficult as model dynamics become more complex and sensitive. Consequently, these techniques often fail for adaptive robotic locomotion tasks involving multiple degrees of freedom. In contrast, reinforcement learning can easily train optimal walking policies. This study applies Deep Q-learning and Augmented Random Search (ARS) to teach a simulated 2D bipedal robot to walk within the OpenAI Gym BipedalWalker-v3 environment. While Deep Q-learning failed to achieve a high-reward policy, frequently converging prematurely to suboptimal local maxima likely due to a coarsely discretized action space, ARS successfully trained a superior robot. The ARS approach generated an optimal policy that officially "solves" the BipedalWalker-v3 challenge. To evaluate the learning algorithm's performance, several naive policies—specifically a random policy, a manually encoded inch-forward policy, and a stay-still policy—were used as benchmarks.

The magnetic properties of BaCuTe$_{2}$O$_{6}$, a member of the $A$CuTe$_2$O$_{6}$ family characterized by complex 3D frustrated spin networks and potential spin-liquid behavior, have been investigated using X-ray diffraction, thermodynamic data, and density-functional band-structure calculations. The temperature-dependent magnetic susceptibility and heat capacity of this barium compound align well with the one-dimensional spin-$\frac12$ Heisenberg chain model, similar to its strontium analog, SrCuTe$_2$O$_{6}$. Although the intrachain coupling constant decreases from 49 K in the Sr compound to approximately 37 K in the Ba compound, the Néel temperature rises from 5.5 K to 6.1 K. In contrast to the Sr variant, BaCuTe$_{2}$O$_{6}$ exhibits only a single magnetic transition with indications of weak spin canting. We clarify the microscopic distinctions between the two compounds, proposing that substituting Sr with Ba induces negative pressure that flips the sign of one interchain coupling. Furthermore, the Néel temperature of BaCuTe$_{2}$O$_{6}$ demonstrates remarkable resilience against magnetic dilution by Zn$^{2+}$, remaining stable even at concentrations up to 20%.

Data compression is extensively employed in modern column-oriented database management systems to reduce storage requirements and accelerate query execution. Early systems adopted compression to alleviate disk bandwidth constraints by sacrificing CPU resources. However, this approach creates a critical trade-off between compression ratios and the computational cost of decompression. Prior research indicated that lightweight compression schemes with minimal decompression overhead outperformed heavier alternatives in columnar stores. Yet, significant advancements have occurred since those findings regarding CPU, RAM, and disk capabilities, alongside the emergence of new compression algorithms.

This paper re-examines compression strategies for disk-based column stores, specifically investigating the I/O-RAM scheme. This approach utilizes two distinct page sizes: compressed pages on disk and uncompressed pages in memory, where the buffer manager handles decompression immediately upon disk arrival. Although widely adopted due to its implementation simplicity and usage in various modern column and row stores, this method warrants re-evaluation. We address three key research questions: (1) Do heavy-weight compression schemes remain unsuitable for disk-based column stores? (2) Have newer lightweight algorithms surpassed older ones? (3) Is there a necessity for SIMD-based decompression algorithms in disk-based environments? These inquiries are explored experimentally using a columnar query engine and the Star Schema Benchmark.

The histopathological evaluation of colorectal polyps is essential for customizing patient care and surveillance strategies, ultimately aiming to prevent or early detect invasive carcinoma. This characterization depends on analyzing tissue samples histologically to assess malignancy and the degree of dysplasia. Although deep neural networks demonstrate remarkable accuracy in recognizing medical patterns, they necessitate extensive sets of annotated training images. We present UniToPatho, a curated dataset comprising 9,536 hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed to facilitate the training of deep neural networks for colorectal polyp classification and adenoma grading. Additionally, we introduce this dataset and offer insights into addressing the challenges of automatic colorectal polyp characterization.

We present a novel numerical technique for addressing time-harmonic acoustic scattering, specifically targeting plane waves interacting with smoothly varying material inhomogeneities. While applicable across all frequencies $\omega$, the method demonstrates particular efficiency in high-frequency scenarios. Built upon a time-domain framework, the approach comprises three stages: \emph{i)} generating an incoming plane wavelet with compact support along the propagation direction; \emph{ii)} resolving the scattering event in the time domain for this wavelet; and \emph{iii)} recovering the time-harmonic solution through a temporal Fourier transform of the time-domain result. A critical component is a front-tracking mesh adaptation algorithm employed in stage \emph{ii)}. By leveraging the localized nature of the wave front, this strategy significantly reduces the dependency of the required degrees of freedom on the frequency $\omega$ to achieve a specified accuracy. Furthermore, we introduce a specialized algorithm for the Fourier transform in stage \emph{iii)} that capitalizes on the reduced degrees of freedom inherent to the adapted meshes. Numerical tests validate the method's advantages and confirm its applicability to external source terms, including point sources and sound-soft scatterers. However, the achieved efficiency is constrained when trapping modes are present.

Cattle farming contributes 8.8% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Beyond methane released through digestion, the expanding demand for grazing land is a significant cause of deforestation. Although regulations exist to protect the Amazon from such clearing, they are frequently violated, creating an urgent need to scale and automate the monitoring of cattle ranching. In partnership with \textit{Global Witness}, we investigated the feasibility of tracking and counting cattle across the continent using satellite imagery. Utilizing a license from Maxar Technologies, we acquired 40cm resolution satellite images of the Amazon and constructed a dataset comprising 903 images with a total of 28,498 cattle. Our experiments yielded promising results, identifying key avenues for future improvements in counting algorithms and data collection methods to address these challenges. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/IssamLaradji/cownter_strike}.

Continuous "bump" attractors serve as a well-recognized framework for modeling cortical working memory involving continuous variables, realizable through diverse neuron and network architectures. This study introduces a versatile methodology for approximating bump states within continuous attractor networks composed of both rate-based and spiking neurons. By employing a low-dimensional parametrization of the spatial firing rate profile, the approach enables the use of efficient numerical optimization techniques. Leveraging this theoretical framework, we derive a correspondence between network architecture and attractor characteristics, facilitating the prediction of how network parameters influence steady-state firing rate profiles and bump existence, as well as the inverse capability to adjust network configurations to generate bumps with specific shapes.

Standard inference methods for cosmic large-scale structure rely on summary statistics matched against analytic models using a Gaussian likelihood and pre-calculated covariance matrices. To address the simplifying assumptions regarding likelihood forms and the data complexity associated with this conventional method, we explore simulation-based inference (SBI). SBI utilizes neural networks to learn the likelihood as a parameterized probability density. We developed a suite of simulated, exactly Gaussian-distributed data vectors tailored for the latest Kilo-Degree Survey (KiDS) weak gravitational lensing analysis, showing that SBI successfully recovers the complete 12-dimensional KiDS posterior distribution using fewer than $10^4$ simulations. Our simulation strategy was refined by first sampling the parameter space with a hypercube, then adding batches of points through active learning. The data compression within our SBI framework proves robust against suboptimal choices of fiducial parameter values and data covariance. Consequently, when paired with a rapid simulator, SBI emerges as a competitive and more flexible alternative to standard inference techniques.
We provide an overview of quantum gravity, string theory, and black holes, summarizing the white papers submitted for this subject as part of the Snowmass process.

Within the quark delocalization color screening model (QDCSM), we examine meson-meson interactions in a fully light four-quark system. Our calculations of effective potentials for all $S$-wave states reveal that vector meson pairs generally experience an attractive force, whereas interactions between a pseudoscalar and a vector meson are either repulsive or only weakly attractive. In contrast, two pseudoscalar mesons always repel each other, with notable exceptions: the $IJ=00$ $\pi\pi$ channel is attractive, while the $IJ=02$ $\phi\phi$ channel remains repulsive. Consequently, the current calculations do not support the use of the $S$-wave $\phi\phi$ state to explain the $X(2239)$, whereas $S$-wave $\rho\rho$ states are more promising candidates for resonance and warrant further investigation. Furthermore, analyzing the contributions of individual interaction terms highlights that both one-gluon exchange and kinetic energy interactions are crucial. Additionally, varying the delocalization parameter demonstrates that kinetic energy contributes to an intermediate-range attraction mechanism within QDCSM, a phenomenon driven by quark delocalization.

In our earlier study, the X-ray spectra of the narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy IRAS 13224$-$3809 were modeled using a disc reflection model with a fixed electron density of $10^{15}$ cm$^{-3}$, necessitating an extra blackbody component to account for the soft X-ray excess below 2 keV. This current work presents a simultaneous analysis of five flux-resolved XMM-Newton spectra totaling 2 Ms of data for this source. We employed a disc reflection model featuring an electron density of $n_{\rm e}\approx10^{20}$ cm$^{-3}$ and an iron abundance of $Z_{\rm Fe}=3.2\pm0.5Z_{\odot}$ to fit the broad-band spectra, finding no need for an additional component to model the soft excess. The resulting best-fit model yields consistent measurements of black hole spin and disc inclination compared to previous models assuming lower disc densities. Finally, utilizing the best-fit density and ionization parameters, we calculated the average illumination distance between the corona and the disc reflection region. Assuming a black hole mass of $2\times10^{6}M_{\odot}$, this distance varies from 0.43$\sqrt{f_{\rm AD}/f_{\rm INF}}$ $r_{\rm g}$ in the lowest flux state to 1.71$\sqrt{f_{\rm AD}/f_{\rm INF}}$ $r_{\rm g}$ in the highest flux state, where $f_{\rm AD}/f_{\rm INF}$ represents the ratio of coronal flux reaching the disc versus infinity. As this ratio relies on the coronal geometry, we evaluate it solely within the context of the simple `lamp-post' model, noting that future detailed modeling of the disc emissivity profile is necessary to determine the exact coronal structure.

Sound field decomposition estimates waveforms in any direction based on inputs from a restricted set of microphones, serving as a critical foundation for downstream applications like source localization, separation, and spatial audio reproduction. Traditional approaches, such as Ambisonics, suffer from limited spatial resolution. This paper introduces a learning-based Neural Sound Field Decomposition (NeSD) framework capable of achieving fine spatial directional resolution using recordings from a few microphone capsules placed at arbitrary locations. The NeSD system takes microphone signals, their specific positions, and the queried directions as inputs, producing outputs that include the waveform and the presence probability at the queried position. Various neural network architectures, including fully connected, time delay, and recurrent networks, are employed to model the NeSD system. Experimental results demonstrate that these NeSD systems surpass conventional Ambisonics and DOANet methods in sound field decomposition and source localization across speech, music, and sound event datasets. Demonstrations can be viewed at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0GIr6doj3BQ.

Multi-view clustering remains a critical but demanding task within machine learning and data mining. A prevalent approach involves matrix factorization, which reduces data to lower-dimensional spaces to mitigate the curse of dimensionality while extracting meaningful features. However, current methodologies face two primary limitations: first, most matrix factorization techniques are restricted to shallow depths, hindering the full extraction of latent information, and existing deep variants lack clear guidance for selecting representation dimensions across layers. Second, prevailing methods prioritize shared information across views while neglecting unique local features specific to individual views. To address these challenges, we introduce MVC-DMF-GGR, a novel Multi-View Clustering framework utilizing Deep semi-NMF and Global Graph Refinement. Our approach captures new representation matrices for each view through hierarchical decomposition and learns a consensus graph by approximating a combination of graphs reconstructed from these representations, thereby refining the new representations iteratively. We further develop an alternating algorithm with proven convergence to solve the associated optimization problem. Experimental results on six multi-view benchmark datasets confirm the efficacy and superiority of our proposed method.

Quantum coherence serves as a defining characteristic that distinguishes quantum mechanics from classical physics. Recent research has increasingly focused on treating coherence as a resource, examining its extraction and utility in quantum technologies. This paper reviews advancements in this field, with a specific emphasis on recent experimental developments. Following a concise overview of the foundational theory, the discussion covers primary experimental platforms, including linear optics, nuclear magnetic resonance, and superconducting systems. The review further addresses methods for detecting and quantifying coherence, state conversion, coherence distillation, and the dynamics of coherence. Additionally, it examines experimental studies linking coherence to uncertainty relations, path information, and the coherence of operations and measurements, while also discussing efforts involving multipartite and multilevel coherence.

The Laboratorio Subterráneo de Canfranc (LSC) serves as the national center for low-radioactivity methodologies and their related scientific and technological applications. Airborne radon concentration represents a significant portion of the radioactive background near the detectors. To address this, the LSC operates a Radon Abatement System (RAS) that supplies air with radon levels below 1 mBq/m³ of ²²²Rn. An Electrostatic Radon Monitor (ERM) continuously tracks radon content. Measurements from double-beta decay demonstrators (NEXT-NEW and CROSS) and gamma HPGe detectors confirm the substantial decrease in radioactive background achieved by using the purified air around the detectors. Additionally, this paper discusses the facility's role in the LSC's current program, which encompasses the NEXT-100 experiment, low-background biology studies, and radiopure copper electroformation equipment housed in a radon-free clean room.

Deep learning semantic segmentation algorithms are capable of localizing abnormalities or opacities in chest radiographs; however, gathering and annotating the necessary training data is costly and demands specialized expertise, creating a bottleneck for algorithmic performance. This study examines how image augmentation techniques can mitigate the need for labeled data in semantic segmentation tasks for pneumonia detection in chest X-rays. We trained fully convolutional networks on varying subsets of the total training data, applying distinct augmentation strategies to each model and comparing their performance against a baseline trained on the full dataset without augmentation. Our results indicate that rotation and mixup are the most effective augmentations among rotate, mixup, translate, gamma, and horizontal flip. These methods reduce the requirement for labeled data by 70% while achieving performance in AUC and mean IoU that is comparable to the baseline.

This work investigates how fluctuations in cosmological fluid fields influence the homogeneous energy density and alter the Friedmann equations. Generally, accounting for backreaction necessitates moving beyond the pressureless ideal fluid model, which can result in a diminished growth of large-scale cosmic structures. Given that observations align closely with the standard linear growth mode, we concentrate on two-component fluids where the non-ideal component is gravitationally linked to cold dark matter, thereby maintaining a standard growth trajectory; this scenario is exemplified by a baryonic fluid interacting with cold dark matter. We compute the backreaction for this specific case and across a broad spectrum of other two-fluid models. In these instances, the effect is either negligible due to the minute magnitude of non-ideal matter properties or constrained by an overly strict ultraviolet cutoff in the power spectrum integral. Finally, we examine matter field backreaction from a wider viewpoint and extend the formalism to accommodate far-from-equilibrium conditions pertinent to late cosmological epochs and non-linear scales for future applications.

Although image captioning has advanced significantly, current models generally lack the flexibility to produce captions with specific styles, such as varying levels of detail or emotional tone. This paper demonstrates that a unified model can effectively operate across diverse domains and seamlessly switch between multiple styles. We achieve this controllability by integrating prompt learning into the image captioning framework. Specifically, we design a set of prompts to fine-tune a pre-trained captioner, enabling it to jointly train on stylized data from various domains without compromising performance in any single domain. Moreover, we optimize these prompts using learnable vectors within the continuous word embedding space, which eliminates the need for heuristic prompt engineering and yields superior results. During inference, the model generates desired stylized captions by selecting the appropriate prompts. Extensive experiments confirm the controllability of our approach, with notable outstanding performance on two distinct benchmarks: the COCO Karpathy split and TextCaps, both utilizing a single unified model.

We define conditions under which global weak solutions to a stochastic Keller-Segel model on $\mathbb{R}^2$, featuring spatially inhomogeneous conservative noise, fail to exist with positive probability. By analyzing the dynamics of both centred and non-centred variances in weak solutions, we derive a criterion linking chemotactic sensitivity to the initial variance, regularity, and noise intensity. Notably, for noise that is arbitrarily spatially uncorrelated, our blow-up condition aligns with that of a deterministic Keller-Segel model characterized by increased viscosity.

Training 3D object detection and semantic segmentation models on lidar point clouds typically demands costly annotations. To address this, we introduce a data augmentation strategy that leverages existing annotated datasets repeatedly. Our proposed framework reutilizes real-world data by automatically identifying appropriate scene locations for augmentation and explicitly managing occlusions. By integrating actual scan points for newly inserted objects, the method preserves the physical attributes of lidar data, including intensity and raydrop. This pipeline demonstrates competitiveness in training high-performance models for both 3D detection and segmentation. Furthermore, the approach yields substantial performance improvements for rare and critical classes, achieving a 6.65% average precision increase for the "Hard" pedestrian category in KITTI detection and a 2.14 mean IoU gain in the SemanticKITTI segmentation challenge compared to state-of-the-art methods.

This paper investigates information leakage to a guessing adversary within the context of zero-error source coding, where the source coding problem is characterized by a confusion graph that defines the distinguishability of source symbols. The leakage metric is defined as the ratio between an adversary's successful guessing probability after and before observing the codeword, maximized across all possible source distributions. This specific measurement, under a basic adversarial model involving a single guess with no distortion between the estimator and the true sequence, is recognized in the literature as maximum min-entropy leakage or maximal leakage. We present a single-letter characterization of the optimal normalized leakage for this basic model, alongside an optimal scalar stochastic mapping scheme. Notably, we observe that the optimal normalized leakage equals the optimal compression rate for fixed-length source codes, and both can be achieved simultaneously by specific deterministic coding schemes. Furthermore, we extend the leakage measurement to generalized adversarial models where adversaries make multiple guesses and tolerate a certain level of distortion, deriving corresponding single-letter lower and upper bounds.

This study demonstrates that the structural characteristics and phase behavior of a self-avoiding polymer chain adhering to a substrate, while being pulled from one end, can be effectively analyzed using a Grand Canonical Ensemble (GCE) framework. We present analytical formulas for the average lengths of fundamental adsorbed structural elements—specifically loops and tails—as functions of adhesive potential and detachment force, and we calculate the universal exponents that dictate their probability distributions. Significantly, our results indicate that the previously debated critical adsorption exponent $\phi$ is fundamentally determined by the interactions between distinct loops. Furthermore, the chain detachment transition is identified as a first-order process, though it is dichotomic, meaning no phase coexistence occurs. These new theoretical insights, along with the proposed phase diagram for the adsorption-desorption transition under external pulling, are corroborated by comprehensive Monte Carlo simulations.

This study examines an integrated visible light positioning and communication (VLPC) system utilizing a single LED lamp. Initially, we exploit the dependency of the VLC channel model on the receiver's location to propose a system model that estimates channel state information (CSI) from positioning data, eliminating the need for pilot sequence transmission. Subsequently, we derive the Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB) for positioning error variance and establish a lower bound on the achievable rate using on-off keying modulation. Building on these performance metrics, we optimize power allocation to minimize the CRLB subject to a rate outage probability constraint. To address the resulting non-convex optimization challenge, we employ worst-case Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) distribution and block coordinate descent (BCD) methods to generate feasible solutions. Finally, numerical simulations illustrate the impact of key system parameters, including outage probability, rate thresholds, and total power limits.

Frame theory is a dynamic and captivating field with diverse applications across pure and applied mathematics. This paper introduces and investigates the notion of Controlled Continuous $\ast$-$g$-Frames within Hilbert $C^{\ast}$-Modules, serving as a generalization of discrete controlled $\ast$-$g$-Frames in the same context. Additionally, we establish several key properties of these structures.

Validating claims involves reasoning across extensive knowledge bases, typically composed of trusted corpora. A prevalent method entails retrieving brief, relevant text segments from reference documents and feeding them into a natural language inference module to determine if the claim is supported or contradicted. However, this approach falters when evidence must be synthesized from multiple documents, as retrieval systems often overlook individual documents that are only tangentially related to the claim. We hypothesize that a graph-based methodology could effectively uncover fragmented evidence. To test this, we constructed a comprehensive graph spanning the entire corpus, linking text segments via mentioned entities, and utilized this structure to identify candidate evidence sets from diverse sources. Our experimental results indicate that employing a graph structure significantly aids in pinpointing a concise set of passages pertinent to a specific claim.

We demonstrate that thermodynamic scaling emerges from the integration of the Murnaghan equation of state (EOS) with the generalized entropy theory (GET) of glass formation. In this framework, thermodynamic scaling manifests within the non-Arrhenius relaxation regime as a property of the fluid's configurational entropy density ($s_c$), when normalized by its value $s_c^*$ at the glass onset temperature $T_A$ ($s_c / s_c^*$). Consequently, a constant $TV^{\gamma}$ signifies a reduced isoentropic fluid condition. Molecular dynamics simulations of a coarse-grained polymer melt validate that the predicted thermodynamic scaling of the structural relaxation time $\tau_{\alpha}$ via GET holds both above and below $T_A$. Additionally, these simulations test whether the extent $L$ of stringlike collective motion, normalized by its value $L_A$ at $T_A$, also adheres to thermodynamic scaling, a requirement for theoretical consistency. While simulations confirm the predicted scaling for both $\tau_{\alpha}$ and $L/L_A$, they reveal that the isothermal compressibility $\kappa_T$ and the long-wavelength limit $S(0)$ of the static structure factor do not exhibit such scaling; this finding seemingly invalidates certain glass formation models that prioritize fluid "structure" over configurational entropy. However, by establishing a low-temperature hyperuniform reference state, we define a compressibility relative to this condition, $\delta \kappa_T$. This transformed dimensionless variable exhibits thermodynamic scaling and correlates directly with $s_c / s_c^*$. Furthermore, the Murnaghan EOS enables the interpretation of $\gamma$ as a quantifier of the intrinsic anharmonicity of intermolecular interactions, a parameter that can be directly derived from the pressure derivative of the material's bulk modulus.

We solve the Dirac equation across three distinct regions of graphene to derive energy spectrum solutions linked to strain, energy gaps, and magnetic fields. By applying the stationary phase approximation after matching wave functions at the interfaces, we calculate the Goos-H\"anchen shifts and group delay time. Our findings indicate that the group delay time is affected by strain in both armchair and zigzag orientations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that gate voltage and strain can modulate the group delay between subluminal and superluminal regimes, a capability with significant potential for high-speed graphene-based nanoelectronics.

This paper introduces an abstract framework for type theory designed to unify the semantics of diverse systems, such as Martin-Löf type theory, two-level type theory, and cubical type theory. We demonstrate fundamental semantic results: each type theory possesses a bi-initial model, every model of a type theory yields an internal language, and the category of theories relative to a given type theory is bi-equivalent to a full sub-2-category within the 2-category of models for that theory.

With the advent of practical quantum computers, it becomes essential to comprehend the constraints of classical support infrastructure and create mitigation strategies for efficient qubit usage. This paper examines three primary bottlenecks in near-term quantum systems: bandwidth constraints caused by data exchange between CPUs and QPUs, latency delays inherent in round-trip hardware communication, and timing limitations stemming from elevated error rates. To illustrate each bottleneck, we analyze a specific near-term quantum algorithm: randomized benchmarking demonstrates bandwidth issues, adaptive algorithms for the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era address latency, and quantum error correction techniques reveal restrictions due to qubit error rates. In every scenario, we explore how these limitations emerge from the current model of offloading all classical computation to the CPU, and we propose that granting access to local classical computing resources within the QPU offers a viable path to mitigation.

In 2011, Nair established a no-go theorem for quantum radar target detection [Phys. Rev. A {\bf 84}, 032312 (2011)], demonstrating that under general conditions, a coherent-state radar's error probability remains within a factor of two of the optimal quantum performance for a pure-loss channel (without background radiation) where the roundtrip transmissivity $\kappa$ is much less than one. We propose first-photon radars (FPRs) to surpass this limit. FPRs emit a periodic train of pulses, each with an average of $N_S$ photons, and utilize ideal photon counting (unit efficiency, no dark counts) on the return signal until either a photon is detected or a maximum of $M$ pulses are sent. A target is confirmed only if at least one photon is registered. We analyze both quantum FPRs (using number states) and classical FPRs (using coherent states), finding that their error-probability exponents are nearly identical when $\kappa \ll 1$. Under the stricter condition $\kappa N_S \ll 1$, the advantage over Nair's limit in terms of error-probability exponent approaches 3 dB as $M$ becomes large. However, since the pulse repetition interval must exceed the roundtrip propagation delay, standoff sensing of moving targets will likely operate with $\kappa N_S \sim 1$ and $M \sim 10$, yielding an approximate 2 dB improvement. This research presents a new no-go theorem for quantum radar target detection.

Quantum reading establishes a general framework for formulating the statistical discrimination of quantum channels, though several approaches have already been explored in this area. Significant work remains, particularly in optimizing channel discrimination through classical coding schemes. Two key open questions stand out: how to design encoding schemes with low complexity that are effective for channel discrimination, and, more critically, how to develop protocols that achieve channel capacity. This paper addresses these challenges by utilizing polar codes. We begin by characterizing the rate and reliability of channels under polar encoding. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed scheme's error probability decreases exponentially as the code length increases. Finally, we provide an analysis of the optimal quantum states suitable for use as probes.

Alongside the recently developed CLIC detector model, CLICdet, a new software framework was released for simulating and reconstructing detector events. This note provides an overview of CLICdet and outlines the experimental conditions at 380 GeV and 3 TeV, covering beam-induced backgrounds. It details the simulation and reconstruction tools and evaluates physics performance regarding single particles, particles within jets, jet energy resolution, and flavor tagging. Additionally, the capabilities of the very forward electromagnetic calorimeters are examined.

Inductive program synthesis, which involves deriving code from examples of intended behavior, provides a versatile framework for creating machine learning systems that are robust, interpretable, and capable of generalization. Successful program synthesis relies on two essential components: a comprehensive function library for constructing programs and an efficient search mechanism to identify solutions for specific tasks. We present LAPS (Language for Abstraction and Program Search), a method that leverages natural language annotations to simultaneously train function libraries and neural search models. When combined with the state-of-the-art library learning system DreamCoder, LAPS generates superior libraries and enhances both search efficiency and generalization across three domains—string editing, image composition, and abstract scene reasoning—even in scenarios where no natural language hints are provided during testing.

How do spousal matching and occupational characteristics collectively influence the distribution of COVID-19 health risks? This study examines the link between COVID-19 incidence and the extent to which couples sort into jobs with varying levels of workplace contact. The proposed mechanism suggests that higher levels of positive spousal sorting reduce intra-household transmission, thereby lowering the overall number of individuals exposed to the virus. Leveraging U.S. state-level data, I argue that spousal sorting is a critical factor in explaining early pandemic disparities in COVID-19 prevalence. First, I find that this sorting pattern exposes approximately two-thirds of U.S. dual-earner couples to elevated health risks due to within-home transmission. Second, I reveal significant variation in the degree of spousal sorting across states. For the first week of April 2020, my estimates indicate that a one standard deviation increase in spousal sorting correlates with a 30% decrease in total cases and a 39.3% reduction in total deaths per 100,000 residents. Additionally, I observe substantial temporal heterogeneity, as these effects diminish over time. These findings highlight the significance of policies designed to mitigate intra-household contagion.

This paper investigates the algebraic characteristics of binary relations associated with smooth digraphs, defined as those lacking sources or sinks. These relations are alternatively characterized as surjective hyper-operations (shops) on their vertex sets or as total binary relations with total inverses, a concept previously termed "multipermutations." We analyze the lattice structure of monoids comprising multipermutations over an n-element domain. Via a Galois connection, these monoids correspond to relation sets closed under definability in positive first-order logic without equality; while the definability side was explored earlier, this work details the monoid side. We examine the inverse property of multipermutations and its role in linking our monoids to groups. Utilizing these findings, we establish a dichotomy theorem for the evaluation problem of positive first-order logic without equality on structures where the preserving multipermutations form a monoid closed under inversion. Consequently, these problems are either solvable in Logspace or are Pspace-complete. Furthermore, we study the monoid of all multipermutations on an n-element domain under standard relational composition, characterizing its Green relations and regular elements, and demonstrating that no polynomial-sized generating set exists for this monoid.

Lyncs-API serves as a Python toolkit tailored for Lattice QCD applications, enabling users to execute diverse Lattice QCD libraries directly within Python code. Its objective is to deliver a streamlined programming environment without compromising performance across different platforms by establishing a unified framework for various Lattice QCD software tools. Consequently, it offers interfaces to packages such as c-lime, DDalphaAMG, tmLQCD, and QUDA. This paper specifically examines the Lyncs-QUDA interface, which connects Lyncs to QUDA, and provides a brief tutorial on utilizing this Python interface to conduct a HMC simulation powered by QUDA.

Nonlinear nanophotonics utilizes engineered nanostructures to concentrate light into minute volumes, thereby amplifying nonlinear optical effects with precise spectral and spatial control. Given graphene's inherently robust and electrically adjustable nonlinear optical response, it stands out as a highly promising nanomaterial for nonlinear optoelectronic applications. In this study, we demonstrate exceptionally high optical nonlinearities within graphene-insulator-metal heterostructures, achieving a three-order-of-magnitude boost in the third-harmonic signal relative to bare graphene. Moreover, by raising the graphene Fermi energy via an external gate voltage, we observe that graphene plasmons drive the optical nonlinearity and modulate the third-harmonic output. These results indicate that graphene-insulator-metal heterostructures are ideal candidates for developing optically controlled and electrically tunable nano-optoelectronic devices.

We demonstrate that Maxwell's equations in $(D+1)$-dimensional Minkowski space-time $\mathcal{M}$, specifically for $D=1$, $2$, and $3$, emerge from an integral formulation of the zero-curvature condition defined on the associated loop space $\mathcal{L}^{(D-1)}(\mathcal{M})$. Within this framework, electric charge conservation arises as a consequence of an underlying symmetry.

Action Unit (AU) detection is a core domain within affective computing focused on identifying distinct facial muscle movements. This capability is essential for developing unbiased computational face representations, sparking significant interest recently. A primary hurdle in constructing efficient deep learning-based AU detection systems is the scarcity of large-scale facial image databases annotated by experts. The ABAW challenge addresses this limitation by providing a dataset comprising 2 million frames annotated with AUs, thereby facilitating advancements in the field. This paper details our submission to the ABAW3 challenge. Briefly, we employed a multi-label detection transformer utilizing multi-head attention mechanisms to determine which regions of the face image are most critical for predicting each AU.

Amid the COVID-19 pandemic, a multitude of visualizations were developed to disseminate information to the general public. During public health emergencies, exposure to such information can shape public attitudes and responses to risks, thereby influencing the pandemic's course. Consequently, there is a pressing need to document, organize, and investigate the range of COVID-19 visualizations shared with the public. This study fills that gap by analyzing 668 such visualizations. Our findings are presented through a conceptual framework derived from this analysis, which explores who utilizes what data to convey specific messages, in what formats, and under what conditions within the context of the COVID-19 crisis. We outline a set of factors to consider for each component of this framework and conclude by offering directions for future research in crisis visualization.
In this brief note, we address and rectify a renowned counterexample presented in Dacorogna's seminal book [2].

Although feature representations from models pre-trained on large-scale datasets demonstrate broad generalizability across various audio analysis tasks, task-specific features often surpass them when ample training data exists, as they can capture properties unique to the specific task. Additionally, the computational overhead of complex pre-trained models during inference is significant. We introduce two regularization techniques that combine detailed task-specific features extracted from spectrograms with generic pre-trained features, ensuring that the inference workload remains minimal since pre-trained features are utilized only during training. Experiments utilizing VGGish, OpenL3, and their combination reveal that our proposed methods not only exceed baseline performance but also enhance state-of-the-art models on multiple audio classification tasks. Furthermore, the results indicate that leveraging a mixture of features yields superior performance compared to using individual feature sets alone.

This study introduces a technique for rejecting out-of-distribution samples that is compatible with any network architecture and eliminates the need for extra training data. A standard ResNet-50 model was trained to identify emphysema using publicly available chest x-rays comprising 38,353 images. Descriptors representing the training data distribution were derived from feature activations in intermediate layers. A new metric, FRODO, was calculated by determining the Mahalanobis distance between new test samples and the established training distribution.
