The approach was evaluated on a held-out test set of 21,176 in-distribution chest x-rays and 14,821 out-of-distribution images featuring incorrect orientation or anatomy. In classifying test samples as either in- or out-of-distribution, the method achieved an AUC score of 0.99.

Observational research on Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) within the mid-infrared spectrum is essential for comprehending AGN and their influence on galaxy evolution. Selecting AGN based on mid-infrared data complements conventional methods, enabling a more comprehensive catalog of AGN activity throughout cosmic history. Mid-infrared observations, which encompass time variability and spatially resolved imaging, have provided distinct insights into the obscuring structures surrounding AGN. The abundance of fine structure, molecular, and dust signatures in this regime allows for the simultaneous investigation of multiple interstellar medium components, facilitating a detailed examination of how AGN impact their host galaxies—a vital step toward understanding the co-evolution of galaxies and supermassive black holes. This review offers a broad summary of these diverse studies, tracing the field's development from its origins in the 1960s, through significant advancements driven by successive generations of space-based and ground-based instruments, to the potential offered by upcoming facilities like the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

Navigating autonomously in densely populated environments remains a significant challenge for robots due to the difficulty of ensuring safe pedestrian interactions in unstructured scenarios. This study introduces a crowd navigation control framework designed for continuous obstacle avoidance and post-contact management, tested on an autonomous personal mobility vehicle. We propose specific metrics to evaluate efficiency, controller responsiveness, and interaction dynamics within natural crowds. Our analysis covers over 110 trials across various crowd types—sparse, flowing, and mixed traffic—at low (< 0.15 ppsm), mid (< 0.65 ppsm), and high (< 1 ppsm) pedestrian densities. Comparative results between two low-level avoidance methods and a shared control baseline reveal a 10% reduction in relative time-to-goal during high-density tests without compromising other efficiency metrics. Furthermore, autonomous navigation demonstrated performance comparable to shared control but with lower relative jerk and significantly higher command fluency, indicating strong crowd compatibility. We conclude that this reactive controller effectively fulfills the need for rapid, continuous adaptation to crowd navigation and should be integrated with high-level planners for enhanced environmental and situational awareness.

Scalar bosons, formed from pairs of chiral fermions within a non-confining potential, exhibit an effective Yukawa coupling ($g$) with free external chiral fermions. At large distances, a Feynman loop of these external fermions produces a scale-invariant potential, $V_{loop}\propto -g^2/{r^{2}}$, which influences valence fermions separated by $\rho=2r$. This interaction typically compels the $s$-wave ground state to transform into a static, massless configuration; for slowly varying, perturbative $g$, this results in a large external "shroud" wave-function, a concept echoing earlier findings by Landau and Lifshitz in quantum mechanics. Consequently, the massless composite scalar boson ground state exists as an extended entity. While infrared effects may induce a small mass for the system, this suggests a perturbative BEH-boson composed of top and anti-top quarks, offering a new dynamical mechanism for spontaneous electroweak symmetry breaking.

Over the past few decades, Multi-Objective Optimization Problems (MOPs) have garnered significant interest. To tackle MOPs, Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithms (MOEAs) have been widely adopted due to their capacity to approximate a set of high-quality, non-dominated solutions. The Multi-Objective Quadratic Assignment Problem (mQAP) constitutes a specific type of MOP. As a generalization of the well-studied classical QAP, the mQAP finds extensive application in real-world scenarios. In this problem, multiple flows between facilities are provided as input, generating several cost functions that require simultaneous optimization. This study introduces PasMoQAP, a parallel asynchronous memetic algorithm designed to solve the mQAP. PasMoQAP utilizes an island model to structure the population into sub-populations, where a memetic algorithm independently evolves a reduced solution set on each island. These islands cooperate asynchronously by exchanging selected solutions with their neighbors. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms all island-based variants of the NSGA-II multi-objective evolutionary algorithm, establishing PasMoQAP as a viable alternative for addressing the Multi-Objective Quadratic Assignment Problem.

We compute curvature tensors for metrics defined on the total spaces of holomorphic fibrations. Our primary method relies on a theory concerning Chern connections and curvature forms associated with potentially degenerate Hermitian forms on holomorphic vector bundles. Within this framework, we establish a version of the Codazzi-Griffiths equations regarding the curvatures of sub- and quotient bundles and utilize these results to investigate genuine Hermitian metrics on fibrations. Specifically, we apply this approach to determine the curvature of metrics on Grassmannian bundles, demonstrating that such bundles possess positive holomorphic sectional curvature whenever the base space does.

This study demonstrates that free boundary problems defined by second-order autonomous ordinary differential equations can be converted into initial value problems. The focus on numerically solving free boundary problems stems from their inherent nonlinearity. While existing literature addresses the invariance properties of scaling or spiral groups of point transformations, this paper presents original theoretical contributions by also exploiting the invariance properties of a translation group. To validate the proposed algorithm, three specific problems are solved: a scenario involving a rope configuration constrained by an obstacle, a dynamical system featuring a nonlinear force, and an issue concerning optimal length estimation for tubular flow reactors.

This article examines a numerical approach utilizing high-precision computations to generate approximations of attractors in chaotic dynamical systems featuring quadratic right-hand sides, and to identify vertical asymptotes in explosive system solutions, including the population explosion model. The study proves a theorem regarding the existence of these asymptotes and outlines the method's extension to piecewise smooth systems, illustrated by the Chua system and systems exhibiting hysteresis.

Within autonomous vehicle technology, environmental perception is critical for understanding the driving environment, such as detecting clear paths and nearby obstacles. Semantic segmentation, a prevalent approach in this domain, classifies every pixel in an image into specific categories. This study evaluates various segmentation models based on their accuracy and efficiency. Experiments conducted on a custom dataset demonstrate that the FasterSeg model operates efficiently enough for real-time applications on low-power embedded systems found in self-driving cars. Additionally, a straightforward technique is proposed for generating synthetic training data. The research further compares the performance of first-person versus bird's-eye view perspectives; specifically, FasterSeg attains a mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) of 65.44% for $320 \times 256$ first-person inputs and 64.08% for bird's-eye view inputs of the same resolution. On the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier, both perspectives process frames at 247.11 FPS. Finally, the study analyzes and compares frame rates and accuracy across both perspectives when utilizing 16-bit Floating Point (FP16) and 32-bit Floating Point (FP32) arithmetic on the target hardware.

We have created a computational framework that utilizes advanced software tools and numerical methods to address critical challenges in earth sciences. Our approach stacks algorithms for multiphase flow physics, coupled geomechanics extending to the surface, and complex field geometries featuring discontinuities in a modular architecture, ensuring ease of use for end users. Currently, the framework focuses on providing tools to evaluate seismic risks linked to energy technologies and to conduct forward simulations for inversion analysis using GPS and InSAR data. This study concentrates on a pivotal development aspect: applying computational geometry within a two-grid method designed for unstructured tetrahedral meshes.

This study investigates how temperature-dependent resistivity evolves under controlled point-like disorder, introduced via 2.5 MeV electron irradiation, in stoichiometric "3-4-13" stannides with the formula $(\text{Ca,Sr})_{3}(\text{Ir,Rh})_{4}\text{Sn}_{13}$. Among the three cubic compounds examined, two display a microscopic coexistence of superconductivity (SC) and charge-density wave (CDW) order, whereas $\text{Ca}_{3}\text{Rh}_{4}\text{Sn}_{13}$ lacks CDW order. As anticipated, irradiation universally suppresses the CDW transition temperature ($T_{\text{CDW}}$) across all three compositions. The behavior of the superconducting transition temperature ($T_{c}$) is more nuanced: in $\text{Sr}_{3}\text{Rh}_{4}\text{Sn}_{13}$, $T_{c}$ initially rises, consistent with a direct competition between CDW and SC, before saturating at higher doses. Conversely, in the other three compounds, $T_{c}$ decreases monotonically with irradiation, with the most pronounced suppression observed in $\text{Ca}_{3}\text{Rh}_{4}\text{Sn}_{13}$, which does not exhibit CDW order. Further analysis of $\text{Ca}_{3}\text{Rh}_{4}\text{Sn}_{13}$ via London penetration depth measurements ($\lambda(T)$) reveals a superfluid density indicative of a weak-coupling, fully gapped, isotropic superconducting state. This finding necessitates an explanation for two apparently contradictory observations: a single isotropic gap alongside a substantial suppression of $T_{c}$ by non-magnetic disorder. A quantitative theoretical analysis utilizing a generalized Anderson theorem suggests an unconventional multiband $s^{+-}$-pairing state, where the order parameter changes sign on one or a few smaller Fermi surface sheets while remaining fully gapped overall.

This work introduces a comprehensive analysis of a non-abelian vector dark matter candidate, $W^\prime$, characterized by a low mass scale in the MeV-GeV range. This candidate exists alongside a dark photon $A^\prime$ and a dark $Z^\prime$ of comparable masses within a gauged two-Higgs-doublet framework featuring a hidden gauge group isomorphic to the Standard Model electroweak group. The model ensures dark matter stability through an accidental discrete $Z_2$ symmetry, known as $h$-parity, eliminating the need for ad hoc imposition. The study rigorously evaluates the model against diverse experimental limits, including dark photon searches from NA48, NA64, E141, $\nu$-CAL, BaBar, and LHCb; electroweak precision measurements from LEP; Planck satellite data on relic density; direct and indirect detection results from CRESST-III, DarkSide-50, XENON1T, and Fermi-LAT; and LHC collider physics. Additionally, theoretical constraints such as the boundedness of the scalar potential from below and tree-level perturbative unitarity in the scalar sector are enforced. The resulting viable parameter space, consistent with all these constraints, is identified. Although resonant annihilation via the dark $Z^\prime$ may dominate the relic density, the dark photon plays an essential role in direct detection. Furthermore, we show that upcoming sub-GeV direct detection experiments like CDEX, NEWS-G, and SuperCDMS offer opportunities to further explore this parameter space.

In the current digital era, data analysis and visualization have gained increasing significance. Drawing a parallel to traditional object imaging, we demonstrate that computational ghost imaging can effectively visualize digital data to reveal their inherent properties, such as periodicity. Our experimental findings indicate that applying optical imaging techniques for data analysis offers distinct benefits, particularly regarding anti-interference capabilities. Specifically, computational ghost imaging enables robust data analysis even in the presence of strong noise and random fluctuations in the amplitude and phase of binarized signals. This resilient approach to data analysis and imaging holds substantial promise for applications across diverse fields, including big data analytics, meteorology, astronomy, and economics.

Detecting emotions offers valuable insights into human behavior; however, the intricate nature of these emotions makes creating annotated datasets for training automated models costly. Consequently, this study investigates the effectiveness of cross-lingual methods, which leverage source language data to develop emotion detection models for target languages. We evaluate three specific strategies: employing inherently multilingual models, translating training data into the target language, and utilizing an automatically tagged parallel corpus. Focusing on English as the source language and Arabic and Spanish as the target languages, we assess various classification models, including BERT and SVMs, using diverse feature sets. Our findings indicate that BERT-based monolingual models trained directly on target language data outperform state-of-the-art results by 4% and 5% in absolute Jaccard scores for Arabic and Spanish, respectively. Furthermore, we demonstrate that relying solely on English data within a cross-lingual framework yields models achieving over 90% and 80% relative effectiveness compared to the Arabic and Spanish BERT baselines. Finally, we apply LIME to examine the specific challenges encountered when training cross-lingual models across different language pairs.

Developing natural language processing systems for non-standardized, low-resource languages presents a significant challenge, a problem that recent large-scale multilingual pretrained language models now help address with new tools. This study investigates the capacity of these models to handle unseen dialects, using user-generated North-African Arabic as a case study. This dialectal variety is resource-scarce, characterized by frequent code-mixing with French and written in Arabizi, a non-standardized transliteration into the Latin script. By focusing on part-of-speech tagging and dependency parsing, we demonstrate that multilingual language models can achieve transfer in both zero-shot and unsupervised adaptation scenarios. Specifically, we highlight success in two extreme cases: (i) transferring across scripts from Modern Standard Arabic as the source, and (ii) transferring from a distantly related language, Maltese, which was not seen during pretraining. These results represent the first successful transfer experiments on this dialect, thereby laying the groundwork for building an NLP ecosystem for resource-scarce, non-standardized, and highly variable vernacular languages.

This study introduces the inaugural beyond closure calculation for neutrinoless double beta decay ($0\nu\beta\beta$) of $^{76}$Ge, specifically targeting the first $2^+$ states of $^{76}$Se. We employ the isospin symmetry restored Quasi-particle random phase approximation (QRPA) utilizing the CD-Bonn realistic force for nuclear structure analysis. Our investigation examines the two-nucleon mechanism nuclear matrix elements and quantifies uncertainties arising from nuclear many-body computations. We determine that the $g_{pp}$ coupling constant is pivotal to these calculations; notably, when quenching is applied, a suppression of the transition matrix element $M_{\lambda}$ is observed. Furthermore, our derived transition matrix elements are approximately an order of magnitude greater than those previously projected using the closure approximation within the Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov framework.

Although self-supervised contrastive learning models have recently achieved significant success in representing 3D point clouds, their adversarial robustness remains a concern. Adversarial contrastive learning (ACL) offers an effective solution to enhance the robustness of these pre-trained models. In contrastive learning, the projector plays a crucial role in filtering out irrelevant feature information during pretraining. Most existing ACL approaches utilize contrastive loss on projected features to create adversarial examples during training, yet rely on "unprojected" features for generating adversarial inputs at inference. This discrepancy between projected and "unprojected" feature distributions limits the models' ability to learn robust representations for downstream tasks. We propose a novel method that leverages virtual adversarial loss with "unprojected" features within a contrastive learning framework to generate high-quality 3D adversarial examples for training. Additionally, we introduce a robust-aware loss function to adversarially train self-supervised contrastive learning frameworks. We further demonstrate that incorporating high-difference points identified by the Difference of Normal (DoN) operator as auxiliary inputs significantly boosts the adversarial robustness of the pre-trained model. Our proposed method, PointACL, is evaluated on downstream tasks such as 3D classification and segmentation across multiple datasets, achieving robust accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art contrastive adversarial learning techniques.

This study employs direct numerical simulations (DNS) to examine how rotation influences the turbulent mixing of two miscible fluids with slight density differences, driven by Faraday instability. We find that at lower forcing amplitudes, turbulent kinetic energy (t.k.e.) rises as the forcing frequency increases until $(f/\omega)^2 < 0.25$ during the sub-harmonic instability phase. This rise in t.k.e. boosts buoyancy variance ($B_V$), thereby increasing total potential energy (TPE). TPE comprises available potential energy (APE), which can convert to t.k.e. via $B_V$ or dissipate into internal energy (raising bulk potential energy, BPE) through $\phi_i$. Additionally, residual TPE converts to BPE via diapycnal flux ($\phi_d$), causing irreversible mixing. Once the instability saturates, this irreversible mixing stops.

When $(f/\omega)^2 > 0.25$, Coriolis forces significantly delay the onset of sub-harmonic instabilities. During this delay, the initial concentration profile diffuses, increasing TPE which subsequently converts to BPE. Strong rotational effects suppress t.k.e., keeping $B_V$ and APE low, causing most TPE to expend into BPE. Because the instability does not saturate in this regime, $B_V$ remains non-zero, leading to a continuous rise in TPE. Consequently, conversion of TPE to BPE via $\phi_d$ persists, resulting in prolonged irreversible mixing. At higher forcing amplitudes, rotation's stabilizing influence becomes negligible; turbulence is less intense and short-lived, causing irreversible mixing to end quickly for $(f/\omega)^2 < 0.25$. In contrast, continuous mixing is observed when $(f/\omega)^2 > 0.25$. We conclude that turbulent mixing is most efficient at lower forcing amplitudes and rotation rates where $(f/\omega)^2 > 0.25$.

Controlling language models (LMs) without retraining remains a significant challenge in natural language generation. Although recent studies have shown success in managing simple sentence attributes like sentiment, progress on complex, fine-grained controls such as syntactic structure has been limited. To tackle this, we introduce Diffusion-LM, a novel non-autoregressive model grounded in continuous diffusion. Leveraging the achievements of diffusion models in continuous spaces, Diffusion-LM iteratively transforms a sequence of Gaussian vectors into word vectors, producing a series of intermediate latent variables. The continuous and hierarchical characteristics of these variables facilitate a straightforward gradient-based algorithm for executing intricate controllable generation tasks. We show that Diffusion-LM successfully handles six difficult fine-grained control tasks, achieving results that significantly surpass previous methods.

An anisotropic MHD turbulence model incorporating nonvanishing cross-helicity is developed using Boldyrev's alignment hypothesis, alongside probabilities $p$ and $q$ describing the likelihood of positive or negative alignment between fluctuations in velocity ($v$) and magnetic field ($b$). Observations indicate that normalized cross-helicity and probability $p$ remain roughly constant across the inertial range, prompting a generalized extension of Boldyrev's theory that relies on the ratios $w^+/w^-$, $\epsilon^+/\epsilon^-$, and $p/q$. This extended framework converges to Boldyrev's original formulation under the specific conditions where $w^+ = w^-$, $\epsilon^+ = \epsilon^-$, and $p = q$.

This study examines the fractional logarithmic Schrödinger equation defined as $\varepsilon^{2s}(-\Delta)^s u + V(x)u=u\log |u|^2$ in $\R^N$, where $\varepsilon>0$, $N\ge 1$, and $V(x)\in C(\R^N,[-1,+\infty))$. Through the introduction of a specific penalized function, we demonstrate the existence of a positive solution $u_{\varepsilon}$ that concentrates at a local minimum of $V$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$. Notably, our results impose no constraints on the decay rates of $V$, allowing it to be compactly supported.

Smart speakers and robots are increasingly integrated into our daily routines. These autonomous agents can perform diverse tasks, necessitating robust control systems. However, current state-of-the-art approaches like (deep) reinforcement learning demand extensive training data, which is frequently unavailable in human-agent interactions. To address this limitation, most existing systems continue to depend on Finite State Machines. We propose Petri Net Machines, a formal extension of state machines grounded in Petri Nets. This framework enables reliable execution of concurrent actions, the simultaneous interleaving of multiple plans, and offers an accessible modeling language. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach using a Human-Robot Interaction scenario set in a shopping mall.

This study introduces fresh spectral and photometric observations of a confirmed LBV star within the NGC4736 galaxy. The object, designated NGC4736_1 (Mbol = -11.5 mag), exhibited distinct spectral fluctuations between 2015 and 2018, coinciding with substantial variations in luminosity. Additionally, we derived an estimated initial mass for NGC4736_1 of approximately 130 solar masses.

This paper investigates the existence and multiplicity of positive standing waves for the specified Chern-Simons-Schr\"odinger equation by integrating variational methods with the Trudinger-Moser inequality. The equation is defined in $\mathbb{R}^2$ as:
\begin{equation}
-\Delta u+u
+\lambda\left(\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{h(s)}{s}u^{2}(s)ds+\frac{h^{2}(\vert
x\vert)}{\vert x\vert^{2}}\right)u=f(x,u)+\epsilon k(x)\quad\quad
\text{in}\,\,\mathbb{R}^2, \\ \end{equation}
where $h(s)=\int_{0}^{s}\frac{l}{2}u^{2}(l)dl$, $\lambda>0$, and the nonlinearity $f:\mathbb{R}^2\times \mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ exhibits exponential growth similar to $\text{exp}(\alpha\vert u\vert^{2})$ as $\vert u\vert\rightarrow \infty$. When $\epsilon=0$, a mountain-pass type solution is established.

Otto's Theorem establishes that bisimulation-invariant PTIME graph queries correspond precisely to those expressible in the polyadic mu-calculus, relying on the Immerman-Vardi Theorem, which links PTIME on ordered structures to First-Order Logic with least fixpoints. This relationship was previously expanded to bisimulation-invariant EXPTIME by augmenting the polyadic mu-calculus with predicate functions, utilizing Immerman's characterization of EXPTIME via Second-Order Logic with least fixpoints. In this work, we demonstrate that bisimulation-invariant versions of every class within the exponential time hierarchy possess logical equivalents derived from the polyadic mu-calculus enhanced by higher-order functions. This result leverages the characterization of k-EXPTIME by Higher-Order Logic (specifically of order k+1) with least fixpoints, as established by Freire and Martins.

We have previously shown that in two-dimensional (2D) coherent electronic spectroscopy utilizing phase modulation and phase-sensitive detection, an \emph{incoherent} nonlinear response—arising from pairs of photoexcitations generated through linear excitation pathways—contributes to the measured signal as an unexpected background [Gr\'egoire et al., J.\ Chem.\ Phys. \textbf{147}, 114201 (2017)]. In this study, we simulate the impact of such incoherent population mixing on photocurrent signals collected from a GaAs solar cell by externally manipulating the transimpedance amplifier circuit employed for phase-sensitive detection. We also identify an effective strategy to detect the presence of incoherent population mixing in 2D data. Our findings indicate that incoherent mixing manifests as cross-talk between the linear amplitudes at the two time-delay variables within the four-pulse excitation sequence; however, we do not observe strict phase correlations between coherent and incoherent contributions, as anticipated from modeling a simple system.

Ensuring the robust operation of future distribution networks (DN) relies heavily on flexible and curtailable resources. This study introduces a network-state driven framework designed for distribution system operators (DSOs) to deploy these resources effectively, addressing voltage and thermal constraints while managing network voltage and current imbalances. By leveraging dynamic network state data and nodal sensitivities, the method calculates a Flexibility Activation Signal (FAS). Inspired by volt-Var and volt-watt inverter controls, this signal is bounded and specifically accounts for imbalances to incentivize the activation of both active and reactive power flexibilities. Consequently, the framework mitigates voltage and thermal issues in three-phase unbalanced networks while simultaneously reducing imbalance. The FAS design mirrors optimal power flow duals, similar to locational marginal prices. Furthermore, the gains from the imbalance component of the three-phase unbalanced resource activation (TPU-RA) objective function are optimized using Pareto optimality. A numerical case study demonstrates the framework's efficacy in preventing network problems and reducing the voltage unbalance factor by over 80%, while also quantifying the DN's flexibility requirements across different locations and times of day.

We introduce new findings on rope hadronization regarding the enhancement of strange hadrons in pp, pPb, and PbPb collisions, utilizing the PYTHIA/Angantyr framework at LHC energies. Employing a rope model for string fragmentation, our results demonstrate a consistent rise in both strangeness and baryon enhancement across all collision systems as a function of average charged central multiplicity, aligning qualitatively with LHC observations. Specifically, in AA collisions, baryonic yields exceed experimental data at high multiplicities; we further explore how integrating rope hadronization with additional string interactions could mitigate this excessive increase.

The oscillating shape motion of freely falling water droplets has long captivated scientists. We introduce dynamic non-linear equations for closed, two-dimensional surfaces under gravity and apply them to examine the shape dynamics of falling water drops. These analytic solutions qualitatively account for why drops oscillate between prolate and oblate forms and exhibit several features that align with experimental observations.

GroundBIRD is a ground-based experiment designed for the precise observation of the polarization of the cosmic microwave background (CMB). To achieve high sensitivity at large angular scales, the experiment employs three key features: fast rotation scanning, microwave kinetic inductance detectors (MKIDs), and cold optics. The rotation scanning strategy effectively suppresses $1/f$ noise and ensures a sky coverage of 40%, corresponding to large angular scales of $l \sim 6$. This capability enables constraints on the tensor-to-scalar ratio through the analysis of the low $l$ B-mode spectrum. The focal plane comprises seven MKID arrays targeting the 145 GHz and 220 GHz bands, with a total of 161 pixels; specifically, 138 pixels operate at 144 GHz and 23 at 220 GHz. Currently under development, the prototype array is scheduled for imminent telescope evaluation. The GroundBIRD telescope, which has been relocated from Japan to the Teide observatory in Tenerife for testing, will observe the CMB. This document outlines the current status and future plans for the GroundBIRD experiment.

Neutron stars provide a laboratory for investigating matter at the universe's extreme densities. Within their cores, this material may shift from hadronic to exotic states, such as quark matter, a process potentially signaled by distinctive features like jumps or sharp peaks in the speed of sound's density profile. Using a model-independent framework, we simulated the speed of sound across various equations of state—some incorporating explicit first-order phase transitions—to determine how well current astrophysical observations can reveal such non-trivial structures. Our comprehensive analysis indicates that existing data do not definitively necessitate the presence of a transition to quark matter.

Multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) offer significant advantages for low-resource languages, including those in the Baltic family, due to their strong cross-lingual transfer abilities. This study investigates the cross-lingual representations within these models, addressing previous contradictory findings regarding whether LMs internally map different languages into a unified shared space. While earlier research argued that "BERT is not an Interlingua," we demonstrate that languages do indeed converge into a common space when alternative pooling strategies or similarity metrics are applied. We conducted a comprehensive representational analysis across 378 pairwise comparisons using the two most prominent multilingual LMs. Our findings reveal that although many languages occupy a shared cross-lingual space, some do not; however, Baltic languages are confirmed to reside within this shared space. The accompanying code can be accessed at https://github.com/TartuNLP/xsim.

With advancements in legged robots and embedded computing, researchers are increasingly turning toward field deployments. Achieving robust autonomy in unstructured settings demands environmental perception to navigate hazards, yet integrating real-time perception with agile movement poses greater challenges for legged robots than for other mobile platforms due to the intricate planners and controllers needed to manage locomotion dynamics. This report examines three recent strategies for perceptive locomotion and explores how vision can be leveraged to facilitate autonomous legged robots.

India and Belgium have collaboratively set up two 4-meter class optical telescopes at Devasthal in Nainital, India. Following the successful installation of the 3.6-meter Devasthal Optical Telescope (DOT) in 2015, the premier leaders of both nations officially activated the facility in Brussels on March 30, 2016. Since that time, the DOT has supported numerous research proposals utilizing both optical and near-Infrared (NIR) observations. The telescope has achieved an angular resolution of 0.4 arcseconds, demonstrating that its optics are high-quality and capable of capturing celestial images with sub-arc-second precision. These results confirm that the low thermal mass of the dome construction effectively preserves the natural atmospheric seeing conditions at Devasthal, which were measured between 1997 and 1999 using a differential image motion monitor. Preliminary scientific findings from recent observations are presented alongside an assessment of the DOT's performance and its global potential within galactic astronomy. Once high-resolution spectrographs and other planned modern back-end instruments become operational, the 3.6-meter DOT will be able to deliver internationally competitive science. Furthermore, the observatory's geographical location holds significant global value for time-domain and multi-wavelength astrophysical studies.

Determining the positions of sensor nodes within the Internet of Underwater Things (IoUT) is critical for applications ranging from navigation and data tagging to underwater object detection. To address this, the paper introduces a hybrid Bayesian Multidimensional Scaling (BMDS) localization framework designed for fully hybrid IoUT networks capable of utilizing optical, magnetic induction, and acoustic communication technologies. While these three methods are established for underwater communication, they currently lack integrated localization solutions; specifically, optical and magnetic induction offer high data rates over short distances, whereas acoustic waves enable long-range communication at lower data rates. The proposed technique leverages ranging data from all three modalities to estimate the precise locations of underwater sensor nodes. Additionally, the study derives the Hybrid Cramér-Rao Lower Bound (HCRLB) to evaluate the scheme, and simulation results offer a comprehensive comparison against existing literature.

In non-abelian gauge theories, the soft function exponentiates, with its logarithmic terms structured by collections of Feynman diagrams known as Cwebs. The color factors within these logarithms are governed by web mixing matrices. Recently, the diagonal blocks of Cwebs were directly constructed using novel concepts such as Normal ordering, basis Cwebs, and Fused-Webs, as detailed in~\cite{Agarwal:2022wyk}. This article establishes a correspondence between the boomerang webs from~\cite{Gardi:2021gzz} and non-boomerang Cwebs. Leveraging this link alongside the Uniqueness theorem and the Fused web formalism from~\cite{Agarwal:2022wyk}, we derive the diagonal blocks for four general classes of Cwebs to all orders in perturbation theory, a framework that also encompasses all four-loop Boomerang Cwebs connecting four Wilson lines. Furthermore, we completely construct the mixing matrix for a specific Cweb to all orders in perturbation theory.

We examined the hydrogen isotopic ratios and water concentrations in pyroxenes from two recent ordinary chondrite falls, Chelyabinsk (2013) and Benenitra (2018), alongside three Antarctic ordinary chondrite finds: GRA 06179, LAR 12241, and DOM 10035. Pyroxenes in the Chelyabinsk and Benenitra meteorites are hydrated (~0.018–0.087 wt.% H$_2$O) and display D-poor isotopic signatures ($\delta$D$_{SMOW}$ ranging from -444‰ to -49‰). Conversely, the Antarctic finds show signs of terrestrial contamination, characterized by higher water contents (~0.039–0.174 wt.%) and isotopic values spanning from -199‰ to -14‰. After assessing various minor parent-body processes that could modify the compositions in the fallen meteorites, we concluded that water loss in S-type planetesimals during thermal metamorphism is negligible. The hydrogen signatures in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk indicate a mixture of D-poor nebular hydrogen and water derived from D-rich mesostases, with 45–95% of the water in these minerals attributed to nebular sources. Furthermore, S-type asteroids, which are primarily made of nominally anhydrous minerals, can retain between 254 and 518 ppm of water. The presence of a nebular water component in nominally dry inner Solar System bodies during accretion implies a diminished requirement for volatile delivery to terrestrial planets during late accretion.

Detecting cyclotron resonance scattering features (CRSFs) remains the sole method for directly and reliably measuring magnetic fields near a neutron star's surface. Leveraging the broad energy range and extensive collection area of \emph{Insight}-HXMT in the hard X-ray band, we identified the CRSF with the highest energy ever recorded, approximately 146 keV, during the 2017 outburst of Swift J0243.6+6124, the first galactic pulsing ultraluminous X-ray source (pULX). This CRSF was notably prominent only near the peak luminosity of $\sim 2\times10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$, marking the highest value observed in any Galactic pulsar to date. The feature is most significant during the main pulse phase of the profile, with its centroid energy shifting from 120 to 146 keV. We classify this as the fundamental CRSF due to the absence of spectral features in the 60–70 keV range. This study represents the first unambiguous detection of an electron CRSF from an ULX. Based on these findings, we estimate a surface magnetic field of $\sim 1.6\times10^{13}$ G for Swift J0243.6+6124. Given that dipole field strengths derived from various magnetosphere radius estimates are at least an order of magnitude lower, we conclude that this high-energy CRSF detection definitively confirms the existence of multipole field components near the neutron star surface. This multipole scenario has been hypothesized for several pulsating ULXs, including Swift J0243.6+6124, and our results provide the first direct validation of this hypothesis.

Although recent advances have excelled at learning from static graphs, mastering time-evolving graphs remains an unsolved problem. This study introduces stricter, real-world-aligned evaluation protocols for link prediction in dynamic graphs to more accurately assess methodological strengths and weaknesses. Initially, we developed two visualization methods to reveal recurring edge patterns over time, demonstrating that many edges reappear in later steps. Leveraging this insight, we proposed "EdgeBank," a pure memorization baseline that surprisingly outperforms others in current settings due to the prevalence of easy negative edges. To address this, we introduced two more rigorous negative sampling strategies to enhance robustness and align better with real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we released six new dynamic graph datasets from diverse domains absent from existing benchmarks, offering fresh challenges and avenues for future research. The associated code repository is available at https://github.com/fpour/DGB.git.

This paper introduces and resolves the bridge consensus problem, which involves a network containing both participating and non-participating nodes. The goal is to achieve distributed and scalable average consensus among all agents based on the initial values of the participating nodes. This is accomplished by utilizing the network connections of non-participating nodes as information bridges while disregarding their own initial values. The proposed solution integrates concepts from both estimation theory and consensus theory. By modeling participating nodes as possessing equal information and non-participating nodes as having none, initial values are mapped into an information space. Two consensus filters operate in parallel on the information state and information matrix. Finally, the conditions required to ensure that the product of the inverse information matrix and the information state for each agent converges to the average of the participating agents' initial values are established.

We examine words over a binary alphabet that exclude mesosomes—defined as sequences $xx'$ where $x'$ is a conjugate of $x$ distinct from $x$ itself. Our work establishes a structure theorem for these mesosome-avoiding words, enumerates their quantity, identifies all infinite instances, and determines the set of minimal forbidden words.

This paper addresses the integrable discretization of a modified Camassa-Holm equation incorporating a linear dispersion term. The central approach relies on constructing a semi-discrete analogue of the bilinear equations associated with this modified equation. First, we demonstrate that both Gram-type and Casorati-type determinant solutions for these bilinear equations can be derived from the discrete KP equation via the Miwa transformation. By analyzing this reduction process, we establish a set of semi-discrete bilinear equations and their corresponding general soliton solutions in determinant form. Subsequently, through the introduction of dependent variables and discrete hodograph transformations, we derive an integrable semi-discrete version of the modified Camassa-Holm equation. Furthermore, we verify that this semi-discrete equation converges to its continuous counterpart in the continuum limit.

Error-tolerant graph matching encompasses a significant class of problems focused on identifying correspondences between two graphs while incorporating an error model. In the Graph Edit Distance (GED) problem, the insertion or deletion of edges and nodes is explicitly defined by this error model. Conversely, the problem commonly known as "graph matching" does not explicitly represent such operations. For many years, these two distinct approaches divided the research community, leading to the development of separate solvers for each. This paper proposes a unification of both problems through a single model. We demonstrate that the two problems are equivalent when the error models are reformulated. This unification enables the application of existing solving methods from both communities to address either problem.

**Background:** The current state of software engineering is defined by a vast array of contributions and significant gaps between them, making it challenging to characterize.

**Questions:** To enhance our understanding of this field, can we pinpoint knowledge gaps at a broad, universally relevant level? Furthermore, what research directions do these gaps imply?

**Method:** The study involved 54 qualitative interviews with senior members of the ICSE community, analyzed using Grounded Theory Methodology.

**Results:** Our grasp of complexity, the concept of "good-enoughness," and developers' strengths remains underdeveloped, while the significance of other factors remains unclear. Additionally, software engineering has not yet evolved into a fully evidence-based discipline.

**Conclusion:** Future research should focus on emergence phenomena, the mechanics of engineering trade-offs, the assumptions underlying current work, and the development of taxonomies. Pursuing these areas will facilitate the transition of software engineering toward an evidence-based practice.

Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) have recently become a focal point for both academic research and industry efforts. Given that AVs are intricate systems comprised of numerous subsystems, they are particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks. Consequently, manufacturers must regularly update the firmware of these subsystems to patch vulnerabilities and add functionalities. This paper introduces a distributed firmware update framework for AV subsystems that utilizes blockchain and smart contract technologies. By employing a consortium blockchain formed by various AV manufacturers, the system guarantees the authenticity and integrity of firmware updates. Rather than relying on centralized third parties, the proposed scheme allows AVs to act as distributors, leveraging their mobility to ensure high availability and rapid delivery of updates. To motivate participation, a reward mechanism is implemented that tracks the credit reputation of each distributor within the blockchain. Furthermore, a zero-knowledge proof protocol facilitates the exchange of updates for distribution verification within a trustless environment. Additionally, an attribute-based encryption (ABE) scheme is applied to restrict access, ensuring that only authorized AVs can download and utilize new updates. Our analysis reveals that the added cryptographic primitives and transaction exchanges do not hinder AV network operations. Moreover, security evaluations confirm that the proposed scheme is both efficient and robust against various attacks.

Standard development relies on human committees convening repeatedly over months or years to reach consensus, including choices about modulation and coding schemes for air interfaces. We introduce a method to "automate" the selection of these schemes, thereby expediting the standards design process and simplifying the extension of standards to accommodate new modulation techniques for emerging applications. This approach utilizes machine learning, where a constructor entity submits proposals to an evaluator entity that assigns scores. The constructor then employs reinforcement learning to refine these proposals until achieving a score that meets pre-agreed design criteria, encompassing performance metrics for transmissions across the interface.

Mathematical models of excitable cells typically rely on cable theory, which assumes a homogenized domain with spatially uniform ionic concentrations. While these models offer useful insights, they fail to account for the impacts of varying ion concentrations or intricate cellular morphology on electrical potentials. This paper presents an alternative method for detailed electrodiffusion modeling in neural tissue. The proposed mathematical framework describes the distribution and temporal evolution of ion concentrations within a geometrically explicit representation of both intracellular and extracellular spaces. By integrating the electroneutral Kirchhoff-Nernst-Planck (KNP) model with the Extracellular-Membrane-Intracellular (EMI) framework, we term this approach the KNP-EMI model. We introduce and numerically assess a novel finite element scheme for the KNP-EMI model that efficiently and flexibly accommodates geometries of any dimension and polynomial degree. Furthermore, we compare the electrical potentials generated by the KNP-EMI and EMI models. Finally, we investigate ephaptic coupling within an unmyelinated axon bundle, demonstrating how the KNP-EMI framework provides novel insights in this context.

Fear is a ubiquitous human experience that fuels urban legends, horror films, and contemporary narratives, yet the specific reasons behind their scare factor and the nature of human fear remain underexplored. This research investigates these issues by examining tens of thousands of horror stories posted on Reddit forums. The study first examines how writing styles have adapted to maintain freshness, followed by an analysis of the enduring techniques writers employ to induce fear. Our findings reveal that story themes have shifted over time, moving from haunted houses to school settings, body horror, and diseases. However, certain elements remain constant; for instance, words linked to pseudo-human entities like clowns and devils appear significantly more frequently in these stories than in baseline texts. Furthermore, we assembled datasets annotating fearful sentences to train a high-accuracy neural network for fear detection. This model identifies specific points within stories where fear is expressed and where vocabulary common in horror spikes, suggesting these moments are strategically placed to sustain reader suspense until the climax. Ultimately, these results offer new insights into how authors tailor their work to audiences and how fear manifests in narrative structures.

This work examines the fluctuations of ergodic averages arising from actions by amenable groups. Within the framework of an abstract ergodic theorem for locally compact, second-countable amenable groups acting on uniformly convex Banach spaces, we establish a highly uniform limit on the number of fluctuations for a specific class of Følner sequences that meet a condition analogous to Lindenstrauss's temperedness. This result is equivalent to proving a uniform bound on fluctuations over extended distances for any Følner sequence. Furthermore, as a corollary, these findings yield corresponding bounds for continuous amenable group actions on $\sigma$-finite $L^{p}$ spaces where $p\in(1,\infty)$.

Deep Ensembles (DE) are a leading method that excels in critical metrics including accuracy, calibration, uncertainty estimation, and out-of-distribution detection. However, the hardware constraints of practical systems restrict ensembles to smaller sizes and lower-capacity networks, which substantially degrades their effectiveness and characteristics. We present Packed-Ensembles (PE), a technique for designing and training lightweight structured ensembles by precisely adjusting their encoding space dimensions. By utilizing grouped convolutions, we parallelize the ensemble into a single shared backbone and forward pass, thereby enhancing both training and inference efficiency. PE operates within the memory budget of a standard neural network. Extensive research demonstrates that PE faithfully maintains the properties of DE, such as diversity, and achieves performance comparable to DE in accuracy, calibration, out-of-distribution detection, and robustness to distribution shifts.

This study evaluates the robustness of maximum likelihood-based uncertainty estimation techniques against outliers in training data for regression tasks. We demonstrate that outliers or noisy labels degrade model performance and lead to inaccurate uncertainty estimates. To address this, we propose employing a heavy-tailed distribution, specifically the Laplace distribution, to enhance robustness. We assess this approach using standard regression benchmarks and a high-dimensional monocular depth estimation task, both of which contain outliers. Our results show that maximum likelihood methods utilizing heavy-tailed distributions yield superior uncertainty estimates, improved separation of uncertainty for out-of-distribution data, and more effective detection of adversarial attacks when outliers are present.

Research into compounds exhibiting antioxidant properties holds significant interest for the scientific community due to its broad implications across disciplines, ranging from Agricultural and Biological Sciences to Food Engineering, Medicine, and Pharmacy. Within the context of human health, antioxidant activity is recognized for its ability to delay or inhibit oxidative cellular damage by mitigating the effects of free radicals, thereby aiding in disease treatment, prevention, or postponement. Among the various classes of compounds with antioxidant properties, phenolic compounds stand out due to their diverse chemical structures. This study utilizes Molecular Topology, focusing on molecular branching and intramolecular charge distributions, to develop a significant topological-mathematical model designed to assess the antioxidant potential of candidate compounds.

Massive Young Stellar Objects (MYSOs) are pivotal to the star formation process. Since MYSOs were historically identified through their extended structures and observational data has been scarce, screening Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) sources for "green" features—representing strong emission in the 4.6 $\mu$m band within three-color composites—provides an effective method to discover additional MYSO candidates. By analyzing WISE imagery across the entire Galactic Plane ($0^\circ<l<360^\circ$ and $\mid b \mid <2^\circ$), we isolated sources with intense 4.6 $\mu$m emissions and categorized them into three groups based on morphology. This effort produced a catalog of 2135 WISE Green Objects (WGOs): 264 exhibit extended structures, 1365 display compact green features without extension, and 505 lack both but possess 4.6 $\mu$m intensities at least 4.5 times those at 3.4 $\mu$m. Spatial analysis reveals WGOs are predominantly concentrated in $\mid l \mid<60^\circ$, aligning with the distribution of giant molecular clouds in the region $\mid l \mid>60^\circ$. Correlations with various maser sources indicate that these three groups correspond to distinct evolutionary phases. Cross-referencing WGOs with existing Young Stellar Object surveys suggests that approximately 50% represent newly discovered YSOs. Furthermore, 1260 WGOs are linked to Hi-GAL sources; based on spectral energy distribution fitting, 231 are classified as robust MYSOs and 172 as candidate MYSOs.

Dwell fatigue, characterized by a shortened fatigue life in titanium alloys caused by stress holds as low as 60% of yield, has been linked to multiple uncontained jet engine failures. Dislocation slip has long been recognized as an intermittent, scale-bridging process analogous to earthquakes but occurring at the nanoscale, prompting hypotheses that significant stress bursts could initiate crack formation. This study observes such stress bursts at the individual grain level in situ using high-energy X-ray diffraction microscopy on Ti-7Al-O alloys. Results indicate that the precipitation of ordered Ti₃Al exacerbates the magnitude of rare prismatic and basal slip bursts linked to slip localization. Conversely, the introduction of trace oxygen interstitials proves beneficial by diminishing the size of basal slip bursts and enhancing the uniformity between basal and prismatic <a> slip. These findings further support the engineering principle that long pathways facilitating easy basal plane slip localization must be avoided to mitigate dwell fatigue in titanium alloys.

With the rapid proliferation of autonomous systems, there is an increasing demand for a legal and regulatory framework to determine when and how these systems cause harm. Although the philosophical literature has attempted to define harm multiple times, no existing definition has successfully addressed the various examples presented, prompting some scholars to propose abandoning the concept in favor of "more well-behaved notions." Since harm is typically an effect of an action, most definitions incorporate causality; however, surprisingly, none utilize causal models or formal definitions of actual causality. This paper introduces a formal, qualitative definition of harm grounded in causal models and based on Halpern's (2016) definition of actual causality. The primary innovation of this definition lies in its reliance on contrastive causation and a comparison between actual outcomes and a default utility. We demonstrate that this framework can effectively handle examples from the existing literature and highlight its significance for reasoning about scenarios involving autonomous systems.

Highly conductive solid-state electrolytes (SSE) are essential for advancing and scaling green energy technologies, including solid-state batteries, fuel cells, and electrocatalysts. However, the extreme complexity of SSE materials has left general rational design principles undefined. This study combines first-principles modeling, computational resources, and advanced data analysis to address this critical challenge. Our data-driven investigation indicates that while correlations between ion diffusivity and various material descriptors are generally monotonic rather than strictly linear, they are strongest when the descriptors are vibrational in nature and account for anharmonic effects. Surprisingly, principal component and k-means clustering analyses demonstrate that elastic and vibrational descriptors, rather than traditional metrics based on chemical composition or ion mobility, are most effective for managing the high complexity of SSE and categorizing them into universal classes. These findings underscore the necessity of utilizing databases that include temperature effects to deepen our understanding of SSE and suggest a generalized framework for designing energy materials.

Rising demands for high-performance microprocessors drive up circuit complexity and data transfer rates, leading to increased power consumption. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a clocking architecture leveraging series LC resonance and inductor matching. This approach utilizes pulsed resonance to recycle switching power dissipation, while the inductor matching technique reduces skew and enhances the robustness of the clock network. Compared to a traditional primary-secondary flip-flop-based CMOS design, this novel resonant architecture achieves over 43% power savings and 91% skew reduction across a frequency range of 1–5 GHz.

Utilizing the algebraic Bethe-ansatz approach, we calculate exact scalar products and form factors for integrable XXZ chains with arbitrary, potentially mixed, higher-spin values. First, we establish the affine quantum-group symmetry, $U_q(\hat{sl_2})$, within the monodromy matrix of the XXZ spin chain to derive these precise expressions. Subsequently, leveraging this symmetry, we explicitly determine the diagonalized forms of the $B$ and $C$ operators in the $F$-basis for the spin-1/2 XXZ chain, thereby confirming a conjecture made during prior algebraic Bethe-ansatz calculations of XXZ correlation functions. These findings are expected to provide a foundational framework for the systematic study of form factors and correlation functions across various solvable models linked to integrable XXZ spin chains.

This paper investigates the generalized Klein-Gordon oscillator equation within the context of Lorentz Symmetry violation, characterized by a tensor field $(K_F)_{\mu\nu\alpha\beta}$ from the Standard Model Extension (SME). We explore a scenario where Lorentz-violating effects interact with a Cornell-type electric field and a linear magnetic field, generating a harmonic-like central potential in the relativistic quantum dynamics of scalar oscillator fields. By applying the parametric Nikiforov-Uvarov method to wave equations featuring Coulomb and Cornell-type potential functions, we derive bound-state solutions. Our results demonstrate that the eigenvalue solutions are altered by Lorentz symmetry-breaking effects when compared to standard Landau levels in flat space without such violations.

This study addresses the homogenization of Schrödinger equations governing non-crystalline matter, where coefficients are defined by stationary functions composed with stochastic deformations. The work establishes two rigorous effective mass theorems relevant to solid-state physics: a general abstract theorem that extends beyond the classical stationary ergodic framework, and a specific result for quasi-perfect materials characterized by limited disorder. The former approach utilizes double-scale limits with wave functions expressed in the Bloch basis, thereby extending Bloch theory, which was previously confined to periodic crystal structures, to non-periodic settings. The latter result employs perturbation theory and focuses on a particular class of stochastic deformations known as stochastic perturbations of the identity.

Time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) has become the preferred approach for computing spectral and response properties across physics, chemistry, and biology, largely due to its favorable system-size scaling that allows for the simulation of significantly larger systems. Although relatively simple functional approximations have successfully addressed increasingly complex and intriguing systems, there is growing recognition that these functionals often fail for specific approximation classes. This review examines the fundamental limitations of approximate functionals in modeling double excitations and charge-transfer excitations, two primary obstacles to applying the theory as a "black box." Concurrently, it outlines the advancements achieved over recent decades in developing functional approximations capable of yielding reliable predictions for these challenging excitations.

Deep generative models, trained via deep learning, serve as effective priors for solving inverse under-determined problems, such as reconstructing images from sparse data. This paper introduces MrSARP, a novel hierarchical deep-generative framework designed for Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery that jointly synthesizes target images at multiple resolutions. During training, MrSARP is paired with a critic that evaluates the realism of these multi-resolution outputs together. We demonstrate the model's utility in recovering high-spatial-resolution images from low-resolution inputs by modifying the generator's cost function to enhance its ability to infer the underlying parameters of the provided resolution set. Finally, we assess the model's performance on simulated data using three standard super-resolution error metrics and compare its results against traditional upsampling and sparsity-based sharpening techniques.

Direct conformation generation models, which derive 3D structures from input molecular graphs, are crucial for machine learning applications like 3D-QSAR and drug design virtual screening. However, current loss functions in these models are either computationally expensive or fail to ensure equivalence during optimization, leading to unfair treatment of different components and suboptimal local geometry. To address this, we introduce the Equivalent Distance Geometry Error (EDGE), a metric that calculates differential discrepancies between conformations while equivalently optimizing three key geometric factors—bond lengths, bond angles, and dihedral angles—with specific weights. Furthermore, an enhanced version of our method incorporates optimization features that minimize linear transformations of atom-pair distances within a 3-hop range. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, relative to existing loss functions, EDGE achieves both effective and efficient performance across two tasks using identical model backbones.

Numerous optimization algorithms have been created to address engineering design challenges where the solution space is too vast for manual optimization. To streamline the development and deployment of these algorithms, the Modular Optimization Framework (MOF) was established. Built on Python 3 and utilizing object-oriented programming, MOF features a modular architecture that enables users to readily integrate new algorithms, methods, or design problems. Furthermore, a standardized input file facilitates the specification of design scenarios, adjustment of optimization parameters, and comparative analysis of different algorithms. The current iteration of MOF includes implementations of genetic algorithms (GA) and simulated annealing (SA), with examples drawn from various nuclear engineering applications. The efficacy of these algorithms within MOF is illustrated through three specific cases: an unconstrained optimization of a nuclear fuel assembly pin lattice, a constrained first-cycle fuel loading optimization for a three-loop pressurized water reactor (PWR), and a constrained third-cycle optimization for a four-loop PWR. In each instance, the algorithms successfully navigated the solution spaces to identify optimized solutions that met all constraints. These outcomes not only validate the capabilities of MOF's existing tools but also offer a suite of benchmark cases for assessing the advancement of future optimization methodologies.

Entanglement, a physical phenomenon driving recent advances in quantum algorithms, remains an underexplored factor in Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) regarding their performance in binary pattern classification. This study offers theoretical insights by introducing and analyzing "negational symmetry," a new invariance property inherent to QNNs applicable to both quantum representation learning and binary classification. Under negational symmetry, a QNN produces identical logits for a given quantum binary signal and its negational counterpart—defined as the result of applying a bitwise NOT operation to each qubit—effectively preventing the network from distinguishing between the two in a binary task. Empirical evaluations using Google's quantum computing framework confirm this property. The findings indicate that negational symmetry is a fundamental characteristic unique to QNNs, absent in classical models, yet it acts as a double-edged sword in practical quantum applications.

The study investigates the $e^+e^- \to \Lambda\bar{\Lambda}$ reaction near threshold, assuming its origin lies in a bound state close to the $\Lambda\bar{\Lambda}$ threshold. The reaction's cross section is modeled using the electromagnetic form factors of the $\Lambda$ hyperon, derived via the vector meson dominance model. Results indicate that a new narrow state with $J^{PC}=1^{--}$ quantum numbers provides the dominant contribution to the reaction at energies immediately near the threshold. This hypothetical state has a mass of approximately 2231 MeV, situated very close to the $\Lambda\bar{\Lambda}$ mass threshold, and possesses a width of only a few MeV. Such a state offers a potential resolution to the issue where prior calculations significantly underestimated the near-threshold total cross section. Additionally, the observed near-threshold enhancement can be replicated by incorporating established vector resonances—specifically $\omega(1420)$, $\omega(1650)$, $\phi(1680)$, and $\phi(2170)$—when applying a Flatté parametrization for their total decay widths and assuming strong coupling to the $\Lambda\bar{\Lambda}$ channel.

The Segmented Pupil Experiment for Exoplanet Detection (SPEED) facility is dedicated to advancing knowledge and expertise in the areas necessary for equipping high-contrast imaging instruments with the extreme angular resolution and complexity anticipated for future Extremely Large Telescopes (ELTs). SPEED integrates an ELT simulator, cophasing optics, wavefront control and shaping, a multi-deformable mirror (DM) system, and optimized coronagraphy designed for a small inner-working angle (IWA). Its primary goal is to demonstrate deep contrast within a dark hole tailored for a narrow field of view and minimal IWA, specifically to facilitate the search for exoplanets in the habitable zones of late-type stars. The facility is configured to deploy an optimized small IWA coronagraph known as the phase-induced amplitude apodization complex mask coronagraph (PIAACMC). This system comprises a multi-zone phase-shifting focal plane mask (FPM) and two apodization mirrors (PIAA-M1 and PIAAA-M2), both subject to rigorous manufacturing standards. Recently, a first-generation prototype of the PIAACMC, optimized for SPEED, has been designed and produced, with components exhibiting optical quality that satisfies all specifications. This paper details the characterization of these components using a metrological interferential microscope and presents the resulting data for the FPM and mirrors. Finally, we discuss the outcomes and future prospects for implementing the PIAACMC components within the SPEED setup.

This paper investigates orthogonally additive operators mapping between Riesz spaces, explicitly relaxing the requirement that the range space be Dedekind complete. First, we establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for a pair of Riesz spaces $(E,F)$ such that every orthogonally additive operator from $E$ to $F$ is laterally-to-order bounded. Second, we derive sufficient conditions for two orthogonally additive operators, $S$ and $T$, to possess both a supremum ($S \vee T$) and an infimum ($S \wedge T$); this further implies that for any orthogonally additive operator $T$, the positive part $T^+$, negative part $T^-$, and absolute value $|T|$ exist, regardless of assumptions regarding the domain or range spaces. Finally, we demonstrate a version of Meyer's theorem concerning the existence of modules of disjointness-preserving operators, adapted specifically to the context of orthogonally additive operators.

Let $\mathbb{N}^d$ represent the $d$-dimensional monoid of non-negative integers. A generalized numerical semigroup is defined as a submonoid $S$ of $\mathbb{N}^d$ where the complement set $H(S) = \mathbb{N}^d \setminus S$ is finite. This work introduces the concept of irreducible generalized numerical semigroups and characterizes them based on the size of a specific subset within $H(S)$. Furthermore, we outline relaxed monomial orders on $\mathbb{N}^d$, define the Frobenius element of $S$ relative to a chosen relaxed monomial order, and demonstrate that for irreducible generalized numerical semigroups, the Frobenius element remains invariant regardless of the specific order selected.

A significant hurdle for autonomous vehicles lies in their interactions with both other cars and pedestrians within urban settings, where unpredictable pedestrian actions at intersections often result in frequent accidents. The first fatality involving an autonomous vehicle occurred in 2018 when a self-driving Uber car hit a pedestrian crossing an intersection in Tempe, Arizona, at night. Consequently, there is an urgent need to develop machine intelligence capable of enabling autonomous vehicles to manage control and adapt to varying pedestrian behaviors to mitigate crash risks. This study achieves three objectives: (a) it develops a Level-$k$ Meta Reinforcement Learning (LK-MRL) model for vehicle-human interactions and defines its solution concept; (b) it evaluates the LK-MRL structure in a scenario where level-0 pedestrians interact with level-1 vehicles, compares the trained policy against multiple baselines, and highlights its benefits for road safety; and (c) it further tests the LK-MRL structure in a level-1 pedestrian versus level-2 vehicle scenario based on level-$k$ thinking properties. Experimental results confirm that LK-MRL retains its advantages by utilizing reinforcement learning to generate agents of varying levels who employ best-response strategies to their lower-level counterparts, thereby enabling the creation of even higher-level scenarios.

This study presents an extension of the de Broglie-Bohm-Bell framework of quantum mechanics by treating intrinsic particle attributes, such as spin, as elements of reality. To circumvent the limitations imposed by the Kochen-Specker theorem, discrete spin values are defined relative to a specific basis—meaning each particle possesses a single, definite spin vector orientation. These orientations are not fixed in advance; instead, they evolve dynamically under the guidance of a (reduced, spin-only) wave function, which depends on the actualized positions of the particles. Consequently, the inherent contextuality of spin arises from the interaction between the wave function and the realized particle configuration, while spin remains a local property of individual particles. Additionally, this formulation incorporates a rigorous discrete-time stochastic dynamics, enabling numerical simulations of entangled spin systems, including Bohm's variant of the EPR experiment.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) utilizes a hybrid quantum-classical framework to address variational optimization problems, depending on a classical component to tune the parameters of a quantum circuit. This study introduces a Bayesian optimization strategy to handle this parameter tuning and evaluates its efficacy against other global optimizers. Our findings indicate that this method substantially decreases the number of required quantum circuit evaluations, which are typically the most resource-intensive aspect of QAOA. Furthermore, we demonstrate the method's robustness in scenarios with slow circuit repetition rates, showing that a minimal number of measurements on the quantum ansatz can yield accurate energy estimates. Additionally, we examined the method's behavior under gate-level noise, discovering that it remains resilient for shallow circuit depths. These results suggest that the proposed approach offers a promising framework for exploiting the hybrid capabilities of QAOA on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices.

Freehand 3D ultrasound (US) holds significant clinical promise because of its cost-effectiveness and wide field of view. Although recent deep learning approaches have eliminated the need for bulky, costly external positioning systems, reconstruction accuracy remains limited by challenging elevational displacement estimation and substantial cumulative drift. To address these issues, we present a novel deep motion network (MoNet) that fuses imaging data with a lightweight inertial measurement unit (IMU) from a velocity standpoint. Our contributions are twofold: first, we pioneer the use of IMU acceleration to estimate elevational displacements out-of-plane, employing a temporal, multi-branch architecture to extract meaningful data from low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) acceleration signals. Second, we develop a multi-modal online self-supervised strategy that utilizes IMU data as weak labels for adaptive optimization, thereby minimizing drift errors and mitigating the effects of acceleration noise. Experimental results demonstrate that our method delivers superior reconstruction performance, outperforming all existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Despite the widespread adoption of neural networks, formally verifying their safety and robustness in real-world scenarios remains a significant challenge. Current approaches, which verify networks prior to deployment, are constrained by simple specifications and static network structures, making them unsuitable for complex or dynamically evolving real-world applications. To address this, verification must occur online as changes happen, yet running existing algorithms in this manner is difficult. Our primary insight is leveraging the temporal correlations of these changes to speed up verification, such as by using prior verified results to warm-start new checks. This paper introduces a novel framework for scalable online verification capable of handling real-world issues involving dynamic specifications (domain shift) and network weights (weight shift). We propose three acceleration techniques—branch management, perturbation tolerance analysis, and incremental computation—to enhance the online verification of deep neural networks. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm is up to two orders of magnitude faster than existing methods, enabling its application to real-world problems.

Beyond symbolic languages, humans also utilize graphical sketches for communication. However, recent research on emergent communication has primarily concentrated on the latter, neglecting sketches and failing to examine the evolutionary trade-off between iconicity and symbolicity that leads to symbolic sign systems. This study takes the initial step toward modeling and simulating this process using two neural agents engaged in a visual communication game where the sender sketches on a canvas. We introduce a novel reinforcement learning approach that co-evolves these agents to achieve successful communication and establish abstract graphical conventions. To analyze these emerging conventions, we define three core properties—iconicity, symbolicity, and semanticity—and develop corresponding evaluation metrics. Our experimental results, conducted under various controls, align with observations from human graphical convention studies. Notably, we discovered that under appropriate environmental pressures, evolved sketches can maintain a continuum of semantics. Furthermore, co-evolved agents demonstrate the ability to switch between conventionalized and iconic communication depending on their familiarity with the referents. We hope this research lays the groundwork for future investigations into emergent communication using sketches as a modality.

Given a cardinal $\lambda$ and a torsion abelian group $K$ with cardinality strictly less than $\lambda$, we establish, under certain mild assumptions (such as $\lambda=\lambda^{\aleph_0}$), the existence of a boundedly endo-rigid abelian group $G$ of cardinality $\lambda$ such that $Tor(G)=K$. Fundamentally, we provide a full characterization of these $(K, \lambda)$ pairs. Our approach utilizes a twofold iteration of the black box method. Furthermore, we apply our construction of boundedly endo-rigid groups to address the problem of identifying co-Hopfian abelian groups of a specific size. Specifically, we introduce new classes of such groups, focusing primarily on mixed abelian groups. Notably, we offer practical criteria for determining when a boundedly endo-rigid abelian group is co-Hopfian and precisely identify the cardinals $\lambda > 2^{\aleph_{0}}$ for which a co-Hopfian abelian group of size $\lambda$ exists.

The linked cluster theorem, a fundamental principle in fermionic and bosonic many-body physics, dictates that vacuum bubbles—virtual particles spontaneously created and annihilated without interacting with real particles—do not influence physical observables. However, this established understanding requires revision when applied to anyons, quasiparticles that follow fractional exchange statistics lying between those of fermions and bosons. We demonstrate that a specific category of vacuum bubbles involving Abelian anyons does indeed alter physical observables. These bubbles correspond to virtually excited anyons that wind around real anyonic excitations, creating topological effects. Consequently, these topological bubbles induce a temperature-dependent phase shift in Fabry-Perot interference patterns within the fractional quantum Hall regime, a phenomenon currently accessible to experimentalists. This effect offers a direct and unambiguous method for observing the elusive fractional statistics of anyons.

In the context of $(n+1)$-webs formed by curves within an $n$-dimensional ambient manifold, we introduce a generalization of the classical two-dimensional Blaschke curvature. This new invariant vanishes if and only if the web achieves its maximum possible rank of one. While all rank-one 3-webs in dimension two are locally isomorphic, we demonstrate that in dimension three, germs of rank-one 4-webs by curves fall into infinitely many distinct isomorphism classes. We outline a construction method for all such classes up to isomorphism and present specific invariants that differentiate them, including the identification of so-called quadrilateral webs.

This work examines the design of optimal heralding schemes within linear optical quantum computing. Leveraging linear optical feasibility criteria from [Phys. Rev. A100, 022301; arXiv:1901.06178], the problem can be formulated with unit fidelity in the appropriate Fock space, and a corresponding solution methodology is outlined. As an application, we evaluate the optimality of several established Bell state generation schemes. The analysis demonstrates that for a system with six modes and two ancillary photons, a success rate of 2/27 is suboptimal.

A transition in a quantum particle's state can alter the physical field it generates within its surroundings. We examine a thought experiment designed to measure the magnetic dipole fields linked to electronic spins. When electrons become entangled, they cease to function as free Dirac electrons and instead represent an excited state within quantum electrodynamics. Consequently, observing the magnetism arising from entanglement and subsequent collapse serves as a test for the Copenhagen interpretation under the framework of quantum electrodynamics. This proposal extends equally to other particles and their corresponding fields and interactions, including neutrons and the electroweak force.
