Non-zero $\sin\Delta\phi$ modulations observed in $ep \rightarrow e'p\pi^+X$ events—where $\Delta\phi$ represents the azimuthal angle difference between the proton and pion in the virtual photon-target nucleon center-of-mass frame—suggest that correlations between hadron spin and transverse momenta across the target- and current-fragmentation regions are significant. Furthermore, the measured beam-spin asymmetries offer the first access in dihadron production to a previously unobserved leading-twist spin- and transverse-momentum-dependent fracture function. These fracture functions characterize the hadronization of the target remnant following the hard scattering of a virtual photon with a quark in the target particle, thereby opening a new pathway for investigating nucleonic structure and hadronization mechanisms.

Consider a viscous fluid filling the gap between a stationary sphere $S_2$ and an inner sphere $S_1$ that oscillates over time with velocity ${\bf U}(t)$ and angular velocity ${\bf \Omega}(t)$, where the time averages of both are zero. It is demonstrated that if this motion exhibits chirality, it can generate a flow capable of exerting a non-zero torque on $S_2$, thereby enabling the transfer of angular momentum through this process.

Natural images frequently consist of superimposed components with distinct geometric properties, such as a blend of cartoon-like and textural structures. Furthermore, these images often contain missing data. This paper proposes a method that simultaneously decomposes an image into its two fundamental parts and restores the missing information. Our separation and inpainting technique relies on an $l_1$ minimization framework employing two specific dictionaries; each dictionary promotes sparsity in one image component while leaving the other unaffected. We provide a thorough convergence analysis of this approach within a general context, utilizing concepts like joint concentration, clustered sparsity, and cluster coherence. As the primary application of our theoretical framework, we address the challenge of separating and inpainting an image into its cartoon and texture constituents.

We demonstrate that any closed $C^1$-smooth surface in a Riemannian manifold with bounded Kolasinski--Menger energy admits a triangulation where the number of triangles is limited by both the energy and the area. Furthermore, each triangle corresponds to a subset of a plane via a diffeomorphism with a distortion bounded by $\sqrt{2}$.

The Fast Timing Micro-Pattern Gaseous Detector (FTM) is a micro-pattern gaseous detector designed to achieve sub-nanosecond time resolution while accommodating large-area instrumentation in high-rate environments. This technology is anticipated for use in high-energy physics experiments at future colliders and in medical diagnostics employing time-of-flight techniques. This study presents systematic investigations of an FTM prototype focusing on Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) foils coated with resistive Diamond-Like Carbon (DLC) films, a development crucial for FTM functionality. The resistive foils were evaluated using various gas mixtures and compared against conductive foils. The findings indicate that current FTM performance is constrained by the manufacturing technology of DLC-coated GEM foils, with high gains achievable only in isobutane-based mixtures.

Unlike in Computer Science, where Logic is a foundational element, it occupies a virtually absent position in Information Systems (IS) curricula. This paper contends that rather than excluding Logic entirely, IS programs should significantly adapt both their content and pedagogical approaches to better align with the requirements of IS practitioners. We outline our vision for this adaptation and detail concrete efforts to implement it in a graduate-level IS course at the University of Haifa. Additionally, we examine the course syllabus and share data regarding student feedback.

Scattering processes involving $W$ and $Z$ bosons that produce pairs of electroweak bosons ($W$, $Z$, and Higgs) serve as sensitive indicators of new physics within the electroweak sector. We examine simplified models representing typical new physics scenarios, parameterizing the spectrum of potential LHC outcomes between Standard Model predictions and unitarity bounds. Moving beyond purely longitudinal scattering, we analyze the significance of transversely polarized gauge bosons. In this context, unitarity plays a critical role, revealing that limits on parameters derived from naive perturbative low-energy effective theories are inherently model-dependent. Finally, we explore the implications of our methodology for interpreting LHC data concerning vector-boson scattering and Higgs-pair production.

Developing a precise, physics-based, and differentiable model for soft robots is essential for enabling advanced optimal control applications. The Finite Element Method (FEM) serves as a powerful technique for representing highly deformable structures, such as dynamic elastomeric soft robots. This study compares virtual simulations utilizing differentiable FEM against data from their physical counterparts, focusing on various soft structures with distinct morphologies, including a force-loaded clamped beam, a pneumatically driven robotic arm, and a soft robotic fish tail. We evaluate and analyze the impact of different meshing resolutions and element types (tetrahedra versus hexahedra), numerical damping settings, and the effectiveness of differentiability for parameter calibration within a simulator built on the fast Differentiable Projective Dynamics (DiffPD) framework. Furthermore, we advance FEM applications in soft robotics by introducing a predictive model for pneumatic actuation. Through our proposed methodologies and case studies, we offer strategies and algorithms for aligning simulated physics with real-world behavior, thereby establishing FEM as a practical tool for soft robotics.

We introduce a straightforward recursive data-driven partitioning approach that generates piecewise-constant or piecewise-linear density estimates over intervals, demonstrating its ability to identify the optimal $L_1$ minimax rate for specific discrete nonparametric classes.

Triangular meshes are the most common way to represent 3D objects, yet many exhibit topological singularities that complicate their display and processing. A specific type of singularity involves self-intersections, which can occur during scanning or deformation processes like offsetting. Mesh foldings represent a unique subset of these self-intersections, where model faces intersect and reverse orientation relative to the unfolded surface. This paper introduces a new approach for detecting and repairing such foldings by leveraging their structural properties to efficiently identify affected regions. Once detected, the foldings are eliminated, and any resulting gaps are filled using the model's existing geometry. The proposed method works directly on simple mesh representations without requiring embedding techniques such as voxelization or projection. Its primary goal is to enable efficient mesh degradation that preserves the original structure based on user input.

Superclusters represent the largest structures in the universe, offering a unique window into the formation of galaxy clusters at cosmic web intersections and the distribution of magnetic fields and relativistic particles beyond cluster boundaries. Radio astronomy is currently experiencing a transformative era driven by the Square Kilometer Array (SKA), supported by the advent of highly sensitive functional telescopes like MeerKAT, which provide exceptional angular resolution and sensitivity to faint, diffuse radio sources. To investigate the radio environments surrounding superclusters, we utilized MeerKAT to observe the core of the {\it Saraswati} supercluster. This paper details the observations and data analysis procedures, including direction-dependent calibration, from the MeerKAT Observation of the {\it Saraswati} Supercluster (MOSS) project. We present initial results from pilot observations of two massive clusters, A2631 and ZwCl2341.1+0000, situated within the dense central region of {\it Saraswati}. Our analysis specifically focuses on ZwCl2341.1+0000, which contains double radio relics and a puzzling diffuse radio source within the filamentary network. Using high-resolution, sensitive L-band MeerKAT data, we imaged these double radio relics and identified a mysterious radio source located between them in a low-resolution image. Additionally, we derived the spectra of the double radio relics by combining MeerKAT data with archival GMRT observations. Subsequent papers will address the formation mechanisms of radio relics and halos, as well as the properties of radio galaxies within the core environment of a supercluster.

This study evaluates three methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, Cartesian irreducible multipoles, and spherical multipoles. We determine that spherical multipoles are most effective for modeling the scattering of electromagnetic radiation, a finding demonstrated using an amorphous silicon sphere. Subsequently, these multipoles are applied to compute the optical forces exerted on semiconductor, dielectric, and metallic particles across a broad spectrum of wavelengths, spanning from the dipolar to the Mie regimes.

Integrating extreme value theory with Bayesian approaches provides distinct benefits, including the quantification of uncertainty in parameter estimation and the capacity to analyze irregular models that frequentist statistics cannot address. However, this combination introduces numerous choices for users regarding model construction, computational algorithms, and inference. Specifically, model parameterization defines a geometry that can complicate calculations and reduce the efficiency of computational algorithms. This study examines the Poisson process characterization of extremes and highlights two primary advantages of an orthogonal parameterization that mitigates these issues. First, diagnostic results indicate that Markov chain Monte Carlo convergence is enhanced relative to the standard parameterization. Second, orthogonalization facilitates the derivation of Jeffreys and penalized complexity priors while ensuring posterior propriety. The findings are validated through simulations and applied to estimating extreme river flow levels within the proposed framework.

Although series and polynomial regression can model the same function classes as neural networks and provide greater interpretability, they are seldom utilized in practice. We attribute this to the sluggish convergence of standard polynomial regression estimators and introduce bagged polynomial regression (BPR) as a compelling alternative. Theoretically, we establish new finite sample and asymptotic $L^2$ convergence rates for series estimators, demonstrating that splitting the feature space and generating polynomial features per partition enhances performance in smooth settings. Empirically, our BPR estimator matches the performance of complex, high-parameter models and achieves results comparable to state-of-the-art methods on the MNIST handwritten digit benchmark.

We introduce a method for reconstructing complete 3D scenes from a single, unseen image. By training on a dataset of realistic, non-watertight scans, our approach predicts a distance function, a technique known for managing complex topologies and expansive spaces effectively. We identify and examine two primary obstacles that have hindered the successful prediction of image-conditioned distance functions on real 3D data: first, the necessity for reasoning across a large receptive field to derive a conventional scene distance from an image; and second, an analytical finding that the optimal network output fails to satisfy all required distance function properties. To address these issues, we propose the Directed Ray Distance Function (DRDF). We demonstrate that a deep network trained to predict DRDFs surpasses all other methods in both quantitative and qualitative metrics for single-image 3D reconstruction on the Matterport3D, 3DFront, and ScanNet datasets.

We examine the chiral characteristics of local, non-derivative baryon fields composed of three quarks under SU(3) flavor symmetry. We explicitly construct independent local three-quark fields that correspond to specific Lorentz and flavor representations. Since chiral symmetry is spontaneously broken, baryon fields may exist in various chiral representations; however, we find that these allowed representations are tightly constrained by the Lorentz group representations, a correlation arising from the color and spatial configuration of the local three-quark fields. Finally, we explore the implications of these permitted chiral symmetry representations for phenomenological Lagrangians featuring chiral U(3)_L \otimes U(3)_R symmetry.

This work investigates the continuous-time extension of Q-learning within reinforcement learning (RL), specifically under the entropy-regularized, exploratory diffusion process framework proposed by Wang et al. (2020). Since the traditional large Q-function degenerates in continuous time, we adopt its first-order approximation, defining it as the "little q-function." This function connects to both the instantaneous advantage rate and the Hamiltonian. We establish a time-discretization-independent "q-learning" theory centered on this q-function. For a given stochastic policy, we characterize the corresponding q-function and value function through martingale conditions of specific stochastic processes. Subsequently, we utilize this theory to create various actor-critic algorithms for solving RL problems, contingent on whether the density function of the Gibbs measure derived from the q-function admits an explicit computation. One proposed algorithm corresponds to the well-known SARSA method, while another recovers a continuous-time policy gradient (PG) algorithm introduced by Jia and Zhou (2021). Finally, simulation experiments are performed to evaluate the performance of our algorithms against those of PG-based methods from Jia and Zhou (2021) and standard time-discretized Q-learning approaches.

Activity monitors are commonly employed to track physical activity (PA) as a marker for mobility, fitness, and overall health. Similarly, real-time monitoring of longitudinal step count trends holds significant clinical promise as a personalized indicator of disease-related changes in daily behavior. However, the clinical applicability of these devices is hindered by inconsistent step counting accuracy across different vendors, body placements, and individual gait variations. This study proposes leveraging the tri-axial accelerometer within PA monitors to enhance step count accuracy across both devices and users. We hypothesize that: (1) raw tri-axial sensor data can be modeled to generate reliable and precise step counts, and (2) a generalized step counting model can be efficiently adapted to unique gait patterns using minimal new data. First, open-source raw sensor data was utilized to develop a long short-term memory (LSTM) deep neural network for step counting modeling. Next, a novel, fully independent dataset was created using a different device and distinct subjects. Finally, a small volume of subject-specific data was employed for domain adaptation to produce personalized models with high individualized accuracy. These findings indicate that models trained on large, freely available datasets can be effectively adapted to patient populations where extensive historical data is scarce.

The Maximum Entropy (MAXENT) method is widely utilized in both theoretical and applied machine learning due to its utility as a non-parametric tool for estimating unknown probabilities, representing a significant contribution from statistical physics to probabilistic inference. Despite this, a systematic understanding of its validity boundaries remains absent. This study investigates MAXENT within a Bayesian decision theory framework, assuming a well-defined Dirichlet prior for unknown probabilities and utilizing the average Kullback-Leibler (KL) distance to assess estimator quality and applicability. This approach enables an evaluation of the relevance of various MAXENT constraints, verification of its general utility, and comparison with estimators ranging from regularized maximum likelihood (ML) to Bayesian estimators with varying prior dependencies. Our findings indicate that MAXENT is effective in sparse data regimes but requires specific prior information. Specifically, MAXENT can surpass optimally regularized ML performance when prior rank correlations exist between the estimated random quantity and its probabilities.

I have employed a straightforward deterministic model to analyze the daily death rate decline across various regions in Italy, Spain, and England, all of which implemented similar nationwide social distancing measures. By comparing these trajectories, I estimated the cumulative fraction of the population already infected by April 10th. In the most severely impacted areas—Lombardy, Madrid, and London—this fraction exceeded expectations at approximately 0.3. This finding allows for an estimation of the infection fatality rate (IFR), yielding a value between 0.0025 and 0.005, which is notably lower than standard assumptions, particularly in London. Alternatively, this data could imply a larger effective infected population than direct counts suggest, potentially due to a variation in individual susceptibility with a variance of roughly 2. Both interpretations, whether applied individually or combined, lead to similar conclusions.

Vision Transformers (ViTs) offer an alternative architecture to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), yet their training remains significantly more challenging due to sensitivity toward hyperparameters like learning rates, optimizers, and warmup epochs. Previous empirical analysis by \cite{xiao2021early} attributed these difficulties to the \textit{patchify-stem} mechanism, suggesting that incorporating early convolutions aids transformer performance. This paper expands upon that finding by demonstrating that early convolutions alone are insufficient for stable training; rather, the critical factor is the scaled ReLU operation within the \textit{convolutional stem} (\textit{conv-stem}). Through both theoretical and empirical validation, we show that scaled ReLU in the \textit{conv-stem} enhances training stability and increases patch token diversity, thereby substantially boosting peak performance with minimal added parameters and computational cost. Furthermore, extensive experiments reveal that existing ViTs are often undertrained, indicating that ViTs possess significant untapped potential to serve as superior alternatives to CNNs.

This paper introduces the Elliptical Quartic Exponential distribution defined over $\mathbb{R}^D$, derived through a maximum entropy approach subject to constraints on the second and fourth moments. The study examines connections to existing literature, provides analytical formulas for the normalization constant and entropy, and analyzes both conditional and marginal distributions.

This article introduces a primal-dual framework for a primal proximal method tailored to a broad range of non-convex models within the calculus of variations. Using standard techniques from functional analysis, convex analysis, and duality theory, the study establishes these results and applies them to a Ginzburg-Landau type model. In the final two sections, we discuss optimal conditions and an additional related duality principle specific to this model.

We suggest utilizing the High Momentum Spectrometer at Hall C in conjunction with the Neutral Particle Spectrometer (NPS) to achieve high-precision measurements of the Deeply Virtual Compton Scattering (DVCS) cross section via a positron beam. The sole unambiguous method for separating the DVCS contribution within the photon electroproduction cross section from its interference with the Bethe-Heitler amplitude involves combining measurements from oppositely charged incident beams. This approach offers a more robust means of constraining the nucleon's Generalized Parton Distributions. Utilizing an 11 GeV beam on an unpolarized proton target will enable coverage of a broad kinematic range, allowing for the independent measurement of the $Q^2$-dependence of each component.

The infinite-width limit enables significant simplifications in the analytical investigation of overparameterized neural networks. When initialized appropriately, an extremely large network can be closely approximated by a Gaussian process, both prior to and throughout training. In this work, we demonstrate a comparable result for a basic stochastic architecture where parameters are treated as random variables. By explicitly computing the output distribution, we facilitate a PAC-Bayesian training method that directly optimizes the generalization bound. Furthermore, empirical evaluations on the MNIST dataset for a large but finite-width network indicate that this training strategy can surpass standard PAC-Bayesian approaches.

We present a framework for tailoring virtual keyboards to individual user habits by adjusting a Gaussian spatial model to incorporate personalized key center offsets and, when applicable, learned covariances. Extensive real-world investigations reveal the critical roles of training data volume, weighting schemes, and the number of key clusters used to prevent overfitting. Although previous studies demonstrated the technique's potential on artificially simplified keyboards, games, or static prompts, we validate its efficacy using the highly optimized Gboard app with a diverse set of users and their authentic typing patterns. Across various major languages, our approach yields modest yet statistically significant gains in both typing speed and decoder accuracy.

We offer a significant update to our lattice study of SU(2) gauge theory featuring a single Dirac fermion in the adjoint representation. This work examines larger lattice volumes alongside four distinct gauge coupling values. Our findings include data on the spectrum—encompassing gluonic, fermionic, and hybrid observables—as well as Polyakov loops and the anomalous dimension of the fermionic condensate derived from the Dirac mode number. These results indicate that the theory lies near the lower edge of the conformal window for adjoint fermions. Furthermore, our analysis yields crucial insights into the potential infrared scenarios conjectured for this system.

Characterizing the semantic relationships between concepts is vital for many applications, where knowledge graphs like ConceptNet serve as valuable resources by representing concept relations as graph edges. Even when concepts lack direct connections, their relationship can be inferred from the paths linking them; however, many such paths are noisy and uninformative, making the success of related applications dependent on the ability to filter for high-quality paths. While existing methods rely on simple heuristics for this selection, this paper proposes learning to predict path quality using crowdsourced human evaluations. To address quality in a generic, task-independent manner, we ask participants to rank paths based on their subjective sense of naturalness, without imposing specific definitions or guiding criteria. We demonstrate that a neural network trained on these assessments achieves near-optimal performance in predicting human judgments for unseen paths. Most significantly, our resulting path selection method outperforms current heuristic approaches in identifying meaningful paths.

This article establishes pointwise convergence theorems for martingale type involving tensor product splines in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space (where $d$ is a positive integer). In this framework, conditional expectations are substituted with their corresponding tensor spline orthoprojectors. We derive versions of Doob's maximal inequality, the martingale convergence theorem, and the characterization of the Radon-Nikodým property for Banach spaces $X$ regarding pointwise $X$-valued martingale convergence within this context. These results mirror their standard martingale equivalents and remain valid regardless of the filtration, spline degree, or the dimension $d$.

A new Stata command, ldvqreg, has been created to estimate quantile regression models for censored data (featuring lower and/or upper bounds) and binary dependent variables. These estimators utilize a smoothed variant of the quantile regression objective function. Simulation results indicate that the command accurately estimates parameters and should be preferred over existing quantile regression methods when censoring occurs. Additionally, the paper includes an empirical study on women's labor supply in Uruguay.

We introduce Human-centered 4D Scene Capture (HSC4D), a method designed to accurately and efficiently generate dynamic digital environments featuring extensive indoor-outdoor spaces, varied human movements, and rich human-environment interactions. By relying solely on body-mounted IMUs and LiDAR, HSC4D operates without external device constraints or the need for pre-existing maps. Addressing the limitations where IMUs suffer from long-term drift despite capturing human poses, and LiDAR offers stable global localization but lacks local precision, HSC4D employs joint optimization to synergize these sensors, enabling effective long-term capture. The system also investigates human-environment relationships to enhance interaction realism. To support downstream applications such as AR, VR, robotics, and autonomous driving, we provide a dataset comprising three large-scale scenes (ranging from 1k to 5k $m^2$) with precise dynamic human motion and location data. Diverse settings, including climbing gyms, multi-story buildings, and slopes, along with challenging activities like stair climbing and exercise, validate the method's effectiveness and generalization capabilities. The dataset and associated code are accessible at http://www.lidarhumanmotion.net/hsc4d/.

We present the development of end-to-end jet image classifiers utilizing simulated low-level detector data from high-fidelity CMS Open Data to distinguish between quark- and gluon-initiated jets. Our work underscores the critical role of precise spatial information and shows that our method achieves performance comparable to current state-of-the-art classifiers. Additionally, we extend this end-to-end framework to event-level classification for quark versus gluon di-jet QCD events. When comparing the fully end-to-end approach to methods relying on hand-engineered features, we demonstrate that the end-to-end algorithm remains robust against underlying event effects and pile-up.

Hardware-based acceleration aims to support computationally intensive mathematical operations. This paper introduces an FPGA architecture designed to speed up convolution, a resource-heavy step common in Convolutional Neural Networks. The design focuses on standard convolution to serve as an edge-AI product, delivering an FPGA IP core capable of processing one convolutional layer at a time. Developed in Verilog HDL, this core can be deployed across various FPGA families. Experimental results indicate that a single synthesized core on a basic edge computing board achieves 0.224 GOPS, while full board utilization yields 4.48 GOPS.

Structural seismic interpretation and quantitative characterization have traditionally been closely linked processes. Historically, quantitative methods generated subsurface property estimates that assisted structural analysis alongside raw seismic data and various seismic attributes. In this study, we reframe this workflow as an inverse problem designed to simultaneously estimate subsurface properties (specifically acoustic impedance) and a piece-wise segmented representation of the subsurface defined by user-specified macro-classes. By inverting for these quantities concurrently, the approach leverages prior knowledge regarding regions of interest while simultaneously constraining these assumptions with actual seismic measurements. Since the proposed functional is separable across the two variables, they are optimized in an alternating manner, with each subproblem addressed using a Primal-Dual algorithm. Following this, each class serves as input to a subsequent workflow intended to delineate the perimeters of detected shapes and generate unique horizons. The efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated through numerical examples utilizing both synthetic and real-world field datasets.

We demonstrate that spin-orbit coupling (SOC) exhibits dual, opposing effects on orbitally-selective Mott transitions within a three-orbital Hubbard model featuring crystal field splitting at a $2/3$ filling, representing a minimal framework for ruthenates. Specifically, SOC promotes a metallic state by enhancing orbital hybridization at low on-site Coulomb repulsions, yet it stabilizes a Mott insulating state at high interaction strengths through the lifting of orbital degeneracies and increased band polarization. Furthermore, an orbitally-selective non-Fermi liquid (OSnFL) emerges between the Mott phase and the Fermi-liquid state, characterized by the simultaneous breakdown and persistence of Fermi liquid behavior across different orbitals. This distinctive phase offers an explanation for the anomalous metallic properties observed in 4$d$ materials like Ca$_{1.8}$Sr$_{0.2}$RuO$_4$, Ba$_2$RuO$_4$ (under strain), and Sr$_2$RuO$_4$ (under uniaxial pressure). We suggest that orbitally-selective Kondo breakdown serves as the underlying mechanism for the OSnFL.

This study introduces a partial least squares (PLS) regression approach designed for function-on-function regression models involving a functional response and multiple functional predictors that exhibit quadratic and interaction effects. Since directly estimating such models is typically ill-posed, practical applications often involve projecting infinite-dimensional functional data into a finite-dimensional space using basis functions. This transformation converts the function-on-function regression into a multivariate regression of the resulting basis expansion coefficients. The proposed method approximates functional variables via finite-dimensional basis expansions during the estimation phase. We demonstrate that PLS regression built from a functional response, multiple functional predictors, and their quadratic/interaction terms is mathematically equivalent to PLS regression derived from the basis expansions of those functional variables. Based on the PLS analysis of these basis expansions, we derive an explicit formula for estimating the coefficient function of the model. Given that true model forms are often unknown, we suggest a forward selection procedure for model building. The method's performance in finite samples is evaluated through multiple Monte Carlo simulations and two empirical case studies, with results showing favorable comparisons to existing approaches.

Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) currently stands as the leading nonparametric approach for solving the two-sample problem. Its statistic measures the difference in expectations of a witness function, which is a real-valued function constructed as a weighted sum of kernel evaluations at specific basis points. Standard practice involves optimizing the kernel on a training set and conducting hypothesis testing on a distinct test set to prevent overfitting and manage type-I error; in this conventional setup, the test set estimates expectations and defines basis points, while the training set merely selects the kernel before being discarded. This paper proposes utilizing the training data to also determine the weights and basis points, thereby enhancing data efficiency. We demonstrate that 1) the proposed test maintains consistency with well-controlled type-I error; 2) the optimal witness function corresponds to a precision-weighted mean within the reproducing kernel Hilbert space linked to the kernel; and 3) empirical evaluations on difficult synthetic and real-world datasets (such as the Higgs data) confirm that the test's power matches or surpasses that of MMD and other contemporary methods.

Sea ice reduces the energy of waves traveling from the open ocean. This study models the progression of energetic, unidirectional random waves within the marginal ice zone using a nonlinear Schrödinger equation that incorporates a frequency-dependent dissipative term, aligning with established modeling frameworks and recent field data. The preferential dissipation of high-frequency components causes a simultaneous downward shift in the spectral peak, resulting in energy decay that is slower than exponential but still less rapid than predicted by a linear model. The interplay between attenuation and the downshifting of nonlinearity causes wave statistics at the ice edge to increasingly resemble a Gaussian distribution as they move further into the marginal ice zone.

The dynamical structure factor is a crucial observable for quantum magnets, yet predicting it for Hubbard-like models in dimensions higher than one remains challenging due to theoretical and numerical constraints. This study investigates magnetic excitations in the triangular lattice Hubbard model, which incorporates next-nearest neighbor hopping. By utilizing self-consistent random phase approximation, we calculate magnon spectra originating from both $120^{\circ}$ and stripe magnetic orders. Within the stripe phase, we identify generic accidental zero modes linked to a classical degeneracy familiar from the corresponding $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg model. We generalize the order-by-disorder mechanism to Hubbard systems, demonstrating how quantum fluctuations stabilize the stripe order. Furthermore, frustration-induced magnon condensation enables us to construct the full phase diagram, showing remarkable consistency with recent numerical studies. Finally, we explore experimental implications for triangular lattice compounds and relate our findings to the proposed chiral spin liquid phase.

Blockchain-based smart contract applications can only achieve their complete potential when they integrate smoothly with legacy software through a programmatic interface. This interface must support the creation and execution of contracts, as well as the monitoring of blockchain state. We introduce a typed API designed for this purpose and define key properties of the resulting hybrid system. Specifically, we present an execution model that allows us to demonstrate type-safe interactions between external programs and the blockchain. We also identify additional properties of this model that inform necessary API requirements. Finally, we present an OCaml prototype of this interface tailored for the Tezos blockchain.

This study introduces a deep learning system designed to predict microsatellite instability (MSI) in colorectal cancer using H&E-stained tissue microarray (TMA) images. The framework features an end-to-end preprocessing pipeline that generates tiles at various magnifications within regions of interest, guided by a tissue classifier and a multiple-bias rejection module. Training and validation datasets were sourced from the EPICOLON project and supplemented with samples from a single institution. A systematic analysis of tile-level biases identified three protected variables influencing baseline model representations: sample origin, patient spot, and the specific TMA glass slide. To mitigate these batch effects, an adversarial training approach was integrated into the deep learning architecture, ensuring the model avoids learning biases associated with these variables. The resulting bias-ablated features demonstrated optimal discriminative capability for the task while maintaining minimal statistical dependence on the identified biases. The study further evaluated the impact of varying magnifications, tissue types, and performance metrics at both tile and patient levels. Across all three tissue categories (tumor epithelium, mucin, and lymphocytic regions) and four magnifications, the area under the curve (AUC) reached 0.87 ± 0.03 at the tile level and improved to 0.90 ± 0.03 at the patient level. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of multiple bias ablation within a deep learning architecture for digital pathology and the inaugural use of TMAs for MSI prediction.

This study introduces a two-dimensional, geometrically nonlinear beam element formulation capable of handling arbitrarily large cross-sectional rotations. Derived from the integrated equilibrium equations combined with kinematic and generalized material relations, the approach yields a system of three first-order differential equations. These are discretized via finite differences, transforming the boundary value problem into an initial value problem through a shooting method-inspired technique. Computational efficiency is enhanced by increasing the accuracy of the numerical approximation through refined integration schemes at the element level without increasing global degrees of freedom. The element has been integrated into an open-source finite element code, and numerical results demonstrate favorable agreement with standard finite-strain beam elements and analytical solutions.

Segmenting vestibular schwannoma (VS) tumors and the cochlea from MRI scans is vital for effective treatment planning. While supervised approaches have demonstrated satisfactory results, they depend on labor-intensive and time-consuming full expert annotations. This study addresses VS and cochlea segmentation within an unsupervised domain adaptation framework. Our method employs image-level domain alignment to reduce domain divergence and utilizes semi-supervised training to enhance performance. Additionally, we introduce a mechanism to fuse predictions from multiple models using noisy label correction. Results from the challenge validation leaderboard indicate that our unsupervised approach achieves promising segmentation performance, with a mean Dice score of $0.8261 \pm 0.0416$ and a mean Dice value for the tumor of $0.8302 \pm 0.0772$, which is comparable to weakly-supervised methods.

This study investigates the rare decays $\Lambda_b \rightarrow \Lambda l^+ l^-$ (where $l=e,\mu,\tau)$ using the Bethe-Salpeter equation framework. Our findings indicate that the branching ratio $Br(\Lambda_b \rightarrow \Lambda \mu^+ \mu^-)\times 10^{6}$ ranges from $0.812$ to $1.445$ for $\kappa = 0.050 \sim 0.060$ GeV$^3$ with a binding energy $E_0=-0.14$ GeV, and spans $1.051$ to $1.098$ when $\kappa = 0.055$ GeV$^3$ as $E_0$ shifts between $-0.19$ and $-0.09$ GeV. These outcomes align with experimental observations. Within these same parameter ranges, the branching ratios for $Br(\Lambda_b \rightarrow \Lambda e^+ e^-)$ and $Br(\Lambda_b \rightarrow \Lambda \tau^+ \tau^-)$, multiplied by $10^{6}$, fall within the intervals of $0.660\text{--}1.028$ and $0.749\text{--}1.098$, respectively, while the corresponding $\tau$-mode values lie between $0.252\text{--}0.392$ and $0.286\text{--}0.489$.

Perfusion imaging represents a promising new method for evaluating and assessing liver cancer treatments. The C-Arm CT offers the capability to conduct these perfusion scans intra-operatively, enabling even quicker assessments. However, the slow rotation speed of the C-Arm CT and inherent noise levels affect reconstruction quality, necessitating the use of model-based approaches. This study implements the Time Separation Technique (TST) to reduce noise, accelerate reconstruction, and enhance the quality of the resulting perfusion images. Using data from animal experiments, we demonstrate that Dynamic C-Arm CT Liver Perfusion Imaging, when combined with TST-based data processing, yields results comparable to those of standard CT liver perfusion imaging.

For years, support mechanisms such as the Feed-in-Tariff (FiT) have significantly driven the adoption of distributed energy resources and facilitated the shift from consumers to prosumers. This process has democratized and decarbonized the energy sector, presenting system operators with both challenges and opportunities that have spurred the development of local energy markets. While the FiT has traditionally been viewed as the minimum economic incentive required for prosumer participation in these markets, it is currently being phased out in various nations. This paper introduces a novel pricing mechanism grounded in the Levelized Cost of Electricity, designed to ensure prosumer profitability while establishing a transparent and equitable price structure for all market participants. Operating on a Distributed Ledger Technology platform, the mechanism adopts a holistic approach by framing the market as a Cyber-Physical-Social-System. The study analyzes and compares fixed and variable contract schemes with wholesale suppliers against both the conventional FiT and its proposed alternatives. Results indicate that while the new mechanism reduces costs for consumers and results in a minor revenue decrease for prosumers relative to the FiT, it offers a substantial net benefit increase for both groups when compared to the actual replacement options currently suggested for the FiT.

Gleason's theorem [A. Gleason, J. Math. Mech., \textbf{6}, 885 (1957)] constitutes a pivotal finding in quantum mechanics foundations, establishing the Born rule as a direct mathematical deduction from the formalism. It offers a fundamental insight into the projective geometry of Hilbert spaces by demonstrating that finitely additive measures defined on the projection lattice $\PH$ can be extended to positive linear functionals on the algebra of bounded operators $\BH$. Over time, numerous researchers have expanded the theorem's applicability from type I algebras to arbitrary von Neumann algebras, excluding those with type $\text{I}_2$ factors. This paper presents a generalization of Gleason's theorem to composite systems, enhancing the original result in two specific ways: first, by extending it to Naimark [M. A. Naimark, C. R. (Dokl.) Acad. Sci. URSS, n. Ser., \textbf{41}, 359 (1943)] and Stinespring [W. F. Stinespring, Proc. Am. Math. Soc., \textbf{6}, 211 (1955)] dilations, and second, by enforcing consistency regarding dynamical correspondences on the local algebras involved in the composition [E. M. Alfsen and F. W. Shultz, Commun. Math. Phys., \textbf{194}, 87 (1998)]. We demonstrate that while neither condition alters the outcome for single systems, both are essential for successfully generalizing the theorem to bipartite systems.

This study offers a comprehensive analysis of the 2016-2017 outburst of the Galactic black hole transient GRS 1716-249, utilizing optical data from the Las Cumbres Observatory, mid-infrared observations from the Very Large Telescope, near-infrared measurements from the Rapid Eye Mount telescope, ultraviolet data from the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope, alongside archival radio and X-ray records. Our findings indicate that the optical/near-infrared and ultraviolet emission primarily stems from a multi-temperature accretion disk, whereas mid-infrared and radio emissions are dominated by synchrotron radiation from a compact jet. During the hard state, the optical/UV flux density correlates with X-ray emission, supporting a model of an X-ray irradiated accretion disk supplemented by viscous disk emission as the outburst wanes. Additionally, we present the long-term optical light curve, determining a quiescent i-band magnitude of 21.39$\pm$0.15 mag. We also critique prior system parameter estimates, arguing they are likely inaccurate due to flawed underlying assumptions. By comparing our dataset with other outbursting black hole X-ray binaries, we observe that while GRS 1716-249 exhibits similar X-ray behavior, it appears significantly optically fainter if the literature distance of 2.4 kpc is correct. Through multiple lines of evidence, we contend that the source lies farther away than previously thought, likely between 4 and 17 kpc, with the most probable distance range being approximately 4 to 8 kpc.

Wikipedia articles on identical subjects across different language editions often rely on distinct information sources. For instance, the English and German versions of the article "Annexation of Crimea by the Russian Federation" contain markedly different sets of linked news references. While variations can be partly explained by differing editor and reader language proficiencies, the lack of significant overlap between English sources cited in the German edition—and the ease of accessing English sources there—suggests a potential bias toward specific national contexts in how facts are referenced. However, manually tracing the national origin of every reference to compare link distributions is impractical for non-technical users or scientists. Wikiwhere addresses this by analyzing and visualizing the geographic origins of external links within Wikipedia articles. Rather than depending exclusively on IP-based location data, the system employs machine learning models that evaluate multiple features to determine where web references originate.

Prior studies have demonstrated that 3D point cloud classifiers are susceptible to adversarial attacks. Nevertheless, most existing techniques focus on white-box scenarios where attacker knowledge of model parameters is unrealistic for real-world settings. To enhance black-box attack performance, the community typically relies on transfer-based methods, yet the transferability of current 3D attacks remains limited. To address this, we introduce the Scale and Shear (SS) Attack, designed to generate adversarial examples with robust transferability. By randomly scaling or shearing input point clouds, our method prevents overfitting to white-box models, thereby boosting transferability. Extensive experiments confirm that the SS Attack can be effectively integrated with state-of-the-art 3D point cloud attack frameworks to create more potent strategies, achieving over 3.6 times better transferability than the baseline. Furthermore, despite significantly outperforming existing methods, the SS Attack attains state-of-the-art transferability across various defensive measures. Our code will be publicly available at https://github.com/cuge1995/SS-attack.

Although dark matter is supported by observational evidence, its intrinsic properties remain unknown, and the origin of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos detected by IceCube is still unclear. Should dark matter interact with neutrinos, they would likely display a non-zero elastic scattering cross-section. An interaction between an isotropic flux of extragalactic neutrinos and dark matter would be most pronounced at the Galactic Centre, where the dark matter column density is highest. This scattering process would reduce the high-energy neutrino flux, potentially creating an observable signature in IceCube data. By utilizing the seven-year Medium Energy Starting Events dataset, we conducted an unbinned likelihood analysis to detect a signal consistent with a dark matter-neutrino interaction scenario. Specifically, we investigated for a suppression of the high-energy neutrino flux toward the Galactic Centre and contrasted these findings with complementary constraints derived from low-energy data, including large-scale structure surveys and the cosmic microwave background.

Explicit formulae for projectors onto the invariant subspaces of the $\operatorname{ad}^{\otimes 2}$ representation for the Lie algebras $so(N)$ and $sp(2r)$ were derived using the split Casimir operator. Additionally, these projectors were analyzed through the lens of the universal complex simple Lie algebra framework via Vogel parametrisation.

Numerous machine learning algorithms have emerged recently to boost model performance across various artificial intelligence domains. However, challenges remain stemming from insufficient data and resources. To some extent, embedding knowledge into machine learning models can mitigate these issues, although this process is intricate due to the diverse formats of knowledge representation. This paper provides a concise overview of these varied knowledge integration methods and evaluates their effectiveness in specific machine learning applications.

While the decay of a massive particle into neutrinos during the early Universe is subject to weaker constraints compared to decays producing other Standard Model particles, the emitted neutrinos inevitably generate secondary particles via electromagnetic interactions that are detectable. We examine in detail the sensitivity of various cosmological probes to these secondary particles, specifically CMB anisotropies, CMB spectral distortions, and Big Bang Nucleosynthesis. For relics with lifetimes shorter than the age of the Universe, this analysis yields novel and rigorous limits on the particle's lifetime, dependent on its mass and abundance.

This work investigates counterfactual explanations for private Support Vector Machines (SVMs), where the classifier is released under a differential privacy guarantee. Although privacy protection is crucial for sensitive data, the noise introduced to the classifier weights inevitably reduces classification accuracy. To address this, counterfactual explanations for such models must remain robust against uncertainties in the SVM weights, ensuring with high confidence that the explained instance is genuinely different from its proposed explanation. We represent these weight uncertainties using a random vector and frame the explanation task as an optimization problem featuring probabilistic constraints. After deriving a deterministic equivalent for this problem, we analyze its solutions. Specifically, for linear SVMs, the formulation becomes a convex second-order cone program, whereas non-linear SVMs result in a non-convex problem. Consequently, we propose a sub-optimal approach utilizing the bisection method. Empirical results indicate that, unlike non-robust explanations, the quality of these robust explanations diminishes as privacy levels increase, a trade-off necessary to maintain a predetermined confidence level for correct classifications.

This paper investigates an abstract Wiener space $(X,\gamma,H)$ and an open subset $O\subseteq X$ that meets specific conditions. For each $p\in(1,+\infty)$, we define the Sobolev space $W_{0}^{1,p}(O,\gamma)$ as the closure of Lipschitz functions with support strictly away from $\partial O$ under the standard Sobolev norm. We demonstrate that, given the assumptions on $O$, this space can be characterized as the set of functions in $W^{1,p}(O,\gamma)$ with a zero trace on $\partial O$, or equivalently, as the space of functions on $O$ whose zero extension lies within $W^{1,p}(X,\gamma)$.

Neural network pruning is a technique used to identify efficient, high-performing subnetworks within pre-trained, dense architectures. Typically, this involves a computationally intensive three-stage workflow—pre-training, pruning, and re-training—requiring the dense model to be fully trained beforehand. However, empirical evidence suggests that high-quality subnetworks can be discovered through pruning even without complete pre-training of the dense model. To theoretically determine the necessary amount of pre-training for a pruned network to perform effectively, we derived a theoretical bound on the number of SGD pre-training iterations required for a two-layer, fully-connected network. Our analysis shows that beyond this threshold, greedy forward selection yields subnetworks with low training error. Furthermore, we found that this threshold scales logarithmically with dataset size, implying that larger datasets necessitate more pre-training to ensure the pruned subnetworks perform well. We validated these theoretical findings empirically across diverse architectures and datasets, including fully-connected networks on MNIST and various deep CNNs on CIFAR10 and ImageNet.

In four-dimensional Yang-Mills theories, we suggest a universal rescaling of the ratio between topological susceptibility and the square of the string tension, relying solely on group factors. This proposal is tested on $SU(N_c)$ and $Sp(N_c)$ groups by comparing data from multiple independent lattice collaborations. We demonstrate that the rescaled numerical sequences for these two group families are mutually compatible. Consequently, we conduct a joint fit and extrapolate to the shared large-$N_c$ limit.

We demonstrate that gravitational wave signals originating from primordial black hole (PBH) binaries at high redshift are detectable. This detectability is amplified by redshift bias and the increased abundance of PBH binaries at such distances. Furthermore, accounting for the initial clustering of PBHs expands the effective mass ranges detectable at high redshift. Future high-redshift gravitational wave observations using space-based instruments like LISA and SKA will allow researchers to constrain both the fraction of dark matter composed of PBHs and their initial distribution.

This work offers analytical and numerical analysis of the phase diagram and related properties of the extended Kitaev-Heisenberg model on a honeycomb lattice, specifically within the *easy-plane* limit where interactions are restricted to spin components lying in the plane of the magnetic ions. This specific parameter range enables a crucial, systematic *quantitative* study of spin excitations within ordered phases and their general characteristics. Specifically, we show that in this limit, magnon interactions can be consistently included in both the zero-field zigzag and field-polarized phases. Regarding the nominally polarized phase, we introduce a regularization method to address the unphysical divergences at the critical field that hinder the $1/S$-approximation in this class of models. Within the explored parameter subspace, all symmetry-allowed terms of the standard extended Kitaev-Heisenberg parametrization—including $K$, $J$, and $\Gamma$—are significant, rendering our findings relevant to a broader parameter space. Furthermore, the dynamical structure factor near the paramagnetic critical point reveals features reminiscent of those seen in $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$, highlighting that these characteristics are not unique to this material but are expected across a wide range of model parameters and, by extension, in other related materials.

Drawing inspiration from direct and indirect maximal center gauge techniques used to detect vortices in lattice computations, and employing the connection formalism, we demonstrate that vortices and vortex chains emerge in the continuum limit of the QCD vacuum under suitable gauge transformations.

This paper addresses the challenge of unsupervised multi-view feature selection. Traditional methods typically merge pre-defined view-specific similarity structures into a single collaborative structure before performing feature selection; however, these two stages are disjoint, leaving the collaborative structure static during selection. Furthermore, naive undirected combination of views can compromise the reliability of the final similarity structure due to inherent noise and outliers in individual views. To mitigate these issues, we introduce Adaptive Collaborative Similarity Learning (ACSL) for multi-view feature selection. Our approach dynamically learns the collaborative similarity structure and unifies this learning process with feature selection within a single framework. Additionally, we design a rank constraint to adaptively optimize the collaborative similarity structure, ensuring appropriate combination weights and neighbor assignments that enhance feature selection performance. We derive an effective solution with proven convergence to iteratively solve the resulting optimization problem. Experimental results confirm the superiority of our proposed method.

Blind image super-resolution (Blind-SR) seeks to reconstruct a high-resolution (HR) image from a low-resolution (LR) input when the specific degradation factors are unknown. While many existing approaches employ an explicit degradation estimator tailored to specific degradation types to guide super-resolution, this strategy is impractical because obtaining concrete labels for numerous degradation combinations (e.g., blur, noise, JPEG compression) to supervise training is infeasible. Furthermore, designing specialized modules for particular degradations, such as blur, limits the model's ability to generalize across different types. Consequently, there is a need for an implicit degradation estimator capable of extracting discriminative degradation representations for all scenarios without relying on ground-truth degradation labels. This paper introduces KDSR, a Knowledge Distillation-based Blind-SR network, comprising a Knowledge Distillation-based Implicit Degradation Estimator (KD-IDE) and an efficient super-resolution network. The KDSR model is trained in two stages: first, a teacher network (KD-IDE$_{T}$) is trained using paired HR and LR patches, optimized jointly with the SR network; subsequently, a student network (KD-IDE$_{S}$) is trained to accept only LR inputs and learn to extract the same implicit degradation representation (IDR) as the teacher. To fully leverage the extracted IDR, we developed a simple, robust, and efficient IDR-based Dynamic Convolution Residual Block (IDR-DCRB) to construct the SR network. Extensive experiments under both classic and real-world degradation conditions demonstrate that KDSR achieves state-of-the-art performance and generalizes effectively to various degradation processes. The source code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available.

We apply canonical quantization to gravity within a Schwarzschild black hole background using the generalized Regge-Wheeler gauge introduced in \cite{Kallosh:2021ors}. Our analysis reveals that the quadratic Hamiltonian is both unitary and free of ghosts. The system features two canonical degrees of freedom linked to the Zerilli-Moncrief and Cunningham-Price-Moncrief functions of metric perturbations, while the ${\ell }<2$ component of the Hamiltonian disappears. Furthermore, this unitary quantization framework for gravity remains valid in Minkowski space when expressed in spherical coordinates.

This paper introduces an enhanced continued fraction approximation for the Wallis ratio, which operates more rapidly than the recently identified asymptotic series. We further derive a double-sided inequality associated with this approximation and conclude by presenting numerical results that highlight its superior performance.

We analyze how a trained autoencoder distorts the input space by examining the Jacobians derived from its trained weight matrices. Under the assumption that eigenvectors are orthogonal, we establish bounds for mean squared errors across points in the input space. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the trace and the product of the Jacobian matrices' eigenvalues effectively predict the MSE for test data. This offers a dataset-independent method to evaluate an autoencoder's generalization capabilities, requiring only the model's parameters rather than knowledge of the training dataset.

We present the discovery of coherent X-ray pulsations at a frequency of 376.05 Hz (corresponding to a 2.66 ms period) within NICER data capturing a 2020 October/November transient outburst from the low-mass X-ray binary IGR J17494-3030. This system is identified as an accreting millisecond X-ray pulsar orbiting in a 75-minute ultracompact binary, with a mass donor likely being a $\simeq 0.02 M_\odot$ finite-entropy white dwarf made of helium or carbon/oxygen. The fractional rms pulsed amplitude stands at 7.4%, and the soft X-ray pulse profile (1–3 keV) exhibits a prominent second harmonic. Both the pulsed amplitude and pulse phase lag display energy dependence, peaking locally at 4 keV and 1.5 keV, respectively. Furthermore, we detected these pulsations in archival XMM-Newton observations from 2012, which enabled us to determine a long-term spin-down rate of $\dot\nu = -2.1(7)\times10^{-14}$ Hz/s and estimate a surface dipole magnetic field strength of approximately $10^9$ G. We demonstrate that mass transfer in this binary is probably non-conservative and examine several potential scenarios for mass loss from the system.

The text provides an explicit description of the virtualization map for the (modified) Nakajima monomial model within crystals, alongside a detailed account of the Lusztig data for these modified Nakajima monomials in type $A_n$.

This work investigates topological terms in $(2+1)$-dimensional sigma models through the lens of bordism group classifications of invertible quantum field theories. We specifically analyze the potential topological terms for the $U(N)/U(1)^N$ flag-manifold sigma model. Our findings indicate that the Hopf-like term is missing, despite the nontrivial homotopy group $\pi_3(U(N)/U(1)^N)=\mathbb{Z}$ suggesting otherwise; consequently, skyrmions cannot acquire arbitrary anyonic statistics. Rather, we identify ${N(N-1)\over 2}-1$ distinct types of Chern-Simons terms, some of which enable skyrmions to behave as fermions, and we provide explicit effective Lagrangians for these cases.

This paper introduces two classes of elements within the enveloping algebra $\mathbf{U}(gl(n))$: the \emph{double Young-Capelli bitableaux} $[\fbox{$S \ | \ T$}\ ]$ and the \emph{central} \emph{Schur elements} $\mathbf{S}_{\lambda}(n)$, which exhibit remarkable action on the highest weight vectors of irreducible Schur modules. Each Schur element $\mathbf{S}_{\lambda}(n)$ is defined as the sum of all double Young-Capelli bitableaux $[\fbox{$S \ | \ S$}\ ]$, where $S$ represents row (strictly) increasing Young tableaux of shape $\widetilde{\lambda}$. It is demonstrated that these Schur elements correspond to the preimages, under the Harish-Chandra isomorphism, of the \emph{shifted Schur polynomials} $s_{\lambda|n}^* \in \Lambda^*(n)$. Consequently, the Schur elements are identical to the Okounkov \textit{quantum immanants}, recently characterized by the authors as linear combinations of \emph{Capelli immanants}. This novel formulation of Schur elements/quantum immanants does not rely on the irreducible characters of symmetric groups. Furthermore, the Capelli elements $\mathbf{H}_k(n)$ function as column Schur elements, while the Nazarov-Umeda elements $\mathbf{I}_k(n)$ serve as row Schur elements. The duality in $\boldsymbol{\zeta}(n)$ arises from a combinatorial description of the eigenvalues of the $\mathbf{H}_k(n)$ on irreducible modules that is {\it{dual}} (in terms of shapes/partitions) to the combinatorial description of the eigenvalues of the $\mathbf{I}_k(n)$. Finally, the limit process $n \rightarrow \infty$ for the algebras $\boldsymbol{\zeta}(n)$ is achieved through both direct and inverse limits within the category of filtered algebras, utilizing the \emph{Olshanski decomposition/projection}.

Grid-forming (GFM) control is increasingly recognized as a viable strategy for integrating large-scale power electronic converters into modern grids, leveraging their voltage-source characteristics on the AC side. In contrast to grid-following (GFL) converters, GFM units operate without relying on phase-locked loops (PLLs) for synchronization and demonstrate superior adaptability to weak grid conditions. Nevertheless, specific guidelines regarding the configuration of GFM converters and the requisite quantity remain undefined. This letter addresses these uncertainties by examining the impact of the GFM-to-GFL capacity ratio on small-signal stability and providing a methodology for selecting an optimal ratio to ensure a desired stability margin. Our approach characterizes the influence of GFM converters on stability margins through the lens of grid strength, with findings validated via high-fidelity simulations.

This Letter presents measurements of the CP violation parameters S_J/{\psi}KS0 and C_J/{\psi}KS0 for the B0 -> J/{\psi} KS0 decay, utilizing 1.0/fb of proton-proton collision data at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV recorded by the LHCb experiment. The analysis results are S_J/{\psi}KS0 = 0.73 +- 0.07 (stat) +- 0.04 (syst) and C_J/{\psi}KS0 = 0.03 +- 0.09 (stat) +- 0.01 (syst). Both measurements align with existing world averages and are consistent with Standard Model predictions.

Finding binary sequences with minimal peak sidelobe levels constitutes a significant computational challenge. To address this, we developed a stochastic algorithm employing two distinct fitness functions that assign varying weights to autocorrelation values based on an exponent. These functions guide separate optimization phases, with the process alternating between them until a stopping criterion is met. Leveraging the Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA), the algorithm utilizes graphics processing units to maximize computational throughput. Validated on sequences of length $L = 2^m - 1$ where $14 \le m \le 20$, the results demonstrate that utilizing dual fitness functions markedly enhances algorithmic efficiency. Consequently, the method achieved new best-known solutions and yielded PSL values substantially lower than $\sqrt{L}$.

A schema represents a naturally defined subset within the space of fixed-length binary strings. While Holland's Schema Theorem establishes a lower bound for the expected proportion of a population matching a schema after a single generation of a simple genetic algorithm, this paper derives formulas for the exact expected fraction. Holland's theorem comprises three components addressing selection, crossover, and mutation; however, only the selection component is exact, with the others being approximations. This work demonstrates how to render the crossover and mutation components exact, from which Holland's theorem emerges as a corollary. Furthermore, the paper exploits the close connection between schemata and the Walsh basis representation of the population to derive these results and enhance the efficiency of computing schema averages. Finally, it presents a variant of the Vose infinite population model in which crossover and mutation are treated as distinct functions instead of a unified "mixing" function.

This work tackles a single-server queue control problem (QCP) under heavy traffic conditions, building on the model established by Lee and Weerasinghe (2011). The framework utilizes a state process representing offered waiting time, with customer arrivals governed by a state-dependent intensity, while service and patience times follow independent, identically distributed general distributions. We define an infinite-horizon discounted cost functional incorporating two components: a control cost dependent on control actions and a penalty for system idleness. Our primary contribution is resolving the QCP using a non-trivial control cost function. Under mild assumptions, the heavy-traffic limit transforms the QCP into a stochastic differential equation-based diffusion control problem (DCP). By applying the Legendre-Fenchel transformation and solving a formal Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation, we derive an optimal control for the DCP. We further establish the existence and uniqueness of the admissible control system through a comparison theorem. Finally, we translate the DCP's optimal strategy to the original QCP, yielding a nearly optimal solution and, consequently, an asymptotically optimal solution to the previously unsolved problem cited in Lee and Weerasinghe (2011).

Materials exhibiting exceptionally low lattice thermal conductivities are crucial for thermal energy management and conversion applications, including thermoelectrics and thermal barrier coatings. While crystal structure and chemical bonding are recognized as key factors influencing heat transfer, utilizing bonding principles to intentionally reduce lattice thermal conductivity remains rare. This study introduces a novel strategy to suppress lattice thermal conductivity by weakening interatomic interactions through chemical bonding principles, alongside a high-efficiency discovery method that screens the local coordination environments of crystalline compounds. Subsequent first-principles calculations identified 30 previously unknown compounds with (ultra)low lattice thermal conductivities across thirteen prototype structures from the inorganic crystal structure database. Additionally, we demonstrate a rational design approach for high-performance thermoelectrics by integrating cations featuring stereochemically active lone-pair electrons. These findings offer fundamental insights into the physical mechanisms behind low lattice thermal conductivity in a broad class of copper-based compounds and provide an efficient framework for discovering and designing materials with specific thermal transport characteristics.

Large-scale pre-training for Vision-and-Language (V+L) models has significantly enhanced performance across various downstream tasks; however, current methods fall short in the fashion domain because they neglect the distinct features of fashion-specific data and tasks. To address this, we introduce FashionViL, a new framework tailored for fashion-focused V+L representation learning. This approach incorporates two innovative pre-training tasks targeting inherent attributes of fashion data. First, unlike other domains where data typically consists of single image-text pairs, fashion datasets often contain multiple images per entry. Consequently, we propose a Multi-View Contrastive Learning task to align the visual representation of one image with the compositional multimodal representation of another image-text pair. Second, recognizing that fashion text (such as product descriptions) is rich in fine-grained concepts like attributes and noun phrases, we implement a Pseudo-Attributes Classification task to ensure that unimodal representations of the same concept remain close. Furthermore, since fashion V+L tasks frequently deviate from standard one-stream or two-stream architectures (e.g., text-guided image retrieval), we develop a flexible, modality-agnostic Transformer-based model capable of adapting to diverse downstream requirements. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FashionViL achieves state-of-the-art results on five downstream tasks, with code available at https://github.com/BrandonHanx/mmf.

Reducing the computational expense of Data Assimilation (DA) is a primary objective in Earth system modeling, especially given the influx of vast observational data. Leveraging Neural Networks' capacity to approximate Partial Differential Equation (PDE) solutions, we integrate Deep Learning (DL) into a DA framework. Specifically, we utilize the latent structure of autoencoders (AEs) to construct an Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter with model error (ETKF-Q) within the latent space, while also propagating model dynamics through a surrogate neural network in that same space. This proposed ETKF-Q-Latent (ETKF-Q-L) algorithm was evaluated on a customized, instruction-based variant of the Lorenz 96 equations, known as the augmented Lorenz 96 system, which features a latent structure that faithfully captures observed dynamics. Numerical results using this system demonstrate that the ETKF-Q-L method achieves both lower computational costs and superior accuracy compared to state-of-the-art algorithms like the standard ETKF-Q.

We examine how Higgs(-like) inflation responds to higher-dimensional operators within both the metric and Palatini formalisms, specifically focusing on nonminimal couplings and the potential. Our findings indicate that while predictions remain robust against these operators near the attractor point in the metric approach, the Palatini formalism exhibits extreme sensitivity. In the Palatini case, inflationary predictions are significantly compromised if $|\xi_4| \gtrsim 10^{-6}$ in the nonminimal coupling term $(\xi_2 \phi^2 + \xi_4 \phi^4 + \cdots)R$, or if $|\lambda_6| \gtrsim 10^{-16}$ in the Jordan-frame potential $\lambda_4 \phi^4 + \lambda_6 \phi^6 + \cdots$ (both expressed in Planck units). This heightened sensitivity arises because the Palatini formalism lacks an attractor mechanism. Consequently, our research highlights the significant difficulties involved in constructing viable inflationary models using nonminimal coupling within the Palatini framework.

This study examines the degree to which contemporary neural language models are vulnerable to structural priming, a phenomenon where a sentence's syntax increases the likelihood of that same structure appearing in subsequent sentences. We analyze how priming can reveal a model's ability to acquire abstract structural knowledge, a foundational capability for effective natural language understanding. To this end, we present a new metric and release Prime-LM, a comprehensive corpus designed to isolate various linguistic factors influencing priming intensity. Our results confirm that Transformer models exhibit structural priming, though these generalizations are partially influenced by semantic content. Furthermore, our experiments indicate that model representations do not merely capture abstract sequential patterns but also encode specific hierarchical syntactic details. Overall, this research demonstrates that the priming paradigm serves as a valuable supplementary method for probing language model capabilities, paving the way for future investigations into the models' internal states using priming techniques.

This work provides a comprehensive kinematic analysis of charged current quasielastic neutrino-nucleus interactions, utilizing the Local Fermi Gas model combined with the Random Phase Approximation. Implemented within the NEUT Monte Carlo framework, this approach enables the investigation of potentially measurable observables, such as hadron distributions. We simultaneously compare our predictions with the latest results from T2K and MINERvA regarding inclusive charged current events, CC0$\pi$ modes, and transverse kinematic-imbalance variables. Our study seeks a microscopic interpretation of the underlying reaction mechanisms to ensure the accurate reconstruction of incoming neutrino kinematics in neutrino oscillation experiments, free from conceptual biases. This research is critical for the current ambitious experimental efforts aimed at precisely determining neutrino properties, testing the three-generation paradigm, establishing the hierarchy of mass eigenstates, and probing leptonic CP violation.

Industrial and security systems frequently utilize sensor arrays to identify sudden shifts in temporal behavior, which often occur locally, meaning only a limited number of sensors provide relevant data. Due to resource limitations, continuously monitoring all sensors is costly, motivating the study of the bandit quickest changepoint detection problem. This approach involves sequentially selecting sensing actions to observe only the corresponding measurements. We establish an information-theoretic lower bound on detection delay applicable to a broad class of finitely parameterized probability distributions. Subsequently, we introduce a computationally efficient online sensing strategy that effectively balances exploring various sensing options with exploiting informative actions. We derive expected delay bounds for this scheme, demonstrating that at low false alarm rates, these bounds align with our theoretical lower limits, thereby proving the method's optimality. Finally, we validate the approach's efficacy through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

This review examines emergent symmetry breaking in small, finite systems, concentrating on strongly correlated electrons in two-dimensional semiconductor quantum dots and trapped ultracold bosonic atoms in harmonic potentials. The discussion highlights universal features and parallels in symmetry breaking across these systems and traditional domains such as nuclear physics and quantum chemistry, despite their distinct interparticle forces. A unified framework for strongly correlated phenomena in finite systems of repelling particles—whether fermions or bosons—is established through a two-step approach: symmetry breaking at the unrestricted Hartree-Fock level followed by symmetry restoration using post-Hartree-Fock projection techniques. The quantitative and qualitative characteristics of this method are analyzed and confirmed via exact diagonalization calculations. Key strongly-correlated phenomena arising from symmetry breaking include: (I) Chemical bonding, dissociation, and entanglement (under zero and finite magnetic fields) in quantum dot molecules and pinned electron molecular dimers within single anisotropic dots; (II) Electron crystallization, featuring particle localization on concentric polygonal ring vertices and the formation of rotating electron molecules (REMs) in circular dots; (III) At high magnetic fields, parameter-free analytic wave functions describe REMs, offering an alternative to Laughlin and composite-fermion theories; and (IV) Crystalline phases of strongly repelling bosons, which, in rotating traps and analogous to REMs, form rotating boson molecules (RBMs).

This work investigates the existence of linear, one-parameter families of polynomials of degree n, where every polynomial in the family possesses the alternating group $A_n$ as its Galois group. The approach employed relies heavily on geometric techniques.

This paper presents decorated merge trees (DMTs) as a new invariant for persistent spaces, integrating $\pi_0$ and $H_n$ data into one structure capable of distinguishing filtrations that merge trees and persistent homology alone cannot. Three distinct DMT variants, focusing on category theory, representation theory, and persistence barcodes, provide varied benefits for both theoretical understanding and computation. The work defines two distance metrics for DMTs—an interleaving distance and a bottleneck distance—and establishes a hierarchy of stability results that both refine and extend prior findings. To address the computational complexity of these distances, the authors propose a novel application of Gromov-Wasserstein couplings to calculate optimal merge tree alignments for a combinatorial version of the interleaving distance, enabling tractable estimation. Additionally, computational frameworks are introduced for generating, visualizing, and comparing DMTs from both synthetic and real datasets. Applications demonstrated include comparing point clouds, interpreting the persistent homology of sliding window embeddings in time series, visualizing topological features in segmented brain tumor images, and performing topology-driven graph alignment.

This work introduces a generic, rapid approach for object classification alongside a technique for dimensionality reduction. These algorithms were successfully applied to real-world chip fabrication data to predict defect states across tens of thousands of chips from various products, utilizing either full or partial measurement sets.
