Unlike conventional neural networks that optimize over vast numbers of weights, the proposed method optimizes a minimal set of variables, thereby enhancing the likelihood of achieving a global optimum. The approach is notable for its speed, strong performance on real wafer data, ease of implementation, and the production of interpretable results with clear physical meaning.

Variations of Hodge structures of weight one linked to square-tiled surfaces naturally give rise to intriguing subgroups within integral symplectic matrices, known as Kontsevich–Zorich monodromies. This paper demonstrates that arithmetic groups appear frequently among the Kontsevich–Zorich monodromies of square-tiled surfaces with low genera $g$.

Since the emergence of modern quantum mechanics in the late 1920s, it has been widely believed that classical probability laws lose their validity within this new framework. However, this presentation aims to demonstrate that this thesis is entirely unfounded and stems from a confused understanding of probability laws. Additionally, the presentation seeks to illustrate that quantum inferences constitute partially exchangeable statistical models subject to specific prior constraints, to explore the nature of these constraints, and to advocate for a dialogue between quantum theory and the theory of exchangeable models.

The late-time manifestations of primordial non-Gaussianity provide a means to probe the physics of inflation and the earliest moments of the Universe. This study examines a specific class of such non-Gaussianity, defined by initial density fluctuations sampled from a non-Gaussian probability distribution, rather than by constructing a specific primordial bispectrum form. We numerically simulated multiple realizations of cosmic structure and analyzed the late-time matter power spectrum, bispectrum, and trispectrum to assess the impact of these altered initial conditions. Our results indicate that initial non-Gaussianity leaves only a minor imprint on the first three polyspectra relative to a standard Gaussian cosmology. Additionally, certain models exhibit intriguing scale-dependent deviations in the bispectrum and trispectrum compared to the Gaussian case, though these signals remain at most at the percent level. Most of our models align with CMB constraints on the trispectrum, while the remainder are only marginally excluded. We conclude by discussing potential extensions of this research.

Recent developments in string-local quantum field theory (SLFT), which inherently preserves positivity and causality, demonstrate the ability to resolve most "No-Go" theorems associated with higher spin systems. Notably, this framework addresses the Velo-Zwanziger causality issue, revealing a significant connection to the resolution of the massless Weinberg-Witten problem. Unlike gauge theories that rely on indefinite metrics and ghosts, SLFT utilizes exclusively physical degrees of freedom that respect positivity. Consequently, it establishes a fully Lorentz-covariant and causal string field theory where light-like or space-like linear strings transform covariantly under Lorentz transformations. The interplay between causality and quantum positivity in interacting $s$-particle systems induces profound conceptual shifts. Specifically, within the Higgs model, $H$-selfinteractions arise not from spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) of a hypothetical Mexican hat potential, but strictly from the enforcement of causality and positivity. These same principles, rather than imposed gauge symmetries, dictate the Lie-algebra structure of the leading terms in self-interacting vector mesons. Furthermore, second-order consistency for self-interacting vector mesons necessitates the existence of $H$-particles; thus, the presence of $H$ is justified by consistency requirements rather than SSB. The foundational tool for SLFT is the S-matrix, whose string-independence acts as a potent constraint that defines interaction densities based on the model's particle content and is essential for constructing physical observables and string-local interpolating fields.

Although neural networks are capable of approximating intricate functions, they often fail at executing precise arithmetic with real numbers. This absence of inductive bias for mathematical operations deprives them of the logical framework needed to generalize in tasks like addition, subtraction, and multiplication. We introduce two novel neural components: the Neural Addition Unit (NAU), designed to master exact addition and subtraction, and the Neural Multiplication Unit (NMU), capable of multiplying specific vector elements. Notably, the NMU represents the first arithmetic neural component known to learn vector element multiplication when the hidden layer size is substantial. Inspired by theoretical analyses of recent arithmetic modules, our findings indicate that optimizing the NAU and NMU requires careful initialization, constrained parameter spaces, and sparsity regularization. Compared to prior neural units, our proposed NAU and NMU demonstrate more consistent convergence, utilize fewer parameters, achieve faster learning, support larger hidden sizes, generate sparse and interpretable weights, and successfully extrapolate to negative and small values.

How can we identify future instances of a rare or minority class of interest within a continuous data stream, given a labeled dataset that also contains a large number of non-interesting majority instances? We present RaRecognize, a method that (i) establishes a general decision boundary separating the rare and majority classes, (ii) learns to identify specific rare subclasses present in the training data, and (iii) detects instances from previously unseen rare subclasses as emerging cases. The general learner in (i) is designed to be distinct from the specialized learners in (ii), allowing it to distinguish minority from majority classes without overfitting to training data. Due to this generality, RaRecognize disregards all future instances classified as majority and focuses solely on recognizing recurrent and emerging rare subclasses. This approach reduces test-time computational effort and ensures that the model's size increases moderately over time, as it only retains specialized learners for minority classes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RaRecognize surpasses state-of-the-art baselines across three real-world datasets featuring rare classes of corporate risk and disaster documents.

Based on a fermionic dark matter model, we analyzed rotation curves from the THINGS HI Nearby Galaxy Survey. Our three-parameter model was compared against other standard profiles found in the literature, including the two-parameter Navarro–Frenk–White and pseudoisothermal sphere models, the Burkert model, and the three-parameter Einasto model (which Chemin et al. proposed in 2011 as a new standard). The fitting results indicate that dark matter likely has a fermionic nature with a rest mass exceeding the keV range.

Optimizing applications intended for entertainment and non-instrumental uses is difficult due to the often ambiguous connections between system parameters and user experience. While crowdsourcing design questions is ideal, current methods focus on evaluating or ranking discrete options rather than optimizing continuous parameter spaces. Furthermore, users naturally express their experiences through informal critiques (e.g., "too cold," "too spicy") instead of the precise feedback required by optimization algorithms. Analyzing this qualitative data is particularly challenging within quantitative modeling frameworks. This article introduces "collective criticism," a critiquing-based method for modeling the relationship between system parameters and subjective preferences. By converting critiques like "too easy" or "too challenging" into censored intervals and applying interval regression, we can address these challenges. This approach offers distinct benefits: it aligns with intuitive user feedback and enables the creation of predictive models for optimal parameterization. We validate the method through two studies modeling aesthetic preferences in neural style transfer images and challenge levels in the game Tetris. These studies highlight the approach's flexibility, demonstrating that it yields robust, easily interpretable results consistent with user preferences.

Although significant efforts have been made, creating a robust model for the precise quantification of COVID-19 in chest CT scans remains highly challenging. Because of indistinct boundaries, supervised segmentation techniques are often prone to annotation biases. To address this and reduce labeling expenses while ensuring unbiased lesion localization, we introduce a data-driven framework that relies solely on image-level labels. This system effectively isolates potential lesions from raw images by leveraging a generative adversarial network and a lesion-specific decoder. Experimental results across two COVID-19 datasets validate the framework's efficacy and demonstrate its superiority over several existing approaches.

This study jointly employs the infinite time-evolving block decimation, linearized tensor renormalization group, and density matrix renormalization group methods to examine the ground state phase diagrams and thermodynamic properties of a spin-1 bond-alternating Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain featuring single-ion anisotropy, subjected to both longitudinal and transverse magnetic fields. In the plane defined by the magnetic field and bond-alternating ratio, a longitudinal field reveals six phases: singlet dimer, Haldane, two Tomonaga-Luttinger liquids, a 1/2 magnetization plateau, and a spin-polarized phase. Conversely, a transverse field identifies five phases, comprising singlet dimer, Haldane, $Z_2$ symmetry breaking, a quasi-1/2 magnetization plateau, and a quasi-spin-polarized phase. A reentrant behavior of staggered magnetization is noted under the transverse field. The quantum critical behaviors in these two field orientations belong to distinct universality classes, characterized by conformal field central charges of $c=1$ and $c=1/2$, respectively. Furthermore, experimental data for the compound NTENP under both field types are well-fitted, confirming the low-temperature specific heat behavior associated with the Luttinger liquid.

This paper presents the construction of a potential, elementary quantum matrix group (in the sense of Woronowicz) that relates to the fundamental formal aspects of General Relativity's Einstein field equations, along with its possible symmetries.

Driven by advancements in rich visual representations and pre-trained language models, video captioning has steadily improved; however, these models remain susceptible to hallucinations, defined as generating descriptions that are pathological and disconnected from the source video. Specifically, video captioning suffers from two types of hallucination: object and action hallucination. Rather than focusing solely on learning superior video representations, this study examines the root causes of hallucination, identifying three primary factors: (i) insufficient visual features extracted by pre-trained models, (ii) improper integration of source and target contexts during multi-modal fusion, and (iii) exposure bias inherent in training strategies. To address these issues, we propose two robust solutions: (a) incorporating auxiliary heads trained in a multi-label setting on extracted visual features, and (b) implementing context gates that dynamically select features during fusion. Since standard evaluation metrics only measure similarity to ground truth captions and fail to adequately capture object and action relevance, we introduce a new metric called COAHA (Caption Object and Action Hallucination Assessment) to quantify the degree of hallucination. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on the MSR-VTT and MSVD datasets, notably outperforming existing methods by a significant margin in CIDEr score.

In heavy nuclei, the ratio of local neutron to proton densities rises toward the surface, creating a "neutron skin" (NS) characterized by a slight difference of less than 0.5 fm between the root-mean-square radii of neutron and proton distributions. This study demonstrates that the NS in $^{208}$Pb results in additional spectator neutrons during ultracentral $^{208}$Pb--$^{208}$Pb collisions at the CERN SPS and LHC. Using an updated Abrasion-Ablation Monte Carlo for Colliders model (AAMCC-MST) that incorporates the NS and pre-equilibrium clustering of spectator matter, we calculated yields for spectator neutrons and protons. While the average counts of spectator neutrons and protons in ultracentral collisions remain nearly constant, the cross sections for emitting specific numbers of spectator neutrons—given 0 to 5 spectator protons—vary by 50% to 250% depending on the NS thickness. Because these cross sections are relatively insensitive to other calculation parameters, measuring them in the ALICE experiment at the LHC could constrain the wide range of existing neutron density parameterizations for $^{208}$Pb.

We examine the exponent $\theta$ in the Łojasiewicz inequality $\|\partial f(\mathbf{z})\| \ge c |f(\mathbf{z})|^\theta$ for two specific classes of analytic functions, providing explicit estimates for this value. Initially, we analyze certain non-degenerate functions, though this approach proves inconvenient. In Section 3.4, we present a polynomial example where the base Łojasiewicz exponent $\theta_0(f)$ varies across the moduli space, and in Section 3.5, we demonstrate via example that the behavior of Łojasiewicz exponents does not necessarily mirror that of Milnor numbers. Finally, in Section 4, we provide estimates for product functions $f(\mathbf{z})=f_1(\mathbf{z})\cdots f_k(\mathbf{z})$ linked to a family of convenient non-degenerate complete intersection varieties. In both categories, the singularities are non-isolated. We derive explicit formulas for the exponent $\theta_0(f)$ based on the combinatorial data of $f$'s Newton boundary and extend these results to non-reduced functions of the form $g=f_1^{m_1}\cdots f_k^{m_k}$.

The inclusion of multiple parallel attention mechanisms, each with distinct heads, significantly enhances the Transformer model's efficacy across diverse tasks such as Neural Machine Translation (NMT) and text classification. In a standard multi-head setup, individual heads focus on different input segments; however, redundancy occurs when multiple heads attend to identical parts, leading to inefficient resource utilization. To mitigate this, one can prune heads deemed least important based on specific scoring metrics. This study introduces a Dynamic Head Importance Computation Mechanism (DHICM) designed to dynamically assess each head's relevance relative to the input. Our approach involves adding a supplementary attention layer that, alongside the multi-head attention outputs and the original input, calculates individual head importance. Furthermore, we incorporate an additional loss function to penalize uniform scoring across heads, thereby ensuring the identification of more critical heads and improving overall performance. Experimental analysis of DHICM within NMT frameworks across various languages demonstrates that it substantially outperforms conventional Transformer-based methods, particularly in scenarios with limited training data.

This study analyzes 991 heartbeat stars (HBSs) drawn from the OGLE Collection of Variable Stars (OCVS), comprising 512 sources in the Galactic bulge (GB), 439 in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), and 40 in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC). Using an analytical model of flux variations based on tidal deformations, we fit the $I$-band OGLE light curves and derive distributions for key parameters such as eccentricity, orbital inclination, argument of periastron, and period-amplitude diagrams. On the Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagram, the sample splits into two distinct evolutionary groups: approximately 90 systems with short periods ($P\lesssim50$ days) feature early-type primary stars on or near the main sequence, while roughly 900 systems with long periods ($P\gtrsim100$ days) contain red giants (RGs). The placement of RG HBSs on the period-luminosity diagram strongly confirms their binary nature, positioning them as an extension of known binary systems including OGLE ellipsoidal and Long Secondary Period (LSP) variables. Additionally, time-series analysis reveals tidally-excited oscillations (TEOs) in about 5% of the sample (78 distinct modes). This large, homogeneous TEO dataset enables the construction of a diagram illustrating the correlation between the orbital harmonic number of the TEOs and the eccentricity of the host binary system.

This study employs a core-radius methodology to analyze nonlocal perimeters driven by isotropic kernels with critical and supercritical exponents, thereby generalizing the established concept of $s$-fractional perimeter (traditionally defined for $0<s<1$) to the regime where $s\ge 1$. We demonstrate that as the core-radius approaches zero, these appropriately scaled, core-radius-regularized $s$-fractional perimeters $\Gamma$-converge to the standard Euclidean perimeter. Under this same scaling, the first variation of these nonlocal perimeters yields regularized $s$-fractional curvatures that converge to the standard mean curvature as the core radius vanishes. Consequently, we establish that level set solutions to the associated nonlocal geometric flows, when suitably reparametrized temporally, converge to the standard mean curvature flow. Furthermore, we derive analogous findings for anisotropic kernels, highlighting applications within dislocation dynamics. Keywords: Fractional perimeters; $\Gamma$-convergence; Local and nonlocal geometric evolutions; Viscosity solutions; Level set formulation; Fractional mean curvature flow; Dislocation dynamics.

This paper addresses the Cauchy problem for the one-dimensional compressible isentropic magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) equations, allowing for vacuum conditions within the domain despite the absence of vacuum at infinity. By deriving a priori estimates that are independent of the resistivity coefficient ($\nu$), we demonstrate the non-resistive limit of global strong solutions for large initial data. Additionally, as a secondary result, we establish the global well-posedness of strong solutions for both the compressible resistive MHD and non-resistive MHD equations.

Automatic language identification (LID) for multiple dialects within noisy conditions presents a significant challenge, particularly when the language identity is only discernible in specific segments of the speech signal. Traditional LID and speaker recognition methods often overlook temporal sequence data by relying on long-term statistical summaries that assume feature frame independence. This paper introduces a neural network framework designed to leverage short-sequence information for language recognition. Specifically, we propose a novel model that incorporates relevance weighting, assigning higher importance to speech segments that are more pertinent to the recognition task. This weighting mechanism is implemented through a bidirectional long short-term memory (BLSTM) network equipped with attention modeling. We investigate two distinct strategies: the first aggregates segment-level i-vector/x-vector representations within the neural model, while the second directly models acoustic features using an end-to-end neural architecture. Experiments conducted on the NIST LRE 2017 Challenge (using clean, noisy, and multi-speaker data) and the RATS language recognition corpus demonstrate that our proposed approach achieves substantial performance gains over conventional i-vector/x-vector methods and other prior models that incorporate sequence information.

Bangladeshi Sign Language (BdSL) serves as a primary communication tool for the hearing-impaired community in Bangladesh. Developing a real-time BdSL interpreter that functions effectively outside controlled laboratory settings holds significant social value and represents a compelling research challenge, particularly due to variations in subjects (such as age, gender, and skin tone), complex sign features, visual similarities between signs, and cluttered backgrounds. Currently, existing BdSL datasets are predominantly created in lab-friendly environments, which restricts the deployment of advanced deep learning technologies. To address this, we present BdSL36, a new dataset featuring background augmentation to enhance versatility, comprising over four million images across 36 categories. Additionally, approximately 40,000 images are annotated with bounding boxes to enable the application of object detection algorithms. We conducted extensive experiments to establish baseline performance for BdSL36 and performed user-level beta testing of our classifiers to validate the dataset's suitability for real-world applications. We anticipate that BdSL36 will accelerate future research into practical sign letter classification. Consequently, we have made the dataset and all pre-trained models publicly available for the research community.

This study examines pulsar timing residuals resulting from the interaction between transverse pulsar acceleration and the R$\rm{\ddot{o}}$mer delay. Although this effect is generally minor and often negligible, it may become significant for pulsars residing in globular clusters. The maximum residual amplitude, observed for pulsars near the cluster core's surface, reaches tens of nanoseconds; however, detecting this signal is currently difficult for most globular clusters. Conversely, an intermediate-mass black hole at a cluster's center can substantially amplify these timing residuals. For pulsars in the innermost core regions, such residuals can become notably large. Residuals exceeding the critical threshold for a given cluster serve as strong evidence for a central black hole or dark remnant of comparable total mass. Additionally, we analyzed timing effects caused by line-of-sight accelerations, simulating their distribution via a Monte Carlo method. A two-dimensional Kolmogorov-Smirnov test was applied to assess the consistency between simulated distributions and reported data across various cluster parameters. Results indicate that the structural parameters of Terzan 5 are well-constrained by comparing measured line-of-sight acceleration distributions with Monte Carlo simulations, yielding an upper limit for the central black hole or dark remnant mass of approximately $ \sim 6000 M_{\odot} $.

At their foundation, artificial neural networks are mathematical constructs, a fact that creates inherent challenges when applied to Natural Language Processing (NLP). A primary issue arises when attempting to quantify similarity or distance between vectors in NLP embedding spaces, as mathematical distance metrics often diverge from linguistic intuition. We propose that the most effective method for assessing linguistic distance is utilizing the Language Model (LM) that generated the vectors. Furthermore, we introduce Language Model Distance (LMD) to evaluate the accuracy of vector transformations grounded in the Distributional Hypothesis (termed LMD Accuracy). The effectiveness of this metric is demonstrated by its application to a simple neural network tasked with learning the Procrustes algorithm for bilingual word mapping.

This study examines the coherence of electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino behavior, and dark matter properties within the minimal scoto-seesaw framework. By extending the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw with the minimal dark sector, we establish a physical mechanism for neutrino oscillation lengths: the atmospheric mass scale originates from tree-level seesaw dynamics, whereas the solar scale emerges radiatively through mediation by the dark sector. We pinpoint parameter regions that satisfy theoretical constraints, align with dark matter relic density, and are viable under direct detection limits. Employing two-loop renormalization group equations, we investigate vacuum stability and the consistency of the fundamental dark parity symmetry, while also deriving a lower bound for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude.

We present an alternative real-space framework grounded exclusively in activated processes to elucidate relaxation dynamics within hierarchical landscapes. Utilizing the cluster model—a coarse-grained lattice representation of jammed systems—we investigate rejuvenation and memory phenomena occurring during aging following a hard quench. In this model, neighboring lattice particles coalesce into clusters via local interactions, which subsequently fragment with a probability dependent on their size. Although the cluster model is conceptually simple, it successfully replicates key observables of aging dynamics in colloidal systems, including metrics for particle mobility and displacement. In this work, we extend the model to examine more intricate quench protocols, demonstrating that it captures the same rejuvenation and memory effects linked to the complex hierarchical architecture of glassy energy landscapes. Beyond analyzing these effects, we further establish the model's utility for predictive insights regarding the termination of memory.

This paper examines the historical development, current advancements, and physical applications of spectral theory regarding two specific categories of random functions. The first category comprises homogeneous and isotropic random fields defined over Euclidean space with values in a real, finite-dimensional linear space. In the context of continuum physics, such fields characterize the physical attributes of a homogeneous, isotropic continuous medium where microstructures are attached to every point. The field's range corresponds to a fixed point set determined by a symmetry class, under the action of two compact Lie groups via orthogonal representations. Within a homogeneous medium, the material symmetry group remains identical at each point and acts trivially, whereas the group of physical symmetries may act nontrivially. In an isotropic random medium, rank 1 (and rank 2) correlation tensors of the field transform under the physical symmetry group according to the specified representation (or its tensor square), thereby ensuring isotropy.

The second category involves isotropic random cross-sections of homogeneous vector bundles defined over a coset space of a compact Lie group. In cosmological applications, the coset space represents the celestial sphere, while the random cross-section models a cosmic background. The Cosmological Principle guarantees that this cross-section exhibits isotropy.

To assist the reader, essential background material covering multilinear algebra, representation theory, and differential geometry is provided in the Appendix.

This paper introduces an incremental text-to-speech (TTS) approach that synthesizes speech in small linguistic segments while preserving natural output quality. Incremental TTS typically faces a trade-off between latency and speech quality, making it difficult to generate high-fidelity audio with low latency without relying on future sentence context (referred to as "lookahead"). To address this, we propose an incremental TTS method that leverages a language model to generate a pseudo lookahead, thereby incorporating future contextual information without increasing latency. This method mimics human incremental reading and utilizes pretrained GPT2 to generate the lookahead, capitalizing on its extensive linguistic knowledge. Evaluation results demonstrate that our approach 1) produces superior speech quality compared to methods using only observed information and 2) achieves speech quality equivalent to that obtained by waiting for future context to be observed.

This paper investigates the connection between the mapping class group of an infinite-type surface and the simultaneous flip graph, a variation of the flip graph for infinite-type surfaces introduced by Fossas and Parlier. We demonstrate that the extended mapping class group is isomorphic to a proper subgroup of the flip graph's automorphism group, contrasting with the finite-type scenario. This finding indicates that Ivanov's metaconjecture, which posits that the extended mapping class group serves as the automorphism group for any "sufficiently rich" object linked to finite-type surfaces, fails to apply to simultaneous flip graphs of infinite-type surfaces.

The cyclic proof system CLKID-omega offers an alternative approach for representing inductive definitions and conducting efficient proof searches. In 2005, Brotherston demonstrated that CLKID-omega is at least as powerful as LKID—first-order classical logic with Martin-Löf-style inductive definitions—and hypothesized that the two were equivalent. However, this equivalence remained unresolved since 2011 until the current paper proved them distinct. By analyzing the 2-Hydra statement within a first-order language comprising zero, the successor function, the natural number predicate, and a binary predicate for 2-Hydra, the study establishes that while CLKID-omega can prove the statement, LKID cannot. This distinction is confirmed by constructing a Henkin model in which the 2-Hydra statement evaluates to false.

The current era is defined by extensive catalogs, making statistical tools like machine learning essential for analyzing large datasets. A prime example is the Sloan Moving Object Catalog (MOC), which records the astrometric and photometric data of all moving objects within the Sloan field. A key strength of the Sloan telescope is its five-filter system, which enables asteroid taxonomy through color analysis. However, previous studies often neglected the color variations induced by changes in the object's phase angle. This paper addresses that gap by utilizing absolute magnitudes for classification. Our objective is to develop a new asteroid taxonomy based on magnitudes that remains unaffected by phase angle variations. We selected 9,481 asteroids with absolute magnitudes ($H_g$, $H_i$, and $H_z$) derived from the MOC using the HG12 system and computed their absolute colors. To execute the classification, we employed the fuzzy C-means algorithm, an unsupervised machine learning method ideal for soft clustering datasets where groups overlap and are not fully distinct. We focused on the four primary taxonomic complexes—C, S, X, and V—as they represent the majority of known spectral types. Ultimately, we classified 6,329 asteroids with a probability of belonging to their assigned class exceeding 60%, including 162 objects that had previously ambiguous classifications. Furthermore, by analyzing the sample within the plane of semimajor axis versus inclination, we identified 15 new V-type asteroid candidates located outside the Vesta family region.

By adopting a functional perspective, we derive a universal formula for the gradient of Mutual Information (MI) concerning system parameters within stochastic systems, explicitly addressing scenarios where inputs depend on those parameters. Applying these findings, we examine K-user Multiple Access Channels (MAC) with feedback to analyze their MI characteristics. When specialized to the additive Gaussian noise MAC, we extend the I-MMSE relationship to the K-user Gaussian MAC with feedback. This derivation reveals that the MI gradient consists of three components: the first stems from noise via the MMSE term, while the second and third capture the impacts of interference and feedback, respectively. Furthermore, by employing Kramer's capacity-achieving Fourier-Modulated Estimate Correction (F-MEC) strategy, we demonstrate how feedback mitigates the detrimental interference effects in the K-user symmetric Gaussian MAC.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data exhibits heterogeneity stemming from variations in equipment manufacturers, scanning protocols, and differences between subjects. Traditionally, this heterogeneity is addressed through preprocessing techniques such as anatomical alignment, voxel resampling, signal intensity normalization, noise reduction, and region of interest (ROI) localization. While these pipelines standardize image appearance, their specific impact on image segmentation quality and other downstream deep neural network (DNN) tasks has not been rigorously evaluated. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of multimodal MRI brain cancer segmentation using the TCIA-GBM open-source dataset. Our findings indicate that most common standardization steps provide no benefit to artificial neural network performance and can even degrade it. We propose that intensity normalization methods fail to enhance accuracy because standardization reduces signal variance. Furthermore, skull-stripping contributes negligibly to clinically relevant metrics. Ultimately, we demonstrate that unifying voxel spacing is the sole essential transformation for accurate analysis, whereas non-rigid atlas registration for anatomical alignment and most intensity equalization steps are unnecessary and do not improve model productivity.

Large-scale vision-language pre-training has shown significant success on downstream tasks. However, current approaches heavily depend on the assumption that internet-crawled image-text pairs exhibit perfect one-to-one correspondence. In practice, this assumption often fails because text descriptions derived from image metadata frequently suffer from semantic mismatches and lack mutual compatibility. To overcome these challenges, we propose PyramidCLIP, which builds an input pyramid featuring distinct semantic levels for each modality. This method aligns visual and linguistic elements hierarchically through peer-level semantics alignment and cross-level relation alignment. Additionally, we relax the loss function applied to negative (unpaired) samples during pre-training to reduce strict constraints, thereby mitigating the risk of forcing the model to incorrectly distinguish compatible negative pairs. Experiments across five downstream tasks validate the effectiveness of PyramidCLIP. Notably, when trained on the same 15 million image-text pairs as CLIP, PyramidCLIP surpasses CLIP in ImageNet zero-shot classification top-1 accuracy by 10.6%, 13.2%, and 10.0% when using ResNet50, ViT-B32, and ViT-B16 encoders, respectively. When scaled to larger datasets, PyramidCLIP achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple tasks. Specifically, PyramidCLIP-ResNet50 trained on 143M pairs outperforms CLIP trained on 400M pairs in ImageNet zero-shot classification, demonstrating a substantial improvement in data efficiency.

For the last twenty years, global electromagnetic facilities have gathered meson photo- and electroproduction data of exceptional quality and volume. Conversely, corresponding meson-beam data for identical hadronic final states are largely obsolete, often low-quality, or missing entirely, rendering them insufficient for interpreting and maximizing the potential of the new electromagnetic datasets. To fully leverage these high-precision electromagnetic measurements, there is an urgent need for new, high-statistics meson-beam data covering a broad spectrum of reactions with comprehensive energy and angular resolution, which is essential for advancing baryon and meson spectroscopy and related hadron physics fields. To resolve this gap, the construction of a cutting-edge meson-beam facility is required. This letter details current unresolved challenges in hadron physics and highlights the significant opportunities and scientific progress that such a facility would enable.

Pretraining with language models (LMs) has consistently enhanced performance across numerous NLP downstream tasks, such as named entity recognition (NER). This paper introduces T-NER, a Python library designed for fine-tuning LMs specifically for NER. Beyond its practical application, T-NER supports the investigation of cross-domain and cross-lingual generalization capabilities in fine-tuned LMs. The library also features a web application that allows non-expert programmers to interactively obtain model predictions for arbitrary text, thereby aiding in qualitative evaluation. To demonstrate the library's potential, we unified nine public NER datasets and assessed cross-domain and cross-lingual performance across them. Initial experiments indicate that while in-domain performance remains competitive across datasets, achieving cross-domain generalization remains challenging even with large pretrained LMs. However, these models demonstrate the capacity to acquire domain-specific features when fine-tuned on combined datasets. To support future research, we have made all our LM checkpoints available through the Hugging Face model hub.

We introduce a method for retrieving values from form-like documents using arbitrary queries, aiming to minimize the manual effort required for form processing. In contrast to prior approaches limited to predefined field items, our technique predicts target values for any query by comprehending both the layout and semantic meaning of the form. To enhance model performance, we also propose SimpleDLM, a straightforward document language modeling strategy that improves document understanding during large-scale pre-training. Experimental findings demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms previous designs, with SimpleDLM further boosting value retrieval performance by approximately 17% in F1 score relative to the current state-of-the-art pre-training method. The code is accessible at https://github.com/salesforce/QVR-SimpleDLM.

This paper presents numerous numerical investigations into low-rank matrix completion, comparing Bayesian methods with a recently introduced de-biased estimator designed to construct confidence intervals. Theoretically, the de-biased estimator achieves a sharp minimax-optimal estimation error rate, whereas the Bayesian approach attains this rate only with an additional logarithmic factor. Our simulation results yield interesting findings: the de-biased estimator performs comparably to Bayesian estimators, yet Bayesian methods demonstrate greater stability and can surpass the de-biased estimator in small-sample scenarios. However, we observe that the confidence intervals provided by the de-biased estimator for individual entries are significantly shorter than the corresponding Bayesian credible intervals. These results suggest a need for further theoretical research into estimation error and concentration for Bayesian methods, as current theoretical bounds remain limited.

A novel optimization framework for sealing leakage pathways using microbially induced calcite precipitation (MICP) has been developed and applied to carbon dioxide (CO$_2$) storage projects. This approach leverages a recently created field-scale MICP mathematical model integrated into the industry-standard Open Porous Media (OPM) Flow simulator. The optimization problem is addressed using the ensemble-based optimization (EnOpt) algorithm, with an objective function designed to maximize calcite precipitation within the minimum feasible operational timeframe. An injection strategy was formulated to efficiently precipitate calcite around and within leakage paths while preventing unwanted clogging in reservoir zones, such as the near-well region. This strategy involves injecting growth and cementation solutions into separate well segments to trigger the MICP process after an initial phase establishes a biofilm in the leakage paths. The proposed procedure was tested on three synthetic CO$_2$ leakage scenarios, with numerical results demonstrating that all leakage paths were successfully sealed while maintaining a low total MICP operational duration.

We employ exact diagonalization to investigate spin-orbit coupling and interaction-driven mixing between $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states within a cubic crystal lattice, a scenario typical of transition metal oxides. Our analysis directly contrasts these findings with the commonly applied $t_{2g}$-only or $e_g$-only models, selected based on electronic filling. Covering all possible $d$-shell occupancies, we calculate the total magnetic moment, spin, individual orbital occupancies, and the effective spin-orbit coupling strength (renormalized by interactions) as functions of bare interaction parameters, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting, with a focus on regimes relevant to 4d and 5d transition metal oxides. We also derive perturbative results for various limits that align with our numerical data. Our findings reveal that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, leading to up to 20% occupancy in orbitals nominally considered "empty." This has critical implications for interpreting experimental branching ratios and influences the effective local moment Hamiltonians used to analyze magnetic phases and excitations in these materials. Ultimately, our results assist in theoretically interpreting experiments on such materials, which often operate in an intermediate coupling regime regarding electron-electron interactions.

We investigated the TeV gamma-ray emission of the supernova remnant RX J1713.7$-$3946 (RX J1713) by comparing it with non-thermal X-rays and the interstellar medium (ISM). Utilizing H.E.S.S. data in two energy ranges ($>$2 TeV and $>$250-300 GeV), we applied a novel approach modeling gamma-ray counts as a linear combination of ISM column density and X-ray counts, representing hadronic and leptonic components, respectively. Fitting this model to individual data pixels revealed that the gamma-ray counts form a flat plane within a 3D space defined by the gamma-ray counts, ISM column density, and X-ray counts. Analysis of the latest H.E.S.S. data at 4.8 arcmin resolution quantified these components for the first time, showing that hadronic processes account for $(67\pm8)$% and leptonic processes for $(33\pm8)$% of the total gamma rays. The dominance of the hadronic component, linked to an associated ISM mass of $\sim$10$^4$ $M_{\odot}$, supports the acceleration of cosmic-ray protons. Additionally, a marginal suppression of gamma rays at high counts was observed, potentially due to second-order effects such as shock-cloud interaction and the penetration-depth effect.

Although Vision Transformers (ViTs) have become dominant in many vision tasks, applying them to large images remains computationally challenging. This difficulty stems largely from self-attention scaling quadratically with the number of tokens, which also scales quadratically with image resolution. For high-resolution images, such as 1080p, over 60% of the network's total computation is consumed by generating and applying attention matrices. We address this problem with Hydra Attention, an ultra-efficient attention mechanism designed for ViTs. Counterintuitively, this efficiency is achieved by maximizing multi-head attention: by employing a number of heads equal to the number of features, Hydra Attention achieves computational linearity in both tokens and features without hidden constants. This makes it substantially faster than standard self-attention in a typical ViT-B/16 model, offering a speedup proportional to the token count. Furthermore, Hydra Attention maintains high accuracy on ImageNet and, in certain instances, even enhances performance.

This study investigates the mean first-passage time (MFPT) for asymmetric continuous-time random walks occurring in continuous space, defined by waiting times with a finite mean and jump sizes possessing both a finite mean and variance. In the asymptotic regime, this well-behaved process is described by an advection-diffusion equation, yielding a finite MFPT when the advection velocity aligns with the boundary. We formulate a nonhomogeneous Wiener-Hopf integral equation that enables the exact determination of the MFPT without relying on asymptotic approximations. This equation depends on the complete distribution of jump sizes and solely on the mean waiting time, making it applicable to general non-Markovian random walks. Using a specific family of asymmetric jump-size distributions—exponential toward the boundary and arbitrary in the opposite direction—we demonstrate that the MFPT is independent of the jump-size distribution away from the boundary. Furthermore, we identify a characteristic length scale determined exclusively by the jump-size distribution in the direction of the boundary. This scale indicates that for starting points near the boundary, the MFPT relies on the specific full distribution of jump sizes, contrasting with the universal behavior observed for starting points distant from the boundary.

This paper revisits the theory of open quantum systems through the lens of fermionic baths, focusing specifically on the dynamics of a central spin-½ particle interacting with a spin bath. We derive the exact reduced dynamics of the central spin and construct the corresponding Kraus operators. Furthermore, we formulate the exact canonical master equation of the Lindblad type for this reduced dynamics. Finally, we briefly examine the issue of non-Markovianity within the context of the central spin's reduced dynamics.

Complex physical challenges are typically addressed using perturbation theory, which yields asymptotic series based on small parameters. However, finite or even large parameter values often hold the greatest physical significance. This paper outlines a technique to forecast the behavior of solutions to nonlinear problems at large variable values using only their small-variable expansions. Rooted in self-similar approximation theory, the approach generates self-similar factor approximants capable of accurately modeling a wide range of functions, including rational, irrational, and transcendental types. The method is demonstrated through various examples from statistical and condensed matter physics, where self-similar predictions align with known large-variable behaviors. It is demonstrated that this approach enables the determination of large-variable solution behavior from just a few terms of small-variable expansions, with numerical convergence of the approximants confirmed.

We introduce a quantum circuit incorporating measurements and post-selection that displays a wide range of space- and/or time-ordered phases, ranging from ferromagnetism to spin-density waves and time crystals. Distinct from unitary models, the time crystals observed in this circuit are \emph{incommensurate} with the driving frequency, and their period can be tuned by modifying the circuit parameters. Furthermore, we show that the phases exhibited by our circuit, including those that are inherently non-equilibrium and dynamical, map onto complex-temperature equilibrium phases of the exactly solvable anisotropic Ising model on a square lattice.

Navigation has been a fundamental aspect of the web from its beginning, allowing both users and scripts to traverse hyperlinks and move backward or forward through history. This paper introduces a formal model consistent with the WHATWG navigation history specification and examines its characteristics. A key property of navigation history is that applying a delta followed by a delta' should equal applying their sum (delta + delta'); specifically, moving forward one step (+1) and then backward one step (-1) should be equivalent to taking no action (0). We demonstrate that the specification-aligned model fails to uphold this property by presenting counter-examples, which lead to four proposed patches for the model. Experimental results indicate that while browser implementations of navigation history are inconsistent, their behavior aligns more closely with the patched model than with the original specification. Consequently, we propose modifications to the specification to ensure it matches the patched model.

This study investigates a two-dimensional extension of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, renowned for its non-trivial topological band structure. Using mean field theory, we examine inhomogeneous superconducting phases driven by an attractive $U$ Hubbard interaction within this single-parameter system, where the hopping ratio satisfies $0 \leq r \leq 1$. Through both analytical derivations and numerical diagonalization, we demonstrate that lattices with open boundaries can host superconducting phases with enhanced order at the edges or corners, contingent upon the filling factor. Specifically, at half filling in finite samples, the superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) at corner sites can significantly exceed that of the bulk. This gives rise to a novel proximity effect in the temperature range $T_{c,bulk} < T < T_{c,corner}$, where the corner induces a non-zero superconducting order parameter tail extending into the bulk. We further establish that such tails are expected to be observable across a specific range of $r$ and $U$ parameters.

Salient object detection focuses on identifying the most visually prominent entities and generating their corresponding masks. Since pixel-level annotations are expensive, image tags are typically employed as weak supervision; however, a single tag can only label one object class. This paper introduces saliency subitizing as a class-agnostic alternative for weak supervision, aligning the supervision with the nature of saliency detection, which often involves multiple object classes within an image. Consequently, we propose a model comprising two modules: the Saliency Subitizing Module (SSM) and the Saliency Updating Module (SUM). The SSM generates initial saliency masks using subitizing information without relying on unsupervised techniques or random seeds, while SUM iteratively refines these masks. Extensive experiments across five benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses other weakly-supervised approaches and achieves performance comparable to certain fully-supervised methods.

To investigate exchange bias effects, researchers utilized nanomechanical resonators coated with bilayers of nickel-iron (permalloy, Py) and cobalt oxide (CoO). By severing one torsion arm, the mechanical compliance along two resonator axes was increased, creating a unique three-axis device capable of resonating to torques produced by a three-axis RF field. This approach enables the simultaneous measurement of three orthogonal torque components. Studies on anisotropies linked to interfacial exchange coupling were conducted. At cryogenic temperatures, observations of shifted linear hysteresis loops verified the existence of exchange bias at the Py/CoO interface. An in-plane rotating DC bias field was employed to detect in-plane anisotropies via out-of-plane torque. Rotational hysteresis data revealed training effects, demonstrating that features arising from interfacial coupling persisted despite significant training of the unidirectional anisotropy. Finally, the data from rotational hysteresis loops were fitted using parameters derived from a macrospin solution to the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, where each parameter in the exchange bias model corresponds to specific characteristics of the rotational loop.

Precise localization and identification of vertebrae are essential for numerous clinical tasks involving spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. Nevertheless, this process faces substantial difficulties due to diverse pathologies—including vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation—as well as varying imaging conditions like restricted fields of view and metal streak artifacts. This study introduces a robust and accurate approach that leverages anatomical spine knowledge to enhance vertebra localization and identification. The method employs a key point localization model to generate activation maps of vertebra centers, which are then re-sampled along the spine centerline to create spine-rectified activation maps. These are subsequently aggregated into one-dimensional activation signals. An anatomically-constrained optimization module is then utilized to simultaneously determine optimal vertebra centers, adhering to a soft constraint on inter-vertebral distances and a hard constraint on consecutive vertebral indices. When tested on a prominent public benchmark comprising 302 highly pathological CT images, the proposed method achieves a state-of-the-art identification rate of 97.4%, surpassing the leading competing method's 94.7% rate by halving the relative identification error.

Graph data management, often categorized as NoSQL, offers distinct advantages in flexibility and scalability by striking a unique balance between query expressivity and schema adaptability. This distinctive benefit has sparked an unexpected surge in the development of specialized graph systems, query languages, and data models, including property graphs, key-value stores, wide-column formats, and Resource Description Framework (RDF). Current graph query languages primarily focus on flexible graph pattern matching (sub-graph matching), while graph computing frameworks prioritize the rapid parallel (distributed) execution of instructions. The proliferation of diverse graph-based data management systems has consequently led to a lack of standardization. Gremlin, a graph traversal language, serves as a common platform to support various graph computing systems, ranging from OLTP graph databases to OLAP graph processors. This work presents a formalization of graph pattern matching for Gremlin queries and consolidates various existing graph algebra operators into a unified framework, accompanied by an analysis and discussion of these components.

The divisor graph is defined as an undirected graph where vertices represent positive integers and an edge exists between $a$ and $b$ if $a$ divides $b$. Let $P(n)$ denote the largest prime factor of $n$, $S(x,y) = \{n \le x : P(n) \le y\}$, and $\Psi(x,y) = |S(x,y)|$. Let $f(x,y)$ represent the maximum number of vertices in a simple path within the divisor graph restricted to $S(x,y)$. This work establishes a uniform lower bound for $f(x,y)$ when $2 \le y \le x$, improving upon a result by Tenenbaum. Specifically, it shows that $f(x) := f(x,x) \ge (c + o(1))x/\log x$ with $c = 0.3$, surpassing the previous value of $c = 0.017$. For smaller values of $y$, it derives the new asymptotic formula $f(x,y) = (1+o(1))\Psi(x,y)$ as $x \to \infty$ and $y = o(\log x)$. Additionally, a lower bound is proven for a variant of $f(x,y)$, intended for use in a subsequent paper to address a question posed by Erdős.

We introduce a stochastic conditional gradient method (CGM) designed to minimize convex finite-sum objectives composed of both smooth and non-smooth components. Current CGM approaches for this class of problems either exhibit slow convergence or necessitate a carefully increasing batch size that eventually requires computing full gradients. In contrast, our proposed method, which utilizes a stochastic average gradient (SAG) estimator, operates with just one sample per iteration while still guaranteeing fast convergence rates comparable to advanced variance reduction techniques. We specifically highlight applications involving a large number of separable constraints, which are common in semidefinite programming (SDP) formulations within machine learning and theoretical computer science. Our numerical experiments cover matrix completion, unsupervised clustering, and sparsest-cut SDPs.

This work examines Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms applied to specific particle systems characterized by both attractive and repulsive interactions, which complicates their convergence analysis. We demonstrate that a variant of these algorithms defined on a bounded state space exhibits uniform ergodicity with a clearly defined quantitative convergence rate. Furthermore, we establish that a version operating on an unbounded state space maintains geometric ergodicity. By employing the shift-coupling technique, we derive an explicit quantitative bound for its convergence rate.

Self-attention demonstrates exceptional capability in modeling long-range dependencies and boosting performance in vision applications like image classification and captioning. However, its reliance on dot-product multiplication and dimension alignment between query, key, and value features creates two significant issues: (1) the dot product leads to exhaustive and redundant computations, and (2) reshaping multi-dimensional tensor features to satisfy alignment requirements can disrupt the internal structure of the visual feature maps. To mitigate these challenges, this paper introduces a self-attention plug-in module with variants called Synthesizing Tensor Transformations (STT), designed to process image tensor features directly. Unlike traditional approaches, the basic STT module avoids query-key-value dot-product multiplication; instead, it employs tensor transformations to derive synthetic attention weights directly from visual information. The efficacy of the STT series is confirmed through evaluations on image classification and captioning tasks. Experimental results indicate that the proposed STT achieves competitive performance and maintains robustness relative to standard self-attention methods in these vision tasks.

Refactoring serves as the standard approach for enhancing software health. Although numerous studies suggest strategies involving design patterns and defect removal to optimize design, there is limited understanding of how developers specifically refactor code to boost reusability. Consequently, we extracted refactorings aimed at improving reusability from 1,828 open-source projects. We evaluated their impact on established reusability metrics and compared the distribution of these reusability-specific refactorings against mainstream refactoring types. Our results indicate that the distribution of refactoring types used for reusability differs significantly from those in general development. Specifically, refactorings intended to enhance reusability involve more design-level changes to source files, whereas typical refactorings affect all code elements, including identifiers and parameters. Furthermore, reusability refactorings significantly influence high-level elements like packages, classes, and methods, unlike typical refactorings which have a broader scope. These findings offer practical insights into current refactoring practices specifically within the context of code reuse.

Recently, covariant scale-invariant dynamics (SID) theory has been suggested to account for dynamical anomalies in galaxies (Maeder & Gueorguiev 2020), proposing that what is typically ascribed to dark matter actually results from a non-standard, velocity-dependent force that expands near-Keplerian two-body orbits. However, we demonstrate that the predicted expansion of the Earth-Moon orbit contradicts lunar laser ranging measurements at a significance level exceeding $200\sigma$. Furthermore, SID implies that the gravitating mass of objects was substantially lower in the past; if accurate, this would require low-mass red giant stars to be significantly older than standard theory allows, potentially surpassing the conventional age of the Universe despite the expectation that the Universe's age remains consistent under SID. Additionally, it remains uncertain whether SID introduces genuine new physics beyond General Relativity, as some prior studies argue the additional degree of freedom is merely mathematical. Ultimately, we conclude that the SID model is falsified at high statistical significance by observational data spanning multiple scales, regardless of its theoretical formulation.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) face significant security vulnerabilities, often exploited by attackers using sophisticated methods to compromise their internal structures. Among these threats, data poisoning-enabled perturbation attacks represent a complex adversarial approach that injects fraudulent data, thereby disrupting the learning process by degrading both accuracy and convergence rates without offering any advantage to deeper architectures. To address this, we introduce an attack-agnostic defense mechanism designed to mitigate such impacts. This approach incorporates a Defensive Feature Layer (DFL) into a standard DNN architecture, enabling the neutralization of illegitimate perturbation samples within the feature space. Furthermore, to enhance the robustness and reliability of the model in correctly classifying compromised inputs, we apply a discriminative regularization technique known as Polarized Contrastive Loss (PCL) to the hidden layers. This loss function strengthens the distinction between different classes while preserving the similarity of samples within the same class. We implemented this combined DFL and PCL strategy within a compact model specifically to counter data poisoning attacks. Evaluated on the CIFAR-10 and MNIST datasets using perturbation attacks, experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms recent comparable techniques.

The Cerebellar Model Articulation Controller (CMAC) stands as a significant brain-inspired computing model widely utilized across various domains. Since its introduction in the 1970s, the CMAC has undergone extensive research, leading to the development of numerous prototype variants, including Kernel-CMAC, Self-Organizing Map CMAC, and Linguistic CMAC. This review examines the progressive evolution and refinement of the CMAC to satisfy the requirements for rapid, adaptive, and robust control. The discussion presents two primary perspectives: viewing the CMAC as a neural network and as a table-look-up technique. Furthermore, three key dimensions of the model are explored: its architecture, learning algorithms, and applications. Finally, the article proposes several promising directions for future research regarding this model.

Modeling dependencies among joints is essential for skeleton-based action recognition, where Transformers demonstrate significant promise in capturing correlations between key joints. However, current Transformer-based approaches fail to account for joint correlations across different frames—a crucial factor, as body parts like the arms and legs in a "long jump" move synchronously in adjacent frames. Addressing this gap, we introduce STTFormer, a novel spatio-temporal tuples Transformer. This method segments skeleton sequences into parts, encoding multiple consecutive frames within each segment. Furthermore, a spatio-temporal tuples self-attention module is designed to capture relationships between different joints across these consecutive frames. Additionally, a feature aggregation module is inserted between non-adjacent frames to improve the model's ability to differentiate similar actions. Experimental results on two large-scale datasets show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

Using a non-relativistic quark model, we calculate the mass spectra for the ground and excited states of doubly heavy $\Xi$ and $\Omega$ baryons. For all states involving $cc$, $bc$, or $bb$ quarks, the mass difference between the $\Omega$ and its corresponding $\Xi$ baryon is estimated at $M_{\Omega}-M_{\Xi}\simeq178$ MeV. We introduce a simple form of the universal Isgur-Wise function to describe the transition form factors between these doubly heavy baryons. By analyzing the close-to-zero recoil limit, we examine the $b \rightarrow c$ semileptonic decay widths and branching fractions, comparing our results with other theoretical predictions.

We demonstrate that no odd-dimensional stable compact minimal immersions exist within the product of two complex projective spaces. Furthermore, we establish that stable compact minimal immersions in the product of a quaternionic projective space and any other Riemannian manifold consist exclusively of products involving quaternionic projective subspaces and stable compact minimal immersions of the second manifold. These findings extend the second author's previous work on low-dimensional or low-codimensional immersions to cases of arbitrary dimension. Additionally, we show that stable compact minimal immersions in the product of an octonionic projective plane with any other Riemannian manifold are precisely the products of octonionic projective subspaces with stable compact minimal immersions of the second manifold.

This letter compares indoor radio propagation measurements and associated channel statistics at 28, 73, and 140 GHz, utilizing extensive data collected between 2014 and 2020 within an office setting. By juxtaposing propagation traits—such as large-scale path loss and multipath time dispersion—across the spectrum from the low millimeter-wave band (28 GHz) to the sub-THz band (140 GHz), the study highlights the principal similarities and distinctions in indoor wireless channels. Both the measurements and models reveal that path loss exponents are remarkably consistent across these frequencies for both line-of-sight (LOS) and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions when referencing a one-meter free-space distance, whereas multipath time dispersion diminishes as frequency increases. Furthermore, the 3GPP indoor channel model is found to overestimate large-scale path loss and predicts an unrealistic quantity of clusters and multipath components per cluster compared to the measured statistics presented in this letter.

The public goods game serves as a framework for modeling societal investment and profit generation, as well as biological populations. While the classic version typically features only two competing strategies—cooperation and defection—a third strategy is frequently introduced to evaluate punishment, a mechanism designed to foster cooperation. Given the game's dynamic nature, we examine time-dependent effects, such as oscillations in the enhancement factor that reflect fluctuating productivity over time. Additionally, we investigate the impact of time delays specifically regarding the implementation of punishment. Our findings indicate that both productivity oscillations and punishment delays negatively affect the level of cooperation.

Virtual environments are increasingly used in robotics research to evaluate systems prior to real-world deployment. The COVID-19 pandemic has further accelerated the need for virtual benchmarks to ensure safe and efficient development, especially as in-person robotics competitions have ceased, thereby restricting opportunities for students and researchers. To address this, we created an extendable and adaptable virtual scoring framework modeled after a service robotics competition. This initiative challenges current state-of-the-art home service robotics by requiring robots to perform realistic household tasks. By providing a virtual foundation, teams can assess their systems when physical access is unavailable. We posit that leveraging virtual environments for assessment will yield additional advantages, including broader accessibility and improved generalization.

We introduce the Novel-Materials-Discovery (NOMAD) Artificial-Intelligence (AI) Toolkit, a web-based platform designed for the interactive, AI-driven analysis of FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable) materials science data. This toolkit functions seamlessly with FAIR data hosted on the central server of the NOMAD Archive—the world's largest repository of materials science information—as well as with locally stored, user-owned datasets. Additionally, the NOMAD Oasis, a standalone local server, offers an alternative environment for executing the toolkit. Utilizing web-browser-based Jupyter notebooks, researchers can query and access NOMAD data, subsequently applying data mining, machine learning, and other AI methodologies for analysis. This infrastructure elevates reproducibility in materials science by enabling the sharing of not only the data underpinning scientific publications but also the complete suite of developed methods and analytical tools. Beyond replicating published findings, users can customize the Jupyter notebooks to advance their own research initiatives.

Accurate visual object localization is a fundamental component of various object detection workflows. Although mainstream strongly supervised approaches in existing literature achieve high precision, they depend on object-level annotations and fail to identify objects from unknown categories; weakly supervised methods encounter comparable limitations. This paper introduces a self-paced learning framework designed to attain precise localization on the ranked list generated by instance search. The proposed system progressively mines target instances from queries and their associated top-ranked search results. Because a common instance exists between the query and the images in the rank list, the target visual instance can be accurately localized without prior knowledge of the object category. Furthermore, this framework addresses few-shot object detection alongside instance search localization. Experiments demonstrate that the method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on both tasks.

We introduce novel quantum algorithms designed to evaluate composed functions where inputs to lower-level gates may be shared. Given an $m$-bit Boolean function $f$, let $F$ be an $n$-bit function constructed by applying $f$ to conjunctions of potentially overlapping subsets of $n$ variables. If $f$ possesses a quantum query complexity of $Q(f)$, our method evaluates $F$ using $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{Q(f) \cdot n})$ queries. This result surpasses the previous $O(Q(f) \cdot \sqrt{n})$ bound derived from treating each conjunction independently, and our bound is proven tight for worst-case selections of $f$. Furthermore, employing distinct methodologies, we establish a comparable tight composition theorem regarding the approximate degree of $f$.

By recursively utilizing these composition theorems, we derive a nearly optimal $\tilde{O}(n^{1-2^{-d}})$ upper bound for the quantum query complexity and approximate degree of linear-size depth-$d$ AC$^0$ circuits. Consequently, such circuits are PAC learnable in subexponential time, even within the difficult agnostic setting. Previously, no subexponential-time algorithm was known for linear-size depth-3 AC$^0$ circuits. Additionally, we demonstrate that AC$^0 \circ \oplus$ circuits of depth $d+1$ necessitate a size of $\tilde{\Omega}(n^{1/(1- 2^{-d})}) \geq \omega(n^{1+ 2^{-d}})$ to compute the Inner Product function, even on average. This improves upon the prior best worst-case size lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1+4^{-(d+1)}})$ established by Cheraghchi et al. (JCSS 2018).

This work investigates the existence and multiplicity of solutions for Dirichlet boundary value problems featuring the (p(x), q(x))-equation, where the nonlinearity is superlinear yet fails to meet the standard Ambrossetti-Rabinowitz condition. The analysis is conducted within Sobolev spaces of variable exponents on complete manifolds. Our primary findings are derived using the mountain pass theorem and the Fountain theorem, both incorporating the Cerami condition. Additionally, we provide an example of a (p(x), q(x)) equation that satisfies all the established results.

We examine the $\rm R$-matrix formulation of quantum deformations for loop algebras $\tilde{\mathfrak{g}}$ associated with non-exceptional affine Lie algebras of types $\hat{\mathfrak{g}}=A^{(1)}_{N-1}$, $B^{(1)}_n$, $C^{(1)}_n$, $D^{(1)}_n$, and $A^{(2)}_{N-1}$. For each $U_q(\tilde{\mathfrak{g}})$, we analyze the commutation rules among the Gauss coordinates of the fundamental $\mathbb{L}$-operators by embedding a smaller algebra into a larger one. We provide a novel current-based realization of these algebras and present the connections between all off-diagonal Gauss coordinates and specific projections of ordered current products. These relationships hold significant importance for applications in quantum integrable models.

Pion exchange forms the cornerstone of nucleon-nucleon interactions in nuclear structure models, with one pion exchange (OPE) appearing at leading order within chiral effective field theory. However, in the $^{2S+1}L_J={^1S_0}$ partial wave, OPE combined with the requisite contact term for renormalization fails to capture both the qualitative and quantitative characteristics of scattering phase shifts. Furthermore, variations in the cutoff indicated a surprisingly low breakdown momentum of approximately 330 MeV for this wave. This study demonstrates that incorporating two pion exchange (TPE) alongside a single contact term resolves these issues, yielding accurate and renormalization group (RG) invariant phase shifts in the $^1S_0$ channel. We show that a leading-order potential including TPE can be systematically refined by adding a contact term quadratic in momenta. For cutoffs below roughly 500 MeV, maintaining RG invariance requires compensating for the removal of relevant physics from TPE loops with additional contacts. Additionally, including the $\Delta$ isobar degree of freedom in the potential does not alter the dominant contributions from TPE.

Ptychography offers highly efficient imaging within scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), yet doubts persist regarding its utility for strongly scattering specimens typical in materials science. While contrast reversals may occur in ptychographic phase images as sample projected potentials increase, we demonstrate that these issues can be readily resolved with a minor degree of defocus. This defocus is minimal; it occurs naturally during focusing via the annular dark field (ADF) signal and can also be tuned after data acquisition. Compared to other STEM methods, ptychographic images of strongly scattering materials remain clearer at finite doses and more effectively highlight light atomic columns embedded in heavy lattices. Furthermore, ptychography data can now be collected concurrently with the swiftest ADF scans. This synergy of sensitivity and interpretability establishes an ideal workflow for materials science applications.

This paper offers an empirical examination of fundamental and depression-specific multi-emotion mining within Tweets, utilizing state-of-the-art multi-label classifiers. Our framework for basic emotions draws from a hybrid model that synthesizes common emotions across four esteemed psychological theories. We further expand this model by incorporating novel emotion categories deemed critical for depression analysis, many of which have not been previously explored in emotion mining studies. Experimental results indicate that both a cost-sensitive RankSVM algorithm and a Deep Learning model demonstrate robust performance, as evidenced by high Macro and Micro F-measures. These findings suggest that both methods effectively tackle the prevalent data imbalance issue in multi-label learning. Notably, the Deep Learning approach yielded the best results, highlighting its advantage in capturing the deep semantic nuances of our extended emotional categories.

This paper establishes a sharp maximal estimate (up to the endpoint) for Weyl sums on the torus $\mathbb{T}^d$ where $d\geq 2$. We further examine two related problems: maximal estimates along rational lines and on generic tori. The applications presented, which yield new upper bounds for the Hausdorff dimension of sets linked to large Weyl sum values, illustrate the interplay between square root cancellation and constructive interference. Additionally, the Appendix features an alternate proof of Theorem 1.1 by Barron, drawing inspiration from Baker's argument in [1]; this proof not only reduces the $N^{\epsilon}$ loss in Theorem 1.1 but also derives Strichartz-type estimates for Weyl sums with logarithmic losses using the same approach.

This research utilizes Particle-in-Cell simulations to examine the core plasma mechanisms behind neutralizing an ion beam's space charge with electrons from a filament. Although filament-based neutralization is cost-effective, prior experiments indicate that various excited waves restrict the efficiency of this process. This study characterizes electrostatic solitary waves (ESWs), which exhibit low dissipation, in both 2D planar and 3D cylindrical beam configurations, revealing that these long-lasting waves impede neutralization. Additionally, a 1D Bernstein-Greene-Kruskal (BGK) analysis demonstrates that the non-Maxwellian distribution of beam electrons generates large ESWs not predicted by theories assuming a Maxwellian electron distribution. Furthermore, the high sensitivity of our PIC simulations allows for the resolution of critical three-dimensional effects within a 3D cylindrical geometry, which trigger Trivelpiece-Gould surface waves due to high-energy electrons present at the onset of neutralization.

Stochastic Thermodynamics models random transitions between observable mesoscopic states using Markovian jump processes. Physical currents are derived from anti-symmetric jump observables defined on the edges of the graph representing the state network. The asymptotic statistics of these currents are described by scaled cumulants. In this study, we leverage the algebraic and topological properties of Markovian models to demonstrate the gauge invariance of the scaled cumulant-generating function. Utilizing this invariance enables an efficient algorithm for computing practical asymptotic averages and correlation integrals. We further explain how our methodology extends the Schnakenberg decomposition of the average entropy-production rate and unifies prior research. Concrete applications of these findings are detailed in a companion publication.

The expansion of neural networks has yielded significant performance gains across diverse tasks, with outcomes often adhering to predictable scaling laws relative to dataset size, model parameters, and computational resources. These laws provide crucial insights as conducting large-scale experiments becomes costlier. However, prior research on scaling laws has largely relied on proprietary data and models or concentrated on single-modal learning in language or vision. To overcome these constraints, we examine scaling laws for contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP) using the public LAION dataset and the open-source OpenCLIP repository. Our extensive experiments involve models trained on up to two billion image-text pairs, revealing power law scaling across various downstream applications such as zero-shot classification, retrieval, linear probing, and end-to-end fine-tuning. We observe that the training distribution significantly influences scaling behavior, as OpenAI and OpenCLIP models demonstrate distinct scaling patterns despite sharing identical architectures and similar training protocols. To promote reproducibility and accessibility in scaling law research, we release our evaluation workflow and all models, including the largest publicly available CLIP variants. The source code and replication instructions are accessible at https://github.com/LAION-AI/scaling-laws-openclip.

While the standard anomalous Hall effect (AHE) typically requires magnetization, electric field, and Hall current to be mutually orthogonal, this study introduces an unconventional variant where these three vectors lie within the same plane.
