**Context.** Sulfur serves as a tracer for the evolution from interstellar clouds to stellar systems; however, the majority of sulfur anticipated in molecular clouds remains undetected. This sulfur vanishes from the gas phase in two stages: an initial depletion during the translucent phase reduces gas-phase sulfur by 7–40 times, followed by a freeze-out step in molecular clouds that reduces it by another order of magnitude. This persistent problem requires an explanation.

**Aims.** This study aims to identify the form in which missing sulfur is sequestered within molecular clouds, specifically investigating depletion onto dust grains.

**Methods.** We conducted experimental simulations mimicking the UV-photoprocessing of H₂S ice in molecular clouds. Infrared spectroscopy monitored the ice, while quadrupole mass spectrometry measured desorbing molecules. Additionally, theoretical Monte Carlo simulations were executed to interpret the experimental data and extrapolate findings to astrophysical conditions.

**Results.** Irradiation at 8 K resulted in the formation of H₂S₂. Molecules of H₂Sₓ (where x > 2) were also identified and observed to desorb during warm-up, alongside S₂ through S₄ species. Larger sulfur molecules (Sₓ) up to S₈ proved refractory at room temperature, remaining on the substrate as a residue. Monte Carlo simulations successfully replicated the desorption patterns during warming and determined that the residues consist of sulfur chains containing 6–7 atoms.

**Conclusions.** We propose that S⁺ in translucent clouds significantly contributes to sulfur depletion in denser regions by forming long sulfur chains on dust grains over approximately 10⁴ years. Furthermore, we suggest that the S₂ to S₄ molecules detected in comets are not the result of fragmenting these large chains. Instead, they likely originate either from the UV-photoprocessing of H₂S-bearing ice formed in molecular clouds or from short sulfur chains established during the translucent cloud phase.

Adaptive Radiation Therapy (ART), which has emerged as a prevailing trend in photon radiation therapy, is founded on Image-guided Radiation Therapy (IGRT). To optimize the utilization of Cone Beam CT (CBCT) images for ART applications, a CBCT system model was constructed using the Monte Carlo method and subsequently validated through physical measurements. The BEAMnrc code was employed to simulate the KV x-ray tube, with IOURCE-13 and ISOURCE-24 utilized to model beam particle trajectories. The calculated Percentage Depth Dose (PDD) and lateral dose profiles (measured in 1 cm of water) were compared against experimental data using the DOSXYZnrc program. Results indicated that the calculated PDD remained within 1% of the measured values up to a depth of 10 cm, while over 85% of the points in the lateral dose profiles fell within a 2% margin. Establishing an accurate CBCT system model facilitates enhanced image quality for dose verification in ART and enables a more reliable assessment of concomitant dose risks associated with CBCT imaging.

This study investigates audiovisual emotion recognition in noisy acoustic environments, emphasizing speech characteristics. We address two primary research questions: (i) How does speech-based emotion recognition perform under noisy conditions? and (ii) To what extent does a multimodal framework enhance accuracy and mitigate performance degradation across varying noise levels? Our analysis examines two emotion datasets corrupted with noise at different signal-to-noise ratios, evaluating three distinct acoustic feature types. Visual inputs are integrated using a hybrid fusion strategy where initial neural network layers are modality-specific, followed by at least one shared layer prior to final prediction. The findings indicate a substantial performance drop when models trained on clean audio are applied to noisy data, demonstrating that incorporating visual features effectively alleviates this decline.

Let ${\bf a}=(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n)$ and ${\bf e}=(e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_n)$ be sequences of real numbers. Define $M_{{\bf e}\rightarrow {\bf a}}$ as the $(n+1)\times(n+1)$ matrix where the $(m,k)$ entry (for $m, k \in \{0,\ldots, n\}$) represents the coefficient of the polynomial $(x-a_1)\cdots(x-a_k)$ in the expansion of $(x-e_1)\cdots(x-e_m)$ relative to the basis $1, x-a_1, \ldots, (x-a_1)\cdots(x-a_m)$. By selecting specific real sequences ${\bf a}$ and ${\bf e}$, this matrix can represent various well-known doubly-indexed combinatorial sequences, including binomial coefficients, both types of Stirling numbers, Lah numbers, and central factorial numbers. In each of these cases, $M_{{\bf e}\rightarrow {\bf a}}$ exhibits total non-negativity, meaning the determinants of all its square submatrices are non-negative. This observation raises the general question: under what conditions is $M_{{\bf e}\rightarrow {\bf a}}$ totally non-negative? While Galvin and Pacurar previously established a simple condition on ${\bf e}$ characterizing this property when ${\bf a}$ is non-decreasing, this work extends their result to arbitrary real sequences ${\bf a}$ and ${\bf e}$. We provide an $O(n^2)$ checkable condition to determine if $M_{{\bf e}\rightarrow {\bf a}}$ is totally non-negative. Furthermore, when the matrix is totally non-negative, we demonstrate this by constructing a planar network with non-negative weights whose path matrix equals $M_{{\bf e}\rightarrow {\bf a}}$; conversely, if it is not, we present an explicit negative minor as proof.

This study examines a cooperative non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) network where a full-duplex (FD) multi-antenna relay facilitates communication from a base station (BS) to distant users experiencing poor channel conditions, concurrently allowing the BS to serve nearby users with strong channels. The analysis accounts for imperfect self-interference (SI) cancellation at the FD relay and imperfect inter-user interference cancellation at the near users. To mitigate SI at the relay, a zero-forcing beamforming approach is employed, leading to a derived outage probability analysis for two user selection strategies: random near and far user (RNRF) selection, and nearest near and nearest far user (NNNF) selection. Our results indicate that employing an FD multi-antenna relay yields substantial performance enhancements over systems utilizing half-duplex relays. This performance gain is contingent upon network parameters including user density, user zoning, path loss, and the magnitude of inter-user interference affecting near users. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the NNNF strategy offers superior outage performance relative to the RNRF strategy, particularly regarding near users.

This paper presents a numerical scheme designed to manage interfaces between computational domains in multi-block frameworks for solving systems of conservation laws. Our primary objective is to transmit shock discontinuities without degrading the method's overall precision. This is achieved by exchanging information solely from the boundary points of adjacent grids, rather than utilizing interior points. We implement the second-order Kurganov-Tadmor (KT) method at interior locations, relaxing it to first order at interfaces. This approach maintains second-order global accuracy (in the appropriate norm) while preserving the scheme's Total Variation Diminishing (TVD) property. Following the development of the method, we conducted various standard one- and two-dimensional tests. Specifically, we employed the one-dimensional advection and Burgers equations to confirm second-order convergence. Additionally, we tested the two-dimensional Euler equations using an implosion scenario and a Gresho vortex. Notably, in the two-dimensional implosion test, shocks traversed the interfaces without significant deformation in either amplitude or front orientation, regardless of their alignment relative to the interface.

This study examines the geometry and topology of submanifolds subject to a stringent pinching condition defined by extrinsic invariants, specifically mean curvature and the length of the second fundamental form. The analysis yields various homology vanishing theorems and establishes an integral bound for the Bochner operator acting on compact Euclidean submanifolds, expressed through Betti numbers.

The Firefighter problem models a scenario where a fire originates at a graph vertex, and at every time step, a firefighter protects one vertex while the fire spreads from all currently burned vertices to their unprotected neighbors. This serves as a simplified framework for simulating disease or gossip propagation in networks. We present a novel two-player variant termed the Pyro game, where the fire spreads from a single burned vertex to all its unprotected neighbors at each step, actively aiming to maximize the number of burned vertices rather than spreading automatically. We demonstrate that, in contrast to the Firefighter problem, a single firefighter can successfully contain the fire on a Cartesian grid within the Pyro game. Furthermore, we analyze the Pyro Game and the Firefighter Problem on the infinite strong grid and examine the computational complexity of the Pyro game.

For a graph $G$, a dominating set $S$ is a collection of vertices where every vertex outside $S$ is adjacent to at least one vertex in $S$. The domination number, $\gamma(G)$, represents the smallest possible size of such a set. The independent domination number, $i(G)$, denotes the minimum size of a dominating set that is also independent. Since every maximal independent set functions as an independent dominating set, such a set exists for all graphs.

Considering a connected $k$-regular graph $G$ that is not $K_{k, k}$ with $k \geq 4$, we generalize a finding by Lam, Shiu, and Sun to demonstrate that $i(G) \leq \frac{k-1}{2k-1}|V(G)|$. This bound is tight when $k = 4$, thereby affirmatively resolving a query posed by Goddard et al. Furthermore, we establish that $\frac{i(G)}{\gamma(G)} \leq \frac{k^3-3k^2+2}{2k^2-6k+2}$, which improves upon a result by Knor, Škrekovski, and Tepeh. Additionally, we prove that for any graph $G'$ with a maximum degree of at most 4, the inequality $i(G') \leq \frac{5}{9}|V(G')|$ holds, a result that is also tight.

The eccentricity matrix $\mathcal{E}(G)$ of a connected graph $G$ is derived from its distance matrix by retaining only the largest nonzero entries in each row and column, setting all others to zero. The $\mathcal{E}$-eigenvalues of $G$ correspond to the eigenvalues of $\mathcal{E}(G)$, and the $\mathcal{E}$-energy (or eccentricity energy) is defined as the sum of the absolute values of these eigenvalues. This article identifies the unique tree with the minimum second largest $\mathcal{E}$-eigenvalue among all $n$-vertex trees excluding the star graph, and it characterizes the trees that achieve the minimum $\mathcal{E}$-energy for any given number of vertices $n$.

Training machine learning models is a resource-heavy task that often becomes memory-bound because of the frequent access to vast training datasets. Consequently, traditional processor-centric systems (such as CPUs and GPUs) incur significant energy and cycle costs due to the expensive transfer of data between processing units and memory. In contrast, memory-centric computing systems featuring Processing-in-Memory (PIM) capabilities can mitigate this data movement bottleneck. This study aims to assess the potential of modern general-purpose PIM architectures for accelerating machine learning training. We achieve this by (1) implementing several classic algorithms—specifically linear regression, logistic regression, decision trees, and K-means clustering—on a practical general-purpose PIM platform, (2) evaluating their accuracy, performance, and scalability, and (3) benchmarking them against equivalent CPU and GPU implementations. Our experiments on a memory-centric system equipped with over 2,500 PIM cores demonstrate that general-purpose PIM architectures can significantly speed up memory-bound machine learning workloads, provided the required operations and data types are natively supported by the PIM hardware. To our knowledge, this is the first evaluation of training machine learning algorithms on a real-world general-purpose PIM architecture.

This paper addresses the inverse first-passage Shiryaev problem, defined for a standard Brownian motion $(W_t)_{t \geq 0}$ and any upper boundary $g: \mathbb{R}^+ \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ that is continuous and satisfies $g(0) \geq 0$. We define the first-passage time as $\mathrm{T}_g^W := \inf \{t \in \mathbb{R}^+ \text{ s.t. } W_t \geq g(t)\}$ and denote its associated density by $f_g^W(t)$. Given any target density $f: \mathbb{R}^+ \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+$ meeting certain smoothness criteria and an arbitrarily large horizon $T > 0$, we demonstrate the existence of a corresponding continuous boundary $g_{f,T}: [0,T] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+$, with $g_{f,T}(0) \geq 0$, such that $f_{g_{f,T}}^W(t) = f(t)$ for all $0 \leq t \leq T$. Our approach offers a more direct existence proof utilizing the Arzel\`a-Ascoli theorem, constructing $g_{f,T}$ as the limit of a subsequence of piecewise linear boundaries. Consequently, while the proof is not entirely direct, we do not derive an explicit formula for $g_{f,T}$ in terms of $f$. Furthermore, these results are extended to the symmetrical two-dimensional boundary scenario.

For the range $1<p<2$ and sufficiently large $q$, we establish the existence of two positive, nonconstant, radial, and radially non-decreasing solutions to the supercritical equation $-\Delta_p u+u^{p-1}=u^{q-1}$ subject to Neumann boundary conditions within the unit ball of $\mathbb R^N$. Employing a variational method within an invariant cone, we differentiate these solutions based on their energy levels: one represents a ground state within a Nehari-type subset of the cone, while the other is derived through a mountain pass argument inside the Nehari set. Furthermore, our proofs yield the limit profile of the low-energy solution as $q$ approaches infinity and demonstrate that the constant solution $1$ acts as a local minimum on the Nehari set.

This study introduces a novel discontinuous Galerkin (DG) fluid solver module for magneto-hydrodynamics, built upon the framework developed by Markert et al. (2021) and integrated into the established multi-physics code FLASH. Our objective is to facilitate future research into the capabilities and benefits of DG methods within complex astrophysical multi-physics environments. We provide detailed insights into the implementation and specific modifications made within FLASH, accompanied by comprehensive validation and test cases that examine interactions with other physics modules, including (self-)gravity and radiative transfer. We conclude that the new DG solver module in FLASH is fully prepared for use in astrophysical simulations, making it suitable for further assessment and investigation.

String theory generically predicts a vast array of axions, termed the "string axiverse." Because these particles possess a natural cosmological production mechanism known as vacuum misalignment, they are strong candidates for dark matter (DM). While much existing research focuses on single, free axions, realistic models suggest string axions span a wide mass range and interact via a shared potential. This study demonstrates that non-linearities within this potential induce a novel form of resonant energy transfer between axions with similar masses. This resonance typically moves energy from axions with higher decay constants to those with lower ones, resulting in diverse observational signatures. These include improved prospects for direct detection of resonant pairs—even if they constitute only a minor fraction of dark matter—and enhanced small-scale structure formation if the pair dominates the dark matter content. Upcoming experiments like ADMX and DM Radio, as well as astrophysical investigations into dark matter substructure, will be capable of probing this scenario.

Simple fiber optic communication systems utilizing energy modulation of isolated, time-limited pulses can be effectively implemented using fundamental solitons. These solitons provide a key advantage: their shape remains stable despite fiber dispersion and nonlinearity, allowing information to be retrieved via a straightforward energy detector at the receiver. However, soliton-based systems struggle to achieve competitive data rates, largely because a soliton's effective duration is tied to its amplitude. To address this, this paper introduces new time-limited waveforms detectable by energy detectors that remain immune to fiber distortions. These waveforms are derived using prolate spheroidal wave functions combined with numerical optimization to minimize time broadening during transmission. Results demonstrate that these new waveforms outperform fundamental solitons; specifically, in binary transmission over a single fiber span, they achieve data rate increases of 33.8% in lossy fibers and 12% in lossless fibers compared to solitons. Additionally, unlike fundamental solitons which are constrained by time-amplitude relationships, the proposed system's transmission rate scales with the number of energy levels. For instance, employing four energy levels yields rate improvements of 164% over lossy fibers and 70% over lossless fibers.

This study examines the ground-state and first radially excited four-quark mesons, $X_0$ and $X_0^{\prime}$, characterized by a $[ud][\overline{c}\overline{s}]$ diquark-antidiquark configuration and $J^{\mathrm{P} }=0^{+}$ spin-parity. The primary objective is to determine if either state corresponds to the $X_0(2900)$ resonance recently observed by the LHCb collaboration. We treat these mesons as tetraquarks formed from either axial-vector or scalar diquark and antidiquark pairs. Using the QCD two-point sum rule method and incorporating vacuum condensates up to dimension 15, we calculate their spectroscopic parameters. For the axial-axial configuration of $X_0^{(\prime)}$, we determine partial decay widths for $X_0^{(\prime)} \to D^{-}K^{+}$ and $X_0^{(\prime)} \to D^{0}K^{0}$, as well as estimate their total widths by computing strong couplings at the $ X_0^{(\prime)}DK $ vertices via the light-cone sum rule method, utilizing soft-meson approximation techniques. Our findings yield masses of $m=(2545 \pm 160)~ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $m^{\prime}=(3320 \pm 120)~\mathrm{MeV}$ (or $m_{\mathrm{S} }=(2663 \pm 110)~ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $m_{\mathrm{S}}^{\prime}=(3325 \pm 85)~ \mathrm{MeV}$ for a scalar-scalar current), alongside total width estimates of $\Gamma_{0}=(140 \pm 29)~ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $\Gamma_{0}^{\prime}=(110 \pm 25)~ \mathrm{MeV}$. These results indicate that neither $X_0$ nor $X_0^{\prime}$ can be identified as the $X_0(2900)$ resonance. Nevertheless, these predictions offer valuable insights into the ground-state and radially excited diquark-antidiquark structures of $X_0$ and $X_0^{\prime}$, suggesting they warrant further theoretical and experimental investigation.

Deep Reinforcement Learning systems have surpassed world-class human players in several complex two-player games, such as Chess, Checkers, and Go. However, due to computational constraints, evaluating the minimax regret of learning systems in these games remains infeasible. This paper addresses this limitation by focusing on simpler games—specifically Noughts-and-Crosses and Hexapawn—where minimax regret can be efficiently calculated. We employ these games to compare Cumulative Minimax Regret across various standard and deep reinforcement learning approaches against two versions of a novel Meta-Interpretive Learning system, MIGO. Our experimental results indicate that all tested variants of both standard and deep reinforcement learning underperformed compared to both MIGO variants in terms of cumulative minimax regret on both games. Furthermore, MIGO's learned rules are highly interpretable and exhibit significant bidirectional transfer learning capabilities between Noughts-and-Crosses and Hexapawn.

A fundamental and shared characteristic of renormalizable field theories is the scale invariance of their action integrals. This note presents \emph{Kanon}, a software utility that enables users to interactively construct arbitrary action integrals and calculate their critical dimensions and scale invariance properties. The tool includes over 60 well-known models, complete with explanatory comments and references to relevant literature.

We introduce the Deep Kronecker Network (DKN), a new framework tailored for medical imaging analysis, including MRI, fMRI, and CT scans. Unlike general images, medical imaging data presents two distinct challenges: i) significantly limited sample sizes, and ii) a higher priority on model interpretability over mere outcome prediction. Consequently, standard approaches like convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are often unsuitable for direct application. To address this, DKN is designed to i) overcome data scarcity, ii) deliver interpretable models, and iii) match the predictive performance of CNNs. The framework is versatile, supporting both matrix and high-order tensor representations as well as discrete and continuous outcomes. Built upon a Kronecker product structure, DKN implicitly enforces piecewise smoothness on coefficients. Additionally, this structure can be expressed in a convolutional format, making DKN akin to a fully convolutional network (FCN). We further demonstrate that using an alternating minimization algorithm, DKN solutions converge geometrically to the true values even when the objective function is highly nonconvex. Notably, DKN shares strong connections with the tensor regression framework by Zhou et al. (2010), which utilizes a CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) low-rank structure for tensor coefficients. Finally, we validate DKN's effectiveness through classification and regression tasks using real Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) MRI data.

We introduce Human Pose Models designed to capture RGB and depth imagery of human poses independently of variables such as clothing textures, backgrounds, lighting, body shapes, and camera angles. Training these universal models necessitates datasets where every pose exhibits variations across all these factors, yet acquiring such data is prohibitively costly. Consequently, we created a framework for synthesizing this training data. The process begins by deriving representative human poses from a vast collection of real motion-captured skeleton data. We then fit synthetic 3D human models with diverse body shapes to these poses and render them from 180 different camera viewpoints while randomly altering clothing textures, backgrounds, and lighting conditions. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are utilized to reduce the discrepancy between the synthetic and real image distributions. Subsequently, Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models are trained to map human poses into a shared, high-level invariant space. These learned CNN models serve as invariant feature extractors for real RGB and depth frames from human action videos, with temporal variations modeled using a Fourier Temporal Pyramid. Finally, a linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) performs the classification. Experiments conducted on three benchmark cross-view human action datasets demonstrate that our algorithm significantly outperforms existing methods in both RGB-only and RGB-D action recognition tasks.

Although deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in machine learning, the specific reasons behind their superior learning capacity remain elusive. This work introduces a framework grounded in statistical physics to analyze the dynamics of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in neural networks. By employing a minibatch gradient ensemble, we define order parameters to describe the behavior of weight updates during SGD. In the absence of mislabeled data, the learning process evolves from a rapid learning stage to a slower exploration phase, marked by significant shifts in order parameters that reflect the alignment and magnitude of SGD gradients relative to their mean. Conversely, when randomly mislabeled samples are present, the dynamics unfold across four distinct phases: Phase I involves finding solutions for correctly labeled data; Phase II consists of wandering around these solutions; Phase III entails discovering a direction to learn from mislabeled samples; and Phase IV achieves solutions satisfying all training data. Consequently, test error drops during Phase I, stabilizes at a low level in Phase II, rises during Phase III, and plateaus at a high level in Phase IV. These phase transitions are explained by variations in order parameters that characterize the alignment and relative strength of mean gradients for correct versus incorrect labels. Furthermore, we observe that individual sample losses for the two datasets are most distinct during Phase II, facilitating a cleaning process that removes mislabeled samples to enhance generalization.

We demonstrate the emergence of the Berry phase within a forced harmonic oscillator situated in a Moyal-type quantum space-time, where time 't' functions as an operator. An effective commutative description yields a time-dependent generalized harmonic oscillator perturbed linearly by position and momentum. Upon diagonalizing the system into a generalized harmonic oscillator, we analyze its adiabatic evolution over a time period $\mathcal{T}$ using the Heisenberg picture to derive the expression for the geometric phase-shift.

We introduce a novel method for constructing Boolean functions. A particular example from this construction yields a 30-variable function with a min-entropy/influence ratio of $128/45 \approx 2.8444$, representing the current highest such ratio achieved by any Boolean function. Consequently, this value also serves as the best-known lower bound for the universal constant in the Fourier min-entropy/influence conjecture.

Computer vision methods hold significant promise for advancing materials design. This study presents AtomVision, a comprehensive and versatile library designed to create, manage, and analyze datasets from scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) while facilitating machine learning applications. To showcase the library's utility, we: 1) compiled and organized an atomistic image dataset covering approximately 10,000 materials; 2) built and evaluated convolutional and graph neural networks for classifying Bravais lattices; 3) implemented a fully convolutional neural network based on the U-Net architecture for pixel-level distinction between atoms and background; 4) employed a generative adversarial network to achieve super-resolution; 5) assembled a natural language processing dataset derived from open-access arXiv publications; and 6) connected the computational framework with experimental microscopy instrumentation. The AtomVision library can be accessed at https://github.com/usnistgov/atomvision.

Individuals living with dementia frequently display behavioral and psychological symptoms that may endanger their own safety or that of others. Although current video surveillance systems in long-term care facilities can monitor these risky behaviors to alert staff and prevent potential harm or death, such events are often heterogeneous and infrequent compared to routine activities. Furthermore, analyzing raw video footage raises significant privacy issues. This paper introduces two novel, privacy-preserving video-based anomaly detection methods designed to identify risky behaviors in people with dementia. Our approaches extract body pose information as skeletons and utilize semantic segmentation masks to replace multiple individuals in a scene with their semantic boundaries. Unlike most existing video anomaly detection methods that rely on appearance-based features—which compromise privacy and are vulnerable to pixel-level noise such as variations in illumination and viewing angles—we trained customized spatio-temporal convolutional autoencoders using anonymized videos of normal activities to detect anomalies. We validated our methods using real-world data from a dementia care unit, comprising approximately 21 hours of normal activity data for training and 9 hours of data containing both normal activities and risky behaviors for testing. When compared against original RGB video analysis, our skeleton-based approach achieved an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUROC) curve of 0.807, while the segmentation mask-based approach reached 0.823. This study represents one of the first efforts to integrate privacy protections into the detection of risky behaviors in individuals with dementia.

Cohort studies are increasingly employing accelerometers to estimate physical activity and sedentary behavior, as these devices are more accurate than self-reports, capture continuous daily activity, and are cost-effective. However, existing methods for analyzing sedentary behavior using hip-worn data often prove invalid or suboptimal in free-living contexts due to inter-individual variability. This paper introduces a local Markov switching model designed to address these challenges, alongside a general framework for posture classification and sedentary behavior analysis that aligns naturally with the model. Our approach incorporates time series changepoint detection and a two-stage classification process that categorizes data into three states: sitting, standing, and stepping. Through a rigorous training and testing framework, we demonstrated that our method achieves over 80% accuracy, while remaining both robust and interpretable.

Most orthopedic and traumatology bone implants are currently non-degradable and often require surgical removal later, particularly in pediatric cases, a process that carries significant health risks. These risks could be reduced by utilizing biodegradable implants, driving ongoing research into magnesium-based alternatives. The efficacy of such materials can be objectively assessed using synchrotron radiation microtomography followed by image analysis. To evaluate material stability over time, precise pixelwise segmentation of these high-resolution scans is essential. Although the fully-convolutional U-Net architecture yields a Dice coefficient of 0.750 +/- 0.102 when trained on a small dataset with dense expert annotations, scaling to larger databases would demand prohibitively high annotation efforts. Consequently, this study implements and compares novel training methods that rely on only a fraction of manually annotated pixels. While direct training on scribble annotations degrades segmentation quality by 26.8 percentage points, a new random walk-based semi-automatic target method achieves the same Dice overlap as dense supervision, presenting a more viable solution for sparse annotation scenarios.

For a Weinstein manifold $X$, we demonstrate that possessing a global field of Lagrangian planes within its tangent bundle $TX$ is equivalent to the presence of a positive arboreal skeleton belonging to the Weinstein homotopy class of $X$.

We establish a rigidity theorem for Einstein manifolds with negative scalar curvature that admit an isometric Lie group action $G$ with a compact, smooth orbit space. Specifically, we demonstrate that the nilradical $N$ of $G$ acts polarly and that its orbits can be extended to minimal Einstein submanifolds. Applying this result, we confirm the Alekseevskii conjecture by proving that any homogeneous Einstein manifold with negative scalar curvature is diffeomorphic to Euclidean space.

Recurrent networks represent a specialized category of artificial neural systems that leverage internal states to execute machine learning computations. A prominent advancement in this field, Reservoir Computing (RC), utilizes an internal architecture—typically a static network with random connectivity—to transform input signals into a nonlinear dynamical system within a higher-dimensional space. Reservoirs are defined by the nonlinear interactions between their units and their capacity to retain information via recurrent loops, enabling the training of systems to master task-specific dynamics. Despite this, the influence of a reservoir's random topology on learning efficacy remains fundamentally unclear. This study addresses that gap by evaluating a range of synthetic networks with distinct topological attributes alongside 45 empirical connectomes derived from brain regions across eight species. These networks were used to construct reservoirs, and their performance in predicting complex input signals was tested. Our results reveal nontrivial correlations between RC performance and both the node count and the rank of the activation states' covariance matrix, with outcomes varying based on whether the input signals are stochastic or deterministic. Notably, reservoir modularity and link density significantly impact RC performance; these effects cannot be anticipated by models relying solely on basic topological metrics. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that complex topological features inherent in biophysical systems like connectomes can inform the design of efficient, bio-inspired artificial neural networks.

When two piezoelectric solids are positioned near each other, acoustic waves can traverse a vacuum gap via tunneling, thereby transferring energy between them. This study provides an analytical proof that this phenomenon is feasible and identifies a specific resonance condition enabling the total transmission of the incident wave. This derivation holds true for any anisotropic crystal symmetry and orientation. Furthermore, we establish that the condition for complete transmission can be expressed in terms of the material's surface electric impedance and effective surface permittivity, allowing for experimental verification. Additionally, numerical simulations illustrate the maximum power transmittance of slow transverse waves tunneling between identical ZnO crystals across all possible crystal orientations. These findings indicate that complete tunneling is achievable within a broad spectrum of orientations.

This study investigates the capacity of overparameterized shallow ReLU neural networks to learn bounded, non-differentiable Lipschitz functions subject to additive noise using Gradient Descent (GD). To address the inconsistency issue where networks trained to near-zero error fail in noisy settings, we concentrate on early-stopped GD, which facilitates the demonstration of consistency and optimal convergence rates. Specifically, we analyze this challenge through the lens of the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) approximation of finite-width networks trained by GD. Our findings indicate that any early stopping criterion capable of achieving an optimal excess risk rate within the Hilbert space defined by the ReLU-induced kernel can likewise attain the minimax optimal rate for learning on the specified class of Lipschitz functions using neural networks. Furthermore, we examine several practically viable stopping rules, both data-free and data-dependent, that ensure these optimal rates.

In [Commun Math Phys 348(1), 129-143, 2016], Cheskidov and colleagues demonstrated that physically realizable weak solutions to the incompressible 2D Euler equations on a torus maintain kinetic energy. These physically realizable solutions are defined as those achievable through limits of vanishing viscosity, contingent upon the key hypothesis that initial vorticity remains bounded in $L^p$ for $p>1$. This study expands upon their findings by incorporating forcing into the flow dynamics.

Theoretical investigation into the steady Poiseuille flow of a Carreau-Yasuda fluid within a pipe, driven by a constant pressure gradient, reveals that the existence of a solution depends on specific viscosity model parameters. Specifically, a classical solution is established under certain conditions, whereas a generalized solution arises under others. For the case of the generalized solution, a necessary and sufficient condition is derived, contingent upon the pressure gradient and the parameters of the Carreau-Yasuda model.

Social media significantly influence how citizens form political views. Data from the Eurobarometer indicates that the proportion of EU citizens using online social networks daily rose from 18% in 2010 to 48% in 2019. This growing intersection between social media and political processes has spurred researcher interest in analyzing user behavior, particularly regarding echo chambers and group polarization during debates. While previous studies have focused primarily on online interpersonal relations, the semantic dimensions of these interactions have been largely neglected. This paper addresses that oversight by employing a two-step methodology. First, we define discursive communities active in the lead-up to the 2018 Italian Elections as clusters of users exhibiting highly similar retweeting patterns. Second, we examine the semantic mechanisms driving their internal discussions by tracking the daily structural evolution of the semantic networks they generate. Beyond characterizing the unique semantic features of the Italian election, our approach advances the field in two key ways. Firstly, it integrates semantic analysis with user behavior through a statistically grounded method that ensures inferences about socio-semantic structures are not skewed by assumptions regarding missing data. Secondly, the method is fully automated, requiring no manual labeling of user attributes or sharing patterns. Consequently, this approach is applicable to Twitter discussions on any topic or in any language.

We explore an all-optical, microscale planar lensing method utilizing coherent fluids of semiconductor cavity exciton-polariton condensates. Our theoretical framework highlights the capability of advanced spatial light modulation of nonresonant excitation beams to direct and focus polariton condensates away from their pumping zones. The spatially tailored nonresonant excitation profile creates an excitonic reservoir that blueshifts the polariton mode and supplies gain, enabling the formation of microscale lens shapes to refract condensate waves. We outline various strategies for manipulating the condensate fluid and demonstrate the creation of highly enhanced, localized condensates distant from the pumped reservoirs. This approach offers new possibilities for guiding quantum fluids of light and generating polariton condensates that are protected from harmful reservoir dephasing effects.

We present a Floquet circuit model for a driven Ising chain incorporating topological defects. This framework utilizes gates representing spin-flipping defects and the duality defect, which explicitly enacts the Kramers-Wannier duality transformation. While the Floquet unitary evolution operator commutes with these defects, the duality defect itself is non-unitary because it projects out half of the states. We demonstrate two applications of these defects: first, analyzing return amplitudes in the presence of "space-like" defects that wrap around the system, where we confirm that the amplitudes align with the defects' fusion rules; second, investigating unitary evolution with "time-like" defects that impose anti-periodic and duality-twisted boundary conditions, revealing a single unpaired localized Majorana zero mode in the latter scenario. We explicitly construct this operator, identifying it as a symmetry of the Floquet circuit, and provide analytic expressions for the entanglement entropy following a single time step for small systems under all described defect configurations.

Using recursion-theoretic methods, we demonstrate that the Cohesiveness Principle (COH) is $\Pi^1_1$ conservative over both $RCA_0 + I\Sigma^0_n$ and $RCA_0 + B\Sigma^0_n$ for every $n \geq 2$. Initially, we characterize COH relative to $RCA_0 + B\Sigma^0_2$ as a `jumped' variant of Weak K\"{o}nig's Lemma (WKL) and construct the necessary tools, including a version of the Friedberg jump-inversion theorem. The primary result follows by integrating these findings with established properties of WKL. Additionally, the appendix provides a proof of the $\Pi^1_1$ conservativity of WKL over $RCA_0$ utilizing the Superlow Basis Theorem, alongside a novel proof of a recent jump-inversion theorem by Towsner.

Saddle points represent a significant obstacle for first-order gradient descent methods. In classical machine learning, these are typically circumvented using stochastic gradient descent techniques. This study demonstrates that the issue of saddle points can be inherently resolved within variational quantum algorithms by leveraging their intrinsic stochasticity. We establish convergence guarantees for this approach and validate its practical efficacy through specific examples. Our argument posits that the natural noise inherent in variational algorithms aids in bypassing strict saddle points—those characterized by at least one negative Hessian eigenvalue. This insight suggests that certain levels of noise can be advantageous in this context, offering a fresh perspective on the development of near-term variational quantum algorithms.

Legal case matching serves as a pivotal operation within intelligent legal systems, demanding high explainability due to its significant downstream effects. Matched cases often act as evidentiary support for judicial judgments, thereby affecting the fairness and justice of legal outcomes. Addressing this challenge, we introduce \textit{IOT-Match}, a novel explainable approach that leverages computational optimal transport to frame legal case matching as an inverse optimal transport (IOT) problem. Unlike prevailing methods that rely solely on sentence-level semantic similarity, our approach extracts rationales from paired cases by integrating both semantic meaning and legal characteristics. These rationales are subsequently utilized to generate faithful explanations and perform matching. Furthermore, \textit{IOT-Match} demonstrates robustness against the scarcity of alignment labels common in practical scenarios, supporting both supervised and semi-supervised learning frameworks. To validate the method's superiority and establish a benchmark for explainable legal case matching, we expanded the well-known CAIL dataset and created a new dataset, Explainable Legal cAse Matching (ELAM), featuring extensive cases with detailed, explainable annotations. Experimental results on both datasets indicate that \textit{IOT-Match} consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in matching prediction, rationale extraction, and explanation generation.

Roger Penrose proposed a model involving two entangled spin-3/2 particles arranged according to a dodecahedron's geometry to formulate a "probability-free" analogue of Bell's theorem. This concept was subsequently reformulated using a Witting configuration comprising 40 rays within a 4D Hilbert space; however, this reformulation requires careful attention to the subtleties of entangling two such configurations to adequately address non-locality and related issues. The present work examines two entangled systems characterized by Witting configuration quantum states. Furthermore, duplicating points relative to the dodecahedron's vertices results in a substantial 432-fold increase in symmetry (25920/60). Finally, quantum circuits serve as a natural framework for describing operations and measurements on these diverse states.

Superconducting nanowire single photon detectors (SNSPDs) are vital instruments in optics, driving progress from basic measurements to quantum information processing. Their capacity to identify individual photons with exceptional efficiency, minimal dead time, high temporal resolution, and broad spectral coverage has significantly advanced the field of quantum optics. Nevertheless, simultaneously achieving near-unity system detection efficiency and superior timing performance remains a critical hurdle. This study presents novel SNSPDs fabricated on membranes, demonstrating system detection efficiencies between 94% and 99.5% (±2.07%) across the 1280–1500 nm wavelength range. The SiO2/Au membrane architecture facilitates broadband absorption within compact SNSPDs, delivering high detection efficiency alongside excellent timing capabilities. By integrating these detectors with low-noise cryogenic amplifiers within the same cryostat, timing jitter is reduced to 15–26 ps. We analyze key challenges in optical design, fabrication processes, and the precise measurement of detection efficiency required to attain high-performance single-photon detection. Consequently, rapidly evolving domains such as quantum information science, quantum metrology, infrared imaging, and quantum networks stand to gain substantially from this advanced quantum detection technology.

Variance reduction (VR) methods have greatly accelerated learning on massive datasets within smooth, strongly convex contexts (Schmidt et al., 2017; Johnson & Zhang, 2013; Roux et al., 2012). Yet, they have not achieved comparable success in large-scale deep learning due to factors like data augmentation and regularization techniques such as dropout (Defazio & Bottou, 2019). This limitation has spurred the development of new VR methods specifically designed for deep learning (Arnold et al., 2019; Ma & Yarats, 2018). This paper advances that direction by leveraging the inherent clustering structure of rich deep learning datasets to create a scalable family of variance-reduced optimizers. We achieve this by integrating existing optimizers (e.g., SGD+Momentum, Quasi Hyperbolic Momentum, Implicit Gradient Transport) with a multi-momentum strategy (Yuan et al., 2019). Our approach demonstrates faster convergence than standard methods on benchmark datasets like CIFAR and ImageNet, exhibits robustness against label noise, and supports distributed optimization. Additionally, we offer a parallel implementation using JAX.

Algorithms that efficiently solve optimal transport problems are crucial for measuring and optimizing distances between functions. Specifically, within the $L^2$ semi-discrete framework, the objective is to determine a mapping from a continuous density to a discrete set of points that minimizes transport cost, utilizing squared Euclidean distance. This approach finds significant utility in image stippling, clustering, resource allocation, and generating blue noise point distributions for rendering. Although recent methods have addressed semi-discrete problems in 2D and 3D, extensions to higher dimensions remain undeveloped, largely due to the computational challenges of calculating power (Laguerre) diagrams in those spaces. This work introduces an algorithm for computing power diagrams applicable to any topological dimension. We initially assess the algorithm's performance across dimensions 2 through 6. Subsequently, we focus on four-dimensional scenarios, demonstrating that our method effectively solves optimal quantization and semi-discrete optimal transport problems by achieving a prescribed mass for each power cell through the computation of an optimized power diagram.

Transfer learning utilizing large pretrained transformer models such as BERT has become the dominant strategy for numerous NLP applications. However, merely fine-tuning these models on downstream tasks or augmenting them with task-specific pretraining often lacks robustness. Specifically, performance fluctuates significantly based on random seed selection or the number of pretraining and fine-tuning iterations, and the resulting models remain susceptible to adversarial attacks. We introduce a straightforward yet effective adapter-based method to address these challenges. This approach involves inserting small bottleneck layers, known as adapters, into every layer of a pretrained model. The pretrained layers are then frozen while the adapter layers are trained on downstream task data through a two-stage process: (1) task-specific unsupervised pretraining followed by (2) task-specific supervised training, such as classification or sequence labeling. Our experiments show that this training protocol enhances both stability and adversarial robustness when transferring knowledge to various downstream tasks.

We re-examine our rope model for string fragmentation, which effectively describes strangeness and baryon enhancement in high-multiplicity pp collisions at the LHC. The model's primary mechanism attributes this enhancement to increased string tension caused by string overlaps in dense environments. By refining the space-time representation of these overlaps to correctly account for non-parallel strings, we can now consistently analyze enhancement effects in both jets and the underlying event.

In a Black-Scholes framework, an investment strategy that maximizes exponential utility is modified by imposing fixed upper and lower bounds on terminal wealth. This approach is mathematically equivalent to integrating the optimal strategy with options. The analysis examines the resulting wealth distribution through the lens of quantile changes. The theoretical framework is demonstrated using quantitative examples, which also evaluate the impact of limiting the strategy to positive-only investments.

This letter introduces a comprehensive Meeting-Merging-Mission framework designed for multi-robot exploration in environments with communication constraints. Addressing real-world limitations in communication bandwidth and range, we propose a lightweight environmental representation method alongside an efficient cooperative exploration strategy. To mitigate low bandwidth issues, each robot employs specific polytopes to track free space and super frontier information (SFI), which serve as the basis for exploration decisions. To minimize redundant exploration, we establish a mission-oriented protocol that facilitates information sharing among robots during stable rendezvous points. Additionally, we develop a full path planning scheme applicable to both centralized and decentralized scenarios. To demonstrate the framework's practicality and generality, we provide an extensive benchmark and successfully deploy the system on both multi-UGV and multi-UAV platforms.

This study investigates the production of heavy Higgs bosons in association with a vector boson, specifically those decaying into a pair of vector bosons, within final states characterized by two same-sign leptons (electrons or muons), missing transverse momentum, and jets. The analysis utilizes a dataset of proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV collected by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider between 2015 and 2018, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 139 fb⁻¹. The observed data align with Standard Model background predictions. Results are interpreted through higher-dimensional operators within an effective field theory framework, yielding upper limits on the production cross-section at a 95% confidence level as a function of the heavy Higgs boson's mass and its couplings to vector bosons. Constraints are established for Higgs boson masses ranging from 300 to 1500 GeV, contingent on assumed coupling values; notably, the highest excluded mass for the explored coupling combinations reaches 900 GeV. Additionally, limits on coupling strengths are reported.

Reasoning about the future—specifically, comprehending how current choices influence future results—represents a core difficulty in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly within highly stochastic or partially observable settings. Although directly forecasting the future is challenging, this work presents a method enabling an agent to "anticipate" without explicit prediction. Specifically, we propose allowing an agent, while training on historical data, to access the \emph{actual} future outcomes that occurred at those times, subject to an information bottleneck constraint that prevents excessive reliance on this privileged data. This approach enables the agent to leverage rich insights into future trajectory dynamics alongside present information. Our method, Policy Gradients Incorporating the Future (PGIF), is straightforward to implement and adaptable to virtually any policy gradient algorithm. By applying PGIF to various off-the-shelf RL algorithms, we demonstrate that it achieves higher rewards more rapidly across diverse online and offline RL domains, including those with sparse rewards and partial observability.

The dissipation of mass and rotational energy from rotating primordial black holes (PBHs) via Hawking radiation follows distinct dynamics. We examine how these dynamics influence the generation of dark radiation—specifically hot gravitons or vector bosons—and non-cold dark matter. Although the production rate of higher-spin particles increases during PBH rotation, we demonstrate that the resulting dark radiation energy density undergoes additional redshift because emission ceases before the PBHs fully evaporate. Incorporating this effect reveals a suppression of $\Delta N_{\rm eff}$ by a factor of $\mathcal{O}(10)$ for maximally rotating black holes compared to earlier findings. By solving the Friedmann and Boltzmann equations to precisely model the evolution of linear perturbations, we reassess warm dark matter constraints on light candidates produced by evaporation across varying black hole spins. Due to the combined influence of enhanced production and late-stage dilution, higher-spin particles are found to be most susceptible to these limits. The accompanying code, FRISBHEE (FRIedmann Solver for Black Hole Evaporation in the Early universe), developed for this study, is available at https://github.com/yfperezg/frisbhee.

Although spring-based actuators enhance energy efficiency and performance in legged locomotion, they complicate controller design. While prior research has relied heavily on modeling and simulation to derive optimal controllers, we propose learning model-free controllers directly on the physical robot. Our method begins by synthesizing gaits using central pattern generators (CPGs), optimizing their parameters to rapidly establish an efficient open-loop controller. Subsequently, reinforcement learning is employed to close the loop, learning corrective actions that build upon the CPGs to increase robustness and further boost performance. We evaluated this approach on DLR's elastic quadruped, bert. Our results demonstrate that for trotting and pronking gaits, the benefits of spring actuator dynamics emerge naturally during the optimization of dynamic motions, resulting in high-performance, model-free locomotion. The entire process completes in under 1.5 hours on the real robot, producing natural-looking gaits.

This study determines the branching fractions and $CP$ asymmetries for the decays $B^{0}\to \bar{D}^{0}\pi^{0}$ and $B^{+}\to \bar{D}^{0}\pi^{+}$ utilizing a dataset of $772\times 10^{6}$ $B\bar{B}$ pairs recorded at the $\Upsilon(4S)$ resonance by the Belle detector at the KEKB $e^{+}e^{-}$ collider. The resulting branching fractions and direct $CP$ asymmetries are $\mathcal{B}(B^{0}\to \bar{D}^{0}\pi^{0}) = [2.70 \pm 0.06~ \text{(stat.)} \pm 0.10~ \text{(syst.)}] \times 10^{-4}$, $\mathcal{B}(B^{+}\to \bar{D}^{0}\pi^{+}) = [4.53 \pm 0.02~ \text{(stat.)} \pm 0.15~ \text{(syst.)}] \times 10^{-3}$, $ {\cal A}_{CP}(B^{0}\to \bar{D}^{0}\pi^{0}) = [+0.42 \pm 2.05~ \text{(stat.)} \pm 1.22~ \text{(syst.)}]\%$, and $ {\cal A}_{CP}(B^{+}\to \bar{D}^{0}\pi^{+}) = [+0.19 \pm 0.36~ \text{(stat.)} \pm 0.57~ \text{(syst.)}]\%$. These $\mathcal{B}$ measurements represent the current highest precision and align well with prior findings, as does the ${\cal A}_{CP}(B^{+}\to \bar{D}^{0}\pi^{+})$ result. Furthermore, this marks the inaugural measurement of ${\cal A}_{CP}$ for the $B^{0}\to \bar{D}^{0}\pi^{0}$ channel, yielding a value consistent with Standard Model predictions.

The swift advancement of science and technology has led to an exponential increase in peer-reviewed publications. However, since each paper requires labor-intensive evaluation by domain experts, ensuring high-quality reviews for this expanding volume presents a major challenge. This study investigates whether scientific reviewing can be automated by leveraging state-of-the-art natural language processing (NLP) models to create initial peer reviews. A primary hurdle in this endeavor is defining what constitutes a "good" review, so we first examine potential metrics for evaluation. Subsequently, we gathered a dataset of machine learning papers, annotated them with specific content aspects, and trained targeted summarization models to generate reviews from these papers. Our comprehensive experiments indicate that while system-generated reviews often cover more aspects than human-written ones, they tend to be less constructive across most categories, except for the explanation of core ideas, which remain factually accurate. Finally, we outline eight challenges and potential solutions for developing effective review generation systems, aiming to inspire further research in this area. All code, the dataset, and the ReviewAdvisor system are publicly accessible at https://github.com/neulab/ReviewAdvisor and http://review.nlpedia.ai/.

Recently, Lad, Sanfilippo, and Agr\`o introduced extropy as the dual counterpart to Shannon entropy. While Tsallis previously defined Tsallis entropy as a generalization of Boltzmann-Gibbs statistics for discrete random variables, this work proposes a new discrimination metric termed Tsallis extropy. The paper examines the properties of this measure, establishes its relationship with entropy, derives several bounds, and illustrates its application in pattern recognition.

This research investigates a system of quasilinear eigenvalue problems subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions on complete, compact Riemannian manifolds. Specifically, we recover Cheng comparison estimates and the Faber-Krahn inequality regarding the first eigenvalue of the $(p,q)$-Laplacian. Furthermore, we provide a new proof of Cheeger-type estimates for the $p$-Laplacian (where $1 < p < \infty$), utilizing these results to construct a lower bound estimate for the first eigenvalue of the $(p,q)$-Laplacian in terms of Cheeger's constant. As a corollary, we demonstrate that the first eigenvalue approaches Cheeger's constant as both $p$ and $q$ tend toward 1.

The need for implementing blockchain services over the Internet has created an urgent requirement for deploying Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) consensus. Deterministic (partial) synchronous protocols offer simplicity and speed under favorable network conditions but are vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks if synchrony assumptions break down. Conversely, asynchronous protocols provide robustness against adversarial networks but are significantly more complex and slower due to their reliance on randomness. To address these limitations, optimistic asynchronous atomic broadcast protocols (Kursawe-Shoup, 2002; Ramasamy-Cachin, 2005) were introduced to enhance the performance of slow asynchronous consensus. These protocols operate a deterministic fast lane when network conditions are good, reverting to a fully asynchronous protocol through a pace-synchronization mechanism if the fast lane fails. However, existing pace-synchronization methods rely heavily on asynchronous multi-valued validated Byzantine agreement (MVBA).

We introduce Bolt-Dumbo Transformer (BDT), a generic framework designed for practical optimistic asynchronous atomic broadcast. At its core, BDT proposes a new fast lane abstraction that is both simple and efficient while ensuring honest parties can gracefully handle fast lane failures caused by malicious leaders or poor network conditions. This design enables a highly efficient pace-synchronization mechanism for fallback, reducing the reliance on cumbersome MVBA to a variant of the conceptually simplest binary agreement. In addition to comprehensive security analyses, we provide concrete instantiations of the framework and implement them. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BDT achieves both the low latency of deterministic protocols (such as the 2-chain version of HotStuff) and the robustness of state-of-the-art asynchronous protocols in practice.

We detected rapid radio brightening from GRB 210702A using the Australian Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) only 11 hours after the burst, monitoring variability over a 5-hour span at ~15-minute intervals across 9.0, 16.7, and 21.2 GHz. A broken power-law fit to the 9.0 GHz data indicated that a 5-hour flare reached a peak flux density of 0.4 ± 0.1 mJy approximately 13 hours post-burst, characterized by a sharp rise and decay. This rapid temporal and spectral evolution contradicts the standard internal-external shock model, which predicts much longer timescales for forward and reverse shock radio emission. Meanwhile, early-time optical and X-ray light curves from the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory displayed typical afterglow forward shock behavior, enabling blast wave physics calculations that suggest a homogeneous circumburst medium and an electron power-law index of p = 2.9 ± 0.1. We propose that the early radio flare resulted from weak interstellar scintillation (ISS), which amplified the radio afterglow above the ATCA sensitivity threshold on minute scales. Applying weak ISS relations allowed us to constrain the blast wave's size in the plane of the sky to ≤6 × 10¹⁶ cm, a value consistent with the theoretical forward shock prediction of 8 × 10¹⁶ cm at ~13 hours post-burst. This marks the earliest ISS-derived size constraint for a GRB blast wave, highlighting the necessity of rapid (<1 day) multi-hour radio follow-ups to capture early afterglow evolution and trace scintillation across a wide frequency range.

This study expands the Standard Model by incorporating TeV-scale scalar leptoquarks to account for neutrino masses and address observed discrepancies, such as the anomalous magnetic moments of charged leptons and $B$-physics anomalies ($R_{K^{(*)}}$ and $R_{D^{(*)}}$). The framework utilizes an $\text{SU}(2)_L$ singlet leptoquark $S_1\sim (\bar{3}, 1, 1/3)$, a doublet leptoquark $\tilde{R}_2\sim (3, 2, 1/6)$, and a triplet leptoquark $S_3\sim (\bar{3}, 3, 1/3)$. We integrate constraints from low-energy lepton flavor violation and meson decay and mixing data to conduct a comprehensive phenomenological analysis. This analysis determines the minimal texture of leptoquark Yukawa matrices required to provide a unified explanation for both the observed anomalies and neutrino oscillation results.

Driven by experimental searches for $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay and collider investigations of lepton number violation at dimensions $d\geq7$, we examine the sensitivity of the $d=5$ Weinberg operator via the non-resonant process $pp\to \ell^\pm \ell'^{\pm} j j$ at the LHC. We establish a prescription for the operator suitable for both collision and decay contexts, concentrating on the $\ell\ell'=\mu\mu$ channel, which lies beyond the sensitivity of nuclear decay experiments. Assuming a Wilson coefficient of $C^{\mu\mu}_5=1$, scales up to $\Lambda\sim 8.3~(11)$~TeV are accessible with integrated luminosities of $\mathcal{L}=300~{\rm fb}^{-1}$ or $3~{\rm ab}^{-1}$. This corresponds to an effective $\mu\mu$ Majorana mass of $\vert m_{\mu\mu}\vert\sim7.3~(5.4)$~GeV, thereby outlining a strategy for testing the Weinberg operator using accelerators.

This study examines how Efimov states influence the post-quench evolution of a three-boson system featuring contact interactions within a spherically symmetric 3D harmonic trap, following a sudden change in interaction strength. Leveraging established hyperspherical solutions for the static three-body problem, we derive semi-analytic expressions for the time-dependent Ramsey signal and particle separation. We analyze quenches transitioning between non-interacting and strongly interacting regimes, as well as the reverse, across a range of Efimov state energies.

This study introduces a fully microscopic model for describing the nuclear level density (NLD) in spherical nuclei. The framework integrates the partition function of the exact pairing solution combined with the finite-temperature independent-particle model (EP+IPM) alongside results derived from collective vibrational states. These vibrational states are calculated using the self-consistent Hartree-Fock mean field with MSk3 interaction, coupled with exact pairing and the random-phases approximation (SC-HFEPRPA). Two critical factors are addressed microscopically: the spin cut-off and vibrational enhancement factors are computed via the statistical thermodynamics and partition function of the SC-HFEPRPA, requiring no fitting parameters. Numerical tests on spherical $^{60}$Ni and $^{90}$Zr nuclei indicate that collective vibrational enhancement is primarily driven by quadrupole and octupole excitations. This marks the first microscopic validation of this effect, which was previously predicted phenomenologically and extensively utilized in various NLD models. Furthermore, the model examines the impact of collective vibrational enhancement on nuclear thermodynamic properties, including excitation energy, specific heat capacity, and entropy.

We establish the convergence in probability of free energy for matchings on random regular, uniform hypergraphs and calculate the limit explicitly. Additionally, we identify a parameter region where replica symmetry is valid.

Since its 1995 discovery, the high-energy peaked blazar 1ES 2344+514 has experienced multiple GeV-TeV flaring episodes and been monitored across various wavelengths. Observations from 1996 and a 2016 flare indicate that this source exhibits transient EHBL-like behavior, a phenomenon also seen in other nearby high-energy peaked blazars. We apply a photohadronic model to interpret the GeV-TeV flaring events of 1995 and 2007. Additionally, we utilize a recently proposed two-zone photohadronic model, known for effectively explaining multi-TeV flaring in similar transient sources, to analyze the spectra from MJD 57611 and MJD 57612. Our results demonstrate that the parameters of zone-2 within this two-zone model are crucial for accounting for these spectra, potentially signaling a new class of transient EHBL-like sources. Furthermore, our spectral fits are comparable to or superior to other leptonic and hadronic models used in previous literature to address these phenomena.

We report the detection of two-fold rotation symmetry within the charge density wave (CDW) state of the recently identified Kagome superconductor, CsV$_3$Sb$_5$. Upon cooling below the CDW transition temperature ($T_{CDW}$), the polarization rotation of the reflected laser beam rapidly appears, reaching approximately 1 mrad, and exhibits distinct two-fold symmetry. Utilizing femtosecond laser pulses, this rotation angle can be readily suppressed and subsequently recovers within several picoseconds, a process accompanied by coherent oscillations. Notably, these signal oscillations undergo a 180-degree periodic shift. Our study offers compelling optical confirmation of nematic order with two-fold symmetry forming immediately below $T_{CDW}$. These findings suggest an immediate onset of nematicity and potential time-reversal symmetry breaking in the CDW state of CsV$_3$Sb$_5$.

This study investigates the behavior of a flexible fiber carried by viscous flow within a Hele-Shaw cell where the cell height matches the fiber's thickness. We demonstrate that long fibers oriented with the flow undergo a buckling instability. The interplay between viscous and elastic forces causes the fiber to deform into a wavy pattern modulated by a Bell-shaped envelope. Our analysis details the wavelength and phase velocity of these deformations, along with the development and expansion of the envelope. Furthermore, examining the spatio-temporal evolution of the deformation uncovers a linear, absolute instability driven by a local mechanism effectively captured by the Ginzburg-Landau equation.

This paper details the design and performance of the calorimeter systems within the ECCE detector, aiming to meet overall specifications cost-effectively through careful management of technical and schedule risks. The system comprises three electromagnetic calorimeters spanning a combined pseudorapidity range of -3.7 to 3.8, along with two hadronic calorimeters. Key performance metrics, including energy and position resolutions, reconstruction efficiency, and particle identification capabilities, will be discussed.

Motivated by string theory, ultra-light axion fields generate a dense condensate, or axion cloud, around rotating black holes via superradiant instability. This cloud induces observable effects, such as black hole spin-down and the emission of monochromatic gravitational waves, offering a novel avenue for astrophysical axion detection. However, incorporating axion self-interaction significantly alters cloud dynamics, potentially triggering an explosive event known as bosenova. Consequently, accurately modeling the evolution of self-interacting clouds is essential for effective detection strategies. This paper introduces a new approach to simulate the full growth process of these clouds using the adiabatic approximation. Unlike conventional methods that rely on non-relativistic or perturbative treatments of self-interaction, our technique avoids these limitations. Our primary finding reveals that in the strongly self-interacting regime, cloud evolution is contingent upon the strength of the gravitational coupling between the axion and the black hole. At high coupling strengths, the system stabilizes into a quasi-stationary state where superradiant energy gain balances energy dissipation to infinity through self-interaction. Conversely, reducing the coupling strength renders the cloud unstable at a specific energy threshold, signaling the onset of bosenova.

This work investigates the texture of Standard Model fermion mass matrices and their mixing patterns within a supersymmetric adjoint SU(5) Grand Unified Theory where modular $S_4$ serves as the horizontal symmetry. In this framework, Yukawa couplings for both quarks and leptons are constructed from modular forms of low weight. The neutrino sector incorporates an adjoint SU(5) representation (24) as a matter superfield, forming a triplet under $S_4$. Light neutrino masses arise via a combination of Type-I and Type-III seesaw mechanisms. The modulus $\tau$ is the sole complex parameter shared between the charged fermion and neutrino sectors. Down-type quarks and charged leptons share identical joint effective operators containing an adjoint scalar; however, their mass differences within the same generation are determined by Clebsch-Gordan coefficients. Notably, for the first two generations, these coefficients yield a double Yukawa ratio of $y_d y_\mu / y_e y_s = 12$, which aligns excellently with experimental data. Furthermore, the model successfully reproduces the correct CKM mixing parameters and all nine Yukawa eigenvalues for quarks and charged leptons. Additionally, it generates appropriate neutrino masses and MNS parameters, favoring a normal mass ordering.

A rapidly expanding field within quantum computing is its integration with machine learning techniques, particularly through quantum kernel methods. However, experimentally assessing these kernels is challenging because it involves measuring the overlap between two quantum states. This article introduces a feasible experimental approach for kernel evaluation utilizing temporally encoded photons and Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference. We provide a comprehensive description of this method and demonstrate its ability to efficiently classify encoded data when combined with kernel mean embedding and maximum mean discrepancy.

This study presents DCPViz, an innovative visual analytics framework that allows climate researchers to interactively investigate large-scale climate datasets without the need to pre-transfer massive volumes of data. By providing more efficient tools, DCPViz facilitates the discovery of emerging trends and patterns within climate projections and their projected impacts. The DCPViz pipeline was specifically engineered to retrieve and extract NEX-DCP30 data from public repositories with minimal data transmission. Furthermore, we implemented DCPViz to validate its scalability and scientific merit, assessing its practical utility across three distinct use cases involving various models and incorporating feedback from domain experts.

Autonomous systems (AS) execute intricate missions by constantly monitoring their environment and acting to achieve specific objectives. While swarms of AS collaborating together can accomplish these tasks more rapidly and efficiently than individual units, current development practices require engineers to manually craft software for observation storage, aggregation, and learning. We introduce the Fleet Computer, a dedicated platform designed for the development and management of AS swarms. This platform offers a programming paradigm that streamlines Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), a growing class of algorithms used to coordinate agent swarms. By utilizing only two user-defined functions, Map() and Eval(), the Fleet Computer compiles and deploys swarms while continuously updating the reinforcement learning models that dictate agent actions. To optimize compute resources, the system implements priority scheduling for models that drive effective actions, establishing a new connection between online learning and resource management. We have applied this technology to create swarms for agricultural unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and for urban traffic video analytics. Relative to individual AS, our swarms demonstrated a 4.4X speedup with four UAVs and a 62X speedup with 130 video cameras. Furthermore, compared to a widely used competing swarm-building approach, our swarms were three times more effective while consuming 3.9 times less energy.

LSTM-based language models play a crucial role in contemporary large-vocabulary continuous speech recognition (LVCSR) systems by substantially outperforming traditional backoff models, though their efficient integration into decoding processes has historically been challenging. This paper introduces a methodology combining one-pass decoding with lattice rescoring. The approach involves initial decoding using the LSTM language model, followed by recombining hypotheses that share the final two words before rescoring the resulting lattice. Evaluated on GPGPU-equipped hardware, our systems achieve competitive performance on the Hub5'00 and LibriSpeech corpora while maintaining real-time or faster processing speeds. Furthermore, we briefly explore the feasibility of executing a full summation over all state-sequences for a given word hypothesis directly during decoding, bypassing the recombination step.

Tri-Structural Isotropic (TRISO) fuel particles are essential for next-generation nuclear fuels, yet characterizing them via X-ray computed tomography (CT) is difficult due to strong X-ray attenuation by the uranium core, which causes severe photon starvation in many measurements. Additionally, high-resolution scans on conventional laboratory systems using standard reconstruction algorithms often require extensive acquisition times. Specifically, analytic methods like the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm produce reconstructions plagued by severe streak artifacts and noise, hindering particle analysis. This article presents the development and application of model-based image reconstruction (MBIR) algorithms to enhance CT reconstruction quality for TRISO particles. We show that these MBIR methods significantly suppress artifacts with minimal pre-processing compared to conventional techniques. Furthermore, the proposed MBIR approach yields high-quality reconstructions comparable to FDK even when utilizing only a fraction of the typical measurements, enabling dramatically faster scan times for TRISO particles.

Event data, defined by the timestamps of occurrences, plays a critical role in numerous real-world scenarios. Recent advancements have utilized neural network-based point processes to model event times, achieving state-of-the-art prediction accuracy. Nevertheless, these models currently lack robust uncertainty quantification. Effective uncertainty estimation in event modeling is essential for enhancing decision-making in practical applications. To address this, we introduce the Bayesian Neural Hawkes Process (BNHP), a novel model that combines the uncertainty modeling strengths of Bayesian approaches with the generalization power of neural networks. We further extend BNHP with spatio-temporal capabilities, enabling it to quantify uncertainty regarding both the predicted time and location of events. Experimental results on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that BNHP significantly enhances both prediction performance and uncertainty quantification for event modeling.

We investigate the evolution of galaxy assembly gradients across a broad redshift range ($0.5<z<1.7$) using spatially resolved H-alpha emission maps of star-forming galaxies. Our data at $z\sim0.5$ derives from deep Hubble Space Telescope WFC3 G102 grism spectroscopy as part of the CANDELS CLEAR Experiment. For galaxies with $\log(M_{*}/\mathrm{M}_{\odot})\geqslant8.96$, the mean H-alpha effective radius is $1.2\pm0.1$ times larger than the stellar continuum radius, indicating inside-out growth driven by star formation. This finding aligns within $1\sigma$ with measurements from the 3D-HST and KMOS-3D surveys at $z\sim1$ and $z\sim1.7$, respectively, suggesting no evolution over time. Conversely, we detect redshift evolution in the stellar mass surface density within 1 kiloparsec ($\Sigma_\mathrm{1kpc}$). Specifically, at $z\sim0.5$, star-forming galaxies with $\log(M_{*}/\mathrm{M}_{\odot})=9.5$ exhibit an H-alpha to stellar continuum $\Sigma_\mathrm{1kpc}$ ratio that is $(19\pm2)\%$ lower than at $z\sim1$. This ratio declines with increasing stellar mass. Most of the redshift evolution in this ratio versus stellar mass arises because $\log(\Sigma_{1\mathrm{kpc, H}\alpha})$ drops twice as much as $\log(\Sigma_{1\mathrm{kpc, Cont}})$ from $z\sim1$ to $0.5$ (at fixed $\log(M_{*}/\mathrm{M}_{\odot})=9.5$). Comparisons with the TNG50 cosmological magnetohydrodynamical simulation rule out dust as the cause of this trend. Our results support a scenario where inside-out quenching follows inside-out growth, with the latter driving the substantial decrease in $\Sigma_{1\mathrm{kpc, H}\alpha}$ from $z\sim1$ to $z\sim0.5$.

Although clinical machine learning has received significant focus and funding, its deployment in real-world clinical settings remains limited. While research drives innovation, translating these advancements is equally critical for ultimately transforming healthcare. We attribute the gap between expectations and reality to an underappreciation of key factors. To gain a comprehensive perspective, we interviewed practitioners with commercial experience in developing clinical machine learning for deployment. Based on these insights, we have identified several primary categories of challenges to guide the design and development of effective clinical machine learning applications.
