This note leverages noncommutative $l$-adic cohomology to broaden the scope of the generalized Riemann hypothesis from algebraic geometry to the extensive domain of geometric noncommutative schemes as defined by Orlov. First, we demonstrate that the generalized Riemann hypothesis remains invariant under derived equivalences and homological projective duality. Second, we establish the validity of the noncommutative generalized Riemann hypothesis in several novel cases.

We introduce the variational separability verifier (VSV), a new variational quantum algorithm (VQA) designed to identify the closest separable state (CSS) for any quantum state relative to the Hilbert-Schmidt distance (HSD). Our initial evaluation of the VSV examines the convergence of its optimization process for Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states comprising up to seven qubits, utilizing both statevector and shot-based simulations. Furthermore, we numerically calculate the CSS for maximally entangled multipartite $X$-states ($X$-MEMS) and derive the analytical expression for these CSS values based on the algorithm's output. Our findings suggest that current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware could effectively tackle the $NP$-hard full separability problem via the VSV, owing to the shallow quantum circuit depth required when using the destructive SWAP test to compute the HSD. Additionally, once refined to determine the closest $k$-separable state ($k$-CSS) for multipartite entangled systems, the VSV may facilitate the broader characterization of such quantum states.

We revisit a nonparametric density model grounded in Gaussian processes. By integrating latent Polya–Gamma random variables and a latent marked Poisson process, we derive a new likelihood that is conjugate to the model's Gaussian process prior. This augmented posterior facilitates efficient inference through Gibbs sampling and an approximate variational mean field method; for the latter, we employ sparse GP approximations to manage the problem's infinite dimensionality. The efficacy of both algorithms, alongside comparisons with alternative density estimators, is validated using artificial and real datasets containing up to several thousand observations.

We have examined the formation of atomic nanoclusters on suspended graphene sheets using molecular dynamics simulations at finite temperatures. Our systematic investigation involved temperature-dependent molecular dynamics simulations of various transition and alkali atoms on these graphene surfaces. Our findings indicate that transition atoms aggregate to form nanoclusters of varying sizes distributed randomly across the graphene surface. In contrast, most alkali atoms tend to form a single atomic layer on the graphene sheets. Notably, potassium atoms exhibit regular deposition on the surface at low temperatures. Based on this behavior, we anticipate that the electrical conductivity of potassium-doped suspended graphene will be significantly higher at low temperatures compared to graphene doped with other atoms.

Achieving unprecedented spatial superpositions of massive objects could enable investigations into quantum mechanics, quantum aspects of general relativity, and the sensing and constraining of classical gravity. In this study, we demonstrate a feasible experimental configuration utilizing realizable magnetic field gradients of ${\cal O}(10-100)$ Tm$^{-1}$. This setup allows for the creation of spatial superpositions ranging from ${\cal O}(10^{-4}-10^{-8})$ m for masses between ${\cal O}(10^{-16}-10^{-14})$ kg, sustained over durations of up to $0.1-10$ seconds.

This study systematically investigates pion emission in heavy-ion collisions at approximately 1 A GeV, utilizing the improved isospin-dependent quantum molecular dynamics (ImIQMD) framework to probe nuclear symmetry energy at supra-saturation densities. The analysis assumes that pions are primarily generated through the decay of $\triangle$(1232) and N*(1440) resonances. Calculations were performed for various Skyrme parameter sets (SkP, SLy6, Ska, and SIII) and for differing stiffness levels of the symmetry energy using the SLy6 baseline. Preliminary findings, when compared with experimental data from the FOPI collaboration, support a hard symmetry energy potential where the density dependence is proportional to $(\rho/\rho_{0})^{\gamma_{s}}$ with $\gamma_{s}=2$.

Jet precession plays a significant role in various astrophysical events, ranging from galaxies to X-ray binaries and gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). Since polarization serves as a distinctive tool for investigating magnetic fields within GRB jets, the precession of these relativistic jets—which alters the geometry of the observable emission region—can influence the polarization observed in the afterglow. This study examines the evolution of polarization and associated light curves in the early optical afterglows of GRBs, considering both ordered and random magnetic field configurations while accounting for jet precession. Our findings indicate that precession driven by long-lived engines can substantially lower the polarization degree (PD), irrespective of the underlying magnetic field structure. The most pronounced reduction in PD occurs when the observer's line of sight is aligned with the precession axis. Consequently, these results suggest that jet precession offers valuable insights into the low polarization degrees detected in the early optical afterglows of GRBs.

Over the last twenty years, graph theory has significantly advanced applied finance, introducing innovative techniques such as asset network estimation, hierarchical selection, and portfolio allocation into the practitioner's toolkit. This paper examines the core challenge of learning undirected graphical models with Laplacian structural constraints using financial time series data. We provide empirically supported rationales for employing the Laplacian matrix as a representation of the precision matrix for financial assets and demonstrate how Laplacian constraints relate to tangible market concepts, including the index factor and conditional stock correlations. These insights offer practical guidelines for graph estimation in financial contexts. Additionally, we develop numerical algorithms utilizing the alternating direction method of multipliers to construct undirected, weighted graphs that account for intrinsic financial characteristics like heavy tails and modularity. We demonstrate the application of these learned graphs in practical tasks, such as stock time series clustering and foreign exchange network estimation, showing that our proposed algorithms surpass state-of-the-art methods in extensive empirical tests. We also present both theoretical and empirical convergence results for these algorithms. Finally, to support reproducibility, we release an R package named `fingraph`, which contains the necessary code and data to replicate all experimental findings.

A recently proposed modification of the Fisher model, grounded in the Landau O(m^6) theory describing free energy near a critical point, yields isoscaling. In this framework, the order parameter is defined as m = (N-Z)/A, a result stemming from specific symmetries of the nuclear Hamiltonian. We demonstrate that isoscaling primarily relies on this order parameter via the 'external (conjugate) field' H, which corresponds to the difference in neutron and proton chemical potentials between two sources. To differentiate this method from prior isoscaling relations, we term it 'm-scaling.' We examine the connection between this new framework and the standard isoscaling formalism, highlighting significant interpretational differences for experimental data that warrant further theoretical and experimental investigation.

Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have attracted significant interest as an energy-efficient alternative to traditional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), primarily due to their naturally sparse activation patterns. Nevertheless, most existing SNN methodologies rely on ANN-inspired structures (such as VGG-Net or ResNet), which may yield suboptimal results when processing binary temporal sequences. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new Neural Architecture Search (NAS) method designed to identify superior SNN architectures. Drawing inspiration from recent NAS techniques that determine optimal structures based on initial activation patterns, our approach selects architectures capable of representing varied spike activation patterns across different data samples without requiring training. Furthermore, to maximize the utilization of temporal information within spikes, our search process explores both feed-forward and backward (temporal feedback) connections between layers. Notably, the resulting architecture, SNASNet, which incorporates backward connections, demonstrates enhanced performance, underscoring the critical role of architectural design in effectively leveraging temporal dynamics. Through extensive experiments on three image recognition benchmarks, we show that SNASNet attains state-of-the-art performance using significantly fewer timesteps (5 timesteps). The source code is accessible via Github.

We formulate the task of moving a Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC) between the wells of a double-well potential as an optimal control problem aimed at determining the time-evolving potential shape. By applying a Galerkin truncation to a finite set of eigenfunctions, we derive a reduced dynamical system and demonstrate that utilizing just three modes is sufficient to effectively manage the full dynamics governed by the Gross-Pitaevskii model. The control functional is discretized into finite dimensions via the chopped random basis (CRAB) method, which is subsequently optimized using a differential evolution (DE) genetic algorithm. Finally, we examine how the accuracy of this reduction-based optimal control approach can be enhanced by incorporating additional modes into the Galerkin reduction.

Earthquake signals are inherently non-stationary, making real-time identification and classification challenging using traditional methods like peak ground displacement or velocity. Even widely used algorithms such as STA/LTA demand extensive research to set appropriate threshold parameters for triggering alarms and are prone to false alarms caused by human error or natural disturbances like thunder and landslides. This study addresses these issues by converting seismograph data into audio signals for enhanced perception and extracting features using Speech Recognition techniques, specifically Filter Bank Coefficients and Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC). These features were utilized to train both a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network. The proposed approach enables automatic earthquake detection from waveforms with minimal human intervention. Testing on a 1000Hz dataset with 0.2-second sample windows yielded a 91.1% accuracy for the CNN model and 93.99% for the LSTM model. The training set comprised 610 audio samples, including 310 earthquake sounds and 300 non-earthquake sounds. During testing, the total alarm generation time was approximately 2 seconds, accounting for data collection, processing, and prediction delays. This demonstrates the method's effectiveness for Earthquake Early Warning (EEW) systems. Given that the input is solely the waveform, the system is well-suited for real-time processing, making it ideal for onsite EEW applications that require low preparation time and workload.

This work addresses the inverse problem of identifying the coefficients of the fractional power of a general second-order elliptic operator defined on the exterior of an open subset within Euclidean space. We demonstrate that this problem can be simplified to determining the coefficients from the boundary Cauchy data of the elliptic operator on the open set, a task equivalent to the Calderón problem. As a consequence, we derive several new findings for nonlocal inverse problems by leveraging corresponding results from local inverse problems. Specifically, under certain regularity conditions on the coefficients, we completely resolve the isotropic nonlocal Calderón problem. Furthermore, we solve the anisotropic Calderón problem up to an isometry that is the identity at the boundary for real-analytic anisotropic conductivities in dimensions greater than two, as well as for bounded and measurable anisotropic conductivities in two dimensions.

Entanglement linking neutral atoms with microwave photons within a superconducting coplanar waveguide (SCW) facilitates hybrid quantum architectures by bridging stationary and flying qubits. We investigate a one-step controlled-Z (C$_{\text{Z}}$) gate connecting a neutral atom trapped adjacent to an SCW and a microwave mode inside the waveguide, extending the approach outlined by J. D. Pritchard et al. in *Phys. Rev. A* 89, 010301(R) (2014). This gate protocol is streamlined, necessitating only a single laser pulse to drive a transition between the atom's ground and Rydberg states.

The collective dynamics linked to color confinement are highlighted as the dominant factor, surpassing point-like mechanisms involving the scattering of proton constituents at the momentum transfer values currently accessible in proton elastic scattering at the LHC. The discussion centers on deep-elastic scattering and its function in distinguishing between absorptive and reflective asymptotic scattering mechanisms, with a specific focus on experimental signatures tied to multiparticle production processes.

Electron acoustic solitary structures in Fermi plasmas featuring two-temperature electron distributions find diverse applications in both laboratory and space environments. Developing a robust theoretical framework is crucial for comprehending various physical systems characterized by differing parameters. Within a quantum Fermi plasma system, the motion of two-temperature electrons significantly influences the system's solitary wave profiles. This study examines a quantum Fermi plasma with two electron populations exhibiting opposite streaming velocities. Utilizing the quantum hydrodynamic (QHD) model, we derive a linear dispersion relation for the system. To investigate non-linear dynamics, we apply the standard perturbation method to obtain the KdV-B equation, demonstrating how solitary profiles evolve across various plasma parameters. Furthermore, we analyze the stable rogue wave structure using the Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation (NLSE) and present corresponding simulation results. Finally, we explore the dynamical properties and phase portraits of a two-stream quantum Fermi plasma system composed of two-temperature electrons.

This work outlines a methodology for analyzing texture in nanostructured materials by employing the real-space texture PDF ($t_xPDF$) framework detailed by Gong and Billinge (2018). The method is applied to a fiber-textured polycrystalline platinum thin film, utilizing 3D PDF techniques to reconstruct the orientation distribution function (ODF) of crystallites directly from diffraction patterns acquired at varying substrate tilt angles relative to the incident beam. A real-space counterpart to the reciprocal-space pole figure is defined using interatomic vectors within the PDF and calculated for multiple vectors in the platinum film. Additionally, the study demonstrates how to derive a valid isotropic PDF through a weighted average of the tilt series and identifies the optimal measurement conditions for approximating an isotropic PDF from a single exposure, which for the fiber-textured sample corresponds to a nearly grazing incidence angle of approximately 10 degrees. Finally, an open-source Python package named Fourigui is introduced to facilitate texture analysis from 3D reciprocal space data, as well as the Fourier transformation and visualization of 3D PDF data.

Graph representation learning is vital for numerous real-world tasks, such as social relation analysis. A core challenge in this field is acquiring effective representations without relying on expensive and time-consuming human labels. Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) tackles this by minimizing the distance between positive node pairs (similar nodes) and maximizing the distance between negative pairs (dissimilar nodes) within the representation space. Although current GCL methods are successful, they predominantly sample node pairs based on local proximity, often neglecting community structures. Consequently, nodes belonging to the same community may incorrectly be treated as negative pairs. We contend that community information must be integrated to identify nodes within the same community, which are inherently semantically similar. To resolve this, we introduce the Graph Communal Contrastive Learning (gCooL) framework, which jointly learns community partitions and node representations in an end-to-end manner. Specifically, gCooL comprises two modules: a Dense Community Aggregation (DeCA) algorithm for community detection and a Reweighted Self-supervised Cross-contrastive (ReSC) training scheme that leverages community data. Furthermore, acknowledging that real-world graphs are complex and often multi-view, we demonstrate that gCooL can be naturally extended to multiplex graphs. Comprehensive evaluations on various real-world datasets reveal that gCooL surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods.

Physics initiatives at the upgraded Jefferson Lab (JLab) and the proposed Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) aim to probe interactions beyond the Standard Model (SM) through parity-violating electroweak processes. Achieving this demands electron polarimetry with a precision exceeding 0.5% uncertainty. Spin-dependent synchrotron radiation, known as "spin-light," offers a viable method for monitoring electron beam polarization. This paper presents a conceptual design for a "spin-light" polarimeter suitable for high-intensity, multi-GeV electron accelerators. Additionally, we describe a Geant4-based simulation of a prototype device and share preliminary results derived from these simulations.

Few-shot learning (FSL), aimed at addressing data scarcity, has garnered significant interest recently. A typical FSL framework consists of two stages: (i) a pre-training phase where a CNN-based feature extractor is trained on base data, and (ii) a meta-testing phase where the frozen extractor processes novel data (which belongs to categories unseen during base training) to design a recognition classifier. To address distributional issues in few-shot data, researchers have introduced Semi-Supervised Few-Shot Learning (SSFSL) by incorporating unlabeled data. Despite SSFSL's proven success, a fundamental issue persists: the pre-trained feature extractor often fails to adapt perfectly to novel data due to the cross-category setting, typically introducing substantial noise into the novel features. We term this the Feature-Extractor-Maladaptive (FEM) problem. To mitigate FEM, we propose two solutions. First, we introduce Isolated Graph Learning (IGL), a novel label prediction method that uses the Laplacian operator to map raw data into graph space, thereby reducing reliance on noisy features during classification and projecting graph representations into label space. Crucially, IGL minimizes the negative impact of feature noise and offers the flexibility to operate independently during both training and testing, making it well-suited for SSFSL. Second, we propose Graph Co-Training (GCT), which addresses the challenge from a multi-modal fusion perspective by extending IGL into a co-training framework. GCT is a semi-supervised approach that leverages unlabeled samples with two modal features to mutually reinforce the IGL classifier.

A primary long-term objective of exoplanet research involves characterizing the atmospheres of numerous small exoplanets to assess their diversity, identify potentially habitable worlds, and detect biosignatures. Realizing this ambition necessitates a space mission of substantial scale. This study quantifies the detection capabilities of a space-based mid-infrared nulling interferometer designed to measure exoplanet thermal emission. To do so, we created an instrument simulator accounting for all significant astrophysical noise sources and integrated it with Monte Carlo simulations of synthetic exoplanet populations orbiting main-sequence stars within 20 parsecs. This approach enables us to determine the number and types of exoplanets a specific mission concept could identify over a defined timeframe. We analyzed various observing scenarios regarding time allocation, aperture sizes, and wavelength ranges. During an initial 2.5-year search phase, an interferometer utilizing four 2-meter apertures, achieving 5% total throughput across a 4 to 18.5 $\mu$m wavelength band, could detect approximately 550 exoplanets with radii between 0.5 and 6 $R_\oplus$ at an integrated signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) $\ge$7. Among these, at least 160 would have radii $\le$1.5 $R_\oplus$. Depending on the observing strategy, 25 to 45 rocky exoplanets (0.5 to 1.5 $R_\oplus$) within the empirical habitable zones of their host stars could be found. Increasing the aperture size to 3.5 meters could raise the total detection count to roughly 770, including 60 to 80 rocky, habitable-zone planets. Conversely, a 1-meter aperture would yield a maximum of about 315 exoplanets, with no more than 20 rocky, habitable-zone planets. In terms of predicted detection yields, such a mission could compete with large single-aperture reflected light missions.

This paper introduces recent nonlinear analytic approximation tools within the classical framework of Hardy spaces defined on the upper half-plane and demonstrates their extension to the higher-dimensional context of harmonic functions in upper half-spaces. Building on the established result [6] that harmonic functions in higher dimensions can be expressed as combinations of holomorphic functions on two-dimensional planes, extended as constants along normal directions, we establish representation theorems accompanied by corresponding isometries. These developments facilitate the application of these methods to the processing of highly oscillatory multidimensional signals.

Although Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are designed to generalize when trained on sufficiently large datasets, they often fail in production because real-world inputs frequently deviate from the training distribution. This limitation stems from the inherent constraint of using finite data, and the situation is compounded when inputs shift over time, leading to inaccurate predictions. To address these runtime mis-predictions, this work introduces a method that focuses on input handling rather than modifying the DNN's internal structure or parameters, treating the model as a black box. The proposed solution involves two stages: first, it identifies and distinguishes "unseen" inputs that preserve semantic meaning using a distribution analyzer built on a Siamese network's learned distance metric. Second, it transforms these anomalous inputs into equivalent samples from the training set by matching their semantics; this process, termed "input reflection," is formulated as a search problem within an embedding space learned by an auxiliary Quadruplet network. We developed a tool called InputReflector based on this two-step framework and evaluated it across three DNN models trained on CIFAR-10, MNIST, and FMINST datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that InputReflector successfully differentiates between normal inputs and out-of-distribution cases, including those that retain semantic properties such as being blurred, brightened, contrasted, or zoomed.

This study examines the scaling behavior of energy spectra in three-dimensional, fully developed, incompressible turbulence within rotating fluids subject to large-scale forcing, a system thought to exhibit universal scaling exponents across its inertial range. To clarify these scaling regimes, we construct a scaling analysis of the 3D Navier-Stokes equations for such forced, rotating fluids. By applying scaling arguments, we derive the exponents that define the distinct regimes of the energy spectra. Furthermore, we explore the intriguing prospect of two-dimensionalization in 3D rotating turbulence based on this theoretical framework. Our findings offer predictions that can be validated through extensive numerical simulations and appropriate laboratory experiments.

Current pre-trained transformer analyses typically examine only one or two model families, often neglecting the diversity inherent in their architectures and pre-training goals. Our study leverages the oLMpics benchmark and psycholinguistic probing datasets to assess a broad range of 29 models, including T5, BART, and ALBERT. We also modified the oLMpics zero-shot framework for autoregressive models to evaluate GPT networks across various scales. Our results indicate that no model can address compositional questions in a zero-shot manner, implying that current pre-training objectives fail to teach this capability. Moreover, we discovered that global model attributes—such as architecture, directionality, dataset size, and pre-training objective—do not predict a model's linguistic proficiency.

Training Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) on advanced platforms at a large scale is anticipated to be heavily limited by communication bottlenecks. While many gradient compression techniques have been introduced to address this with high compression ratios, most struggle to scale effectively in large distributed environments due to gradient accumulation issues and lack robust evaluation of model fidelity on extensive datasets. To resolve these challenges, we introduce Scalable Sparsified Gradient Compression (ScaleCom), a novel approach that exploits similarities in gradient distributions across learners to achieve superior scalability. Theoretical analysis confirms that ScaleCom offers favorable convergence properties and integrates seamlessly with gradient all-reduce methods. Experimental results indicate that ScaleCom incurs minimal overhead, significantly cuts gradient traffic, and delivers compression rates between 65x and 400x. It also demonstrates excellent scalability, supporting up to 64 learners and enabling batch sizes 8-12 times larger than standard training, all while maintaining high accuracy across diverse applications in image, language, and speech domains.

This study examines how partisan content from national cable news channels impacts local reporting in U.S. newspapers. We introduce a novel machine-learning metric for assessing cable news bias, developed using a dataset of 40,000 transcribed episodes from Fox News Channel, CNN, and MSNBC between 2005 and 2008. When applied to a corpus of 24 million local newspaper articles, our findings reveal that an exogenous rise in local viewership of Fox News relative to CNN or MSNBC leads local articles to align more closely with Fox transcripts (and conversely). Aligning with the hypothesis that newspapers adapt to shifts in reader preferences, we observe a change in the framing of local news rather than mere direct copying of cable content. Additionally, cable news bias polarizes local reporting: right-leaning outlets increasingly adopt the language of right-wing Fox News, while left-leaning outlets shift further toward the left. Ultimately, media slant proves to be contagious.

This paper details our approach to SemEval 2020 Task 4, which focuses on commonsense validation and explanation. We introduce a new method for retrieving evidence and selecting various large-scale pre-trained models as the backbone for three subtasks. The findings indicate that our evidence-searching strategy enhances model performance on the commonsense explanation task, securing a 2nd place rank for our team in subtask C based on human evaluation scores.

Building an ensemble from diverse unsupervised anomaly detection methods is difficult due to the absence of class labels or ground truth, which renders traditional ensemble strategies relying on response variables inapplicable. To address this, we employ Item Response Theory (IRT)—a modeling framework from educational psychometrics designed to evaluate student and question attributes—to create an unsupervised anomaly detection ensemble. The latent trait calculations inherent to IRT facilitate anomaly detection by revealing hidden ground truth. By applying a new IRT mapping to the anomaly detection domain, we develop an ensemble capable of diminishing the influence of noisy, non-discriminatory methods while highlighting more effective ones. We validate the efficacy of this IRT-based ensemble across a vast data repository, contrasting its performance against other ensemble approaches.

The observation of interference in increasingly massive objects offers striking validation for quantum theory. While this phenomenon is typically interpreted as evidence for "wave-particle duality" and, by extension, "complementarity," we begin by outlining the historical evolution of these concepts. This review reveals that they lack rigorous definitions and serve primarily as heuristic tools. We then examine recent interference experiments involving large, complex molecules, which appear to reinforce the heuristic utility of "duality." However, we demonstrate that in these experiments, the diffraction of a {\em delocalized} center-of-mass wave function relies on the interaction between the molecule's {\em localized} structure and the diffraction apparatus. Consequently, the molecules exhibit "dual features" simultaneously, contradicting the conventional interpretation of wave-particle duality. We conclude that the concept of "wave-particle duality" has no legitimate place in contemporary quantum physics.

We introduce a second quantization framework for frequency-based continuous-variable quantum computation within the single-photon subspace. By defining frequency and time operators via the free field Hamiltonian and its Fourier transform, we demonstrate that, when confined to the one-photon-per-mode subspace, these observables satisfy canonical position-momentum commutation relations. Consequently, frequency and time operators enable the construction of a universal gate set for this specific subspace. We examine the physical realization of these gates and their impact on single-photon states, further illustrating that frequency and time variables can facilitate continuous-variable quantum information protocols, analogous to how polarization serves as a two-dimensional quantum degree of freedom.

In an earlier work, we presented several moduli stacks corresponding to two-dimensional tamely potentially Barsotti-Tate representations of the absolute Galois group of a p-adic local field, along with associated stacks of Breuil-Kisin modules featuring descent data. This paper examines the irreducible components of these stacks, specifically demonstrating that the components of the representation stacks are naturally classified by particular Serre weights.

Prosopography examines the shared traits of historical groups by collectively analyzing their biographies to address historical questions; when full biographies are missing, it relies on extant documents and secondary data. Quantitative prosopography specifically analyzes information regarding "ordinary people" drawn from diverse sources. This paper introduces a machine learning framework designed to automatically construct a people gazetteer, which serves as the foundation for quantitative prosopographical studies. This gazetteer is trained on noisy newspaper text using a Named Entity Recognizer (NER) and identifies influential individuals via a custom Influential Person Index (IPI). The study's corpus consists of 14,020 articles from the 1896 New York local newspaper, "The Sun." Notable figures detected by the algorithm include Captain Donald Hankey (English soldier), Dame Nellie Melba (Australian soprano), Hugh Allan (Canadian shipping magnate), and Sir Hugh John McDonald (Canada's first Prime Minister).

This study examines two-particle binding factors for the \ch{H2} molecule using our proprietary Exact Diagonalization \textit{Ab Initio} (EDABI) method. Specifically, we reformulate many-particle covalency and ionicity factors as functions of interatomic separation. We highlight the limitations of these fundamental descriptors and introduce the concept of \textit{atomicity}, which aligns with Mott and Hubbard criteria regarding localization in many-particle systems. This new metric incorporates an atomic component into inherently molecular states, thereby correcting the unphysical behavior of the standard covalency factor at large interatomic distances and offering a physically grounded reinterpretation of the chemical bond.

This letter introduces a protocol for quantizing nonlinear transport within two-dimensional ultracold atomic Fermi gases confined by a harmonic trap. The proposed method involves sequentially applying two optical pulses in the left and lower half-planes, followed by counting the excess atoms in the first quadrant. Under ideal conditions, the nonlinear density response to these successive pulses becomes quantized, with the quantization value reflecting the Euler characteristic of the local Fermi sea at the trap's center. We examine practical experimental factors—such as finite pulse duration, limited pulse edge width, and finite temperature—that may cause deviations from perfect quantization. To mitigate these deviations, we suggest averaging measurements taken in both the first and third quadrants, a strategy grounded in symmetry principles. Employing this approach allows for the observation of quantized nonlinear responses under experimental conditions easily achievable with ultracold atoms.

This paper introduces a new method for creating dual controllers designed for unknown linear time-invariant systems, aiming to minimize a quadratic cost function while simultaneously reducing uncertainty. The proposed synthesis problem requires the feedback law to concurrently acquire knowledge of the system dynamics and robustly optimize the cost. By modeling the scenario within a finite horizon framework, the optimization problem formally captures the trade-offs inherent in tasks that involve both identification and control. The results demonstrate that leveraging the problem's structure leads to efficient exploration strategies.

We derive mean-field bounds for the critical exponents of the Poisson-Boolean continuum percolation model under a moment condition on the radii, specifically $\gamma \ge 1$, $\delta \ge 2$, and $\triangle \ge 2$. While these bounds were previously established only for fixed radii in the case of $\gamma$ or remained unknown for $\delta$ and $\triangle$, we obtain them as direct consequences of the recent mean-field bound $\beta \le 1$ by Duminil-Copin, Raoufi, and Tassion, which also relies on the same moment condition, utilizing a relative entropy method developed by the authors in earlier research.

Facial Action Unit (FAU) intensities are commonly used to analyze facial behavior, yet they often suffer from sparse representation when only a limited number of units are active simultaneously. This study investigates the feasibility of modeling facial expression dynamics by adapting algorithms typically employed in natural language processing for word representation. Specifically, we cluster a large-scale dataset containing 5.3 million temporal facial expression frames prior to applying the Global Vector (GloVe) algorithm to generate embeddings for these facial clusters. We assess the utility of these learned representations on two downstream tasks: estimating schizophrenia symptoms and regressing depression severity. The experimental findings demonstrate the potential effectiveness of this approach in enhancing the assessment of mental health symptoms compared to baseline models that rely solely on FAU intensities.

Comprehending the dynamics of outbreaks such as COVID-19 is essential for formulating effective control strategies. This research introduces an agent-based model designed to simulate infection progression by adjusting various parameters within a synthetic population. The model incorporates individual attributes—including age, gender, and employment status—as well as other factors influencing disease spread. By varying the number of infection epicenters, the location of initial cases, detection sensitivity, the proportion of asymptomatic individuals, and the frequency or duration of lockdowns, the simulator tracks every person to map the community's infection trajectory over time.

In a closed community of 10,000 residents, the model reveals that without intervention, cases peak around the sixth week and subside by the fifteenth. However, if the primary case originates in a dense cluster like a slum, the peak occurs earlier and the decline is slower. Implementing a lockdown slows the rate at which cases peak. Furthermore, reduced sensitivity in identifying infections leads to higher case and death counts, whereas an increased proportion of asymptomatic cases correlates with a decline in total cases. The model demonstrates robustness and reproducibility with realistic parameters, offering guidance for controlling outbreaks. It is highly flexible, accommodating diverse variables such as the infectious period, testing yield, socio-economic status, travel patterns, awareness levels, population density, social distancing, and lockdown measures, allowing it to be adapted for studying other infections with similar transmission dynamics.

Accurately estimating weather forecast uncertainty using ensemble systems demands a meticulous selection of perturbations to reliably sample error growth potential within the model's phase space. Traditionally, singular vectors from the tangent linear model propagator are employed to pinpoint the fastest-growing modes via the classical singular vector (SV) method. This paper introduces a computationally efficient, matrix-free block Krylov approach for generating rapid-growth perturbations in high-dimensional dynamical systems. We define a specific matrix, the Evolved Increment Matrix (EIM), which captures the non-linear evolution of perturbations. Rather than solving an equivalent eigenvalue problem, we apply the Arnoldi method to directly approximate the leading singular vectors of the EIM without explicitly computing the matrix itself. This strategy eliminates the need for linear and adjoint models but necessitates forecasts utilizing the complete non-linear system. We evaluate the performance of these approximated perturbations against the singular vectors of a fully computed EIM, rather than comparing them to the classical SV method. Promising outcomes are demonstrated for both the Lorenz96 differential equations and a shallow water model, where a small number of Arnoldi iterations yield robust approximations of the fastest-growing perturbations.

We introduce Fast text2StyleGAN, a natural language interface designed to adapt pre-trained Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for synthesizing human faces guided by text. By utilizing recent advancements in Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP), our approach eliminates the need for text data during the training phase. Formulated as a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE), the model enhances control and diversity in generated images at test time without requiring re-training or fine-tuning of the underlying GANs or CLIP for new text prompts. Unlike previous methods, Fast text2StyleGAN avoids test-time optimization, resulting in a speed improvement of orders of magnitude. Empirical evaluations on the FFHQ dataset demonstrate that our method achieves faster and more accurate image generation from natural language descriptions of varying detail levels compared to existing approaches.

The LHC can access vast, uncharted kinematic regions through fixed-target collisions of $pp$, $pA$, and $PbA$ at center-of-mass energies ranging from 72 to 115 GeV. Designed as a fully instrumented forward spectrometer capable of fixed-target operations, the LHCb detector currently houses a gas cell target for data collection during Run 3. The LHCspin initiative seeks to expand this physics agenda into Run 4 and introduce polarized physics at the LHC. This document provides an overview of the project's physics potential along with a description of the LHCspin experimental configuration.

We demonstrate that nonextensive entropy can induce spontaneous symmetry breaking when a parameter shifts from a value associated with a symmetric domain, mirroring phenomena in field theory. We provide the underlying physical rationale and further illustrate that even with symmetric Dirichlet priors, this specific entropy definition combined with a particular parameter value can result in asymmetry upon entropy maximization.

This paper presents h(x)-Fibonacci polynomials within an arbitrary finite-dimensional unitary algebra over a field K (where K is either R or C), extending the concepts of h(x)-Fibonacci quaternion and octonion polynomials. For these polynomials in such algebras, we establish a summation formula, a generating function, a Binet-style formula, a Catalan-style identity, and a d'Ocagne-type identity.

This study investigates disorder and interaction effects on Bogoliubov-Fermi surfaces within a low-energy effective model coupled to bosonic degrees of freedom, assuming preserved inversion symmetry. It demonstrates that non-ideal Bogoliubov quasiparticles (bogolons) typically generate an odd-frequency pair amplitude, indicating Cooper pairing across different times. In the low-frequency limit, bogolon self-energy is predominantly driven by disorder effects, mirroring behavior in standard electron liquids. Depending on specific parameter choices, two distinct solutions emerge: one frequency-independent (though incorporating a frequency sign function) and another proportional to the inverse frequency, both present in the normal and anomalous self-energy components. These distinctive self-energy patterns are distinctly observable in the single-particle spectrum. Furthermore, since bogolons originate from electrons, the connection between them is explored using a concrete $j=3/2$ fermion model, revealing that the odd-frequency pairing of bogolons primarily consists of the odd-frequency pairing of electrons.

This research explores diversity-aware clustering, a variation of classical clustering focused on algorithmic fairness. The problem involves selecting facility subsets such that each predefined group contributes a minimum number of facilities, all while minimizing the cost of a $k$-median or $k$-means objective. We analyze the fixed-parameter tractability of these challenges, demonstrating significant hardness and inapproximability results that persist even when exponential time is permitted relative to certain parameters. Guided by these findings, we define natural problem parameters and develop fixed-parameter approximation algorithms achieving ratios of $\big(1 + \frac{2}{e} +\epsilon \big)$ for diversity-aware $k$-median and $\big(1 + \frac{8}{e}+ \epsilon \big)$ for diversity-aware $k$-means, arguing these bounds are essentially optimal under the gap-exponential time hypothesis. Additionally, we introduce a straightforward, more practical bicriteria approximation algorithm with superior runtime efficiency and propose efficient heuristics. Finally, through rigorous experiments on both real and synthetic datasets, we assess the scalability and effectiveness of our proposed methods.

This paper introduces a sample-based method for deriving straightforward and computable approximations of chance-constrained sets. By defining families of simple-approximating sets with specified complexity levels, the procedure enables control over the resulting set's complexity. A subsequent probabilistic scaling step adjusts these sets to meet desired probabilistic guarantees. The authors demonstrate the approach's applicability across various systems and control problems, including the development of Stochastic Model Predictive Control strategies and the resolution of probabilistic set membership estimation tasks.

The rapid proliferation of Machine Learning (ML) solutions has outpaced the ability to process their associated algorithms and data, leading to a surge in interest regarding Algorithm Recommendation (AR). AR is increasingly treated as a learning task, specifically a Meta-Learning problem aimed at identifying the optimal algorithm for a given dataset. This approach typically involves using ML to learn the mapping between datasets encoded with meta-features and the most suitable techniques. A primary challenge in this domain is selecting the most valuable features, as the abundance of available meta-features can lead to high dimensionality. This paper provides an empirical analysis of feature selection and extraction at the meta-level for AR, evaluating three key criteria: predictive performance, dimensionality reduction, and pipeline runtime. The findings indicate that while Dimensionality Reduction (DR) methods generally do not enhance predictive performance, they successfully reduce the number of meta-features by approximately 80% while maintaining performance levels similar to the original setup, albeit with significantly lower runtimes. The sole exception was Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which exhibited runtimes comparable to the full meta-feature set. Furthermore, experiments revealed that many datasets contain numerous non-informative meta-features, demonstrating that high predictive performance can be achieved using only about 20% of the original features. Consequently, given the inherent tendency of meta-features toward high dimensionality, DR methods are recommended for both meta-feature selection and extraction.

This study employs a direct approach to derive the longitudinal structure function at the next-to-leading order in the number of active flavors, utilizing parton distribution parametrizations. Specifically, it accounts for the contributions of charm and bottom quarks associated with the gluon distributions defined at $n_{f}=3$ and $n_{f}=5$. The resulting longitudinal structure function for $n_{f}=4$ is compared against H1 experimental data [Eur.Phys.J.C{\bf74}, 2814(2014) and Eur.Phys.J.C{\bf71}, 1579 (2011)], the findings of L.P.Kaptari et al. [Phys.Rev.D{\bf 99}, 096019(2019)] derived via Mellin transforms, and the CT18 [Phys.Rev.D103, 014013(2021)] parametrization model. The analysis demonstrates that nonlinear effects within the gluon distribution enhance the agreement of the longitudinal structure function with both the H1 data and CT18 results at low $Q^{2}$ values.

Conventional approaches to diagnosing autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are often costly, subjective, and labor-intensive, frequently delaying confirmation until adolescence or adulthood. Recently, graph-based learning methods have shown significant promise when applied to resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) data from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE). This paper presents IMAGIN, a multI-granular, Multi-Atlas spatio-temporal attention Graph Isomorphism Network designed to model dynamic functional brain connectivity (chronnectome) rather than static patterns (connectome). Experimental findings indicate that IMAGIN reaches a 5-fold cross-validation accuracy of 79.25%, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods by 1.5%. Furthermore, the analysis of spatial and temporal attention scores offers additional support for the neural mechanisms underlying autism.

We present a novel graphical bilinear bandit framework wherein a learner assigns arms to graph nodes, observing noisy bilinear rewards for each edge that reflect the interaction between connected nodes. Focusing on the best arm identification task, our goal is to determine the node allocation that maximizes the total bilinear reward. By leveraging the geometric properties of this bandit setting, we develop a \emph{decentralized} allocation strategy utilizing random sampling, complete with theoretical assurances. Specifically, we analyze how graph topology—such as star, complete, or circular structures—affects the convergence rate and conduct empirical studies that validate this relationship.

Let $B_E$ represent the open unit ball within a complex Hilbert space, whether finite or infinite dimensional. For a function $f$ in the Bloch space $\mathcal{B}(B_E)$, we demonstrate that the dilation map defined by $x \mapsto (1-\|x\|^2) \mathcal{R} f(x)$ is Lipschitz continuous with respect to the pseudohyperbolic distance $\rho_E$ in $B_E$, where $\mathcal{R} f$ is the radial derivative of $f$. This finding generalizes the known result for the classical Bloch space $\mathcal{B}$ to higher dimensions. To establish this, we first prove that $\rho_E(zx, zy) \leq |z| \rho_E(x,y)$ for $x,y \in B_E$, subject to specific constraints on $z \in \mathbb{C}$. The resulting Lipschitz continuity yields several applications that extend classical theorems from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{B}(B_E)$. Specifically, we address interpolating sequences for $\mathcal{B}(B_E)$ by showing that separation is a necessary condition for a sequence in $B_E$ to be interpolating, and we prove that any such sequence can be slightly perturbed while retaining its interpolating property. Furthermore, following an in-depth analysis of the automorphisms of $B_E$, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for a composition operator on $\mathcal{B}(B_E)$ to be bounded below.

Network interactions are commonly modeled as networks, with the latent position model being a prevalent tool that situates actors within a latent space. However, determining the appropriate dimensionality of this space remains difficult; while researchers often default to two dimensions or rely on model selection criteria, these approaches entail selecting a specific criterion and the computational cost of fitting multiple models. To address this, the Latent Shrinkage Position Model (LSPM) is introduced, which automatically infers the effective dimension of the latent space. By utilizing a Bayesian nonparametric multiplicative truncated gamma process prior, the LSPM ensures that variance in latent positions shrinks across higher dimensions. Consequently, dimensions exhibiting non-negligible variance are identified as most relevant for describing the network, enabling automatic dimension inference. Although the LSPM is broadly applicable, this study specifically develops logistic and Poisson variants for binary and count networks, respectively. Inference is conducted using a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm enhanced by novel surrogate proposal distributions to minimize computational demands. The model's properties are validated through simulations and demonstrated on real-world network data, with open-source software provided to facilitate broader adoption.

How do shared objectives influence the language used by intelligent agents? We investigate the learning dynamics within Latent Language Policies (LLPs), where instructor agents formulate natural-language subgoals and executor agents translate these into low-level actions. While LLPs effectively tackle difficult long-horizon reinforcement learning tasks and offer a robust framework for examining task-oriented language, prior research indicates that training LLPs is susceptible to semantic drift, where messages diverge from their original meanings. In this work, we theoretically and empirically demonstrate that multitask training serves as an effective solution to this issue. We prove that multitask training eradicates semantic drift in established signaling game families and show that applying this approach to neural LLPs in a complex strategy game significantly reduces drift while enhancing sample efficiency.

This study employs a hedonic regression model to identify the determinants of residential property prices in Boulder, Colorado. Given that urban housing markets are complex and not homogeneous, market segmentation is necessary. To determine whether properties in Boulder should be analyzed or predicted at an aggregate or disaggregate level, we stratified the housing market by property type and location, estimating separate hedonic price models for each submarket. The findings reveal that the implicit values of property characteristics vary across different property types and locations in Boulder, confirming the existence of market segmentation.

This research examines a discrete dynamical system within the class of contour systems introduced by A.P. Buslaev, featuring two closed contours. Each contour comprises $n$ cells and hosts a cluster—a group of particles occupying adjacent cells that move in unison. At every discrete time step, each particle advances to an adjacent cell along its path of motion. The contours intersect at two nodes, where clusters experience delays because two particles cannot occupy the same node simultaneously. While previous studies of this system assumed a constant number of particles per cluster, this paper investigates a scenario where cluster lengths vary. The study derives analytical results regarding the system's limit cycles and the spectrum of average cluster velocities.

Simulating flow in fractured porous media typically results in extensive systems of linear equations, necessitating specialized solvers. This study introduces an efficient linear solver and its practical application for mixed-dimensional scalar elliptic problems. We propose a robust preconditioner utilizing approximate block factorization combined with algebraic multigrid methods. Numerical experiments on benchmarks featuring intricate fracture networks confirm the solver's efficacy and its stability across varying physical and discretization parameters.

This work utilizes Heegaard Floer homology techniques to characterize the topological attributes of complex curves within the complex projective plane. Specifically, we settle an open conjecture regarding the Alexander polynomial of the link associated with the singular point of such a curve, under the conditions that the curve has genus 0, the link is connected, and there is precisely one singular point. Furthermore, these results extend to scenarios involving multiple singular points.

Topological Insulators (TIs) hold great promise for diverse applications, particularly due to the robust surface and edge states found in both three-dimensional (3D) and two-dimensional (2D) regimes. While the conducting surface states in 3D systems create an "electron bath" known to support catalysis, the analogous effects in 2D scenarios—where conducting helical edge states lead to Fermionic accumulation—have been rarely explored. Using density functional theory-based first-principles calculations, we show that the conducting edge states in 2D TIs, such as LiMgAs, can effectively enhance catalytic performance for the hydrogen evolution reaction. In these cases, the Gibbs free energy reaches a remarkably low value of $-$0.02 eV, outperforming other materials reported in the literature. This approach can be generalized to other established 2D TIs to develop novel topological quantum catalysts capable of ultra-high efficiency and performance.

End-to-end automatic speech recognition has reached high accuracy through increasingly deep architectures; however, the expanded receptive field associated with greater depth can degrade performance in streaming contexts. We introduce an alternative method termed the Neural Mixture Model, which substitutes a single deep network with a parallel ensemble of shallow networks. To test this concept, we developed CarneliNet, a CTC-based architecture featuring three mega-blocks, where each block comprises multiple shallow sub-networks utilizing 1D depthwise-separable convolutions. Evaluations on the LibriSpeech, MLS, and AISHELL-2 datasets demonstrate that our model achieves performance comparable to the state-of-the-art for CTC-based systems. Furthermore, we show that the number of parallel sub-networks can be dynamically adjusted to meet computational demands without the need for retraining.

Superconformal blocks and crossing symmetry equations are fundamental components of superconformal field theories. We present a review of the methodology based on harmonic analysis on the superconformal group, originally introduced in [J. High Energy Phys. 2020 (2020), no. 1, 159, 40 pages, arXiv:1904.04852] and [J. High Energy Phys. 2020 (2020), no. 10, 147, 44 pages, arXiv:2005.13547]. By elevating conformal four-point functions to functions defined on the superconformal group, we demonstrate how to derive compact forms for Casimir equations and crossing constraints. These equations facilitate the expression of superconformal blocks as finite sums of spinning bosonic blocks.

Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) have gained significant interest recently because their controllable scattering elements can steer electromagnetic waves toward desired directions. While RISs share certain characteristics with relays, they also possess fundamental differences that affect their performance. This paper proposes a multi-user communication system where a relay and an RIS cooperate to enhance energy efficiency. To maximize RIS utility, the discrete phase shifts of its elements are optimized alongside the beamforming matrices at the transmitter and relay, aiming to minimize total transmit power under a quality-of-service (QoS) constraint. Two efficient suboptimal solutions are developed for the resulting non-convex, discrete optimization problem: one leveraging singular value decomposition (SVD) and uplink-downlink duality, and the other combining SVD with zero-forcing. Simulation results demonstrate that these proposed solutions outperform systems using only a relay or only an RIS, particularly when both devices are located closer to the users than to the base station.

Computer Algebra Systems, such as Cadabra Software, are vital to various research endeavors in physics and associated domains. We demonstrate the straightforward integration of the Cadabra language within the mature Python ecosystem, achieving superior flexibility and customization to tackle tensor perturbations in General Relativity. Our approach yields an efficient algorithm capable of decomposing tensorial quantities up to arbitrary perturbative orders of the metric. The capabilities of this code are validated through an analysis of specific computational challenges arising in research concerning first- and higher-order gravitational waves.

Kidney transplants in the United States face severe demand shortages. A recent innovation to mitigate this is the kidney exchange, where medically incompatible patient-donor pairs swap donors to enable successful transplants. While proposed matching rules often focus on static fairness for specific groups, such as highly-sensitized patients, prioritizing time-critical pairs appears more intuitively fair in dynamic settings. This study examines the trade-off between established sensitization fairness and time fairness. We developed two algorithms, SENS and TIME, to evaluate patient loss and demonstrated a theoretical advantage to prioritizing time-critical patients, evidenced by an approximate 9.18% improvement on U.S. data compared to prioritizing sensitized patients. These findings indicate that time fairness must be integrated into kidney exchange protocols. Furthermore, we propose a batching algorithm for existing branch-and-price solvers that balances both fairness requirements.

Introduced in 2010 by V. Futorny and S. Ovsienko, Galois orders constitute a category of associative algebras encompassing significant examples such as the enveloping algebra of $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ (along with its quantum deformation), generalized Weyl algebras, and shifted Yangians. These structures were developed to facilitate the study of specific infinite-dimensional irreducible representations known as Gelfand-Tsetlin modules. In 2017, J. Hartwig defined Principal Galois orders as a subset of Galois orders possessing an additional property that streamlines their analysis; notably, all previously cited examples fall into this category. Subsequently, in 2019, B. Webster introduced principal flag orders, which are generally Morita equivalent to principal Galois orders and offer an even more simplified framework for investigation. This paper outlines methodologies for linking pairs of standard flag and Galois orders with corresponding data. These techniques include establishing sufficient conditions for morphisms between these order types, identifying properties of flag orders concerning differential operators on affine varieties, and constructing tensor products of standard, principal flag, and Galois orders.

Building on the methods of De, Mossel, and Neeman [FOCS, 2019], we present two distinct findings regarding the tolerant testing of juntas. With black-box access to a Boolean function $f:\{\pm1\}^{n} \to \{\pm1\}$, we introduce a query algorithm running in $poly(k, \frac{1}{\varepsilon})$ time that differentiates between functions $\gamma$-close to $k$-juntas and those $(\gamma+\varepsilon)$-far from $k'$-juntas, where $k' = O(\frac{k}{\varepsilon^2})$. In the non-relaxed scenario, we adapt our approach to achieve a $2^{\tilde{O}(\sqrt{k/\varepsilon})}$ (adaptive) query complexity for distinguishing functions $\gamma$-close to $k$-juntas from those $(\gamma+\varepsilon)$-far from $k$-juntas. As far as we are aware, this represents the first subexponential-in-$k$ algorithm for approximating the distance of $f$ to a $k$-junta, surpassing prior work by Blais, Canonne, Eden, Levi, and Ron [SODA, 2018] and De, Mossel, and Neeman [FOCS, 2019], which necessitated exponentially many queries in $k$. Our methodology relies on Fourier analysis and incorporates Talagrand's [AoP, 1994] concept of "normalized influences."

State and input constraints are fundamental challenges in control system design. Control Barrier Functions (CBF) have emerged as a recent solution, converting state constraints into input-space conditions. Consequently, CBF-based controllers integrate these conditions alongside input constraints within a quadratic program, but they are only well-defined when the CBF conditions are compatible. For perturbed systems, ensuring robust compatibility becomes critical. This paper presents an algorithmic approach to verify or disprove the compatibility (or robust compatibility) of specified CBFs before implementation. By utilizing the Lipschitz properties of the CBF conditions, we propose a grid sampling and refinement method supported by theoretical analysis and guarantees.

This article introduces four novel odd-magic-type colorings—odd-edge graceful-difference, odd-edge edge-difference, odd-edge edge-magic, and odd-edge felicitous-difference total coloring—to construct twin-graphic lattices for topological cryptography. We employ RANDOMLY-LEAF-ADDING algorithms that generate continuous graphs by appending random leaves, ensuring these structures admit the newly defined colorings. Furthermore, we utilize complex graphs to form caterpillar-graphic and complementary graphic lattices, where every graph within these lattices supports a uniformly $W$-magic total coloring. Investigating the relationship between graphic and integer lattices is presented as both a compelling research avenue and a critical application for the quantum computing era. Finally, we establish twin-type $W$-magic graphic lattices (distinguishing public from private variants) and $W$-magic graphic-lattice homomorphisms to generate more intricate topological number-based strings.

We theoretically and numerically demonstrate that for a linearly polarized electromagnetic plane wave normally incident on cylindrical passive scatterers, a single energy diagram can unify absorption, scattering, and extinction cross-sections for any scattering system, regardless of its internal structure, material properties, or dimensions. In systems with specific resonant orders, the boundary of the energy diagram requires both the magnitudes and phases of the scattering coefficients to be identical, a condition associated with superabsorption or superscattering. Furthermore, the energy diagram domain for systems with higher resonant orders can entirely encompass those with lower ones. Consequently, systems with different resonant orders can exhibit identical energy characteristics, illustrating an energy degeneracy in light scattering. This degeneracy offers greater flexibility in functional design applications, including energy harvesting, imaging, and sensing devices. We validate these findings by demonstrating various systems constructed from real materials.

Printing has gained significant interest as a cost-effective, high-throughput method for patterning graphene inks to manufacture scaled-up, thin-form-factor devices. However, conventional printing is limited to flat surfaces and cannot pattern 3D objects. In this study, we introduce a conformal printing approach to create functional graphene patterns on arbitrarily shaped surfaces. Through experimental design, we developed a water-insoluble graphene ink with optimized conductivity. We utilized standard screen printing to deposit single and multi-layered electrically functional structures onto a sacrificial layer. These prints were then floated on water to dissolve the sacrificial layer while preserving the functional patterns, enabling direct transfer onto 3D objects without any post-deposition processing. We demonstrated the conformal printing of single and multi-layer functional devices—including Joule heaters, resistive strain sensors, and proximity sensors—on diverse hard, flexible, and soft substrates such as glass, latex, thermoplastics, textiles, candies, and marshmallows. This straightforward strategy holds great promise for imparting new device and sensing capabilities to previously inert 3D surfaces.

Federated Learning (FL) allows multiple devices to collaboratively train a global neural network while retaining data locally. Unlike centralized training, FL faces non-IID, imbalanced, and distribution-shifted data across the network, leading to increased divergence between local and global models and degraded performance. This paper introduces FlexCFL, a flexible Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) framework that: 1) groups clients based on similar optimization directions to minimize training divergence; 2) employs an efficient cold-start mechanism for newcomers to ensure scalability and practicality; and 3) enables flexible client migration to address client-level distribution shifts. By decomposing joint optimization into sub-groups, FlexCFL improves performance while balancing accuracy and communication efficiency in distribution-shift scenarios. We analyze convergence and complexity to demonstrate its efficiency and evaluate it on several open datasets against related CFL frameworks. Results indicate that FlexCFL significantly boosts absolute test accuracy, achieving +10.6% over FedAvg on FEMNIST, +3.5% over FedProx on FashionMNIST, and +8.4% over FeSEM on MNIST. Furthermore, experimental results confirm that FlexCFL maintains communication efficiency even in distribution-shift environments.

During programming and debugging, developers frequently engage in "edit-run cycles" by repeatedly modifying and executing their code. Although live programming techniques aim to facilitate this workflow, the specific characteristics of these cycles remain largely unexplored. To address this, we examined 28 hours of work from 11 professional developers, covering over 3,000 development activities. By categorizing actions into edit or run steps, we identified 581 debugging cycles and 207 programming cycles. Our analysis reveals that these cycles occur frequently: developers average seven edit-run iterations to fix a defect and two to introduce one. Additionally, developers wait longer before re-running code during programming (mean cycle length: 3 minutes) compared to debugging (mean cycle length: 1 minute). The majority of cycles consist of editing a single file followed by a run to check output changes. However, cycles involving additional activities like file navigation, resource consultation, or IDE interaction are significantly longer, averaging 5 minutes versus 1.5 minutes for simple cycles. We conclude by offering design recommendations to enhance tool fluidity for these cycles.

We investigate the Gram determinant and establish bases for the hom spaces within Khovanov's recently formulated one-dimensional topological theory of decorated unoriented one-dimensional cobordisms, specifically in the case where the pair of generating functions is linear.

The disintegrating planet candidate K2-22 b exhibits periodic and stochastic transits that are best attributed to an escaping debris cloud, though the mechanism generating this cloud remains unidentified. Determining the grain size and sublimation rate of the debris offers crucial insights into the disintegration environment. Using the Large Binocular Telescope, we conducted simultaneous photometry in the g band (0.48 microns) and KS band (2.1 microns). During an event characterized by minimal dust activity, we established a new upper limit for the planet's radius at 0.71 Earth radii (4500 km). Additionally, we detected a medium-depth transit that helps constrain dust particle dimensions, revealing that the median particle size likely exceeds 0.5 to 1.0 microns, contingent on debris composition. These findings imply a high mass loss rate of approximately 3 × 10^8 kg/s, which aligns with hydrodynamic escape models; if driven by alternative mechanisms like explosive volcanism, such a rate would demand extraordinary geological activity. By combining our planetary size constraints with the high mass loss rate, we estimate the planet's lifetime to be under 370 million years, dropping to merely 21 million years if the 0.02 Earth masses predicted by hydrodynamical models are adopted.

Recent extensive research on Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers in diamond has enabled numerous NV-based applications, yet certain aspects of their energy levels and dynamic properties remain elusive. This study introduces a charge conversion pulsed sequence designed to identify the energy level of the NV center singlet manifold through multi-color excitation with a tunable laser. We evaluate two readout methods—photo-induced current and NV$^0$ population—and analyze their respective efficiencies across various regimes within the relevant spectrum.

This study examines how a vertical cylinder penetrates a dry granular medium under repeated impacts. The penetration depth, $z_N$, initially increases linearly with the number of impacts $N$ before transitioning to a power-law behavior proportional to $N^{1/3}$. Observations indicate that while the final depth grows with higher impact energy, it diminishes as the cylinder's diameter or the granular medium's density increases. We propose a model incorporating both quasi-static and inertial granular forces to explain these findings, identifying two distinct intrusion regimes for large and small impact counts that allow data to collapse onto a single master curve. Furthermore, we investigate the influence of sidewalls on the impactor's dynamics, demonstrating that lateral confinement alters the relationship between depth and impact number, $z_N(N)$. This modification is explained by the enhanced granular drag resulting from lateral confinement.

The art gallery problem seeks to determine the minimum number of guards required to fully secure a simple polygon $P$. While most standard formulations of this problem are NP-hard, Ghosh introduced a deterministic $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$-approximation algorithm for vertex and edge guards in simple polygons in 1987, simultaneously conjecturing that constant-ratio approximation algorithms also exist. This work presents three polynomial-time algorithms achieving constant approximation ratios for guarding an $n$-sided simple polygon $P$ with vertex guards: (i) an algorithm with a ratio of 18 that guards all vertices in $\mathcal{O}(n^4)$ time, (ii) another with a ratio of 18 that guards the entire boundary in $\mathcal{O}(n^5)$ time, and (iii) an algorithm with a ratio of 27 that covers all interior and boundary points in $\mathcal{O}(n^5)$ time. These methods can be adapted to achieve similar ratios using edge guards. These findings resolve Ghosh's 1987 conjecture regarding constant-factor approximations, a longstanding open problem despite numerous prior attempts. Additionally, the algorithms leverage intricate visibility structures inherent to simple polygons, which are of independent interest.

We re-examine the renormalizable polynomial inflection point model of inflation, specifically targeting the small-field regime, which allows for a complete analytical treatment. Notably, the model predicts a running spectral index given by $\alpha = -1.43 \times 10^{-3} +5.56 \times 10^{-5} \left(N_{\rm CMB}-65 \right)$, a prediction that may be verified in future studies. Furthermore, we investigate reheating mechanisms driven by perturbative inflaton decays into fermionic or bosonic states via trilinear interactions. While successful Big Bang nucleosynthesis imposes lower limits on these couplings based on the reheating temperature, radiative stability of the inflaton potential establishes corresponding upper limits. Combining these constraints yields a lower bound for the near-inflection point location $\phi_0$, specifically $\phi_0 > 3 \cdot 10^{-5}$ in Planck units. The inflationary Hubble parameter spans a wide range, from approximately $1$ MeV up to $\sim 10^{10}$ GeV. Likewise, the reheating temperature is bounded below by $\sim 4$ MeV and above by roughly $4 \cdot 10^8$ GeV for fermionic decays or $4 \cdot 10^{11}$ GeV for bosonic decays. Finally, we consider the "prehistory" of the universe within this framework, suggesting it could have featured an era of eternal inflation.

Code-switching refers to the phenomenon where a speaker alternates between languages within a conversation. Although this behavior naturally occurs in spontaneous spoken interactions, most current research relies on code-switching data derived from read speech rather than natural dialogue. ASCEND (A Spontaneous Chinese-English Dataset) addresses this gap by providing a high-quality corpus of Mandarin Chinese-English code-switching, sourced from spontaneous multi-turn conversations recorded in Hong Kong. This paper details ASCEND's design, data collection methodology, and annotation procedures. The dataset comprises 10.62 hours of clean audio from 23 bilingual speakers fluent in both Chinese and English. Additionally, we present baseline experiments utilizing pre-trained wav2vec 2.0 models, which achieved a best-case character error rate of 22.69% and a mixed error rate of 27.05%.

We characterize the expected maximum behavior within a random assignment process defined by a square matrix of independent entries. Given mild conditions on the base distribution, the solution is formulated using its quantile function.

In quantum field theory, the $i\epsilon$ prescription connects in and out states to the full Hamiltonian, and a subsequent Wick rotation transforms correlation functions into Euclidean spacetime for better-defined integrals, facilitating analytical work. However, applying an infinitesimal $\epsilon$ or performing a Wick rotation on numerical functions presents significant challenges. To address this, we introduce two novel numerical approaches: an Integral Basis method utilizing linear regression and a Beta Regulator method grounded in Cesàro/Riesz summation. Additionally, we incorporate a class of partition-extrapolation techniques previously employed in electromagnetic engineering. Benchmarking these new strategies against existing methods using in-in formalism integrals demonstrates their superior performance in both computational efficiency and accuracy.

Microtearing modes are extensively recognized as a plasma instability driven by the electron temperature gradient with tearing parity, causing fine-scale disruption of magnetic flux surfaces, reconnection of field lines, and the creation of magnetic islands. While prior research in slab geometry indicated that a finite collision frequency was necessary for the drive mechanism, our linear gyrokinetic simulations demonstrate that a collisionless, fine-scale tearing parity instability persists even at low or zero collision frequencies. In-depth analysis reveals that these slab modes are also fueled by the electron temperature gradient but are sensitive to electron finite Larmor radius effects; they exhibit a radial wavenumber significantly smaller than the binormal wavenumber, which is comparable to the ion Larmor radius. Notably, these modes exist within the electrostatic limit, where electromagnetic effects actually provide a stabilizing influence. An analytic model confirms that this collisionless small-scale tearing mode aligns with a tearing parity slab electron temperature gradient (ETG) mode, which can be more unstable than the frequently studied twisting parity ETG mode. Ultimately, this small-scale tearing parity mode can generate magnetic islands, thereby affecting turbulent transport in magnetized plasmas.

This study investigates collective modes in doped two-dimensional crystalline materials—specifically graphene, MoS$_2$, and phosphorene, across both monolayer and bilayer configurations—using density functional theory simulations combined with the random phase approximation. We employ an {\it ab initio} model incorporating material-realistic physical properties to determine the many-body dielectric functions. Following the calculation of electron energy loss, we analyze the collective modes for each system, distinguishing between in-phase and out-of-phase behaviors in bilayers. Additionally, due to complex band structures and interband transitions, we identify high-energy excitations within these systems. We argue that achieving realistic plasmon dispersions requires a material-specific dielectric function that accounts for crystalline polarizability, particularly in cases like MoS$_2$. Finally, we characterize the distinct collective modes found in each studied material and elucidate their physical origins.

This thesis explores both the strong and weak manifestations of the Banach-Tarski paradox, deriving them from the Hausdorff paradox. It offers contemporary proofs of these paradoxes alongside essential characteristics of equidecomposable and paradoxical sets. The work also examines the historical impact of the paradox on measure theory, including its erroneous attribution to Banach and Tarski. Furthermore, it analyzes the indispensable role of the axiom of choice, contrasting it with other axiomatic and topological conditions that permit such paradoxes.

Numerous partial identification issues involve determining the optimal value of a function defined over a set, where both the function and the set must be estimated from empirical data. Although progress has been made regarding convex scenarios, statistical inference for this broader context remains underdeveloped.
