Drawing on Green et al.'s abstraction of provenance semirings, where relation tuples are annotated with elements from a commutative semiring that propagate through positive RA operators, we propose an "annotator" extension. This extension maps each string to an annotated relation over spans. As a concrete instance, we examine weighted VSet-automata, which attach semiring values to transitions akin to weighted automata and transducers. We analyze critical expressiveness properties, such as closure under positive RA, and computational complexity issues, including the enumeration of ranked annotated answers for ordered semirings. For several of these challenges, fundamental semiring characteristics, particularly positivity, are essential for determining tractability.

Robust text recognition systems urgently demand vast quantities of labeled data. Yet, gathering handwriting samples across diverse styles and extensive lexicons is prohibitively costly. While data synthesis offers a viable solution to this data scarcity, significant challenges regarding style representation and content embedding in handwriting synthesis remain unresolved. To address these issues, we introduce SLOGAN, a novel Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) capable of synthesizing parameterized, controllable handwriting styles for arbitrary-length and out-of-vocabulary text. Our approach employs a style bank that encodes specific handwriting styles as latent vectors, serving as style priors for the generator to produce corresponding handwritten outputs. Notably, training this style bank relies solely on writer identification from source images, eliminating the need for attribute annotations. Additionally, text content is embedded by utilizing readily available printed style images, allowing flexible content diversity through input variation. The generator is further guided by dual discriminators to accurately capture both isolated character features and the flow of cursive connections. Consequently, SLOGAN can generate words outside the training vocabulary in various new styles. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method produces high-quality text images with significant style diversity and a rich vocabulary, ultimately enhancing the robustness of text recognizers.

This position paper examines the utility of rebellion and disobedience (RaD) within human-robot interaction (HRI). We identify two primary benefits of employing controlled and well-designed RaD: i) revealing insights into the efficacy of collaboration (or its absence) and ii) averting errors and correcting user actions when it serves the user's best interest. By utilizing handheld robots as a close interaction modality, we explore RaD use cases that offer applicability to other HRI scenarios.

Sampling-based Model Predictive Control (MPC) techniques, including Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI), have demonstrated significant potential across diverse robotic applications. However, these methods can generate infeasible trajectories if the sampled distributions cluster within high-cost or infeasible regions. To address this, we introduce log-MPPI, a novel approach utilizing an enhanced trajectory sampling distribution policy that markedly improves constraint satisfaction. The core innovation involves drawing trajectory samples from a normal log-normal (NLN) mixture distribution instead of a standard Gaussian distribution. Additionally, this study outlines a strategy for collision-free navigation in unknown, cluttered environments by integrating 2D occupancy grid maps directly into the sampling-based MPC optimization framework. We validate the efficiency and robustness of this control strategy through extensive simulations covering various cluttered 2D navigation scenarios and a cartpole swing-up task. Furthermore, real-world experiments confirm the applicability of log-MPPI for 2D grid-based collision avoidance in unknown environments, demonstrating its superiority over local costmap methods without increasing optimization complexity. Video demonstrations of both simulation and real-world results are available at https://youtu.be/_uGWQEFJSN0.

We demonstrate that the right ideal of a Novikov algebra, which is generated by the square of a right nilpotent subalgebra, is itself nilpotent. Additionally, we establish that a $G$-graded Novikov algebra $N$ over a field $K$ is solvable if its $0$-component $N_0$ is solvable, provided that $G$ is a finite additive abelian group and the characteristic of $K$ does not divide the order of $G$. Finally, we prove that any Novikov algebra $N$ possessing a finite solvable group of automorphisms $G$ is solvable whenever its algebra of invariants $N^G$ is solvable.

Attention mechanisms are extensively utilized in acoustic scene classification; however, our empirical observations indicate that they often discard valuable information despite enhancing performance. To address this, we introduce the attentive max feature map, which integrates attention with a max feature map to refine the attention process and alleviate information loss. Additionally, we investigate various joint training strategies, such as multi-task learning, which assign supplementary abstract labels to audio recordings. Our system achieves state-of-the-art results for single models on Subtask A of the DCASE 2020 challenge by employing these two techniques with a relatively compact parameter count. Moreover, the implementation of the proposed attentive max feature map enabled our team to secure fourth place in the DCASE 2021 challenge.

Predicting human actions is critical for applications like autonomous driving and human-robot collaboration. Yet, most current algorithms rely primarily on visual features, neglecting the extraction of spatial relationships between humans and their environment, as well as causal links within temporal action sequences. Since humans naturally excel at using spatial and causal reasoning to anticipate others' actions, we developed a Spatial and Causal Relationship based Graph Reasoning Network (SCR-Graph) to model these dynamics. This framework predicts actions by capturing action-scene interactions in the spatial domain and causal dependencies between actions in the temporal domain. In the spatial dimension, we implemented a hierarchical graph attention module that iteratively aggregates features from various scene elements across different levels. For the temporal dimension, we introduced a knowledge graph-based causal reasoning module that utilizes a Diffusion RNN to map past actions into temporal causal features. Furthermore, causality features are integrated into a heterogeneous graph as "shadow nodes," while a self-attention mechanism determines the optimal timing for activating knowledge graph information. Extensive experiments on the VIRAT dataset confirm the framework's superior performance.

Elegant Objects (EO) represents a variation of the object-oriented programming paradigm that emphasizes pure objects and decoration. Proposed by Bugayenko, the EO programming language serves as an intermediate representation for object-oriented programs. This paper offers plausible EO representations of certain class-based constructs found in Java, C++, and Python. It then reformulates the classical fragile base class problem within the context of these EO representations. Finally, the paper discusses an algorithm for identifying a subset of fragile base class patterns in EO programs. The authors demonstrate the viability of using EO as an intermediate language and explore potential enhancements to the language to facilitate more comprehensive static analysis.
These lecture notes outline the theory of QCD and its application using perturbation theory at particle colliders.

This study continues the work presented in [1]. Similar to the prior article, this paper outlines intriguing concepts and introduces numerous new theorems within the realm of plane geometry associated with them.

This study analyzes flux-integrated semiexclusive differential cross sections for charged-current quasielastic and neutral-current elastic neutrino scattering on argon. Calculations employ the relativistic distorted-wave impulse approximation, utilizing nucleon axial mass values of 1 GeV and 1.2 GeV. Additionally, elastic cross sections are computed varying the strange quark contributions to the neutral-current axial form factor. For the SBN experiment's near and far detectors, flux-integrated differential cross sections are evaluated as functions of reconstructed neutrino energy, incorporating short baseline neutrino oscillations within a 3+1 framework. The results indicate that the ratios of cross sections between the far and near detectors are dependent on oscillation parameters, making them suitable for investigating sterile neutrino oscillations.

We introduce the concept and term XV (eXtended meta/omni/uni/Verse) as a generalization and alternative to the widely recognized "metaverse," defining it essentially as shared or social Extended Reality (XR). Building on XR as a comprehensive umbrella term—where "X" represents any variable reality from the physical to the virtual or augmented—XV inherits this broad scope. Our framework begins with a foundational taxonomy of realities constructed from two primary elements: (1) physical reality (PR), composed of "atoms," and (2) virtual reality (VR), composed of "bits." XV expands this by integrating an extended society as a three-dimensional space, creating a taxonomy of "atoms" (physical), "bits" (virtual), and "genes" (social). This new field allows researchers operating in the intersection of VR, AR, and the metaverse to categorize their work within XV. XV encompasses the metaverse and extends beyond it to include shared perception across the entire spectrum of reality, such as infrared, ultraviolet, electromagnetic radio waves, sound, and electric currents. For instance, maintenance workers could collectively view a pump in real-time while overlaying the live waveform of its motor's rotating magnetic field. This presentation was delivered at the IEEE Standards Association event, "Behind and Beyond the Metaverse: XV (eXtended meta/uni/Verse)," on Thursday, December 8, 2022, from 2:15 to 3:30 PM EST.

A first-order phase transition occurring at the electroweak scale could generate gravitational waves detectable by future space-based observatories like LISA. Since the Standard Model does not predict such a transition, LISA offers a means to probe new physics by searching for a stochastic gravitational wave background. This study evaluates LISA's sensitivity to the thermodynamic parameters governing the stochastic background from a phase transition, employing the sound shell model to describe the gravitational wave power spectrum and the Fisher matrix to quantify uncertainties. We examine a parameter space defined by transition strengths $\alpha < 0.5$ and phase boundary velocities $0.4 < v_\text{w} < 0.9$, assuming transitions nucleate at $T_{\text{N}} = 100$ GeV with mean bubble separations of $0.1$ and $0.01$ Hubble lengths and a sound speed of $c/\sqrt{3}$. Our results demonstrate that the power spectrum within the sound shell model can be accurately approximated by a four-parameter double broken power law, with the peak power and frequency measurable to about 10% precision for signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) exceeding 20. Although degeneracies complicate the determination of underlying thermodynamic parameters, the phase boundary speed remains the most tightly constrained variable in all scenarios. Analysis of the Fisher matrix's principal components reveals that an SNR above 20 yields relative uncertainties below 3% for the two highest-order components, suggesting favorable prospects for parameter combinations; notably, the highest-order component is dominated by the wall speed. These sensitivity estimates serve as preliminary accuracy targets for theoretical calculations of thermodynamic parameters.

We introduce a framework for extensible lexicon development grounded in Lexical Conceptual Structure to aid in social engineering detection and the generation of appropriate responses. This approach utilizes core concepts of "ask" (the solicitation of specific behaviors, such as granting monetary access) and "framing" (the implied risk and reward associated with the ask). By refining our lexical organization, we demonstrate enhanced detection capabilities for asks and framings, showing that response generation quality improves correspondingly as detection performance increases. Ultimately, this paradigm offers a systematic and efficient method for adapting resources to achieve superior task-specific performance.

We provide deep near-infrared (NIR) imaging of Sh 2-209 (S209), a low-metallicity HII region within the Galaxy characterized by an oxygen abundance of [O/H] = -0.5 dex. By combining these NIR images with Gaia EDR3 astrometric data, we determine S209's distance to be 2.5 kpc. This proximity allows us to clearly resolve individual cluster members with separations of approximately 1000 AU, reaching a mass-detection limit of roughly 0.1 $M_\odot$. Consequently, we have identified two star-forming clusters within S209, each spanning scales of about 1 pc. Utilizing model luminosity functions, we derived the ages and underlying initial mass functions (IMFs) for both clusters. The resulting IMFs display slightly flatter high-mass slopes ($\Gamma \simeq -1.0$) than the Salpeter IMF ($\Gamma = -1.35$), and their break mass of $\simeq$0.1 $M_\odot$ is lower than the typical $\sim$0.3 $M_\odot$ observed in the solar neighborhood. Notably, because the main cluster in S209 contains significantly more members ($\sim$1500) than previous studies in similar environments ($\sim$100), this work enables the first high-accuracy derivation of the IMF in a low-metallicity setting across the broad mass range of 0.1--20 $M_\odot$.

We propose three adjustable parameters designed to enhance the fidelity of continuous-variable quantum teleportation within nonideal frameworks. Leveraging the characteristic function formalism, we establish the conditions under which teleportation fidelity remains invariant to the amplitude of input coherent states, regardless of the entangled resource employed. Subsequently, we analyze how these tunable parameters influence fidelity in the presence and absence of environmental noise and imperfect measurements, deriving analytical expressions for fidelity across three distinct input coherent state distributions. Our findings demonstrate that, for linear distributions, optimization utilizing all three parameters outperforms single- or two-parameter strategies. Ultimately, our results highlight the efficacy of tunable parameters in boosting teleportation fidelity and increasing resilience against decoherence.

Conducting a thorough literature review has long been a fundamental prerequisite for any significant research endeavor. However, the recent proliferation of vast amounts of information across both open-access and subscription-based databases in all disciplines has rendered it increasingly challenging, if not impossible, to guarantee the completeness of a literature survey. Consequently, reviewers may doubt the novelty of proposed research directions, regardless of the actual quality of the work. In this context, statistical analyses derived from published literature can offer valuable quantitative and visual insights into research trends, knowledge gaps, and collaborative networks within various fields. Our tool delivers an automated and efficient method for generating such insights to support systematic reviews across any research domain.

TORCH is a newly developed time-of-flight detector engineered to identify pions, kaons, and protons within a momentum range of 2–20 GeV/c across a 10-meter flight path. The detector utilizes a module featuring a 10mm thick quartz plate that generates Cherenkov photons; these photons travel via total internal reflection to one end, where they are focused onto an array of custom Micro-Channel Plate Photo-Multiplier Tubes (MCP-PMTs) to record position and arrival time. With a target single-photon time resolution of 70 ps, detecting approximately 30 photons per particle yields a time-of-flight resolution of 10–15 ps. A 1.25m prototype module incorporating two MCP-PMTs has been constructed and evaluated at the CERN PS using an 8 GeV/c charged hadron beam. The document details the module's construction, MCP-PMT characteristics, and readout electronics. Photon yield measurements and single-photon time resolutions were analyzed relative to particle entry points on the plate and compared with theoretical expectations, demonstrating that the TORCH prototype's performance aligns closely with the design objectives for the full-scale detector.

This study addresses the extraction of features from passive, multi-channel electroencephalogram (EEG) systems to support downstream inference regarding high-level mental states, including stress and cognitive load. Our approach utilizes recently developed multi-graph techniques applied to time-series graph structures derived from the statistical dependencies (such as correlations) among multiple sensors. Through three classification experiments, we compared our proposed features against traditional band power-based features, discovering that both sets provide complementary predictive value. Finally, we demonstrate that the significance of specific channels and channel pairs identified by our method holds neuroscientific validity in the context of classification.

This work establishes conditions ensuring that all eventually positive, increasing solutions to a half-linear delay differential equation are regularly varying, alongside deriving exact asymptotic formulas for these solutions. These findings are novel even within the linear context, and certain observations offer original insights applicable to non-functional equations as well. Additionally, a significant distinction between delayed and non-delayed cases regarding eventually positive decreasing solutions is highlighted.

I propose a revisionist view of Galileo's place in the history of science, arguing that he possessed limited mathematical aptitude, a deficiency that directly shaped his career. Specifically, his poor math skills explain his strong preference for experimentation and empiricism, as well as his rapid adoption of the telescope. Rather than representing a pioneering advance in scientific method, his reliance on practical, hands-on research was a compensatory strategy for a mind ill-suited to mathematical rigor. Similarly, his extensive writings on the fundamental principles of scientific method stemmed from his inability to contribute through mathematics, echoing the adage, "Those who can't do, teach." Ultimately, Galileo's vision of science was less original than traditionally believed; these ideas had long been accepted by mathematicians who, too occupied with advanced scientific work, did not feel the need to elaborate on them in philosophical prose.

Driven by practical scenarios like fast fashion retail and online advertising, the Multinomial Logit Bandit (MNL-bandit) has become a prominent model in online learning and operations research over the last ten years. Despite its popularity, the fundamental problem of pure exploration within the MNL-bandit framework has surprisingly received limited attention. This paper introduces efficient algorithms for pure exploration in the MNL-bandit setting, achieving instance-sensitive pull complexities. Furthermore, we establish an almost matching lower bound to complement the derived upper bounds.

We introduce a smoothening criterion for group actions on manifolds involving singular diffeomorphisms. Specifically, we demonstrate that for a countable group $\Gamma$ possessing the fixed point property FW for walls (such as groups with property (T)), every aperiodic action by $C^r$ diffeomorphisms with countably many singularities is conjugate to an action by genuine $C^r$ diffeomorphisms on a manifold that is homeomorphic, though potentially not diffeomorphic, to the original. As applications, we extend Navas's findings on Kazhdan group actions on the circle and recent resolutions to Zimmer's conjecture to encompass aperiodic actions defined by diffeomorphisms with countably many singularities.

To achieve successful measurements within constrained experimental timeframes, leveraging preliminary data efficiently is vital. This study demonstrates that a straightforward feedforward neural network approach for learning such initial data enables rapid simulation of experiments within the learned domain. This method is particularly advantageous for physical property measurements involving multi-axis scanning, where derivatives or integrations are necessary to derive the target quantity. Given its simplicity, the learning process is sufficiently swift to allow users to perform real-time learning and simulation by combining open-source optimization tools with deep-learning libraries. Consequently, this proposed tool aims to augment experimental data, assisting researchers in identifying optimal experimental conditions prior to conducting expensive real-world trials. Additionally, the tool facilitates the repurposing and reutilization of previously published data, thereby accelerating data-driven exploration of functional materials.

Time-resolved scattering techniques allow for the visualization of materials at the molecular level with femtosecond precision; however, within disordered media, they are restricted to a single radial dimension, thereby hindering the investigation of orientational dynamics and structure. This study presents a robust and practical theoretical framework designed to predict and interpret experiments that integrate optically induced anisotropy with time-resolved scattering. By combining impulsive nuclear Raman and ultrafast X-ray scattering data from chloroform with simulations, we demonstrate that this framework can precisely forecast and clarify both the spatial and temporal characteristics of such experiments.

Addressing information disclosure in databases with expansive conceptual schemas is a complex challenge, particularly when formulating ad-hoc queries. While current solutions include graphical interfaces, query-by-navigation, query-by-construction, and point-to-point queries, this article introduces the "spider query" mechanism as a crucial component for an accessible, computer-aided query formulation system within InfoAssisant. The core concept involves constructing a partial query comprising all data deemed relevant to a specific object type, resulting in a tree structure that expands across the conceptual schema—referred to as a "spider." Additionally, the paper outlines how this spider query mechanism integrates with existing methods such as query-by-navigation, query-by-construction, and point-to-point queries.

This work addresses finding the $\R$-minimizing solution to the ill-posed equation $Ax = y$, where $A$ is a bounded linear operator mapping from a Banach space $X$ to a Hilbert space $Y$, and $\R: X \to (-\infty, \infty]$ is a strongly convex function. A dual gradient flow method is introduced to approximate this solution using noisy data. Given the ill-posed nature of the problem, the flow exhibits semi-convergence, necessitating a carefully selected stopping time to obtain reasonable approximations. We examine various strategies for choosing this stopping time, including {\it a priori} rules, the discrepancy principle, and the heuristic discrepancy principle, and derive corresponding convergence results. Additionally, convergence rates are established under variational source conditions regarding the target solution. Finally, numerical experiments are presented to evaluate the performance of the proposed dual gradient flow.

We introduce an algebraic framework that characterizes the complexity classes Logspace and Nlogspace, utilizing an algebraic structure with a composition law derived from unification. This novel connection between unification and complexity theory stems from proof theory, particularly linear logic and the geometry of interaction. We demonstrate how to construct a computational model within this unification algebra and, through a syntactic representation of finite permutations, establish that determining whether a program (represented algebraically as an observation) accepts a specific word can be performed within logarithmic space. Furthermore, we show that this construction inherently aligns with pointer machines, offering a practical perspective on logarithmic space computation.

This study introduces two innovative approaches for investigating temporal and morphological phenotypic changes induced by various experimental conditions through imaging data. As a proof of concept, these methods are applied to evaluate drug impacts on 2D cancer cell cultures. We develop a convolutional autoencoder trained on a dataset of one million images, utilizing random augmentations and multi-cropping, to serve as a feature extractor. This model is systematically benchmarked against pretrained state-of-the-art architectures. The feature extractor is leveraged in two distinct manners: first, by employing distance-based analysis and dynamic time warping to cluster the temporal patterns of 31 drugs, thereby categorizing them as cytotoxic, cytostatic, mixed, or non-effect; second, by implementing an adversarial/regularized learning framework to enhance drug classification and visualize the image regions driving these improvements. This approach yields an average 8% increase in top-3 classification accuracy and enables the extraction of morphological feature importance maps. We make the feature extractor and model weights publicly available to support transfer learning initiatives in biology. Additionally, we discuss the potential of other pretrained models and the broader applicability of our methodologies to diverse biomedical datasets.

Tsallis' thermostatistics has gained significant traction for its ability to describe phenomena exhibiting atypical thermodynamic characteristics. Within this framework, the generalized Saha equation must adhere to a condition of generalized thermal equilibrium between matter and radiation. This study investigates non-Gaussian impacts on Saha ionization using Tsallis statistics. To achieve this, we extended the number density formulation by incorporating a non-Gaussian Fermi-Dirac distribution and derived the Saha equation for cosmological recombination. Consequently, we identified two novel non-Gaussian effects: $i$) two distinct generalized chemical equilibrium conditions, applicable to relativistic and non-relativistic regimes respectively; and $ii$) the hydrogen binding $q$-energy. We demonstrated that producing smooth shifts in binding energy requires the $a$-parameter to be extremely small. Furthermore, we observed that the binding $q$-energy displays symmetrical behavior relative to the standard binding energy. Additionally, we utilized the $q$-energy to probe other hydrogen energy levels, determining the specific $a$-parameter values required to access these levels and their correlation with temperature. Finally, we applied these findings to analyze the non-Gaussian effects associated with the deuterium bottleneck, recombination, and the particle-antiparticle asymmetry.

This note investigates $\mathrm{ZHH}$ production within the all-hadronic final state during $\mathrm{e}^{+}\mathrm{e}^{-}$ collisions at the Compact Linear Collider operating at the 3 TeV energy level. At this stage, this specific Higgs pair production mode remains sub-dominant compared to the $\mathrm{W}^{+}\mathrm{W}^{-}$ fusion cross-section associated with $\mathrm{e}^{+}\mathrm{e}^{-}\rightarrow\mathrm{HH}\nu\nu$. The resulting events exhibit a six-jet topology, where the masses of three distinct pair-wise jet combinations align with the decay signatures of two Higgs bosons and one Z boson. The event selection strategy prioritizes the primary Higgs decay channel into two b-quarks by necessitating the detection of multiple b-jets. This analysis relies on complete simulations utilizing the CLICdet detector model, incorporating beam-induced backgrounds from $\gamma\gamma\rightarrow\mathrm{hadrons}$, and presents findings on the measurement of the total $\mathrm{ZHH}$ cross section.

Software security and privacy are frequently overlooked and seldom prioritized by developers. This prevailing insight largely stems from research focused on populations in the United States, Europe, and the United Kingdom. However, given the global nature of software production, significant technology hubs outside these regions remain inadequately studied. The Turkish software startup ecosystem is particularly influential, yet knowledge regarding security and privacy mitigation within this sector is underexplored. To address this gap, we conducted a semi-structured interview study involving 16 developers from Turkish startups to examine how they ensure software security and user privacy. Our primary finding indicates that developers rarely prioritize these aspects due to insufficient awareness, skills, and resources. We also observed that regulations can positively influence security and privacy practices. Consequently, we offer recommendations tailored for industry practitioners, individual developers, researchers, educators, and regulators. These insights aim to support a more globalized approach to securing software development.

This study aims to improve captions produced by image-caption generation systems. We introduce a method that enhances caption generation by selecting the output most semantically aligned with the image, instead of relying solely on the model's most probable predictions. Our approach revises the beam search process in language generation from a visual context standpoint. By utilizing a visual semantic metric at both the word and sentence levels, we ensure the selected caption accurately reflects the image's content. This post-processing technique can be integrated into any existing caption generation system.

Malicious actors can exploit image cropping to distort layouts and change an image's meaning. While prior detection methods merely identify if an image has been cropped without specifying the location, this paper introduces a novel Robust Watermarking Network (RWN) designed for precise crop localization. The approach involves training an Anti-Crop Processor (ACP) to embed an imperceptible watermark into a target image, which is then shared on social media. Upon receipt, the ACP extracts the watermark from the modified image, and feature matching against the original watermark pinpoints the cropping position within the source image plane. The framework is also extended to detect tampering attacks on the compromised image. Additionally, we propose an efficient JPEG-Mixup technique to enhance generalization in JPEG robustness. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that RWN achieves the first high-accuracy, robust image crop localization, while its tamper detection performance rivals many state-of-the-art passive methods.

Crowd counting has recently garnered significant attention, particularly regarding high-density environments where existing methods often fall short. To address this, we introduce a Multi-level Attentive Convolutional Neural Network (MLAttnCNN). This architecture extracts high-level contextual information by applying multiple scales through pooling and employs multi-level attention modules to enhance features across different layers, facilitating more efficient multi-scale feature fusion. Combined with dilated convolutions and $1\times 1$ convolutions, this approach generates highly accurate density maps. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that our proposed network outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches.

For any subset $A \subseteq \mathbb Z_n$, the $A$-weighted Gao constant $E_A(n)$ is defined as the minimal natural number $k$ such that every sequence of $k$ elements in $\mathbb Z_n$ contains a subsequence of length $n$ with an $A$-weighted sum equal to zero. Sequences of length $E_A(n)-1$ in $\mathbb Z_n$ that lack any $A$-weighted zero-sum subsequence of length $n$ are termed $A$-extremal sequences for the Gao constant. Specifically, a sequence containing $n-1$ zeroes is classified as being of the standard type. In cases where $A=U(n)$ (the set of units in $\mathbb Z_n$) and $n$ is odd, we identify all such sequences and demonstrate that they adhere to the standard type. Conversely, when $n$ is even, we provide examples of $A$-extremal sequences that do not follow the standard type. Furthermore, we characterize the $U(n)$-extremal sequences for the Gao constant when $n=2^rp$, where $p$ is an odd prime.

This study presents an algorithm designed to detect change-points and identify associated subsequences within transient multivariate time-series data (MTSD), a task gaining critical importance as data availability expands across various industrial sectors. Labeling, sorting, or filtering highly transient measurements for condition-based maintenance (CbM) training is often laborious and prone to errors. While simple thresholds or mean-value/variation change-point detection suffice for certain applications, they fail to provide robust diagnosis for components with complex non-linear correlations among multiple sensors, rendering the resulting data incoherent for CbM model training. To address this, we propose an algorithm utilizing an iteratively trained Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) based Autoencoder (AE). This approach employs a scoring function derived from reconstruction error and latent space information. The algorithm saves models of identified subsequences to facilitate the recognition of repeating patterns and enable efficient offline clustering. Furthermore, we introduce a novel curvature-based similarity measure to provide a more intuitive metric for clustering time-series subsequences. Evaluation against seven state-of-the-art algorithms across eight datasets demonstrates the proposed method's enhanced capability and performance for online and offline clustering of MTSD within mechatronic systems.

This report presents measurements of anisotropic flow coefficients, determined using two- and multi-particle cumulants for inclusive charged particles in Pb-Pb collisions at center-of-mass energies of $\sqrt{{\textit s}_\text{NN}} = 5.02$ and 2.76 TeV. The analysis covers the pseudorapidity interval $|\eta| < 0.8$ and transverse momentum range $0.2 < p_\text{T} < 50$ GeV/$c$. Data collected by the ALICE detector in 2015 (and 2010), corresponding to integrated luminosities of 12.7 (2.0) $\mu$b$^{-1}$ across the 0-80% centrality range, are utilized. Results include flow coefficients up to the sixth harmonic ($v_6$), accompanied by a detailed comparison between the two collision energies. The study investigates the transverse momentum dependence of these flow coefficients and their evolution with respect to centrality and harmonic number $n$. An approximate power-law scaling, $v_n(p_\text{T}) \sim p_\text{T}^{n/3}$, is observed for all flow harmonics at low $p_\text{T}$ ($0.2 < p_\text{T} < 3$ GeV/$c$). Simultaneously, the ratios $v_n/v_m^{n/m}$ are found to be largely independent of $p_\text{T}$ for most centralities up to approximately $p_\text{T} = 10$ GeV/$c$. By examining differences among higher-order cumulants of elliptic flow ($v_2$) with varying sensitivities to flow fluctuations, the standardized skewness of the event-by-event $v_2$ distribution $P(v_2)$ is measured, along with constraints on its higher moments. The Elliptic Power distribution parametrizes $P(v_2)$, with parameters extracted via fits to cumulants. Finally, these measurements are compared against various model predictions to distinguish between initial-state models and to constrain the temperature dependence of the shear viscosity to entropy-density ratio.

We introduce a novel algorithm for Promise Constraint Satisfaction Problems (PCSPs) known as CLAP, which integrates the Constraint Basic LP relaxation with the Affine IP relaxation. By characterizing CLAP's capabilities through a minion homomorphism, we define a specific, albeit weak, form of symmetry; if this symmetry holds for infinitely many polymorphisms of a PCSP, it ensures the problem is tractable. Furthermore, we show that CLAP solves certain PCSPs that no existing algorithms can handle, including the BLP+AIP method proposed by Brakensiek et al. [SICOMP'20] and approaches that reduce the problem to tractable finite-domain CSPs.

Casalbuoni and Gomis [1] introduced a conformally invariant model describing two interacting massless particles in Minkowski space. We extend this framework to de Sitter space by utilizing geodesic distance, ensuring the generalized action converges to the original formulation as the de Sitter radius approaches infinity. Following Dirac's prescription for constrained Hamiltonian systems, we analyze the Hamiltonian structure and perform canonical quantization in the coordinate representation using DeWitt's method. This process yields a fourth-order differential wave equation for bilocal fields, which correctly reproduces the equation derived for the Minkowski space case in the limit of an infinite radius.

This study presents the inaugural global QCD analysis that simultaneously incorporates spin-averaged and spin-dependent parton distribution functions (PDFs), utilizing single jet production data from both unpolarized and polarized hadron collisions. We rigorously evaluate how SU(3) flavor symmetry and PDF positivity constraints influence quark and gluon helicity PDFs, identifying significant biases—especially regarding gluon polarization—arising from these assumptions. Furthermore, this unified analysis enables, for the first time, the extraction of individual helicity-aligned and antialigned PDFs while maintaining a consistent approach to uncertainty treatment.

This paper introduces the spectral and scattering theory of the Casimir operator applied to the radial component of SL(2,R). Following an appropriate decomposition, the analysis focuses on a specific family of differential operators defined on a half-line. For these operators, we derive explicit formulas for the resolvent, spectral density, and Møller wave operators, all expressed using the Gauss hypergeometric function. Additionally, an index theorem is presented and examined; the associated equality connects diverse asymptotic behaviors of the hypergeometric function.

When a group $\Gamma$ acts geometrically on a CAT(0) space $X$ that lacks 3-flats, it follows that either $X$ possesses a $\Gamma$-periodic geodesic which fails to bound a flat half-plane, or $X$ is a rank 2 Riemannian symmetric space, a 2-dimensional Euclidean building, or non-trivially decomposes as a metric product. As a result, every such group fulfills a robust version of the Tits Alternative.

Nitrogen isotopic ratios found in primitive Solar System bodies exhibit a wide range of values, the origins of which are currently unclear. A primary inquiry concerns whether these nitrogen reservoirs formed before or after the stage of comet accretion, while another critical issue involves identifying the mechanisms responsible for the observed 14N/15N variations. Circumstellar disks around pre-main-sequence stars offer a unique vantage point to observe the chemical composition of protosolar nebula analogs, thereby aiding in the construction of a comprehensive model for nitrogen's origin in both planet-forming disks and the Solar System. This study presents spectrally and spatially resolved observations of the hyperfine structure of the 4-3 rotational transition of HCN, along with its main isotopologs H13CN and HC15N, within the disk surrounding the 8 Myr old T Tauri star TW Hya. The spatially averaged abundance ratios of HCN/H13CN and HCN/HC15N were determined to be 86 ± 4 and 223 ± 21, respectively. The latter figure is notably lower than the CN/C15N ratio of 323 ± 30 in this disk, marking the first evidence of two distinct nitrogen isotopic reservoirs existing in a disk during the epoch of giant planet and comet formation. Additionally, a clear radial gradient was detected, with the HCN/HC15N ratio increasing outward: it is 121 ± 11 at the comet formation zone (r = 20 au), approximately three times lower than the outer disk value of 339 ± 28. This outer disk ratio aligns excellently with direct measurements from the local interstellar medium and galactic evolution predictions. While this radial trend qualitatively supports a scenario where selective photodissociation of N2 is the dominant fractionation process, the measured isotopic ratios and kinetic temperatures of the HCN-emitting layers quantitatively conflict with existing disk nitrogen chemistry models.

Large language models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance across numerous tasks. However, training these models demands substantial computational resources. With an increasing number of open-source pre-trained models available, it is valuable to explore methods for maximizing their utility. We propose a technique to reduce both training time and resource costs by adapting smaller, well-trained models into larger ones. This is accomplished by initializing a larger target model using the weight values from a smaller source model, supplemented with zero-padding or small initialization values. This approach ensures that the source and target models produce similar outputs, leveraging the block matrix multiplication and residual connections inherent in transformer architectures. Experimental results on several datasets show that the target model performs comparably to the source model. Furthermore, when continued training is applied to the target model, the initial training loss begins from a lower value.

Private permissioned blockchains like Hyperledger Fabric are extensively adopted in the industry to streamline cross-organizational workflows and offer superior performance relative to public alternatives. Nevertheless, the absence of empirical and theoretical data hinders accurate forecasting of their real-world capabilities. This study bridges that gap by performing a comprehensive performance evaluation of Hyperledger Fabric. The paper offers a detailed synthesis of diverse performance metrics using an upgraded Distributed Ledger Performance Scan (DLPS) tool. These findings serve as practical guidelines for researchers and practitioners to optimize blockchain configuration and deployment, while also enabling the application of the DLPS framework for custom performance assessments.

Constructing matching costs is a fundamental component of light field (LF) depth estimation, yet it has been largely overlooked in recent deep learning research. Existing deep learning approaches typically generate these costs by sequentially shifting each sub-aperture image (SAI) across a set of predefined offsets, a process that is both intricate and computationally expensive. This paper introduces a streamlined and efficient cost constructor designed for LF depth estimation. Utilizing a sequence of convolutions with tailored dilation rates, our method integrates pixels corresponding to specific disparities directly from SAI arrays, eliminating the need for any shifting operations. Furthermore, the proposed constructor is occlusion-aware; it dynamically adjusts pixel contributions from various views to effectively manage occlusions. Leveraging this cost constructor, we developed a deep network for LF depth estimation that achieves the lowest mean square error (MSE) on the standard 4D LF benchmark and operates faster than other state-of-the-art techniques.

To achieve the realization of all possible KMS-bundles on the Jiang-Su algebra, we define a new class of C*-algebras termed rationally approximately finite dimensional (RAF). Leveraging this class, we demonstrate that for any proper simplex bundle $(S, \pi)$ where the fiber over zero is a singleton, and for a unital separable monotracial C*-algebra $A$ that absorbs the Jiang-Su algebra tensorially (such as the irrational rotation algebra), there exists a flow on $A$ such that its KMS-bundle is isomorphic to $(S, \pi)$.

This article investigates the local constancy of the mod $p$ reduction for specific $2$-dimensional crystalline representations of $\mathrm{Gal}\left(\bar{\mathbb{Q}}_p/\mathbb{Q}_p\right)$ via the mod $p$ local Langlands correspondence. By deriving an explicit lower bound for the local constancy radius around weights up to $(p-1)^{2} +3$ with slopes fixed in $(0, \ p-1)$ under certain constraints, we establish local constancy in the weight space. This bound is determined by explicitly calculating the mod $p$ reductions at neighboring weights and applying a local constancy result from Berger.

This study examines quasinormal modes (QNM) of a scalar field surrounding a noncommutative Schwarzschild black hole. We assess the impact of noncommutativity on quasinormal frequencies using two established techniques: the sixth-order Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin (WKB) approximation and the continuous fraction method proposed by Leaver. Furthermore, our results indicate that increasing the noncommutative parameter leads to a reduction in the shadow radius. Additionally, we observe that the shadow radius remains nonzero even in the zero mass limit, provided the noncommutative parameter is finite.

This paper introduces an extension to the $\texttt{matryoshka}$ suite of neural-network-based emulators, collectively named $\texttt{EFTEMU}$. Developed to accelerate Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure (EFTofLSS) analyses of galaxy power spectrum multipoles in redshift space, the $\texttt{EFTEMU}$ achieves prediction accuracies exceeding 99\% across scales of $0.001\ h\ \mathrm{Mpc}^{-1} \leq k \leq 0.19\ h\ \mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$, using BOSS-like bias parameters and counterterms. We conducted mock full-shape analyses to evaluate its performance in parameter inference, confirming that the $\texttt{EFTEMU}$ recovers true cosmological parameters within $1\sigma$ at redshifts $z=[0.38,0.51,0.61]$ and under various noise levels, including the most stringent Gaussian covariance for a $5000^3 \ \mathrm{Mpc}^3 \ h^{-3}$ volume. Comparisons with fully analytic EFTofLSS models reveal no significant bias while demonstrating a three-order-of-magnitude speedup in inference. The $\texttt{EFTEMU}$ is publicly accessible via the $\texttt{matryoshka}$ $\texttt{Python}$ package.

This paper investigates free mappings of the plane, defined as orientation-preserving, fixed-point-free homeomorphisms of $\mathbb{R}^2$. Utilizing Haefliger-Reeb theory regarding plane foliations, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for determining when two such free mappings, which are embedded in flows, are conjugate.

This paper addresses the control of a radially symmetric, friction-driven tripod robot. The device consists of a 3-D printed chassis with three servo motors positioned 7 cm from the center of mass and spaced 120 degrees apart. These motors actuate limbs that generate frictional reactive forces against the body. A mathematical model of the robot's motion, validated through experiments on a uniform friction surface, was utilized to develop a gait map enabling instantaneous omni-directional control. The system successfully demonstrated line-following capabilities using real-time data from an overhead tracking camera. On a rectangular course, a Proportional-Integral (PI) error compensation strategy was benchmarked against a standard position update method. The PI controller achieved a path error reduction of approximately 46%. Furthermore, this error compensator effectively mitigated aerodynamic disturbances caused by a high-volume industrial fan (with a mean flow speed of 5.5 m/s), lowering the path error by 65% compared to the basic position update approach.

In massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) architectures, hybrid analog-digital (AD) beamforming offers high directional gain without necessitating a radio frequency (RF) chain for every antenna element, thereby markedly lowering hardware expenses and power usage. Although massive MIMO transceiver design usually adheres to the conventional mean-square error (MSE) metric, directly minimizing the symbol error rate (SER) yields superior performance. This paper initially formulates the hybrid transceiver design problem under a minimum SER (MSER) criterion and subsequently develops an MSER-driven gradient descent (GD) iterative algorithm to identify stationary points. We then introduce a deep-unfolding neural network (NN) that unfolds the iterative GD process into a multi-layer architecture, incorporating trainable parameters to accelerate convergence and boost overall system performance. For the training phase, the inter-layer gradient relationship is derived using the generalized chain rule (GCR). The proposed deep-unfolding NN is applicable to both quadrature phase shift keying (QPSK) and $M$-ary quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) signals, with its convergence analyzed theoretically. Additionally, we examine the network's transfer capability, computational complexity, and generalization potential. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms conventional methods while maintaining reduced complexity.

This work introduces SeRP, a framework designed for the self-supervised learning of 3D point clouds. SeRP utilizes an encoder-decoder architecture that ingests perturbed or corrupted point clouds with the goal of reconstructing their original, uncorrupted forms. The encoder is tasked with learning high-level latent representations within a low-dimensional subspace to recover the underlying structure. For implementation, the study employs both Transformers and PointNet-based autoencoders. The framework specifically mitigates certain limitations found in Transformer-based Masked Autoencoders, such as location information leakage and uneven information density. Models were trained on the full ShapeNet dataset and subsequently evaluated on ModelNet40 for a downstream classification task. Results demonstrate that the pretrained models achieve classification accuracies 0.5% to 1% higher than networks trained from scratch. Additionally, the authors propose VASP, a Vector-Quantized Autoencoder for Self-supervised Representation Learning of Point Clouds, which leverages vector quantization to facilitate discrete representation learning within Transformer-based autoencoders.

This paper introduces a novel class of automorphisms for Leavitt path algebras associated with arbitrary graphs. As a result, we derive Anick-type automorphisms within these algebras and identify new irreducible representations for Leavitt algebras of type $(1, n)$.

Nonstationary Gaussian process models are capable of modeling intricate, spatially varying dependency patterns found in spatial data. Nevertheless, the sheer volume of observations in contemporary datasets renders fitting these models computationally infeasible using traditional dense linear algebra techniques. Furthermore, optimization approaches that lack derivatives or rely solely on first-order methods often struggle to converge efficiently when estimating numerous spatially varying parameters. This work introduces a computational framework that integrates an algebraic block-diagonal plus low-rank covariance matrix approximation with stochastic trace estimation. This approach enables the efficient application of second-order solvers for maximum likelihood estimation in Gaussian process models with many parameters. The efficacy of these methods is demonstrated by simultaneously estimating 192 parameters in the widely used Paciorek and Schervish nonstationary model using 107,600 sea surface temperature anomaly measurements.

While deep neural networks excel at recognizing many video activity classes, they still lag behind human performance, particularly when distinguishing between difficult-to-tell-apart actions. Humans manage to differentiate these complex scenarios by identifying key spatio-temporal connections among recognized objects and body parts, such as an item entering a container. Deep networks often fail to learn these critical relationships effectively. To address this, we propose a human-inspired method that analyzes videos in sequential temporal stages to extract specific object-hand relationships within those phases. Random forest classifiers are then trained on these extracted features. When applied to a challenging subset of the Something-Something dataset, this approach demonstrates more robust performance on difficult activities compared to neural network baselines.

This paper examines the Fokas-Lenells equations using a bilinear method. We first bilinearize the unreduced system to derive double Wronskian solutions, then apply a reduction technique to generate a wide range of solutions for the reduced equations. This approach provides a comprehensive overview of solutions for both classical and nonlocal Fokas-Lenells equations, with specific results illustrated through asymptotic analysis. A significant new finding is the derivation of solutions related to real discrete eigenvalues, which have not previously been reported in analytic methods; these solutions exhibit behavior similar to (multi-)periodic waves or solitary waves with algebraic decay. Furthermore, we derive solutions for the two-dimensional massive Thirring model based on the solutions of the Fokas-Lenells equation.

This work examines measure-valued diffusion processes defined on a simplex for a graph with vertex set $V$, governed by the stochastic differential equation $dx_i=\sum_{j\in N(i)}\sqrt{x_ix_j}dB_{ij}$ for $i\in V$. In this formulation, $\{B_{ij}\}$ represent independent standard Brownian motions exhibiting skew symmetry, and $N(i)$ denotes the neighbors of vertex $i$. To analyze the system, a dual Markov chain on integer partitions is constructed relative to the Markov semigroup of the diffusion, demonstrating that the support of an extremal stationary state for the adjoint semigroup corresponds to an independent set of the graph. Additionally, the study explores the diffusion incorporating a linear drift, which induces a killing mechanism in the dual Markov chain on a finite integer lattice. This chain facilitates the investigation of the diffusion's unique stationary state, a distribution that extends the Dirichlet distribution. Finally, two applications are presented: the analysis of an algorithm for identifying independent sets in graphs and a Bayesian approach to graph selection, which relies on sample probability computation via coupling from the past.

Excitability, a phenomenon observed across disciplines ranging from biology and neuroscience to optics, is defined by a system's all-or-none reaction to external disturbances. When these excitable systems experience delayed feedback, they can maintain multistable pulsing states, manifesting as either regular or irregular sequences of pulses recurring at the delay interval. This study examines an excitable microlaser under delayed optical feedback to explore the development of intricate pulsing behaviors, such as periodic, quasiperiodic, and irregular regimes, driven by experimental evidence of these dynamics. Utilizing a mathematical framework of delay differential equations, we conduct a detailed bifurcation analysis. Our findings indicate that resonance tongues are pivotal in generating complex dynamics, including non-equidistant periodic pulsing and chaos. The configuration of these resonance tongues is highly sensitive to the pump parameter. Specifically, successive saddle transitions of bounding saddle-node bifurcations create a merging process that yields surprisingly extensive locking regions, which then detach from the relevant torus bifurcation curve; the presence of these disconnected periodic pulsing regions aligns perfectly with experimental data. We demonstrate that the transition to these unconnected regions stems from a universal mechanism: the local interaction of resonance tongues at an extremum of the rotation number along a torus bifurcation curve. Furthermore, we illustrate the two generic scenarios of disconnecting and vanishing resonance tongues and show how maxima and minima in the rotation number naturally arise when two torus bifurcation curves undergo a saddle transition, connecting in distinct ways.

To identify an effective interaction suitable for both the mean-field and residual components within beyond mean-field frameworks, this study examines Skyrme interactions as a residual force. Employing time-dependent density-matrix theory (TDDM) as the beyond mean-field approach, ground states for $^{16}$O and $^{40}$Ca were computed using five standard Skyrme parametrizations, each varying in their density and momentum dependencies. The results indicate that the Skyrme interaction characterized by strong density dependence and weak momentum dependence generates significant ground-state correlations, yielding outcomes comparable to those of other theoretical methods.

Reaction-diffusion mechanisms serve as a versatile framework for modeling diverse biological and physical phenomena across various spatial scales, including intracellular dynamics, cell migration, vegetation patterns in semi-arid regions, and domain growth associated with embryonic development and wound healing. While numerous numerical frameworks exist to simulate these systems on expanding domains, each is optimized for specific spatial scales and particle counts. Recently, spatially extended hybrid methods have been introduced for static domains to bridge gaps between different modeling paradigms and capture multiscale behaviors; however, these approaches have not yet been adapted for growing domains. This paper presents three novel hybrid methods tailored for expanding domains, extending three leading static-domain techniques. We provide comprehensive algorithms to facilitate their implementation and demonstrate that these methods can accurately and unbiasedly model three representative reaction-diffusion systems.

This study reconstructs the $\gamma$-photon energy spectrum using our modified EQMD model, achieving excellent consistency with experimental data for the $^{86}$Kr + $^{12}$C collision at $E/A$ = 44 MeV. We examined the directed and elliptic flows of free protons and direct photons by incorporating the $\alpha$-clustering structure of $^{12}$C. Relative to free protons, direct photon flows provide more distinct insights into the early stages of the nuclear reaction. Our results reveal variations in collective flows across different $^{12}$C configurations, demonstrating that direct photon flows are highly sensitive to the initial setup. Consequently, the $\gamma$ bremsstrahlung process could serve as an effective alternative probe for investigating $\alpha$-clustering structures in light nuclei within heavy ion collisions at Fermi energies.

The spectral signatures of magnetic skyrmions excited by microwave fields hold fundamental significance and promise for high-frequency applications. Although these topological solitons can be engineered within multilayered thin films, observing their spin wave dynamics experimentally has remained challenging, largely due to substantial damping. In this study, we examine Pt/FeCoB/AlO$_x$ multilayers that support dense, robust skyrmion lattices at room temperature with a Gilbert damping of approximately 0.02. We employed magnetic force microscopy to analyze their static magnetic phases and broadband ferromagnetic resonance to investigate their high-frequency responses. Micromagnetic simulations accurately replicated the experimental results, enabling the identification of distinct resonant modes within the skyrmion lattice phase. Low-frequency modes (below 2 GHz) and intermediate-frequency modes (2–8 GHz) involve excitations localized at skyrmion edges alongside the precession of the uniform background magnetization. Conversely, a high-frequency mode (above 12 GHz) corresponds to in-phase precession of the skyrmion cores, which emits spin waves into the uniform background with wavelengths between 50 and 80 nm, matching the lattice structure. These results may prove crucial for exploring room-temperature wave scattering and developing new microwave processing schemes using reconfigurable arrays of solitons.

Using Hubble Space Telescope imaging across UV, optical, and NIR wavelengths, combined with optical spectroscopy from Keck/LRIS and MMT/Binospec, we analyzed 18 main-sequence OB stars in the nearby, extremely metal-poor (Z~5% Z_sun) galaxy Leo A (D~0.8 Mpc), focusing on massive stars (M>8 M_sun). Our findings reveal that: (a) emission lines appear in 12 of the 18 stars, even without association with an H II region, suggesting stellar activity such as mass loss, accretion, or binary interaction, which aligns with prior predictions of heightened activity at low metallicity; (b) six of the stars are Be stars, representing the first spectroscopic study of such objects at this metallicity level, which exhibit unusual panchromatic spectral energy distributions; (c) for stars effectively modeled by TLUSTY non-LTE simulations, photometric and spectroscopic determinations of T_eff and log(g) agree within approximately 0.01 dex and 0.18 dex, respectively, demonstrating that NUV/optical/NIR imaging can reliably characterize massive (M ~ 8-30 M_sun) main-sequence properties compared to optical spectroscopy; (d) the properties of the most massive stars in H II regions match constraints from earlier nebular emission line research; and (e) 13 stars with M>8 M_sun are located more than 40 pc away from any known star cluster or H II region. This sample accounts for roughly 50% of all known massive stars with Z < 10% Z_sun that have derived stellar parameters, high-quality optical spectra, and panchromatic photometry.

This work investigates the boundary states of the prototypical three-dimensional topological order, specifically the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ toric code. We examine three distinct elementary types of these boundaries. Within the phase diagram encompassing these three boundary types, a multi-critical point emerges, characterized by a deconfined quantum critical point (DQCP) featuring "easy-axis" anisotropy. Furthermore, an emergent $\mathbb{Z}^d_2$ symmetry arises that exchanges two of the boundary types, eventually becoming part of the DQCP's global symmetry. This boundary-specific emergent $\mathbb{Z}^d_2$ symmetry originates from a particular surface defect within the bulk. Additionally, we identify a gapped boundary possessing a surface topological order that remains invariant under this emergent symmetry.

Annually, countless innocent lives are lost to heart attacks, many of which strike unexpectedly because current medical insurance often excludes the cost of detecting coronary calcification via scanning. Consequently, unless a patient is already suspected of having cardiac issues, they cannot undergo a gated CT scan to identify potential disease, as non-gated scans are less effective at locating arterial calcification and serve different primary purposes. Furthermore, real-time coronary artery calcification scores are exclusively calculated from gated scans, not non-gated ones. After training a U-Net model on gated Coronary Calcium and chest CT scans, it achieved a DICE coefficient of 0.95 on an unseen test set. When applied to non-gated scans, the model initially yielded a mean absolute error (MAE) of 674.19 and a bucket classification accuracy of 41% across five classes. However, by deriving mathematical equations from image analysis to automatically crop the heart region, and subsequently employing semi-supervised learning, the cropped non-gated scans were successfully transformed to closely mimic gated CT scans. This approach improved the MAE by 91% (down to 62.38) and increased accuracy by 23%.

Dissipationless flows in single-component superfluids exhibit a high level of universality. In He4, mass flows without dissipation driven by a superfluid velocity defined by the gradient of the superfluid phase. Conversely, interacting superfluid mixtures introduce novel effects. This Letter introduces a new type of dissipationless phenomenon occurring in mixtures of interacting bosons within optical lattices. Specifically, for a certain class of optical lattices, bosons condense into a state where the superflow of one component induces dissipationless mass transport in the other component along a direction distinct from either component's superfluid velocity. This behavior arises because the system's free-energy density includes a vector-product-like interaction between superfluid velocities, resulting in dissipationless noncollinear entrainment. This effect serves as the superfluid analog to the Spin Hall effect.

We investigate energy deposition in a one-dimensional interacting quantum system featuring a point-like potential at $x=0$ that combines a constant component with a small time-dependent oscillation of frequency $\omega$. Employing bosonization, renormalization group methods, and linear response theory, we calculate the resulting energy deposition, which follows a power-law dependence on frequency indicative of the system's Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid (TLL) character. The specific interactions, defined by the TLL parameter $K$, can induce a crossover between weak and strong coupling regimes for backscattering caused by the potential. We determine the characteristic frequency scale $\omega_\ast$ associated with this crossover and observe that the energy deposition from backscattering exhibits distinct exponents for $K>1$ and $K<1$. Finally, we explore the potential experimental implications of these findings within the context of cold atomic gases.

When an integer $n$ can be expressed as the sum of two biquadrates in two distinct ways, the elliptic curve $y^2=x^3-nx$ possesses a rank of at least 3. Furthermore, if $n$ is odd and the parity conjecture holds, the rank is guaranteed to be an even integer no less than 4. Additionally, specific instances yielding ranks of 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 10 are presented.

The MUon RAdiography of VESuvius (MURAVES) initiative focuses on analyzing the summit cone of the active Mt. Vesuvius volcano near Naples, Italy, by determining its density profile via muon flux attenuation. By integrating this data with results from gravimetric and seismic surveys, the project seeks to more precisely characterize the volcanic plug at the crater's base. This paper details the creation of a comprehensive end-to-end simulation framework designed to rigorously evaluate experimental constraints and compare outcomes across different model hypotheses against real-world observations. The detector simulation utilizes GEANT4, alongside a comparative study of cosmic particle generators to select the optimal source for the framework. To replicate actual data conditions, GEANT4 raw hits are processed through simulated digitization: energy deposits are aggregated per scintillator bar and transformed into photoelectron counts using a data-driven method. Subsequently, the same clustering algorithms and tracking codes employed in real analyses are applied. Additionally, the study examines muon transport through rock using both PUMAS and GEANT4. The authors discuss the reasoning behind these technical decisions, including the balance between computational speed and accuracy. These developments hold general significance for the field of muon radiography and are applicable to analogous scenarios.

By adapting the Horowitz and Hubeny method originally designed for asymptotically anti-de Sitter black holes, we demonstrate the classical stability of quasinormal modes within de Sitter spacetime. Additionally, employing a direct approach, we compute the gravitational perturbation frequencies for de Sitter quasinormal modes and examine specific characteristics of their associated radial functions.

For many decades, researchers have sought efficient numerical techniques to tackle the quantum many-body problem, a challenge complicated by a Hilbert space that expands exponentially with system size. Despite these efforts, existing approaches remain constrained by significant limitations. Recently, deep learning methods have emerged as a promising avenue for addressing these long-standing issues. This study demonstrates that a deep learning-based simulation protocol can achieve state-of-the-art precision within Hilbert spaces as vast as $2^{1296}$ for spin systems and $3^{144}$ for fermion systems. Leveraging a HPC-AI hybrid framework on the new Sunway supercomputer, our applications, which scale across up to 40 million heterogeneous cores, achieved 94% weak scaling efficiency and 72% strong scaling efficiency. This achievement paves the way for simulating spin and fermion models on previously unattainable lattice sizes with extreme precision.

We examine the repeated balls-into-bins model proposed by Becchetti et al. (2019), which begins with $m$ balls distributed arbitrarily among $n$ bins. In each step $t=1,2,\ldots$, a ball is selected from every non-empty bin and relocated to a bin chosen uniformly and independently at random. Our findings include:

*   For $n \leq m \leq \mathrm{poly}(n)$, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(m/n \cdot \log n)$ for the maximum load. When $m=n$, this aligns with the $O(\log n)$ upper bound from [BCNPP19] and confirms their conjecture that the maximum load exceeds $\log n/ \log \log n$ over a polynomially large window. However, for $m$ in the range $[\omega(n), n \log n]$, our lower bound refutes the [BCNPP19] conjecture that the maximum load stays $O(\log n)$.
*   For $n \leq m \leq \mathrm{poly}(n)$, we derive an upper bound of $O(m/n \cdot \log n)$ for the maximum load over a polynomially large window, which matches our lower bound within constant factors.
*   For any $m \geq n$, our analysis indicates an $O(m^2 / n)$ waiting time to reach a state with $O(m/n \cdot \log m)$ maximum load, regardless of the worst-case initial distribution.
*   When $m \geq n$, we demonstrate that each ball visits every bin within $O(m \log m)$ steps. In the case $m=n$, this improves upon the prior $O(n \log^2 n)$ bound from [BCNPP19]. Furthermore, we prove that this upper bound is tight up to multiplicative constants for all $n \leq m \leq \mathrm{poly}(n)$.

At the conclusion of each fiscal year, companies distribute annual reports to shareholders detailing their operational and financial status; these documents typically average 80 pages but can reach up to 250. This paper introduces PoinT-5, a methodology combining Pointer Networks and the T-5 (Test-to-text transfer Transformer) algorithm, developed for the Financial Narrative Summarisation (FNS) 2020 challenge. Our approach employs pointer networks to isolate key narrative sentences from the reports, followed by T-5 to paraphrase these into concise, informative summaries. We assessed the method using ROUGE-N (1,2), L, and SU4 metrics. Results indicate that our method attained the highest precision across all measures, secured the top F1 scores for ROUGE-1 and LCS, and was the sole solution to surpass the MUSE baseline in ROUGE-LCS performance.

The surge in accessible mobility data, including GPS traces, web queries, and climate information, has heightened the need to leverage these resources for improved urban mobility support. Nevertheless, data from individual entities like information providers and transportation systems often remains siloed within specific modes, lacking sufficient support for holistic analytics across integrated sources. This paper details our ongoing research within the Data4UrbanMobility (D4UM) project, which focuses on holistic data analytics for urban mobility applications. First, we examine challenges in urban mobility analytics and introduce the D4UM platform currently under development to enable comprehensive analysis of heterogeneous, integrated data sources. Second, we showcase the MiC app, a tool designed to augment existing datasets with intermodal mobility data through a citizen science methodology. Finally, we highlight selected use cases and outline our future research directions.

The increasing scale and complexity of single-cell RNA-seq datasets now facilitate the investigation of cellular composition shifts across diverse biological and clinical settings. However, there is a critical need for scalable dimensionality reduction methods capable of separating biological variation while addressing both technical and biological confounders. This study extends a widely used probabilistic non-linear dimensionality reduction technique, the Gaussian process latent variable model, to handle massive single-cell datasets by explicitly incorporating these confounders. Our core approach utilizes an augmented kernel that maintains the factorizability of the lower bound, thereby enabling rapid stochastic variational inference. We validate this method by successfully reconstructing latent innate immunity signatures from Kumasaka et al. (2021) with a nine-fold reduction in training time. Additionally, analyzing a COVID dataset across a cohort of 130 individuals, we demonstrate that this framework effectively integrates data while revealing interpretable infection-related signatures. Specifically, we utilize COVID severity as a latent dimension to improve patient stratification and identify disease-specific gene expression patterns.

A vertex-coloured graph is defined as $k$-ultrahomogeneous when any isomorphism between induced subgraphs containing at most $k$ vertices can be extended to an automorphism of the entire graph. Similarly, such a graph is $t$-tuple regular if the count of vertices adjacent to every node in a set $S$ of size at most $k$ relies solely on the isomorphism class of the subgraph induced by $S$. This work categorizes finite vertex-coloured graphs that are $k$-ultrahomogeneous (for $k \geq 4$) and those that are $l$-tuple regular (for $l \geq 5$). Notably, our findings include a classification of finite vertex-coloured ultrahomogeneous graphs, a term reserved for graphs that satisfy the $k$-ultrahomogeneity condition for all possible values of $k$.

Nanopore sequencing is a prevalent, cost-effective, high-throughput method capable of converting long genomic fragments into raw electrical signals. However, achieving accurate downstream analysis requires two computationally intensive stages: basecalling, which converts electrical signals into nucleotide bases (A, C, G, T), and read mapping, which locates reads within a reference genome. Current pipelines typically execute these steps separately, a workflow we identify as causing substantial data transfer and redundant calculations that slow overall analysis. This paper introduces GenPIP, an in-memory accelerator that tightly couples basecalling and read mapping. GenPIP enhances pipeline performance through two primary mechanisms: (1) parallel, in-memory, fine-grained collaborative execution of major analysis steps, and (2) a novel early-rejection technique that halts processing for low-quality or unmapped reads, thereby eliminating inefficient computation. Experimental results demonstrate that GenPIP achieves a 41.6X (8.4X) speedup and 32.8X (20.8X) energy reduction with negligible accuracy loss compared to state-of-the-art software tools running on top-tier CPUs (GPUs). Furthermore, relative to a design integrating separate state-of-the-art in-memory accelerators for basecalling and mapping, GenPIP delivers a 1.39X speedup and 1.37X energy savings.

Primordial non-Gaussianity serves as a sensitive indicator of the inflationary epoch, yet many key theoretical predictions lie an order of magnitude beyond the detection limits of current Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) data. While large-scale structure maps theoretically possess the statistical sensitivity to access these targets, the complexities of nonlinear evolution are often viewed as formidable, perhaps even insurmountable, barriers. This paper contends that the difficulty posed by nonlinear structure formation has been exaggerated. The signal from primordial non-Gaussianity is encoded in nonlocal density field correlations spanning three or more points across cosmological distances. Conversely, nonlinear evolution modifies the density field only locally and cannot generate or eliminate these long-range correlations. Consequently, the local nature of late-time non-Gaussianity remains hidden in Fourier space and within standard bispectrum analyses. We therefore advocate for measuring non-Gaussianity directly in position-space maps of large-scale structure. Using equilateral non-Gaussianity as a proof of concept—where the confusion with late-time nonlinearities is most acute—we demonstrate that a map-level analysis can disentangle this degeneracy, significantly enhancing constraining power compared to prior estimates. Our results indicate that "simulation-based inference" through the forward modeling of large-scale structure maps holds the potential to revolutionize the search for primordial non-Gaussianity.

Network pruning offers a substantial reduction in the computational and memory demands of large neural networks. However, achieving an optimal balance between model size and performance typically relies on manual heuristics and requires expert knowledge to set layer-specific compression ratios, a process that is often time-consuming. This paper introduces NAP, a unified and automated framework capable of performing both fine-grained and structured pruning. By utilizing a theoretically grounded criterion, NAP automatically identifies unimportant network components and determines suitable compression ratios for each layer. Specifically, NAP employs an efficient Kronecker-factored Approximate Curvature method to approximate the Hessian for evaluating component importance. Despite its ease of use, NAP significantly outperforms existing pruning methods. For fine-grained pruning, it achieves 25x compression on AlexNet and VGG16, and 6.7x on ResNet-50, with no loss in ImageNet accuracy. In structured pruning scenarios, such as channel pruning, it reduces FLOPs by 5.4x for VGG16 and 2.3x for ResNet-50 with merely a 1% accuracy drop. Crucially, NAP requires almost no hyper-parameter tuning or expert knowledge, making it accessible to start and use effortlessly.

The numerical discretization of large-scale Maxwell's equations results in an ill-conditioned linear system that is difficult to solve, making the selection of an efficient solver a critical requirement for successive solutions. This work employs Perfectly Matched Layers (PML) to enhance efficiency. While PMLs have traditionally been utilized to truncate wave equation simulations by improving solution accuracy over absorbing boundary conditions (ABCs), we propose an alternative application: using PML as transmission conditions at the interfaces within a domain decomposition method. We solve Maxwell's equations using this approach and evaluate the convergence rate of our results against scenarios where ABCs serve as the transmission conditions.

This paper investigates the flexibility of weak solutions to the Monge-Ampère system using convex integration.
