This system serves as a natural generalization of the Monge-Ampère equation in two dimensions, originating from problems in isometric immersions and nonlinear elasticity. The core technical component is the "stage" construction, which ensures $\mathcal{C}^{1,\alpha}$ Hölder regularity for the approximating fields across all $\alpha < \frac{1}{1+ d(d+1)/k}$, where $d$ represents an arbitrary dimension and $k \geq 1$ denotes an arbitrary codimension.

This research examines the species and mechanisms responsible for repetitive pulsed streamer initiation in CO$_{2}$. A 10 kV high-voltage pulse, featuring a 1 ms width and 10 Hz repetition rate, was applied to a pin electrode positioned 160 mm from a grounded plane. Using a photo-multiplier tube, inception times—defined as the delay from the pulse's rising edge—were recorded over 600 cycles, revealing a single histogram peak with a median of 1.2$\mu$s. To determine the origin of this peak, low-voltage (LV) pulses were applied prior to the main high-voltage (HV) pulse to manipulate residual space charges, resulting in three distinct phenomena: drift, neutralization, and ionization. At low LV amplitudes and widths, the inception time peak shifted toward faster or slower values under positive or negative LV pulses, respectively. However, the magnitude of this shift differed between positive and negative configurations under identical pulse settings. We propose a hypothesis to account for this asymmetry, attributing it to differences in detachment processes between air and CO$_{2}$.

This study investigates the electronic band structure and elastic properties of the Cd${}_{16}$Se${}_{15}$Te solid solution using density functional theory. The sample's structure is modeled based on the cubic phase of the binary compound CdSe. Utilizing the calculated electronic band structure, effective masses for electrons, heavy holes, light holes, spin-orbit interactions, and reduced mass at the G point are determined. Furthermore, the exciton binding energy, refractive index, and high-frequency dielectric constant are computed. Theoretical calculations also yield the Young's modulus, shear modulus, bulk modulus, and Poisson ratio. Finally, acoustic velocity and Debye temperature are derived from the results of the elastic coefficients.

Lagrangian data assimilation for complex, nonlinear turbulent flows is a critical yet computationally demanding challenge. This study introduces an efficient, data-driven reduced-order modeling algorithm that statistically maintains accuracy while drastically improving computational speed. The method begins by applying a Fourier transform to the high-dimensional flow field, followed by a targeted model reduction that preserves only a limited set of Fourier coefficients representing energetic modes. A linear stochastic model is subsequently constructed to approximate the nonlinear dynamics of these coefficients. To account for modes displaying Gaussian and non-Gaussian statistics, respectively, the approach incorporates effective additive and multiplicative noise processes. All parameters within the reduced-order system, including multiplicative noise coefficients, are derived systematically using closed-form analytical expressions. These linear stochastic models effectively forecast uncertainty and enable an exceptionally rapid data assimilation process. The proposed Lagrangian data assimilation technique was tested against observations of sea ice floe trajectories driven by atmospheric winds and turbulent ocean currents. Results indicate that monitoring approximately 30 non-interacting floes within a 200km × 200km domain is adequate to reconstruct the primary multi-scale characteristics of ocean currents. Furthermore, angular displacement data serve as valuable supplements to center-of-mass positions for enhancing assimilation accuracy. Additionally, large and small floes prove more effective for recovering large-scale and small-scale ocean features, respectively. Finally, Fourier domain data assimilation successfully retrieves ocean characteristics in regions where cloud cover obstructs direct observations.

This paper comprises two distinct sections. The first section advances the study of the class $(\Sigma)$ by introducing a novel characterization of its stochastic processes, presenting new properties, and solving the Bachelier equation. The second section examines the class of stochastic processes $\Sigma(H)$, which was originally defined in \cite{f}. In that work, the authors utilized martingale theory with respect to a signed measure from \cite{chav} to establish a general framework and methods for handling such processes. In our contribution, we develop additional properties for this class and embed a non-atomic measure $\nu$ within $X$, a process belonging to $\Sigma(H)$. Specifically, we identify a stopping time $T<\infty$ such that the law of $X_{T}$ corresponds to $\nu$.

Originally, the logistic map gained prominence as a simplified representation of population growth. Despite its apparent simplicity, increasing the growth rate reveals a wide spectrum of behaviors, including bifurcation cascades that transition from periodic to chaotic states. Investigating coupled maps reveals further qualitative shifts in collective dynamics, such as pattern formation and hysteresis. Specifically, hysteresis involves the emergence of distinct attracting sets depending on whether the control parameter is raised or lowered, creating a multi-stable region. This study presents an experimental investigation into the bifurcations and hysteresis of nearly identical, coupled logistic maps. Our implementation uses an electronic system with discrete-time evolution and a high signal-to-noise ratio ($\sim10^6$), enabling precise and reliable manipulations, including the design of a modifiable circuit for diffusive coupling. We observe that the dynamics of both isolated and coupled maps align excellently with theoretical and numerical predictions, including critical bifurcation points and Feigenbaum's bifurcation velocity. Furthermore, we demonstrate robust multi-stable regions across various configurations, even in the presence of unavoidable electronic noise and direct parameter mismatches measured within the circuit components.

This study examines the evolution of quantum correlations in three independent qubits, where each qubit interacts locally with a zero-temperature non-Markovian environment, utilizing the Geometric measure of quantum discord (GQD). We analyze how these correlation dynamics depend on the strength of non-Markovian effects, the initial degree of quantum correlation, and the purity of the initial states. Our findings reveal that, in the presence of an appropriate level of non-Markovianity, the quantum correlations within this three-qubit system recover following a brief period of instantaneous disappearance. Furthermore, we compare these results with the dynamics of pairwise quantum discord and entanglement in the same system.

Certain false vacua do not undergo decay through bounces. This typically occurs when a scale-invariant flat direction in the tunneling action is tilted into a sloping valley by a scale-breaking perturbation, driving the bounce solution to infinity. We examine two recently proposed alternative decay mechanisms: pseudo-bounces and new instantons. Despite their structural similarities, our findings indicate that the pseudo-bounce action is lower than that of the new instanton and more accurately represents the minimum of the action valley. Furthermore, pseudo-bounces span a broader region of field space compared to new instantons, potentially resulting in actions that are orders of magnitude lower.

Inspired by the Weak Gravity Conjecture within AdS holography, it has been suggested that operators carrying charges under global symmetries in three-dimensional or higher CFTs must exhibit specific convexity properties within their spectra. A crucial aspect of this proposal concerns the charge scale at which convexity emerges, which was hypothesized to never be parametrically large. This work extends that constraint to scenarios involving multiple Abelian global symmetries. We posit that the convex directions in the multi-dimensional charge space must form a sub-lattice of the total lattice of charged operators, with an index that cannot become parametrically large. In the specific case of two-dimensional CFTs, we demonstrate via an explicit example that the index can indeed be parametrically large; however, we also prove that convex directions always exist which generate a sub-lattice whose index is bounded by the levels of the global symmetry currents. Consequently, for two dimensions, the conjecture requires a slight modification to incorporate these current levels to remain provable. In dimensions greater than two, we show that the index of the sub-lattice generated solely by marginally convex charge vectors corresponding to BPS operators can be made parametrically large. Nevertheless, when all operators are taken into account, we find no evidence supporting a parametric delay in the onset of convexity.

Controlling chaotic systems has long been a significant challenge in engineering. This study introduces Physics-Informed Deep Operator Control (PIDOC), a framework that encodes control signals and initial positions into the loss functions of a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) to guide a nonlinear system along a desired trajectory. PIDOC is particularly applicable to scenarios where physical commands are received as input signals; for instance, when learning chaotic data from the nonlinear van der Pol system, the PINN outputs the controlled signal. In benchmark tests, PIDOC demonstrated a fluctuating acceleration behavior that oscillated at the same frequency as the target signal, suggesting that while neural networks introduce stochasticity into higher-order terms, they can still effectively enforce control to match the desired frequency. Case studies further confirmed PIDOC's ability to converge to various target trajectories. Although initial positions slightly impacted early-stage control accuracy, numerical experiments showed the system eventually converged to the control signal. It is worth noting that for highly nonlinear systems, PIDOC achieved lower accuracy compared to the benchmark but still converged to reasonable trajectories with predictable behavior. Additionally, variations in the depth and width of the neural network structure had minimal impact on convergence across low and high nonlinearity van der Pol systems. Surprisingly, multiplying the control signal by a Lagrangian multiplier caused PIDOC to fail in converging to the desired trajectory, indicating that amplifying the control signal does not enhance control quality, contrary to intuition. Ultimately, this framework holds potential for controlling chaos in a wide range of nonlinear systems.

Non-Riemannian gravitational frameworks offer new pathways for investigating quantum gravity characteristics and establishing a rigorous environment to analyze condensed matter systems exhibiting non-relativistic symmetry. However, formulating an action principle for these theories has historically been difficult due to various obstacles. In this technical note, we utilize the double field theory formalism to construct actions across a range of such theories. This approach eliminates ambiguities often found in their corresponding equations of motion. Specifically, we incorporate Torsional Newton-Cartan gravity, Carrollian gravity, and String Newton-Cartan gravity into double field theory, derive their respective actions, and contrast these findings with existing results in the literature.
This paper demonstrates that for spinor groups, every exponent exceeding degree 2 is a divisor of the Dynkin index 2.

Collisionless magnetic reconnection usually necessitates computationally intensive kinetic models, which are significantly more demanding than fluid-based approaches. This study employs the MHD-AEPIC framework to examine the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. This novel approach integrates adaptive particle-in-cell (PIC) zones within a global magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) domain, restricting kinetic calculations to areas where such physics is critical. We evaluated three scenarios: (1) MHD with adaptive PIC regions, (2) MHD with fixed PIC regions, and (3) a comprehensive PIC simulation. The results demonstrate strong consistency across all cases regarding reconnection rates, magnetic island separation, ion pressure tensor components, and ion agyrotropy. Achieving this alignment required extensive adaptive PIC regions within the MHD domain, suggesting that magnetic island coalescence is fundamentally a kinetic process where the interaction between macro-scale MHD and micro-scale kinetic effects plays a pivotal role.

The rare inclusive decay $\bar{B}\rightarrow X_s\gamma$ serves as a critical tool for investigating physics beyond the standard model. The dominant uncertainties regarding both the decay rate and CP asymmetry originate from operators emerging at the $1/m_b$ order within the heavy quark expansion. One of the three primary contributions in this expansion, $Q_1^q-Q_{7\gamma}$, is characterized by a non-local function whose moments correspond to HQET parameters. Leveraging recent advancements in our understanding of these parameters, we aim to more precisely constrain their impact on the total rate and CP asymmetry.

This paper introduces the concept of weighted (harmonic) chromatic polynomials for graphs and explores their properties. Additionally, we define weighted (harmonic) Tutte--Grothendieck polynomials for graphs and extend the recipe theorem connecting harmonic Tutte--Grothendieck polynomials of graphs with harmonic Tutte polynomials of matroids. Furthermore, we provide constructions for weighted (harmonic) Tutte--Grothendieck invariants in graphs and weighted (harmonic) Tutte invariants in matroids. Finally, we offer a remark on the categorification of harmonic chromatic polynomials for graphs and harmonic Tutte polynomials for matroids.

We utilize time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (50 fs resolution) to examine the non-equilibrium electronic structure and characteristic time scales in the potential excitonic insulator Ta$_2$NiSe$_5$. Upon strong photoexcitation, the band gap closes transiently within 100 fs, occurring faster than typical lattice vibrational periods. Additionally, we observe that the time required for photoemission intensity to rise above the Fermi energy shortens as excitation strength increases, whereas the electron population's relaxation time toward equilibrium exhibits the opposite trend. We attribute these findings to an excitonic origin of the band gap, a hypothesis supported by microscopic calculations using non-equilibrium Green's function formalism for an interacting two-band system. Specifically, we interpret the fluence-dependent acceleration of the rise time as resulting from enhanced scattering between photo-excited electrons and excitons, which drives an initial rapid decay of the order parameter. Furthermore, while incorporating semi-classical electron-phonon coupling alters quantitative details, it leaves the qualitative dynamics unchanged. Ultimately, our combined experimental and theoretical analysis yields a simple, intuitive phenomenological model describing the primary post-photoexcitation dynamics in Ta$_2$NiSe$_5$.

Many modern mobile augmented reality systems include range sensors; for example, the Microsoft HoloLens features a Time-Of-Flight (ToF) camera that generates coarse triangle meshes suitable for custom applications. This paper proposes leveraging these meshes to automatically create indoor models that act as a foundation for adding location-specific information to physical environments. We introduce a novel voxel-based method for reconstructing indoor spaces from unstructured 3D geometries, such as triangle meshes. The process begins by voxelizing the input data, after which rooms are identified by segmenting connected components of potential ceiling voxels and extruding them downward to locate corresponding floors. Subsequently, a rule-based voxel sweep algorithm assigns semantic labels—such as 'Wall', 'Wall Opening', 'Interior Object', and 'Empty Interior'—to the voxels situated between the detected ceiling and floor. Finally, the geometry of identified walls and their openings is refined within the voxel framework. Unlike methods limited to Manhattan World assumptions or requiring planar room surfaces, this approach remains applicable without such constraints.

Deep-HP serves as a scalable extension of the \TinkerHP\ multi-GPU molecular dynamics (MD) framework, facilitating the integration of PyTorch and TensorFlow-based Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). This extension dramatically expands the capabilities of DNN-driven MD, enabling nanosecond-scale simulations of 100,000-atom biological systems and allowing seamless coupling between DNNs and various classical force fields (FFs) as well as many-body polarizable force fields (PFFs). Specifically, it supports the ANI-2X/AMOEBA hybrid potential for ligand binding research, where solvent-solvent and solvent-solute interactions are handled by the AMOEBA PFF, while solute-solute interactions are managed by the ANI-2X DNN. This hybrid approach leverages AMOEBA's efficient Particle Mesh Ewald implementation for physical long-range interactions while maintaining the quantum mechanical accuracy of ANI-2X for short-range solute dynamics. Users can define the partitioning between DNNs and PFFs to incorporate essential biophysical elements such as polarizable solvents and counter ions. To enhance performance, a multiple-timestep strategy is employed, focusing on low-frequency nuclear force modes; this prioritizes AMOEBA force evaluation and incorporates ANI-2X forces only through correction steps, achieving an order-of-magnitude speedup over standard Velocity Verlet integration. Simulations exceeding 10 microseconds have successfully calculated solvation free energies for charged and uncharged ligands across four solvents and determined absolute binding free energies for host-guest complexes from SAMPL challenges. With average errors within chemical accuracy, the ANI-2X/AMOEBA framework paves the way for large-scale hybrid DNN simulations at force-field computational costs, advancing applications in biophysics and drug discovery.

This study presents high-precision measurements of the transverse momentum ($p_\mathrm{T}^{\ell\ell}$, where $\ell=e,\mu$) and the angular variable ($\phi^{*}_{\eta}$) distributions for Drell-Yan lepton pairs within a mass range of 66–116 GeV. Utilizing 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data at a centre-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, collected by the ATLAS experiment at the LHC during 2015 and 2016, the analysis combines results from electron-pair and muon-pair final states after correcting for detector effects and applying them to the same fiducial volumes. Relative to earlier measurements at $\sqrt{s}=$7 and 8 TeV, these new results investigate perturbative QCD at a higher energy scale with a distinct initial state composition, achieving a 0.2% precision for normalized spectra at low $p_\mathrm{T}^{\ell\ell}$. When compared against various QCD predictions, the data indicate that models employing resummation approaches successfully describe the entire spectrum within the stated uncertainties.

This work investigates diffeomorphometric geodesic landmark matching, aiming to identify a diffeomorphism that aligns two landmark sets through its group action. It is established that landmark motion, and consequently the diffeomorphism, can be represented by an initial momentum, transforming the matching task into an optimization problem over these momenta. Our contribution introduces a derivative-free Bayesian inverse method to learn the optimal momentum that encodes the diffeomorphic mapping between a template and a target. Specifically, we utilize the ensemble Kalman filter, which extends the Kalman filter to handle nonlinear observation operators. We detail an efficient implementation of this algorithm and present numerical results demonstrating its performance across various target shapes.

Through the expansion of two finite products of square sums, combined with series expansions of composite hyperbolic and trigonometric functions (specifically sine, cosine, and their inverses) and leveraging properties of partial Bell polynomials, the author derives Taylor series for real powers of two functions involving squared inverse (hyperbolic) cosines expressed via Stirling numbers of the first kind. Additionally, an explicit formula is provided for specific partial Bell polynomials regarding a sequence of derivatives of a function containing the square of an inverse cosine function. The work also establishes several combinatorial identities involving Stirling numbers of the first kind, presents multiple series representations for the circular constant Pi and its real powers, recovers series expansions for positive integer powers of inverse (hyperbolic) sine functions using Stirling numbers of the first kind, and arrives at other significant and meaningful conclusions.

LoRa wireless networks serve as a pivotal technology for future Internet of Things (IoT) infrastructures. Emerging IoT applications, such as smart cities, may deploy thousands of devices per square kilometer, resulting in significant power demands for connectivity. This study examines green LoRa networks powered by a hybrid system combining grid electricity and renewable energy sources, addressing the challenges of intermittent energy supply and harvested power. The paper introduces resource management strategies for limited channels and spreading factors (SFs) aimed at enhancing gateway energy efficiency. First, an optimization problem is formulated to minimize grid power consumption while meeting quality of service (QoS) requirements, analyzing both uncorrelated and time-correlated channel scenarios. The optimal solution, which involves decoupling the problem into channel and SF assignment alongside energy management, is characterized by high computational complexity. Consequently, online heuristic algorithms are proposed to minimize grid energy usage. Furthermore, adaptable resource management schemes leveraging Reinforcement Learning (RL) are developed to account for correlations in channel and energy data. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed schemes effectively optimize the utilization of renewable energy within LoRa wireless networks.

This paper introduces a robust approach for assessing the quantitative accuracy of various tomographic phase microscopy (TPM) techniques using a multiple-scattering 3D-printed microphantom with a defined geometry and refractive index distribution. We validate this approach by constructing such a phantom and comparing the 3D refractive index reconstructions generated by three distinct TPM methods operating at visible and near-infrared wavelengths. One of these methods operates under a weak-scattering assumption, whereas the other two account for multiple scattering effects. Furthermore, this study can be easily expanded to include more intricate microphantoms designed to better mimic the scattering properties of real-world objects, such as biological tissue.

This work aims to deduce the 3D shape and pose of objects from single images by introducing a learning-based method trained on unstructured image collections, supervised solely by segmentation masks from pre-existing recognition systems (termed "shelf-supervised"). Initially, we estimate a volumetric representation within a canonical frame alongside the camera pose. We constrain this representation to be geometrically consistent with both visual appearance and segmentation masks, ensuring that synthesized novel views are indistinguishable from the source image collection. Subsequently, the coarse volumetric output is transformed into a mesh-based format, which is further refined within the predicted camera frame. These two stages enable both shape-pose factorization from image sets and detailed per-instance reconstruction. We evaluate the approach on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its scalability across 50 categories in the wild—an increase of an order of magnitude compared to current methods.

To meet the rising demands of next-generation home WiFi networks for high throughput and low latency—driven by applications like virtual reality, online gaming, and high-definition video—deploying multiple access points (APs) offers a significant performance boost by enhancing average coverage and data rates. However, this approach introduces the challenge of identifying the optimal AP for each station (STA). This article investigates the performance improvements achievable through the use of secondary APs, known as Extenders, focusing on throughput and delay. To address this, we propose a centralized, easily deployable selection mechanism that leverages IEEE 802.11k/v capabilities to gather STA data and manage association decisions. These decisions, calculated either at the AP or by an external controller, utilize a metric that considers not only RSSI but also the load on both access and backhaul links for potential connections. Initial evaluations using a custom simulator demonstrated that this channel load-aware mechanism improves key metrics, increases traffic capacity by at least 35% without causing congestion, and outperforms traditional RSSI-based association. These findings were validated in a real-world deployment, where associating STAs with the recommended APs or Extenders resulted in a 77.12% increase in total throughput.

Cloud computing is widely recognized as a successful IT paradigm that offers mutual benefits to both providers and customers. Despite these advantages, it faces specific challenges, notably the inefficient provisioning of resources for dynamic workloads. Precise workload forecasting can enhance resource allocation and minimize waste; however, the high dimensionality and variability of cloud workload features make accurate prediction difficult. Current dominant methods, relying on regression or recurrent neural networks, often fail to capture long-term workload variations. To overcome these limitations, we propose esDNN, an efficient supervised learning-based Deep Neural Network approach. First, we employ a sliding window to transform multivariate data into supervised time series suitable for deep learning. Next, we utilize a modified Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) to ensure accurate predictions. We validated esDNN's effectiveness through comprehensive experiments using realistic traces from Alibaba and Google cloud data centers. Results show that esDNN predicts cloud workloads accurately and efficiently, significantly reducing mean square errors compared to state-of-the-art baselines, such as a 15% improvement over standard GRU. Furthermore, applying esDNN to machine auto-scaling demonstrates its ability to efficiently reduce the number of active hosts, thereby optimizing service provider costs.

A symmetric doubly stochastic matrix $A$ is defined as being determined by its spectrum if the only symmetric doubly stochastic matrices similar to $A$ are those obtainable via permutation similarity, i.e., of the form $P^TAP$ for some permutation matrix $P$. This paper addresses the characterization of such matrices. A closely related, yet more challenging problem, was previously proposed by M. Fang in a 2010 publication regarding the inverse eigenvalue problem for symmetric doubly stochastic matrices. Specifically, Fang asked for the characterization of all $n$-tuples $\lambda = (1, \lambda_2, \dots, \lambda_n)$ such that, up to permutation similarity, there exists exactly one symmetric doubly stochastic matrix with spectrum $\lambda$. This short note first derives general results for both of these problems and then provides a complete solution for the case where $n=3$. Furthermore, the study explores connections with spectral graph theory. Finally, two open questions concerning the general case are presented, along with a conjecture.

Consider a rational function $R(x)=g(x)/h(x)$ of degree three defined over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$. We determine the number of irreducible polynomials in $\mathbb{F}_q[x]$ of a specific degree that can be expressed as $h(x)^{\mathrm{deg}\, f}\cdot f\bigl(R(x)\bigr)$ for some $f(x)\in\mathbb{F}_q[x]$. This result allows us to rederive the count of irreducible transformation shift registers of order three, a figure previously established by Jiang and Yang.

We examine a repeated game in which a player voluntarily declares their service usage, and a central authority charges them accordingly. The center receives a partial signal reflecting a portion of the player's actual consumption, drawn from a known public distribution. The player may report any value consistent with this signal, after which the center determines the payment. This framework applies to scenarios like net metering in electricity markets, where verifying a customer's exact network consumption is often impossible due to data masking. When the true underlying value remains relatively stable, we introduce a penalty mechanism that encourages honest self-reporting. Specifically, in addition to charging the reported amount, the mechanism imposes a penalty proportional to inconsistencies in the player's reports. We demonstrate that the fear of future uncertainty motivates the player to act truthfully in the present. For Bernoulli distributions, we provide a full analysis of optimal strategies for any given penalty. Since perfect truthfulness is unattainable with continuous distributions, we derive approximate truthful outcomes by reducing the problem to Bernoulli cases. Furthermore, we extend this mechanism to a multi-player cost-sharing environment and establish corresponding equilibrium results.

The surge in data volume, coupled with the growing need for real-time analysis of the most recent information, has led to the development of database systems that simultaneously handle transactions and analytics. Known as hybrid transactional and analytical processing (HTAP) systems, these platforms enable real-time analysis without the high expenses associated with synchronizing separate single-purpose databases. However, for applications with high data update rates, current HTAP systems suffer from significant throughput reductions in both transactional (up to 74.6%) and analytical (up to 49.8%) workloads compared to isolated execution. These losses stem from (1) data transfer between CPU and memory, (2) the overhead of propagating updates from transactional to analytical tasks, and (3) the cost of maintaining consistent data views. To address this, we introduce Polynesia, a hardware-software co-designed system for in-memory HTAP databases that eliminates the substantial throughput penalties found in traditional approaches. Polynesia achieves this by (1) partitioning the system into distinct transactional and analytical islands, (2) deploying custom hardware to optimize software for reduced update propagation and consistency costs, and (3) utilizing processing-in-memory for analytical islands to minimize data movement overhead. Our evaluation demonstrates that Polynesia surpasses three state-of-the-art HTAP systems, delivering average throughput gains of 1.7x for transactions and 3.7x for analytics, while cutting energy consumption by 48% compared to the most energy-efficient prior system.

This document outlines the content of a Stanford course offered in the Spring 2018 quarter. Drawing from cognitive and systems neuroscience, the course explores the development of hybrid systems that combine connectionist and symbolic reasoning. These systems aim to advance machine learning by merging human and artificial intelligence. A primary focus is on digital assistants that, through ongoing dialogue with expert software engineers, initially function as powerful analytical, computational, and mathematical experts. Over time, these assistants acquire domain-specific problem-solving strategies and develop intuitions based on heuristics and experience gained from their human counterparts. This learning process enhances their innate analytical capabilities, enabling them to collaborate as equal partners. Effectively acting as cognitive extensions or digital prostheses, these assistants emulate the flexible thinking of their human partners and facilitate greater access and control over robust computing resources.

Accurately and efficiently evaluating Newtonian potentials across general two-dimensional domains is crucial for numerically solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations. Complex geometries usually necessitate unstructured mesh discretization, making direct potential evaluation via quadrature computationally expensive. This paper introduces a straightforward, high-order algorithm for calculating Newtonian potentials by leveraging Green's third identity to convert volume integrals into boundary integrals, which are then processed using the Helsing-Ojala method. Consequently, the time required for traditionally costly near-field and self-interaction calculations on unstructured meshes becomes comparable to that of far-field interactions computed via the Fast Multipole Method (FMM). A central component of this algorithm is the high-order 2-D monomial approximation of functions over mesh elements; although often viewed as an ill-conditioned problem due to the resulting Vandermonde linear system, it is well-established that sufficiently smooth functions can be approximated uniformly with high accuracy when paired with a backward stable solver. We rigorously formalize this observation in the present work. The algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through various numerical experiments.

Efficient urban traffic management is a cornerstone of smart city development, making the integrity of traffic sensory data critical. Yet, such data often suffer from imperfections, resulting in missing measurements. This paper addresses the completion of inter-region traffic data by modeling it as a spatiotemporal tensor with missing entries. We introduce an improved CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) completion method that accounts for both urban and temporal dimensions. To capture urban characteristics, the study area is segmented into regions, and urban feature vectors—inspired by biodiversity metrics—are calculated to generate an urban similarity matrix. For the temporal dimension, we first perform an entropy analysis to identify the most regular time series, followed by a joint Fourier and correlation analysis to determine periodicity and build a temporal matrix. These matrices are integrated into a modified CP-completion objective function, which is solved using an alternating least squares algorithm applied to the vectorized inputs. We validate our method through a comprehensive comparative study involving two scenarios: one simulating random missing values and another simulating missing data within specific spatial and temporal bounds. The results indicate that our approach achieves superior recovery performance, outperforming state-of-the-art CP methods by 26% and generative model-based approaches by 35%.

We employ low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy to investigate the function of narrow electronic bands in two 1$T$-TaS$_2$-related materials: bulk 1$T$-TaS$_2$ and the superconducting compound 4$H_{\rm b}$-TaS$_2$. The latter consists of alternating 1$T$-TaS$_2$ and 1$H$-TaS$_2$ layers; the 1$H$-TaS$_2$ layers exhibit a weak charge density wave (CDW) pattern that diminishes CDW coupling between adjacent 1$T$-TaS$_2$ layers. Within the 1$T$-TaS$_2$ layers of 4$H_{\rm b}$-TaS$_2$, we detect a narrow electronic band near the Fermi level, with a spatial distribution matching tight-binding calculations for two-dimensional 1$T$-TaS$_2$. Due to weak electronic hybridization between the 1$T$-TaS$_2$ and 1$H$-TaS$_2$ layers in 4$H_{\rm b}$-TaS$_2$, this narrow band shifts slightly above the Fermi level, thereby suppressing electronic correlation-induced band splitting. Conversely, bulk 1$T$-TaS$_2$ features an insulating gap caused by interlayer CDW coupling. Comparing the spatial distributions of electronic states in both materials reveals that the insulating gap in bulk 1$T$-TaS$_2$ arises from the formation of bonding and antibonding bands resulting from the overlap of narrow electronic bands in the dimerized 1$T$-TaS$_2$ layers.

Quantum Measure Theory (QMT) interprets quantum mechanics through the path integral framework, viewing it as a generalized stochastic process. While a core postulate of QMT asserts that events with zero quantum measure are impossible, this alone fails to fully describe the quantum realm. As determining additional postulates remains an ongoing effort, this paper examines the Multiplicative Scheme for QMT, which posits that the physical world consists essentially of histories derived from the path integral. Applying this scheme to Sorkin's $n$-site hopper—a discrete, unitary model of a single particle on an $n$-site ring inspired by free Schrödinger propagation—the study demonstrates that the scheme's global characteristics imply that no non-trivial, time-finite event can occur.

It is commonly accepted that natural images possess a low-dimensional structure, even though they are represented by high-dimensional pixel arrays. This concept forms the basis for the widespread intuition explaining deep learning's remarkable achievements in computer vision. In this study, we utilize dimension estimation tools on standard datasets to examine the significance of low-dimensional structures in deep learning. Our findings confirm that common natural image datasets exhibit very low intrinsic dimensions relative to their pixel counts. Furthermore, we observe that neural networks learn from low-dimensional datasets more easily and demonstrate superior generalization from training to test data. During this process, we developed a method to validate our dimension estimation tools using synthetic data generated by GANs, enabling us to actively manipulate intrinsic dimensions by controlling the image generation process. The code for our experiments is available at https://github.com/ppope/dimensions.

Many problems grounded in physical theory have been demonstrated to be undecidable, including the spectral gap problem and determining membership for quantum correlations. These findings predominantly stem from reductions applied to a limited set of undecidable issues, such as the halting, tiling, Post correspondence, and matrix mortality problems. A shared characteristic of these problems is that their bounded variants are NP-hard. This study elucidates the connection between unbounded undecidable problems and their bounded, NP-hard counterparts. Specifically, we demonstrate that the NP-hardness of a bounded version naturally follows from the reduction of the unbounded problem. Consequently, this approach yields new and streamlined proofs for the NP-hardness of bounded versions of the Post correspondence problem, matrix mortality, positivity of matrix product operators, reachability, tiling, and ground state energy problems. Ultimately, this work illuminates the intractability inherent in theoretical physics problems and highlights the computational implications of imposing bounds on parameters.

The upcoming XRISM and Athena missions will achieve unprecedented depth and resolution in high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy. Deciphering the resulting spectra demands a thorough grasp of how uncertainties in fundamental atomic parameters—specifically collisional cross sections, transition rates, and wavelengths—influence spectral modeling. Since generating even a basic model of an optically thin hot plasma necessitates millions of values, and most of these rates rely on theoretical calculations rather than experimental data, we have devised methods to estimate the uncertainty in final spectral results using available experimental data and reasonable approximations for underlying atomic uncertainties. This work introduces an extension to the pyatomdb code that incorporates these methods and examines the sensitivity of key diagnostic lines within the X-ray bandpass (0.3–12 keV).

Chemotaxis describes a particle's reaction to chemical gradients within its surroundings. Although initially noted in biological systems, it holds significant relevance for synthetic active particles like nanomotors. Previous literature has documented chemotaxis in chemically driven colloidal nanomotors, specifically within still fluids or microfluidic channels where gradients are maintained by distinct inlet designs. This study employs mesoscopic particle-based simulations of both the colloid and solvent to demonstrate chemotaxis in a microfluidic channel. Utilizing this particle-based framework, we analyze chemical concentration distributions around passive and chemically active colloids, calculate the resulting chemotactic forces, and develop a stochastic model to explain our observations regarding colloidal chemotaxis. Furthermore, this model successfully accounts for results from prior simulations using simpler geometries and expands upon their interpretation.

The primary objective is to derive Gagliardo-Nirenberg-type inequalities within the frameworks of fractional homogeneous Sobolev and homogeneous Besov spaces, specifically by generalizing several findings previously presented in references [1, 2, 3, 7, 16, 21].

In solid-state physics, numerous physical quantities are determined through k-space summations. Specifically, spectral functions involve a frequency-dependent component that separates into an energy-conserving delta function and a nondissipative principal value. The tetrahedron method serves as a highly effective scheme for performing these k-space summations. While this approach has been extensively applied to compute the energy-conserving delta function portion, such as the imaginary part of the dielectric function, its application to the nondissipative principal value part, like the real part of the dielectric function, remains limited. This paper addresses the technical challenges associated with applying the tetrahedron method to the nondissipative component and introduces a stable, easy-to-implement solution. We validate this approach by calculating both static and dynamical spin Hall conductivity in platinum. Furthermore, the proposed method is broadly applicable to determining linear static or dynamical conductivity, electron self-energy, and electric polarizability, among other quantities.

A model for NH$_3$CH$_2$COOH$\cdot$H$_2$PO$_3$, adjusted to include the piezoelectric coupling between ordering structure elements and strains $\varepsilon_i$, $\varepsilon_j$, is employed to investigate phenomena arising under external pressure. Utilizing the two-particle cluster approximation, the study calculates the polarization vector components and the static dielectric permittivity tensor for both mechanically clamped and free crystals, along with their piezoelectric and thermal properties. The impact of hydrostatic pressure on phase transitions and the resulting physical characteristics of the crystal is examined, yielding a robust quantitative agreement with experimental data for these materials.

This study introduces a stochastic decentralized algorithm designed to identify the most suitable Charging Station (CS) for Plug-in Electric Vehicles (PEVs) requiring power. To accommodate varying driver priorities—such as minimizing expenses, reducing charging duration, or shortening travel distance—we employ distinct cost functions. Furthermore, we utilize an IoT framework grounded in permissioned Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) to ensure driver compliance and mitigate malicious behaviors. The proposed PEV assignment mechanism is validated through extensive simulations using the SUMO mobility simulator within realistic city-wide networks, demonstrating its practical operation and performance.

This study constructs multiple one-parameter families of explicit self-similar solutions for porous medium equations incorporating fractional operators. The associated self-similar profiles, known as \emph{Barenblatt profiles}, maintain the same structural form as those found in the classical porous medium equations. These newly derived exact solutions augment existing theoretical frameworks for these equations and are anticipated to offer valuable insights for future quantitative research.

Outcomes from joint analyses of existing cosmological data have sparked significant debate regarding the potential detection of non-zero spatial curvature. Confirmation of such a finding would necessitate a revision of our current comprehension of cosmic evolution, yielding substantial theoretical and observational repercussions. This paper examines the validity of combining currently available data sets and investigates their ramifications for a non-flat universe and modifications to the standard cosmological model. Employing a robust tension estimator, we conduct a quantitative assessment of the physical consistency among recent measurements from the Cosmic Microwave Background, type Ia supernovae, Baryonic Acoustic Oscillations, and Cosmic Chronometers. Our analysis encompasses both flat and non-flat scenarios within the $\Lambda$CDM framework, as well as two dark energy models characterized by constant and evolving equations of state. This study enables a clearer understanding of whether discrepancies between these data sets are significant enough to render joint analysis results misleading, alongside an evaluation of how these outcomes depend on spatial curvature and dark energy parameterizations.

We investigate the emergence of nonequilibrium collective motion in disordered, non-thermal active matter by simulating a two-dimensional model of polydisperse self-propelled particles, focusing on the competition between persistent motion and crowding. Unlike monodisperse systems, we observe that polydispersity stabilizes a homogeneous active liquid even at arbitrarily large persistence times, which exhibits remarkable velocity correlations and irregular turbulent flows. At high densities, this active fluid undergoes a nonequilibrium glass transition regardless of the persistence value. As persistence increases, the nature of this collective motion evolves from near-equilibrium spatially heterogeneous dynamics at low persistence to a qualitatively distinct intermittent regime at high persistence, characterized by a complex temporal evolution of the correlated displacement field.

Many Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) tasks demand not only answer prediction but also the identification of supporting evidence sentences. However, annotating these evidence sentences is typically labor-intensive and time-consuming. To address this challenge, we introduce U3E, an unsupervised evidence extraction method designed to overcome the limitations of existing semi-supervised approaches. U3E operates by utilizing changes resulting from sentence-level feature erasure within a document, thereby simulating the reduction in problem-solving capability associated with memory loss. Furthermore, to ensure selections are made based on a comprehensive understanding of the original text's semantics, we propose specific metrics for rapidly selecting the optimal memory model for these input variations. Experiments conducted across various datasets compare U3E with standard evidence extraction techniques to evaluate its efficacy. The results demonstrate that U3E is both simple and effective, achieving higher accuracy in evidence extraction and significantly enhancing overall model performance.

Recommendation systems are integral to the modern digital landscape, with widespread adoption in domains like music (e.g., Spotify) and film streaming (e.g., Netflix). Conversely, fewer studies have focused on recommendation systems for physical exercise. Given that sedentary behaviors are a primary cause of numerous health issues and rising medical expenses, this paper introduces a system designed to suggest daily exercise routines by leveraging user history, profiles, and peer similarities. The proposed model employs a deep recurrent neural network enhanced with user-profile and temporal attention mechanisms.

Furthermore, unlike streaming platforms where click data is readily available, exercise recommendation systems lack direct user feedback. To address this, we propose a real-time, expert-in-the-loop active learning framework. In this approach, the system evaluates the recommender's uncertainty at each time step for every user and solicits expert input when confidence is low. We derive the probability distribution function of marginal distance to precisely determine the moments for expert consultation. Experiments conducted on a mHealth dataset demonstrate that integrating this real-time active learner significantly improves the system's accuracy.

In drug discovery, aqueous solubility is a critical pharmacokinetic attribute that influences drug absorption and assay feasibility. Consequently, *in silico* solubility prediction has gained traction for virtual screening and lead optimization. Recently, machine learning (ML) approaches leveraging experimental data have become popular, as physics-based methods such as quantum mechanics and molecular dynamics are often unsuitable for high-throughput applications due to their high computational costs. However, ML models are prone to overfitting in data-scarce scenarios, a common challenge for chemical property datasets. Furthermore, ML methods are often viewed as "black boxes," making it difficult to interpret how hidden features contribute to outputs, which hinders the analysis and modification of structure-activity relationships. To address these challenges, we developed Bayesian graph neural networks (GNNs) incorporating a self-attention readout layer. Unlike typical GNNs that apply self-attention during node updates, applying it at the readout layer allows the model to enhance prediction accuracy while identifying atom-wise importance, aiding lead optimization as demonstrated with three FDA-approved drugs. Additionally, Bayesian inference enables the separation of results based on prediction uncertainty. We anticipate that this accurate, reliable, and interpretable model will facilitate more informed decision-making and support various applications in drug development.

Although Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) are becoming increasingly popular, they often face challenges with high dropout rates and low completion rates. Consequently, predicting student success early to facilitate targeted interventions is crucial to prevent students from falling behind. While extensive research exists on predicting MOOC success, most studies train models from scratch for specific courses, a method that is impractical for early prediction since student performance data is only available at the end of a course. This paper proposes early success prediction models capable of transferring across MOOCs with different topics and domains. We introduce three novel transfer strategies: pre-training on a diverse collection of courses, incorporating meta-information about courses to leverage the pre-trained model, and fine-tuning on prior iterations of the same course. Experiments involving 26 MOOCs with over 145,000 enrollments and millions of interactions demonstrate that models combining interaction data and course metadata perform comparably to or better than those relying on historical course iterations. These models aim to effectively allow educators to initiate predictions for both new and ongoing courses.

We theoretically examine the thermoelectric transport characteristics of a T-shaped double quantum dot side-coupled to a topological superconducting nanowire containing Majorana zero-energy modes. Utilizing the numerical renormalization group method, we focus on the transport regime characterized by the two-stage Kondo effect. Our findings indicate that the leakage of Majorana quasiparticles into the double dot system causes a half-suppression of the second Kondo stage. This phenomenon manifests as fractional charge and heat conductances and generates novel resonances within the Seebeck coefficient. Furthermore, the heat conductance adheres to a modified Wiedemann-Franz law. Lastly, we discuss how the interaction between Majorana-induced interference and strong electron correlations influences the spin Seebeck effect, a distinctive attribute of this configuration.

Ensuring the safe operation of machinery relies heavily on intelligent fault diagnosis. Nevertheless, deep learning approaches often suffer from over-fitting and limited generalization due to data heterogeneity and the scarcity of fault samples in real-world machinery. To address these challenges, this study introduces a privacy-preserving, personalized federated learning framework designed for multi-task fault diagnosis across various factories. Initially, rotating machines from different sites exhibiting similar vibration characteristics are clustered into specific groups via a federated clustering technique. Subsequently, a multi-task deep learning model utilizing convolutional neural networks is developed to diagnose diverse machinery faults through the fusion of heterogeneous information. Finally, the proposed framework employs an adaptive hierarchical aggregation strategy to resolve data heterogeneity among different machines within the personalized federated learning setup. Empirical validation using data from actual machines confirms the framework's efficacy, demonstrating that diagnosis accuracy improves significantly, particularly for machines with limited fault sample data.

The memory effect, a fundamental property of fractional calculus, has garnered significant attention since its inception due to its critical role in addressing various practical problems. This study integrates fractional derivatives with memory effects and grey modeling theory to establish a unified framework for existing fractional grey models. By utilizing diverse kernel and normalization functions, this framework enables the derivation of novel fractional grey models. To enhance predictive performance, four prominent intelligent algorithms are employed to optimize the coefficients of the UFGM(1,1) model. The model's validity is verified using two published cases, which also investigate the impact of the fractional accumulation order and initial values on prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the model is applied to two real-world examples to demonstrate its efficacy and illustrate the practical implementation of the proposed unified framework.

This study revisits the Alexander et al. (2006) model describing the closure of a circular hole within a molecularly thin, incompressible Langmuir film resting on a Stokesian subfluid. While the original framework simplifies the surface phase as inviscid—predicting a constant reduction in cavity area governed by the ratio of edge tension to subfluid viscosity—we reformulate the problem to incorporate a regularizing monolayer viscosity. Our analysis reveals that viscosity-dependent corrections to hole dynamics are significant, even at low monolayer viscosity levels, potentially accounting for discrepancies between experimental data and theoretical predictions when the hole radius approaches the Saffman-Delbruck length. Through curve fitting, we estimate that the edge tension may be approximately eight times higher, reaching ~5.5 pN, under these relaxed assumptions compared to previous reports.

A Cayley (di)graph $Cay(G,S)$ associated with a group $G$ and a subset $S \subseteq G$ is defined as normal when the right regular representation of $G$ forms a normal subgroup within the full automorphism group of $Cay(G,S)$. It is termed a CI-(di)graph if the condition $Cay(G,S) \cong Cay(G,T)$ for any $T \subseteq G$ necessitates the existence of an automorphism $\sigma \in Aut(G)$ such that $S^\sigma = T$. A group $G$ is classified as a NDCI-group if every normal Cayley digraph of $G$ satisfies the CI-property, and as an NCI-group if every normal Cayley graph of $G$ satisfies the CI-property. This paper establishes that a cyclic group of order $n$ is a NDCI-group if and only if $8$ does not divide $n$, and it is an NCI-group if and only if $n = 8$ or $8$ does not divide $n$.

Cell-free systems can effectively eliminate inter-cell interference by allowing multiple base stations (BSs) to cooperatively serve users without cell boundaries, albeit at the high cost of hardware and power consumption resulting from extensive BS deployment. To address this challenge, low-cost reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) offer a promising solution to enhance the energy efficiency of cell-free systems. This paper investigates an RIS-aided cell-free MIMO system where multiple RIS units are strategically placed around BSs and users to facilitate favorable propagation conditions through low-cost, reconfigurable reflections, thereby boosting cell-free MIMO performance. A hybrid beamforming (HBF) scheme is proposed to maximize energy efficiency, combining digital beamforming at the BSs with RIS-based analog beamforming. The study formulates an energy efficiency maximization problem and develops an iterative algorithm to solve it. Furthermore, the impact of transmit power, the quantity of RIS units, and the size of individual RIS elements on energy efficiency is analyzed. Both theoretical analysis and simulation results demonstrate that optimal energy efficiency is contingent upon the number and size of the RIS units. Additionally, numerical evaluations confirm that the proposed system achieves superior energy efficiency compared to conventional approaches.

This study demonstrates that machine learning can enhance the precision of simulations for stress waves in one-dimensional composite materials. We introduce a data-driven approach to derive nonlocal constitutive laws for stress wave propagation models. This optimization-based method approximates the nonlocal kernel function using Bernstein polynomials. By determining both the functional form and parameters of the kernel, we ensure that when integrated into a nonlocal solver, it produces solutions that align closely with high-fidelity data. Consequently, the optimized kernel functions as a homogenized nonlocal continuum model that accurately replicates wave dynamics observed in detailed, multi-material small-scale models. We applied this technique to analyze wave propagation in a heterogeneous bar featuring a periodic microstructure. Multiple one-dimensional numerical experiments confirm the algorithm's accuracy. Furthermore, the optimal kernel successfully reproduces high-fidelity data for composite materials in applications that differ significantly from the training datasets.

Our previous study (Ayral et al., 2020 IEEE Computer Society Annual Symposium on VLSI) demonstrated the initial implementation of the Quantum Divide and Compute (QDC) approach, a technique that partitions quantum circuits into smaller segments requiring fewer qubits and reduced circuit depth. This method addresses the constraints of noisy, intermediate-scale quantum processors, specifically their limited qubit counts and brief coherence times. The present article examines how various noise factors—readout error, gate error, and decoherence—affect the success rate of the QDC process. By conducting comprehensive noise modeling on the Atos Quantum Learning Machine, we identify trade-offs and propose recommendations for prioritizing the optimization of specific hardware noise sources. Furthermore, we provide a detailed exposition of the noise models employed to replicate experimental results from IBM's Johannesburg processor. This work also features a thorough derivation of the equations governing the QDC procedure, which calculates the output distribution of the original circuit from those of its fragments. Finally, we evaluate the computational complexity of the QDC method for the specific circuit using tensor-network analysis and discuss its relationship to tensor-network simulation techniques.

Automated classification of crop types using Sentinel-2 satellite time series data is vital for agricultural monitoring. Recently, deep learning models leveraging transformer encoders have emerged as a promising solution for this task. Applying explainable machine learning techniques to illuminate the internal mechanisms of these models is a crucial step toward enhancing stakeholder trust and optimizing agricultural oversight.

This paper presents a new explainability framework designed to clarify the essential crop disambiguation patterns learned by a state-of-the-art transformer encoder. Specifically, we analyze the attention weights of a trained model to identify critical dates for distinguishing crops and employ domain knowledge to expose the phenological events underpinning the model's performance. Furthermore, we introduce a sensitivity analysis method to better comprehend the attention mechanism's ability to detect crop-specific phenological events.

Our findings demonstrate that attention patterns are strongly correlated with key dates and, by extension, with the critical phenological events necessary for accurate crop-type classification. These insights could be instrumental in bolstering stakeholder confidence and refining agricultural monitoring workflows. However, our sensitivity analysis also highlights a limitation of attention weights in identifying significant phenological events; we empirically show that the revealed events vary depending on the other crops included in the training dataset.

**Background:** Although numerous phenomenological models for nuclear fission exist, achieving a microscopic understanding of this process remains one of the most difficult challenges in nuclear physics.

**Purpose:** This study examines the applicability of the generator coordinate method (GCM) as a microscopic framework for cluster radioactivities in heavy nuclei. These events can be viewed as a form of fission characterized by large mass asymmetry, representing a phenomenon intermediate between standard fission and $\alpha$-decays.

**Methods:** Building upon Gamow theory, we calculate the preformation probability of a cluster using the GCM, while estimating Coulomb barrier penetrability via a potential model. To achieve this, we utilize Skyrme interactions and solve the one-dimensional Hill-Wheeler equation incorporating the mass octupole field. Furthermore, we incorporate dynamical pairing correlations by employing BCS wavefunctions derived with enhanced pairing interaction strength.

**Results:** We apply this approach to the cluster decay of $^{222}$Ra (specifically $^{222}$Ra$\to^{14}$C+$^{208}$Pb), demonstrating that the experimental decay rate is reproduced within approximately two orders of magnitude. We also briefly address cluster radioactivities in $^{228}$Th and $^{232}$U; for these actinides, our calculations yield decay rates with similar accuracy, reproducing them within one to three orders of magnitude, respectively.

**Conclusions:** The methodology outlined in this paper offers a promising avenue for the microscopic description of cluster decays in heavy nuclei.

Reference [M18] details a construction of strongly regular Cayley graphs on finite field additive groups utilizing three-valued Gauss periods. Combined with findings from [BLMX], it was demonstrated that strongly regular Cayley graphs possessing negative Latin square type parameters $(q^6,r(q^3+1),-q^3+r^2+3r,r^2+r)$, with $r=M(q^2-1)/2$, exist under three specific conditions: (i) $M=1$ where $q\equiv 3\,(\mod{4})$; (ii) $M=3$ where $q\equiv 7\,(\mod{24})$; and (iii) $M=7$ where $q\equiv 11,51\,(\mod{56})$. The question of whether such graphs exist for odd $M>7$ remained unresolved. This paper addresses that gap by proving that if there exists an integer $h$ ($1\le h\le M-1$) satisfying $M\,|\,(h^2+h+1)$ and the multiplicative order of $2$ modulo $M$ is odd, then infinitely many primes $q$ yield strongly regular Cayley graphs with the specified parameters.

Reciprocity within social networks illuminates information exchange between pairs of individuals and reveals their interaction patterns. However, a recent study found that the reciprocity coefficient of a standard directed preferential attachment (PA) model fails to align with empirical data. To address this, we expand the classical three-scenario directed PA model by introducing a parameter that regulates the likelihood of forming reciprocal edges. Furthermore, our proposed model permits edge creation between existing nodes, offering a more realistic framework for fitting real-world datasets. Beyond analyzing the theoretical characteristics of this reciprocity-enhanced PA model, we present and compare two estimation methods for fitting the extended model to both simulated and actual data. The resulting models demonstrate a strong correspondence with the empirical tail distributions of both in-degrees and out-degrees. Nevertheless, other diagnostic mismatches indicate that further generalization of the model is necessary.

Producing extensive hydrodynamical simulations for cosmological predictions is a computationally intensive requirement for upcoming observational efforts. In this study, we develop a new fully convolutional variational auto-encoder (VAE) designed to synthesize hydrodynamic fields based on dark matter inputs derived from N-body simulations. Following training on a single hydrodynamical simulation, the model successfully probabilistically translates new dark matter-only simulations into corresponding full hydrodynamical outputs. By sampling within the VAE's latent space, we generate posterior samples to analyze the mapping's variance. Our results indicate that the reconstructed fields accurately represent target hydrodynamical data and offer reasonable variance estimates. This methodology shows significant potential for rapidly generating mock data and for integration into a comprehensive Bayesian inverse model for observed data.

Although multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has advanced significantly in recent years, achieving coordination in complex domains remains difficult. Existing MARL research typically targets scenarios where agents interact with every other entity in the environment; however, real-world tasks often consist of multiple isolated local interaction instances (subtasks). In such composite tasks, agents can effectively concentrate on a single subtask while ignoring the rest. Successful strategies in these settings involve a two-level decision-making process: first, assigning agents to specific subtasks, and second, having each agent act productively toward its assigned goal. This decomposed approach offers a powerful structural inductive bias, drastically reduces observation spaces, and promotes the reuse and composition of subtask-specific policies during training, rather than treating every new task composition as entirely unique. We present ALMA, a general learning framework designed to leverage these structured tasks. ALMA concurrently learns a high-level policy for subtask allocation and low-level policies for individual agents. We show that ALMA achieves sophisticated coordination in various challenging environments, surpassing strong baselines. Furthermore, ALMA's modularity enhances its ability to generalize to new environmental configurations. Finally, we observe that while ALMA can combine separately trained allocation and action policies, optimal performance is achieved only when all components are trained jointly. The code is available at https://github.com/shariqiqbal2810/ALMA.

We define the concepts of locally visible and locally Gromov hyperbolic domains within $\mathbb C^d$. We establish that a bounded domain in $\mathbb C^d$ possesses these local properties if and only if it is globally visible and Gromov hyperbolic under the Kobayashi distance. This result enables the construction of novel classes of Gromov hyperbolic domains where biholomorphisms admit continuous extensions to the boundary.

This study introduces a new framework for tail-risk forecasting that integrates forecast combination with weighted quantiles to mitigate modelling uncertainty. The methodology utilizes a two-stage estimation process: initially, Value-at-Risk (VaR) forecasts across a spectrum of quantile levels are combined, drawing from a universe of various parametric and semi-parametric models, with weights derived by optimizing quantile loss. Subsequently, Expected Shortfall (ES) is calculated as a weighted average of these combined quantiles, where the weighting structure is optimized by minimizing a strictly consistent joint VaR and ES loss function belonging to the Fissler-Ziegel class. Applied to six stock market indices, the framework's performance was benchmarked against individual models, simple averaging, and weighted quantile methods, with results indicating that the proposed approach yields superior forecasting outcomes.

We have compiled a comprehensive catalog of spatially resolved binary stars from the Gaia eDR3 data, covering distances up to approximately 1 kpc from the Sun and projected separations spanning from a few astronomical units to 1 parsec. The likelihood of each pair being a chance alignment was determined empirically by leveraging the Gaia catalog itself to compute alignment rates based on various observables. This dataset includes 1.3 million (1.1 million) binaries with greater than 90% (>99%) confidence of being gravitationally bound, comprising 16,000 white dwarf–main sequence systems and 1,400 white dwarf–white dwarf binaries. The complete catalog, along with the necessary queries and generation code, is made publicly accessible. We subsequently utilized this sample to refine the published Gaia DR3 parallax uncertainties, exploiting the near-identical parallaxes of binary components. Our analysis reveals that while these uncertainties are generally reliable for faint stars ($G\gtrsim 18$), they are significantly underestimated for brighter stars. For isolated sources with stable astrometry, underestimates are typically $\le 30\%$, whereas they can reach up to 80% for apparently well-behaved sources with companions within $\lesssim 4$ arcseconds, and are even more severe for sources with poor astrometric fits. We provide an empirical fitting function to adjust published $\sigma_{\varpi}$ values for isolated sources. The public catalog facilitates diverse follow-up studies, including the calibration of spectroscopic surveys, precise age determination for field stars, investigations into white dwarf masses and the initial-final mass relation, and dynamic mapping of the Galactic tidal field.

To effectively mitigate threat propagation in interconnected networks, it is crucial to allocate defense resources optimally. Although most electric power utilities operate under resource constraints, the methodology for balancing costs during the design of threat reduction strategies remains unclear. Consequently, this study proposes a vulnerability propagation and defense framework grounded in an epidemic model. The efficacy of this novel defense mechanism is validated by analyzing the sensitivity of propagation parameters regarding optimal investment across both two-node and N-node scenarios. Furthermore, the model's effectiveness is assessed through its application within a communication network of a cyber-physical power system, with a specific emphasis on the impact of network topology on optimal nodal investment. Results indicate that optimal investment in neighbors with lower connectivity degrees exhibits high sensitivity to fluctuations in vulnerability exploitability probability.

We demonstrate that for a broad category of Banach spaces consisting of analytic functions within the unit disc $\mathbb{D}$, an unbounded operator defined by $Af=G\cdot f'+g\cdot f$ (where $G$ and $g$ are analytic in $\mathbb{D}$) generates a $C_0$-semigroup of weighted composition operators precisely when it generates a standard $C_0$-semigroup. This finding encompasses classical Hardy spaces as specific cases. Our work extends earlier studies in this area and connects to cocycles associated with flows of analytic functions on Banach spaces. Furthermore, for a wide range of non-separable Banach spaces $X$ of analytic functions in $\mathbb{D}$ that are subsets of the Bloch space, we establish that no non-trivial holomorphic flow can induce a $C_0$-semigroup of weighted composition operators on $X$. This result broadens previous findings concerning $C_0$-semigroups of unweighted composition operators.

By encoding X-ray images, radiology reports, and other diverse medical data into binary representations within a shared space, clinicians can efficiently retrieve pathology-related information across heterogeneous modalities through hashing-based cross-modal retrieval. This approach offers a novel perspective for enhancing computer-aided diagnosis. However, a significant challenge remains: improving retrieval accuracy by uncovering the ambiguous semantics of medical data while filtering out irrelevant information. To address this limitation, we introduce Deep Supervised Information Bottleneck Hashing (DSIBH), a method that significantly enhances the discriminability of hash codes. This is achieved by extending the Deep Deterministic Information Bottleneck framework, originally designed for single-modality data, to a cross-modal context. This extension effectively minimizes superfluous information, thereby improving the distinctiveness of the generated hash codes. Experimental results confirm that the proposed DSIBH outperforms state-of-the-art methods in cross-modal medical data retrieval tasks.

We investigate the energy of a frustrated spin system exhibiting ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic properties, where spins are constrained to two separate circles on the 3-dimensional unit sphere within both one-dimensional and two-dimensional domains. The total energy comprises a component based on nearest-neighbor and next-to-nearest-neighbor interactions, alongside a penalty term accounting for magnetic anisotropy transitions. We examine the system's asymptotic energy behavior as it approaches the helimagnet/ferromagnet transition point in the limit of an infinite number of particles. In one dimension, we calculate the first- and second-order $\Gamma$-limits of the renormalized energy, thereby quantifying the energetic cost associated with any magnetic anisotropy or chirality transition. In two dimensions, by determining the second-order $\Gamma$-limit of the renormalized energy, we demonstrate and analyze the emergence and geometric rigidity of chirality transitions.

Unsupervised near-duplicate detection offers significant practical utility across domains such as social media analysis, large-scale web retrieval, and digital image forensics. The process involves executing threshold-constrained queries on image descriptors to identify all near-duplicates while minimizing false positives caused by visually similar but distinct images. Because false alarm rates increase with dataset size, realistic applications demand extremely high specificity, reaching $1 - 10^{-9}$, a critical requirement that is frequently neglected in existing literature. Although deep convolutional neural network descriptors have recently matched or exceeded traditional feature extraction methods in content-based image retrieval, to our knowledge, this work is the first to evaluate the performance range of these deep learning descriptors for unsupervised near-duplicate detection across diverse datasets and definitions. We utilize both established and novel benchmarks, including the Mir-Flick Near-Duplicate (MFND) dataset, which provides ground truth for all pairs within a large-scale image collection. To assess specificity, we frame unsupervised detection as a binary classification problem distinguishing near-duplicates from non-duplicates, characterized via Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves. Our results generally support fine-tuning deep convolutional networks over using pre-trained features, though performance differences at high specificity levels vary by dataset and are often minimal. The optimal results were achieved on the MFND benchmark, yielding 96% sensitivity at a false positive rate of $1.43 \times 10^{-6}$.

Research on the one-dimensional Bose-Hubbard model in the large-$U$ regime has involved simplifying and mapping the Hamiltonian to a more tractable form. Within subspaces characterized by fixed counts of single and double occupancies—excluding configurations with multiple occupancies—exact eigenstates and eigenvalues have been derived, allowing for the calculation of the system's thermodynamic properties. Furthermore, these exact solutions facilitate a novel perturbative approach to the model, enabling the precise determination of the ground-state energy to first order in $1/U$.

The evolution time of a qubit driven by a Hamiltonian is a fundamental challenge in quantum control, information processing, and computing. In Hermitian systems, this duration is bounded below by the coupling between qubit states; however, it has been theorized that non-Hermitian systems could significantly reduce this time without breaching the time-energy uncertainty principle. We experimentally validated this proposal using a single dissipative qubit, demonstrating that in a non-Hermitian Parity-Time-Symmetric ($\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric) system, the evolution time from an initial to an arbitrary state can be regulated by adjusting the dissipation intensity. As dissipation intensity rises, the evolution time decreases, yielding a stricter bound on the quantum speed limit (QSL). Conversely, we observed that the time required for the reversal operation increases with higher dissipation. These results provide a precise mechanism for accelerating qubit operations, facilitating rapid and practical quantum computation capable of tackling complex problems with minimal qubit resources.

The study of competing or coexisting quantum many-body phases remains a captivating domain within condensed matter physics. A prominent example of such phase competition involves superconductivity and magnetism, an area that, despite decades of inquiry, continues to yield novel discoveries. Although these phenomena are intuitively viewed as opposing forces, specific conditions allow them to cooperate, coexist, and mutually enhance one another, resulting in exotic quantum states. This chapter examines a unique superconducting phase that emerges in "Pauli-limited superconductors" when there is an imbalance in the population of the fermionic species forming pairs. This disparity gives rise to a non-trivial, spatially modulated superconducting state known as the Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov (FFLO) phase. Defined by finite-momentum pairing between fermions, the FFLO phase supports a non-zero magnetization, thereby creating an unconventional phase where superconductivity and magnetism coexist.
