The astrophysics of the cosmic dawn, marking the onset of star formation in the first collapsed structures, is expected to manifest as spectral and spatial features in the long-wavelength cosmic radio background. Specifically, the sky-averaged redshifted 21-cm absorption line of neutral hydrogen serves as a key probe of this era. The shape of this line is governed by the gas's evolving thermal conditions, the radiation background, Lyman-$\alpha$ radiation from stars scattering off cold primordial gas, and the relative populations of hyperfine spin states in neutral hydrogen. We present radiometer data measuring the radio sky spectrum between 55 and 85 MHz, demonstrating that the profile previously identified by Bowman et al. using the Experiment to Detect the Global Epoch of Reionization Signature (EDGES) low-band instrument is not of astrophysical origin; their best-fitting profile is rejected with 95.3% confidence. Although this profile was initially interpreted as a signature of the cosmic dawn, its amplitude far exceeded predictions from standard cosmological models. Proposed explanations for this anomaly included non-standard cosmology, additional baryon cooling mechanisms—potentially through interactions with millicharged dark matter—and an excess radio background at redshifts greater than 17. Our non-detection validates earlier concerns and indicates that the profile reported by Bowman et al. does not constitute evidence for new astrophysics or non-standard cosmology.

This paper aims to construct the unification of q-extension Genocchi polynomials and presents several significant relations involving these polynomials. Furthermore, by applying the Mellin transformation to the generating function that interpolates these unification q-extension Genocchi polynomials, we derive q-extensions of Hurwitz-zeta type functions.

This study investigates light scalar mesons using QCD sum rules by constructing both diquark-antidiquark currents, $(qq)(\bar q \bar q)$, and meson-meson currents, $(\bar qq)(\bar qq)$. We identify five independent currents for each configuration and establish the relationships connecting them. Specifically, the five independent meson-meson currents arise from products of either color singlet or color octet $\bar q q$ pairs; however, these can be interrelated through derived equations. Our calculations yield masses for the light scalar mesons that align with experimental observations.

Decision-guided viewpoints on model uncertainty broaden conventional statistical approaches to handling, evaluating, and merging inferences across multiple models. Bayesian predictive decision synthesis (BPDS) strengthens conceptual and theoretical underpinnings while introducing a methodology that explicitly incorporates decision-analytic results into the assessment, comparison, and possible integration of candidate models. Building on recent theoretical and practical progress in both Bayesian predictive synthesis and empirical, goal-oriented model uncertainty analysis, BPDS is facilitated by a new subjective Bayesian framework for weighting models within predictive decision contexts. Applications are demonstrated through real-world scenarios, such as optimal design for regression prediction and sequential time series forecasting for financial portfolio management.

Subwavelength pillar-based optical metasurfaces have enabled versatile control over light's amplitude, phase, and polarization. This study demonstrates that an efficient dielectric metasurface lens can trap and image individual neutral atoms at a working distance of 3 mm. We characterize these high-numerical-aperture optical tweezers using the trapped atoms and validate our findings against numerical simulations of the lens performance. We anticipate that future metasurfaces designed for atom trapping will utilize ongoing advancements in metasurface engineering to facilitate multifunctional control in complex quantum information experiments involving neutral-atom arrays.

The H$\alpha$ equivalent width (EW) serves as an observational indicator for the specific star formation rate (sSFR) and traces episodic star formation. Prior studies indicate a strong anti-correlation between EW and stellar mass, scaling as $M^{-0.25}$, which mirrors the sSFR--mass relationship; however, this link might stem from selection biases. This research examines the correlation between H$\alpha$ EWs and galaxy properties, as well as the impact of selection biases, using a $z = 0.47$ narrowband-selected sample of 1572 H$\alpha$ emitters from the Ly$\alpha$ Galaxies in the Epoch of Reionization (LAGER) survey. Covering 3 deg$^2$ of the COSMOS field and $1.1\times10^5$ cMpc$^3$, the study constructs mock samples based on an intrinsic EW distribution and applies selection criteria to mimic observations, thereby isolating the effects of selection bias. The findings reveal an intrinsic EW--stellar mass correlation of $W_0 \propto M^{-0.16\pm0.03}$, where EW decreases by approximately a factor of three between $10^{7}$ and $10^{10}$ M$_\odot$. Additionally, low-mass H$\alpha$ emitters are roughly 320 times more likely to exhibit rest-frame EWs greater than 200\AA\ than their high-mass counterparts. Integrating the intrinsic EW--mass correlation with the observed star formation function successfully reproduces the observed H$\alpha$ luminosity function, whereas failing to account for selection effects leads to an underestimation of bright H$\alpha$ emitters. This implies that the intrinsic EW--mass correlation is physically meaningful and simultaneously explains three statistical distributions of galaxy populations (luminosity function, star formation function, and EW distribution). Even after correcting for selection effects, high-EW outliers remain more common in low-mass galaxies. Consequently, the results indicate that high sSFR outliers, signaling bursty star formation, are intrinsically more frequent in low-mass H$\alpha$ emitters rather than being artifacts of selection bias.

This work examines recent developments in analyzing the Wang--Landau algorithm, a method for directly estimating the density of states (DOS) via Monte Carlo simulations. For systems with discrete energy levels, we propose an approach utilizing a transition matrix in energy space (TMES) that fully characterizes a random walk biased by Wang--Landau probabilities. The properties of this TMES elucidate specific algorithmic features, such as histogram flatness. We demonstrate that the Wang--Landau probability, when paired with the true DOS, defines a Markov process in energy space, where the inverse spectral gap of the TMES estimates the process's mixing time. We argue that an efficient implementation comprises two stages: an initial Wang--Landau procedure followed by a $1/t$ modification. The mixing time dictates the convergence rate to the true DOS during the second stage, while the convergence parameter is defined by the deviation of the TMES's largest eigenvalue from unity. Finally, the characteristic time for the first stage corresponds to the tunneling time required for the system to access all energy levels.

This note examines a specific class of matrices arising in the numerical approximation of distributed order fractional differential equations (FDEs). While these matrices appear conventional as they are real, symmetric, and positive definite, they pose unique challenges that render classical tools ineffective. Specifically, the matrix sequence is ill-conditioned with respect to matrix size, lacks a single generating function, and instead involves a complex sequence of generating functions. Despite these difficulties, we establish a real interval containing the smallest eigenvalue and analyze its asymptotic behavior. Our derived bounds surpass existing literature, offering more precise spectral data essential for designing fast numerical algorithms to solve the large linear systems associated with distributed order FDEs. The paper includes critically discussed numerical results and concludes with a section on findings and open problems.

We present an end-to-end platform designed for precise brain activity recognition by integrating multiple processing tiers. The system ingests massive electroencephalogram (EEG) datasets, initially converting time-frequency spectrograms into episode-wise feature matrices, designated as tier-1. A subsequent tier employs a spiking neural network (SNN) to extract essential information from sparse features via spike-streams, thereby preserving the temporal dynamics inherent to EEG signals. Tier-3 then transforms these spike patterns across time and spatial domains, feeding the resulting matrices into a specialized artificial neural network (specifically a Transformer) at tier-4. This fourth tier utilizes a unique spanning topology to accommodate the two-dimensional input structure, enabling high-accuracy cognitive tasks such as classification. As a proof-of-concept, the platform addresses sleep stage scoring using extensive EEG datasets, including a record of 42,560 hours from 5,793 subjects. Experimental results demonstrate that our system achieves an overall accuracy of 87% using only EEG data, surpassing state-of-the-art methods by 2%. Furthermore, the proposed multi-tier methodology provides interpretable, graphical insights into the temporal characteristics of EEG by identifying critical episodes, a capability essential for neurodynamics but often absent in traditional cognitive frameworks.

We suggest employing trapped electrons as high-$Q$ resonators to detect meV-scale dark photon dark matter. When the dark photon's rest energy aligns with the energy gap between the two lowest cyclotron levels, it resonantly excites the electron's first cyclotron excited state. A proof-of-principle experiment using a single electron confirmed that this approach is background-free over a 7.4-day observation period. This study establishes a limit on dark photon dark matter at 148 GHz (0.6 meV), improving upon prior constraints by a factor of approximately 75. Furthermore, dark photon dark matter within the 0.1–1 meV mass range (corresponding to 20–200 GHz) could likely be detected with comparable sensitivity using an apparatus specifically designed for such dark photon searches.

Predicting molecular properties, such as energy, is a critical challenge in chemistry and biology. However, many supervised learning approaches struggle with the scarcity of labeled molecules in chemical space, as these labels typically require computationally expensive Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations. An effective remedy is to integrate unlabeled molecules using semi-supervised learning. Nevertheless, learning semi-supervised representations for vast molecular datasets remains difficult due to the dual challenge of jointly capturing molecular essence and structure, as well as the conflict between representation learning and property prediction. To address this, we introduce Active Semi-supervised Graph Neural Network (ASGN), a novel framework that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data. ASGN utilizes a teacher-student architecture: the teacher model employs a new semi-supervised method to derive general representations that combine structural and distributional information, while the student model focuses on property prediction to resolve learning conflicts. Furthermore, we propose a novel active learning strategy based on molecular diversity to select informative samples throughout the training process. Extensive experiments on multiple public datasets demonstrate the framework's remarkable performance.

This paper presents DIRECTGO, a novel MATLAB toolbox designed for derivative-free global optimization. It aggregates multiple deterministic DIRECT-type algorithms capable of handling box-constrained, generally-constrained, and problems with hidden constraints. Every sequential algorithm in the toolbox is available in two implementations: one utilizing static data structures and another using dynamic ones to enhance information storage and organization efficiency. Moreover, parallel processing schemes have been integrated into several promising algorithms. The toolbox includes a graphical user interface (GUI) to facilitate user-friendly access to all its features. These capabilities are validated through extensive computational studies employing the comprehensive DIRECTGOLib v1.0 library of global optimization test functions. Additionally, eleven classical engineering design problems demonstrate DIRECTGO's effectiveness in addressing complex real-world challenges. Finally, the appendix provides examples of supplementary MATLAB code and outlines its application on test problems involving both box and general constraints.

The question of whether late-time modifications to the Universe's dynamics can resolve the $H_0$ tension has been widely debated, while alternative arguments suggest the tension actually lies within the supernova absolute magnitude, $M_B$. In this study, we rigorously constrain $M_B$ by analyzing Pantheon Type Ia Supernova (SN) data alongside Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO) and Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) observations. We then evaluate the $M_B$ tension across three theoretical frameworks: standard $\Lambda$CDM, $w$CDM, and an IDE model featuring non-gravitational interactions between dark energy and dark matter. Our findings indicate that the IDE model successfully resolves the $M_B$ tension with a non-zero coupling strength at 95% confidence level, a result that aligns with previous analyses utilizing an $H_0$ prior.

This paper demonstrates that k-dimensional spherical integrals are asymptotically equivalent to the product of their 1-dimensional counterparts. This finding enables the extension of several large deviations principles in random matrix theory, which were previously established solely for one-dimensional cases. Specifically, we examine the universality of large deviations for the k largest eigenvalues of Wigner matrices (as well as Wishart matrices and matrices with general variance profiles) featuring sharp sub-Gaussian entries, alongside the large deviations principles governing extreme eigenvalues of Gaussian Wigner and Wishart matrices subject to finite-dimensional perturbations.

Although there has been remarkable success in rapidly developing effective vaccines against Cov-SARS-2, global vaccination initiatives are hindered by disparities in distribution and public acceptance, resulting in inadequate herd immunity. While current research primarily focuses on modeling vaccine acceptance through social-demographic factors, the specific characteristics of this acceptance remain poorly understood, particularly regarding the impact of information diffusion. This study investigates the influence of information spread on vaccine acceptance by creating a comprehensive agent-based computational model. This approach addresses the complexities associated with socio-demographics, vaccine types, population statistics, and information propagation. Calibrated using vaccine acceptance survey data from Canadian provinces and territories, our analysis provides robust evidence that information dissemination significantly affects acceptance rates. Specifically, the spread of negative narratives about COVID-19 vaccines can generate substantial hesitancy, undermining the objective of achieving high public immunity. These findings suggest that addressing vaccine hesitancy requires a greater focus on individual opinions and behaviors.

This study investigates the branching ratios for the decays $B^{0}_{s}\rightarrow a_{0}(980)[ \rightarrow K\overline{K}, \pi\eta]a_{0}(980)$, $B^{0}_{s} \rightarrow f_{0}(980)[ \rightarrow \pi^{+}\pi^{-}, K^{+}K^{-}]f_{0}(980)$, and $B^{0}_{s} \rightarrow f_{0}(500)[ \rightarrow \pi^{+}\pi^{-}]f_{0}(500)$ using the perturbative QCD (pQCD) framework, treating the scalar mesons $a_{0}(980)$, $f_{0}(980)$, and $f_{0}(500)$ as the lowest-lying $q\overline{q}$ states. Accounting for the mixing between $f_{0}(980)$ and $f_{0}(500)$ within the SU(3) nonet to ensure more reliable results, we calculate with mixing angles $\theta$ ranging from $[15^{\circ}, 82^{\circ}]$ and $[105^{\circ}, 171^{\circ}]$. Leveraging isospin symmetry, we also predict the branching ratios for the $B^{0}_{s} \rightarrow f_{0}(980)[ \rightarrow \pi^{0}\pi^{0}]f_{0}(980)$ and $B^{0}_{s} \rightarrow f_{0}(500)[ \rightarrow \pi^{0}\pi^{0}]f_{0}(500)$ processes. Our findings indicate that the branching ratios for $B^{0}_{s}\rightarrow a_{0}(980)[ \rightarrow K\overline{K}, \pi\eta]a_{0}(980)$ are significantly smaller, whereas the rates for $B^{0}_{s} \rightarrow f_{0}(980)[ \rightarrow \pi\pi, K\overline{K}]f_{0}(980)$ and $B^{0}_{s} \rightarrow f_{0}(500)[ \rightarrow \pi\pi]f_{0}(500)$ fall within the $10^{-6}\sim10^{-5}$ range, making them promising candidates for verification by the LHCb and Belle II experiments.

This paper introduces a training strategy for convolutional neural networks designed to mitigate interference caused by competing hypotheses regarding inter-categorical information. Rooted in the concept of feature binding—the integration of spatial and layer-wise activations to ensure correct inferences—we apply this to dense image labeling by blending images via categorical clustering or category co-occurrence likelihood. A feature binding network is then trained to simultaneously segment and separate these blended images. Following feature denoising to eliminate noisy activations, we observe enhanced desirable properties and high prediction accuracy. Ultimately, we demonstrate a novel mechanism that improves base segmentation and saliency network performance while bolstering robustness against adversarial attacks, distinct from existing methods.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) rely on layers of neurons linked by synaptic weights, where high bit-precision is typically necessary to ensure accuracy across various applications, and minimizing error accumulation between layers is crucial for scaling these networks. However, current photonic neural network demonstrations face limitations in bit-precision due to crosstalk and the high sensitivity of optical components like resonators. In this study, we experimentally achieve a record-high precision of 9 bits for photonic synapses using a dithering control scheme. Furthermore, numerical simulations illustrate how increased synaptic precision impacts a wireless signal classification task. This research supports the practical realization of photonic neural networks for numerous real-world applications.

This study addresses the learning of product graphs from multi-attribute graph signals, driven by the prevalence of multilayer networks exhibiting interactions both within and across layers. Concentrating on product graphs with homogeneous layers, we introduce a bivariate polynomial graph filter model. To tackle topology inference, we adapt established spectral methods, proposing two approaches for the necessary spectral estimation: a simplified technique that unfolds multi-attribute data into matrices, and an exact method utilizing nearest Kronecker product decomposition (NKD). Notably, we demonstrate that while strong inter-layer coupling can impair the unfolding approach, the NKD method remains robust against such coupling. Numerical experiments confirm the effectiveness of these proposed techniques.

The solution to the wave equation for a Cauchy problem with initial conditions at $t=0$ is exclusively retarded. Likewise, in quantum radiation theory, defining Heisenberg picture photon creation and annihilation operators at $t>0$ via their $t=0$ counterparts inherently produces purely retarded source fields. Nevertheless, we demonstrate that two-time quantum correlations between the retarded source fields of a stationary dipole and the quantum vacuum contain advanced wave-like components. Although advanced in nature, these correlations remain fully consistent with Einstein causality. While they do not significantly impact photo-detection amplitudes in the vacuum state, they do influence the statistics of measurements concerning the radiative force on a point charge within the dipole's field. Specifically, the dispersion in the charge's momentum is observed to grow over time. This finding suggests the potential for direct experimental verification of advanced waves in physical reality and offers another signature of the quantum nature of the vacuum.

This study examines the dynamics of G band bright points (GBPs) in the quiet Sun to characterize distinct motion patterns. Utilizing a high-resolution image sequence from the Hinode/Solar Optical Telescope (SOT), GBPs are automatically identified by segmenting three-dimensional evolutionary structures within a space-time cube. Following the exclusion of stationary GBPs, the remaining non-stationary points are classified into three categories using a motion-type index: straight motion for those traveling in linear or near-linear paths, rotary motion for those following curved trajectories, and erratic motion for the remainder. The average horizontal velocities for straight, erratic, and rotary motions are 2.18 km/s, 1.33 km/s, and 1.63 km/s, respectively. Observations indicate that GBPs moving in straight lines maintain a higher, constant velocity throughout their lifespan, whereas those on rotary paths exhibit lower, variable velocities. Regarding diffusion processes, straight motion displays ballistic diffusion, erratic motion shows super-diffusion, and rotary motion exhibits sub-diffusion. The corresponding diffusion indices and coefficients are 2.13 and 850 km²/s for straight motion, 1.82 and 331 km²/s for erratic motion, and 0.73 and 13 km²/s for rotary motion. In terms of direction, the motion is homogeneous and isotropic, typically persisting between adjacent frames regardless of the specific motion type.

The Free Energy Principle (FEP) posits that, under conditions of weak coupling, random dynamical systems possessing ample degrees of freedom act to minimize variational free energy, which serves as an upper bound on surprisal (also known as self-information). This bound functions as a measure of Bayesian prediction error; conversely, its negative provides a lower bound on Bayesian model evidence, or marginal likelihood. Essentially, specific random dynamical systems exhibit a form of self-evidencing. In this work, we recast the FEP within the framework of scale-free, spacetime-independent quantum information theory. We demonstrate that generic quantum systems can be viewed as observers, and under the standard assumption of free choice, as agents capable of imbuing observational outcomes with semantic meaning. Furthermore, we illustrate how these agents reduce Bayesian prediction error when operating in uncertain environments marked by limited learning capacity and quantum contextuality. We establish that the quantum formulation of the FEP is asymptotically equivalent to the Principle of Unitarity. Based on these findings, we propose that biological systems utilize quantum coherence not only as a computational asset but also, implicitly, as a communication resource. Finally, we outline several avenues for future inquiry, with a specific focus on the resources necessary for classical communication and for identifying and reacting to quantum context switches.

The COVID-19 pandemic has drastically altered transportation systems both qualitatively and quantitatively, rendering existing networks obsolete. This paper investigates identifying an optimal subnetwork that ensures three conditions: (i) the shortest access time from any urban node to the new network remains comparable to the original system; (ii) the delay introduced by removing nodes does not exceed acceptable limits for any given itinerary; and (iii) the total number of nodes is reduced by at least a specified factor. A solution is deemed optimal if it minimizes the overall global delay. We formulate this challenge as a Mixed Integer Linear Program and subsequently apply the model to a real-world case study of Lyon's bus network.

Following the initial detection of a fast radio burst (FRB) in 2007 and their subsequent confirmation as a plentiful extragalactic phenomenon in 2013, research into these sources has accelerated dramatically. Our 2019 review described a burgeoning yet enigmatic population comprising 60 distinct sources, two repeaters, and a single identified host galaxy. However, within just a few years, enhanced observations and new discoveries have yielded a vast amount of data. The catalog of FRBs now exceeds 600 published sources, includes 24 repeaters, and identifies 19 host galaxies. Improvements in time resolution, continuous monitoring, and precise localization have deepened our understanding of repeater behavior, host galaxies, burst morphology, source activity, progenitor models, and the potential of FRBs as cosmological tools. Notably, the recent detection of a luminous FRB-like event from the Galactic magnetar SGR~1935+2154 establishes a crucial connection between FRBs and magnetars. Other unexpected findings include periodic activity modulation in repeaters and the localization of an FRB source to a nearby globular cluster within the M81 galaxy. This review summarizes these compelling recent observational results and underscores their significance for refining our knowledge of the FRB population and theoretical progenitor models. Building upon the foundational introduction to FRBs from our earlier work, we update readers on the latest findings and explore promising future directions as the field transitions into an era where hundreds to thousands of new FRBs are discovered and reported annually.

Simulation models addressing complex dynamics in both natural and social sciences often lack a tractable likelihood function, making traditional likelihood-based statistical inference unfeasible. Recent machine learning advancements have introduced new algorithms to estimate these previously intractable likelihoods by employing a likelihood ratio trick grounded in binary classifiers. This enables the derivation of efficient likelihood approximations whenever high-quality probabilistic classifiers are available. We propose a kernel classifier designed for sequential data that utilizes path signatures derived from the recently developed signature kernel. Our findings indicate that the representational capacity of signatures results in a highly effective classifier, particularly when sample sizes are limited. In such low-data scenarios, our method can surpass sophisticated neural networks in common posterior inference tasks.

The varied near-Earth radiation landscape, driven by cosmic rays and solar activity, significantly influences human civilization. Given the rising trend in air travel, understanding the specific radiation dose impacts on the human body during flights is crucial. This study employs the Geant4 toolkit via Monte Carlo simulations to quantify radiation exposure at aviation altitudes, accounting for the protective shielding of aircraft structures. The simulation incorporates a precise 3D model of the atmosphere and geomagnetic field, an updated profile of incoming cosmic ray particles, and relevant physics processes. To calculate effective doses, we utilized quasi-realistic computational phantoms representing male and female human bodies, alongside a simplified mathematical model of a Boeing 777-200LR to analyze shielding effects. Radiation environments were simulated at cruising altitudes across geomagnetic latitudes of 45°–50° and at various points within the aircraft fuselage. Subsequently, dose rates for different organs were computed for both phantoms in accordance with the latest guidelines from the International Commission on Radiological Protection. Results indicate a sex-averaged effective dose rate of 5.46 μSv/h. When calculating the weighted sum of equivalent dose contributions separately, the female phantom received 5.72 μSv/h, while the male phantom received 5.20 μSv/h. Furthermore, the simulation quantified the production of numerous cosmogenic radionuclides within the phantoms through activation and spallation processes, which could lead to long-term biological effects.

Research on decision-making impacts has predominantly examined decision fairness, the long-term consequences of decision pipelines, and utility-based perspectives for both decision-makers and individuals. Conversely, there has been little attention paid to precarity, a concept that captures the instability in people's lives, where negative outcomes can cascade into other areas of well-being. Investigating precarity requires shifting the analytical lens from the decision-maker to the decision subject. Prioritizing this subject is a crucial direction that emphasizes moving beyond aggregate measures to analyze the long-term effects of decision-making. To address this gap, we propose a modeling framework that simulates how compounded decision-making influences precarity over time. Our simulations demonstrate the heterogeneity of precarity, revealing how negative decisions produce non-uniform, ruinous aftereffects across different income classes within the population, and illustrate how policy interventions can mitigate these impacts.

We derive geodesic normal forms for the general series of complex reflection groups G(de,e,n) by leveraging the presentations of Corran-Picantin and Corran-Lee-Lee for G(e,e,n) and G(de,e,n) (where d > 1), respectively. This process necessitates developing a combinatorial method to explicitly identify minimal word representatives for the elements of G(de,e,n). By utilizing these geodesic normal forms, we establish natural bases for the Hecke algebras linked to the complex reflection groups G(e,e,n) and G(d,1,n). Furthermore, as an application, we provide a novel proof of the BMR freeness conjecture for these groups.

This study establishes, for the first time, the existence of a non-trivial, positive, and bounded critical traveling wave solution within a diffusive disease model featuring a reaction system with infinitely many equilibria. This finding resolves an open problem previously posed in [X. Wang, H. Wang, J. Wu, Traveling waves of diffusive predator-prey systems: disease outbreak propagation, Discrete Contin. Dyn. Syst. Ser. A 32 (2012) 3303-3324]. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the critical traveling wave in this model exhibits a hybrid nature, combining characteristics of both front and pulse types.

Lidar data enables the creation of point clouds essential for navigating autonomous vehicles and mobile robots. Scan matching, which calculates the optimal rigid transformation to align two point clouds, serves as the foundation for lidar odometry, a dead reckoning technique especially valuable when absolute sensors like GPS are unavailable. This paper introduces the Iterative Closest Ellipsoidal Transform (ICET), a scan matching algorithm that offers two novel enhancements over the current state-of-the-art Normal Distributions Transform (NDT). Similar to NDT, ICET partitions lidar data into voxels and fits Gaussian distributions to points within them. Its first innovation mitigates geometric ambiguity on large flat surfaces by suppressing solutions along those directions. The second innovation involves inferring the output error covariance for the position and orientation transformation between consecutive point clouds; this covariance is highly beneficial when ICET is integrated into state-estimation frameworks such as an extended Kalman filter. We conducted a 2D simulation comparing ICET and NDT performance, both with and without geometric ambiguity, demonstrating that ICET yields superior estimates while accurately predicting solution accuracy.

This study investigates the analytic characteristics of the density function $h(x;\gamma,\alpha)$ defined for $x \in (0,\infty)$, $\gamma > 0$, and $0 < \alpha < 1$. This function emerges from the domain of attraction problem concerning a statistic that bridges the gap between the supremum and the sum of random variables. Within this framework, $\alpha$ governs the interpolation between these two extremes, while $\gamma$ specifies the underlying extreme value distribution. Specifically, when $\alpha = 0$, the Fréchet density is obtained; conversely, at $\alpha = 1$, the result corresponds to a specific Fox H-function, representing a natural generalization of hypergeometric functions within fractional calculus. However, for intermediate values of $\alpha$, a previously unknown function arises, distinct from existing hypergeometric extensions. We provide series, integral, and continued fraction representations for this novel function.

Throughout history, numerous datasets have been created for different object detection applications. While maritime object detection is critical for ensuring ship safety and navigation, a significant shortage of large-scale, publicly accessible datasets exists in this specific field. To address this gap, we introduce KOLOMVERSE, an open-source, large-scale image dataset developed by KRISO (Korea Research Institute of Ships and Ocean Engineering) for maritime object detection. This collection comprises approximately 2,151,470 images at 4K resolution, derived from 5,845 hours of video footage recorded across 21 territorial waters in South Korea. Following a rigorous data quality assessment, the dataset captures a wide array of environmental conditions, including variations in weather, time of day, illumination, occlusion, viewpoints, background complexity, wind speed, and visibility. It features five distinct object classes: ships, buoys, fishnet buoys, lighthouses, and wind farms. With image dimensions of 3840×2160 pixels, KOLOMVERSE represents, to our knowledge, the largest publicly available resource for maritime object detection. We conducted object detection experiments using several pre-trained state-of-the-art architectures to validate the dataset's effectiveness and utility. The dataset can be accessed at: \url{https://github.com/MaritimeDataset/KOLOMVERSE}.

To genuinely understand reasoning capabilities, Natural Language Inference models must be assessed using counterfactual data. TabPert supports this by aiding in the creation of such data to evaluate issues within model tabular reasoning. The tool enables users to modify tables, alter their associated hypotheses and labels, and emphasize rows critical for hypothesis classification. Furthermore, TabPert records details regarding the automatic table generation techniques and the strategies used to formulate challenging hypotheses. These counterfactual tables, hypotheses, and accompanying metadata can subsequently be utilized to systematically and quantitatively investigate the limitations of existing models.

Timely identification of cardiovascular conditions is vital for successful treatment, with electrocardiograms (ECG) serving as a cornerstone for diagnosis. Recently, Deep Learning techniques for classifying ECG signals have advanced to match the diagnostic accuracy of cardiologists. While clinicians typically rely on standard 12-channel ECG recordings, the automatic analysis of these multi-channel datasets remains underexplored, highlighting the necessity for a multi-channel approach. We introduce a model that capitalizes on the data from standard 12-channel ECGs to identify patterns at the beat, rhythm, and individual channel levels. Experimental evaluation on the PTB-XL dataset demonstrates that our model achieved a macro-averaged ROC-AUC of 0.9216, an average accuracy of 88.85%, and a peak F1 score of 0.8057. Furthermore, we validated the model's correctness and practical utility by comparing its attention visualization outputs against established cardiologist guidelines.

This study examines the finite temperature Casimir effect arising from a massive, charged scalar field that induces Lorentz violation in a CPT-even, aether-like manner. The analysis covers parallel plates subject to Dirichlet and mixed (Dirichlet-Neumann) boundary conditions, omitting pure Neumann conditions as they yield identical outcomes to Dirichlet ones. Employing the $\zeta$-function method, the research derives the Helmholtz free energy and Casimir pressure under a uniform magnetic field oriented perpendicular to the plates. Three distinct scenarios of Lorentz asymmetry are explored: timelike, spacelike and perpendicular to the magnetic field, and spacelike and parallel to it. For each asymmetry type and boundary condition combination, asymptotic limits involving small plate separations, high temperatures, strong magnetic fields, and large masses are analyzed. Consequently, simple yet highly precise analytic expressions for thermal corrections to Casimir energy and pressure are derived, revealing that these corrections are significantly influenced by the orientation of the unit vector responsible for breaking Lorentz symmetry.

Segmenting renal compartments from abdominal CTA images aims to reconstruct their three-dimensional structures, a critical step for diagnosing and treating kidney conditions. However, this deep-learning task is hindered by ambiguous boundaries, delicate structures, and significant anatomical variations in 3D kidney CT scans. To address these challenges, we introduce the Cycle Prototype Network, a novel weakly supervised learning framework. This approach features three key innovations: First, Cycle Prototype Learning (CPL) ensures generalization by deriving pseudo labels via a forward process and applying consistency regularization in reverse, rendering the model robust to noise and highly label-efficient. Second, the Bayes Weakly Supervised Module (BWSM) leverages cross-period prior knowledge to extract insights from unlabeled data across different time points, automatically correcting errors to produce precise pseudo labels. Third, the Fine Decoding Feature Extractor (FDFE) enhances fine-grained feature extraction by integrating global morphological context with local details to generate feature maps with sharp boundaries, enabling accurate segmentation of thin structures. Using only four labeled images, our model achieves Dice scores of 79.1% and 78.7%, representing a substantial 20% improvement over the standard prototype model, PANet.

The "reproducibility crisis" has recently sparked intense controversy, debate, and demands for institutional reform within science. To address both current challenges and future hurdles, I propose establishing a novel research organization dedicated to randomly auditing the scientific literature. I suggest that analyzing a digitized scientific corpus through data analytics could empower broadly trained scientists to pinpoint critical results worthy of deeper investigation across all fields. Furthermore, I contend that a brief pilot program involving a small group of researchers acting as a simplified auditing firm would offer valuable insights into the practical viability of this initiative.

Quantum theory presents a transformative framework for information processing, but converting its mathematical foundations into practical algorithms demands highly complex systems with minimal error rates. These systems require robust hardware capable of coherent storage, processing, and retrieval of data, alongside effective quantum error correction (QEC) protocols to identify and mitigate faults. Circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) emerges as a promising platform for building such resilient quantum devices. Specifically, bosonic encoding schemes within cQED—which utilize multi-photon states in superconducting cavities to store information—have demonstrated significant success in achieving hardware-efficient QEC. This review examines recent advancements in both the theoretical and practical aspects of QEC using bosonic codes, highlighting progress toward realizing fault-tolerant quantum information processing with cQED technology.

This paper investigates the Helmholtz transmission eigenvalue problem within inhomogeneous anisotropic media where the refractive index $n(x)$ equals 1, covering both two and three dimensions. Building upon a nonlinear fourth-order formulation introduced by Cakoni, Colton, and Haddar [2009], we introduce auxiliary variables to derive an equivalent mixed formulation and subsequently apply finite element discretization. We rigorously demonstrate that the proposed scheme achieves optimal convergence rates for transmission eigenvalues across both convex and nonconvex domains. However, the resulting sparse generalized eigenvalue problem is so large, even on coarse meshes, that the smallest real eigenvalues cannot be computed using the shift-and-invert method. To address this, we partially resolve the issue by deflating the vast majority of the $\infty$ eigenvalues, which possess huge multiplicity. This approach drastically reduces the matrix size while maintaining sparsity. Finally, extensive numerical examples are provided to validate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed methodology.

The decay channels $B\rightarrow D_{\left(s\right)}^{\left(*\right)}h$ (where $h=\pi,\rho$) are analyzed within the confined covariant quark model under the naive factorization hypothesis. Our findings indicate that the calculated branching fractions consistently surpass experimental measurements, a trend previously documented by other researchers for analogous processes.

Accurately forecasting the future movements of road users is a pivotal component of autonomous driving systems. This study tackles the challenge of generating scene-level, joint trajectory predictions within multi-agent driving environments. We introduce FJMP, a Factorized Joint Motion Prediction framework designed for interactive multi-agent scenarios. FJMP represents future scene interaction dynamics as a sparse directed graph, with edges signifying explicit agent interactions. By pruning this graph into a directed acyclic graph (DAG), we decompose the joint prediction task into a series of marginal and conditional predictions based on the DAG's partial ordering, utilizing a directed acyclic graph neural network (DAGNN) to decode the joint future trajectories. Experiments conducted on the INTERACTION and Argoverse 2 datasets show that FJMP yields more accurate and scene-consistent joint trajectory predictions compared to non-factorized methods, particularly for highly interactive and kinematically complex agents. Consequently, FJMP achieves the top rank on the multi-agent test leaderboard for the INTERACTION dataset.

**Background:** Creating computationally manageable models for atomic nuclei has been a primary objective in nuclear structure physics. While the configuration-interaction shell model (SM) offers a flexible framework capable of incorporating excited states and many-body correlations, its basis size grows exponentially, necessitating an efficient truncation method that ideally accounts for both deformation and pairing effects.

**Purpose:** This study introduces a streamlined truncation approach for the SM. The method begins with a pair condensate derived variationally from Hartree-Fock single-particle states within the particle-number conserved Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (NBCS) approximation, followed by the projection of states possessing definite angular momentum.

**Methods:** The procedure involves generating Hartree-Fock single-particle states with Kramers degeneracy within an SM space. Subsequently, pair amplitudes in the NBCS are optimized by minimizing energy, and states with good angular momentum are constructed using linear algebra projection (LAP). Both the NBCS and LAP techniques are computationally efficient.

**Results:** The calculations demonstrate strong agreement with full configuration-interaction SM results for low-lying states in transitional and rotational nuclei exhibiting axially symmetric or triaxial deformation across medium- and heavy-mass regions, specifically $^{44,46,48}$Ti, $^{48,50}$Cr, $^{52}$Fe, $^{60,62,64}$Zn, $^{66,68}$Ge, $^{68}$Se, and $^{108,110}$Xe. Additionally, the method successfully predicts low-lying states for $^{112-114}\textrm{Ba}$ and $^{116-120}\textrm{Ce}$, systems that are typically inaccessible via large-scale SM computations.

**Conclusions:** The findings indicate that both pair correlations and configuration mixing among various intrinsic states are essential for accurately modeling collectivity and shape coexistence, thereby validating the effectiveness of this truncation scheme for investigating transitional and deformed nuclei.

Hybrid quantum systems, comprising an ensemble of two-level systems coupled to a single-mode electromagnetic field, are pivotal for advancing quantum information processors and related devices. These systems are defined by energy level hybridizations separated by collective Lamb shifts that emerge during coherent interaction between the ensemble and the field mode at high cooperativity. However, calculating the complete set of Lamb shifts is typically infeasible due to the high dimensionality of many such devices. This work introduces techniques enabling a compact representation of Lamb shift statistics across all collective angular momentum subspaces of the ensemble without imposing restrictive approximations on the state space. We apply these methods to analyze the Lamb shift within every subspace and excitation manifold, as well as to characterize the average observed Lamb shift weighted by the degeneracies of all subspaces.

Inspired by the initial research of Gilbarg and Weinberger regarding the asymptotic behavior of steady plane solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations near infinity \cite{GW1978}, we examine these properties for solutions defined on a half-neighborhood of infinity that possess a finite Dirichlet integral and satisfy the Navier-slip boundary condition. Our findings indicate that the solution's velocity increases at a rate slower than $\sqrt{\log r}$, and the pressure approaches zero along every ray originating from the center.

Accurate localization is critical for numerous modern applications involving Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) and Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), offering significant benefits in control, safety, and power efficiency. The widespread deployment of 5G New Radio (NR) cellular networks presents new avenues for enhancing the localization capabilities of these vehicles. This paper reviews radio frequency (RF) based localization approaches, examining specific RF features and investigating current methods applicable to unmanned vehicles, categorized into range-based and fingerprinting techniques. Furthermore, the study analyzes existing state-of-the-art literature on RF localization for both UAVs and UGVs, explores the potential of 5G NR to improve localization, and outlines future research directions.
Marking fifty years of partnership and camaraderie with Chris Isham.

Federated Edge Learning (FEEL) often causes energy-constrained edge devices to deplete their power reserves due to the high energy costs of training and uploading local machine learning models, thereby shortening their operational lifespan. To address this, we introduce novel strategies for energy-efficient FEEL that jointly optimize local training data, available computational and communication resources, and round deadline constraints to minimize energy usage. The proposed system model features an edge server with multiple antennas utilizing beamforming and orthogonal channels to communicate with local users. Our objective is to determine optimal user resources—including fine-grained selection of relevant training samples, bandwidth, transmission power, beamforming weights, and processing speeds—to achieve minimum total energy consumption within a specified deadline for FEEL rounds. We develop tractable solutions by first introducing a new fine-grained training algorithm that filters out less relevant samples to retain only those enhancing model performance. Subsequently, we derive closed-form solutions and employ a Golden-Section-based iterative algorithm to identify the optimal computation and communication resources for energy minimization. Experimental results using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets show that our algorithms significantly outperform state-of-the-art methods, reducing energy consumption by 79% for MNIST and 73% for CIFAR-10.

This study examines how boundary impurities influence entanglement entropy within an antiferromagnetic Heisenberg open spin-1/2 chain. Utilizing the density-matrix renormalization-group technique to calculate bipartite entanglement, the findings indicate that entropy rises as the subsystem length grows, eventually stabilizing at a constant value for very large system sizes. Furthermore, under identical impurity interaction conditions, spin-1 qutrit impurities are shown to enhance the entanglement entropy.

This paper centers on a classical tracking model based on subspace learning, which operates under the assumption that targets in consecutive frames exist within a low-dimensional subspace or manifold because of their visual similarity. Although various subspace trackers have recently been developed with impressive outcomes, this work is motivated by findings that tracking accuracy improves when utilizing a discriminative subspace learned from recently localized targets and their immediate backgrounds. Consequently, the study addresses the challenge of learning a robust, low-dimensional subspace capable of accurately and discriminatively representing both target and background samples. To achieve this, a discriminative method that effectively distinguishes the target from its surroundings is integrated into the subspace learning process through joint learning, resulting in a dimension-adaptive subspace with enhanced discrimination capabilities. The proposed approach undergoes extensive evaluation and comparison against state-of-the-art trackers on four widely used benchmarks. The experimental results indicate that the new tracker performs competitively, specifically surpassing existing subspace trackers by over 9% in performance.

Extending the worldline effective field theory (EFT) formalism for spinning bodies from the Post-Newtonian regime to Post-Minkowskian (PM) dynamics, we establish a manifestly covariant framework that incorporates rotational degrees of freedom. We present a systematic method for calculating the total momentum and spin changes during the gravitational scattering of compact objects. Specifically, for configurations where spins are aligned with orbital angular momentum, we demonstrate the construction of radial actions for elliptic-like orbits via the Boundary-to-Bound correspondence. As a key example, we solve the scattering problem to next-to-leading PM order, including linear and bilinear spin effects with arbitrary initial conditions, thereby incorporating finite-size corrections for the first time. From the resulting scattering data, we derive the aligned-spin radial action, as well as the periastron advance and binding energy for circular orbits. Additionally, we provide the square of the center-of-mass momentum up to ${\cal O}(G^2)$, enabling Hamiltonian reconstruction. Our findings align perfectly with existing literature while advancing the understanding of PM dynamics for compact binaries at quadratic spin order.

Accurately treating d electrons is crucial for predicting the electronic properties of prototype chalcopyrite semiconductors. The influence of d states correlates with the anion displacement parameter $u$, which directly affects the bandgap of these materials. While semilocal exchange-correlation functionals often provide good structural predictions for semiconductors and insulators, they frequently fail to estimate reasonable values for $u$ due to bandgap underestimation caused by the strong interaction between d electrons. This study demonstrates that the meta-generalized gradient approximation (meta-GGA) derived from cuspless hydrogen density (MGGAC) [Phys. Rev. B 100, 155140 (2019)] offers an improved approach to capturing the essential electronic features of chalcopyrites, with bandgaps comparable to those from state-of-the-art hybrid methods. Furthermore, the assessment highlights the significance of the Pauli kinetic energy enhancement factor, $\alpha=(\tau-\tau^W)/\tau^{unif}$, in describing d electrons within these systems. The findings strongly suggest that the MGGAC functional, operating within semilocal approximations, is a superior and preferred option for investigating chalcopyrites and other solid-state systems, owing to its enhanced performance and significantly reduced computational cost.

Non-deterministic recursion schemes recognize languages of finite trees. This highly expressive model can simulate, among other things, higher-order pushdown automata equipped with collapse. We demonstrate the decidability of the diagonal problem for these schemes. This finding yields several significant implications; notably, it provides an algorithm to compute the downward closure of word languages recognized by such schemes. Consequently, this enables immediate applications to separability issues and the reachability analysis of concurrent systems.

This paper establishes sharp maximum principles, specifically characterizing the geometric structure of minimum sets for supersolutions of equations governed by the $k$-th fractional truncated Laplacian or the $k$-th fractional eigenvalue. These are fully nonlinear integral operators characterized by a nonlocality of $k$-dimensional nature.

This research examines Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) that are weakly interacting components of an Electroweak multiplet. Specifically, we focus on real SU(2) representations with zero hypercharge, which naturally evade direct detection limits arising from tree-level Z-boson exchange. For the first time, we calculate all thermal masses for both scalar and fermionic WIMPs, incorporating Sommerfeld enhancement and bound state formation at leading order in gauge boson exchange and emission. Our analysis demonstrates that WIMP masses in the few hundred TeV range remain consistent with s-wave unitarity constraints on the annihilation cross-section and perturbative limits. We also quantify theory uncertainties for all multiplets, noting that these uncertainties become substantial for large SU(2) multiplets. Finally, we propose a strategy for investigating these scenarios at future experimental facilities. Electroweak 3-plets and 5-plets, with masses reaching approximately 16 TeV, could be effectively detected at a high-energy muon collider. We analyze various experimental signatures, including single and double gauge boson emission accompanied by missing energy, as well as disappearing tracks, and determine the necessary collider energy and luminosity to probe thermal Dark Matter masses. While larger multiplets remain beyond the reach of any realistic future collider, they could potentially be tested using future gamma-ray telescopes and large-exposure liquid Xenon detectors.

This study examines a magnetoelectric effect based on the Katsura-Nagaosa-Balatsky mechanism within a spin-1/2 $XY$ chain subjected to a transverse magnetic field. By selecting a specific spatial orientation for the electric field, the model is solved exactly using free spinless fermions. The analysis also covers the simplest quantum spin chain exhibiting this effect: the zero-temperature spin-1/2 $XX$ chain in a transverse magnetic field under the Katsura-Nagaosa-Balatsky mechanism. This model features the most straightforward forms for magnetization, polarization, and susceptibility functions, with their dependence on electric and magnetic fields expressed in a simple manner. For arbitrary $XY$ anisotropy, a non-monotonic relationship between magnetization and the anisotropy parameter is identified. This irregular behavior is controlled by a critical point associated with the system's ability to transition between gapped and gapless states via the electric field. Furthermore, singularities in the magnetoelectric susceptibility at critical parameter values are demonstrated.

Traditionally, the compilation of commonsense knowledge in AI has relied on manual efforts, but recent developments in web data processing now facilitate automated methods. This demonstration presents three systems for the automatic construction of commonsense knowledge bases, each emphasizing a distinct area of interest for data management. First, Quasimodo is utilized to demonstrate knowledge extraction systems engineering; second, Dice illustrates how schema constraints aid in cleaning fuzzy commonsense knowledge; and third, Ascent highlights the importance of conceptual modeling. These demonstrations can be accessed online at https://quasimodo.r2.enst.fr, https://dice.mpi-inf.mpg.de, and ascent.mpi-inf.mpg.de.

Tracking Lagrangian coherent structures is crucial for various fields, including meteorology and oceanography. This paper introduces a collaborative robotic control framework aimed at following stable and unstable manifolds. Unlike methods requiring global fluid dynamics data, this approach relies on local sensing, prediction, and correction mechanisms. We demonstrate the strategy using a trio of robots to track coherent structures and manifolds in both static flows and a noisy, time-dependent wind-driven double-gyre model typical of ocean environments. The study includes both simulation and experimental outcomes, alongside a discussion of the theoretical guarantees underpinning the collaborative tracking approach.

We introduce a novel framework for conditional image synthesis that accommodates semantic layouts across varying precision levels, spanning from pure text to detailed 2D canvases with exact shapes. Specifically, the input comprises one or more semantic regions featuring free-form textual descriptions and adjustable precision, allowing users to tailor controllability to their needs. At its most basic level, the framework functions as text-to-image (T2I) generation without shape data, while at its most detailed level, it operates as segmentation-to-image (S2I). By bridging these extremes, the system offers flexibility for users with diverse drawing skills and at various stages of the creative process. To overcome the challenges inherent in this setup, we developed several new techniques: a training data collection pipeline, a precision-encoded mask pyramid combined with a text feature map representation to jointly encode precision, semantics, and composition, and a multi-scale guided diffusion model for image synthesis. For evaluation, we assembled a test dataset featuring user-drawn layouts across diverse scenes and styles. Experimental results demonstrate that our method generates high-quality images that strictly adhere to the specified layout precision, outperforming existing approaches. Project page: \url{https://zengxianyu.github.io/scenec/}

Mercury telluride (HgTe) quantum wells (QWs) exhibit a remarkable progression of physical states, transitioning from insulators to two-dimensional Dirac semimetals and finally to three-dimensional topological insulators. This versatility stems from the profound influence of film thickness on the QW band structure. However, despite their significance, these energy dispersion relations have historically remained elusive in experimental settings due to insufficient measurement techniques. This study presents both experimental and theoretical investigations of two HgTe quantum wells featuring an inverted energy spectrum that supports two-dimensional semimetallic states. By employing sub-THz magneto-optical spectroscopy, we successfully determined electron and hole cyclotron masses across various Fermi levels and charge densities. These findings are corroborated by Shubnikov-de Haas analysis of capacitance data, which reveals the degeneracy of active modes. Utilizing these datasets, we reconstructed the electron and hole dispersion relations. A detailed comparison with theoretical models confirms strong agreement, capturing nuanced details such as band splitting, the second conduction band, and overlaps between the first conduction and valence bands. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that cyclotron resonance experiments offer an effective method for directly mapping the band structures of semimetallic two-dimensional materials.

Recent years have seen the emergence of image-to-image (I2I) translation techniques capable of generating varied outputs from a single input image. However, these methods predominantly address translation between only two domains, leaving multi-domain I2I translation as an unresolved challenge. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel unsupervised multi-domain image-to-image translation (MDUIT) framework. This approach utilizes decomposed content features and appearance-adaptive convolution to transform an image into a target style while maintaining its original geometric structure. Additionally, we employ a contrastive learning objective that enhances disentanglement capabilities and efficiently leverages multi-domain data by pairing semantically similar images. Consequently, our method learns diverse mappings across multiple visual domains within a single unified framework. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach generates visually diverse and realistic outcomes across various domains, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods.

Process discovery techniques have achieved significant success in Process Mining by generating interpretable models that boost management effectiveness. Nevertheless, choosing the optimal method for a given event log remains heavily dependent on human expertise, which limits widespread adoption. Meta-learning (MtL) approaches offer a promising avenue for developing systems that require minimal human intervention. This paper introduces an MtL framework designed to recommend process discovery methods that maximize model quality across complementary dimensions. Leveraging our MtL pipeline, we achieved a recommendation accuracy of 92% using lightweight event log features. Furthermore, our experimental analysis yielded valuable insights into the critical role of log features in generating recommendations, facilitating a deeper comprehension of discovery algorithms.

Cosmic rays (CRs) exert significant influence on the multiphase interstellar medium (ISM), driving dynamical activity in low-density plasmas and altering the ionization, temperature, and chemical makeup of denser atomic and molecular gas. This study investigates CR propagation from the ionized ISM into a neutral cloud. Utilizing one-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic particle-in-cell simulations that incorporate ion-neutral drag to suppress Alfvén waves within the cloud, we simultaneously evolve the kinetic behavior of CRs and the fluid dynamics of the multiphase gas. By embedding a cloud within a periodic domain, our simulations break translational symmetry, enabling the development of spatial structures in the CR distribution function. Specifically, a negative spatial gradient emerges across the fully ionized ISM, whereas a positive gradient develops across the neutral cloud. We validate these findings against CR hydrodynamics models by calculating wave-particle scattering rates derived from quasilinear, fluid, and Fokker-Planck theories. For momenta where the mean free path is significantly shorter than the simulation box size, we observe strong consistency among all scattering rate predictions. Furthermore, by varying cloud dimensions and ion-neutral collision frequencies, we demonstrate the robustness of our results. This work offers a first-principles validation of CR hydrodynamics during particle streaming down a pressure gradient and establishes a route for comprehensive calibration of transport coefficients based on self-generated Alfvén wave scattering by CRs.

Absolute Pose Regressor (APR) networks are designed to infer camera pose from images by regressing position and orientation from latent representations. While APRs offer a distinct balance of accuracy, speed, and memory usage compared to structure-based localization methods, this paper introduces Camera Pose Auto-Encoders (PAEs). These multi-layer perceptrons utilize a Teacher-Student framework, where APRs serve as teachers to encode camera poses. The resulting latent representations match APR performance and prove effective for related tasks. Specifically, we propose a lightweight test-time optimization that encodes the nearest training poses to refine position estimates, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy for APRs on the Cambridge Landmarks and 7Scenes benchmarks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that training images can be reconstructed from these learned encodings, enabling the integration of visual data at low memory costs. Our code and pre-trained models are accessible at https://github.com/yolish/camera-pose-auto-encoders.

This work serves two main objectives: first, to review current stability findings for Sobolev, Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev (HLS), and associated inequalities; second, to advance the field by offering insights into constructive stability estimates specifically for the HLS inequalities.

This study examines the nonlinear stability of a composite wave structure consisting of a viscous contact wave and two rarefaction waves within the one-dimensional bipolar Vlasov-Poisson-Boltzmann (VPB) framework, a model describing charged particle transport subject to electrostatic forces. Utilizing a novel micro-macro decomposition centered on the local Maxwellian—developed in our prior work [26]—we demonstrate that this superposition of waves is time-asymptotically stable for the 1D bipolar VPB system, provided the initial perturbations and wave amplitudes satisfy specific smallness criteria. This finding establishes the nonlinear stability of this particular composite wave pattern under the simultaneous influence of binary collisions, electrostatic potential forces, and interactions between distinct charged species. Notably, this represents the first result addressing the nonlinear stability of a combination of two distinct wave patterns for the Vlasov-Poisson-Boltzmann system.

We demonstrate that the Morita equivalences $\mathrm{Cliff}(4) \simeq {\mathbb H}$, $\mathrm{Cliff}(7) \simeq \mathrm{Cliff}(-1)$, and $\mathrm{Cliff}(8) \simeq {\mathbb R}$ are derived from the quantization of the Hamiltonian reductions ${\mathbb R}^{0|4} // \mathrm{Spin}(3)$, ${\mathbb R}^{0|7} // G_2$, and ${\mathbb R}^{0|8} // \mathrm{Spin}(7)$, respectively.

This article provides a comprehensive survey of all established optimal isosystolic inequalities for two-dimensional Finsler tori, focusing on the Busemann-Hausdorff and Holmes-Thompson definitions of Finsler area. Furthermore, we complete this overview by establishing a novel optimal isosystolic inequality: for a Finsler reversible 2-torus with a unit systole, the Busemann-Hausdorff area is at least $\pi/4$. The core of our proof relies on verifying a conjecture by Burago and Ivanov, which asserts that transitioning from a Finsler reversible metric to its stable norm on a 2-torus results in a reduction of the Busemann-Hausdorff area.

Natural language generation models are computational systems capable of producing coherent text based on provided word sequences. Although these models are widespread and offer numerous benefits, they can also cause social harm by creating discriminatory, hateful, or profane content, making their ethical evaluation essential. However, conducting such assessments is difficult because it demands specialized knowledge in areas like computational linguistics and social justice. Despite notable progress by researchers, broad public access remains restricted due to high entry barriers. To address this, this article presents TEAL (Tool for Ethical Assessment of Language generation models), a new instrument designed to standardize and democratize ethical evaluations within the Credo AI Lens, an open-source framework.

This paper presents findings that could have significantly influenced the early trajectory of quantum mechanics had they been recognized sooner. First, we derive Planck's blackbody radiation spectrum without assuming quantized energy levels; instead, the sole departure from classical theory is the inclusion of zero-point fluctuations in the electromagnetic field, which implies a non-trivial vacuum derivable through classical methods. Subsequently, we establish the Unruh-Hawking effect for the electromagnetic field within a purely wave-based framework, avoiding both dualities and the concept of photons. This leads to a pivotal question: how might the history of quantum mechanics have unfolded if Planck had been aware of these possibilities?

In their 2015 work published in *Quantum Information Processing* (Vol. 14, pp. 4237-4244), Qin and Dai introduced a proactive quantum secret sharing protocol. This study examines the security of that scheme and concludes it is vulnerable. Specifically, during the distribution phase, two colluding dishonest participants can intercept the dealer's secret without generating any detectable errors. Furthermore, we propose an improvement to address this vulnerability in the distribution phase.

Contemporary business and social engagements have increasingly shifted online, underscoring the critical need to establish digital trust. Reputation mechanisms serve as a primary method for quantifying this trust by tracking historical interactions and performance to derive a reputational score. This paper identifies that many current systems mirror real-world social dynamics, categorizing them as "social reputation mechanisms." The study examines various social phenomena and aligns them with existing mechanisms across three distinct scopes. Initially, it addresses the individual scope, where personal reputation is self-managed and communicated via recommendations. Next, it explores the acquaintances scope, in which reputation is linked to others through endorsements or exclusive networks. Finally, it analyzes the neighborhood scope, where an individual's standing is significantly influenced by the actions of those within their immediate social group.

Significant portions of metals are absent from the observable gas phase in the interstellar medium (ISM) because they are locked within dust grains, a process known as dust depletion. Investigating this phenomenon is crucial for understanding the origins and evolution of cosmic dust and metals. This study aims to characterize dust depletion across various environments, ranging from the Milky Way to distant galaxies. We compiled metal column densities from absorption-line spectroscopy found in existing literature and additionally measured Ti and Ni densities for a sample of 70 damped Lyman-$\alpha$ absorbers (DLAs) toward quasars using UVES/VLT. Utilizing ISM relative abundances, we estimated the depletion levels for 18 metals (C, P, O, Cl, Kr, S, Ge, Mg, Si, Cu, Co, Mn, Cr, Ni, Al, Ti, Zn, and Fe) across different settings, including the Milky Way, Magellanic Clouds (MCs), DLAs toward quasars, and toward gamma-ray bursts. We identified linear relationships between the depletion of each metal and the overall strength of dust depletion, indicated by the observed [Zn/Fe] ratio. In the neutral ISM of the MCs, we detected slight deviations from linearity, characterized by an overabundance of $\alpha$-elements (Ti, Mg, S) and an underabundance of Mn. These discrepancies vanish when assuming that all OB stars in our MC sample exhibit $\alpha$-element enhancement and Mn deficiency, suggesting that the MCs may have recently been enriched in $\alpha$-elements, possibly due to recent star formation bursts. The strong correlations observed in metal depletion sequences from low-metallicity QSO-DLAs to the Milky Way imply that cosmic dust shares a common origin, regardless of the varying star formation histories among these galaxies. This supports the significance of grain growth in the ISM as a major mechanism for dust production.

We present an analysis of the planetary microlensing event OGLE-2018-BLG-1185, which was monitored by numerous ground-based observatories and the $Spitzer$ Space Telescope. The ground-based light curve reveals a low planet-to-host star mass ratio of $q = (6.9 \pm 0.2) \times 10^{-5}$, positioning it near the peak of the wide-orbit exoplanet mass-ratio distribution. Host and planet masses were derived via Bayesian analysis utilizing the measured angular Einstein radius, assuming a uniform prior for host star masses. Although the flux variation detected by $Spitzer$ was marginal, it constrains the microlens parallax. Applying a conservative limit where the flux variation is $\Delta f_{\rm Spz} < 4$ instrumental flux units yields a host mass of $M_{\rm host} = 0.37^{+0.35}_{-0.21}\ M_\odot$ and a planet mass of $m_{\rm p} = 8.4^{+7.9}_{-4.7}\ M_\oplus$. Conversely, a Bayesian analysis incorporating the complete parallax constraint from $Spitzer$ indicates lower masses: $M_{\rm host} = 0.091^{+0.064}_{-0.018}\ M_\odot$ and $m_{\rm p} = 2.1^{+1.5}_{-0.4}\ M_\oplus$. Future high-resolution imaging using $HST$ or ELTs could differentiate between these scenarios and further elucidate the system's characteristics.

Following a binary black hole merger, the remaining black hole can experience a significant recoil, or "kick," with speeds potentially reaching 5000 km/s. This effect holds substantial importance for gravitational wave astronomy, black hole formation theories, general relativity tests, and galaxy evolution. Focusing on the gravitational wave signal from the merger GW200129_065458 (GW200129)—which displays strong evidence of orbital precession—we utilized numerical relativity surrogate models to constrain its final kick velocity. At 90% credibility, we determined the velocity to be $v_f \sim 1542^{+747}_{-1098}$ km/s, or alternatively, $v_f \gtrsim 698$ km/s as a one-sided limit. This represents the first time a large kick velocity has been identified for a specific gravitational wave event. Based on this velocity, we estimate the probability of the remnant black hole being retained by globular clusters is less than 0.48%, dropping to 7.7% for nuclear star clusters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that kick-induced biases are not anticipated in ringdown tests of general relativity for this particular event, though future advancements in detector sensitivity may alter this conclusion.

This study examines the initial boundary value problem for a nonlinear parabolic equation featuring nonlocal absorption, subject to nonlinear nonlocal boundary conditions and nonnegative initial data. We establish the comparison principle and demonstrate both the global existence and blow-up of solutions.

We reside in the information age. Although Claude Shannon, regarded as its father, established a communication theory that quantified the "amount of information," he explicitly noted that he did not define the concept of information itself. Logical entropy fills this gap by offering a definition grounded in distinctions, differences, distinguishability, and diversity. It serves as a normalized quantitative measure of the distinctions within a partition on a set, mirroring how Boole-Laplace logical probability measures the elements of a subset. Since partitions and subsets are mathematically dual concepts, the logic governing partitions is dual to standard Boolean logic, justifying the term "logical entropy." The logical entropy of a partition can be simply interpreted as the probability of obtaining a distinction (a "dit," where elements fall into different blocks) upon two independent draws from the set. Furthermore, Shannon entropy is also rooted in this notion of information-as-distinctions; it represents the average minimum number of binary partitions (bits) required to join to capture all distinctions of a given partition. Consequently, concepts such as simple, joint, conditional, and mutual logical entropy can be converted into their Shannon counterparts through a uniform non-linear dit-bit transform. Finally, logical entropy naturally extends to the quantum realm. Quantum logical entropy, defined for an observable applied to a state, equals the probability that two independent projective measurements of that observable on that state yield different eigenvalues.

**Keywords:** logical entropy, Shannon entropy, partitions, MaxEntropy, quantum logical entropy, von Neumann entropy

Cylindrical gravitational pulse waves are characterized by a radial pulse profile within cylindrical gravitational waves. Their dynamics are controlled by a two-dimensional integrable sigma model possessing an infinite-dimensional hidden symmetry known as the Geroch group. Piran, Safier, and Katz derived an exact solution for a single pulse wave by applying a double analytic continuation to the Kerr metric; this solution depicts a wave originating from infinity, reflecting off the symmetry axis, and returning to infinity. In this work, we derive an exact solution for a double pulse wave by performing a double analytic continuation on the double Kerr metric. This new solution represents a pair of waves arriving from infinity, scattering off one another, and returning to infinity. The pulses traverse each other and emerge with their original shapes preserved, mirroring standard soliton scattering. However, unlike conventional soliton interactions, this process involves no time delay. Additionally, the resulting metric is free from the conical singularity present in the double Kerr metric. Future research should aim to elucidate how the Geroch group operates within the quantum framework of gravitational pulse wave scattering.

A high pulse-energy VECSEL operating in a single transverse mode has been created. This GaSb-based device operates at a 2.04-micron wavelength, achieving peak powers over 500W with excellent beam quality. Its cavity design utilizes a Pockels cell paired with a low-loss thin film polarizer to extract intracavity energy into a 10ns pulse. This laser shows potential for applications in incoherent LiDAR, material processing, gas sensing, and nonlinear optics.

u} R_{\mu
u}$, $\phi R_{\mu
uho\sigma} R^{\mu
uho\sigma}$, and $\phi R_{\mu
uho\sigma} 	ilde R^{\mu
uho\sigma}$. These interactions arise naturally when heavier particles exist. We systematically derive these couplings by integrating out these massive particles. These interactions hold significant phenomenological value, as certain operators facilitate the decay of the scalar into graviton pairs. Notably, such decays can generate a substantial stochastic cosmic graviton background at high frequencies, because the suppression scale corresponds to the mass of the heavy particles rather than the Planck scale. We calculate the resulting graviton spectrum using specific models.

Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) have demonstrated remarkable efficacy in image super-resolution; however, their performance declines significantly in real-world scenarios where paired high- and low-resolution (LR) images are missing, and LR inputs suffer from complex, unknown degradation kernels. To overcome these challenges, we introduce the Unsupervised Bi-directional Cycle Domain Transfer Learning-based Generative Adversarial Network (UBCDTL-GAN), which integrates an Unsupervised Bi-directional Cycle Domain Transfer Network (UBCDTN) and a Semantic Encoder-guided Super Resolution Network (SESRN).
